# THE EPISTLE

Of the royal blood of Chinese Emperors <note>original: "Regio Sinensium Imperatorum sanguine"</note>, he is called Confucius. By the universal consensus of the Chinese, he is considered the wisest of all who ever flourished among them, a master and oracle of both moral and political philosophy.

Just as three thousand disciples once hung upon his every word, so now a vast empire is governed by his sayings. Laws are established, the customs of the nation and civil duties are arranged according to them; finally, in the thorough study of his doctrine lies the sole hope and method for obtaining the highest honors and magistracies of the state <note>original: "Reipublicæ." This refers to the Chinese Imperial Examination system, where knowledge of Confucian classics was the requirement for government office.</note>. All the Chinese <note>original: "Sinae"</note> marvelously revere his memory, his books, and his very name. Even the emperors themselves do not disdain to visit with reverence the very houses where he once taught (which are preserved as shrines of wisdom) and his schools. And indeed, not without cause; for from such a great master they learned to adore and fear the "Supreme Emperor of Heaven" <note>original: "Summum cæli Imperatorem." This reflects the Jesuit attempt to show that ancient Chinese philosophy was compatible with monotheism.</note>, as he called Him—the moderator and judge of all kingdoms and empires. They learned to rule the peoples subject to them with great equity and charity, to foster the arts, and finally to govern the Chinese world—which has flourished for so many years in both peace and war—with the most holy institutions and laws.

Here, therefore, that very Confucius presents himself to you, **GREAT KING**, as if transported into France <note>original: "in Gallias"</note> by your care and royal generosity. He approaches, prostrating himself at Your Majesty's feet, to openly admire your wisdom. He comes to confess that his own wisdom—though celebrated with incredible fame and esteem among his own people—nevertheless yields to yours, just as the stars give way to the sun.

He will, I believe, be transfixed at the first approach and sight of you, rooted to the spot by both admiration and joy, having found for himself at last

# E P I S T L E.

*Born of the royal blood of the Chinese Emperors, they call him Confucius; by the unanimous consent of the Chinese, he is held to be the wisest of all who ever flourished among them, and the Master and Oracle of both Moral and Political Philosophy.*

*Just as three thousand disciples once hung upon his every word, so now is that most vast empire governed by his sayings. Laws are established, the customs of the nation and civil duties are composed by them; finally, the only hope and method for attaining the highest honors of the State and the rank of Magistrate <note>This refers to the Imperial Examination system, where mastery of Confucian texts was the sole requirement for becoming a government official (Mandarin).</note> is contained in the thorough learning of his doctrine. All the Chinese hold his memory, his books, and his very name in marvelous reverence; even the Emperors themselves do not disdain to frequent his temples—which are preserved as sanctuaries of wisdom—and his schools with great veneration. Nor is this without merit; for they have learned from so great a Master to adore and fear the Highest Emperor of Heaven <note>original: "Summum cæli Imperatorem." The Jesuits used this term to translate the Chinese concept of 'Shangdi' or 'Tian', arguing that ancient Chinese religion acknowledged a single Supreme Deity similar to the Christian God.</note> (as he himself called Him), the ruler and judge of all kingdoms and empires. They have learned to rule the people subject to them with great equity and charity, to foster the arts, and finally to govern the Chinese world—which has flourished for so many years in both peace and war—by the most sacred institutions and laws.*

*Here, therefore, that very Confucius presents himself to you, **GREAT KING**, carried as it were into France <note>original: "Gallias"</note> by your cares and Royal generosity. He approaches, prostrating himself at Your Majesty's feet, openly to admire your wisdom. He comes to confess that his own wisdom—though celebrated among his own people with incredible fame and esteem—nevertheless yields to yours, no differently than the stars give way to the Sun.*

...foreign <note>original: "peregrina," completing the word "peregrina" from the previous page</note> doctrines, which he used to say repeatedly were born for the destruction of peoples and the ruin of Monarchies, he might utterly drive away. From this comes that saying of his, which even today is most celebrated among the Chinese: *Cum hu y tuon* <note>original: "Cum hu y tuon." A transliteration of the Chinese *Gōng hū yì duān* from the *Analects* (2.16), which the Jesuits translated here as "Oppugna hæretica dogmata" or "Attack heretical doctrines."</note> "Attack heretical doctrines." How much joy, then, would it bring to a man so fond of piety, if indeed he had been able to reach these most happy times of the "law of grace" <note>A theological term referring to the era of Christianity.</note>, to see your care, **O King**, for protecting and enlarging Religion, uprooting heresy, and propagating piety? With what praises would he extol You, when he saw heresy—that most foul enemy of the ancestral faith and of a most flourishing kingdom—trampled and crushed; the edicts <note>A reference to the Edict of Nantes, which Louis XIV revoked in 1685, shortly before this book's publication.</note> by which it seemed to live repealed; its temples destroyed, its very name buried; so many thousands of souls led back so sweetly, so strongly, and so happily from their former errors to the truth, and from destruction to salvation; and finally all of France, under its Greatest and truly **Most Christian King**, seen as truly Most Christian?

Surely he would not only admire and proclaim the other miracles of Your France: not just the many fortresses, fortified by all the defenses of both art and nature, which were partly cast down and captured by You, and partly built and erected; nor the most powerful and numerous fleets with which You brought terror to Asia and Africa; nor the many victories reported over enemies, upon which You placed that most glorious crown, the trophy of public peace; nor those sights in which You display Your Royal splendor and magnificence, the Palaces; nor rivers carried across mountains <note>Refers to the impressive engineering of aqueducts and canals built during Louis XIV's reign, such as those supplying Versailles.</note>; nor the seas opened and joined <note>Refers to the *Canal du Midi*, which linked the Atlantic Ocean to the Mediterranean Sea, completed in 1681.</note>; nor the many schools and nurseries of arts and sciences. All these things, I say, would not strike so much admiration into the wisest Philosopher as this one triumph of Religion over Heresy, achieved under Your leadership and auspices.

->### THE EPISTLE<-

...[majesty] <note>original: "-tis," likely completing "majestatis."</note> of such a victory, which no one before had dared to attempt in such a way, nor even to hope for; truly, future generations will scarcely be able to believe it, and they will certainly never be able to sufficiently admire or proclaim it.

I, indeed, struck especially by the incredible fame of this one achievement and victory, have come here from the furthest shores of **China** <note>original: "Sinarum."</note>. Having successfully crossed the vast Ocean, I consider the great effort to have been well worth the prize, because it has been my lot to see with these eyes those things which rumor had spread everywhere—though I found that rumor was actually less than the reality itself. How sweet it will now be for me, by God's favor, to sail back across so many seas, to revisit my most longed-for **China** <note>original: "Sinam."</note>, and there to proclaim those miracles of which I have been an eyewitness! Truly, the memory of them will wipe away the sense of so many labors and dangers, erase their memory, and make the path for my return easier and, as it were, smooth it out. Already I seem to see myself in the midst of a most joyful assembly of **new converts** <term>Neophytes: individuals recently converted to Christianity, specifically in the Jesuit missions of China.</term> flocking toward me, and even of the **pagans** <note>original: "Ethnicorum," referring here to the non-Christian Chinese population.</note> themselves, as I recount what I have seen here. I see them standing by with ears and minds alert, hanging on my words, stunned at the magnitude and novelty of these things, while at the same time congratulating You, **GREAT KING**, as well as the Church and **France**.

With what joys, then, will they be moved when they hear that their own **Confucius** has been held in such high esteem and honor by You, that You willed him a place among the other books of the **Royal Library**? They will learn that he has been gifted with the Latin language; that his image, his books, and even the records of their own princes have been printed not just on those wooden blocks which **China** uses, but on copper plates and with the most elegant type. They will hear that he, who until now was known only within the Chinese Empire, is soon to be spread through **France**, and from France throughout all of **Europe**, to be held everywhere by all in such high regard as is his due. What great [joys]... <note>original catchword "MA-" likely leads to "MAGNAS" (great) or "MAXIMAS" (greatest) on the following page.</note>

# THE EPISTLE

*...to your **Majesty** <note>Completes the word "Majestati" from the previous page.</note> they will give thanks; with what praises will all people celebrate your Name, and with what joyful prayers will they follow you! What vows will the **neophytes** <term>Neophytes: From the Greek for "newly planted," these are the recent converts to Christianity within the Jesuit missions in China.</term> eagerly offer for your safety, for the successful outcome of all things you have undertaken, and for the most prosperous course of your flourishing Kingdom and the Catholic Religion? PHILIPPE COUPLET

# THE WORK’S
## ORIGIN AND SCOPE
->AS WELL AS<-
->CHINESE BOOKS, INTERPRETERS,<-
->SECTS, AND THE PHILOSOPHY WHICH<-
->THEY CALL NATURAL,<- <note>original: "NATUTALEM"; the Latin text contains a printer's error, intending "NATURALEM" (Natural).</note>

# INTRODUCTORY DECLARATION.

The European Reader will, I hope, grant us pardon if throughout this entire work—but especially here while we are laying, as it were, the foundations of the whole—we pursue many matters with great care, and indeed more minutely and at greater length than the sharp minds of many might desire, who, being as they are, are perhaps also fond of brevity. For although we certainly desire our labors <note>original: "lucubrationem," literally "work done by lamp-light," implying late-night scholarly effort.</note> to please these readers, and indeed hope they will not be unpleasing to the learned curiosity of many (especially since we are dealing with such a great and refined antiquity, so far removed from their own eyes and lands), yet we must state this clearly once and for all: our purpose is not so much to serve the delight and curiosity of those living in Europe, as it is to serve the utility of those who sail from Europe to bring the light of the Gospel to these most distant lands. Therefore, we have deemed a certain prolixity <term>Prolixity: The quality of being long-winded or using more words than necessary.</term>—which might otherwise be considered a fault—to be not only worthy of pardon but plainly necessary in the face of such great obscurity concerning this concise <note>original: "Laconicæ," referring to the Laconians or Spartans, known for their brief, pithy speech. Couplet is describing the dense and difficult nature of the Chinese language.</note> and foreign people. We believe we must take account of even the smallest details, all the more so because we have chosen to carry a torch not only for this explanation, but for all those which others may hereafter undertake in this field, and to lay those foundations which will support this structure, however much by the work of others thereafter...

<summary>In this preface, Philippe Couplet explains that his detailed and lengthy writing style is intended to assist future missionaries in China rather than just entertaining European scholars. He justifies his "wordiness" as a necessary tool for navigating the dense and difficult history and language of the Chinese people.</summary>

...or brought up from a deep level, or expanded upon, they may be able to be sustained. Before we proceed to these matters, it will not be unpleasant for the Reader to learn the occasion and the reasons for undertaking this work.

From the first time the <term>Society of Jesus</term> <note>The Jesuits, the Catholic religious order to which the author belongs.</note> opened a path for itself into the <term>Empire of the Chinese</term> (it has been a hundred years and more), we attempted to proclaim the Gospel among the Chinese in the very same way that the <term>Heralds of the Gospel</term> <note>Missionaries.</note> had used among all other nations: namely, as religious men, following religious customs, dress, and rituals. However, the actual experience and the outcome of our affairs—which by no means answered our prayers—soon taught us that a completely different path had to be taken if we wished to achieve anything worthwhile. This was because among this nation, not only does all religion lie in neglect, but furthermore, those who publicly profess a certain stricter and holier way of life (not unlike our own monks) are held in very little honor. We commonly call these men <term>Bonzes</term> <note>original: "Bonzios"; a term used by early travelers and missionaries to describe Buddhist monks in East Asia.</note>. They are generally from the lowest dregs of the people and are distinguished neither by any learning nor even by those shadows of virtue in which the heathens boast.

Therefore, there were very grave men among the Chinese, whom we had already bound to us through private friendship and who had inspected our affairs and goals more closely and deeply. These men strongly urged us that, since we were so highly cultivated in letters and the sciences (as they had already discovered for themselves), we should join ourselves to their own <term>order of the Literati</term> <note>The "Literati" or scholar-officials were the elite ruling class of Imperial China, educated in Confucian classics.</note>. They suggested that we could sufficiently—and more than sufficiently—protect and profess the sanctity of a stricter life (which the priests of their own nation only feigned) through the actual holiness of our conduct, without the external harshness of that local religious dress. In this way, they said, there would finally be hope of making progress and of persuading even the Provincial Governors and the leading men of those things we most desired. Furthermore, we would no longer be liable to those harassments and insults with which the insolence of wicked men is accustomed to pursue foreigners—despising them specifically because they bore the appearance of the <term>Bonzes</term>. Indeed, the first companions of our Society had already endured many such insults, and yet without any benefit to the Christian cause.

It was not at all difficult to persuade us of what reason and experience had long since suggested—especially to those for whom no other goal was set than to win all for Christ, and for the sake of this goal, to become not only "literati to the literate Chinese nation," but to become "all things to all men." <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 9:22, a guiding principle for Jesuit "accommodation" or cultural adaptation.</note> Therefore, from 그that time onward, we assumed the persona and the dress of the <term>Literati</term>. Scarcely had we assumed it (which may seem incredible to many) when both the highest and the lowest began to respect us—the latter in awe and the former in reverence—as if we were "new men." Even the <term>Magistrates</term> <note>original: "Magistratus"; high-ranking government officials or Mandarins.</note> themselves began to visit us more frequently with splendid entourages. But indeed, it was difficult to maintain the name and reputation of the Literati for long by external dress alone and the testimony of a few who dealt with us familiarly, especially...

-># INTRODUCTORY DECLARATION.<-

...certainly among those who, through a remarkable and pride-filled ignorance, considered whatever lands lay outside their own borders to be unrefined barbarism. For this reason, it was necessary, besides the native language, to also learn their <term>characters</term> <note>original: "literas"; here referring to the written Chinese script as opposed to the spoken language.</note> thoroughly, and to heap labor upon labor. The language of the Chinese is, if any other in the whole world, the most difficult. It is contained in many grammatical rules; the people use monosyllabic words, and very few of them, which are affected by such a subtle inflection of the tongue, or a hiss, and even a <term>tone</term> <note>original: "tono"; the author is describing the tonal nature of Chinese, where the pitch of a word changes its meaning.</note> (almost musical). By being affected now this way, now that, words take on one meaning after another, and often of the most contrary things. Thus, it can hardly be said how much trouble this matter creates for foreigners.

Furthermore, such a scarcity of vocal sounds gave rise to a great abundance of written characters; for by the greatest variety of these, they distinguish the similarity and identity of their spoken words. Do you ask the number of these characters? It surpasses belief. Let it suffice to have said one thing: the number is so great that no one yet within the memory of the Chinese has been able to remember them all, even though many of them, beginning from the sixth year of their age, spend their whole life thereafter consumed in studying them. However, I would not wish to hide this: he who has learned to use five or six thousand characters appropriately can not only understand most of the books which the Chinese have written in great numbers regarding morals, duties, the State, and history; but he himself also, even though he be a European, will be able to write conveniently about any subject which must be debated between us and the Chinese.

Therefore, men of mature age—and not a few already advanced in years—who had long ago been endowed with a literary (if not a laurel) crown in their own native homes, became like children again among the Chinese for the love of Christ. Starting from the very elements of the language with incredible labor and constancy, within a few years—with the <term>Divine Power</term> <note>original: "Numine"; a reference to God's providence.</note> always breathing upon them—they attained such skill in both language and characters that they even published European sciences and the mysteries of the most holy Christian Religion in print. The amazed Chinese understood that these men were truly worthy of the name of <term>Literati</term> <note>original: "literatorum"; the scholarly class that held high social and political status in China.</note>, since they could learn the Chinese script so quickly and were instructed in so many and so famous sciences and disciplines. They decided for themselves that the suspicions were by no means true (which, as is common in a highly political nation, had settled in many minds at the beginning) that we had come into their lands under the guise of promulgating a foreign law, but were in truth driven by a desire for profit or honors. This was especially clear when, having set out from such distant lands, we lived among them in such a way that we were a burden to none of the natives; rather, we constantly rejected money offered as a gift, freely professing that we lacked nothing of the things necessary for life.

In this manner, that first labor and industry of the <term>Companions</term> <note>original: "Sociorum"; referring to the members of the Society of Jesus (Jesuits).</note> had happily dispelled the first shadows and suspicions of the nation, and already concerning the fortification...

For Europeans, there were many exchanges, not only with people, but also regarding sciences and academic disciplines; nevertheless, these exchanges were not so productive as to prevent most of the Chinese from still looking down on our achievements compared to their own. They frequently asserted that we were not so much approaching the heights of their wisdom as we were merely moving a little further away from the laziness and crudeness of other barbarians. Indeed, some jokingly remarked that, according to an ancient proverb of their people, only the Chinese <term>Sinae</term> <note>The Latin term for the Chinese people.</note> were gifted with both eyes, while the rest of mortals were plainly blind; they did, however, grant Europeans one eye. Therefore, it pleased the <term>Companions</term> <note>The "Socii," referring to the members of the Society of Jesus, or Jesuits.</note> to explore all the secrets of this nation. Just as they had already penetrated the lands themselves, fortified by so many barriers and guards, they also sought to create an entrance for themselves into the innermost sanctuaries of that proud philosophy which holds such a high opinion of itself. Their plan was this: once they had thoroughly learned and understood all their tenets, institutions, and especially their ancient records, they might seek—in imitation of the <term>Apostle</term> <note>A reference to St. Paul, who in the New Testament (Acts 17) adapted his preaching to the culture and philosophy of the Athenians to win them over.</note>—whatever light or strength could be found there to announce and confirm the truth of <term>Christian Philosophy</term> <note>A term used by the authors to present Christianity not just as a religion, but as a supreme system of wisdom and logic.</note>. Thus, these proud men might finally recognize, even against their will (unless a wicked self-love should utterly blind them), that it was they rather than we who truly lacked a "second eye," since they were completely ignorant of our sciences, to which we had now joined their own philosophy.

Therefore, after a diligent examination, the Companions realized that nearly the whole of <term>Chinese Philosophy</term>—certainly the flower and marrow of it—is contained in four principal books <note>These are the "Four Books" of Confucianism: the *Great Learning*, the *Doctrine of the Mean*, the *Analects*, and *Mencius*.</note>. There is no member of the <term>literati</term> <note>The educated class of scholar-officials in Imperial China.</note> who does not hold these in his memory from youth. The more one drinks from this pool of political and moral knowledge, the more quickly he is promoted to literary degrees, honors, and <term>Magistracies</term> <note>Official government positions.</note>. From these books, finally, the chief oracles of the nation and the "eternal truths" of the Chinese are sought. 

They undertook this task with great courage, first working to understand these books; it is impossible to describe how much they labored and sweated over them. Since they found nothing in them that opposed reason or the Law of Nature, but much that marvelously supported it, they decided to learn them thoroughly and turn them to their own use. This great labor was met with an equally great reward. For when Christian truths were presented—deduced (as they believed) from Chinese principles, supported and illustrated by the authority and testimony of their ancient Kings and sages, and finally adorned with their own words and maxims—the Chinese no longer received them with fear or contempt as foreign and barbarian, but welcomed them with listening ears and even with reverence as their own. Not a few, upon whom the divine light shone more kindly, followed with ready minds; soon they were the ones encouraging and leading their relatives and friends to "enroll" in this same philosophy. Others, however, who were entangled in the bonds of greed and lust, or who were more alienated from us by their devotion to superstitions, nevertheless looked up to the intellect, memory, and wisdom of the Europeans.

...of men: Finally, in a spirit of competition, the leading men, governors of cities and provinces, and even the **Colai** <note>original: *Colai*. These were the Grand Secretaries or highest-ranking imperial officials, second only to the Emperor in the Ming and Qing dynasties.</note>, whose dignity and authority is foremost after the Imperial rank, honored our books with their own Prefaces. They did so with truly wonderful praise, honoring both our men and, indeed, the divine law (which was our one true wish).

Therefore, since the ancient world never granted as much faith or authority to any of the philosophers among the Europeans—nor even, I believe, to the Oracle of Delphic Apollo itself—as China grants to its **Confucius**; and furthermore, since this philosopher is so far from opposing the doctrine and light of the Gospel that, on the contrary, we may not without reason expect there to be those who say he rather favors it, and in a way leads his countrymen by the hand toward it; and since they will observe in his books so many flashing sparks of right reason, not without admiration and pleasure: since, I say, such is the authority of **Confucius** even among the neighboring kingdoms of the Chinese, who does not see that excellent uses can arise from this for the Herald of the Gospel? While he brings knowledge of the True and Supreme Deity to these nations, he will confirm the truth of his doctrine not by the authority of the Poets (which that **Doctor of the Gentiles** <note>A traditional title for Saint Paul the Apostle.</note>, even among the Athenians, did not hesitate to do), but by the authority of that very Philosopher, than whom these nations have known nothing more truthful or wise up to our own times. 

Who then would not hope (provided the Deity is always favorable) that these people—convicted by the testimony of their own Master and happily defeated by their own weapons—will eventually surrender to the truth of the Gospel? Certainly, such a surrender was made by one who was once famous for Chinese wisdom and the dignity gained through it (the highest after the Imperial rank), but far more illustrious for his Christian virtues and heavenly wisdom: the pillar of the newborn Church, **Siu Paulus** <note>original: *Siu Paulus*. This refers to Xu Guangqi (1562–1633), a high-ranking official and one of the most famous Chinese converts, known as one of the "Three Pillars of the Chinese Church."</note>, formerly a **Colao** of the Chinese Empire. When someone asked him what this new doctrine we Europeans brought was achieving, he responded with the characteristic brevity <note>original: *Laconismo*. A reference to the concise style of the Spartans of Laconia.</note> of this nation, in both speech and writing: **Pu ju; çive se**;

> *that is, It supplements and perfects what is missing in our Master Confucius and our philosophy of the scholars; but it removes and radically uproots wicked superstitions and the worship of demons.*

For these reasons, therefore, we give this work of our nightly study to the public light. We do so not to show off Chinese wisdom to Europeans, but so that it might be of use to the candidates of the Eastern Missions; that weapons might be supplied to the soldiers with which these nations, under the leadership and auspices of Christ, might not only be conquered by you, but might even rejoice in it; that the fishers of men might have bait ready at hand with which the Chinese, once enticed, might be driven into the nets; and finally, so that the sacred merchants might be equipped with those goods by which a hundred and more years of experience has taught us these nations are powerfully captured and delighted. And indeed, in that Europe of ours, where now the Socrates and the Platos, where the Senecas and the Plutarchs have almost become cheap—

There were many discussions among Europeans, not only concerning the people of China, but also regarding their sciences and disciplines. However, these discussions were not so productive that many of the Chinese did not still look down on our achievements in comparison to their own; they used to say that we had not so much approached the praise of their own wisdom, but had merely moved a little further away from the laziness and crudeness of other barbarians. Thus, some amusingly remarked—following an old proverb of that nation—that only the **Chinese** <note>original: *Sinas*</note> were gifted with both eyes, while the rest of mortals were clearly blind; nevertheless, they granted the men of Europe at least one eye. It pleased the **Members of the Society** <note>The Jesuits, or Society of Jesus.</note>, therefore, to explore every secret of the nation. Just as they had already penetrated the lands themselves, which were fortified by so many barriers and guards, they also sought to make an entrance for themselves into the innermost sanctuaries of that prideful and high-minded Philosophy. They did so with this specific plan: that once all their opinions, institutions, and especially their ancient monuments were thoroughly known and understood, they might—imitating the **Apostle** <note>Saint Paul, who used the "Unknown God" of the Greeks to preach the Gospel.</note>—seek from those sources whatever light or strength could be used to announce and confirm the truth of Christian Philosophy to them. Thus, these proud men might finally recognize, even against their will (unless an excessive self-love should happen to blind them completely), that it was they rather than we who lacked "the other eye," since they were utterly ignorant of our sciences, to which we had now joined their own Philosophy.

Therefore, after the matter was diligently examined, the Members realized that almost the whole of **Chinese Philosophy**—at least the flower and marrow of the entire system—is contained in four principal books. There is not one among the literate class who does not already hold these in his memory from youth. From these books, the more one has drawn knowledge of moral politics, the more quickly he is promoted to literary degrees, to honors, and to magistracies. From these, finally, the principal oracles of the nation and the virtually eternal truths of the Chinese are sought. Consequently, they approached the task with great courage, making it their first priority to understand those books. It cannot be expressed how much labor and sweat was expended on this; but since they found nothing in them that opposed reason or the law of Nature, and indeed much that wonderfully supported it, they decided to learn them thoroughly and turn them to their own use. Furthermore, a great harvest answered this great labor. For the Chinese now received Christian truths—deduced from what they considered their own principles, stabilized and illustrated by the authority and testimony of their ancient Kings and sages, and finally presented and adorned with their own words and maxims—not as something foreign and barbaric with a certain fear or contempt, but as their own, with receptive ears and indeed with reverence. Nor were there few who, upon whom the divine light shone more kindly, followed with ready minds; and soon they became encouragers and leaders to their relatives and friends to give their names to the same Philosophy. Others, however, who were entangled in the chains of greed and lusts, or who were more alienated from us by their devotion to superstitions, nevertheless looked up to the talent, memory, and wisdom of the Europeans.

...hesitated to do, or should we hope that it is possible for our Chinese **Epictetus** <note>original: *Epictetus*; the author compares Confucius to this Greek Stoic philosopher (c. 50–135 AD), who was known for his practical ethics and moral discipline.</note> to receive applause? This would be true even though that instrument might perhaps be rude and unrefined, and by now almost entirely eaten away by rust, and by no means to be compared with the shine and elegance of those instruments with which Europe now abounds. But it would certainly delight Europeans to see that which had existed in the **Far East** <note>original: *ultimo Oriente*</note> for two thousand four hundred years.

We ourselves cannot deny that the work of our **Confucius** is something rude and unpolished, if indeed it is compared with European elegance and beauty. For although Confucius was born in the year 551 before Christ, he himself repeatedly affirms that the doctrine and the politico-moral principles which he handed down to posterity are not his own, but were received from the legislators **Yao** and **Shun** <note>original: *Yao & Xun*; legendary sage-kings whom Confucius regarded as the perfect models of virtue and government.</note>. Since these Princes governed that most ancient monarchy three thousand eight hundred years ago (as the **Chronological Table** <note>original: *Tabula Chronologica*</note> that we have attached to this study of ours will explain to the reader), it must be fully admitted that this doctrine has long flourished among the Chinese. And so, just as we have a nearly certain hope that this study of ours will be welcomed and pleasing to the Missionaries because of the most abundant fruits they will gather from it, we also hope it will be held in at least some value among all those who venerate antiquity. Let these words suffice regarding the reasons for undertaking this work.

## FIRST PARAGRAPH.

# WHICH BOOKS ARE CLASSICAL AND OF THE FIRST AUTHORITY.

Let us now descend to those matters which will serve as our foundation: first, the books and the principal monuments of this nation, their authors and their commentators. We do this so that Europeans may understand which books in this long-cultivated vineyard belong to the first class and which to the second. From among these, we shall see which may be read with confidence, which should be explored with a slow and cautious step, which are to be rejected like apocryphal works, and which are to be shunned as pestilential and impious, not to be greeted even from a distance. We shall do the same for the commentators (of whom there is a vast abundance, variety, and diversity)—which ones it is right to avoid and which to follow, how much faith and credit should be given to each, and in which specific matters.

For since the very times of **Confucius**, faith, piety, and the majesty of the Imperial family were neglected by many, and the customs of the ancestors had strayed significantly from their original path. Not long after, civil wars between local lords broke out one after another, in which nearly all the royal houses were eventually entangled. There also occurred a general and most terrible burning of books, the likes of which neither Alexandria nor any other part of the world ever experienced or heard of <note>The author refers to the "Burning of Books and Burying of Scholars" in 213 BC under the First Emperor, Qin Shi Huang.</note>. As usually happens, the laws were silent amid the clash of arms. Amid such great license for weapons and vices and lack of punishment, it is hard to believe how many sects, errors, and heresies—how many monsters of opinion and plagues of superstition—grew up like useless and harmful weeds in a neglected and deserted field within this "Garden at the Center of the Lands" <note>original: *medio terrarum horto*; a Latin rendering of *Zhongguo* (the Middle Kingdom).</note> (for so the Chinese call their Empire), as will be declared more fully below.

Among this people, there is no limit to the books already written, nor any end to the writing of new ones. Nevertheless, the most important of all, those of the first class, are and always have been partly those which are known by the title <term>Wujing</term> <note>original: *U kim*; meaning the "Five Classics."</note>, that is, the *five volumes*; and partly those called the <term>Sishu</term> <note>original: *Su xu*; meaning the "Four Books."</note>, or the *Four-Fold Book*. These are the four books we spoke of previously, the explanation of which we have translated into Latin. Furthermore, since these Four Books serve as commentaries on the Five Classics, although they are surpassed in authority and antiquity, they surpass them in practical use and utility. Now the first and most excellent among the five mentioned volumes is called the <term>Shujing</term> <note>original: *Xu kim*; the "Classic of History" or "Book of Documents."</note>; it consists of six books and encompasses the deeds of three great Kings: **Yao**, **Shun**, and **Yu**. Of these, **Yu** was the leader of the **Xia** <note>original: *Hia*; the first traditional dynasty of Chinese historiography.</note> family, the first of the Imperial families; the others were the Lawgivers and the true **Solons** <note>original: *Solones*; the author compares the legendary sage-kings to Solon, the famous lawmaker of ancient Athens.</note> of the Chinese nation.

It is well established that the excellent and politically prudent records, laws, and institutions of each [ruler], as well as the advice and opinions of their counselors, were carefully committed to writing, although many are now missing. Regarding the antiquity of this Work, there is no need to say much, since it must be admitted that the matters related in the first two books were written long before Moses.

Therefore, those things done and established by King *Yao* over the span of a hundred years (for he held the Empire for that long, having begun his reign in the year 2357 before Christ) were passed down for the memory of posterity by those who served as chroniclers to his successor, *Xun* [Shun]. Although through the corruption of later times almost everything perished, those things which remain deal chiefly with the Calendar and the use and order of the intercalary year, as well as the nine-year flood which the good Prince endeavored to remedy. Similarly, much has been lost of what the high officials of King *Xun* recorded in writing. What has reached us, however, are mostly those things he observed as a pious and wholesome example while surveying the various regions of his Empire: always sacrificing solemnly and purely to *Shangdi* <note>original: "Xam ti"</note>, the Supreme Emperor of the Heavens, as well as to the Guardians of the noble mountains and rivers, though to these with a lesser rite. There also survive not a few things regarding the rites to be observed in sacrifices, music, the punishment of criminals, and the proper governance of subjects. Even more abundant than these are the traditions concerning King *Yu*; and first, indeed, with what labor and industry he diverted the waters of the Chinese flood into the sea; in what manner he divided the Empire into exactly nine Provinces, and taught which region of the heavens and which constellations corresponded to each; what each of the Provinces ought to pay in the name of tribute, and other matters of that kind. Besides certain distinguished records which both he himself and his high officials produced for the common comfort and instruction of their subjects. And indeed, just as these Princes were elevated to the Empire by no other right or title than that of virtue and wisdom, so they are most celebrated for both praises; and whatever examples or records they left to their posterity hold almost the force of Oracles and laws.

In the third book are contained those things established during the reign of the Second Family, or Imperial house, called *Shang* and *Yin* <note>original: "Xam & Yn"</note>, especially by its founder *Cheng Tang* <note>original: "Chim tam"</note>, who entered upon the Empire in the year 1776 before Christ, after he had defeated and expelled the impious *Jie* <note>original: "Kie"</note>; he also gave an account of this deed in the Assembly in a painstaking and weighty speech. It is well-established that the excellent and wise political documents, laws, and institutions of each individual ruler, as well as the advice and opinions of their counselors, were carefully recorded in writing, even though many are now missing. Concerning the antiquity of this Work <note>The *Shujing*, or *Book of Documents*, one of the Five Classics of Chinese literature.</note>, there is no need to speak, since it must be admitted that the events related in the first two books were recorded long before the time of Moses.

...faith must be maintained. Certainly, it can be proved by the sole testimony of *Confucius* <note>The Latinized name for Kong Fuzi (c. 551–479 BCE).</note> that the ancient monuments of the *Odes* <note>The *Shijing*, or Classic of Poetry, a collection of 305 poems dating from the 11th to 7th centuries BCE.</note> were free from this kind of stain, when he says: *The entire teaching of the Three Hundred Poems is reduced to this one point: "Si Wu Xie," which is to say: Let no depraved or shameful thing be thought.* <note>original: "Trecentorum Poëmatum doctrinam totam ed dumtaxat reduci, ut Su Uu Sic, hoc est: Ne quid pravum, aut turpe cogitetur."</note> Nevertheless, the authority of these poems is great; but the style is indeed difficult and obscure. This obscurity is caused by a brevity that is always Laconic, and often metaphorical, and adorned with the most ancient proverbs. However, this very obscurity wins a certain reverence and authority for such secret and ancient poetry (as we see happen with certain healthy traditions).

The third volume (if indeed it can be called a volume) is called the *Ye-Kim* <note>The *I Ching*, or Classic of Changes.</note>, and it is much more obscure even than the Odes I have mentioned; indeed, it is a mere enigma. It is by far the most ancient of all the volumes, if you exclude the Commentaries; for its author is said to be *Fo hi* <note>Fuxi, the legendary first emperor and cultural hero of China.</note>, the founder of the Chinese nation and the first teacher—another Orpheus—to a rude and rustic people. The entire matter consists of <term>Lineolis</term> <note>Small lines, referring to the broken and unbroken lines that form the trigrams and hexagrams of the I Ching.</note>, and quite a few of them at that. We shall depict them here shortly, and at the same time explain how often and in what way they vary to create new figures and, as it were, new meanings for things. The Monarchy had stood for one thousand eight hundred years when finally an Oedipus <note>A reference to the Greek figure who solved the riddle of the Sphinx; here used to mean a "riddle-solver."</note> appeared: I mean the petty king *Ven vam* <note>King Wen of Zhou (1112–1050 BCE).</note>. He, by mutually exchanging the eight lines eight times among themselves, attempted to explain the mutual changes of the eight principal things. His son *cheu cum* <note>The Duke of Zhou (r. 1042–1035 BCE).</note> attempted the same, and indeed more copiously than his father; but in truth, both the one and the other involved everything in mysteries and enigmas, using hieroglyphic signs and new riddles to entangle the old ones. Finally, nearly five hundred years later, *Confucius* himself attempted to untie the knot. He interpreted the secret <term>Lineolas</term> of the Founder and the earlier interpretations in such a way that he referred everything partly to the natures of things—especially the elements and the affections and qualities proper to each—and partly to the morals and disciplines of men. Therefore, although the root of the work is, as I said, most ancient, because all the rest came forth a long time afterward, the three mentioned Interpreters hold the name and authority of Authors here rather than mere Interpreters. Furthermore, since everything is obscure and most difficult to grasp, we have judged that this book should only be reviewed in the third place. *Confucius*, certainly not being satisfied with those first Commentaries of his, desired to comment upon the enigmatic work anew in his old age; but death anticipated the man's efforts and wishes.

Furthermore, an obscurity so ancient, and an antiquity so obscure, offered more than one occasion for error to a vain and superstitious posterity. Indeed, thinking that more mysteries lay hidden there the less they understood, they began to misuse the enigmatic lines for lots and auguries. Nor were there lacking masters of error and folly from the sects of *Tao* <note>Taoism.</note> and *Fe* <note>Buddhism (from the Chinese term "Fo" for Buddha).</note> to support this. But concerning this enigmatic work, there will be a more copious place for discussion below.

Confucius wished the title of the fourth volume to be *Chun cieu* <note>The *Chunqiu*, or Spring and Autumn Annals.</note>, which words signify *Spring and Autumn* <note>original: "Ver & Autumnum"</note>; it was written by him when he was already quite old. In this work, he follows, in a historical narrative, the deeds, vices, virtues, punishments, and rewards of various Princes. He begins from the 49th year of the Emperor *Pim vam* <note>King Ping of Zhou (r. 770–720 BCE).</note>, the thirteenth from the house and family of *Cheu* <note>The Zhou Dynasty.</note>. He carries this history from the petty king <note>The author uses *Regulo* to refer to the feudal dukes of the era.</note> *Yn cum* <note>Duke Yin of Lu.</note>, who held the Kingdom of *Lu* (which also provided the Philosopher his birthplace) by feudal right, through ten successive petty kings over 241 years, leading up to *Ngai cum* <note>Duke Ai of Lu.</note>, the twelfth petty king, with whom he ends the history. He sought the title of his work from *Spring* and *Autumn* because, with the virtue and wisdom of the Prince, the State flourishes like the most pleasant *Spring*; just as, on the contrary, with his foolishness and wickedness, like leaves and flowers under an *Autumnal* sky, the whole must scatter, wither, and—like something growing old—finally die. He used to say that there would one day be those who, having read through this labor, would know themselves—that is, they would perceive his zeal for public utility and truth; but there would also be those who would hate and condemn it—namely, those who would behold, even against their will, themselves and their own baseness expressed there in vivid colors, and the just punishments set forth for their lust, cruelty, and tyranny. This book was commented upon with great erudition by *ço xi* <note>Zuo Qiuming, the traditional author of the *Zuo Zhuan* commentary.</note>, who is said to have been a disciple of Confucius; he also published another work entitled *Que-yu* <note>The *Guoyu*, or Discourses of the States.</note>; that is, the *Decrees* or axioms of the Kingdoms.

Finally, the fifth Volume, which is inscribed *Li-ki* <note>The *Liji*, or Book of Rites.</note>, (as if to say) the *Memorial of Rites and Duties*, consists of ten books. Confucius had collected these from various books and monuments of the Ancients; but since about three hundred years later, all copies of this were also burned by order of the barbarian Emperor *Xi hoam ti* <note>Qin Shi Huang (r. 221–210 BCE), famous for his "Burning of Books and Burying of Scholars."</note>; and they could not be restored afterwards except by consulting the memory of the aged; there is no doubt (and indeed the *Interpreters* <note>Commentators.</note> so affirm) that some parts are missing. Some things, through the fault of senile memory—not to mention the industry and malice of certain people—have crept in which are foreign and apocryphal. Therefore, the cautious and prudent reader will imitate the industry of bees here, and will select for himself those things which serve the purpose, while rejecting the others. This entire volume deals with rites, both sacred and profane; likewise with duties of every kind which were in use during the time of the three leading Families <note>The Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties.</note> *Hia*, *Xam*, and *Cheu*, but especially the latter (during whose rule Confucius lived). These include the duties of parents toward children, and those of children in turn toward parents, those of spouses toward each other, those of friends, and those of guests at home, abroad, among banquets, etc. Again, it describes what vessels, what victims for heaven, in what sacrifices and Temples, what dishes for the now-deceased ancestors, what feasts and gifts in their funeral Halls, by what rite, or with what preparation, either Kings, or No-

# INTRODUCTORY DECLARATION.
<meta>catchword: if to it</meta>

[...it teaches what rituals] should be observed by the nobility, or even the common people themselves; indeed, it also diligently pursues the liberal arts—music in particular—as well as military skills like archery and chariot-driving; and for the sake of clarity, each is distinguished by its own titles. Finally, certain "miscellanea" are read, inserted by the disciples of Confucius, whose authors are said by interpreters to have been both the disciples and their Master themselves, although these are rejected by others as apocryphal. Father Francesco Saverio Philippucci <note>A Jesuit missionary (1632–1692) who wrote extensively on Chinese rites and philosophy.</note> has learnedly woven these together in a singular treatise, in which he brings to light in English <note>original: "Latinè"</note> from the Chinese the judgments and critical annotations of the interpreters regarding the aforementioned five classic books.

And these are those five volumes of the first class and authority, the primary sources, as it were, of the political and moral science of the Chinese. Next to these are the four books called the *Su xu* <note>The *Sishu*, or "Four Books," which became the standard curriculum for the imperial examinations.</note>, the work of the philosophers Confucius and *Memcius* <note>Mencius, the most famous follower of Confucius.</note>. Furthermore, although these can truly be considered interpretations of the five volumes—seeing as they drew nearly all their doctrine from them—their books are nevertheless held in the highest esteem. In terms of utility, they undoubtedly surpass the five classic volumes of the ancients mentioned before, and they are even equal in authority. Hence they are called the *Lo kim* <note>The "Six Classics." The author explains that the "Four Books" are sometimes grouped with the "Five Classics" to form a complete body of authoritative literature.</note>, that is, the six volumes; or the *U kim su xu*, that is, the five volumes and four books. 

Certainly, whoever aspires to literary degrees and laurels is required to be skilled in only one of the five volumes (whichever he has chosen to study by his own will); however, as for these four books, there can be no student who does not embrace them entirely in memory and understanding. There are several reasons for this law: first, because both philosophers extracted nearly whatever "better juice" was in the volumes of the ancients and made it their own; second, because they themselves added not a few things to the discoveries of their ancestors; third, because they set forth their doctrine much more plainly and clearly than the ancients; and finally, because they polished the primitive roughness of the old style and adorned the naked simplicity of the golden age with a more refined style, yet without deceit or pride. Therefore, these same reasons have persuaded us to translate these books—from which Europeans might form a judgment about the whole of Chinese philosophy—from Chinese into English <note>original: "Latinum"</note>, rather than others. However, we do not dismiss those other volumes so entirely that we do not consult them from time to time when the matter requires it; we go to the sources ourselves and derive pure waters for our own painstaking work.

Furthermore, there are four parts or books in total of the *Tetrabiblium* <note>A title used by the Jesuit translators to refer to the collection of the "Four Books."</note>. The first is titled *Ta hio*, that is, the *Great Science* <note>Now commonly translated as "The Great Learning."</note>. It is the smallest in comparison to the others; it teaches leading men how to rule well and happily. It begins first with the care and cultivation of the soul and one’s whole self, then proceeds through the correct instruction of one’s family or domestic court, to the administration of the Kingdom, and finally of the whole Empire...

...if heaven carries them to it, to take a step. *Zengzi* <note>original: "çem-çu"; a key disciple of Confucius to whom the "Great Learning" is often attributed.</note>, a disciple of Confucius, brought this work to light.

The title and subject of the second book, called the *Zhongyong* <note>original: "Chum yum"</note>, is the "Eternal Mean," or the consistency of the middle path or the "golden mean" <term>Golden Mean: The ancient philosophical ideal of finding the desirable middle ground between two extremes, such as excess and deficiency.</term>. *Zisi* <note>original: "çu fu"</note>, the grandson of Confucius through his son, a disciple of *Zengzi* <note>original: "Cemciique"</note>, and also the teacher of *Mencius* <note>original: "Memcii"</note>, published this and added some things of his own; however, much is also missing, so that it has the appearance of fragments rather than a complete book. Furthermore, because the sublimity of the doctrine handed down sometimes seems to exceed the limits of nature itself, the Chinese Masters, regarding it as somewhat obscure and difficult to grasp, explain it in the last place in the schools, even though it is second in the traditional numbering.

The third book also has wonderful uses, and is much easier and more clear than the second. It consists of ten parts and is titled the *Analects* <note>original: "Lun yu"; literally "Classified Sayings."</note> (as if to say "Conversations or Discourses of those Reasoning"), because it consists entirely of the aphorisms of Confucius, as well as those of his disciples, and various questions and answers gathered from here and there. Thus, there is much discussion here about vices, virtues, duties, and proper governance; there are also many things—not to say more than is strictly necessary—which the disciples, having observed in their Master Confucius, passed down for the memory of posterity, so that they might either imitate or at least admire them.

The fourth book, if you look at its physical bulk, equals the other three combined; its author is *Mengzi* <note>original: "Mem-çe"</note>, or *Mencius* <note>original: "Memcius"</note>, whom we have already mentioned several times. He disputes concerning nature, rituals, customs, and duties; none of the ancient thinkers has come closer to our own way of philosophizing. He is sharp and far more prolific than Confucius. And indeed, he undoubtedly surpassed Confucius in eloquence, though not in the innocence of his life, modesty, austerity, and uprightness. And let these things suffice regarding the authentic books of the "first rank." After these, the Chinese chronicles hold the next place and authority; and after these again—though at a great distance—come other books, among which are the *Jiayu* <note>original: "Kia yu"</note>, that is, "Family Sayings"; the *Xiaoxue* <note>original: "Siao hio"</note>, or "Instruction for the Young"; the *Xiaojing* <note>original: "Hiao-Kim"</note> regarding filial piety <note>original: "de obedientia"</note>; and the *Zhongjing* <note>original: "Chum-Kim"</note> regarding loyalty <note>original: "de fidelitate"</note>. Parts of these are attributed to Confucius and his disciples, but all of these must be read "with a grain of salt" <note>original: "cum grano salis"; meaning with healthy skepticism or discretion.</note> and carefully adapted for our own purposes.

# INTRODUCTORY DECLARATION.

## SECOND PARAGRAPH.

### CONCERNING THE *Interpreters* OF THE CLASSIC BOOKS.

**T**here cannot but be an abundance of interpreters where there is such a great abundance of books that have been written and continue to be written. Certainly, every age has had its own. Indeed, of those books contained in the *Wujing* <note>original: "U Kim"; the Five Classics of Confucianism</note> and the *Sishu* <note>original: "Su xu"; the Four Books</note>—namely the five volumes mentioned previously and the four-volume collection, which we shall henceforth call the *Classics* <term>Classics: The foundational texts of the Chinese intellectual tradition, comparable in authority to the Western canon.</term> by way of excellence—it is rumored that there have existed a total of six hundred interpreters and more. Not all of them interpreted every book, but some focused on one and some on others; thus, some worked on the *Shujing* <note>original: "Xu Kim"</note> or historical books; others on the Odes; some on the books of Rites and offices; and finally others on different parts; not a few interpreted only a portion of a single book.

However, the authors of the work called the *Xingli Daquan* <note>original: "Sim li ta çiven"; literally "The Great Compendium of Natural Philosophy," a massive Ming-dynasty collection of Neo-Confucian thought</note> cast suspicion of falsehood upon this rumor. For these authors number no more than twenty interpreters of the Classic volumes, whom they record as having lived during the reigns of the *Zhou* <note>original: "Cheu"</note>, *Han*, and *Tang* <note>original: "Tam"</note> families <term>Families: Referring to the imperial dynasties of China.</term>. Even among these, they teach that much is lacking and they criticize many points; they ultimately (because they either judge them to be counterfeit or certainly suspect them to be) unhesitatingly prefer the "Neoteric" <note>Modern or "New" interpreters, referring to the Neo-Confucians.</note> interpreters of their own age as the legitimate ones. Meanwhile, they cite a total of one hundred and eighteen of their own who flourished under the two most recent families, the *Song* <note>original: "Sum"</note> and *Yuan* <note>original: "Yven"</note>.

Indeed, if we deal with the more ancient writers—those specifically who wrote toward the end of the third family, called the *Zhou*—we find a troubled record. *Mencius* <note>original: "Memcius"</note>, who belonged to that same family and followed *Confucius* by a century, testifies to the calamity of his times, deploring that the heresies of *Yang Zhu* <note>original: "Yam"</note> and *Mozi* <note>original: "Me"</note> were prevailing, while the doctrine of the ancient Kings and Sages was being neglected and obliterated. Not without cause are we suspicious of the writers and interpreters of that time, when not only were errors running rampant, but the "Seven Kingdoms" (vying among themselves for the Empire) gave these errors license and impunity through their warfare. Two of the others, easily the leaders, named *Liezi* <note>original: "Lie çu"</note> and *Zhuangzi* <note>original: "Chuam çu"</note>, are openly accused and condemned of error by an interpreter of later times named *Cheng Zi* <note>original: "Chin-çu"</note> and others, because they mixed into their commentaries not a few ravings drawn from the sects of *Laozi* <note>original: "Lao-Kiun"; the legendary founder of Daoism</note> and others that flourished at that time.

The Fourth family, called the *Qin*, succeeded the Imperial *Zhou* family. They were primarily warlike and triumphant over all the petty kings, whose jurisdictions and kingdoms they eventually reduced into provinces; but this same family, regarding literature and...

deserved the very worst from the community of learned men. Though this sin was not so much the fault of the whole Family <note>Here "Family" refers to a Dynasty.</note> as it was of a single man, with whom that line may be said to have both begun and perished. This was *Shi Huangdi* <note>original: "Xi hoam ti"; the first Emperor of the Qin dynasty</note>, the builder of the Great Wall of China, who was second to none of the Chinese Kings in wars and victories. Driven by some unknown madness and a truly fatal hatred of literature, he ordered all books throughout the entire Empire to be burned, with the exception of those dealing with agriculture, medicine, and divination—at the instigation, it is said, of *Laozi* <note>original: "Lao Kiun"; the legendary founder of Daoism</note>, or rather his followers, whom the Emperor favored more excessively as he took greater delight in the delusions and lies of impostors. When, therefore, these orders were carried out under penalty of death, all the books of the Ancient Kings and Philosophers—especially those of *Confucius*—as well as those of their interpreters, were consumed by flames everywhere in the land, resulting in an irreparable loss to the world of letters. And lest any cruelty be missing from this monstrous crime, many learned men were buried in the earth up to their necks and perished, some by the sword and others by arrows.

But a few years later, when that family became extinct upon the death of the Prince, the dynasty that succeeded it—commonly called the *Han*, now the fifth in order—though it was also itself devoted to the sect of *Laozi*, nevertheless produced Princes who were not so estranged from the literature, doctrines, and customs of the Ancients. They immediately ordered the half-burnt remains of books, wherever any might still exist, to be collected. They likewise commanded that those hidden in walls and tombs, even if already half-eaten and ruined by decay, be brought into the light. Furthermore, they ordered that the elderly be consulted, to see if by chance they still held in their minds what they had once committed to memory as boys. In short, they spared no effort or industry to heal such a great loss of literature. Thus, a greater remedy was provided than had even been hoped for. Yet, it was not so complete that many things did not remain either gaping with fragments and, as it were, mutilated in some of their members, or deformed by foreign words and sentences—like scars left behind by a wound. Nevertheless, the Chinese political authority willed that these remain untouched, so that by law it has never been permitted to change or add even a single mark <term>mark: the original "apex" refers to the smallest stroke or diacritic in a character</term> to them.

In the meantime, under this Dynasty, several interpreters of books flourished: *Liu*, *Zhang*, *Ban*, *Jia*, *Zheng*, *Wang*, and others <note>original: "Lieu, Cham, Pan, Kia, Chim, Vam"</note>. All these interpreters are enumerated by a man named *Hu*, who wrote during the reign of the *Song* <note>original: "Sum"</note> Dynasty. But before we descend to the interpreters of later times, it will be worthwhile to first provide some notice of the two sects that have most especially infected this Empire, and have either entirely depraved or at least partially corrupted the senses and minds of the literati. In this way, the European reader will more easily discern which interpreters are to be followed and which, in truth, are to be utterly cast out.

## SECTION THREE.

### A BRIEF ACCOUNT OF THE SECT

->Of the Philosopher Laozi, and of his followers, whom they call the Daoshi in China.<-

To give the reader a more abundant account, it should be known that the author of this sect was the Philosopher commonly called *Li Lao-jun* <note>original: "Li lao Kiun"; known today as Laozi</note>, otherwise named *Boyang* <note>original: "Pe yam"</note> or *Laodan* <note>original: "lao tan"</note>. He was a contemporary of *Confucius*, although somewhat older than him. They tell fables, however, that after he had been carried in his mother's womb for eighty-one years, he finally burst forth into the light through an opening made in her left side; his mother is said to have died soon after such a miraculous birth. His books still exist, but they are believed to have been corrupted in more than one place by his followers. He wrote several things in which he inserted thoughts worthy of a philosopher regarding virtues, the fleeing of honors, the contempt for wealth and human affairs, and that blessed solitude which the Soul, rising above human matters, is able to enjoy. But where he deals with the production of things, he brings forward this sentence among others, which his followers constantly chant as the most noble axiom of his philosophy, namely: *The Way produced one, one produced two, two produced three, and three produced all things.* <note>original: "Tao sem ye, Ye sem ulh, Ulh sem san, San sem van ve"</note> Although this pronouncement of the man is ambiguous and obscure, as those oracles of the Ancients usually are, one thing is nonetheless certain: he possessed knowledge of a certain first and supreme Divinity, although his knowledge was in truth flawed, as he believed that the Divinity was corporeal <note>possessing a physical body</note>, even if he admitted that he ruled over other Divinities like a King over his subjects. They also commonly report that he was the Prince and Author of the chemical art <note>Alchemy</note>.

Furthermore, whatever kind of Master he himself may have been, it is beyond controversy that several centuries later, many of those who were—or falsely claimed to be—his disciples turned out to be wicked and ruined men; indeed, they were either the inventors of the magical arts among the Chinese or certainly their propagators. For although there are not lacking those who trace the beginning of magic to the Emperor of the fourth Family <note>Dynasty</note>, the *Qin* <note>original: "çin"</note>, called *Shi Huangdi* <note>original: "xi hoam ti"</note>—that famous enemy of the learned, and likewise of books, nearly all of which he ordered to be burned—it was because he allowed himself to be persuaded by the magicians and impostors who were disciples of the aforementioned *Laozi* that a medicine of immortality <term>Chang sheng yao: the "elixir of life"</term> <note>original: "Cham sem yo"</note> could truly be given as a drink...

Magic, however—if it did not take its beginning then—certainly received its greatest growth during the times of the next dynasty, called the **Han**; it was then that its sixth Emperor, surnamed **Wudi** <note>Han Wudi, r. 141–87 BC, famous for his interest in immortality</note>, devoted himself entirely to the nefarious studies of Magic under a Master named **Li Shaojun** <note>original: "Li xao kium"</note>. This philosophy, as is believable, was by then already corrupted, but for this very reason, it was more acceptable to feminine curiosity and desire. When this became common knowledge, there immediately arose a great gathering at the Court of those men who professed that new Sect. And since during that time one of the Queens had died, for whom the Prince was dying of love, and he could no longer bear the longing for her loss, there was one from that herd of Magicians who, through his illusions, offered the shadow of the deceased woman to be seen by the astonished and trembling King. Entangled thus in such destructive arts, the King—after he had committed many follies and had frequently swallowed the "potion of immortality"—at last felt himself to be mortal. Already close to death, he deplored his own credulity with late-coming tears, detesting the nefarious arts and the Masters of those arts.

This plague, however, was by no means extinguished with the King; nay rather, if he did not come from the same school, certainly the famous **Zhang Daoling** <note>original: "Cham tao lin"; the first "Celestial Master"</note> lived while that same family was ruling, whose descendants thereafter spread the diabolical arts far and wide. Among them, a certain **Zhang Daoyuan** <note>original: "Cham tao yven"</note> again achieved principal name and fame. Therefore, all the Shrines of this Sect that exist in the whole Empire, consecrated to those wonders, were entrusted and credited to the care and even the protection of both men. This is evident from the tablets and small images for sale everywhere, which show that whole herd of demons and men along with their followers, whom they have enrolled in the number of the gods and call **Xianren** <note>original: "Sien gin"</note>, that is, **immortals**. 

And indeed, the superstition and insanity of the Emperors under the **Tang** <note>original: "Tam"</note> dynasty honored the Ministers of this Sect with the very honorable title of **Tianshi** <note>original: "Tien su"</note>, that is, **Celestial Master**. Indeed, the founder of that family consecrated a Temple to **Laozi** <note>original: "Lao Kiun"</note> as if to an idol, and the Emperor who was sixth in order, **Xuanzong** <note>original: "Hiven çum"</note>, introduced his statue into his Palace. And now, even the descendants of these impostors are held in no common honor, especially those who, being descended from the first stock, were born in the first place; for they enjoy a perpetual dignity of a somewhat Mandarin rank. They inhabit very large and splendid houses in a certain village of the Province called **Jiangxi** <note>original: "Kiam si"; likely referring to the Dragon and Tiger Mountain, Longhu Shan</note>. Many indeed frequent this place, either seeking a remedy for their diseases, or desiring to be informed of their fate and the entire course of their life. These people, having been mocked by the lies and illusions of the one who then performs the dignity and office of **Celestial Master**, and being instructed in his hieroglyphic contract and other diabolical arts, are for the most part sent away joyful,

Furthermore, these diabolic arts seem to have gained the greatest strength during the times of the **Song** <note>original: "Cum"</note> family under its third Emperor, called **Zhenzong** <note>original: "Chin çum"; r. 997–1022</note>. Impostors and Magi—or the demons who serve as their ministers—had hung it by night from the most noble gate of the royal city. The credulous Emperor sought this book (which was filled with magic) on foot, and having received it with great veneration, he ordered it to be carried into the inner parts of his Palace with royal pomp and kept preserved in a golden casket.

From all of this, it becomes clear that the miserable Empire of the Chinese has always gone from bad to worse, and (as we were saying at the beginning) that the arts and observations which this pestilential sect of men now uses are full of superstitions and bound by a manifold pact with demons. Since they are such, not a few among the Chinese are so far from despising them that, after Idolatry was introduced—with this sect as its primary teacher—they pursued these same arts even more zealously and accumulated the old ones with the addition of new ones; so much so that their use is frequent and very common among the Chinese even today. 

If the Reader desires some specimen of these arts: at times, they offer to the astonished and credulous crowd images of both their Heresiarch <note>The leader of a sect; here referring to the founder of Daoism</note> and their Idols to be seen in the empty air. At other times, in a very large basin full of water, they represent the "changes of the empire" and the fantastic dignities and new prefectures to be obtained by their followers. Sometimes, after consulting the fates and invoking demons, they describe I know not what monstrous letters with a brush hanging in the air, either on a paper placed beneath it, or on the wall itself, or in the ashes; and they practice other illusions and superstitions of this kind, which it would be useless to recount here at length.

But truly, the age of the **Ancient Chinese** was not only free from such wickedness, but even ignorant of it. However, whatever that age may have been, we, since the very beginnings of the Chinese Mission, have always made it our goal to utterly extirpate all observations, both ancient and of this current age; and the efforts of Christian writers have been the same, following our advice and exhortation. # SECTION FOUR.
## A BRIEF ACCOUNT OF THE SECT
### called **Buddhism** <note>original: "Foe Kiao"</note>, and of its followers.

TWO HUNDRED and seventy years after the **Han Family** had begun to hold power—and sixty-five years after Christ—a most foul pestilence, more destructive than any fire, invaded China by royal authority: the nefarious sect of the Idol **Buddha** <note>original: "Fe"</note>. It was brought from **India** <note>original: "Indiis"</note> into China along with the **Pythagorean doctrine of reincarnation** <note>original: "metempsychosi"; the belief that souls move into new bodies after death</note>, many fables and superstitions, and finally atheism, along with many books in which the principles, decrees, and dogmas of the sect were contained. Because this pestilence currently spreads very widely and has long since infected almost all the books and sects of the Chinese (if one perhaps excludes the Muslims), and is indeed the mother of many of them; and furthermore, because it is most especially contrary to Christian truth and our own efforts, I think it necessary to give the reader a brief account here. I shall recount from somewhat further back what its origin was among the Indians, what its growth was among the Chinese, and what dogmas it introduced.

A small king named **Suddhodana** <note>original: "in fan vam"; the father of the historical Buddha</note> held that part and region of India which is midway between the North and the South, called by the Chinese **Zhong Tianzhu** <note>original: "Chum tien cho"; meaning "Central India"</note>. His wife's name was **Maya** <note>original: "Mo-ye"</note>. From her was born to him...

...his son, first called **Shaka the First** <note>original: "Xe primùm"</note>, or **Shakyamuni** <note>original: "Xe Kia"; the historical Buddha, Siddhartha Gautama</note> (a name by which the entire filth and superstition of the **Bonzes** <note>a term used by Europeans for Buddhist monks</note> is designated; the Japanese, however, have made it **Shaka** <note>original: "Xaca"</note> from a corrupted Chinese term). Later, when he reached the thirtieth year of his age, he was named **Fo** <note>original: "Fœ"; the Chinese word for Buddha</note>. Whether he was truly a man or a mere phantom of the devil (as the Apostle of Japan, **Francis Xavier**, believed) is a matter of uncertain controversy. Certainly, if the stories his followers recount about his birth are not fables, one must agree with Saint Xavier. They tell that a vision of a **white elephant** was offered to his mother in a dream, which insinuated itself into her womb through her mouth; hence the rumor that he was conceived from an elephant. Others have a much truer suspicion: that by the work of a demon, he was conceived from human seed brought from elsewhere under the appearance of that beast. Among the Indians, a white elephant is not only highly prized but even held in such veneration that if its possession is in doubt, it sometimes drives kingdoms to war, and the controversy is not ended without much bloodshed. They recount again that he was brought into the light from the **right side** of his mother, who died soon after the birth. Thus, this "Savior of the human race" (as his followers boastfully call him) could not even look after the safety of his own mother. Indeed, from this you may understand that this monster of a man had more of the viper in him than the human. And truly, the character **Fo** <note>the Chinese character 佛</note>, being composed of the signs for **not** and **man** <note>the author refers to the components 亻 (man) and 弗 (not)</note>, implies as much. Immediately after birth, he stood on his feet and walked exactly seven paces, pointing to heaven with one hand and to the earth with the other, pronouncing in a clear voice: *Tien xam, Tien hia to ngo guei çun* <note>original: "天上天下唯我獨尊"; In heaven and on earth, I alone am to be venerated</note>, so that no one could hereafter doubt by which father he was begotten.

These things happened in the year 1909 of the Chinese Monarchy, in 1026 BCE, at which time **Zhao Wang** <note>original: "Chao vam"; r. 1052–1002 BCE</note>, the fourth Emperor of the third family called **Zhou** <note>original: "Cheu"</note>, held power among the Chinese. In the 17th year of his age, **Shakyamuni** <note>original: "xe kia"</note> took three wives. He fathered a son whose name the Chinese express with the three letters **Lo-heu-lo** <note>original: "Lo heu lo"; Rahula</note>. Not long after, renouncing human affairs and cares—perhaps to do penance for the mother who died because of him—he withdrew into the wilderness at nineteen years of age. Here he gave himself over to be instructed by four **Gymnosophists** <note>ancient Greek term for "naked philosophers," here referring to Indian ascetics</note> who are called **Yogis** <note>original: "Jogues"</note> in India. Finally, in the thirtieth year of his age, while he happened to be contemplating the **morning star** <note>original: "phosphorum"</note> as the herald of the sun, by that single gaze at the star he suddenly perceived the entire essence of the **First Principle**. Suddenly inspired by some sort of divinity, he emerged as **Fo**, or a **Deity** <note>original: "Numen"; he notes that in India this is called a "Pagode"</note>. Thus, from a disciple he became a Master, and from a man now a God, he began to impart his doctrine to mortals. Nor was the son (or certainly his minister) lacking the help of an evil demon, by whose power he performed many deeds that gripped blind mortals, who were utterly astonished by the novelty of the matter or by the apparent miracles. The Chinese have published these very deeds in many great volumes and quite elegant images. For [many] years...

...altogether, this dire impostor <note>The author is referring to the Buddha</note> published forty-nine dogmas far and wide throughout the East at the very same time that **King Solomon** was watering the West with the streams of his flowing wisdom.

It exceeds belief what is recounted concerning the multitude of his disciples; it is said that eighty thousand existed, for each of whom there was a specific rank of either **Gymnosophy** <term>Gymnosophy: From the Greek for 'naked wise men,' a term used by Westerners to describe Indian ascetics or yogis</term> or **Idolatrous dignity**.
