They say that from that monstrous multitude, five hundred were selected; from these, one hundred; and from those hundred, another ten, who, being distinguished by the name and dignity of "Magnates," compiled the praises of their Master into five thousand volumes after he departed from this life.

Indeed, this "new God" eventually realized he was not numbered among the immortals when, in the 79th year of his age, he felt his strength failing, weighed down by disease and fate. But he was never more ruinous to the human race than when he ceased to be ruinous: for as he was dying, he vomited forth the most foul poison of **Atheism**. He expressly professed that for forty years and more he had not declared the truth to the world, but had hidden the naked truth, contenting himself with shadowy and metaphorical teachings through figures, similes, and parables. But now at last, being close to death, he wished to signify the secret meaning of his mind: that outside of the **vacuum** and the **void** <note>original: "vacuum & inane"</note> (which the Chinese call **Kong xu** <note>original: "Cum hiu"; the Buddhist concept of Śūnyatā or 'Emptiness'</note>), there is nothing to be sought, and nothing in which our hopes should be placed. This was the final word of the dire impostor and the first root of Atheism; although even today, hidden by the darkness of lies and superstitions, it remains concealed from the unlearned common folk like something buried in the ground. From this also comes that famous distinction of the doctrine into the "exterior" and "interior," which we shall soon explain.

His corpse was burned with scented wood according to the custom of the nation, and the ashes were distributed (so they say) among men, spirits, and sea dragons. One tooth was sent as a gift to the King of the **Island of Ceylon** <note>Sri Lanka</note>. Later, **Constantine**, the brother of the **Duke of Braganza**, while managing the affairs and arms of the Portuguese in India, ordered this tooth—which had been captured among other spoils—to be handed over to the flames. After it was reduced to ashes, he ordered them to be scattered into a flowing river. He did this while despising, with a Christian and princely spirit, an immense weight of gold which the barbarian King offered through his legate to ransom it. As for the claim by **Maffei** <note>Giovanni Pietro Maffei, a Jesuit historian</note> and other historians of our nation that the tooth belonged to a certain monkey which was worshipped with great superstition: this should not be attributed to an error. Rather, it is because that wicked demon is worshipped in different places with various forms and names; in those lands from which the Portuguese took the tooth, he was held in veneration under the figure of a monkey.

Besides other most absurd fables, the followers of this sect also persuade the credulous multitude that this Master of theirs was born eight thousand times through **metempsychosis** <term>metempsychosis: the philosophical term for the migration of a soul into a new body after death; reincarnation</term>, appearing now in the form of this beast, now in the form of another. They claim he was most recently conceived in the form of a **white elephant**, returning to the world for the sake of bringing aid to mortals.

Therefore, in addition to that aforementioned crowd of disciples, he left behind one disciple who was by far his most beloved, the primary heir and propagator of his impiety; his name was *Mo o Kia ye* <note>Mahākāśyapa, one of the principal disciples of the Buddha</note>. He gave this disciple instructions that in all the books he published concerning his doctrine, he should prefix these words: *Ju xi ngo ven* <note>original: "Ju xi ngo ven"; the Chinese translation of the Sanskrit "Evam mayā śrutam," meaning "Thus have I heard"</note>. He was to use no other reasons or arguments; thus it clearly appears that he learned this arrogance, along with his other insanities, from this Master—a style which the **Pythagorean School** <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, known for the phrase "Ipse dixit" or "The Master has said it," valuing authority over proof</note> followed roughly five centuries later.

Furthermore, *Fo* (or *Shaka*) himself makes mention in his books of another Master even older than himself (who was in truth an evil demon). The Chinese call him *O-mi-to*, and the Japanese, using a corrupted version of the word, commonly call him *Amida* <note>Amitābha, the Buddha of Infinite Light</note>. He lived in Eastern India, or Bengal, where the **Bonzes** <note>Buddhist monks</note> falsely claim the **Elysian Fields** <note>The author uses the Greek term for the blessed afterlife to describe "çim tu," the Pure Land or Western Paradise</note> are located. Indeed, such great holiness is attributed to *Amida*, and so many are his merits, that whoever prays to him may obtain pardon for their crimes, however innumerable they may be. Consequently, nothing is more frequently on the lips of the Chinese people than these two names, *O mi to, Fo*, so that by joining the names and merits of both, they might emerge entirely purified—though soon, by the impulse of these same figures, they will again and again loosen the reins on their former lust, avarice, treachery, and every kind of disgrace with impunity.

Moreover, the power and reason of the **two-fold doctrine** which we mentioned before is this: that the "exterior" leads, as it were, by the hand to the "interior." This exterior doctrine (which they call *Kiven* <note>Chinese: "Quan," meaning expedient or provisional teachings</note>) remains in use only until the other doctrine—which they call *xe* <note>Chinese: "Shi," meaning real or solid</note> and teach to be the true and solid one—has taken firm root in the minds of those capable of it (though these are very few among the common people). They explain the matter with a similar example: when someone builds a stone arch, they undoubtedly first erect a wooden frame which acts as a support for the stone until the arch is finished and attains its strength. Once it is perfected and firm, the wooden frame is dismantled and cast aside, as it no longer has any use.

This is the summary of the **exterior and substituted doctrine**: that there is a distinction between good and evil, right and wrong; and thus there are both rewards and punishments, and places destined for each. It teaches that blessedness is obtained through thirty-two figures and eighty qualities; that *Fo* (or *Shaka*) himself is a deity and the Savior of mortals; that he was born for their sake because he took pity on those wandering from the path of salvation; and that their crimes are expiated through him. By this expiation, they achieve salvation from death and are reborn more happily in another world. Finally, it teaches that there are **five precepts**: the first, that no living thing...

Six works of mercy are likewise prescribed for his followers: First among these is that they kindly cherish and nourish the **Bonzes** <note>From the Japanese word *bōzu*, referring to Buddhist monks</note>, and build their monasteries and temples; for in this way, there will be no lack of those who, through their prayers and voluntary penances, may pay the punishments due for sins. The sum of the doctrine, which they call the *inner*, solid, and true doctrine, is this: that *Cum hiu* <note>original: "Cum hiu"; likely the Chinese *Kōngxū*, representing the Buddhist concept of *Śūnyatā* (emptiness or the void)</note>, a certain vacuum and void, is the beginning and the end of all things. Indeed, they say this vacuum itself is ours, and is our substance, so that from it and from the elements equally, whatever things exist anywhere are produced; and into the same they are then resolved and return through death. All things are distinguished and differ entirely only by shapes and qualities, just as water placed in different and various vessels: now refined into snow by flakes, now...

...like air spread out into mists, sometimes forged into the breastplates of freezing waters, sometimes binding itself into stones of hail; similarly also as bronze and gold, from which an **Artisan** <note>original: *Artifex*</note> might cast now a man, now a lion, or any other household object—all different in form, certainly; yet once the metal is melted down again, they are altogether one and the same thing. Thus, therefore, all things that exist—endowed with life, sense, and mind—though they differ among themselves in use and shape, are nevertheless intrinsically one and the same thing, for they are indistinct from their very beginning.

This beginning, however, they teach to be an altogether wonderful thing: pure, clear, subtle, and infinite; something that can neither be created nor destroyed, which is the perfection of all things and is itself supremely perfect and quiet. *Yet they deny* that it is equipped with a heart, or any **virtue, mind, or power** <note>original: *virtute mente potentiave*</note>. Indeed, they claim this is the most defining characteristic of its essence: that it agitates nothing, understands nothing, and desires nothing. Therefore, whoever is desirous of living well and happily must strive toward this through constant meditation and victory over oneself—to become as similar as possible to one's beginning, taming and utterly extinguishing all human affections. Such a person should no longer be disturbed or distressed by anything, but like one entirely absorbed in an **ecstatic state** <note>original: *extatici prorsus instar*</note>, should enjoy that deepest contemplation, without any use or reasoning of the intellect, in that divine quiet than which nothing is more blessed. Once someone has achieved this, they may pass on the common way of living and teaching to others, and follow it themselves in appearance; but in secret, they should devote themselves to their own soul and to the truth, enjoying that hidden quiet and the way of a heavenly life. This is the sum of the mystery. Meanwhile, there is no mention of right or wrong, no mention of reward or punishment, no divine providence, and no immortality of souls. They speak of a single **vacuum** <note>original: *vacuum*</note>, and a real **nothing** <note>original: *nihil*</note>; and that, as we have seen, is a most confused concept. To this they refer the origin and destruction of all things; indeed, they say this "nothing" is itself all things, into which it constantly transmigrates and transforms itself through one of four ways: **from the womb, from eggs, from seed, or through mutual transformation** <note>original: *vel uteri, vel ovorum, vel seminis, vel mutuæ conversionis*</note>. Thus, one and the same chimeric principle is at once man, lion, stone, and everything else. It is from the contemplation of that chimera that their entire happiness (as I was relating) is sought; and those who devote themselves more intensely to this contemplation are considered to belong to a specific and new sect.

This is called by another name, *Vu guei Kiao* <term>Wuwei Jiao: The "Teaching of Non-Action," a school of thought emphasizing emptiness and spontaneity</term>, or the **sect of those who do nothing** <note>original: *nihil agentium secta*</note>. It is not much different from that which we have already mentioned, which flourished long ago among the **Gymnosophists** <term>Gymnosophists: "Naked philosophers" of ancient India known for their asceticism and meditation</term> of India, and then began to flourish among the Chinese as well during the reign of **Huidi** <note>original: *hoei ti*</note>, who was the second emperor from the seventh dynasty called the **Jin** <note>original: *çin*</note>, about two hundred and ninety years after Christ. But what you might wonder at more is that this insanity invaded and occupied the minds of the highest nobles of the Empire and all the greatest men, to such an extent that the closer one approached the nature of a stone or a tree-trunk—remaining for many hours without any movement of body or mind, without...

# INTRODUCTORY DECLARATION.

...without any use of the senses or powers, it is thought that one has progressed more successfully, becoming nearer and more similar to one’s **airy beginning** <note>original: *principio suo aërio*</note>, to which one would eventually return.

Thus they say that **Bodhidharma** <note>original: *Ta mo*; the monk credited with bringing Zen Buddhism to China</note>, the twenty-eighth descendant from the lineage of **Shakyamuni** <note>original: *Xa ca*; the historical Buddha</note> himself, sat for nine whole years facing a wall. During all this time, he contemplated nothing except that chimerical principle of his, the **void and nothingness**; and having finally conformed to it, he emerged as a deity. He has certainly long held the veneration of a deity among the **Chinese** <note>original: *Sinas*</note>, with very large and magnificent temples built for him. Although they bestow the far more principal honors, and the title **Fo** <note>original: *Fœ*; the Chinese word for Buddha</note>, primarily upon two: namely **Amitabha** <note>original: *Amida*</note> and Shakyamuni, because they say these two were perfectly complete images of the first principle, absolute in every detail. Others, who represent only a single attribute of the same principle, they wish to be called **Bodhisattvas** <note>original: *Pu sa*</note>. Such is **Guanyin Pusa** <note>original: *Quon in pu sa*</note>, which is an idol in the appearance of both a mother and a virgin embracing a small son, being the image of **mercy** alone. Those lower than these, and not far different from the ancient Roman "gods of the lesser nations" <note>the *Dii minorum gentium*, or minor deities in the Roman pantheon</note>, they call **Arhats** <note>original: *Lo han*</note>.

Meanwhile, the **Grand Secretary** <note>original: *Colaus*; a Latinization of the Chinese title *Gelaou*</note> **Poei guei** <note>likely a phonetic rendering of a high-ranking Confucian official</note>, a follower of Confucius, attacked this sect of contemplatives in a written volume and proves at length that **Aristotelian** maxim: **out of nothing, nothing is made** <note>original: *ex nihilo nihil fieri*</note>. From this, he then concludes that there undoubtedly existed long before that "principle" something from which so many things, which we see most clearly to exist, have flowed. However, that excellent man was not able to refute this error so completely that it did not spread very widely; even in our own time, many devote themselves to such insane contemplations. I say further that many of the **Literati** <note>the scholar-official class in China</note> have been, and still are, poisoned by both the native **Laozi** <note>original: *Lao Kiun*; the founder of Daoism</note> and the Indian Shakyamuni. Many of them, born and educated among the rustic and superstitious dregs of the common people, even if they rise by their own talent to the highest duties and dignities in the State, can scarcely or only with great difficulty shed those native and domestic superstitions which they sucked in from their tender years, almost with their mother’s milk—especially since they are provoked and confirmed by the examples of their own princes, whose favor they seek.

Some indeed condemn this foreign novelty and teach with grave words and maxims that it is heretical and ruinous; yet in truth, it seems to me that they do not so much wish to demolish a stone archway as a wooden one with their censures <note>meaning their criticism is superficial or targets the weak points rather than the core philosophy</note>. And while they hated the dogmas of the "outer" doctrine, its many rituals, the abstinence from meat and wine, the many monstrous idols, and the idle crowd of **Bonzes** <note>original: *Bonziorum*; Buddhist monks</note> who are useless to the State; nevertheless, not a few have embraced the "inner" and secret doctrine, and have at last fallen headlong into the deep abyss of **Atheism**, toward which they were already leaning by the weight of their own proud arrogance and vices.

# INTRODUCTORY DECLARATION.

These wicked men hide under the simple name of **"Natural Philosophy"** <note>original: *Sim-li* (Xingli); a Neo-Confucian term referring to the study of the principles of nature and the human heart</note>, treating it like a well-worn, flat, and royal road. They do not hesitate to use the authority of their ancestors, whose virtue and wisdom were so exceptional, to confirm their own impiety and foolishness.

Those who have sinned most in this regard—though they were not the first—were the four interpreters, **Chen, Cham, Chim, and Chu** <note>The author refers to the major Song Dynasty Neo-Confucian masters: the brothers Cheng Hao and Cheng Yi, Zhang Zai, and Zhu Xi</note>. Nevertheless, the later age followed them as masters. In the beginnings of the **Ming** <note>original: *Taimingæ*</note> Dynasty, a new and destructive doctrine soon emerged, established by the opinion and authority of no others more than those four interpreters.

### PARAGRAPH FIVE.
## CONCERNING THE SECT OF THE LITERATI;
#### *or the proper philosophy: what foundation or principle the ancients established for it, and what the modern interpreters have established.*

The **ancient age of the Chinese** <note>original: *Prisca Sinarum ætas*</note>, a sincere cultivator and teacher of wisdom, prudence, and the other virtues, not only always admired the wonderful order and constancy of heaven and earth, but also tried with great care and zeal to imitate it. From this, they derived their monarchical rule, which has now flourished for four thousand years; from this, they sought a way of governing so fit and easy: the lowest through the middle, and the middle through the highest. It truly seems that the ancient Kings and Sages of this nation labored with all the struggle of mind and body on this one goal. Indeed, they never even tasted with the tips of their lips the more sublime delights of **Greek philosophy** <note>original: *philosophantis Graeciae*</note>, which are more remote from the senses. Perhaps they would have even turned away in their minds—forbidding entry not only to their ears but even to their borders—if some **Aristotle** or any clever **Sophist** from the **Stoic** or **Peripatetic** <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle's school</note> schools had migrated from there into China. Their only prayer was for peace and a constant, equitable system of both morals and laws. To achieve this, they first looked to religion, then to political govern—

# INTRODUCTORY DECLARATION.

...they devoted their efforts to the nation: In that Ancient Age, they rightly worshipped a certain Supreme Deity, whom they called ***Xam ti*** <note>original: *Xam ti*; Shangdi, the "High Sovereign" or "Supreme Lord"</note>, the Supreme Emperor of Heaven, as well as other spirits who preside over things beneath the moon. Truly, they did not pry too curiously into the secrets of that nature which is so sublime and so far removed from human eyes; indeed, they forbade such scrutiny in explicit words, lest heresies easily arise among a people who are ingenious but unstable and most eager for novelty, which would harm the public peace and truth. The height of their political wisdom and industry was this: that those who ruled believed they ruled over sons, and those who obeyed believed they obeyed fathers. And this was the entire system and Philosophy of the Ancient Age, which we must treat more copiously in the "Chinese Science" <note>The author refers to *Scientia Sinica*, likely the ongoing project to translate and explain Chinese classics for a European audience</note> which we have undertaken to explain.

Therefore, it remains to be examined whether some other Philosophy was introduced in later times, which the Ancient Sages were entirely ignorant of, and which only the ***Modern Interpreters*** <term>Modern Interpreters: *Neoterici Interpretes*; the author's term for the Neo-Confucian scholars of the Song Dynasty</term> finally brought into the light of their Chinese world after it had been buried—as they say—for forty centuries. So that we may proceed in an orderly fashion, we must first investigate who those men were, of what authority they were, and at what time they appeared. Then, we must ask from what source they drew that doctrine of theirs, or "new philosophy." Finally, we must determine what principle and foundation of their entire doctrine or nature they ultimately strove to establish. In this way, it will be easy to decide which opinion a European should especially follow: that of those who fight for the innocence, rectitude, and sincerity of the Ancients, or that of those who, having almost no regard for that antiquity, devised a new doctrine in the most corrupt times and transmitted it to posterity.

Furthermore, as for the Modern Interpreters, I call those here who existed while the ***Sum*** <note>original: *Sum*; the Song Dynasty (960–1279 AD)</note> family was ruling (not the one that was eighth in order, but the one of the same character that was nineteenth in order). Indeed, the year 960 after the birth of Christ gave the beginning to this family. This was eight hundred and ninety-nine years after idolatry, along with ***Pythagorean dreams*** <note>The author compares the Buddhist doctrine of reincarnation/metempsychosis to the theories of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras</note>, was brought into China from the Indies by royal authority. From that Sect, one after another arose—to say nothing now of the nation’s own "domestic" Sects and Heresies, such as those of ***Lao Kiun*** <note>Laozi, the founder of Taoism</note>, and ***Yam*** and ***Me*** <note>Yang Zhu and Mozi, ancient philosophers whose radical views on egoism and universal love were often condemned by traditional Confucians</note>, which were already dominant in China long ago. Therefore, since the Imperial family of ***Sum*** was more devoted to Letters and the Learned than all previous families, and thus very prolific, it had Interpreters of outstanding talent and dignity. They undertook to explain not only the interpretation of the five Classic books and the Chronicles, but also the Commentaries of the Interpreters themselves—namely ***Confucius***, ***Mencius***, and others—and their own night-studies, much more copiously and eloquently.

Those called ***Chim çu*** <note>original: *Chim çu*; referring to the Cheng brothers, Cheng Hao and Cheng Yi, key figures in Neo-Confucianism</note> wrote around the year of Christ 1070, during the reign of ***Xin çum*** <note>Emperor Shenzong of Song</note>, the sixth prince of the ***Sum*** <note>Song</note> Family. This Interpreter also held the highest offices in the Empire, and because he served literature so well, he was honored with the title ***Ven cum*** <note>Wengong</note>, or "Prince of the Literati." Furthermore, although these men all flourished nearly six hundred years ago, we confidently call them ***Moderns*** <term>Modern Interpreters: *Neoterici*; the author uses this to distinguish the medieval Neo-Confucians from the "Ancient" Sages like Confucius</term>, insofar as they are compared with the ancients whom we cited above, who preceded them by more than one thousand five hundred years. 

In that long interval of time, fifteen imperial families <note>dynasties</note> had their rise and fall, burning with almost perpetual civil wars, and claiming the supreme right for themselves through trickery, snares, slaughter, and parricide, whether by right or wrong. Added to this, they were miserably entangled and contaminated by various sects of idols <note>The author likely refers to the spread of Buddhism and Taoism</note> which, like the many-headed hydra, sprouted daily from nearly the same single source we mentioned above. In the midst of such darkness and disturbances, what place could there finally be for the liberal arts and the study of literature? Indeed, they themselves admit and even lament that there was scarcely any; thus it is less surprising that the writers of those times (for there were some) were so rare, so fragmented, and so brief that ***Chu çu*** and others did not hesitate to say that for more than a thousand years, no truly learned man had existed. 

Regarding these ***Modern*** Interpreters whom I just mentioned, some Emperors of the ***Sum*** <note>Song</note> Family expressly affirm that after the death of ***Confucius***, ***çemcii*** <note>Zengzi</note>, ***çu fu*** <note>Zisi</note>, and ***Memcii*** <note>Mencius</note>—the ancient Interpreters—no others arose who explained the meaning of the ancient books more successfully or clearly, or who revived the doctrine of the ***Ancients*** <note>original: *Priscorum*</note> that had been buried for so many centuries, as did these later Interpreters under the Song Family. 

This is also the reason why other Interpreters, who were much more recent than these—namely, those who flourished during the reign of ***Yum lo*** <note>The Yongle Emperor</note>, the third emperor of the twenty-first family, the ***Tai mim*** <note>The Ming Dynasty</note> (which immediately preceded the one under which we are now writing)—issued a royal edition of the five ancient books or doctrinal works. By his mandate, and through the labor and study of forty-two selected Literati from the court, these works were laboriously revised and brought to public light by a new press. It was established by general consensus that the schools should follow and explain no other Interpreters than the aforementioned ***Chim çu*** and ***Chu çu***. Indeed, they attempted to attach all other Interpreters to these two, and nearly everyone wished to swear by the words of these two men alone. Thus, their labors, divided into many volumes, were finally brought to light in the year 1415 after Christ, which was the thirteenth year of the aforementioned Emperor ***Yum lo***. ...of those books to which they added an explanation of the *Four Books* <note>original: *tetrabiblii*; referring to the four foundational texts of Confucianism</note> or the works of ***Confucius*** and ***Mencius***, they moreover produced another work, which contains twenty significant volumes, titled ***Sim li ta çiven*** <note>original: *Xingli Daquan*, or "The Great Compendium on Nature and Principle," commissioned by the Yongle Emperor in 1415</note>, that is, the *Pandects* <term>Pandects: a complete body of knowledge or a comprehensive compendium</term> on Nature or Natural Philosophy. This stain of evil has spread even to our own age, in which we see not a few of the Literati class devoting themselves to those new commentaries; and although they are by no means considered Classics, they still attribute to them a weight and authority they least deserve. The cause of the error was undoubtedly the attractive novelty of the matter; since it disputed there concerning the procreation of things, principles, and causes, and it was disputed with talent, richness of speech, and elegance. Moreover, the work was completed by Royal authority, as well as by the effort of forty-two men, who were all foremost in literature and rank. 

Some of the more credulous Chinese embraced this new and false Philosophy (if it can even be called Philosophy) as if it had fallen from heaven, the more eagerly because they certainly believed it to be a friend to truth and heaven, when in fact it was most hostile to both. For what? Can anything more contrary to truth be said or even imagined, or anything more alien to the light of reason infused in us from heaven, than to deny the existence of Him who is the maker, Lord, and Moderator of heaven, earth, and all things? 

Yet this is denied among that nation which, by the most constant use and custom of four thousand years, has professed (as if in a most eloquent speech) that every body needs its head, and every assembly of men needs its Prince, so that it might be preserved and governed for a long time. Unless perhaps we say that the Ancient Chinese, when they so studiously measured all their affairs by the pattern of heaven and earth, nevertheless thought that this very thing was lacking in the prototype, which was by far the greatest part of the prototype's example; I mean, that heaven lacks its King and Lord, which the Monarchy—the imitator of heaven—could never lack. Or that they believed that the most beautiful and constant state, motion, and order of heaven proceeds from no Divine Will or counsel, but that everything is owed to chance and accident; when nevertheless, in order to imitate that state, motion, and order, they considered nothing so necessary for themselves as to apply counsel and wisdom, and to entrust the highest state of their affairs to one head and one King...

->## SECTION SIX.<-

### **FROM WHAT SOURCE**
### *the Modern Interpreters drew this new kind of Philosophy.*

The root of the entire doctrine is one and the same, and clearly has a single foundation: the book *Ye kim* <note>The *Yi Jing* or *I Ching*</note> or the *Book of Changes*, which we placed above in the third position among the five Classical books. This is true if indeed hieroglyphic lines and figures deserve the name of a "book"—and very few lines at that—which <margin>Fo hi</margin> ***Fo hi*** <note>Fuxi, the legendary first emperor and hero of China</note>, the founder of the Chinese nation, left to his posterity to be untangled like another Gordian knot <note>A metaphor for a complex or unsolvable problem</note>, since there was no use of letters at that time. And because the Interpreters begin their encyclopedias <note>original: *pandectas*</note> with this book and found their entire doctrine chiefly upon it, it seems worthwhile, before we proceed further, to explain a certain summary and model of this little book to the curious European. Indeed, it is established that the Author’s <note>Fuxi's</note> intention was nothing other than to set before the eyes of mortals the mutual connections and alliances, or the dissociations and battles, of created things; and furthermore, to show their influences, order, and vicissitudes. Through these steps, as if by degrees, he intended to lead the unrefined infancy of the Chinese nation toward the knowledge of its own beginning and ultimate end, and of the supreme intelligence of spirits. To this intelligence, even then, prayers and sacrifices were offered; for this reason, ***Fo hi*** is called by another name, ***Pao hi***, which means "embracing the sacrificial victims." This most evidently proves that the worship of the true deity existed at the very beginning of the nation.

First of all, he seems to have proposed for the consideration of posterity those things which happened to heaven, earth, and man. Indeed, while he contemplated a certain wonderful society and, as it were, a mutual affinity and symmetry among these three, he himself described the eight Figures, in Chinese ***Pa qua*** <note>The *Ba Gua* or Eight Trigrams</note>, that is, the "eight hanging images or figures." The Interpreter explains the character *Qua* with these words, ***Quahiven-chi-fiam*** <note>Likely a phonetic rendering of a Chinese commentary explaining *Gua* as "to hang" or "manifest symbols"</note>, although it is now commonly used by mistake to refer to "fortunes" or "lots." And he described these figures in such a way that each one consisted of three small lines, some whole and some broken. From these, eight combinations then arise, in much the same way that the three-syllable feet of our metric art are combined—if, in place of a whole line, you imagine a long syllable, and in place of a broken line, two short ones. From these three-part combinations...

<header>->INTRODUCTORY DECLARATION.<-</header>

...through the doubling of paths and the eightfold multiplication of these combinations among themselves, sixty-four figures finally emerge. When inquisitive posterity later arranged these in various positions or structures, they sketched out—as if in a rough painting—the diverse and multifaceted nature, movement, and order of things through their placement and variety.

To understand this deeply, one must know that from the earliest times, the Chinese <note>original: *Sinas*</note> have held this view: that there is a dual material principle of all things. One they call *Perfect*, the other *Imperfect*; they name the latter *Yn* <note>Yin</note> and the former *Yam* <note>Likely a typographical variant for "Yang".</note>. These two were produced from the *Tai Kie*, that is, the *Great Axis* <note>The *Taiji*, or "Supreme Ultimate," which the author translates literally as *Magnum Axem*</note>, which seems to be a kind of chaos or material mass encompassing all things. Alternatively, as the Chinese Doctors—and not a few among the Pagans <note>original: *Ethnicos*</note> and those of us illuminated by the light of faith—unanimously explain it, this is *Yuen che*, which is to say, the *Primary Matter* <note>original: *Materia prima*; the basic, unformed substance from which the universe was created according to Aristotelian philosophy</note>. 

When discussing the first production of things, many Interpreters seem to imagine in their minds a certain vast sea, which is split into two smaller seas. This split is such that in one remains whatever is more mobile, lighter, purer, and more perfect; in the other, whatever is less mobile, heavier, and more dross-filled <note>original: *fæculentum*</note> and imperfect. These two principles, like two seas but now smaller, split again and are subdivided into two others, always with the same separation of the pure and *perfect* from that which is dross and imperfect. From these four, eight similarly divided and distinct ones emerge; soon eight become sixteen, like spacious rivers; these become thirty-two, then sixty-four; and finally, dispersed into many flows and streams (always following the rule of the first division and separation), they constitute this visible World <note>original: *Mundus*</note>. 

To move from this metaphor to the reality itself, the Chinese Philosophize in this way: they say that everything consists of the power and virtue of both *Yn* and *Yam*, as a multifaceted quality. Thus, any given thing is more or less perfect depending on how much or how little of either principle it possesses.

Therefore, the entire construction of the map or table is formed, as I have said, from two

Those lines which are not interrupted, but are continuous and whole, signify something perfect and solid, and that which, in the same category, surpasses the other; they also signify something happy and fortunate. However, those which are not whole or are interrupted designate the opposite of these. By the interrupted lines, therefore, they designate the *imperfect*—for example, the earth, the moon, water, cold, night, the female, the native moisture which we commonly call "radical moisture" <note>original: *humorem nativum quem vulgò radicalem dicimus*; "radical moisture" was a common concept in early medicine and alchemy, referring to the essential fluid that sustains life.</note>, diseases, and calamities. By the continuous and whole lines, they designate the *perfect*—for example, heaven, the sun, fire, heat, day, the male, the native fires or primordial heat, prosperous health, and fortune.

They teach, moreover, that it is the property of the perfect to manifest itself, to go forth, to move, to dilate, to rarefy, to ascend, to increase, and to open. On the contrary, they teach that it is the property of the imperfect to hide itself, to enter within, to rest, to restrict, to condense, to descend, to diminish, and to close. Furthermore, they teach that from each of these two principles, another two subordinate principles exist: two from the *Perfect*, of which one is the "greater-perfect" <note>Old Chinese: *Tai Yang*, or Great Yang</note> and the other is the "lesser-imperfect" <note>Old Chinese: *Shao Yin*, or Lesser Yin</note>; and two from the *Imperfect*, of which one is the "lesser-perfect" <note>Old Chinese: *Shao Yang*, or Lesser Yang</note> and the other is the "greater-imperfect" <note>Old Chinese: *Tai Yin*, or Great Yin</note>.

Confucius calls these four emanations from the two principles the *Su siam* <note>original: *Su siam*; the Romanization used by the author for the *Si xiang* or "Four Images" in the I Ching.</note>, that is, the *Four Images*. By these—according to the opinion of the Interpreters—the *Sun*, the *Moon*, the *Greater Stars* (or those that shine more brightly), and the *Lesser Stars* (those that shine less) are denoted. How they are able to prove and defend this opinion is not sufficiently clear. 

Certainly, they seem to admit here a certain mutual root, or as we say, a kind of causality; for example, that the cold is born from the hot—or at least follows from it—and conversely, the hot from the cold. While the Interpreters attempt to defend and prove this opinion, they use an example of this sort: water and metal are cold by their nature (they say), but it cannot be denied that the brightness and clarity inherent in both are produced by heat—specifically, by no other heat than that which resides within all water and metal. Similarly, fire is hot by nature; but that blackish and blue-like color which is usually observed in a surging flame—from what cause does it proceed, if not from the cold contained within the fire? 

Undoubtedly, when heat is at its most intense, it generates cold in a certain way; likewise, when cold has obtained the highest degree of its efficacy, it generates heat. And so, since the cold is most intense in the North <note>original: *Septentrione*</note>, it happens (they say) that in this very place heat takes its beginning, which

## PREFATORY DECLARATION.

Regarding the eight figures <note>The *Ba Gua* or eight trigrams.</note> already mentioned, and their communication or dissociation with one another, in another place of the same book, the *I Ching* <note>original: "Ye kim"</note>, the same Philosopher <note>Referring to Confucius.</note> describes the production of things through the steady cycle of the whole year in a perennial course and undisturbed order. This occurs through its four seasons and through the eight regions of the world—or cardinal directions—returning upon itself, according to his own opinion as well as those of King Wen <note>original: "Ven vam"</note> and the Duke of Zhou <note>original: "Cheu"</note>, along with the views of the Interpreters.

The Emperor of Heaven <note>A translation of *Shangdi*, the supreme deity or celestial principle.</note> (he says) in the first production of things came forth and manifested himself from the region of the rising sun <note>The East.</note> in full spring. Then, continuing his course and work in a certain way, he arranged all things rightly in that region which lies between the east and the south <note>The Southeast.</note>, toward the end of spring when it joins with summer. He then caused all things to emerge and come into mutual view, standing lively and vigorous in the south itself, in the heat or the middle of summer. After this, he gave growth to all things and sustained them through the earth and the elements; and indeed in that region which is between the west and the south <note>The Southwest.</note>, joining the end of summer with the beginning of autumn. From there, he is said to have gladdened all things, when every thing, having attained what it required, rested in its own end; and this in the west itself during the middle of autumn. But truly, toward the end of autumn, when it begins to mix with the beginnings of winter, he also mixed in struggles and wars, in that region which is equidistant from the west and the north <note>The Northwest</note>. This was surely the struggle of heat with cold, which dominates it; then, with the struggle ceasing and cold predominating, he brought peace again to all things in the north itself, in the season of midwinter. At the last, he wove together and completed all things, connecting the end to the beginning, in that region which divides the north from the east <note>The Northeast</note>, as winter ends and its final parts join with the start of spring.

These are the words of Confucius, according to the explanation of the Interpreter Zhang Juzheng <note>original: "Cham Colai", a phonetic rendering of Zhang Ge-lao, a title for the prominent Ming dynasty Grand Secretary.</note>, who then concludes thus: "All these things are by the dominion and governance of the Supreme Emperor" <note>original: *Kiai xam ti chi chu çai*, likely 皆上帝之主宰 (Jiē Shàngdì zhī zhǔzǎi).</note>. Having explained as best as possible the eight Figures and their mutual conjunction or opposition, it remains that from these eight, when each is doubled, sixteen arise; from sixteen likewise doubled, thirty-two; and finally from thirty-two, sixty-four. Each of these <term>hexagrams</term> <note>The 64 six-lined symbols formed by combining two three-lined trigrams.</note> is composed of two of the aforementioned eight Figures, while these are arranged in various positions and orders and are mixed among one another.

# PREFATORY DECLARATION.

### xlvi

M

These sixty-four Figures <note>The 64 hexagrams of the *I Ching* or *Book of Changes*.</note>, the table of which we have just provided, King Wen <note>original: "Ven vam"; referring to the founder of the Zhou Dynasty (c. 1100 BCE).</note> was the very first to attempt to explain. He interpreted each of them, it is true, but in a very concise—and therefore quite obscure—manner. Since each of the figures consists of exactly six lines, as may be seen here, the entire series of them consists of exactly as many lines as there are days in what the Chinese call an intercalary year: namely, three hundred and eighty-four. Furthermore, the son of the aforementioned King, the Duke of Zhou <note>original: "Cheu cum"; a historical figure credited with writing the "Line Judgments" of the *I Ching*.</note>, attempted to explain the individual lines of the figures. He considered them according to how the highest lines relate to the middle and lowest, and these in turn with the middle, and finally the middle with the lowest and highest—obtaining various connections, orders, and relations. Thus, they communicate more or less with one another and participate in perfection or imperfection. While he studied these things diligently, often using analogies, he was sometimes more successful than his father; yet even so, he interpreted many things enigmatically. Therefore, while he declares each of the figures, or rather each of the lines, he always ascends step by step from the bottom line to the sixth, which is the highest. He likewise assigns his own numbers to each of the lines: to the solid lines, he assigns the number nine (or three times three), while not omitting other numbers that the order of the lines requires.

That all these things are not devoid of mystery can be understood from this: in the opinion of the Chinese, an odd number is perfect, and an even number is imperfect. This even number they refer to *Yin* <note>original: "Yn"</note>, or the imperfect; they ascribe it to cold, night, the moon, water, earth, etc. The odd number, which they teach belongs to *Yang* <note>original: "Yam"</note>, or the perfect, they attribute to heat, day, the sun, fire, and heaven. From this principle, they further teach that from the number of heaven (which is three) and the number of earth (which is two), there exists the number five; if this is doubled, it makes ten. Indeed, they believe all numbers are reduced to ten as if to their root and completion.

And this, finally, is that table of sixty-four Figures—a gloomy, not to say useless, exercise or labyrinth for so many Chinese minds—from which the singular Confucius attempted to extricate himself with the highest praise. Even as an old man, he confessed that he was possessed by a desire to investigate it again more accurately. Therefore, interpreting those "Princes of Interpreters," King Wen and his son the Duke of Zhou, he declares everything quite clearly and abundantly in a moral sense. From the natural connection, order, and vicissitude of things, and their power of producing effects, he derives most beautiful lessons—both for the private conduct of each individual and domestic education, and especially for the public administration of Cities, Provinces, and the entire Empire. Meanwhile, as far as lots and divinations are concerned, he does not deny that the Ancient Chinese believed a certain power and nature was implanted in these things, by which the outcomes of events, whether favorable or unfavorable, could be fore-

# PREFATORY DECLARATION.

### xlvi

...to be able to announce, just as it is generally customary to seek some knowledge of future events from each person's horoscope—and this, in the judgment of the Sages, is not entirely vain or erroneous. Nevertheless, Confucius himself (as the Interpreters testify), having no regard for lots or auguries—just as if they were something vain and entirely useless, or at least certainly of no concern to him—was content with the guidance and light of reason alone. He labored here upon virtue alone; to this alone he gave his effort. Even if this matter were passed over in silence by the Interpreters, it could be sufficiently established for us by the testimony of *Confucius* himself. In the book *Ye kim* <note>The *I Ching* or *Book of Changes*.</note>, page 3, he expressly says that the ancient saints wrote that book and illustrated it with their commentaries with this primary intention: not that it should be used for auguries and divinations, but (as *Cham Colaus* <note>Zhang Juzheng (1525–1582), a prominent Ming dynasty statesman and commentator highly regarded by the Jesuits.</note> explains) so that men might know the nature which they received from heaven, and follow it as their guide and mistress; and further, that they might have a clear perception of the mandate of heaven, or the providence of the supreme Deity <note>original: "Numinis"</note>, from which nature proceeded.

So that this may be clearer to all, it is pleasing to bring forward what those forty-two Interpreters <note>Refers to a standard collection of Confucian commentators used by the Jesuit translators.</note> noted in express words at the very beginning of that table of 64 mutations <note>The 64 hexagrams.</note>, while they fortify the reader and take precautions for all posterity, teaching that there is a certain supreme Lord and Governor whose name is the Emperor <note>original: "Imperator"; here referring to *Shangdi*, the "Supreme Deity" or "Lord on High" in Chinese tradition.</note>. "Who, however, is he," they ask, "who is called Lord and Governor?" And they immediately respond: "He is Lord and Governor of Himself. For heaven is indeed a thing most solid and perfect, which revolves naturally without interruption; but that it always revolves in this way is, without doubt, from some Lord and Governor who effects it. This foundation having been laid, it is necessary that men know Him by themselves: for words are not sufficient with which we might reach the point of explaining Him."

Truly, so that the Reader may see the truth of the matter with his own eyes, and at the same time may form a judgment of the whole work from one small part of it, and finally understand where this Chinese Philosophy <note>original: "Sinarum Philosophia"</note> tends—which has been so very suspect to those who have not examined the matter—it will be worth the effort to bring forward one of the 64 Figures. This is the one which is number 15, and is shorter than the rest; the Chinese praise it above all others and establish it as a prognostic of every kind of happiness. We present it here with the commentaries of the two Princes, King Wen <note>original: "Ven vam"</note> and the Duke of Zhou <note>original: "Cheu cum"</note>, as well as those of Confucius and Zhang Juzheng <note>original: "Cham Colai"</note>, translated from Chinese into Latin.

# PREFATORY DECLARATION.

### xlvij

This figure is called *Kien* <note>The 15th hexagram, *Qian* (谦), representing Modesty. Note that the author uses the same transliteration for this and the first hexagram below.</note>. *Kien* signifies humanity, or modesty and humility of mind. And since the fourteen preceding figures lead to this one like so many steps, it seems necessary for us to touch upon each of the steps here in their own order and number as they are designated in the table, at least with a word, just as *Confucius* runs through them in his appendix called the *Hi çu* <note>The *Xici*, or "Appended Remarks," a traditional commentary on the I Ching.</note>. We do this so that we may be clear and so that the logic of all the remaining figures may be established for the reader by the example of this one. Furthermore, the beginning is taken from the procreation of heaven and earth, while in this very book, the *Ye Kim* <note>The *I Ching* or *Book of Changes*.</note>, *Confucius* speaks thus:

> *After heaven and earth existed, then all things existed; once all things existed, then male and female existed; once male and female existed, then husband and wife existed; once husband and wife existed, then father and son existed; once father and son existed, then Prince and client existed; once Prince and client existed, then superior and inferior existed; once superior and inferior existed, then there was a place and order for one's duties and justice.*

Thus far the Philosopher <note>The Jesuits frequently referred to Confucius simply as "The Philosopher."</note>. Now let us come to the matter proposed.

The first of the figures is called *Kien* <note>The 1st hexagram, *Qian* (乾), representing Heaven.</note>, and in both its upper and lower parts, it designates the material *Heaven*, from which, as if from some emblem, *Confucius* seeks the form of the King and the royal virtues.

The second, *Quen* <note>The 2nd hexagram, *Kun* (坤), representing Earth.</note>, similarly designates the *Earth* in its entirety; it is a kind of emblem or symbol of subjects. Indeed, heaven and earth are both foundations and, as it were, natural principles of all things, to which the names of father and mother are attributed by metaphor. The Philosopher sought the example for the establishment of Kings and subjects first from heaven and earth—that is, from that perennial firmness and equable order and course of all things. This order is expressed by four characters, *Yven, hem, li, chim* <note>The four "virtues" or qualities of the first hexagram: *Yuan* (origin), *Heng* (success), *Li* (benefit), and *Zhen* (persistence).</note>, that is: "ample and perpetual," "clear and manifest," "fitting and decent," and "upright and solid." Moreover, the Philosopher strives to explain these through four "Cardinal Virtues," namely *Gin, li, y, chi* <note>The core Confucian virtues: *Ren* (Benevolence), *Li* (Ritual/Propriety), *Yi* (Righteousness), and *Zhi* (Wisdom).</note>, that is: benevolence <note>original: "pietatem"</note>, propriety <note>original: "convenientiam"</note>, justice, and wisdom.

Therefore, with heaven and earth established and the active mixing with the passive, seeds of all things soon emerge: yet in such a way that they lie hidden, as if received and held back in a womb; this is what the third figure, called *Chun* <note>The 3rd hexagram, *Zhun* (屯), representing "Difficulty at the Beginning" or a sprout.</note>, signifies.

Then, gradually nourished in that embrace of the maternal womb, they are formed into a fetus, and at last emerge into the light in some part of themselves, just as the rising grape tends to show itself from its bud; this is taught by the Fourth Figure, which takes its name from the character *Mum* <note>The 4th hexagram, *Meng* (蒙), representing "Youthful Folly" or childhood.</note>, which sounds like "infancy."

Nevertheless, just as the rising grape requires the juice of the earth and the heat of the Sun to grow, so this common infancy of all things—lest, having barely been born, it should soon perish like a withered thing—first...

<page-num>xlviij</page-num>
-> # PREFATORY DECLARATION. <-

...requires its own milk and juice, so to speak (which the Fifth Figure indicates by the name *Siu* <note>original: "Siu"; refers to the 5th hexagram, *Xu* (需), often interpreted here as "Nourishment" or "Waiting."</note>); thereafter, it indeed requires more solid food and other aids and comforts of life, so that it may grow successfully and reach its maturity and perfection.

At this point, while every thing strives to preserve itself, and because what is gained for the use and benefit of one must generally be taken from another, disputes, lawsuits, and wars cannot help but arise—especially among men, whose greed is as insatiable as their nature is satisfied with little. This is what the Sixth Figure, called *Sum* <note>original: "Sum"; refers to the 6th hexagram, *Song* (讼), meaning "Conflict" or "Litigation."</note>, designates.

There would thus be a need for some law and for judges here to settle these disputes and decide what is fair and just. But since the law is often either unclear, or private interests and advantages are placed before law and equity—especially when there is as yet no city, no Commonwealth <note>original: "Respublica"; referring to a structured political community.</note>, and no common ground—mortals are very easily inclined to disagree, first in their opinions and soon also in their goals and desires. As that early form of society, such as it was, is broken, it is torn into parties and factions; armies are raised on both sides, and finally men of the same nature are separated by camps and weapons. The symbol of this is the word *su* <note>original: "su"; refers to the 7th hexagram, *Shi* (师), meaning "The Army" or "The Multitude."</note>, by which the Seventh Figure is expressed.

In such a crisis and confusion of affairs, unless there are men present whose virtue and wisdom can restrain the disorderly multitude and cause those groups, blindly huddled together, to coalesce into a single body, they would most likely either devour one another like wild beasts or, while each strives only for himself, all would gradually wither and perish. Therefore, there is a need for certain outstanding men who, as the Eighth Figure—called *Pi* <note>original: "Pi"; refers to the 8th hexagram, *Bi* (比), meaning "Union" or "Holding Together."</note>—denotes, know how to win over the hearts of men and then, by their industry, prudence, and authority, calm and govern those in turmoil. To these men the individual groups might then yield, as if to their Masters and Lords, following them as Leaders and Shepherds.

From this there will immediately emerge a closer bonding and society of all people; by the reciprocal giving, receiving, and exchanging of resources and benefits, no one will lack anything. Instead, an abundance will be provided of those things necessary for protecting and sustaining life, and thus the beginning of a City and a Commonwealth will be seen. Its symbol is shown by the Ninth Figure, called *Siao cho* <note>original: "Siao cho"; refers to the 9th hexagram, *Xiao Chu* (小畜), meaning "The Small Taming" or "Lesser Nourishment."</note>, which means *A certain small union and bonding.*

Nor will it be difficult to gradually win over through laws and duties those who are held together by the utility and pleasure of the new society—which they have already begun to experience—as well as by mutual charity and respect, joined and bound to one another and to their leader. It will flourish...

...therefore, every kind of duty will grow, and in their paths, people can steady their footsteps, which until that time may have been wavering (as designated by the Tenth Figure, *Li* <note>original: "Li"; Hexagram 10, often translated as "Treading" or "Conduct," representing how one moves through the world.</note>).

Furthermore, a great eagerness of spirit cannot help but arise, along with a certain breadth (which the Eleventh Figure, *Tai* <note>original: "Tai"; Hexagram 11, meaning "Peace" or "Pervasiveness," symbolizing a time of harmony between heaven and earth.</note>, denotes) of peace and harmony, where each is given his due, where the interests of mind and body are so studiously consulted, and where the preservation of both laws and duties flourishes so strongly.

However, because human happiness is usually very brief and fleeting, it cannot be avoided—as the character *Pi* <note>original: "Pi"; Hexagram 12, "Obstruction" or "Stagnation," the opposite of "Tai."</note> prefixed to the Twelfth Figure teaches us—that some whirlwind of discord and war should follow the serenity of long-lasting peace and harmony. Though it may be brief, as between citizens and brothers, it may be judged not so much as discord, but as a kind of restoration of former love and respect.

Once this relationship has been stirred by some contention like a wind, it usually sinks its roots much deeper and binds subjects more closely to one another and to the Sovereign himself. Hence the name of the Thirteenth Figure, *Tum gin* <note>original: "Tum gin"; refers to *Tongren* (同人), Hexagram 13, "Fellowship with Men," symbolizing universal brotherhood.</note>, which means *unanimity* <note>original: "unanimitate"</note>.

If this unanimity remains constant and is joined with a zeal for the public good and love for the Fatherland, the Commonwealth will flourish and grow remarkably strong. As the Fourteenth Figure, called *Ta yeu* <note>original: "Ta yeu"; refers to *Dayou* (大有), Hexagram 14, "Great Possession" or "Great Abundance."</note>, bids us hope, there will be a vast abundance of *wealth* <note>original: "opum"</note> and riches, a great splendor and breadth of dignity, and moreover, an immense reputation for an excellently constituted Empire. Neighboring nations, and even those in distant regions, moved by this fame, will of their own accord seek our friendship and alliance, submitting themselves to us and preferring the protection of our good faith and equity to their own liberty.

But when everything flows so prosperously according to our will, and when the affairs of the Empire stand at such a lofty peak of happiness and glory, one caution must be applied by all (and especially by him who is the Prince and head of all): let us not, puffed up by pride—as often happens to those placed in high positions—vanish and fall all the more heavily the higher we have been raised. Therefore, all pride, haughtiness, and arrogance must be shunned; instead, one must devote oneself earnestly to moderation, modesty, and lowliness of spirit. The teacher of this virtue and doctrine is Figure 15, taking its name from *Kien* <note>original: "Kien"; refers to *Qian* (谦), Hexagram 15, "Humility."</note>, that is, *humility*. ## SECTION EIGHT.
## THE FIFTEENTH FIGURE

### Explanation.

Having briefly set these things forth, let us come to the explanations of the three Interpreters we mentioned. And since this Figure shall serve as a single example for all the rest, let us bring into the open whatever they have commented upon. Thus King Wen <note>original: "Ven vam"; King Wen of Zhou, the legendary founder of the Zhou dynasty and traditional author of the Hexagram judgments.</note>, who was the very first to attempt to untie the knot, says: *Humility is a virtue that spreads most widely. Even if a perfect man is hidden and lowly at the start, he will eventually obtain success and a prosperous outcome.*

<margin>
<image-desc>A hexagram diagram consisting of six horizontal lines. The top three lines are each interrupted in the center (representing the trigram for Earth). The bottom three lines consist of a single solid continuous line followed by two interrupted lines beneath it (representing the trigram for Mountain).</image-desc>
<unclear>Monastery</unclear>
<unclear>S. M.</unclear>
</margin>

In order to clarify this brief interpretation, Confucius explains the two words *Kien hem* <note>original: "Kien hem"; likely a phonetic rendering of "Qian Heng," the Chinese name of the hexagram meaning "Humility: Success."</note> in this manner: *The substance (or the power and meaning of the two words) says: Humility spreads most widely. This is the way and nature of Heaven: that although it is exalted and stands above all things, yet through its influences it descends, as it were, and lowers itself to join with the humble Earth. Thus its virtue and efficacy shine forth more and more through its effects in creating and preserving things, and it is finally made manifest to all. The nature of the Earth is not unlike this; for even if it stays hidden in the lowest place, gathered within itself, it nonetheless exerts itself and rises high through its effects, which it joins with Heaven. Again, it is the way and nature of Heaven to diminish what is overflowing and to bring down what is swollen; it prunes back what is rank. Yet it fosters and makes fruitful with a kindly influence, and increases with great growth that which is humble, lowly, and like an empty vessel. The Earth acts in the same way, for it restrains and destroys what is redundant and immoderately swollen; on the contrary, it increases and perfects what is moderate and humble.* (Cham Colaus <note>original: "Cham Colaus"; likely referring to a high-ranking Chinese official or "Colao," specifically the neo-Confucian scholar Cheng Yi, whose commentaries were standard for the Jesuits.</note> explains these very things at length using the natural effects of heaven and earth; but since the European reader will easily grasp them on his own, and it is right for us to strive for brevity even in this single example among many, we deliberately pass them by.) *Finally, the Spirits <term>Spiritus</term> <note>Referring here to 'Shen' or spiritual beings/powers in the Chinese worldview that govern the moral order of the cosmos.</note> themselves cast down the proud and bless the humble; and the principle among men is very similar: namely, to hate the proud and to love the humble.*

[...ju]st and humble man established in a position of dignity becomes famous and celebrated for that very reason, even if he does not seek it; the light of his virtues shines forth more happily from such a sublime place. If that same man were placed in a humble and obscure position, since virtue shines by its own light, he could not fail to be illustrious and happy, and nothing could be added to his praise and felicity. And this is the happy and glorious end of the humble and therefore perfect man.

These are the words of Confucius, who, gathering the meaning or doctrine of the entire figure into a summary, says: *this is the significance of the great image which shows us the aforementioned virtue: "Mountains arise from the middle of the earth; they are the symbol of humility—of an exalted humility, I say—as they reach toward the clouds and stars with their sublime peaks from the humble and lowest bosom of the earth."* <note>The "Great Image" (Dazhuang) commentary for Hexagram 15 describes the mountain (Ken) within the earth (Kun).</note>

Wherefore, the **Perfect Man**, <note>Latin: *Vir perfectus*; a translation of the Chinese term *Junzi*, often rendered as "Superior Man" or "Gentleman."</note> being not at all ignorant of the fact that it is a vice of mortals to magnify themselves and their own affairs while despising those of others, achieves a daily victory over himself by depressing the swelling of his own soul. He prunes away whatever is excessive, first in himself and then also in others, and whatever is born of its own abundance or splendor to generate pride and arrogance. On the contrary, by studiously supplying and accumulating what he understands to be lacking in himself or others—just as if he were weighing all things, both his own and those of others, on a water-scale—he thus distributes to each his own with admirable equity. He accommodates and tempers himself to all, both prudently exalting the humble and, through the authority he wields, healthfully depressing the prideful; he levels all things and administers affairs most successfully. Thus far speaks **King Wen**, <note>original: "Ven vam Rex"</note> through his interpreter **Confucius**, and the interpreter of Confucius himself, **Grand Secretary Chang**. <note>original: "Cham Colao"; likely referring to the Ming dynasty Grand Secretary Zhang Juzheng, whose commentaries were frequently used by Jesuit translators.</note>

Let us now hear the King's son, the **Duke of Zhou**; <note>original: "Cheu cum"; Zhou Gong, traditionally credited with the authorship of the line statements (Yao) of the I Ching.</note> he is indeed somewhat more wordy than his father, yet he is not so clear that we will not have need here of the same interpreters we used before. He does not interpret the complex of six lines as his father had done, but rather each of the lines individually, ascending step by step from the lowest. Since Confucius explains each of these interpretations in turn, this explanation is called the **minor image**, <note>original: "minor imago"; referring to the *Xiaoxiang* or "Lesser Symbolism" commentary.</note> so that it may be distinguished from the **major image**, which pertains to the whole complex.

Thus, the **Duke of Zhou** says: *The first line of the sixes* (he calls it the first because it is the lowest; a "six" because it is a broken line) <note>In I Ching numerology, "six" represents a broken Yin line.</note> *designates a man humble and humble again, and thus upright and perfect. While a man of this sort applies himself to virtue, he must indeed swim across and navigate great and wide rivers of struggles and labors; yet let him not lose heart, for he shall at last successfully reach the port of merits.*

Confucius, illustrating this commentary in turn with his own notes, says the meaning of the minor image is that *the man who is thoroughly humble and perfect conducts himself modestly and submissively at any time and place; he attends primarily to himself and dwells within himself, so that he may feed himself upon the happy fodder of virtues and make wonderful progress.* The **Duke of Zhou**, making a step toward the next line from the bottom, says: *the second six designates a man whose...*

Confucius adds: *That that humility should be revealed and celebrated, as the image signifies—because it is pure, genuine, and solid—and that it goes excellently with him who is endowed with it, happens because he possesses it in the center of his heart, and not merely in his mouth or in some empty, external appearance of virtue.*

The **Duke of Zhou** <note>original: "Cheu cum." The Duke of Zhou is the traditional author of the "Line Statements" in the I Ching.</note>, explaining the third line, or the third from the end (which, since it is a solid line, refers to that which is more perfect, and is thus designated by the odd number nine and is called **The Ninth** <note>In the I Ching, a solid "Yang" line is represented by the number 9, while a broken "Yin" line is represented by the number 6.</note>), teaches us that if anyone joins great merits toward the King and the people with humility, as a **perfect man** <note>original: "vir perfectus." A translation of the Chinese term *Junzi*, often rendered as "Superior Man" or "Gentleman."</note> persevering without pride or insolence, he will undoubtedly, sooner or later, have a prosperous outcome for his affairs and a worthy reward for his labors.

The meaning of the Image, says Confucius, is this: *if that perfect man, though so excellently deserving, should never depart from the state of a moderate and modest man, it will result in all people whatsoever obeying and submitting themselves to such great virtue with a tranquil mind.*

The **Fourth Six** <note>original: "Senarium quartum." This refers to the fourth line from the bottom, which is a broken "Yin" line.</note> (says the Duke of Zhou) designates for us a man who indeed surpasses the preceding one in virtue and dignity; nevertheless, he is not yet distinguished by any merits toward the State. Yet, he himself profits from everything; in whatever change of circumstances or times, he gathers the fruit of his virtue: *Truly, because he understands himself to be devoid of merits, he displays and manifests his modesty and lowliness of mind more and more; and thus he is not stirred by any impulse of anger or envy.*

The meaning of the Image (says Confucius) is that *a man who is so great, and who profits from everything, and thus behaves more and more lowly and humbly, does not easily sin; nor does he commit anything that would clash with the laws and reason.*

The Duke of Zhou says regarding the **Fifth Six** (this number is usually assigned to the one who commands the others): A Prince, he says, *endowed with that moderation of soul and modesty, does not expend the wealth and power of the Empire to keep his subjects bound and obedient to him, because such great virtue—more powerful than even the most profuse liberality or any military strength—wins over and subdues the minds, zeal, and wills of everyone to him. But if, however, there should exist those who cast off humanity, throw away all justice, and refuse to obey such great virtue, then it will certainly be right to employ wealth and arms to tame and break the rebels; and then indeed, armed virtue, and virtue so great, shall accomplish everything.*

Confucius, confirming this doctrine, says the meaning of the Image is, *it is right and just for a King, with royal power and through war and arms, to conquer and break the stubborn and rebellious when equity, reason, and virtue...*

Finally, the **Duke of Zhou** <note>original: "Cheu cum."</note> explains the supreme and last line: by the top **Six** <note>original: "Senario." In the I Ching, a broken "Yin" line is represented by the number 6.</note> is designated the great humility of a private Prince—one that indeed shines widely and is celebrated; however, as far as practical use is concerned, it is enclosed within narrower limits. This refers to a private and modest domain (the broken line itself signifies these constraints and the lack of power), since heaven does not destine for him that supreme dignity which is proper to Emperors. He certainly lacks that vastness of both works and lands, as well as the multitude of clients and subjects, all of which usually follow Imperial majesty. Therefore, if he should ever decide it is in his interest to levy a soldier or keep an army in arms, he will do so with no other purpose than to subdue rebels and keep the people of his own domain and Kingdom in their duty.

Subscribing to this opinion and exposition, **Confucius** says thus:
> *The sense of the sixth and supreme image is this: that virtue is indeed great, and fame no less than virtue; however, because supreme dignity is lacking, and other protections are absent, it happens that the greatest and most beautiful things he revolves in his mind, he cannot perfect. Therefore, he does this one thing—and if ever the situation requires, he does it even with an army and arms—to keep the subjects of his private domain and Kingdom in their duty.*

Here is a brief exposition of the **fifteenth Figure** <note>original: "Figura." The author uses this term for the Hexagrams of the I Ching.</note>, a clear specimen of all the rest; for in this way both the fourteen that precede and the forty-nine that follow are explained in almost no other sense than a moral and political one. Thus, absolutely everything that pertains to the morals and duties of Princes, Clients, Parents, Children, and Spouses; what likewise must be observed toward Guests, Foreigners, and Enemies; finally, what kind and how much veneration is owed to the Spirits; and with what great religion and constancy it is right to obey Heaven—all these things, I say, are treated in this place, some more copiously than others, yet none are left untouched.

That Figure, therefore, which follows next, sixteenth in number and called **Yu** <note>Hexagram 16, *Yu*, often translated as Enthusiasm or Excess.</note>, places before our eyes a common and most festive joy, which flows from such great virtue of so moderate and modest a Prince onto his subjects, and is diffused, as if from the head, into the whole body.

The seventeenth, called **Sui** <note>Hexagram 17, *Sui*, translated as Following.</note>, teaches subjects to do the bidding of their Prince in all things, and to follow the nod of their head eagerly and promptly, just like members of a body. And so on.

So it can clearly be said that the whole work of the first founder <note>Likely referring to the legendary Fuxi, credited with creating the hexagrams.</note> was nothing other than an enigmatic emblem, or an emblematic enigma, from which curious posterity has since sought various teachings for itself. If among these anything is found even among the first of the Interpreters, which strong...

# PREFATORY
## DECLARATION.
### PART TWO.

---

#### FIRST PARAGRAPH.

### *EXPLANATION OF THE PRINCIPLE*
### *of things, both material and efficient, established by the Chinese,*
### *both Ancient and Modern.*

After we have explained to some extent the origin and diversity of the Chinese Sects, it remains for us to finally advance higher and explain that very thing for whose sake we brought forward almost all the preceding matters: namely, what <term>material and efficient principle</term> <note>In the philosophy of the time, the "material principle" is the substance things are made of, while the "efficient principle" is the force or agent that creates them.</note>, and what base and foundation for heaven, earth, the elements, and all things, the sages of China established. This is so that we may determine whether they had any knowledge of a supreme <term>Numen</term> <note>A Latin term for a divine power or deity.</note> and the first creator of things, and if so, of what kind. Furthermore, we shall see whether our **Matteo Ricci** <note>The founding figure of the Jesuit mission in China (1552–1610), famous for his "accommodation" strategy of blending Chinese culture with Christian teaching.</note>, the Founder of the Chinese Mission, acted not rashly but prudently and with a just foundation when he tried to oppose and uproot the modern errors of the Chinese using their own testimonies and authorities. In this way, he sought to derive certain principles of Christian truth from the very books and ancient monuments of that ancient nation, while paying little heed to the later Interpreters <note>Refers to the Neo-Confucian scholars of the Song Dynasty (960–1279 AD) whose more materialistic interpretations Ricci rejected in favor of older texts.</note> and the scholars of this current age; he focused instead only on the written characters, especially those which the Chinese themselves admit are their own and which—though they may differ from them in their current customs and way of life—they nonetheless cherish as ancestral and revere as sacrosanct.
