Regarding first the material principle of things, the aforementioned book *The Great Compendium of Nature and Principle* <note>original: *Sim li ta çiven* (Xingli Daquan). A massive 15th-century collection of Neo-Confucian philosophy.</note>, or *On Nature*, takes its starting point from this, and then disputes it most copiously through several chapters. The Neo-Confucians <note>original: *Neoterici*. The author refers to the Song Dynasty (960–1279 AD) scholars who revived and reshaped Confucianism.</note> call this principle of theirs *Taiji* <note>original: *Tai kie*, usually translated as the "Supreme Ultimate."</note>. And since (as *Zhu Xi* <note>original: *Chu çu*. The most influential Neo-Confucian philosopher.</note> says) neither *Fu Xi*, the founder of the Chinese nation, nor *King Wen*, the first interpreter of the Fohian table <note>The "Fohian table" refers to the system of trigrams and hexagrams attributed to Fu Xi.</note>, nor his son *Zhou* mentioned a name of this kind, these innovators rely on no other authority than a single book, or rather an appendix and addition called the *Appended Phrases* <note>original: *Hi çu* (Xici).</note>, which Confucius added to the *Book of Changes* <note>original: *Librum Mutationum* (I Ching).</note> which he interpreted. That appendix is of the same authority as the rest of the interpretation. In that place, these express words are read: *The Change contains the Great Axis or Pivot: This produced the two virtues*—namely, the perfect and the imperfect, like heaven and earth. *The two virtues produced the four images; the four images produced the eight hanging figures* <note>original: "Ye yeu tai kie : Xi sem leam y : leamy sem su siam sem su siam : su siam sem pa qua." This is a Latin transliteration and translation of a famous passage from the *I Ching* describing the evolution of the universe from the Supreme Ultimate to the Eight Trigrams.</note>. Outside of this text, no mention of this *Taiji* is made anywhere in the Five Classics or the Four Books <note>original: *tetrabiblio*. The foundational canon of Confucianism.</note>, and so, whatever they bring forward or however they dispute concerning their principle of things, they have essentially devised it all themselves. For this reason, all praise for such a new Philosophy is attributed to them alone by the Interpreters of the penultimate Imperial Family, the *Ming* <note>original: *Ta mim*.</note>; for they confess and indeed proclaim that those two chief Interpreters, *Cheng* and *Zhu* <note>The Cheng brothers and Zhu Xi.</note> under the *Song* <note>original: *Sum*.</note> Dynasty, discovered what all antiquity was ignorant of, and thus after *Confucius* and *Mencius* <note>original: *Memciumque*.</note> no others existed who brought into the light a doctrine hidden for so many centuries.

Furthermore, although they say that *Taiji* is something inexplicable to human minds, something spiritual, and a power which we cannot investigate, nor is it a name by which it can be expressed, they nevertheless laboriously pile up many similarities with which they try to prove their opinions. Indeed, because the two words *Taiji* from their earliest establishment denote a "Great Terminus" or "Pole," they have borrowed a likeness from the axis of the world, or the pole; likewise from the axis of a house, which is that transverse beam that holds together almost all the connections and members of a Chinese building. Elsewhere they also compare it to the root of a tree or the axle of a chariot; they call the same thing the base, the pivot of things, the column, and the foundation. They plainly deny that it is something merely imaginary, or similar to what the sect of the Bonzes <note>Buddhist monks.</note> calls *the void and the empty*, or what the Sect of *Tao* <note>The Taoists.</note> calls *nothingness*. They assert, therefore, that it is a true and truly existing thing, which ought to be conceived as having been before all things, but in reality is not distinguished from things themselves—such as the perfect and imperfect heaven and earth and the five elements—but is one and the same thing with them. Thus, individual things can be said, in their own way, to be *Taiji*; in much the same way as the delirious Servetus <note>Michael Servetus (1511–1553), a Spanish theologian executed for heresy, who held pantheistic views.</note> asserted in his 6th letter to Calvin that God was truly in a stone and...

This page details the mechanical and cyclical nature of Taiji and compares it to Western concepts of "prime matter" and "divinity."</meta>

...that a stone is properly a stone, a tree trunk is a trunk, and so on; from which they finally conclude that all things are of one single substance. Elsewhere they also say that **Taiji** <note>original: *Tai Kie*. The "Supreme Ultimate" or fundamental ground of existence in Neo-Confucian thought.</note> must be conceived as something immobile and quiet in its first state <note>original: *actu primo*. A Scholastic term referring to a thing's potential or essential existence before it acts.</note>; while it moves, it produces **Yang** <note>original: *Yam*. The active, masculine, or "perfect" principle.</note>, and when it stops or rests from this motion, it produces **Yin** <note>original: *Yn*. The passive, feminine, or "less perfect" principle.</note>. They say this is almost like a man meditating on something within himself and revolving it in his mind, and then shortly thereafter speaking aloud what he has meditated upon. Or, they illustrate it as an emotion of the soul which, before it exerts itself, resides unmoved in the soul like a root. 

Finally, they illustrate all these things by an analogy taken from a mass of **quicksilver** <term>mercury: the author uses the Latin *argentum vivum* (living silver) to describe the fluid, transformative nature of the Supreme Ultimate</term> which lies hidden and immobile, enclosed in a round box; as soon as it is opened, the mercury immediately flows out and disperses itself into a thousand rays, as it were, which are indistinguishable from the matter and form of the mercury itself. 

They teach that the alternation of this kind of motion and rest in this universe is perpetual, like a circle or a wheel, or like a water pump <note>original: *anthleæ aquaticæ*</note> revolving in a perennial motion. Just as they deny that a time can be assigned when this perennial revolution of things did not exist, so too, when they are about to explain the motion and rest of these things (if indeed it is rest or merely an interval), they again seek an analogy from the perpetual alternation of day and night, or from the **contraction and expansion** <note>original: *systoles item diastolesque*. These are Greek medical terms for the beating of the heart, used here to describe the "breath" of the universe.</note> as we breathe; just as night follows day and day follows night, or summer follows winter and winter follows summer. 

And although they attribute **29,600 years** <note>This likely refers to the "Great Cycle" of time. Most Neo-Confucian sources cite 129,600 years (a *yuan*); the "29" here may be a transcription error in the original Latin or OCR for "129".</note> to the entire course and, as it were, the full age of all things, after which they intend for things to begin their course and age anew, they nevertheless indicate by their manner of speaking that they recognize a certain eternity of rising and falling things preceding that aforementioned numerical course of years, repeated infinite times. In this, they certainly clash with the common sense of **Chinese antiquity** <note>original: *antiquitatis Sinicæ*</note>, which held from its traditions that heaven and earth, and the first man and woman, had a definite beginning; so much so that they do not hesitate to assign the very hour in which they began to exist.

Meanwhile, the things which these new Commentators <note>The Song Dynasty Neo-Confucians, particularly Zhu Xi.</note> confidently attribute to their *Taiji* are marvelous and nearly similar to divine attributes: capacity, magnitude, extension, and a power of penetrating and harmonizing with all things. What more can be said? They call it the first and self-caused, the highest, the subtlest, the purest, the most beautiful, the supreme mean, and the most perfect and good; the exemplar and idea of all things, lacking beginning and end. 

Indeed, they even seem to attribute life to it elsewhere when they grant it the name of "mind" or "spirit." In the end, if they were only consistent with themselves, the reader would hardly doubt that they were dealing with the true, first, and supreme **Divinity** <note>original: *Numine*</note>; and indeed there are not a few who think so, and that some have understood it thus may be proven by certain temples consecrated in the name of *Taiji* itself.

But since they consider it to be mere **prime matter** <note>original: *materia prima*. In Aristotelian philosophy, the pure potentiality that lacks all form; the author is accusing the Chinese of being materialists.</note> along with the [Western] Philosophers...

...so that our people may understand, it is confirmed by the fact that they ascribe another name to that **Taiji** <note>original: *Tai Kie*</note> of theirs: they call it **Li**. This word among the Chinese, no differently than the word **Reason** <note>original: *ratio*</note> among the Latins, has a very broad meaning. Here, however, they explain the aforementioned **Taiji** using this word such that they say the essential differences of things emanate from this one **Reason**; they also philosophize about this in such a way that they seem to establish a certain universal "thing-in-itself," which works its way through the species and individuals of things. Thus it is more probable that, just as they correctly understand **Taiji** as **prime matter** <term>prime matter: in Aristotelian philosophy, the pure potentiality or "stuff" that has no form of its own but can become anything</term>, so by **Li** they truly mean a certain "reason" or constitutive form that makes a thing what it is and distinguishes it from others. 

For they reason in this way: that which constitutes a chair, in the "reason" <note>in the sense of the defining logic or essence</note> of a chair, is **Li**; that which constitutes a table in the "reason" of a table, is likewise **Li**; and so on for the rest. Break the chair, take apart the table, and the **Li**—the "reason" of the chair and table—has ceased to be. Nor do they hesitate to philosophize about Morals in the exact same way as Physics. For example, the "reason" of mutual right and duty between King and subject, between father and son, or between husband and wife—and ultimately any "reason" that constitutes virtue—they call **Li**. Indeed, they even call the affections of the mind or body, and even the soul itself insofar as it **informs** <term>informative: a technical term meaning to give shape, life, or essential character to a body</term> the body, by the name **Li**. 

Consequently, this **Li** is destroyed in its own way when it ceases to "inform" the body; they say it is much like water frozen into ice: when it is melted again by heat, it is restored to its original liquid state and status, but it ceases to be "ice." But they do not stop here; from this line of reasoning, they are finally carried away into a far greater and most shameful error. For when they have argued at length concerning their **Li** and **Taiji** (though in a very intricate and confused manner), they seem to slide gradually into **Atheism**, insofar as they exclude every supernatural efficient principle. Although they occasionally seem to speak abstractly of things beyond the senses and matter, in reality they persist in a material view. To spirits and the effects of spirits, whatever they may be, they certainly attribute a more subtle and effective power; yet they do so in such a way that they never seem to exceed that sphere which our own Philosophers attribute to both active and passive principles. Therefore, they labor all the more to twist—by any means necessary—the many famous texts of the ancient books (where the spirits presiding over things and the justice and providence of the **Supreme Mind** are so frequently and eloquently discussed) to fit their own material and coarse opinion.

But then elsewhere they seem to contradict themselves while they expressly teach that every mortal can, from his own **heart** <note>original: *corde*. Likely referring to the Chinese concept of *Xin*, the heart-mind.</note>—insofar as the heart has a certain command over all movements and affections of the mind or body—arrive at the knowledge of that great and **Supreme Heart**; namely, the divine mind and the supreme moderator. They teach again from that admirable connection and propagation of things, by which it happens that so...

...constantly produces its like, it can be clearly proven that there exists a certain **Great Brain** <note>original: *Ta teu nao*, a term likely referring to a governing "Master Principle" or chief organ of the world's order</note>, which preserves and governs all things with such steady cycles and leads each thing to its fitting end. Therefore, they deny—and this indeed logically follows—that such a thing is dead; they deny it is material; rather, they assert elsewhere that it is a spirit, independent, embracing all goodness and all (as they say) the "reasons" or definitions of all things. You might believe you are hearing some followers of **Plato** <note>Plato: an ancient Greek philosopher who taught that the physical world is a reflection of higher, spiritual realities</note>, or other philosophers who hold no bad opinions **concerning God**.

For this reason, I believe I must proceed even more cautiously; these **innovators** <note>referring to the Neo-Confucian scholars of the Song Dynasty (960–1279 AD) who reinterpreted ancient texts</note> should not be immediately condemned for **Atheism**, unless perhaps for a "material and negative" kind (as it is called). Nevertheless, they are certainly suspect of "formal and positive" atheism <note>Scholastic distinction: "material" atheism might be unintentional or poorly defined, whereas "formal" atheism is a conscious rejection of God</note>, as their new and unusual way of speaking has led many of their readers into the abyss of true atheism. For whenever they find anything concerning a supreme mind or providence in the ancient texts, they reduce it all to their own concepts of **Taiji** <note>original: *Tai Kie*, the "Supreme Ultimate"</note> and **Li** <note>Principle</note>. Furthermore, they do not distinguish between **material, formal, efficient, ideal, and instrumental causes** <term>causes: in the Aristotelian tradition used by Jesuits, these are the different factors explaining why a thing exists (e.g., the material it's made of, the design, the creator, and the purpose)</term>; indeed, they teach that all these are distinguished only by name. Thus, they contend that even **Heaven** and **Shangdi** <note>original: *Xam ti*, the "Lord-on-High" or Supreme Emperor</note>, along with all his attributes, are the same as their **Li** and **Taiji**, or the same as the natural influence and power of heaven and earth. Therefore, even if they sometimes speak of this "celestial power" as if it were truly a divine mind, one may rightly suspect they are speaking more in the manner of poets than philosophers, using nothing more than metaphors. 

Consequently, we rightly judge their doctrine to be a poisonous one that leads to explicit atheism, especially for those of a political or worldly mind. Thus, these innovators must be attacked as fiercely as possible by the Gospel preacher with the weapons and arrows of reason, as has always been done. They can be convicted of their errors from their own contradictory commentaries; just as **Lactantius** <note>Lactantius: an early Christian author known for his skill in using pagan philosophy to prove Christian truths</note> used to say that no one could refute **Cicero** more forcefully than Cicero himself, so these innovators can be refuted by no one more certainly than by themselves.

Truly, however, how differently they have felt, how far they have strayed from their ancestors, and how vain a foundation everything the innovators have devised rests upon, can be proven most clearly from the chronological sequence in which their books were written and published. For the older a book is, the more it opposes their novelties. This will be clear from the truly brilliant testimonies that the **Classic of History** <note>original: *Xu kim*, also called *Xam xu*</note>—so called by way of excellence because it is the first and oldest among all authentic books—will provide for us in more than one place. I ask you then? The **I Ching** <note>original: *Ye kim*; the *Book of Changes*, one of the oldest Chinese classic texts</note>, or rather that book inscribed "On Changes"; for its author is the same as the founder of the Chinese nation, **Fu Xi** <note>original: *Fo hi*; a legendary figure in Chinese mythology credited with creating humanity and the writing system</note>. You are quite right: but tell me, I pray, what sort of book was it whose author you proclaim to be **Fu Xi**? It consisted of sixty-four enigmatic figures, or 384 small lines, partly continuous and partly broken—and besides these, nothing else. That is all well and good. But if they are enigmatic, then they are very obscure; and if they are so obscure, then an **Oedipus** <note>In Greek mythology, Oedipus solved the riddle of the Sphinx; the author uses this to mean a person capable of decoding profound mysteries</note> was needed to bring light to them. And who was he? Was it perhaps the same man who was the author?

You will say that nothing remains from the author himself, but the "Oedipuses" were that great Prince and near-founder of the third Imperial Family, the **Zhou** <note>original: *Cheu*</note>, named **King Wen** <note>original: *Ven vam*</note>, as well as his son, the **Duke of Zhou** <note>original: *Cheu cum*</note>. These men solved the enigma and interpreted the figures. But were these men perhaps contemporaries of **Fu Xi** himself? On the contrary, they lived one thousand seven hundred years later. For that long, indeed, did that first creation of the founder lie in darkness, exactly as if it had not existed in the nature of things.

Was **China** then, during all that time, unrefined and devoid of letters? Not at all: rather, how rich and fertile it was then is brilliantly attested by the illustrious monuments of letters in which the deeds of the first Kings and times were commended to posterity, recorded almost at the very time they were performed. Yet in these monuments of letters, the **innovators** <note>Referring to the Song Dynasty Neo-Confucians who reinterpreted ancient texts through a more metaphysical lens</note> will surely find nothing that favors their "novelty"; instead, they will find much that opposes it. Let them search indeed for that term **Taiji** <note>original: *Tai Kie*; the "Great Ultimate" or supreme source in Chinese cosmology</note> from which they extract so many mysteries; they will not find it once. Nor will they find that other word **Li** <note>translated as "Principle" or "Reason"</note> in the sense which they themselves have devised.

And yet, how frequently, how clearly, and how solemnly do these texts treat the wisdom and providence of the one **Supreme Deity**, and the worship and sacrifices to be offered to Him and to the spirits? What of the fact that those very Princes, **King Wen** and the **Duke of Zhou**, the first interpreters of that enigmatic table, do not make mention of this **Taiji** or **Li** even once? Only one man, I say—**Confucius**—mentions them; and even he, living six hundred years after the aforementioned **King Wen** and **Duke of Zhou**, brings those two words **Taiji** into the light only once in his appendix, where he says this one thing: *The Change contains the Taiji, or the Great Pivot. This produced the two virtues, etc.*

Therefore, two thousand three hundred years after **Fu Xi**, the founder of the Chinese nation, the **Taiji** finally came forth like a **god from a machine** <note>original: *Deus è machinâ*; a theatrical term for a sudden, unexpected solution to a plot</note>. Nor was it poorly understood then, according to the interpretation of the most learned men, who assert that the Philosopher understood nothing else here than **prime matter** <note>original: *materia prima*; the formless substance that is the basis of all physical reality in Aristotelian philosophy</note>, as is sufficiently hinted at by the very manner of speaking just cited.

But then, one thousand six hundred years after **Confucius** himself, you "good innovators" finally came forward, and you caused such a **Taiji** to emerge as all of antiquity had never heard of before. And what was much more absurd and intolerable: you wished to adapt all of antiquity to your own infantile understanding, dragging it, as if **by the neck** <note>original: *obtorto collo*; a Latin idiom for forcing someone to do something against their will</note>, into

...to draw your own opinion into line, and to persuade posterity that for three thousand years, your ancestors felt and wrote nothing else about God and the spirits than what you yourselves were asserting: that they were merely some mute power <note>original: *mutâ aliquâ virtute*; the author is arguing that modern scholars reduced a personal God to an impersonal force</note> and the airy, accidental influences of the heavens, which you were calling by the grand names **Taiji** <note>original: *Tai Kie*; the "Supreme Ultimate" in Chinese philosophy</note> and **Li** <note>original: *Li*; often translated as "Principle" or "Reason," central to Neo-Confucian thought</note>.

## SECOND PARAGRAPH.

### HOW PERPLEXED AND anxious the first heralds of the divine Law (especially Ricci) were made by such great variety and confusion of dogmas, sects, books, and interpreters.

This, furthermore, was the deep chaos of the Chinese nation; this was the labyrinth, these were the crags. The first sight of these things certainly struck **Matteo Ricci** <note>The founding figure of the Jesuit China missions (1552–1610)</note> and his companions, who laid the foundations of the Chinese Mission, and forced them to proceed with a very slow and hesitant step. Thus, when they were carried into this new sea of various dogmas—after traversing so many oceans and so successfully breaking through the barriers of so many centuries—they imitated skillful and prudent ship-captains and progressed with the sounding-lead <note>original: *bolide*; a weight used by sailors to determine the depth of water</note> always suspended. They sought to explore everything diligently: what bays and estuaries were in this new region, and where the sandbanks and shallows lay.

They sought, I say, to examine which dogmas were most prevalent, upon what foundations they relied, and how safe or certain they were. First, therefore, not without wonder and lamentation, they caught sight of frequent "monsters of idols" everywhere—namely, those very same ones with which they had seen the regions of India swarming, brought into China by the **Bonzes** <note>original: *Bonziis*; a term used by early Europeans to refer to Buddhist monks</note> in the time and manner we have already mentioned. 

Temples were most frequent everywhere, along with numerous herds of petty sacrificers and the greatest variety of errors. Many other sects had been born from this one, and the authority and favor of the **Bonzes** among the unlearned common people—even though these same monks were almost neglected by most of the literati and the more honored classes—cast sharp anxieties into the missionaries' minds. 

Besides this, another face of a "new" sect, no less foul, offered itself, commonly called **Tao** <note>Daoism</note>. It is older here than the former [Buddhism] and born in the very bowels of the Empire itself. Not a few of the literati followed it. As a superstitious cult, it attributes a certain divinity and immortality on earth not only to spirits but also to men—to say nothing of the sorceries and magical arts to which it is devoted. 

Increasing this filth were the frequent **Muslims** <note>original: *Mahometani*</note> found everywhere. They had entered China in great numbers and with much liberty almost seven hundred years ago, bringing their errors with them. They had taken such deep roots everywhere that it seemed human strength alone could never hope to uproot them.

<meta>This page continues the "Prefatory Declaration," transitioning from a critique of Neo-Confucian philosophy to a broader sociological and historical overview of the "Sect of the Literati" (Confucianism) and its relationship with other faiths in China, setting the stage for Matteo Ricci's missionary strategy.</meta>

<page-num>lxj</page-num>
<header>->PREFATORY DECLARATION.<-</header>

Furthermore, one sect especially, called **Ju Kiao** <gloss>The School of the Learned, or Confucianism</gloss> <note>original: 儒教 *Rujiao*</note>, stood out among all others in wealth, dignity, and authority. This authority was won through its antiquity and a reputation for wisdom; letters brought it riches, honors, and power. It was, in both fact and name, the "sect of the literati." In former times, it looked down upon—and even persecuted—those two sects we mentioned in the first and second place <note>Referring to Buddhism and Taoism</note>, even though various Emperors of the nation, and their flattering ministers following their example, embraced those other sects out of private zeal and goodwill. They even had their own struggles with the **Muslims** (I believe because they were of foreign origin), yet these were neither as frequent nor always as sharp and bitter as their conflicts with the others. This was perhaps because (as those who describe their customs and religion write) the Muslims **Su tien** <gloss>serve Heaven</gloss> <note>original: 事天 *Shitian*</note>, which is the very thing the literati magnificently profess regarding their own sect. From this, one might clearly gather that when the Chinese Literati say that they themselves worship and adore "Heaven," they mean not the physical sky, but the **Lord of Heaven**, whom the Muslims also worship.

However, since the path to honors and magistracies is open only through literature, many of those who rise through their studies are born of humble status, sometimes even from the lowest dregs of the common people. The common people, as I have said, are almost entirely worshippers of idols. Thus it happens that many transition to the Sect of the Literati in such a way that they do not entirely reject those native superstitions. I also believe this was the reason why some among the literati eventually did not hesitate to enter into a "friendly league" (so to speak) and partnership with the two sects of idol-worshippers. Political men were driven toward this by a desire for uniformity and public tranquility. Therefore, they wished to fuse one single doctrine or sect out of the three: their own, that of the Indian **Bonzes** <note>A term used by early missionaries for Buddhist monks</note>, and the native one which is called **Tao** <gloss>The Way</gloss> <note>original: 道 *Dao*</note>. I believe the handle for such an innovation was provided by those dreams and errors which the sect of the literati had produced while the **Song** <note>original: *Sum*; the Song Dynasty (960–1279 AD), during which Neo-Confucianism flourished</note> family was ruling, even though at that time the sect was attacking the sects of the idols in writing, as we noted above. For since they philosophize about their **Tai Kie** <gloss>Supreme Ultimate</gloss> <note>original: 太極 *Taiji*</note> and **Li** <gloss>Principle</gloss> <note>original: 理 *Li*</note> in such a way that at times nothing seems more empty, yet at other times nothing seems so solid and sublime, it is no wonder that it provided fertile material for the aforementioned innovation. This pleased the Bonzes, who preach a certain "emptiness" that is not empty at all <note>A reference to the Buddhist concept of Śūnyatā or Vacuity</note> and their own internal doctrine; nor did it displease the others <note>The Taoists</note> who boast of their own equally chimerical "nothingness." Most of all, this was possible because they allowed all sorts of superstitious rites and the external doctrine to persist—along with the idols themselves and the petty priests of the idols—for the sake of the unlearned multitude. Meanwhile, they themselves slide shamefully into **Atheism**.

What was our **Ricci** to do here, about to announce the law of Christ to the Chinese world? Where was he to turn in such a great variety of dogmas and religions?

<header>->PREFATORY DECLARATION.<-</header>

at once, what perversity! Hard struggles weighed upon his mind, battles he would have to enter—and not only against idolaters <note>Refers to Buddhists and Taoists</note>, **Muslims**, and the common populace, but against the very **Magistrates** and almost the entire class of the **Literati**. Among these, more than a hundred thousand were distinguished by their academic degrees; they were, I say, the very flower, strength, and foundation of the Empire. These were men of a <term>secular-atheistic</term> <note>original: "Atheopoliticis." This refers to the Neo-Confucian elite who prioritized state stability and natural ethics over supernatural or religious belief.</note> mindset, from whom all others sought law and justice. They were men swollen with pride and power, content with a mere appearance of virtue, while in truth, for the most part, they were covered in the filth of their vices. 

He had to do battle with the most famous writers of that time, and with the modern—yet still considered "Classic"—interpreters of the ancient books <note>Ricci distinguished between the original ancient classics and the "modern" Song Dynasty interpretations (Neo-Confucianism), which he found more difficult to reconcile with Christianity.</note>, whose commentaries were worn thin by the hands of everyone who read them. Their authority had to be uprooted, and their deceptions and shadows dispelled. For if it were true (as these **Innovators** <note>The Neo-Confucian scholars</note> so studiously taught) that their own thoughts and opinions were the same as those of all the Ancients, then Ricci would have to struggle bravely against the entire torrent of antiquity—an authority strengthened by more than forty centuries—even at the risk of his own life. 

Consequently, he would have to condemn the authors of these errors: the ancient Kings and Sages, and even the master of the empire himself, **Confucius**. All posterity, even today, venerates these men as the world's oracles and as illustrious prototypes of virtue and wisdom. If he were asked legally and formally what he thought of them, he would have to respond boldly and plainly: that they had all erred and were eternally lost <note>A reference to the theological position that those outside the Church were damned, a point of great friction in Chinese ancestor worship.</note>. How would a nation so proud, so clinging to ancient custom, and so observant of its ancestors, bear such a thing? Surely, detesting such a hated novelty, they would constantly affirm that their people had by no means erred; nor could so many thousands of sages of such great name have possibly erred so consistently through so many centuries. Whatever the case, they would prefer to tread in the footsteps of their ancestors, even with the risk of error, rather than follow the opinions of a few **foreigners** <note>original: "hominum exteriorum"</note>—opinions unheard of until that time.

Ricci also remembered that he was an outsider—that is, in the opinion of the Chinese, a **Barbarian**. He remembered that the Religion he had come to propagate was new here, and brought from a "New World." For if the very name of "foreigner" was an object of contempt; if every novelty was suspected—especially because it was born to disturb public tranquility—it would always be hated by a political nation so tenaciously holding to its ancient laws and customs. Indeed, the Magistrates and the King's Counselors had more than once expressed the opinion that all religions and sects, except for their own "Sect of the Literati," should be utterly abolished. In practice, various Princes had raged with fire and sword against the followers of those sects (even though they were already established residents, and had been greatly increased and strengthened by the private superstition of many Emperors). What, then, could be hoped for a religion that was so new and foreign, and which challenged the pride of such a nation?

### PARAGRAPH THREE.

## RICCI’S DELIBERATION ON THE MANNER
### *of announcing Gospel truth to the Chinese. He reads and examines the Monuments and Annals of the Ancients.*

Anyone relying on human strength alone would undoubtedly lose heart amidst so many worries and fears. But Ricci, relying on God, stood his ground. While he turned over in his mind day and night the institutions and laws of such a great and ancient Monarchy <note>Refers to the Chinese Empire</note>, he reasoned with himself roughly in this manner: 

"If it is true, as everyone constantly assures me, that it has been fifteen hundred years or more since idols and the cult of idols were first brought into China from India by Royal authority <note>Ricci refers to the traditional introduction of Buddhism during the Han Dynasty, which he contrasts with the much older native traditions</note>: It is certain, however, that this Empire has stood for four thousand years and more—if indeed it is right to give credit to the Annals of the Empire, which are certainly worthy of no less trust than those written by the Greeks and Romans about their own affairs. 

What, then, shall we say of all that time which preceded idolatry—namely, those two thousand five hundred years? Could they have been ignorant of every divinity, both true and false? Such a thing has hardly been heard of, even regarding a people however savage and barbaric (as <term>Cicero</term> <note>original: "Tullio." Ricci cites the Roman statesman Marcus Tullius Cicero, who argued that belief in a divinity is innate to all mankind.</note> testifies). Could that voice of the human race—that there is some Divinity—have escaped the ears of the Chinese alone? Could the Chinese alone—otherwise always so sharp-sighted—have been blind to that light, and to the appearance and magnitude of creation, through which (as <term>Paul</term> <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul's argument in Romans 1:20 that God's power is visible through nature.</note> testifies) the Creator of all things can be so clearly seen? 

Or could that insanity, that internal murmur of those saying in their heart: *'There is no God'* <note>original: "Non est Deus." A reference to Psalm 14:1.</note>—which <term>Augustine</term> <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo</note> says belongs only to a few—have always occupied the minds of all the Chinese without exception? Could wise, cultured, and gentle men have always been ignorant of what the illiterate, the rustic, and the wild have always known? These people have always admired the constant and steady movements of the Stars and the rotations of the heavens; since the dawn of their Monarchy, they have always strived to observe that same steadiness, constancy, and inviolate order in the administration of their own Empire. Can it be believed that they never thought of the mover and Lord of the heavens? Did they never think of that supreme Monarch—invisible and incorporeal—whose deputy and almost adopted son they believed their own Monarch <note>The Emperor of China, traditionally titled the "Son of Heaven" (Tianzi).</note> to be, for the purpose of governing this sublunary world? 

But if there was at least some faint knowledge of the true Divinity here, then from where did so much [ensuing darkness] come..."

He seeks to harmonize the Chinese concept of the "Son of Heaven" with Christian monotheism to find a cultural bridge for evangelization.</summary>

The perversity of opinions and morals, the cesspool of so many sects that we see today—whence come so many arts of harming and deceiving? The cause is readily apparent: it stems from the inconstancy of a depraved nature, and specifically from the pestilential servitude of idols. How often do people among us preach about the innocence, faith, and sanctity of ancient times! 

Virtue, it seems, soon grows old, and human weakness falls toward the worse of its own accord, even if there is no one to push it. The first age of the Romans was sufficiently severe, simple, and innocent; yet how great was the corruption of morals later brought into the city along with the <term>Asian triumphs</term>! <note>The author refers to the Roman conquest of the Hellenistic East in the 2nd century BCE, which historians of the time blamed for introducing luxury and decadence to Rome.</note> And what of the Church of Christ itself? How many and how great were the vicissitudes it underwent? How quickly did that fire of the Holy Spirit—by which the Church was inflamed and carried away at its birth—begin to cool? Therefore, one cannot rightly say that what now lies in ruins never stood upright. One might rightly say that it is a human thing, and by its very nature, fragile. The nation is depraved, let it be so. Morals are most corrupt, I do not deny it; but I say that even from this, it is clear that it once possessed something sincere and upright. 

The matter stands entirely thus: China was not in the past what we see it to be now. But just as has happened in our own Europe in these recent times—where after a notable corruption of both opinions and morals, and after so many swarms of heresies sprouting daily like <term>hydras</term> <note>A multi-headed monster from Greek mythology; here used to describe how new heresies seem to multiply as soon as one is suppressed.</note>, atheism has also infected many—this too has happened to China. This execrable plague spreads here all the more cruelly because there is less of a remedy present, and more fuel always available to feed it.

What plan, then, should be taken in such a desperate matter? Should we begin to apply a cure through reason and philosophy? But in this field, they [the Chinese] think we have come from Europe so that we might be cultivated by *them*, as if they were the masters. Shall we fight, then, with the holier weapons that the divine pages supply in abundance? But they will foolishly contend that their own books are similar to the divine ones; and if they should even say theirs are older, it will certainly be very difficult to convict them of error. 

Why not, then, relying on the great God, seize the image of our Savior Christ hanging from the cross and rush forth boldly into public? Why not carry the trophy of our faith through the crossroads and marketplaces? The Lord himself would be present for such pious efforts, and if we could not confirm his doctrine with miracles and signs, we would certainly confirm it with our blood and our lives. 

Would that this were so! However, we have not learned that even the <term>Apostle of the Gentiles</term> <note>St. Paul.</note>—although he burned to die for Christ and preached Christ and him crucified—entered upon this path or method of preaching Christ in the <term>Areopagus of the Wise</term> <note>The high court in Athens where St. Paul delivered a famous sermon (Acts 17). Ricci uses this to justify his intellectual approach.</note>. There, although his spirit was provoked within him seeing the city given over to idolatry, he nevertheless made mention of Christ the Redeemer and man in such a way that he spoke first of the Creator and God. Only then did he return to the Redeemer, but as one miraculously raised from the dead and destined to judge the human race in glory. While this same Apostle performed so many and such wonderful signs among other nations, yet in this theater of intellects and wisdom...

### PROEMIAL DECLARATION.

...on this stage, he judged that they must be moved by the solid weight of reason, with God's inspiration.

   What if, therefore, we imitate the Apostle <note>Saint Paul, referencing his speech to the Athenians in Acts 17.</note> as he debated in the **Areopagus**? Just as he did not hesitate to draw out the faintest ray of the first light from the very mist of the **Poets**, let us likewise seek from the older monuments of **Chinese Philosophy** at least something that might be like the twilight or the dawn, opening a path for the **Sun of Justice** <note>original: *solique justitiæ*; a traditional Christian title for Christ.</note>. It is now clear enough that there is no lack of ancient books: and perhaps, the closer they were to the origin and the fountains of truth, the more purely and clearly they discussed it. But we must fear that while the ancients may favor us, the **Interpreters** of the ancients may oppose us. For I hear that the ancient books are explained no less copiously than ingeniously by certain Interpreters who, although they appeared barely five hundred years ago, nevertheless pass judgment with great confidence on the meaning and doctrine of forty centuries. Add to this that the natives themselves are highly skilled in their national literature, and because these men have deserved so well of it (as is commonly said), and for that reason formerly held the highest offices, their labors are read with singular zeal and applause by the highest and lowest alike. Why, then, would they defer to one man, especially a foreigner, who—I suspect—they consider worth nothing compared to even one of their own masters and Interpreters? And yet, one might rightly doubt whether those who wrote in these recent, most corrupt times have truly grasped the mind and genuine doctrine of the **Ancients**, especially in those matters which pertain to the Religion of the Ancients, or which are further removed from our own senses and common opinion. Indeed, a constant agreement among Interpreters—especially if they are many and not from a single age—is quite rare and nearly a miracle. A later age almost always delights in either adding something to or taking something away from the previous one. Thus, the **Chinese Literati** <note>The scholar-official class of China.</note> of our age have devised that new religion forged from three, two of which those who flourished under the **Song** family <note>original: *Sum*; the Song Dynasty (960–1279), during which Neo-Confucianism rose to prominence.</note> attacked most fiercely as false and depraved. Why then should these men not have been equally deluded, and have departed even further from those first times and the dogmas of their ancestors? Especially when they themselves freely admit that a thick night of a thousand years or more intervened, during which the ancient **Philosophy of the Chinese** lay as if asleep and extinguished?

   Pondering these and similar thoughts day and night, **Matteo Ricci**, though he vehemently desired to establish a base as soon as possible in the very citadel of the Empire—the Royal city of **Beijing**, I say, which is the head of the whole Monarchy (as the great **Xavier** <note>St. Francis Xavier, the Jesuit pioneer who died before he could enter mainland China.</note> had so greatly desired)—nevertheless, because he did not yet think himself sufficiently ready for that expedition, and because he feared that unless a way were paved there little by little, such a headlong acceleration might bring much more harm than benefit...

...he judged it better to make haste slowly <note>original: *festinare lentius*; a classical adage suggesting that a cautious, systematic approach is more effective than rushing.</note>, and to seek whatever fruit he could from the nearest places and provinces. He intended to practice, in a sense, outside the Royal Court for those contests which he would eventually enter within the Palace itself. Thus, having spent a total of sixteen years in the provinces of **Southern China**, he laid successful foundations for the Christian cause in more than one place, both by himself and through his companions. Although he was tested by various and heavy labors and dangers throughout all that time, his spirit was never broken; instead, relying on God, he drew courage and resources even from adversity. Meanwhile, he acted continually with a singular zeal and skill toward one goal: to investigate everything and weigh it silently within himself. With that purpose, he repeatedly consulted the books of the nation and as many men outstanding in literature as he could find among his friends. Finally, in the year 1598, judging the expedition to **Beijing** <note>original: *Pekinensem*</note> to be ripe, he undertook it eagerly. But behold, having been brought to Beijing, he saw everything boiling with the terror and preparations for a recent war <note>This likely refers to the Imjin War, the Japanese invasions of Korea, which involved Chinese forces and created a climate of suspicion toward foreigners.</note>. Therefore, prudently yielding to the difficulty and the time, he returned to **Nanjing** <note>original: *Nankinum*</note>, the **Southern Capital**. There, however, after gathering many to Christ, he founded a Church and a residence for the **Society of Jesus**. After about two years, when the affairs of the Beijing Court were calmer, and after many prayers and tears poured out before God—for whose cause alone this was undertaken—he was filled with great hope and heavenly confidence. Indeed, he had been divinely assured that Christ would be favorable to him in Beijing, just as He had once been to **Ignatius** <note>Saint Ignatius of Loyola, the founder of the Jesuits, who experienced a famous vision at the chapel of La Storta where God the Father promised to be favorable to him in Rome.</note> when he was seeking Rome. At last, in the year of Christ 1600, he set out again to raise the trophy of the Cross of Christ in that citadel of such a flourishing Empire. Under these auspices, he was to fight against idolaters, atheists, and Muslims <note>original: *Mahometanis*</note>, and, if it were pleasing to God, to triumph over them and the whole of Hell. Furthermore, he intended to establish a monument of eternal truth, even by trampling upon the authority of forty-four centuries <note>A reference to the long recorded history of China, which the Jesuits estimated at 4,400 years.</note> if necessary, and to seal it with his own blood if the truth required it.

Thus, in the year of human salvation 1601, in the month of January (which was the last month of the 28th year of the reign of **Wanli** <note>original: *Van lie*; the Wanli Emperor, who reigned 1572–1620.</note> of the **Ming** <note>original: *Tai-mim*; the "Great Ming" dynasty.</note> family, the thirteenth in order), **Matteo Ricci** entered the Royal Court of Beijing and offered gifts to the Prince. These were precious and welcomed for no other reason more than their novelty: and first, in the place of honor, an image of **Christ the Savior** and of the **Virgin Mother of God** elegantly expressed in colors, as well as the trophy of the Cross itself. The Emperor accepted everything (a rare sign of favor and benevolence), and he received the sacred images with a particular sign of a venerating mind. When such an unusual favor became common knowledge, everyone's interest was kindled to greet the new guest. People of almost every rank and dignity rushed to Matteo’s lodging, most eager to learn what this new guest and stranger brought from those lands which they, up to that time, [believed were] under the sky...

they had never imagined that such things existed. Many people began to ask many questions; Matthew [Ricci] himself, being wise, would voluntarily offer much information. They heard him discussing the elements, the position or motion of the heavens and the earth, and in these matters, many things were entirely new and unheard of. He spoke in their own native language, explaining these topics no less ingeniously than clearly. They also loved and deeply respected the gravity of his character, which was tempered by such singular courtesy and modesty. Amidst these interactions, this most prudent man repeatedly took steps toward more sublime matters—moving from the earth and the sky, naturally, to the Creator and Lord of both. Soon, he also began to demonstrate His nature and divine perfections—His unity, providence, wisdom, omnipotence, and goodness—using solid reasoning. Furthermore, when he discussed the first principle or Creator of all things, everyone easily agreed; not a few even confidently asserted that this was the very same being whom the ancient kings and sages of their nation had called by the most appropriate name *Shangdi* <note>original: *Xam ti*</note>, that is, the **Supreme Emperor**, and whom they had truly worshipped. Yet, others were not lacking who suggested a far different and chimerical principle belonging to the "innovators" <note>The "innovators" refers to the Neo-Confucian philosophers of the Song Dynasty (960–1279 AD), whose metaphysical interpretations Ricci often opposed.</note> mentioned above: the *Taiji*, *Li*, and *Kong* <note>original: *Tai kie, li, cum*</note>, that is, the **Great Ultimate, universal reason, and the empty void**. Meanwhile, he listened to them, just as he had to others with whom he had dealt more familiarly in **Southern China**, as they extolled with wonderful praise the innocence and simplicity of their own ancient times. He heard them cite ancient authorities and old literary monuments in which mention was made—quite clearly—of both the natural law and other matters that Ricci was preaching. At the same time, they admitted that the integrity and brilliance of that golden age had long since ceased. Indeed, they confessed that most of the "sages" of their own age were followers of **Confucius** in name only; they had almost nothing at heart except the wealth, dignities, and pleasures of this world, and the glory of a false eloquence. They were little concerned about what might happen in the future because they believed in almost nothing except what could be perceived by the senses. Such were the conversations and complaints of those whose native light of truth was less obscured by vices and errors. Among them were even certain literati of the highest reputation who—by an instinct, I believe, that was more than human—were so captured and convinced by the singular learning of our Matthew and the great firmness of his doctrine that they began to attach themselves to him quite studiously. They even voluntarily invited him to at least sample the books of their nation, especially the older ones; for they said that after talking with him two or three times, they themselves perceived many things contained in the ancient monuments much more clearly than ever before, and they urged him not to find it burdensome to sample them himself. ...to exist, they had never imagined. Many people began to inquire about many things; Matteo himself, being wise, proactively introduced many topics. They heard him speaking—no less ingeniously than clearly, and in their own native language—about the elements, the position and motion of the heavens and the earth, and many other things among these that were entirely new and unheard of. They also loved and greatly admired his dignity of character, which was tempered with such singular courtesy and modesty. 

Amidst these interactions, that most prudent man repeatedly made the step toward more sublime matters: moving from the earth and sky to the Creator and Lord of both. Soon, he also demonstrated with solid reasoning His nature and divine perfections—His unity, providence, wisdom, omnipotence, and goodness. 

Furthermore, as he spoke of the first principle or maker of all things, everyone easily agreed, and not a few even confidently asserted that He was the very one whom the ancient Kings and sages of their nation had called by the most fitting name *Xam ti* <note>original: *Xam ti*; a transcription of *Shangdi*, the "Supreme Emperor" or "Lord-on-High"</note>, and indeed had worshiped. 

Yet others were not lacking who, in turn, thrust forward a far different principle—that chimeric one of the "innovators" <note>This refers to the Neo-Confucian scholars of the Song Dynasty, whom Ricci viewed as having corrupted ancient traditions.</note> mentioned above: *Tai kie*, *li*, and *cum* <note>original: *Tai kie, li, cum*; referring to *Taiji* (the Great Ultimate), *Li* (Principle/Reason), and *Kong* (the Void/Emptiness)</note>, that is, the **Great Ultimate**, the **universal reason of being**, and likewise the **vacuum** and **void**. Still others pushed the idol *Fo* <note>original: *Fœ*; the Buddha</note> brought from India, while others finally obtruded the native sect called *Tao* <note>Taoism</note>. 

Matteo attacked and conquered the errors and empty dogmas of all these groups with arguments drawn from both natural and supernatural truth, doing so no less firmly than gently. Meanwhile, he listened to these men (just as he had to others with whom he had dealt more familiarly in **Southern China**) as they extolled with wonderful praise the innocence and simplicity of their ancient times. He heard them cite ancient authorities and old literary monuments in which there was a clear mention of both the natural law and other matters which **Ricci** was preaching. 

At the same time, they themselves confessed that it had been a long time since the integrity and sincerity of that golden age had ceased. They claimed that most of the sages of their own age were disciples of **Confucius** in name only, as they had hardly anything at heart except the wealth, honors, and delights of this world and the glory of a deceptive eloquence. They were little concerned about what might happen in the future, because they believed almost nothing except what could be perceived by the senses. 

Such were the conversations and complaints of those whose native light of truth was less clouded by vices and errors. Among these were even some scholars of the highest reputation who—by an inspiration, I believe, that was more than human—were so captured and convinced by the singular teaching of our Matteo and the great stability of his doctrine that they began to attach themselves to him more studiously. They voluntarily invited him to at least sample the books of their nation, especially the older ones; for they said that after having held a conversation with him two or three times, they themselves now understood some things contained in the ancient records much more clearly than ever before, and they hoped he himself would not find it a burden to examine them. Thus...

...for he would clearly learn what all antiquity once thought under the guidance and mastery of nature itself; what those leading men—who were also the sages of that ancient age: *Yao*, *Shun*, *Yu*, *Tang*, *Wen-wang*, *Wu-wang*, *Zhou-gong*, and *Kong-zi* <note>original: *Yao, Xun, Yu, Tam, Ven-vam, Vu-vam: Cheu-cum, Cum-çu*; these are the legendary sage-kings and founders of Chinese civilization, ending with Confucius.</note>, or *Confucius*—judged concerning the supreme Emperor and Lord of the heavens, and what they thought of spirits and Religion. All of posterity has at least consistently venerated these men, even if they have perhaps followed them with less success. Surely, if these sages were alive today, they would approve of these new truths—as if announced from heaven—and why should they not even embrace them? If Matteo himself should find certain seeds and sparks of that same light and Religion in the records of their ancients, then they asked him to kindly awaken what has lain dormant for so long (seeming almost extinguished), and to kindle and perfect that ancient light of native truth with the new radiance of celestial doctrine.

Very similar had been the encouragements and wishes of other most serious men with whom he had dealt through previous years. Even then, complying with their wishes, he had worked significantly in this area. Nevertheless, prudently concealing his progress at this moment, he most kindly replied that since they so ordered it, he would certainly obey. He spoke of his great hope of learning and progressing from the books written by such a highly literate nation, especially from that age whose wisdom and holiness they themselves so highly praised. Meanwhile, he exulted entirely with secret joy and gave immortal thanks to Christ, his leader and protector, because he saw a huge door opening for the dissemination of the Gospel. Yet he also understood that this door would be shut tight if, by chance, he were to condemn the entire antiquity of this scholarly nation. Such a move would have incited the hostile minds and "weapons" of all the literati <note>The *literati* were the scholar-official class who governed China through their knowledge of the Confucian classics.</note> and even the Magistrates against him. It was surely better to win them over through a shared interest in studies and opinions than to alienate them with excessive novelty and difference. In this way, the foundations of the Christian Religion in this Empire might rely not only on divine firmness (which must always be the primary concern) but also on human support, so far as law and reason would allow.

Therefore, with these teachers of the highest rank acting as his encouragers and guides, he resolved to explore everything more deeply with new fervor and zeal. He went, I say, to the very sources of Chinese doctrine, turning over the records of ancient dogmas and the oldest annals again and again. In addition to this, he diligently examined obscure and doubtful passages, partly by consulting the commentaries of both ancient and modern interpreters, and partly by consulting the living masters of letters and philosophers. (During the twenty-seven years that Ricci stayed in China, more than five thousand such scholars were recorded). He was visited by them, and he in turn visited them, consulting them on all matters. In short? He saw, he heard, he read, and with the greatest...

### SECTION FOUR.

->*FROM THE AUTHENTIC BOOKS OF THE CHINESE*<-
->*it is concluded that they had no commerce with other nations.*<-

It is therefore worthwhile to declare here how solid a foundation our Ricci rested upon, and with what authority, fruit, and applause he performed this work. This man, as perceptive as he was prudent, understood first of all that there is great reliability in the Chinese annals <note>original: *annalium Sinicorum*; the official historical records of China.</note>, as well as a truly rare authority and antiquity. He understood that those who write the annals are chosen by the Emperor of the nation himself, and that almost at the same time, all events are both carried out among the Chinese and recorded; although these records are usually not printed until much later—specifically, after the fall of a ruling family and the arrival of a new one. Therefore, he determined that the opinion with which almost all of us from our Europe have been imbued and preoccupied must be entirely corrected: namely, the idea that every single nation without exception (always excepting the Hebrew nation) lost the knowledge of the true Deity within a few centuries after the Great Flood and during the very beginnings of each nation. For the matter is not so, and whatever may be said of others...

judgment is made concerning nations, but such a judgment can by no means be applied to the Chinese <note>original: *Sinica*</note>, as they have always been, and remain today, very different from other peoples—not only in the distance of their lands, but in their customs, dress, and literature. Indeed, they have reached such a point that they believed no other nation existed under the sun and sky besides their own, except for a few neighboring barbarian tribes and islands. Thus, both in speech and in writing, they are accustomed to call their Empire *Tien hia* <note>literally "Under Heaven"</note> or *Sui hai chi nuy* <note>literally "Within the Four Seas"</note>, which means "that which is under heaven," or "whatever is contained within the four seas."

Indeed, if this Empire had possessed trade with more remote lands and nations during its first two thousand years, could so many ancient monuments of other nations—Egyptians, Hebrews, Greeks, or Romans—have ignored or failed to mention it? Again, around ninety years after Christ, the seventeenth Emperor of the same family, *Ho ti* <note>Emperor He of Han</note>, under the leadership of General *Pan chao* <note>Ban Chao</note>, advanced into India and beyond; in a journey of 200 days, he subjected forty kingdoms to the Chinese Empire.

However, so that this may be clearer: if we consider the ancient Empire of the Assyrians, which took its beginning from Nimrod, the grandson of Ham <note>original: *Nemrodo Chami nepote*; referring to the biblical lineage in Genesis</note>, it is well established that almost from its very start, it revolted from true worship to idolatry. It was so contaminated and obscured by cruelty, lust, and other crimes that almost nothing has reached the knowledge of posterity except the empty names of its Princes. When that Empire was subsequently devolved to the Medes, and from them to the Persians, from the Persians to the Greeks (or Macedonians), and finally from the Greeks to the Romans, who does not understand that their vices—and idolatry, the parent and nurse of all vices—passed along together with the spoils and triumphs? The Roman Empire then infected the rest of the world with this idolatry, adding to itself even those monstrous idols which the particular superstition of individual nations had manufactured.

Therefore, although the Empire of the Assyrian nation was very ancient and, founded in the heart of Asia, extended itself to Arabia, Egypt, and India, no one will suspect that the Empire of the Far East <note>literally "Extreme Asia"</note> or of the Chinese was derived from it. This is clear to anyone who considers that China persisted for 4,222 years under its native Princes before it underwent the yoke of the Western Tartars <note>The Mongols</note>. Anyone who carefully observes the customs, language, rituals, letters, and all other things of these two nations will see how different they are from one another. And yet, could it have been possible for so great a river to have nothing in common with its source? Especially that "poison" of vice which flows so quickly, and from those vices, the poison of idolatry? And yet...

<meta>This page continues the argument regarding the antiquity and independence of the Chinese Empire. # PREFATORY DECLARATION. lxxi

If someone only briefly consults the annals of the Chinese people <note>original: *Sinicæ gentis*</note>, it will immediately become clear to them that the plague of idolatry was not introduced here by Royal authority until nearly three thousand years after the founding of the Chinese Monarchy, and indeed more than nine hundred years after the end of the Assyrian Empire.

But if we distance China from commerce with the Assyrians, Egypt must be distanced even further. Although some assert that certain Chinese hieroglyphic <term>hieroglyphic: script using symbols or pictures rather than an alphabet</term> characters bear a resemblance to those of the Egyptians, why is it not argued instead that the Egyptians took their origin from the Chinese—who preceded them by several centuries—rather than the Chinese from the Egyptians? Furthermore, what prevents different nations from inventing certain things that are entirely the same and common to other very distant peoples? After all, what is easier or more obvious than to draw characters that reflect the likeness of a thing, such as the Sun, the Moon, birds, trees, and so on, so that they may teach what each signifies? Must a passage and migration from the Egyptian nation into China have occurred across the whole of Asia for that reason?

Nor can it be said that any vice or error was propagated in China by the Indian <term>Gymnosophists: literally "naked philosophers," a term used by Greeks and later Europeans for Indian yogis or ascetics</term> before Idolatry itself was spread here. For the chief propagator of this sect, called **Foe** <note>original: *Foe*; the Chinese name for Buddha, *Fó*</note>, is said to have been born in India in the 16th year of the reign of **Chao vam** <note>King Zhao of the Zhou Dynasty</note> (who was the fourth from the **Cheu** <note>Zhou</note> family) in the year 1308 before Christ—about 400 years before the birth of **Pythagoras** and **Confucius**. At that time, this Monarchy had already stood for 1600 years or more, consistently governed by its own laws and rituals, not foreign ones. Indeed, the dogmas of that pestilential man were not introduced into China by Royal authority until about nine hundred years after his death, along with the formal worship of idols.

It is even less believable that the origin of the Chinese people can be sought from the Japanese (whom the proud Chinese used to call **Vo nu** <note>original: *Vo nu*; likely *Wōnú*, a derogatory term meaning "dwarf slaves"</note>), even though they share written characters and many other things with the Chinese. For the Empire of the Chinese had stood for two thousand five hundred years when (as their own annals record) several thousand families migrated from China to the Eastern Islands—specifically, in the year 200 before Christ. From this, however, I would not wish to conclude that Japan is a colony of the Chinese, especially since it is clear that the Japanese began to number their Kings from the year 660 before Christ; until the year 1608 of this century, one hundred and eight are counted. This is evident from a Chinese book printed in Japan, which is kept in the Royal Library. Because of this, another opinion seems more probable to me: that the Japanese drew their origin instead from the **Tartars** <note>A general European term for the nomadic peoples of North and Central Asia, including Mongols and Manchus</note> (who dwell near their Northern sea), and that this origin is very ancient. Indeed, around the year 1196 before Christ, when (as the annals testify) the Northern Barbarians (namely, the Tartars) [sent] many...

...the multitude of their race demanding it, they betook themselves to the islands of the Eastern Sea. To believe this more readily, we are also persuaded by the very warlike character of the Japanese people, who far surpass the Chinese in strength of spirit and constancy, and by the fact that they use a language very different from Chinese.

These facts are confirmed by many embassies, both of other barbarians and of the Japanese. The first embassy from Japan to China is recorded as having occurred in the second year of the fourteenth Emperor, **Guangwu** <note>original: *Quam vu ti*</note> of the fifth **Han** family (which was the year 28 after the birth of Christ). In the thirty-third year of the same Emperor, there was a second embassy, by which they were first presented with a Royal seal. The third embassy, in the first year of **An** <note>original: *Ngan ti*</note>, the nineteenth Emperor, consisted of 160 persons. Thereafter, the embassies were interrupted for many years due to civil wars in that region, until they were resumed and continued under seven imperial families. One occurred under the second Emperor, **Taizong** <note>original: *Tai çum*</note> of the thirteenth family, the **Tang** <note>original: *Tam*</note>, in the fifth year of his reign (specifically three years before the arrival of the preachers of the Gospel from Syria). Under the subsequent Emperor, **Gaozong** <note>original: *Cao çum*</note>, the name of their kingdom was first changed: for thereafter it was called ***Riben*** <note>original: *Ge puen que*</note>, that is, the *Kingdom of the Sun's Rising* (which to us is Japan). In the ninth year of the second Emperor, **Taizong**, of the nineteenth family, the **Song** <note>original: *Sum*</note>, Buddhist monks <term>Bonzes: a term used by early European travelers to describe Buddhist monks in East Asia</term> first performed the duties of the embassy, and they continued to do so thereafter. Under **Yongle** <note>original: *Yum lo*</note>, the third Emperor of the family of the **Great Ming** <note>original: *Tai mim*</note>, they were ordered to come to the court only once every ten years. From these records, the reader may recognize from where, chiefly through mutual commerce, their ancestral customs and letters, along with printing <note>original: *Typographia*</note>, and even the contagion of vices and superstitions, were transmitted. Likewise, it is well established that amidst so many vicissitudes of empire, public tumults, and calamities at various times, the Chinese fled to neighboring lands and islands such as Tibet, Cambodia, Siam, Tonkin, Malacca, the island of Formosa <note>modern-day Taiwan</note>, the Moluccas, Java, and especially, as we have already said, Japan. Nevertheless, our Europeans have by no means reasoned correctly from the aforementioned facts; for beyond what they had observed and learned among the Japanese, they wished to be the interpreters and judges of Chinese affairs and—what you might wonder at more—of Chinese origins and books at the beginning of this century, passing judgment on the entire antiquity and learning of the Chinese based on the present age of the Japanese.

But perhaps there will be someone who thinks that the people of this furthest part of Asia were propagated from the Hebrew people, insofar as they trace their lineage from one and the same Patriarch **Shem** <note>original: *Sem*</note>, the founder of Asia. Those who first arrived here from Europe testify that some Hebrews, and those well-versed in the sacred volumes, were found in China. And indeed, to say nothing of the character and temperament of the Chinese, who almost entirely gape at earthly happiness, riches, comforts, and honors—just as if they expect no other blessing than that which comes from the **dew of heaven and the fatness of the earth** <note>A biblical allusion to the blessing of Isaac in Genesis 27:28</note>—the practice of polygamy...

The probability of this opinion <note>the theory of Hebrew origin</note> could also be increased by that singular piety of the **Chinese race** <note>original: *Sinicæ gentis*</note> toward their deceased ancestors, which they are accustomed to testify through the splendor and care of their tombs, various rites and funeral lamentations, as well as the offerings they perform at appointed times.

In truth, so many rites and ceremonies, so many observations and minute details in the proper preparation of victims, and furthermore these sacrifices—so many and so varied, consisting of bulls, rams, bread, and wine; indeed, even the **burnt offerings** <note>original: *holocausta*</note> with which they made atonement to the Supreme Emperor of the heavens by consuming victims and precious items; likewise, there was one supreme Priest (who was also the Emperor), for whom alone it was lawful to sacrifice to the Supreme Emperor of the heavens whenever the necessity of the state required it; which he usually did while surveying the empire, upon the mountains and hills themselves; and finally, the fact that the Chinese, above all other nations, seem to have preserved the knowledge of the true Deity for much longer: all these things could certainly offer a European man reason to doubt whether many rites and customs might not have passed from **Judea** <note>original: *Judæa*</note> into **China** <note>original: *Chinam*</note>, and whether the race itself might have been propagated from the Hebrew people.

But the monuments of the Chinese annals <note>ancient historical records</note> stand against this opinion (to which I solely appeal the Reader throughout this entire work). For besides the fact that China was highly civilized and most thoroughly instructed in laws and rites, both sacred and profane, long before the dispersion of the Israelite Tribes, this one fact should suffice: fully one hundred years and more before **Moses** <note>original: *Moyses*</note> received the law from God, that pious Emperor and founder of the second family, the **Shang** <note>original: *Xam*</note>, named **Cheng Tang** <note>original: *Chim*</note>, being then already over eighty years old, in the seventh year of a famine <note>original: *sterilitatis*, literally "sterility" of the land</note>—which the **Sacred Pages** <note>the Bible, specifically the story of Joseph in Egypt</note> testify prevailed throughout the entire world—devoted himself as a victim for the salvation of the people with a solemn rite and specific words addressed to heaven. What of the fact that even more than two hundred years before Abraham, the Emperor **Shun** <note>original: *Xun*</note> is mentioned more than once to have made atonement with burnt offerings and other sacrifices to the Supreme Emperor, and then to have worshipped the spirits presiding over mountains and rivers with other sacrifices of a lower name and order? As is reported in the book ***Classic of History*** <note>original: *Xu kim*</note> by the Royal historian of that time, near the first imperial family, the **Xia** <note>original: *Hia*</note>, around the year 2200 before Christ.

## PARAGRAPH FIVE.

## EVIDENCE THAT THE CHINESE WERE VERY NEAR TO THE FLOOD,
### *and thus imbued with the knowledge and worship of the true Deity at their very origin.*

Therefore, we must either completely discard our trust in their annals—which are so accurately organized by their "Olympiads" <note>A reference to the Chinese sexagenary cycle, a 60-year calendar system used to track time, which the author compares to the four-year Greek Olympiads.</note> or 60-year periods—or we must certainly ascend higher and trace the beginnings of the **Chinese** <note>original: *Sinarum*</note> back to the times immediately following the Flood. If we do this, it will finally become clear that the laws, sciences, and most institutions of the **Chinese** could have originated from no other nation on earth except from the Patriarch **Noah** <note>original: *Noëmo*</note> himself, or from his sons or grandsons. 

To make this clearly evident, let us consider the founder of the Chinese race himself, named **Fuxi** <note>original: *Fo hi*; Fuxi is the legendary first emperor of China, credited with creating the I Ching and teaching hunting and fishing.</note>. His lineage and homeland are not explicitly stated in the Chinese Chronicles, except for the report that he lived in the westernmost and northernmost province, namely **Shaanxi** <note>original: *Xen si*</note>. Indeed, it was necessary to arrive first at this very province if one were migrating from **Mesopotamia**, or the land of **Shinar** <note>original: *Sennaar*; the biblical location of the Tower of Babel.</note>, during the dispersion of languages and nations, to reach the heart of China, the province of **Henan** <note>original: *Ho nan*</note>. It is written that he first established his court in that region, where the town of **Chenzhou** <note>original: *Chin cheu*</note> is now located, which is subject to **Kaifeng** <note>original: *çai fum fu*; historically the capital of many dynasties</note>, the metropolis of that same province, also known by the name **Bianliang** <note>original: *Pien leam*</note>.

Indeed, consider that modesty and humility of heart shown by those princes in their prayers to Heaven, by which they called themselves "little ones" and "infants" in the presence of the Supreme Majesty. Consider the charity with which they held themselves guilty of all the sins their subjects might have committed, and how they voluntarily took upon themselves those punishments which everyone feared from an angry Heaven. Consider that care, that anguish, that fear and trembling they showed in the worship and veneration of the Supreme Emperor, even in private—matters often mentioned in their books. Does all this not declare that true Religion was seated in their souls?

Now, if these things we have just touched upon were so observed by Emperors and Princes, what do we think was done by the people who were subject to them? This is especially true since the royal edicts commanded that the highest and lowest alike should worship the Supreme Emperor as well as the other spirits who preside over particular places.

I ask you now: if someone had seen **Aristotle**, or any other Philosopher, daily bowing his knees in veneration at appointed times, burning incense, prostrating his whole body on the ground, and pouring out prayers with his eyes and hands repeatedly raised to heaven, could any doubt arise in that observer’s mind as to whether that Philosopher recognized a Divine Power <note>original: *Numen*</note>? This would be true even if, by chance, he made no mention of a Divine Power in any of the books he wrote. What if the same observer had noticed these very similar signs of Religion in a whole nation or sect, and simultaneously in the Prince of that entire nation? How then could anyone dare to accuse ancient China of such wicked ignorance and impiety? For one does not merely hear of these examples of rare piety and the many rites and sacrifices usually performed by their kings, but one reads of them described in monuments and books of the highest authority—written, in fact, at the very time when these practices were most flourishing. 

If you had found these things, or things very similar to them, recorded by authentic writers in any other nation of the world—among the Assyrians or Egyptians, in Gaul among the **Druids**, or in the most ancient records of Spain or Germany—just as China possesses regarding its earliest ages, what, I pray, would you feel? What would you say? What outcries of praise and applause would you give? With what honors would you celebrate each and every thing of that era? How much admiration and praise would you stir up for your ancestors who thought so piously of God?
