# SEVENTH PARAGRAPH.

## *THROUGH VARIOUS ARGUMENTS, it is confirmed that a knowledge of the true God existed among the Chinese.*

Since indeed, just as frequent and serious crimes and the dissolution of morals eventually pave the way to the greatest of all crimes, Atheism; so too, every virtue, the right way of living, and the pious administration of a people are no obscure signs of true Religion. Let us see what the ancient age of the Chinese performed, both in word and example, with the light of nature as their only guide. They always taught that this nature was good and upright from its origin, and was equipped from heaven with the protections and aids of piety and the rest of the moral virtues. This opinion of the ancients is demonstrated philosophically by <term>Mencius</term> <note>A Confucian philosopher (c. 372–289 BCE) who famously argued that human nature is fundamentally good.</note>, the philosopher who follows after <term>Confucius</term>. However, although these same seeds of virtue are implanted in all nations by God, the author of nature, where true Religion is lacking, it is inevitable that those seeds are greatly weakened and oppressed, and almost all virtue lies dormant. It is not surprising that these virtues were missing in many other nations, since among them, vices themselves were already considered religious and sacred; they were not so much avoided as they were worshiped, as <term>Lactantius</term> <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325) who critiqued pagan morality.</note> says. For indeed, what place could there be for modesty and honesty where the marriages and adulteries of the Gods were celebrated, and where a naked <term>Venus</term> <note>Goddess of love</note>, <term>Cupids</term>, and <term>Priapi</term> <note>A minor rustic fertility god, often depicted with permanent arousal</note> were honored? What place for peace, friendship, and faith, where <term>Mars</term> <note>God of war</note>, <term>Bellona</term> <note>Goddess of war</note>, and <term>Mercury</term> <note>God of thieves and commerce</note> were worshiped as Divinities? What place for obedience, where <term>Jupiter</term>, who usurped the Kingdom for himself after driving out his father, was adored as the supreme King of Gods and men? What place for prudence, and the natural light of reason, where even mindless monsters—such as calves, she-wolves, crocodiles, snakes, and even the onions and garlic <note>original: *cœpæ & allia*; a reference to the Roman satirist Juvenal's mockery of Egyptian animal and vegetable worship</note> grown in gardens—were celebrated with insane ritual?

Where, I ask, can one find even a shadow of such monsters in all of Chinese antiquity, either on their land or even in the heavens and their star-bearing globe? Where is there any mention of a disparity of sexes among spirits (whom they consider incorporeal), or the marriages of Gods and Goddesses?

...and transformations: Where are the likenesses, images, or statues—I do not say of animals, but even of men or spirits—which China would have worshipped with religious devotion? If such things had existed in the ancient age, would not later generations have added some of the ancient idols to the new ones after idolatry was brought in from India <note>A reference to the introduction of Buddhism, which reached China via the Silk Road in the 1st century CE.</note>? Would so many commentators on the annals have attacked Emperor **Ming Ti** <note>Emperor Ming of Han (r. 58–75 CE), who according to legend dreamt of a golden man and sent envoys to India, leading to the arrival of Buddhist monks.</note> with such heavy words and sharp pens for being the first to introduce idolatry, if that plague had already been prevalent in the Empire before him? Would they have written that he was even more execrable for this single reason than the tyrants **Jie** and **Zhou** <note>Jie (the last ruler of the Xia dynasty) and Zhou (the last ruler of the Shang) were the archetypal "evil kings" of Chinese history.</note>, if the monsters of idols had already been exposed for public worship in earlier times? Could they have been ignorant of it, or remained silent, if anything similar had existed before, either in the ancient and authentic monuments of their books, or in the provinces and cities of so great an Empire?

Since, therefore, it is known that no such portents existed here formerly as were common among other nations—nations with whom China had even forbidden eternal commerce by law—there is no reason for you to expect or believe that there were bloody or shameful sacrifices here. There were no such things as the *Priapeia*, *Floralia*, or *Saturnalia* <note>Festivals of ancient Rome involving Priapus (fertility), Flora (flowers), and Saturn, which Christian writers often characterized as debauched.</note>, through which that sacred *Senate and People of Rome* <note>original: "Senatus Populusque Romanus"</note>, the master of all nations, allowed their youth to be depraved. There were no victims of infants, which the **Latins** used to sacrifice to their **Saturn**, and which the **Jews** also sacrificed to foreign gods; no human victims, which the "pious" **Aeneas** sent as funeral offerings to the spirits of the dead; and following his example, later Roman Emperors and Senators did the same. There were no theatrical games performed in human blood, nor other such things which **Lactantius** <note>A 4th-century Christian apologist known as the "Christian Cicero," who wrote "The Divine Institutes" to critique paganism.</note> extensively recounts and rejects. The **Chinese** <note>original: "Sinarum"</note> were always so far removed from all these things that they could scarcely bear to hear them recounted by a European with impartial ears and minds.

Regarding the superstitions of those other nations and their ancient religions, we know of them from the earliest literary monuments of each race—from **Orpheus**, I say, and from the earliest poets **Hesiod**, **Homer**, and others. As the same Lactantius says, they existed long before the name of "Philosophy" was born and were considered wise men; and yet they brought forth such foolish fictions and fables regarding God and the generations of the gods. But regarding the Ancient Religion of the **Chinese**, we have those who wrote two thousand and more years before Christ—that is, long before Orpheus or other writers had come to light.

Just as the ancient age of the **Chinese** attributed nothing unbecoming or shameful to the supreme Emperor of Heaven and the spirits—nothing in common with earthly contagion or corporeal and visible substance—and on the contrary, they confidently attributed to Him whatever is joined with right reason: namely, virtue, providence, power, knowledge, justice, and mercy; so too, they did not offer other honors and sacrifices than those worthy of supreme majesty, nor in any other way...

...[they taught that He] should be worshipped through the cultivation of virtues and a righteous mind, teaching this as much by words as by deeds and examples. I will say nothing here of their external manner—their gravity, modesty, self-restraint, abstinence, grace, and decorum—except to say that they denied all such external devotion could please Heaven unless it was imbued with the cultivation of the soul and internal virtue.

What shall I say now of the obedience of the Ancients <note>original: *Priscorum*</note> and their piety <note>The Latin *pietas* here refers specifically to "filial piety" (*xiao*), the foundational Confucian virtue of devotion and duty toward parents and ancestors.</note> toward their parents and ancestors? They wished this devotion to be continued and practiced in its own way even after death. To ensure that children learned the zeal and veneration they ought to show toward their living progenitors by this example, they believed they should serve those who had already departed this life just as they had served them when they were alive and present. This is the origin of that exquisite care for funerals, rites, sarcophagi, and tombs, aimed at preserving forever, if possible, the remains and memory of those who gave them life. And what of the three-year mourning period for a father and mother? It was such that even those performing the highest duties in the Empire would immediately resign from their appointed office for a period of three years. Why say more? So great was the solicitude, care, and diligence toward deceased ancestors that they might justly seem guilty of superstition—were it not clear from their own authentic books that they had no other goal or end in mind than pure filial observance and grateful piety and reverence toward their ancestors, which was not to be broken even after death. We must admit, however, that over time—or rather through the influence of so many sects and idolatrous superstitions—the original, ancient institution of the ancestors was corrupted in some people.

What shall I say of the respect toward elders and those advanced in age? Even the Emperor himself, while surveying the Empire, did not disdain to visit them; he would order them to be sought out and would decorate those who were well-deserving with honorary titles, increasing their wealth from the royal treasury if necessary. What of their clemency and that munificent compassion toward the poor, the blind, widows, orphans, the lame, and others? In former times, specific dwellings and incomes were assigned to them; indeed, even to this day, in every city and town of so great an Empire, a certain number are supported by the Royal grain-supply. This continues even under Tartar rule <note>A reference to the Manchu (Qing) dynasty, which had conquered China in 1644. The author suggests the Manchus maintained Chinese social welfare systems out of respect for their antiquity.</note>, for the sheer antiquity of this piety deterred the Tartar from abolishing this holy custom, even though he had already considered doing so in his mind. And although the rigor of justice was maintained toward those guilty of crimes, there was still a place for clemency here as well; specifically, throughout so vast an Empire, it was unlawful for anyone condemned to a capital offense to be put to death unless the sentence had first been approved by the Emperor himself—to say nothing of the periodic public pardons of offenses and the release of prisoners.

Now, what shall I say of the virtue of women, their modesty, and their simple manner of dress and appearance? For even up to these times, although

So too was the inviolability of the lawful marriage bed among the Ancients, even if it was corrupted by abuses in the course of time. > *What you do not wish to be done to yourself, do not do to another.* <note>original: "Quod tibi non vis fieri, alteri ne feceris." This is the "Silver Rule" of Confucius, which the author is presenting here in its Latinate, Christian-adjacent form.</note>

And since the Chinese world <note>original: *orbis Sinicus*</note> is composed most especially after the example of the King, let us consider only those things which are related below concerning the two Lawgivers and the founders of the three princely families, from the princes of Philosophers, *Confucius* and *Mencius* <note>The Latinized names for Kong Fuzi and Meng Ke, the primary architects of Confucian thought.</note>. He was content with a simple and poor house, food, and carriage, abhorring every appearance of luxury or haughtiness; he even wore common clothing (except when it was time to sacrifice). *Xun* <note>Emperor Shun</note> was the heir to this virtue as well as the Empire, having been raised to it by *Yao* himself, with no consideration given to his sons (though he numbered nine of them), but only to his virtue. In turn, he who was the founder of the first Family <note>The Xia Dynasty</note>, called *Yu*, was the imitator and chosen heir of this man. But also the founder of the second Family <note>The Shang Dynasty</note>, *Cheng Tang* <note>original: *Chim tam*</note>, when after a seven-year famine he offered himself as a victim to heaven for his people, he suppliantly asked of heaven itself whether perhaps he or his magistrates had sinned in the administration of the Republic; whether any corruption had crept in through the giving of gifts; whether slanders and murmurings were being heard; whether in the Palaces and buildings, or in the finery and dress of women, there was anything immoderate or unseemly, etc. Did he not declare, more than sufficiently, how joined his administration was then to all honesty, virtue, and moderation?

Indeed, how much innocence, frugality, and moderation governed such a great Empire for one thousand two hundred years and more, will be attested by the truly rich witness *Jizi* <note>original: *Ki çu*</note>, a Prince and also the uncle of the last of the second Family, the eighteenth Emperor called *Zhou* <note>original: *Cheu*</note>. For when he saw *new and foreign things being imported into the Palace, he said, not without a groan and like one prophesying:*
> *“Now for the first time,” he said, “ivory chopsticks are produced, and cups made of Rhinoceros horn; the simpler and shorter style of dress is changed for long robes, proud with silk and gold. The roofs inhabited by our ancestors now displease them, and ample ones are built with towers, and these made of precious stone. Even so, human greed will not be satisfied; I already perceive in my mind stones of immense price and other things of that kind being imported here from remote lands <gloss>a)</gloss> and at the same time, I see the ruin of the Empire.”*

Thus he spoke. Let him who wishes consult the annals and the books we are explaining. Truly, he will find hardly anything offensive.

...established by common use or public authority, anything that might be alien to virtue or reason.

Since things are so, and because the antiquity of the Chinese <note>original: *Sinarum*</note> sought the proper administration of the State <note>original: *Reipublicæ*</note> from virtue alone, why should we wonder if, by that example of virtue, they so gently led the neighboring barbarians on all sides of their lands toward the laws of humanity? Through this, the nation grew over so many centuries into the form and magnitude of a most vast Empire, and brought even the Princes of neighboring kingdoms into a state of clientage, and often even tributary obedience. Certainly, long ago around the year 1100 BC, legates arrived from Cochinchina <note>An ancient name used here to refer to the regions of modern-day Vietnam.</note>, led by fame alone, because China possessed "holy heroes" who knew how to pray for and obtain fertility from heaven. They had come to implore the patronage of these heroes and to seek a remedy for the sterility and famine under which Cochinchina was then piteously suffering. Why should we also wonder if this Empire, in those ancient times, was so fortunate and long-lasting that the three founding Families <note>The Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties.</note> possessed and preserved it longer than the nineteen Imperial Families that followed them combined? For although these later dynasties attempted to recall certain customs received from the Ancients and mentioned by us above, they nevertheless—due to so many wars, heresies, sects, and parricides <note>In this context, the assassination of rulers or heads of state.</note> increasing more and more with the slip of time—never returned to that ancient innocence and integrity, except during certain brief, lucid intervals.

There will perhaps be someone who, judging from the truly depraved morals of this age—in which, besides innumerable vices, fraud and pretense reign, and if any virtue shines forth, it is not so much virtue as a certain painted appearance of virtue—there will be, I say, perhaps someone who forms a judgment and passes sentence on the Ancient era based on the present age. Such a person might think that the art of feigning and lying about Religion flourished even then, and that Princes and Magistrates used it to more successfully keep the unlearned multitude in their duty. This follows the suggestion mentioned above regarding a "double doctrine": one being exterior or popular, and another being interior or belonging specifically to the politicians; and that whatever they said or did in this regard, they said or did solely out of a desire to preserve public peace and tranquility.

But, besides the fact that no one will find even a trace of this "double doctrine" in the authentic books of the Ancients, I certainly oppose to this opinion—not to say the rashness of those so judging—the very sentiment of later ages and of the literati <note>The *Ru* or Confucian scholar-officials.</note>, who with unanimous speech and writing praise and extol nothing so much as the candor, simplicity, and sincerity of Ancient times. They confess, not without a groan, that these qualities are greatly missed in their own times. Certainly, those who read Confucius and other authentic books of the highest authority and antiquity will find nothing more frequently instilled and emphasized than that, following the example of the Ancient Kings, all things should be done with truth,

...and all words and deeds should always proceed from the innermost heart; hence those words so often repeated by the commentators, *Chim xe* and *Vu vam* <note>In modern Pinyin, these likely represent *Chengshi* (誠實 - sincere/true) and *Wuwang* (無妄 - without falsehood).</note>—that is, *The true and solid, without pretense or falsehood*. In all their actions, then, and in their words and duties that pass between King and subjects, parents and children, between brothers, friends, and spouses, the Ancients always wanted sincerity and faith to be preserved whole and unsullied, with every shadow of deceit excluded. Would they, then, have been feigned and cunning politicians only in the most serious matter of Religion? And did they assume Religion itself only as a deceptive means to keep the common people in their duty?

This would certainly never be conceded even by those "atheistic-political" innovators, the Interpreters of the *Song Family* <note>The author refers here to the Neo-Confucian scholars of the Song Dynasty (960–1279 AD). Early Jesuit writers often viewed these later commentators as having introduced a materialistic or "atheistic" interpretation of the ancient texts.</note>. Although they fashioned some empty monster of their own "political divinity," they nevertheless did not hesitate to establish the entire foundation of their philosophy in truth and solidity (which they express by the word *Chim* <note>The Chinese character *Cheng* (誠), meaning sincerity or integrity.</note>). And just as they contend that all things in the universe—even those that seem to happen by chance—are ruled and preserved by some solid and predominant virtue (of whatever kind that may be), so too in the administration of the State, and in man himself, they want all actions and movements to proceed from an integrity of mind and a sincerity entirely without pretense.

And indeed, if you were to object, the Interpreters would ask: on what foundation, I pray, would they say such things? What text, finally, could they bring forward from the ancient five Books of teachings <note>The *Wujing* or Five Classics of the Confucian tradition.</note> to prove that religion was a fraud? And even if they were to bring forward some passage in which it was said that the Ancient and holy Kings and their sages held the people of the Empire subject to them through the protections of Religion, would it immediately follow that Religion was their own invention to keep the people in their duty? For who does not know that true Religion is—if it is permitted to speak thus—not a human invention, but a divine one, by which States and Empires ought to be established and preserved? For, as Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure whom Renaissance and Baroque scholars believed was an ancient Egyptian sage who possessed "primal" wisdom consistent with Christianity.</note> says, Religion is to be loved and followed for its own sake, because it is good and true, and not as a deceptive means for the preservation of the State. Thus, the ancient Kings of the Chinese <note>original: *Sinarum*</note> adopted a thing that was true and holy, received from their ancestors nearly at the time of the Flood, for the public good and for the safety and happiness of their subjects.

For why? Would the first founder of the Empire, *Fo hi* <note>Fuxi, the first of the legendary Three Sovereigns of ancient China.</note>, having soon cast aside the Religion he received from the sons or grandsons of Noah <note>original: *Noëmi*. The author follows the common 17th-century theory that the Chinese were descendants of Noah who migrated east after the Flood.</note>, invent a new and fictitious one, in which he even used a fictitious name (which sounds like "sacrifice") to keep the people in their duty and laws? If so, the entire ancient institution and political norm of the Chinese would also be a fiction and mere deception, since it would be resting on a deceptive and empty foundation. The faith and obedience of subjects toward their Princes, and of children toward their parents and ancestors, would always have been a fiction. Why so? For since they teach that the Prince must be served by his subjects in the same way as Princes and pe—

Who then could now believe that those ancient Sages and Kings imposed upon their subjects with such wicked and impious simulation; that they wished to contaminate themselves with such an infamous and execrable lie regarding Religion and holiness? Finally, that such a great harmony of such nefarious simulation and impiety could have existed through so many ages, and among so many men so dissimilar in talent, nature, and condition, and across such great intervals of space and time? Truly, even if it were clearly evident to the people of this age that their ancestors had thus lied about Religion and the uprightness of life; yet they would studiously conceal and cover this; indeed, they themselves would not hesitate to lie, lest perhaps they should deprive their ancestors and those Kings and Philosophers of such great holiness (as they say) of the praise for their sincere candor, faith, and truth. The strength of our arguments will therefore always remain; we will always be able to hurl this inevitable spear, by which they will either be compelled to admit, along with their ancestors, the providence of the supreme Deity and His religious worship, or to free these ancestors from the suspicion of madness (which they will never be able to accomplish), or finally to confess that they have departed from the opinions and institutions of their ancestors with a degenerate and shameful levity and inconstancy.

# PARAGRAPH EIGHT.

## BY WHAT NAME THE ANCIENT CHINESE addressed the true God. The etymology and propriety of the name are examined.

BUT another question remains for us to discuss here; it concerns a name, certainly, but it is not at all to be dismissed as those disputes commonly called "merely about names." For if in those earliest times, close to the era of the Flood, the Chinese knew the true Deity and worshipped Him once known (which I think all will now easily grant me), by what name, by what word, and by what letters did those ancient worshippers express that supreme Deity? Certainly, if no nation has ever existed, however barbaric, that did not call the Deity it worshipped by some name, whether true or false (for as *Tullius* <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator and philosopher.</note> testifies, there are as many names for gods as there are human languages), how could the Chinese people—so civilized, cultured, and precise—have lacked a name for the God they worshipped? Could that language—which in the division of languages and nations was probably one of those seventy "mother tongues" <note>The author refers to the traditional belief that seventy-two distinct languages arose after the fall of the Tower of Babel.</note>—possess names, words, and letters to explain all created things, the names of herbs, and their natures, and yet lack the very name by which the Creator and Lord of the universe (whose existence all nature proclaims) might be rightly addressed? No sensible person, I think, would suspect this.

But you may ask: what was that name? Was it significant of some supreme power or perfection, or did it denote a relationship to created things? For as long as we are "wayfarers" <note>A technical theological term (*viatores*) referring to humans on their earthly journey toward God, who cannot yet see the divine essence directly.</note>, we know that a name which perfectly signifies the divine and ineffable essence as it truly is cannot even be conceived by man, much less expressed by any sign.

I say, therefore, that among the ancient Chinese, the name by which they addressed the true God was *Shangdi* <note>original: "Xam ti." This title is often translated as "Lord on High" or "Supreme Emperor."</note>. The antiquity of this name is the same as that of their very letters, the foundations of which were laid by *Fuxi* <note>original: "Fo hi," the legendary first sovereign of China and creator of the I Ching hexagrams.</note>, the founder of the Chinese nation; these were further refined and organized into a system during the reign of the third Emperor, *Huangdi* <note>original: "Hoam ti," the "Yellow Emperor."</note>, through the work of *Cangjie* <note>original: "çâm kie," the legendary four-eyed official credited with inventing Chinese characters.</note>. Regarding this Emperor, it is also recorded that he built a Palace or Temple for *Shangdi* himself; this occurred approximately 600 years before the birth of Abraham, if one chooses to trust the annals and the chronology of the "Seventy Interpreters" <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, which provides a different chronological timeline for early history than other versions.</note>. This was, of course, long before the name *God* <note>original Greek: "Θεὸς" (Theos).</note>—from which the Latins derived their word for the Deity—was found written by anyone. That

If you prefer to follow the common reckoning, the antiquity of that name *Xam ti* <note>original: *Xam ti*; the modern transliteration is *Shangdi*, meaning "Supreme Deity" or "Lord on High."</note> is certainly established by the Royal Scribe and Historiographer who, around the time of *Yu* <note>Yu the Great, the legendary founder of China's first dynasty.</note> (who was the founder of the first *Hia* <note>Xia</note> Dynasty), recorded the deeds of *Yao* and *Xun* <note>Sage-kings Yao and Shun.</note>. Although many of those records have perished (for out of the sixteen chapters of which they consisted, eleven are entirely missing), it is nevertheless clear from the remaining fragments how the Emperor *Xun*—who modeled himself entirely after his predecessor *Yao*, by whom he had been chosen—offered sacrifice to *Xam ti*. Following this, he sacrificed by a different, lower rite to the six princely spirits, and finally to the guardians of the mountains and rivers, as well as those of all other things. It is also recorded that he sacrificed to *Xam ti* with a burnt offering called *Ghai* <note>original: *holocaustico Ghai dicto*; likely referring to the *Lì* or *Jiao* sacrifice where precious items and animals were consumed by fire.</note>, in which the victim and the most precious items were burned. This was written by the Royal Scribe of that era, approximately 2,220 years before Christ. Seek now, if you please, another monument among any other nation of the world that is older or more authentic; seek, I say, and assign me another name, if you can, in the whole of Chinese antiquity, by which the ancient age of the Chinese addressed the true God (whom you must admit was recognized everywhere in the times closest to the Flood).

But if you seek the true etymology <term>Etymology: the study of the origin of words and the way in which their meanings have changed throughout history.</term> of this name *Xam ti*: the character and word *Ti* in its primary, ordinary, and indeed its unique and proper meaning, is the same as Emperor, Governor, and Lord. It is the very same word and character by which the Chinese have generally addressed their Emperors from nearly the beginning until the present day. However, among the first eighty-eight princes of the Empire, only thirteen are found who used this title, while the others used either their own names at the time, or *Vam* <note>Wang</note>, which means King. This continued until the Emperor *Xi hoam ti* <note>Qin Shi Huang, the "First Emperor."</note> of the fourth *Çin* <note>Qin</note> Dynasty, who, presuming that he had surpassed the merits and virtues of the three founders and princes of the Empire—*Yao, Xun, Yu, Tam* <note>Tang</note>, and *Vu-vam* <note>Wu Wang</note>—first decreed that the name *Ti* should be preceded by *Hoam* <note>Huang</note>, that is, Great or August Emperor. By this title, all the princes who followed from that time on have been addressed. 

Furthermore, the other character which is placed before the character *Ti* when they signify God is *xam* <note>Shang</note>, which means Supreme. When this is added simply to the name *Ti*, no Emperor has hitherto dared to use it, even though some among them were impiously proud and by far the most insolent. Therefore, just as they used this name *Ti*—which earthly princes usurped—to designate their dominion and power over the kingdoms and peoples subject to them, so by the addition of *Xam*, they signified a certain supreme majesty, power, and dominion, higher than all things, over all spirits, over heaven and earth, over Empires and Kingdoms, Kings and peoples. And so, just as China has always pursued a monarchical government on earth under one head with the greatest zeal, so it also believed that there exists a certain invisible Monarch in the heavens, seeking...

...meanwhile, by the established rule of his administration—drawn from the balanced order of the heavens and the earth, as well as of the seasons and the elements—the one supreme and visible Monarch on his own lands might moderate his Empire in imitation of the supreme and invisible Divinity <note>original: *Numen*; a term for a deity or divine power.</note>, whose majesty he even withdraws from the eyes of his subjects as if by a veil.

But, you will say, do they not also in the most ancient and most authentic texts frequently use the name *Tien* <note>original: *Tien*; the Chinese term *Tian*, meaning Heaven.</note>, that is, *Heaven*, and attribute to it the same qualities as to *Xam ti* <note>original: *Xam ti*; *Shangdi*, the Supreme Emperor.</note>, the Supreme Emperor? For example: intelligence, will, providence, law and dominion, justice, piety, and so forth. It is exactly so; nor do I deny that the name and word *Tien*, or *Heaven*, is also very ancient and perhaps coeval <note>existing at the same time.</note> (if I may speak so) with the term *Xam ti*. 

But if you grant me that the Chinese <note>original: *Sinas*.</note> existed in the times closest to the Flood, and thus must have had both a knowledge of the true Divinity and, consequently, a name by which they might express that true Divinity: certainly, whether this name was *Xam ti* or even *Tien*, it must always be concluded that they knew and intended to signify none other than the true God under these names. And in truth, since they saw nothing in the nature of things more beautiful or more august than heaven—and moreover, since heaven calls forth the eyes and hearts of all mortals to itself, especially in times of danger—will anyone wonder that they bestowed the name of "Heaven" upon the Lord of Heaven? 

This is even more likely if you were aware of the most common mode of speaking used by the Chinese from every age, more so than other nations: they have constantly been accustomed to name the "Palace" for the "King," the "City" for the "Governor of the City," the "Court" for the "Magistrate," and the "House" itself for the "Father of the Family." This practice indeed has a place among other nations as well, and is found in the Holy Scriptures and used by Christ our Savior himself. 

To make this clearer to you, I beg you to consult the old and classic books: the *Li Ki* <note>original: *Li Ki*; the *Liji* or *Book of Rites*.</note>, the *Xu kim* <note>original: *Xu kim*; the *Shujing* or *Classic of History*.</note>, the *Ye kim* <note>original: *Ye kim*; the *Yijing* or *Book of Changes*.</note>, and others. It is impossible that you would not be convinced by them that the ancient age acknowledged and worshipped the spirits of mountains and rivers and the presiding guardians of cities. And yet these very spirits are in some texts explicitly called "spirits of mountains and rivers," while in others they are simply called "rivers and mountains"; likewise, the tutelary spirits of cities, the *Chim hoam* <note>original: *Chim hoam*; *Chenghuang*, the City God, literally meaning "Wall and Moat".</note>, are simply called "walls and ditches." 

If, therefore, they signify the spirits presiding over lower things by the names of the places over which they preside, why would you not conclude, with even greater force, that when they use the name of "Heaven," they understood the Lord and Moderator of Heaven? To this is added the significant testimony of both major lexicons, the *çu guei* <note>original: *çu guei*; the *Zihui*, a famous 1651 Chinese dictionary.</note> and the one commonly called *Chim çu* <note>original: *Chim çu*; the *Zhengzitong*, a 1627 dictionary.</note>. In these, while multiple uses and definitions of the word *Tien* (or "Heaven") are provided, this is explicitly taught among other things: that when you wish the character *Tien* to indicate the Lord and Governor of Heaven, it is designated by another word, namely *Ti* <note>original: *Ti*; the character *Di*, meaning Emperor or Lord.</note>, that is, the Supreme Emperor.

...deals with the City of Rome, and calls it Apostolic, Holy, and the mistress of the Christian world; and likewise says that orthodox doctrine flows from it and that Ecclesiastical dignities are conferred by it, and other things of this kind: if (I say) we were to claim that he was speaking of no other City than the one visible to the eyes of many as a mere collection of buildings, would we not surely say he was speaking nonsense and had lost his mind? Or indeed, if we ourselves were to deny the spiritual meaning, would we not seem to be speaking nonsense and to have departed from a sound state of mind? 

Yet not only *Confucius*, but all the *Chinese* everywhere—and not only in antiquity, but even in this current age of ours—call Heaven <note>original: *Caelum*; referring here to the Chinese term *Tien*.</note> intelligent, pious, and propitious. They attribute the titles of *Parent* and *Lord* to it. Furthermore, they say that the light of right reason is infused into mortals by it; that from it descend the rewards of the virtuous and the punishments of the wicked; that from it are sent and delegated Sages and the teachers of Kingdoms; and finally, that crowns and empires are conferred upon, taken away from, and transferred between Princes by it. 

What more? They even metaphorically ascribe speech and senses to it. Thus, there are those who, if they believe they are being treated unfairly, complain with impious indignation: "Does Heaven then not have eyes?" They mean by this: does it not see by whom and how unjustly they are harmed, so that it may inflict due punishment on the one acting unjustly? Ultimately, they attribute to it a heart, anger, compassion, joy, and love. Now, if they themselves did not ascend much higher in their thought than where they can reach with their physical eyes, would they not rightly seem to be speaking nonsense? For they would be attributing life to a dead machine, and the faculty of seeing and speaking to the blind and mute—indeed, they would be granting the right of Empire over Kings and Kingdoms themselves quite pointlessly and ridiculously to a physical object.

But when the Chinese speak of the incorporeal Heaven and the corporeal one, they use words and phrases so diverse that these very differences declare the vast distinction between the two "Heavens." This is no less clear than when they distinguish the court of their Emperor from a common hall, commending it sometimes for its structure, elegance, and firmness, and at other times for its power and equity. 

Thus, when the Philosopher <note>This refers to Confucius or his grandson Zisi, the traditional author of the text mentioned next.</note> in the book *The Doctrine of the Mean* <note>original: *Chum yum*; the *Zhongyong*, one of the "Four Books" of Confucian philosophy.</note> speaks of the perpetual and equable succession of the four seasons of the year; of the approach, retreat, and unperturbed course of the Sun and Moon; of the magnitude of heaven covering all things and warming all things in its embrace; of its concurrence with the earth itself for the production and conservation of things, and other matters of this kind—then surely no one can doubt that he is dealing with the corporeal and visible heaven. 

But when he deals with that Heaven from which all mind and reason flows; when the discourse is of that mandate, the nod of heaven, and that providence upon which it is necessary for us to depend entirely at all times; when he says this must be the rule for our actions; that this can in no way be eluded or deceived; that riches and honors are dispensed by it; and that from this alone, together with rational nature itself, are conferred gifts more precious than wealth—prudence, fortitude, justice, and piety—from this [Heaven], whoever [seeks] riches...

# xciii
->PREFATORY DECLARATION.<-

...nt, and they say those who neglect their duties and apply themselves too eagerly to amassing riches err unhappily; that by its benefit Magistrates and Empires come about, and that these are preserved by one and the same Family through many generations; then surely one must consider that it deals entirely with that invisible and secret majesty which presides over the heavens.

Therefore, let the authority and proper meaning remain for those two words, *Xam ti* <note>original: "Xam ti"; the Jesuit transcription for *Shangdi*, often translated as "Lord on High" or "Supreme Emperor."</note>—whether for the sake of brevity and the custom of speaking used here, one addresses Him under the name of "Heaven" through a figurative usage, or whether one uses His own proper names: *Xam ti*, the Supreme Emperor of the heavens, I say.

And this is indeed the first and most ancient name used by the Chinese <note>original: "Sinarum"</note>. Upon hearing it, this nation conceives of that than which it knows nothing greater or more excellent. It is in use among that sect <note>Referring to the Literati or followers of original Confucianism.</note> which is considered better than all others and more in conformity with natural law, and to that extent even with Christian truth; thus, it produces here an easier concept of the true God. Just as it is the most ancient, so for many centuries it has been the sole and supreme name of God, to whom the Emperor alone, as an adopted son and vicar on earth, performed sacrifices. This was to show that he felt toward *Xam ti* what his own subjects felt toward himself: namely, that he is the supreme and sole one chosen by God for his Chinese Empire, just as the God of the heavens and earth is the supreme and only Emperor of Himself. And from this it also happened that when he was about to sacrifice, having prepared the solemn rite, he would order the date of such a great solemnity to be announced to his subjects by a decree sent to all the jurisdictions of his Empire. To the other spirits, however, the Princes and Magistrates performed sacrifices each according to his own rank, to show that those spirits, when compared with the supreme Emperor *Xam ti*, are what Princes and Magistrates on earth are when compared with their King:
> *For thus (to use the words of Lactantius) we say the world is ruled by God (and the Chinese have always judged so) as a Province is by a governor, whose attendants no one would call partners in ruling the Province, even though the business is carried out through their ministry.* <note>original: "Sic enim... Lactantii..."; Lactantius was a 4th-century Christian author. The author uses this quote to argue that Chinese "spirits" are merely God's heavenly bureaucrats, not independent deities.</note>

Since, therefore, that name *Xam ti* is primary and not a personal name, like *Saturn*, etc., but a title like *Deity* <note>original: "Numen"</note> or *God*; and since, according to its etymology, it denotes no imperfection but, on the contrary, power and majesty (and indeed the supreme kind); and since, according to the opinion of St. Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century philosopher-theologian.</note> and all theologians, the true God can be called by those names which denote some perfection without imperfection; we confidently and deservedly affirm that the Ancient Chinese knew, signified, and worshipped the one and true Deity by that very name. This is sufficiently clear from the authority of so many centuries, and also from so many authentic monuments and testimonies of books, in which you will find (surprisingly) absolutely nothing that is unworthy or unbecoming of that name and supreme majesty, or alien to reason—

## PARAGRAPH NINE.

### THAT THE CORRUPT INTERPRETATION OF THE INNOVATORS
### cannot abolish the primeval meaning of the name *XAM TI*.

NOR indeed can the perverse opinion and interpretation of the "Innovators" <note>original: "Novatorum"; here referring to the Neo-Confucian scholars of the Song Dynasty (960–1279 AD) who reinterpreted ancient texts through a more naturalistic or materialistic lens.</note>—shamefully hallucinating after so many centuries—derogate from such an ancient and clear meaning and etymology of this name, which is illustrated by so many attributes and properties that belong to the one and only God. This is true whether those innovators were from the sect of *Tao* <note>Taoism</note>, by which the meaning was first somewhat corrupted when various "Divinities" of the same name were introduced into heaven, to each of whom they seemed to attribute a certain independent power over individual elements; or whether they were two or three Emperors, such as *Tven çum* <note>The Song Emperor Zhenzong (r. 997–1022), though the text labels him as the 13th Tang Family Emperor.</note> from the thirteenth Tang Family, and *Hoei çum* <note>The Song Emperor Huizong (r. 1100–1126).</note> from the nineteenth Song Family, who attributed the name and title of *Xam ti* <note>Shangdi, the "Supreme Emperor."</note>—that is, of supreme power and excellence—to two men: *Lao kiun* <note>Laozi, the founder of Taoism.</note> and *Cham y* <note>Zhang Yi, often associated with the Jade Emperor.</note>. The former of these was a contemporary of Confucius, while the latter flourished under the fifth Han Family, as we have related more extensively above. Therefore, an impious abuse could no more detract from the legitimate use, nor take away the significative force of the ancient Chinese word, than the usurpation of the word *God* <note>original: "Θεὸς"; the Greek word for God.</note> by demons or men could take away its own proper power of signifying; just as a rebel who wickedly usurps the title and name for himself by force of arms does not take away the name and power of a legitimate King.

Much less certainly (whatever the atheistic-political thinkers <note>original: "atheopolitici"; a term the author uses for those who interpret Chinese philosophy in a purely secular or materialistic way.</note> of this age may contend) can the spurious interpretation of certain secularists—brought to light after forty centuries—take away or change the proper and most ancient force and meaning of the name *Xam ti*. By this interpretation, they endeavor to elude the supreme Deity of heaven and His attributes, reducing everything to a certain mute and inanimate virtue and the natural efficacy of things, and thus twisting the monuments and sense of all past antiquity into their own opinion.

Let it be permitted here, therefore, to bring forward a few points out of many, which those "Innovators" <note>The Neo-Confucian scholars of the Song Dynasty (960–1279 AD) who reinterpreted ancient texts through a more naturalistic lens.</note> explain more laboriously in their commentaries and in that work of theirs on nature. For what, I ask, can be imagined more absurd than to say that the Emperor of the Chinese sacrifices to the Supreme Emperor only because—since he is himself *Tien çu* <note>original: "Tien çu"; *Tiānzǐ* (天子), or "Son of Heaven."</note>, that is, the son of heaven (adoptive, naturally, because all power according to them is from heaven)—he participates more fully in that purer and refined virtue and efficacy of heaven? Wherefore, they claim that while he sacrifices to heaven, he does so so that his own "air" <note>original: "aër"; the author uses this to translate the Chinese concept of *Qi* (氣), the vital energy or vapor that Neo-Confucians believed permeated the universe.</note> or influence, being purer, may be united with heaven through a certain natural sympathy, and thus be preserved and increased. And hence also, they say, fasts and abstinence are performed beforehand, so that he may purify his "air"—which may perhaps be obscured and polluted by cares and shameful allurements, like certain mists—and thus, having recalled that royal and heaven-infused spirit within himself, he may approach the sacrifice rightly disposed.

And they also say this is the reason why there were holy Kings in those first centuries, and why the golden and opulent ages occurred under two Princely Families; because in those times, just as the air and its vigor and virtue were fresher, so too was everything that was communicated from heaven to the Ancient Kings more vivid, vigorous, and abundant. This is quite different from what happened in later ages, as the aforementioned virtue and effective power of the heavens gradually grew thin and sterile; just as, they say, water is pure at its source, but the further it flows, the more it is infected by filthy and muddy places, and contracts grime.

Elsewhere also, while they explain how heaven is said to procreate Kings, Masters, and Saints, they affirm that this happens through a fortuitous celestial influence which falls upon this or that person. When, however, it is recorded in the texts that heaven or the supreme emperor of heaven grants the prayers and vows of pious Princes, they wish it to be understood that since the Pious and Religious mind of such Princes is entirely united with heaven and its influence, that very celestial influence—which is naturally sympathetic—spontaneously and immediately insinuates itself into such pious vows and desires, from which the hoped-for successes follow. In like manner, the Interpreter *Hu u sum* <note>Likely a reference to a Neo-Confucian commentator.</note>, while attempting to explain that singular favor which the supreme Emperor of heaven bestowed upon the Empress *Kiam yven* <note>Jiang Yuan, the legendary mother of the Zhou dynasty's ancestor, said to have conceived after treading in a footprint of God or sacrificing.</note>, when she conceived a son after prayers and a sacrifice offered together with her husband to *Xam ti* <note>original: "Xam ti"; *Shàngdì* (上帝), the "Supreme Emperor" or God.</note>, wrote thus (I say, 3400 years after that event is said to have happened): "While," he says, "*Kiam yven* was sacrificing to the Supreme Emperor with all her mind's affection, to wherever the full intention and affection of the mind was directed, there also a certain celestial influence was immediately carried. Where this was carried, a certain generative power flowed together, and thus her vow and sacrifice were accepted. That she therefore conceived and gave birth to a son is not so marvelous."

How absurdly, indeed, they philosophize—or more truly, trifle—concerning the pro-

...[the pro]vidence of the Deity, and the just retribution for merits or crimes. For they teach that the prosperous successes of human affairs arise from heaven in such a way that they attribute them entirely to the "air" <note>original: *aër*; refers to the concept of *Qi* (氣), the vital energy or vapor that Neo-Confucians believed permeated the universe.</note> or to some more benign and fruitful influence, which unfolds, expands, and spreads itself for the sake of those who are well-deserving; while adverse successes they attribute again to that same "air," but now restricting itself and in a certain way withdrawing from the use of men who have deserved so poorly. It is helpful to hear what they say regarding the Emperor *Wu Yi* <note>original: *Vu ye*; an Emperor of the Shang Dynasty known for his impiety.</note>, who was the 25th in order from the second *Shang* <note>original: *xam*</note> Family, and who, being impiously bold and blasphemous against heaven, died struck by lightning while hunting in the year 1195 before Christ, in the fourth year of his reign. What, I ask, do the Interpreters of the *Song* <note>original: *sum*; referring to the Neo-Confucians of the Song Dynasty (960–1279 AD).</note> Family say? These are the ones whom *Zheng Nanhu* <note>original: *Tim nan hu*; likely a reference to a specific scholar of the era.</note>, himself an Interpreter, rejects. *Lightning*, they say, *is a certain spirit of heaven and a burning and violent exhalation; because it thus encountered the violent and impious air and spirit of a man so as to extinguish the impious Wu Yi, the matter was entirely consistent with reason.* Again, in what way do they explain the very thoughts of man, whether wicked or good? When someone, they say, entertains a good or pious thought, it is nothing more than what is said in the *Book of Odes* <note>The *Shijing*, one of the Five Classics of Chinese literature.</note>: *Shangdi lin ru* <note>original: *Xam ti lin ju*; "The Supreme Emperor approaches you and descends to you."</note>, while when someone entertains a wicked thought, this is what is meant by *Ti chen nu* <note>original: *Ti chin nu*; "The Supreme Emperor is gravely angered"</note>, and nothing more. And thus, with those adulterated commentaries of theirs, they contend that the Deity of heaven is nothing other than the mind of man itself. Fearlessly affirming that this mind is the *Supreme Emperor* <note>original: *xam ti*; Shangdi.</note>, and this mind is heaven. Where, however, it treats the soul of man—whenever it is said in the text that at death the body returns to the earth, but the spirit ascends on high, or even where the souls of pious Kings are mentioned as *standing before the Supreme Emperor of heaven*—they certainly understand those things as referring to that "airy" substance which, mixed with the heavens, is carried here and there by a fortuitous impulse; and now descending, now even ascending, it persists nowhere in a stable state.

And who of sound mind would not reject these few points (which we have just reported out of many), and would not also be justly and deservedly angry that men, otherwise learned—sometimes discoursing so excellently on virtues and vices, as well as on the successful administration of the Commonwealth—are seized by I know not what madness, and so foully and filthily corrupt so many and such illustrious monuments of all antiquity concerning the Supreme Deity and Religion left to posterity? And they do this indeed not without applause and pride, as if, by the subtlety of their own genius, they had found a way of explaining everything through those "airy" and inanimate efficacies of the heavens and new dogmas of a chimerical Philosophy, which were unknown and ignored for nearly 40 centuries, or (as they themselves indeed judge) buried, as it were, in the shadows of oblivion brought about by the long passage of time. In exactly that way, the heterodox <note>A term often used by Catholic writers of this period to refer to Protestant reformers or other heretics.</note> do not blush to confirm their own new and pestiferous dogmas by the authority of the Sacred Scriptures and the Doctors of the Church, and to drag them—as if they were the reformers of all antiquity—to their own depraved sense and judgment.

And will there be any of the European heralds <note>original: *Europæorum præconum*; referring to the Christian missionaries, particularly the Jesuits, who acted as "heralds" of the Gospel.</note> who would prefer to cling stubbornly to these adulterated and impiously political interpretations? By doing so, they might once again awaken the most beautiful lights implanted by the Author of Nature during the golden age of the Chinese, and recall, to some extent, the entirely unfeigned innocence, piety, and religion of the Ancients. This is especially true since, among this nation (if only one brings a mind free of prejudice), one will find so many and such appropriate aids sought from ancient monuments, which open the way and even, in a certain sense, smooth the path for a more easy course of Gospel preaching.

## PARAGRAPH TEN. ##

### BY THE EXAMPLE OF THE APOSTLE TO THE GENTILES ###
### *and the Fathers of the primitive Church, it is concluded by other reasons that the true Deity may be addressed by the same name used by the Ancient Chinese.* ###

Furthermore, all that we have reported so far has been intended primarily to persuade the first founders of the Chinese Mission <note>original: *Sinicæ Missionis*</note> to cast aside these corrupted commentaries of the [modern] interpreters and insist upon the footprints of naked antiquity. To signify the God whom they come to announce, they should use that appellative name and word from the most ancient language, *Shangdi* <note>original: *Xam ti* (上帝); the "Highest Deity" or "Emperor on High" in ancient Chinese classics.</note>, which was used for so many centuries and remained uncorrupted both in their speech and in their written books. 

That this may be done confidently and without any hesitation, much hard labor and study over many years in turning and re-turning the monuments and books of the ancients has opened the way. Moreover, the judgments of very grave men—so often consulted on such a great matter—and the prayers and votes of many who think rightly, as well as their encouragements and impulses, are by no means lacking. However, by far the most effective motive in a matter of such weight and importance would be to imitate the Apostle to the Gentiles <note>original: *Apostolum gentium*; referring to St. Paul.</note>, as well as the holy Fathers and Doctors who were his imitators. One should also follow the practice and method of the Councils and the universal Church in announcing the true Deity <note>original: *Numen*</note> among all nations. Indeed, in almost every part of the world, they used no other name than the one they found among the individual nations, even if they found that name had been most corrupted through many centuries by the dreams of various pagans and innumerable fictions, and was almost entirely obliterated. # PREFATORY DECLARATION. #

...there was a controversy) namely, that the name **God** <note>original: *Θέὸς* (Greek) or *Deus* (Latin)</note> was to be preferred among the Greeks and Latins. This was because, upon hearing this name, the gentiles whom they were instructing would come to the knowledge of some Divinity, even though those same people understood that name to mean the material sky, the earth, the elements, the planets, or even most wicked men. Thus, they erred more gravely and shamefully than the **Chinese** <note>original: *Sinæ*</note>, who attached nothing shameful or unseemly to that name, except when they transferred it to two particular men.

Let us ask those who are perhaps troubled by fears and scruples: what word did Augustine and other orthodox Fathers use in the past when they disputed with the Manichaeans <note>Followers of a dualistic religion that viewed the material world as evil; Augustine famously argued against them after leaving the sect.</note> about **God**? Did those religious and timid men perhaps abstain from that word, **God**, because they knew that to those with whom they were disputing, it already signified something corporeal, according to the heretical and depraved use of the word? And the very Princes of the Church and the Apostles—when they announced God to the Romans and Greeks in the past, what word do we think they used? They will say: they used that very word, **God**. But what else could that word signify to the heathens of that time than some Divinity similar to Saturn, Jove, or Mercury? For indeed, many of them—if not all—had never perceived anything of any other Divinity, even by rumor. Was the use of that word therefore liable to produce errors? Not at all, you will say; for the Saints used that word in such a way that, partly by affirming what belonged to the divine nature and partly by denying what did not belong to it, they taught the ignorant and unrefined that the God they were announcing was entirely different, and distant by infinite intervals, from those whom blind heathendom adored.

Well then. What else will the first heralds <note>A term for the missionaries spreading the Gospel.</note> in this **China** achieve through word and writing? When they pronounce the two words **Shangdi** <note>original: *Xam ti*; the ancient Chinese name for the "Supreme Deity" or "Highest Lord."</note>, they will simultaneously and most eloquently teach that He is incorporeal, eternal, immense, infinite, most perfect, and the Creator and Lord of heaven and earth. Could it be that **God** <note>original: *Θέὸς* or *Deus*</note> could be safely pronounced by Paul in Athens and Rome, but **Shangdi** cannot be pronounced in **China** without danger? This is despite the fact that this name, both literally and from its first institution, signifies the "Supreme Emperor," and according to the native interpreters, **the Lord and Governor of Heaven** <note>original: *Tien chi chu çai* (Tian zhi zhu zai).</note>?

I ask further: if a European teacher were legally questioned by the most grave **Chinese** Doctors as to what name the first Gospel heralds once used in heathen Europe, and whether the name of **God** always remained untouched and uncorrupted—never once applied to mortals or material things—what ought a prudent man to respond? That the name of **God** in Europe always remained whole and inviolate? Who would dare to assert that? And yet, did the first heralds of the Gospel in Europe not use this very word constantly?

# PREFATORY DECLARATION. #

Suppose, then, that a **Chinese person** <note>original: *Sina*</note> were to ask for a reason why a European hesitates to use the name **Shangdi** <note>original: *Xam ti*; a Chinese term meaning "Highest Lord" or "Supreme Deity."</note> in his Empire. This is despite the fact that the name has been found corrupted—both by the followers of **Laozi** <note>original: *Lao kiun*; the legendary founder of Daoism.</note> and by false interpreters who have attributed that name to some mute power of the heavens or to an atmospheric influence. I ask you: what reason should or can a European provide against the use of the name **Shangdi** that would not likewise apply—and even more strongly—in Europe against the name **God**? For in Europe, that name was corrupted much more frequently, for a longer time, and more foully than the name **Shangdi** ever was here.

But, you will say, at least this care and fear should deter the European preacher from using the name **Shangdi**: by doing so, the Christian law might seem to agree in many respects with the **Sect of the Literati** <note>The "Literati" refers to the Confucian scholar-officials, whose philosophy the Jesuits often tried to align with Christian ethics.</note>, and thus their conversion to the faith would be delayed. Yet, if this argument carries weight, it also works against what was just mentioned: for the same reason, the Apostles and other early preachers should not have used the names **God** <note>original: *Θεὸς* (Greek) or *Deus* (Latin)</note>, especially since other names established by God himself were available, such as **Eloe, Adonai, or Jehovah**. Nor would it be permitted for Christians living among Muslims to use the name **Allah** <note>original: *Halla*</note> when speaking Persian or Turkish, nor to use Hebrew names when speaking Hebrew, lest they be thought to agree with Muslims or Jews. It is not necessary for every single dogma or name to differ just so that one sect may be distinguished from another. Some things are common to the Christian law as well as to the Jewish and Muslim laws, and even to the **Sect of the Literati**—such as the belief that there is a supreme mind governing all things, that parents must be honored, and that principle: **"What you do not wish to be done to yourself, do not do to another"** <note>The "Golden Rule," which appears in both the Bible and the Confucian Analects.</note>, and so on. Indeed, the more we have in common with the Literati, the easier will be the path to their desired conversion. 

Who, I ask, would criticize **Jerome** <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his Bible translation.</note> for writing that the Christian religion is very similar to the **Stoic** discipline? (From which very discipline many passed over to Christianity and thereafter defended it with their writings and their blood). Who would argue with **Augustine** when he writes that he found the beginning of the Gospel of Saint John—**"In the beginning was the Word"**—among the **Platonic** philosophers? Who would condemn **Lactantius** <note>An early Christian author (c. 250–325) who frequently quoted pagan oracles to prove Christian truths.</note>, who throughout his work uses the authorities of the heathens against the Gentiles, and after reviewing which dogmas of our religion were also handed down by various philosophers, finally concludes: *“Therefore, the philosophers touched upon the whole truth and every secret of the divine Religion.”*

If the law of grace does not abolish the law of nature but rather perfects it, why should it not be permitted to bring forward the most beautiful "lights of nature" that can be found in the monuments of the ancients? This is especially true when even the sacred writers and the Fathers of the Church attempted to confirm those very things—which we know through God's revelation and which are most remote from human understanding—by the testimonies and authorities of the heathens; for example, the **Sybils**—

## SECTION ELEVEN. ##

### IT IS SHOWN THAT ONE SHOULD NOT ALWAYS ###
### *Abide by the authority of Modern Interpreters, but rather stick to the bare text as much as possible.* ###

BUT you will say: shouldn't the European Preacher be deterred by the authority of so many interpreters who have explained the authentic books of the **ancient Chinese** <note>original: *Sinarum veterum*</note> and forged a new kind of philosophy? This philosophy has been confirmed by the authority of Emperors and is celebrated today by the praise of everyone. But certainly, all these interpreters—even though some appeared five hundred years ago and others about three hundred years ago—must rightly be considered **Moderns** <note>original: *Neoterici*; the author refers to the Neo-Confucian scholars of the Song Dynasty (960–1279 AD) and later, whom the Jesuits viewed as having corrupted the original, "pure" monotheism of ancient China</note>. This is because four thousand years have passed since the founding of the Monarchy, and about 1,700 years since the time of **Confucius**, the common Teacher of the Empire. After so many monsters of idolatrous sects, so many wars, rebellions, murders of kin, and shifts in the Empire—which (by their own admission) interrupted the course and splendor of literature and the doctrine of the ancients for more than ten centuries—these scholars finally appeared with their new and imaginary commentaries. Thus, they should be viewed with suspicion by the European preacher.

But do we also think there will be those among the literati of the **Chinese nation** who will accuse us of rashness and pride? They might say that because we are outsiders, we neglect their long labors and commentaries to seek out the hidden meanings and secrets of the Ancients on our own. They might complain that we are now, in a way, proving those from whom we ought to learn to be in error, and attempting to teach them instead. For indeed, if they wished to apply themselves to Latin or Greek literature, we could act as their masters even here in **China**; but surely Chinese literature ought to be handed down by the Chinese, and whatever remains doubtful or obscure in it should be explained by the Chinese. Why then should we reject as false and counterfeit those interpretations with which legitimate sons have tried to illuminate the monuments of their ancestors? Why should we—strangers and unknowns who have so lately entered the "Ocean of Chinese literature"—rashly and arrogantly prefer the things we have thought up ourselves over a doctrine that has been so accepted for so long throughout the entire Empire? # PREFATORY DECLARATION #

...if they happened to migrate to Europe for the purpose of thoroughly learning the sacred volumes <note>The Bible</note>, they would by no means act in such a way. For they would surely be certain that they must stand by and acquiesce to the exposition of us Europeans—especially those who flourished in holiness and learning—mindful that they had come to Europe for the sake of learning, and not for teaching.

What a plausible speech! And if we contemplate its first appearance, how consistent it is with reason, and how full of fairness! Wherefore it is also less surprising if there have been some among the Europeans who were persuaded by it. This, therefore, is the foundation of the whole controversy; from here come all the scruples and anxieties by which they confess they are tormented. Before I attempt to tear these scruples from their minds, I would like to ask them this: Do they think they truly know those "Sages" and learned men whose opinions and interpretations they say we ought to follow? 

They are men of abandoned and ruined lives, who are content with a certain painted appearance of faith, integrity, and fairness, and with the lie of virtue rather than virtue itself. Meanwhile, they have hearts heaped with greed and ambition, deceit and plunder, and six hundred other vices. They are men "whose god is their belly" <note>A reference to the biblical verse Philippians 3:19, describing those focused on worldly desires</note>, who, immersed in the filth of their vices and most shameful lust, admit every kind of impurity. And although they lie cast down lower than four-footed beasts, yet by pride and insolence they raise themselves above the stars, boasting that they are Masters of the World and the wisest of men. 

And since they cannot gaze upon that light of Ancient Truth with the eyes of their corrupted minds—and even if they could, they would not want to—they naturally cloud and envelop everything in their own darkness and errors; and thus they disagree and fight, both within themselves and much more with one another. And so, those things which learned and religious antiquity piously and wisely attributed to a certain supreme Spirit, the Lord and Ruler of the Heavens, they themselves, no less impiously than stupidly, wish to attribute to their I-know-not-what <term>Taiji</term> <note>original: *Tai kie*; the "Supreme Ultimate" or fundamental principle in Neo-Confucianism</note>, <term>Li</term> <note>The "Principle" or underlying pattern of reality</note>, and <term>Qi</term> <note>original: *Ki*; the vital energy or material force</note>, <term>Yin</term> <note>original: *Yn*</note>, and <term>Yang</term>—by some accidental influxes, and other monsters not so much of things as of letters and words. 

They themselves have invented the meanings of these terms, adapted to their own errors and <term>atheism</term> <note>The author, like many Jesuit contemporaries, viewed the Neo-Confucian "Li" as a materialistic or atheistic departure from ancient Chinese monotheism</note>. But indeed, these ideas are so foreign to every appearance of truth, and so distant from the minds of their Ancestors, that I believe it could never have entered the minds of those Ancient Sages, even in a dream, that their depraved descendants would come up with such ridiculous fictions and daydreams.

And will there be anyone who thinks anything should be granted to men of this sort? Who thinks trust should be given to them? Who wants us to stand by their opinions and interpretation? "But," they will say, "if it happened that they were staying in our Europe, and some doubt or controversy arose concerning the genuine sense <note>original: *Germano sensu*; meaning the authentic or true meaning</note> of the **Bible** <note>original: *Bibliorum*</note>, they would certainly stand not by their own opinion, but by ours—that of the Europeans, and especially by the opinion and interpretation of the **Holy Fathers** <note>original: *SS. Patrum*; the authoritative early Christian theologians</note>. Why then should we, in turn, who are staying in **China**, not listen to and follow them?"

What of the fact that *Confucius* himself and *Mencius* <note>original: "Memcius"</note> could be called Interpreters, as their chief praise was that they faithfully interpreted the books of the Ancients?

It would have been better never to have undertaken a contest of this kind than to have undertaken it so inauspiciously at the whim and will of treacherous enemies. What then is required to be done here, someone might ask? What counsel do you yourself suggest to us? None other, indeed, than what the matter itself and reason would suggest to any prudent person, and which those Wise and Holy Men <note>The Church Fathers</note> would undoubtedly have adopted if such a situation had arisen in their times: Namely, that since they did not hesitate to leave their homeland, cross the seas, and expose their lives to a thousand dangers for the sake of Christ, they should not refuse to devote their effort to thoroughly learning the Hebrew language and its letters for the sake of that same Christ. And though it might be necessary to be hidden away in a certain solitude, as Saint Jerome was, and there for three or four years devote effort to studies that are by no means pleasant, they should nevertheless perform this with an eager and strong spirit, always keeping the great utility and necessity of the task before their eyes.

But once they have achieved proficiency in the language, let them then begin to weigh the Hebrew texts for themselves, and "turn those Sacred Pages" <note>original: "nocturnâ versare manu, versate diurnâ"; a reference to the Roman poet Horace’s advice to study classic texts "by night and by day."</note>—the masters of indubitable truth—with a nightly and a daily hand. As for others who are known to be perverse and obstinate, even if they are learned and possess the greatest authority among their own people, let the missionaries disregard them and not listen to them at all. 

However, when the true and genuine sense of the Hebrew text is finally established for them, let them "descend into the arena" and engage with the <term>Rabbis</term> <note>Jewish scholars and teachers of the law</note> themselves. Jerome, certainly that great light of the Christian world, followed no other path; and with what reward for his work, with what success and fruit of labor, all lands and all ages now bear witness.

However, what reward for his efforts do we believe a person will gain if they follow this path? What fruit will they eventually bring back from their labor? Is it to lead people from their errors to the **Gospel truth**? Certainly, the result would be nothing other than to leave the enemies of truth even more hardened in their errors. And one must hope that the missionary himself does not return home infected by the pernicious principles of **Mohammedanism** <term>Mohammedanism: An archaic Western term for Islam, used here to refer to the religious influences encountered during travel through Central or Western Asia.</term>, the dogmas of heretics, or—if he should happen to reach China—the poison of **Atheism** and **Idolatry**.

From all these things, let a fair judge decide what the duty of a wise man should be, especially one who travels to remote lands for the purpose of proclaiming the **Gospel Law**. Truly, when he reaches a region whose inhabitants he desires to gather to Christ, if that nation happens to possess certain monuments of literature and wisdom received from their ancestors, he must not condemn or approve them with a hasty or blind judgment. Nor should he rashly condemn or approve those who have interpreted the ancient books of that nation, whether they are foreigners or natives. 

Avoiding extremes, a wise man should insist on a middle path. Thus, having implored the help of the Supreme Deity, he first exerts himself to learn the language and letters of the nation accurately. Then, he should diligently study the books he finds to be of greater value there, as well as the interpretations of those books, examining and weighing them again and again. Meanwhile, he must most studiously investigate whether the sincerity and truth of the ancient text remain intact, or if, on the contrary, it has been corrupted by the negligence or even the wickedness of later generations. Furthermore, he must see whether those who act as interpreters here consistently follow in the footsteps of their ancestors, or whether they deprave their doctrine and twist it toward their own errors—or perhaps toward the desires of their Prince, whom they wish to flatter (however corrupt he may be). In this way, they might use the authority and wisdom of the Ancients to provide a defense for their own insanity, the insanity of others, and the corruption of morals. Finally, he should see whether there is a single mind and doctrine among them all, or if, conversely, they disagree and clash with one another and within themselves.

When all these things have been properly understood and perceived in this manner, if he realizes that nothing solid or true is contained in the aforementioned monuments and books, he should certainly not touch them, nor even make mention of them. But if the ancient Kings or Teachers of the nation, with nature also as their guide and mistress, achieved many things that are so far from opposing the **Gospel light** and truth that they even benefit and favor it—appearing like the morning twilight opening the path for the **Sun of Justice** <note>original: "Soli justitiae"; a traditional Christian title for Jesus Christ, derived from the biblical book of Malachi 4:2, suggesting that ancient wisdom can prepare a people for the arrival of the "true light" of Christ.</note>—then the **Heralds of the Gospel law** <term>Gospel Heralds: A term for Christian missionaries.</term> should by no means (if they would listen to me) despise those things. Instead, they should use them constantly. Thus, with the native juice of the local doctrine (which, because it is of their own country, is naturally suited to please the palate of the citizens), they will instill the foreign ambrosia of heavenly doctrine into the tender minds of the **Neophytes** <term>Neophytes: A term for new converts to the Christian faith, from the Greek for "newly planted."</term>.
