# TWELFTH PARAGRAPH.
## FATHER MATTEO RICCI RELEASES A BOOK
### *on Divine Law; with what success and fruit.*

Therefore, after all these things had been maturely weighed before God; after the most constant and arduous labor, after day and night vigils, and after repeated conversations and disputes with so many literati of distinguished reputation for nearly twenty years; after severe examinations of books both ancient and modern, finally that new stranger from the West, that new proclaimer of a doctrine both new and ancient, Matteo Ricci, brought forth into the public light of the Chinese world a work on the Christian Religion consisting of two volumes. Its title was *Tien hio xey* <note>original: "Tien hio xey" — usually transliterated as *T'ien-chu shih-i*, or "The True Meaning of the Lord of Heaven."</note>, that is, *The True Meaning of the Celestial Doctrine*. It was printed in the very court of the Empire in the 31st year of the reign of *Van lie* <note>The Wanli Emperor, who reigned from 1572 to 1620.</note>, which was the 40th year of the seventy-second Chinese period or cycle, called *Quei mao* <note>The Gui-mao year in the Chinese sexagenary cycle.</note>, and the year of our salvation 1603.

First of all, on the very threshold of the entire work, he boldly declares how gravely the whole nation has sinned against the supreme Divinity of Heaven and against the Emperor through such wicked dogmas, through so many sects and such pernicious heresies, and finally through such great corruption of morals. He argues that for this very reason, so many and such great calamities and such a miserable disturbance of affairs and times followed. He then begins a discourse on the supreme Lord of all, the Creator and Preserver, and His names, properties, and divine excellencies. 

After this, he proceeds to loosen that "triple cord" of the three sects <note>The "Three Teachings" of China: Confucianism, Buddhism, and Taoism.</note>. Here the Bonzes <term>Bonzes: A term used by early European explorers and missionaries to refer to Buddhist monks.</term> see their dreams eluded, along with the foundation of nearly all those dreams and lies: *Metempsychosis* <term>Metempsychosis: The transmigration of souls, or reincarnation; a core tenet of Buddhism that Ricci argued against.</term>. Here the sectarians of *Tao* <note>Taoism.</note> see their superstitions and empty dogmas utterly overturned. Here the principles of the recent family of Interpreters from the *Sum* <note>The Song Dynasty (960–1279 AD), whose Neo-Confucian scholars reinterpreted the ancient classics.</note> collapse, along with their new commentaries. Their entire philosophy regarding *Tai kie* <term>Taiji: The "Supreme Ultimate," which Neo-Confucians viewed as an impersonal first principle, but which Ricci argued was being misinterpreted as a material cause.</term> and *Li* <term>Li: "Principle" or "Reason," a central concept in Neo-Confucianism.</term>, and the notion *that all things are one*, are thoroughly crushed by the weight of reason and eternal truth. Indeed, he courageously summons them to judgment; he orders these degenerate descendants to appear before their own ancestors—the kings and wise men of the ancient age—as if before so many incorruptible judges. There, they must give an account of their doctrine, every part of which he examines like a severe prosecutor of the most ancient literary monuments, treating them as codes of ancient law. He asks in what part of those classic volumes they ever read of sacrificing to, serving, obeying, or fearing...

...to worship, revere, and pray to their own *Taiji* <note>original: "Tai kie" — the "Great Ultimate," a cosmological term in Chinese philosophy.</note> or *Li* <note>original: "Li" — often translated as "Principle" or "Reason."</note>, even though one very frequently reads that all these things were done for *Shangdi* <note>original: "Xam ti" — the "Supreme Emperor" or "High Deity" found in ancient Chinese classics.</note>, the Supreme Emperor of the heavens. According to these very same records, this figure is identical to the Supreme Lord and Governor of the heavens whom Ricci came to announce.

Furthermore—something you might find surprising for a foreigner living among so many scholars who despise outsiders, especially under the exceptionally proud Ming <note>original: "Mim"</note> dynasty—Ricci even dared to utter these words in the capital of Beijing, the very theater of the Chinese world: *"The error of the scholars of this present age in explaining the books of the Ancients cannot be sufficiently expressed in words. As far as the ornament of flowery writing is concerned, they are ready and sharp; but as far as the understanding of meanings, they are most negligent."* He concludes, therefore: *"Although the modern writing style is exceedingly flowery and ornate, the truth and solidity of works and right actions are lacking."* Since he rebuked all the living in this way, even in the imperial court, should we be surprised that certain deceased Interpreters were punished with a most well-deserved censure?

Because the foundation of the Christian faith is the knowledge and belief in the true God, he initially imparted this under the name *Tianzhu* <note>original: "Tien chu" — "Lord of Heaven."</note>. We began using this name at the start, when we did not yet have mastery of Chinese books, and we have chosen to keep it even to this day. Afterward, once he had studied the books of the Ancients, he most confidently bestowed the name *Shangdi* <note>original: "Xam ti"</note> upon the Chinese. To remove all danger of error or offense, and to take away any occasion for doubt or perplexity—both from the idolaters when they hear *Tianzhu*, and from the politically-motivated atheists <note>original: "atheopoliticis" — likely referring to Neo-Confucian scholars who interpreted traditional spiritual terms in a purely physical or social sense.</note> when they hear *Shangdi*—he deliberately calls God by various other names. At times he calls Him the Lord of Heaven and Earth and the Supreme Emperor; at others, the Supreme King and Governor of the Heavens; sometimes the Majesty of the Supreme Emperor; sometimes the Creator and Conserver of all things; sometimes the Common Parent of the human race, the Beginning and the End, and other such titles. Finally, he preaches God with so many and such distinguished attributes that no one who reads could be so blind as not to see the divine clarity radiating before the eyes of the mind.

Meanwhile, many of the scholars—specifically those who had frequently heard Ricci's discussions and had even joined him as close associates—rejoiced in a wonderful way. They were learning not only what their own ancient citizens thought about the Supreme Deity and the immortality of the soul, but also more illustrious things they had never heard or even imagined concerning that Supreme Majesty. For instance, they learned how He created all things from nothing, the order of creation, the fall of the Angels, the first man, and other such truths which the Eternal Truth has revealed to us. Moreover, they derived a fruit of the sweetest consolation from one particular thing: they understood that Divine Mercy did not seem to have been always turned away from their nation, but that those ancient citizens and pious fathers of theirs had been [visited] by a certain saving light of truth...

...[that they] had been enlightened, and that that ancient age, once certain blemishes and clouds were removed, had remained safe and whole for several centuries, as they piously believed.

A curious reader might ask here: with what success or fruit did this work of our Matteo [Ricci] come to light? I answer: it was absolutely admirable, and such as could never have been hoped for according to human reasoning. Certainly, any European who has a deep understanding of China—what the constitutions and laws regarding religion are here, how great the authority of the scholars <note>The *literati*, or scholar-official class, who held immense power in Ming China.</note> was at that time, how great the contempt was everywhere for things coming from abroad and for foreigners themselves, and how great the horror of any foreign law or novelty (especially one brought in by a foreigner without any public faculty or authority)—if such an European, I say, maturesly considers all these things, he cannot help but acknowledge and profess that "the finger of God" was in this work and its success. For what the Lord had promised Ricci as he was entering—*that He would be favorable to him in Beijing* <note>original: "Pekini propitium se fore"</note>—was indeed fulfilled according to his wishes, and even beyond his expectations.

Indeed, Ricci did not come in the manner of an official ambassador, but as a private person, though equipped with his own modest gifts; nor did he come summoned or invited, as the followers and masters of Indian superstition <note>A common, though derogatory, 17th-century Jesuit term for Buddhism, noting its origins in India.</note> once arrived.

To set aside the testimonies of our own Society [of Jesus], let the single testimony of the Reverend Father Friar Dominic Sarpetro suffice for many. He was a most religious man of the Holy Order of Preachers [the Dominicans] who stayed in China for nearly 30 years and was exceptionally skilled in Chinese literature; he was clearly outstanding in doctrine, virtue, and religious observance. In those letters which he sent from the metropolis of Guangzhou <note>original: "Cantonensi"</note> (our residence for those exiled for the faith) to the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith <note>The Vatican department responsible for missionary work.</note> and to his own Most Reverend General—after he solemnly professed that he was driven to write by no favor, persuasion, or prayers, but by the love of truth alone—he says thus:

> *Concerning this book (namely, that of Matteo Ricci) which I have often read attentively, I testify that it has frequently come to mind that the said book was a work of such a kind that it could not have been completed by the author without divine revelation or other special help from God. In witness of which I have signed with my own hand on the ninth of May, 1667, in the metropolis of Guangzhou <note>original: "Quam-cheu"</note> in the Province of Guangdong <note>original: "Quam-tum"</note>.*

-> DOMINIC MARY SARPETRO. <-

...even though those little books were suppressed by the wickedness of certain ill-wishers, it can hardly be believed how much power they exerted on the minds of wise and sensible men. Thus, there was by no means a general conspiracy of everyone against the divine law, but rather the opposition of only one or two atheistic politicians <term>Atheopolitici</term> <note>A term used by the Jesuits to describe Confucian officials who held secular or naturalistic views, rejecting the supernatural aspects of Christianity.</note>, or idolaters, or even those jealous of European glory and wisdom. There was a time when eighteen petitions against the law of Christ were offered to the last Emperor of the preceding family <note>The Ming Dynasty (1368–1644).</note>, who rejected them all. He even punished the official who stubbornly offered them, demoting him to a lower rank of dignity. He would have inflicted an even greater punishment, had not the wise Emperor (as he ordered to be announced to Father Johann Adam Schall <term>Joanni Adamo Schall</term> <note>A German Jesuit (1592–1666) who became a high-ranking official in the Chinese Bureau of Astronomy.</note>) considered that this matter involved "exterior men" <note>original: "hominum exteriorum"; a term for foreigners.</note>, and a heavier punishment against a native official might cause great hatred toward the foreigners among their own people.

And indeed, it has long been found through use and experience that those things which most offend and irritate the minds of the Chinese <term>Sinenſium</term> are not so much the laws and institutions of the Christian faith itself, as the fact that all other sects (even those of the modern literati) are condemned by the one Christian Religion. They also criticize certain ceremonies and rites, as well as the gatherings that are held of men and especially of women, although they are not gathered at the same place and time. The frequency of "exterior men" settling in various Provinces also displeases them, as does their authority among their followers and disciples, and the singular favor they enjoy even among the pagan <note>original: "Ethnicos"; referring to non-Christian Chinese officials.</note> Magistrates. 

We learned this very thing most especially by experience during these last years, when a far more savage storm arose against us under the rule of the Tartar <term>Tartaro</term> <note>Refers to the Manchu rulers of the Qing Dynasty, specifically during the regency of the Oboi (1661–1669) when the Jesuits were persecuted.</note>. For we were brought under suspicion of rebellion and condemned for teaching a false and depraved religion. However, when at last, by God’s mercy, the slanders of the wicked were exposed, and the innocence and integrity of the Christian Religion was legally declared in the solemn assemblies of the Kingdom and published through all the Provinces by Royal edicts, a great care and fear nevertheless remained in the Tartar ruler (whom his own small numbers here force to fear everything in order to remain safe). 

After the Emperor himself <note>The Kangxi Emperor (reigned 1661–1722).</note>, with an unusual sign of honor and benevolence, had permitted the Priests of our Society <note>The Jesuits.</note> who live at court to live according to the Christian rite and with almost their former liberty, he likewise granted a certain unspoken liberty and approval of the divine law to the rest of our associates who were soon recalled to their former residences. This was most evident when, on July 12, 1675, the Emperor himself, visiting our Temple and House, wrote with his own hand and Royal brush two large-scale characters <note>original: "trabales litteras"; literally "beam-sized letters," referring to a large calligraphic plaque.</note> ***Kim tien***, that is, ***revere heaven*** <note>original: "reverere cælum"; the Chinese characters *Jing tian* (敬天).</note>, or, what is the same among them, ***revere the Lord of heaven***. These letters, protected by the Royal seal—or rather, copies of them—were placed upon our churches and houses in three orders <note>Possibly referring to the three different styles of calligraphic presentation or different ranks of buildings.</note>. It is marvelous how much authority they secure for the Christian faith and its heralds, even for the centuries to come.

# PREFATORY DECLARATION. 112

->CONCLUSION.<-

And here at last let there be an end to our Prefatory Declaration—if indeed the size of the work and the subject matter allow for such a name, since it could well be called a distinct Book in its own right. In this, we seem to have been not quite mindful enough that we are writing for Europeans, for whom indeed, as wise men, even a few words would have sufficed. However, I hope they will, out of their benevolence, forgive our wordiness when they consider that we had to travel through ages spanning two thousand years and more. Furthermore, what is being dealt with is by no means of slight importance, since the goal is to vindicate the entire ancient age of so numerous and cultured a nation from the suspicion of abominable atheism. There was also this reason: that these things are written especially for the sake of those who will one day come here to announce the truth <note>The Christian Gospel.</note>. We would certainly not want them to come here imbued with such a suspicion; for besides being far from the truth, it brings this additional disadvantage: it would disarm the soldier of Christ of a truly suitable and powerful weapon with which he could successfully attack either the worshipers of false Deities or the worshipers of no Deity at all, and by that same weapon—with Christ always as leader and protector—conquer them.

In addition, it pleased us to follow our own affairs and those of the Chinese <term>Sinicas</term> simultaneously by narrating, explaining, and debating. For we narrate the first efforts and labors of those who brought the light of the Gospel into these lands; we deal with the moral and political science of the people; we review the Classical books and all the principal monuments of literature, both ancient and modern. We also mention the sects, partly native and partly foreign but now settled here. We also explain their natural philosophy to some extent from the *Ye kim* <note>original: *Ye kim*; the *I Ching* or *Book of Changes*.</note>, or the most ancient "book of mutations," all of which we leave to be discussed by the sharp minds of Europeans. Finally, we discuss at length what kind of "principle of all things" the scholars <term>litterati</term> <note>The Confucian scholar-official class.</note> of both the Ancient and later ages established; specifically, how they once knew the true Deity, by what name they signified Him, and how long this knowledge and true Religion can be considered to have flourished. And although from the sequence of time it seems it can probably be inferred that it persisted in China until the times of King You <note>original: *Yeu* vam; King You of Zhou (r. 781–771 BCE).</note>, the twelfth ruler of the third Dynasty, the Zhou <note>original: *Cheu*</note>, about two hundred years before the birth of Confucius, and nearly eight hundred years before Christ; yet we do not wish to establish a certain and evident foundation for our opinion from this, but leave the whole dissertation to the judgment of Europe. Let it suffice for us here to have shown that, from times very close to the flood (whether you calculate them according to the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament, which offered a longer chronology than the Hebrew text.</note> or according to the Vulgate), the first Chinese had knowledge of the true God, and held it under the name *Xamti* <note>original: *Xamti*; *Shangdi*, or "Supreme Deity."</note>, the Supreme Emperor, or even *Tien* <note>original: *Tien*; *Tian*, or "Heaven."</note>.

<sig>f f</sig>

<summary>The author concludes his introduction by arguing that ancient Chinese culture was originally monotheistic rather than atheistic, identifying "Shangdi" and "Tian" as names for the true God. He positions this historical research as a vital "weapon" for missionaries to use when converting the Chinese by appealing to their own ancient traditions.</summary>

# PREFATORY DECLARATION. cxiv

As for the interpreter of *Confucius*, or Chinese Knowledge, he is *Zhang Juzheng* <note>original: "Cham Kiu Chim"; Zhang Juzheng (1525–1582) was a powerful Grand Secretary during the Ming Dynasty.</note>, a native of the city of *Jiangling* <note>original: "Kim lim"</note>, which is under the jurisdiction of the city of *Jingzhou* <note>original: "Kim cheu"</note> in *Huguang* Province. This interpreter is second to none in the richness and abundance of his speech or the clarity of his style. Consequently, the Emperor *Wanli*, at the age of ten, so cherished and revered him as his Tutor and Master, and as the first Minister of the Empire, that he would visit him when he was ill. The Emperor, like a disciple to a master, would even offer him a medicinal drink he had prepared himself. After his death, the Emperor also honored him with the posthumous title *Wenzhong* <note>original: "ven chum"</note>, which means *a man distinguished by letters and loyalty* <note>original: "viri litteris <unclear>ε)</unclear> fide præstantis"</note>. He delegated a Mandarin of the highest rank to escort the deceased's body from the court where he had died back to his ancestral tomb in *Huguang* Province with great ceremony. Nevertheless, in the second year after his death (which was the twelfth year of the Emperor *Wanli's* reign), he was gravely accused by his rivals. By imperial decree, he and his descendants were stripped of their dignities and titles, and all his fortunes were confiscated by the Royal Treasury.

When the Senate <note>The Grand Secretariat or Board of Rites.</note> moved to extinguish his memory entirely, even suggesting that his books and commentaries be destroyed by fire, the Emperor refused, saying:

> *The books did not sin; why then should works so profitable and innocent perish?*

As for why it pleased us to select him as our chief Interpreter above all others, the reason was that his commentaries are in everyone's hands and are most highly celebrated. Although he is nearly the most recent among the modern scholars, he seems to have paid less heed to the chimerical novelties of others; for this reason alone, he is worthy of being the primary guide we follow. We have, however, occasionally trimmed his style—which is often quite lush for the sake of the Chinese youth—for the benefit of Europeans. Even so, I suspect we shall not escape the criticism of wordiness. This would be a fair point of attack if we were writing these things for the amusement of a fastidious Europe rather than for the practical use of the Chinese Mission. Yet, even here, remedies for such boredom will not be lacking, drawn studiously from their ancient books and monuments, as well as the Chronological and Genealogical Table of the annals of this nation, which it pleased us to add to the work. Farewell, and commend China to God, the Best and Greatest. Whether you look at the vastness of the land and the multitude of its people, or the maturity of their manners and character and the excellent lights implanted in them by the Author of Nature <note>A common Jesuit term for God as perceived through natural reason.</note>, she will perhaps seem not unworthy of having all of Europe spend and exhaust itself to promote her conversion and eternal salvation.

->PHILIPPE COUPLET of the Society of JESUS<-
->Procurator of the Chinese Mission to the City [of Rome].<-

->TO GOD ALONE BE HONOR AND GLORY.<-

->CONFUCIUS<-

<image-desc>A decorative rectangular woodcut header featuring symmetrical scrolling acanthus leaves, floral motifs, and a central stylized mask or face.</image-desc>

## OF THE CHINESE PHILOSOPHERS
### THE LEADER
# C O N F U C I U S
## L I F E

<image-desc>An ornate square woodcut initial 'C' containing a large flower and surrounding foliage, beginning the word 'CUM'.</image-desc>

*CUM FU CU*, or Confucius, whom the *Chinese* follow and revere as the Leader of their *Philosophy*, was called by the common or rather domestic name *Kieu* <note>Kong Qiu</note>; and by the courtesy name *Chum nhi* <note>Zhongni</note>. He had his birthplace in the Kingdom of *Lu* (which kingdom is today called *Shandong* <note>original: Xantum</note>) in the village of *çeu ye* of the *Changping* <note>original: Cham pim</note> territory, which belongs to the city of *Qufu* <note>original: Kio seu</note>; moreover, this city is subject to the city called *Yanzhou* <note>original: Yen cheu</note>. He was born in the 21st year of the Emperor *King Ling* <note>original: Lim vam; r. 571–545 BCE</note>. This emperor was the twenty-third from the third Family, or Imperial house, called *Zhou* <note>original: Cheu</note>, in the 47th year of the 36th cycle, called *Kem fio*; likewise in the twenty-second year of King *Xiang Gong* <note>original: Siam cum</note>, who at that time held the Kingdom of *Lu*: on the 21st day of the eleventh moon called *Kem çu*, around the second hour of the night, in the year 551 before the birth of Christ. His mother was *Zheng* <note>original: Chim</note>, originating from the very noble *Yan* <note>original: Yen</note> family; his father was *Shu-liang He* <note>original: Xo leam he</note>, who was illustrious not only for the first-order magistracy which he held in the Kingdom of *Song* <note>original: Sum</note>, but also for the nobility of his lineage; for he traced his descent (as the *Chinese Chronicles* testify, and the genealogical table inserted in the annals clearly teaches) from the 27th or penultimate Emperor, *Di Yi* <note>original: Ti ye</note>, of the 2nd family, *Shang* <note>original: Xam</note>. Furthermore, Confucius was born when his father was already seventy years old, whom he soon lost as an infant of three years; but his mother then survived as the guardian of the ward for twenty-one years, her husband having been buried on Mount *Fang* <note>original: Tum fam</note> in the Kingdom of *Lu*. Already as a six-year-old boy, with a certain premature maturity, being more like a man than a child, he was never seen playing with his peers. He would not taste offered food before he had reverently offered it to heaven according to the ancient rite called *zu dou* <note>original: çu teu; referring to the use of ritual sacrificial vessels</note>. As a youth of fifteen years, he began to devote himself entirely to unrolling the books of the ancients, and having rejected those things which seemed less useful, [choosing] all the best...

<image-desc>An ornate square woodcut initial 'C' decorated with floral and leaf patterns.</image-desc>CUM FU CU, or Confucius—whom the Chinese <note>original: "Sinenses"</note> follow and revere as the Prince of their *Philosophy*—was known by his common or rather domestic name, Kieu; his courtesy name was Chum nhi. This Emperor was the twenty-third from the third Family, or Imperial House, called Cheu <note>The Zhou Dynasty</note>, in the 47th year of the 36th cycle <note>The Chinese sexagenary cycle, a sixty-year calendar system</note>, called Kem fio; likewise, it was in the twenty-second year of King Siam cum, who held the Kingdom of Lu at that time: on the 13th day of the eleventh moon, called Kem çu, at about the second hour of the night, in the year 551 before the birth of Christ. His mother was Chim, descended from the most noble Yen family; his father was Xo leam he, who was illustrious not only for the first-rank <term>Magistracy|A high-ranking administrative or judicial office</term> which he held in the Kingdom of Sum, but also for the nobility of his lineage. Indeed, he traced his ancestry (as the Chinese Chronicles testify, and the genealogical table inserted in the annals clearly shows) from the 27th or second-to-last Emperor, Ti ye, of the 2nd family, the Xam <note>The Shang Dynasty</note>. Furthermore, Confucius was born when his father was already seventy years old, and as a three-year-old infant, he soon lost him; however, his mother survived her ward for twenty-one years, while her husband was buried on Mount Tum fam in the Kingdom of Lu. Even as a six-year-old boy, possessing a certain premature maturity—making him seem more like a man than a child—he was never seen playing with his peers. he selected documents, first intending to express them through his own character, and then to set them forth for others to imitate. Not long after, together with *Mem çu* <note>Mengzi or Mencius, though here likely referring to a contemporary student or associate</note> and *Nan cum kim xo*, he applied himself to learning civil rites. In his nineteenth or, as others say, his twentieth year of age, he took a wife, who was his only one, *Kien quon xi*, from whom he received a son, *Pe yu* <note>Kong Li, also known as Boyu</note>, in the following year; but he was later deprived of this son when the son was fifty and he himself was 69 years old, his wife having been lost three years prior. However, the lineage was by no means extinguished with his son, but through his grandson *çu su* <note>Zisi, the famous philosopher and author of the 'Doctrine of the Mean'</note>, who, being a student of his grandfather's praise and Philosophy, wrote commentaries on his grandfather’s books; having performed great duties in the Empire, the lineage continues through a perpetual succession of descendants with no common wealth and dignity even to these present times.

The Philosopher held the office of <term>Magistrate|A civil officer or lay judge who administers the law</term> in various places with great praise: indeed, he accepted cares and dignities of this kind for no other reason than for public utility and the hope of propagating his doctrine. If by chance he saw himself frustrated in this hope, he would voluntarily abdicate his office. He gave an illustrious testimony of this matter many times, but especially in the 55th year of his age; for when he served as a **Mandarin** <note>original: "Mandarinum"</note> in the Kingdom of *Lu* (I speak here in the manner of the Portuguese, by whom those who administer public affairs among the Chinese <note>original: "Sinas"</note> are called **Mandarins**), such great observation of the laws and such a happy conversion of affairs and customs followed within a three-month period that neighboring Kings and rivals were soon seized by envy and fear. They were well aware that Republics are preserved and grow by nothing more happily than by discipline and the observation of laws. Therefore, the King and nobles of the neighboring Kingdom called *Çi* <note>Qi</note>, intending to lay snares for the excellent government of their rivals, covered them—as is often done—with gifts: they sent as a gift to the King of the Kingdom of *Lu* girls surpassing in beauty, the grace of singing, and other talents. The King, unaware of the snares, accepted the deceitful gift and was immediately captured by the charms of the young women. The nobles were also captivated, so much so that for an entire three months, while they indulged in those new delights, public business ceased and the way to approach the King was blocked. Confucius did not tolerate this: he resigned his office, left the court, and went as a voluntary exile to the Kingdoms of *Çi* <note>Qi</note>, *Guei* <note>Wei</note>, and *Çu* <note>Chu</note>. But these nations did not know how to enjoy the good which they had envied in others. The Philosopher was not admitted, and thus he was forced to seek the Kingdom of *Chim* <note>Chen</note>; here he was reduced even to an extreme penury of food. Not long after, while he traveled through the Kingdom of *Sum* <note>Song</note>, he was more than once sought for death by a certain *Huon tui* <note>Huan Tui</note>, an exceedingly powerful but remarkably wicked man. Meanwhile, amidst so many hardships and dangers, he remained always like himself, with an unconquered spirit, and ready to lay down his life for so good a cause. However, relying on the conscience of his right deeds and on heavenly protection, he declared that no one could harm him, since he was furnished with that virtue which rested upon heaven itself. He did not relax his ardent and indefatigable study of spreading sounder doctrine throughout the whole Empire until his very last breath; and since the man’s passion could hardly be contained within his native borders, he more than once thought of sailing the sea and visiting more remote lands.

<meta>This page continues the biography of Confucius, moving from his political career and personal lineage to a description of his school, the classifications of his many disciples, and the core tenets of his moral philosophy, often drawing parallels to Christian ethics.</meta>

<page-num>CXIX</page-num>
<header>THE LIFE OF CONFUCIUS.</header>

He counted 3,000 disciples. Of these, it is recorded that five hundred emerged to hold positions as <term>Magistrates|Government officials or civil administrators</term> in various Kingdoms. However, seventy-two were particularly eminent in virtue and letters; their names, surnames, and the native lands from which each originated are preserved in the historical record.

He established four levels, as it were, of his doctrine, and an equal number of ranks for his disciples. The **highest rank** placed its study in cultivating the soul through the virtues. In this rank, the foremost were *Min çu Kien* <note>Min Ziqian</note>, *Gen Pe Nieu* <note>Ran Boniu</note>, *Chum cum* <note>Ran Yong (Zhonggong)</note>, and finally *Yen yven* <note>Yan Hui</note>, the disciple dear to the Master above all others. The Master continually mourned his untimely death, for he died in the thirty-first year of his age.

The **next rank** devoted its labor to the faculty of reasoning and eloquence; the leaders of this group were *çai ngo* <note>Zai Wo</note> and *çu cum* <note>Zigong</note>.

The **third rank** dealt with political governance and the proper administration of public duties; *Gen yeu* <note>Ran You</note> and *Ki lu* <note>Zilu</note> excelled here.

Finally, the labor and occupation of the **fourth and last rank** was to explain matters pertaining to ethics in a fit and elegant style; two disciples, *çu yeu* <note>Ziyou</note> and *çu hia* <note>Zixia</note>, performed this with particular praise. Indeed, among the seventy-two, these ten were the most select disciples and the "flower" of the Confucian school.

Every study and doctrine of the Philosopher aimed primarily at this: that he might recall human nature—which had been obscured by the darkness of ignorance and corrupted by vices—to its original light and integrity, with which it was endowed when created by Heaven itself. From this would follow a merciful and just administration of affairs, and consequently a happy and most peaceful state of the Empire. Moreover, so that this goal might be more surely attained, he wished all people to obey Heaven, and to fear and worship it; to love one's neighbor as oneself; to conquer oneself and subject one’s appetites to reason; and to do, say, or even think nothing that was alien to this path.

Furthermore, what he taught by the spoken and written word, he was the first to express through his own character and life. Sufficiently clear testimony of this is provided by the great number of so many illustrious men who joined his discipline, and those who, as eyewitnesses, passed down to posterity everything he did and said, even the smallest details. To this, the constant favor of so many Princes and the great honor of so many centuries (which we shall discuss shortly) serves as proof that the Philosopher possessed true virtue, not a mere appearance or pretense of it.

What more shall I say? In our own times, there have been many from the order of Literati <note>The scholar-official class in China</note> who—having either already embraced the Christian Religion or at least having clearly perceived its integrity and holiness—affirmed without hesitation their hope that their Philosopher, had he lived in our age, would have been the first to transition to the law of Christ. Certainly, as his followers pass down, there was a wonderful gravity in the man, a moderation of both body and soul, and a singular faith, equity, and gentleness. He was a severe and vigilant observer and censor of himself: a despiser of wealth and honors, acting with an utterly tireless zeal to impart his doctrine to as many mortals as possible.

However, that which we Europeans admire most in him, and which we find lacking even in our own philosophers of ancient times, was that Confucius possessed such great humility of soul...

The leading men were also captured, so much so that for three whole months, while they indulged in those new delights, public business ceased and the way of approaching the King was blocked. But these men also did not know how to enjoy the good which they had envied in others. The Philosopher was not admitted, and thus he was compelled to seek the Kingdom of Chim <note>Chen</note>; here he was reduced even to an extreme penury of food. Not long after, while he traveled through the Kingdom of Sum <note>Song</note>, he was more than once sought for death by a certain Huon tui <note>Huan Tui</note>, a very powerful man but remarkably wicked. Meanwhile, amidst so many hardships and dangers, he was always like himself, with an always unconquered spirit, and ready to lay down even his life for so good a cause. However, relying on the consciousness of his right deeds and on heavenly protection, he declared in turn that no one could harm him, since he was equipped with that virtue which leaned upon Heaven itself. <meta>This page continues the biography of Confucius from page 118, moving from his early life and family to the structure of his school, the character of his disciples, and his core philosophical teachings.</meta>

<page-num>cxix</page-num>

-> # THE LIFE OF CONFUCIUS <-

He counted three thousand disciples in total. Among them, it is recorded that five hundred went on to serve as <term>Magistrates|High-ranking civil officials or governors</term> in various Kingdoms. However, seventy-two were considered truly eminent in both virtue and letters; their names, surnames, and even their birthplaces have been preserved by history. Confucius established four levels, or grades, for his teachings, and categorized his disciples into four corresponding orders. 

The **highest order** focused their study on cultivating the soul through the practice of virtues. In this rank, the most prominent were Min çu Kien <note>Min Ziqian</note>, Gen Pe Nieu <note>Ran Boniu</note>, Chum cum <note>Zhong Gong</note>, and finally Yen yven <note>Yan Hui</note>, the Master’s most beloved disciple. Confucius mourned him incessantly after his untimely death, for he passed away in only his thirty-first year. 

The **second order** dedicated themselves to the faculty of reasoning and eloquent speech <note>original: "ratiocinandi, dicendique facultati"</note>. The leaders of this group were çai ngo <note>Zai Wo</note> and çu cum <note>Zi Gong</note>. 

The **third order** dealt with political governance and the proper administration of public duties; here, Gen yeu <note>Ran You</note> and Ki Lu <note>Zilu</note> excelled. 

Finally, the labor and occupation of the **fourth order** was to express matters of morality in a fitting and beautiful style, a task performed with particular praise by çu yeu <note>Ziyou</note> and çu hia <note>Zixia</note>. 

These ten were the most select among the seventy-two, representing the very flower of the *Confucian* school. The entire study and teaching of the Philosopher aimed primarily at this: to call back human nature—which had been clouded by the darkness of ignorance and corrupted by vice—to its original light and integrity, the state in which it was first created by Heaven itself. From this restoration would follow a merciful and just administration of affairs, and thus a happy and profoundly peaceful state for the Empire. To ensure this goal was reached more certainly, he desired all people to obey Heaven, to fear and worship it, to love one’s neighbor as oneself, to conquer oneself, and to subject one's desires to reason. He taught that one should never do, say, or even think anything that might be alien to this path.

Furthermore, whatever he taught through the written or spoken word, he was the first to express through his own character and life. Quite clear testimony of this is provided by the great number of illustrious men who placed themselves under his discipline, and by those who—as eyewitnesses—recorded even his smallest actions and sayings for posterity. Moreover, the constant favor shown to him by so many Princes, and the great honor paid to him over so many centuries (which we shall soon discuss), serve as proof that the Philosopher possessed true virtue, not a mere appearance or facade. 

Indeed, in our own times, there have been many from the order of the <term>Literati|The scholar-official class in China (Shi)</term> who, having either already embraced the *Christian* Religion or at least recognized its integrity and holiness, have affirmed without hesitation their hope that their Philosopher, had he lived in our age, would have been the first to transition to the law of Christ. 

Certainly, as his followers pass down, the man possessed a wonderful gravity, a moderation of both body and mind, and a singular sense of faith, equity, and gentleness. He was a strict and ever-watchful observer and censor of himself. He was a despiser of wealth and honors, driving himself with tireless zeal toward a single goal: to share his doctrine with as many mortals as possible. However, what we *Europeans* admire in him most—and what we find lacking even in our own ancient philosophers—is that Confucius possessed such great humility of soul.

<page-num>CXX</page-num>

-> ### THE LIFE OF CONFUCIUS ### <-

...so that he spoke not only of himself and his affairs with great modesty, but also went so far as to openly and publicly rebuke himself. He claimed that he was neither tireless in learning nor constant in teaching, nor did he apply himself with the necessary vigilance to the correction of his own faults or the diligent practice of virtue. He gave the most certain proof of his modest and sincere spirit when he openly and ingenuously professed that his doctrine was not his own, but belonged to the Ancients—specifically the Kings and Legislators Yao and Shun, who had preceded him by fifteen hundred years or more. Since there were some who believed and even proclaimed that he was born with innate wisdom, he bore this with difficulty and expressly denied that he could ever reach the level of perfect and consummate virtue or sanctity. 

He was often accustomed to say (as is passed down by the Chinese): *In the West, there exists a holy man* <note>original: "Si fam, Yeu Xim gin." This phrase was historically interpreted by Jesuit missionaries as a prophecy of Christ, though it likely referred to the Buddha or was a later interpolation.</note>. It is uncertain of whom or by what spirit he pronounced this. What is certain is that in the year 65 AD, the Emperor Ming Di (who was the seventeenth ruler of the fifth Han Dynasty), moved by the words of the Philosopher and even more by a vision offered to him in a dream of a holy Hero from the west, sent ambassadors named Cai Yin and Qin Jing in his name toward the west. Since he could not go himself, they were tasked with seeking this holy man and his holy law. When these ambassadors reached a certain island not far from the Red Sea, they did not dare to proceed further. Instead, they brought back to this Empire a certain idol and a statue of a man called Fo <note>Buddha</note>—who had flourished in India about five hundred years before Confucius—along with his detestable law. 

How fortunate they would have been, and how eternally well-deserving of their country, if instead of this plague they had brought back the saving doctrine of Christ, which the Apostle Thomas was propagating among the Indians during those very same times. But indeed, human prosperity, and the pride of a wealthy, powerful, and most flourishing nation that grew from it, had at that time (in my opinion) blocked the path to true happiness. 

The Chinese, therefore, as they began to venerate idols more and more—not without the example of certain kings who followed this new superstition quite intensely—gradually departed from the genuine doctrine of their Master and the noble institutions of the Ancients. Finally, they fell into a contempt for all religion and into true **Atheism**. Furthermore, the scholars and the more sharp-witted among them were led into this, as if by the hand, by the doctrine of that very Fo, or Shakyamuni <note>original: "Xe kia"</note>, who stood as a master of idolatry for the unrefined common folk. 

For that most ruinous impostor and prince of atheists left behind a two-fold doctrine. The first teaches that the beginning and end of all things is **nothingness**; those who follow this are atheists and call this the "secret" or "interior" doctrine. The other is called the "exterior" doctrine, which is a sort of shadow of the first, adapted to the understanding and superstition of the common and unrefined people. Regarding Confucius, however, there can be no doubt that he was free from both of these plagues. Certainly, not even those who now venerate idols due to the corruption of the times would dare to assert that he was a worshiper of idols. As for how foreign he was to atheism, we declare this not only from his own words, but from the entire ancient age of the Chinese in our explanation of the book *Zhongyong* <note>original: "Chum yum," often translated as The Doctrine of the Mean</note>. 

Confucius departed from this life...

In the 73rd year of his age, on the 4th moon, on the day commonly called *Ki cheu*, in the fifty-ninth year (named *gui-si*) <note>original: "cui gin sio nomen"</note> of the thirty-seventh Chinese cycle, Confucius passed away. This was the forty-first year of the reign of King Jing <note>original: "Kim vam"</note>, the twenty-fifth Emperor of the Zhou <note>original: "Cheu"</note> Family. At that same time, Duke Ai <note>original: "Regulus Ngai"</note> had been ruling the Philosopher's native Kingdom, called Lu, for sixteen years. Shortly before he was seized by the illness that would be his last, mourning the disturbances of his times, he was heard to sing this verse with a swan-like voice: *The great mountain (by which he meant his own teaching) how you have fallen! The supporting beam is overturned; and the holy ones have withered away.* Soon after, beginning to grow weak, on the seventh day before his death, he turned to his disciples and said: *Last night, in a dream, it seemed to me that funeral rites were being performed in the hall. The Kings do not observe what I teach: Is there anyone throughout our Empire who is a follower and practitioner of my system? Only one thing remains: for me to die.* Having spoken this, he was seized by a lethargy, and when he had remained as if sleeping for seven full days, he finally ceased to live. 

He was buried in his native Kingdom of Lu (for he had returned home with his disciples) near the city of Qufu <note>original: "Kio feu"</note>, on the bank of the river Si <note>original: "Su"</note> in his very own Academy where he had been accustomed to teach, which today is seen surrounded by walls like a city. There, his disciples mourned their Master in mourning attire, with much fasting and tears, no differently than a son for a parent; they did this for a whole year. There were even some who remained for a full three years, while Zigong <note>original: "Çucum"</note> remained in that same place and in mourning for six years. 

The Philosopher was of a very tall stature—even giant, if it is right to believe the Chinese—and his broad shoulders and ample chest gave him a sense of grace and majesty. On the very crown of his head, he had a rather large bump, for which reason he was named by his father *Kieu* <note>original: "Kieu," likely referring to the name Qiu</note>, that is, "a little hill," which the bump somewhat resembled; the modest man would also call himself by this same name from time to time. He had a broad face, a dusky complexion, black and very large eyes, black hair, a long beard, a flat nose, and a deep voice like the sound of thunder, as the Chinese relate.

Furthermore, as to how much honor the grateful posterity of the Chinese has bestowed upon their Master—or rather upon his labors and doctrine—for more than two thousand years, let all those speak for me who have been raised to dignities and public offices throughout the entire Empire by the protection of letters. All of these men certainly confess that their wealth, honors, and illustrious names have come to them primarily from the school of Confucius and from the books upon which they are examined for their degrees. Let the schools <term>gymnasia</term> <note>The author uses 'gymnasia' to refer to the Confucian temples or academies found in every Chinese district.</note> erected and dedicated to the man in every town and city also speak; as often as those of the literary order who hold public magistracies pass before their doors, they immediately descend with reverence from the high and majestic chair in which they are carried according to the custom of the nation, and follow their path on foot for several paces. Finally, let the truly honorary titles speak, which are seen carved into the beams of those schools I just mentioned in gilded letters: "To the Great Master," "To the Illustrious King of Letters," "To the Holy One," or (as is said among...

*...is the same as the people themselves) <note>original: "ipsos idem est"</note> adorned with a certain extraordinary wisdom, and other similar titles, by which the Emperors of the families of Han, Sui, Tang <note>original: "Tam"</note>, Song <note>original: "Sum"</note>, and Yuan <note>original: "Yven"</note> (this last being of the Western Tartars <note>The Mongols</note>) have raised this Teacher of their nation almost above human praise. Although the Founder of the family called Ming <note>original: "Mim"</note> (which immediately preceded the modern Qing <note>original: "Cim"</note> of the Eastern Tartars <note>The Manchus</note>) forbade royal honors to be paid to Confucius, permitting only that style with which the memory of the Xianshi <note>original: "Sien su"; meaning the First Teacher</note>—that is, the life of the Holy Teacher—was formerly celebrated. Furthermore, he allowed no other offerings than those which his disciples were accustomed to present to their masters while they were living. In addition to this, he forbade statues of Confucius or his disciples to be erected in the Academies <note>original: "Gymnasiis"</note>; for he said they are not to be honored with the same rite as other spirits or idols. Instead, he commanded that only tablets be displayed, upon which the titles and names of each individual are inscribed. Therefore, those funeral tablets are merely commemorative signs of the Teachers (and the same reasoning applies to the tablets of ancestors), lest the pious memory of those who served letters well after their lives ended, or of the parental family, should die out among posterity. Nor are tablets of this kind any more liable to produce error than our European paintings, which depict for us the living likenesses of our ancestors in a most graceful way; showing these to friends and guests, we say without hesitation and even with reverence: "This was our grandfather; that man was our Teacher." Therefore, we ought not to be offended if we see the Chinese <note>original: "Sinas"</note> bend the knee <note>original: "curvare poplitem"</note> before these tablets according to the custom most common among them, any more than we are offended if we see some European take off his hat while passing by chance before the image of his father or his King—just as we recently saw the Lords Ambassadors of the Kingdom of Siam, who, whenever they passed before the image of LOUIS THE GREAT <note>King Louis XIV of France</note>, immediately stopped their pace, and with hands joined high and a bowing of the whole body, lowered themselves as if at the feet of such great majesty. Indeed, those Confucian honors and rites are clearly civil; they are performed not in a Temple or shrine of idols (which is forbidden by Imperial law), but in the academy, a place open only to the learned, by the prefects of the literary faculty, among whom are even Muslims <note>original: "Mahometani"</note> (not to mention the "atheist-politicians" <note>original: "atheopoliticis"; a reference to Neo-Confucian philosophers whom the authors viewed as secular or materialistic</note>) who recognize nothing divine here and detest the superstitions and idols of the Gentiles. Indeed, if we speak of those literati already tainted from childhood by the poison of idolatry (such as men of the lowest rank), when the time approaches for undergoing an examination to obtain some degree, they either first consult their own domestic household gods <note>original: "penates"</note> and implore their divinity and help, or they go as suppliants to the public shrines of demons for the sake of desired success; but they never think of going to the academy of Confucius. To hold or name him as a Pusa <note>original: "Pu sa"; a term for a Buddhist deity or idol</note>, or to ask or hope for anything from him, is unheard of and unusual among them.*

...and if their integrity and faithfulness in performing their duties as magistrates (authentically proven by the testimonies of many through the Governors <note>original: "Prætores"</note> of the Provinces to the Emperor) is established, they are also added to the register and number of the disciples of Confucius by public decree and royal favor even to the present day. Because of the memory of his ancestor—though removed by an interval of more than two thousand two hundred years and sixty-eight generations—both the highest and the lowest in society honor him. This descendant enjoys a perpetual and hereditary title of Duke <note>original: "ducis"</note> and dignity, with a rare privilege granted to none except Princes of the royal blood: he pays no tax to the Emperor. In addition to this, every three years, as many scholars as are raised to the degree of Doctor are accustomed to pay a pledge of a grateful mind—a sort of "teacher’s fee" <term>Minerval</term> <note>In Roman antiquity, a fee paid to a teacher in honor of Minerva; here, a symbolic tribute given to Confucius's living heir.</note>—to the grandson, which they can no longer pay to the grandfather himself.

This is something that we Europeans may rightly praise and even wonder at: although China has indeed experienced great shifts in fortune, and has undergone the disasters and calamities of so many wars, and has seen the rise and fall of so many ruling families, the honors I have mentioned and the monuments of a grateful posterity toward Confucius have never been interrupted. We must, however, except a few years in which—three centuries after the Philosopher died—Qin Shi Huang <note>original: "çin xi hoam ti," the first Emperor of a unified China (r. 221–210 BC)</note>, the second Emperor of the fourth family, the Qin <note>original: "çin"</note>, raged barbarously and cruelly not only against books but also against the learned. However, upon his death, literature soon revived, and with those increases of honors which we see today even under the Tartars <note>The Manchu Qing Dynasty</note>, the name and fame of Confucius grew.

What the ultimate purpose and intention is behind these posthumous honors and titles is nowhere more clearly established than from a single testimony among many: a decree from the third Emperor of the preceding Ming <note>original: "Mim"</note> family, named Yongle <note>original: "Yum lo," r. 1402–1424</note>. > I venerate Confucius, the Teacher of Emperors and Kings. Emperors and Kings are the Lords of the People. Confucius, however, proposed the right instruction of the People, specifically those three bonds (namely, between King and subjects, parents and children, husband and wife), and likewise the norm of the five universal virtues (piety, justice, prudence, fidelity, and civility), and the great symmetry and form of the Chinese Empire. This is so that his reputation and that of his doctrine—which is already nearly greater than is just—does not increase excessively through our testimony and authority, especially among a nation naturally proud and prone to despising foreign things compared to their own. And while we might perhaps despise or condemn him who taught things so consistent with **reason**, and who is believed to have conformed his life and character to his doctrine, we Europeans might seem, at least to the Chinese, to want to fight not so much against their Master as against reason itself, and to extinguish its light rather than the name of Confucius.*

# CHINESE KNOWLEDGE,
# BOOK ONE.

This book, authored by **Confucius** <note>The Latinized name of Kong Fuzi (Master Kong), the 6th-century BCE philosopher whose teachings form the foundation of Chinese social and political ethics.</note> and commented upon by **Zengzi** <note>original: "çemçu"; Zengzi was one of Confucius’s most influential disciples, credited with preserving the "Great Learning."</note>, his second disciple, now begins to see the light of public day. It serves as a kind of door and first threshold for those beginning to enter the inner sanctums of wisdom and virtue. Its subject matter is threefold: first, the right instruction and governance of oneself; next, of others; and finally, resting—or as I might say, remaining consistent—in the highest good. Furthermore, because the Author intended this threefold doctrine to be primarily recommended to Princes and Great Men who govern the peoples and kingdoms subject to them, it received the name **The Great Learning** <note>original: "Tá-Hiǒ" (Daxue); "Magna Scientia" in the Latin text.</note>.

*Note: The English version of this work is literal; it is distinguished by numbers and corresponds exactly to the Chinese phrasing, text, and characters (which are printed separately), following their order precisely. For the rest, the explanation is drawn from the interpreters, especially **Zhang Juzheng** <note>original: "Cham-Colai"; Zhang Juzheng (1525–1582) was a powerful Ming dynasty statesman and Grand Preceptor whose commentaries were standard for the Imperial Examinations.</note> and the **Royal Master.** <note>original: "Magistri Regii"; likely another reference to the authoritative Ming commentaries used by the Jesuits.</note>*

<margin>1.</margin>
The $^1$ Great $^3$ institution $^2$ of learning $^4$ for leading men $^4$ consists in $^5$ polishing or cultivating $^6$ the rational $^7$ nature $^7$ bestowed by heaven; so that this nature, like a perfectly clear mirror, once the stains of wicked appetites are wiped away, can return to its original clarity. $^8$ It consists next in $^9$ renewing or reforming $^{10}$ the people $^{11}$ through one's own example and encouragement. $^{12}$ It consists, finally, in $^{13}$ standing firmly, or persevering, $^{15}$ in the highest $^{14}$ good: by which the Interpreters here wish to be understood the highest conformity of all actions with right reason. And these are the three points to which everything else in this book is reduced.

### §. 3.

In the present paragraph, the Author teaches by an enumeration of parts which things are more or less fundamental, what comes first and what comes later, and what constitutes the root versus the branches, and so on. ¹ The ancients ² wishing ³ to polish ⁴ <note>The Latin *expolire* suggests refining or perfecting one's innate moral nature.</note> rational nature ⁵ ⁶ in ⁷ ⁸ the empire—or rather, wishing that the people of the entire Empire might have the means by which to polish their own rational nature—they themselves, as a prototype for those to come, ⁹ first rightly governed ¹⁰ their own ¹¹ private ¹² Kingdom. By their own example, they ensured that their subjects also polished and cultivated their rational nature well. In this way, they moved step-by-step from that which was closer—that is, their private Kingdom—to that which was more remote—that is, to the whole Empire. For indeed, the ordering of a private Kingdom is like a root from which the successful administration of the Empire grows. To such an extent that, besides a few smaller Kingdoms of "Barbarians" (as they call them) adjacent to their lands, they have known nothing of the world until now—or if by chance they did know of it, they thought it could not be counted in the same category as their own Empire.* )

one's own intention, insofar as it is removed from all pretense, truly wants nothing except what is truly honorable and at the same time useful, and truly avoids nothing except what is shameful and destructive. Thus, the root of rectifying the mind—the primary thing which must be cared for first—is this truth of our intention. For this reason, the author says that he who wishes to rectify his mind must first solidify his intention in truth. Furthermore, ⁴⁵ those wishing ⁴⁶ to verify ⁴⁷ their ⁴⁸ intention, ⁴⁹ first ⁵⁰ perfected and brought ⁵¹ their ⁵² intellect (or intellectual power) to the highest peak they could, so that this power had nothing that it did not see through. And this is what the Author means when he says that he who wishes to verify his intention and will must first perfect his intellect; for nothing is willed unless it is first known <note>original: "nihil enim volitum quin præcognitum." This is a famous Scholastic philosophical maxim used here by the Jesuit translators to explain Confucian psychology.</note>. Ultimately, to perfect or bring the intellectual power to its highest peak in this way consists in penetrating, or rather exhausting, all things—that is, the underlying reasons <note>original: "rationes"</note> of all things. Since there are different modes of knowing (which Philosophers call "knowabilities" <note>original: "cognoscibilitates"</note>) according to the diversity of things and beings, and since the mode of knowing follows the mode of being, the intellectual power will be judged to have reached the peak of science or knowledge only when it has exhausted the reasons and essences of all things according to all their "knowability" (so far as human strength allows). And this is what the Author means: that perfecting or bringing the intellectual power to its peak consists in comprehending and, in a manner of speaking, exhausting the reasons of all things.

> *Of these eight steps enumerated above, the last five—namely, intimately penetrating all things, bringing the intellectual power to its peak, verifying the intention, rectifying the heart, and rightly composing one’s own person—are what constitute that cultivation and polishing of rational nature which everyone must care for first regarding themselves. On the other hand, rightly ordering the family, rightly administering the Kingdom, and polishing the rational nature of subjects in the whole Empire, are what constitute the "renovation of the people." He who performs these in the proper and not a reversed order will find that he has attained a rational nature polished in himself and renovated in the people. Thus, he will have achieved the highest good, in which he may finally rest, according to the prescription of this great science.*

->p. 2. §. I.<-

1. **A** ² From the **Son of Heaven** ³ or the Emperor, ⁴ all the way ⁵ down ⁷ to the **common** ⁸ people, ⁹/¹⁰ all ¹¹ as one must establish the right ¹² composition of their ¹³ **person** ¹⁴ as their ¹⁵ **primary principle**. It is as if he were to say: although the conditions and statuses of men are diverse—some being born to the scepter and others to the plow—the study of cultivating one's own person through virtues ought to be common to all, from the highest to the lowest. For to penetrate all things, to perfect the intellectual power, to verify the intention, and to rectify the heart—all these actions belong to the right composition of one's person. From these things, the other matters follow: namely, the right administration of the domestic family, the private Kingdom, and finally the whole Empire. This latter part is not common to all, and is thus less of a "primary principle"; the first part must be common to everyone without exception, from the Emperor himself to the lowest commoner, and is the more primary principle.

*Note.* The Chinese denote their Emperor with these two characters <term>*tien çu*</term> <note>The pinyin for this is *Tiānzǐ*.</note>, which signify *Son of Heaven*: *for the Chinese also believe that Kingdoms and Empires are conferred as well as taken away by Heaven, as is clear from various monuments of the Ancients.* Hence they assert that the Emperor is from Heaven and is called <term>*tien çu*</term>, that is, *Son of Heaven*; because he is <term>*tien hoe*</term> <note>original: "tien hoe". This likely refers to *Tiānhuò*, meaning "obtained from Heaven."</note>, that is, obtained from Heaven or by Heavenly means, namely by a peculiar privilege.

1. With one's primary concern (that is, the individual person) <gloss>1</gloss> disturbed or neglected, it is <gloss>4</gloss> nevertheless <gloss>5</gloss> impossible for the secondary or less important concerns—namely, the Family, the Kingdom, and the Empire—to be <gloss>6</gloss> governed <gloss>7</gloss> rightly. Otherwise, you would be wishing for a tree to still flourish with green boughs and leaves even though the root is already withered. <gloss>8</gloss> To make <gloss>11</gloss> a minor matter <gloss>9</gloss> out of that which <gloss>10</gloss> is of greater importance, <gloss>12</gloss> and <gloss>13</gloss> to make <gloss>16</gloss> a major matter <gloss>14</gloss> out of that which <gloss>15</gloss> is of lesser importance, <gloss>17</gloss> is not <gloss>18</gloss> according to right reason. He cannot possibly put those whom his condition has made more distant ahead of those to whom the bond of family or blood has joined him more closely.

And this is the very doctrine of the "Oracle of the Chinese," *Confucius* <note>The Latin text refers to Confucius as an "Oracle," reflecting the high esteem the Jesuit translators held for his wisdom.</note>, specifically adapted for the instruction of Princely Men; it turns upon a double hinge: first, the right governance of oneself, and then the right governance of others. In the following sections, *Zengzi* <note>original: "çem-çu"</note>, his disciple, pursues these individual points according to the mind of his Master, strengthening and illustrating them with the authorities and examples of ancient Princes.

->f. 3. p. 1. §. 1.<-

**T**he first authority which *Zengzi* uses to declare his Master's superior doctrine regarding the right governance of oneself and others is sought from an ancient book composed by *King Wu* <note>original: "vù-vâm"</note>, the son of *King Wen* <note>original: "vên-vâm"</note>. In this book, he celebrates the virtues of his father and presents them to his brother *Kang Shu* <note>original: "cam-xo"</note>. Therefore, that book, <gloss>1</gloss> called the *Kang Gao* <note>original: "cam-caó"</note> (which is also part of the Chronicles of the *Zhou* <note>original: "cheu"</note> Empire), <gloss>2</gloss> says: <gloss>4</gloss> "He"—namely, *King Wen*—"was able to polish his own <gloss>5</gloss> rational nature." <note>The "rational nature" refers to the innate moral light or conscience that Confucians believe must be "polished" like a mirror to remain clear.</note>

->§. 2.<-

**A** second authority is sought from an even older book called the *Tai Jia* <note>original: "tái-kia"</note>, which was written by that famous man *Yi Yin* <note>original: "y-yn"</note>, the Governor of the *Shang* <note>original: "xam"</note> Empire. For when he saw that *Tai Jia*, the grandson of the Emperor *Cheng Tang* <note>original: "chim-tam"</note> (who was the founder of the *Shang* family), was degenerating from his ancestral institutions, he ordered him to dwell for three years in the sepulchral garden <note>The tomb complex or mourning grounds.</note> of his grandfather. Moreover, in this little book, he exhorted him to follow the virtues of his grandfather. And indeed, the prince repented, and was afterward led back to the Empire by this same *Yi Yin*; he then administered it for a long time and with great success, having used such a great man as his teacher and assistant. Therefore, this book <gloss>1</gloss> called the *Tai Jia* <gloss>3</gloss> says: [King Tang] <gloss>4</gloss> "always held the eyes of his mind intent <gloss>5</gloss> upon cultivating <gloss>7</gloss> this rational nature <gloss>6</gloss> given by <gloss>6</gloss> heaven."

<header>BOOK ONE.</header>

### §. 3.

Finally, a third authority is sought from a very ancient book of King **Yao** <gloss>1</gloss> called the **Canon of Yao** <gloss>2</gloss> <note>original: "ti-tièn"; likely the *Yaodian* section of the Classic of History</note>; this book, along with the two just cited, is included in the **Classic of History** <note>original: "xu-kim"; the *Shujing*</note>. Furthermore, <gloss>3</gloss> it says: <gloss>4</gloss> he (namely, King **Yao**) was able <gloss>5</gloss> to polish or cultivate this great and <gloss>6</gloss> sublime <gloss>7</gloss> gift, or <gloss>6</gloss> sublime <gloss>7</gloss> virtue—that is, our rational nature.

### §. 4.

<margin>1.</margin> All <gloss>2</gloss> by themselves <gloss>3</gloss> polished their own rational nature. This is as if to say: although this great and sublime gift and light of rational nature has been sent and implanted by heaven into all men, most mortals have nevertheless clouded and diminished it by their disordered appetites and vices, and some have even nearly extinguished it. However, the aforementioned Kings **Yao**, **Cheng Tang**, and **Wen Wang** <note>These are three of the most revered sage-kings in Chinese tradition, representing the Xia, Shang, and Zhou periods respectively.</note> were able, through their own labor and constancy, to polish and illuminate it to such an extent that they never thereafter lost it; on the contrary, they radiated its vast splendor and light far and wide through the whole world of the Chinese people.

### Part 2. §. 1.

<margin>1.</margin> On the washbasin of King **Tang** <note>The founder of the Shang Dynasty</note>, in which he used to wash his body, the <gloss>3</gloss> inscribed <gloss>4</gloss> letters said: "Every <gloss>5</gloss> day—that is, constantly—wash yourself and <gloss>7</gloss> renew yourself; indeed, <gloss>8/9</gloss> daily <gloss>10</gloss> renew yourself; and again, <gloss>12</gloss> day by day <gloss>13</gloss> renew yourself." It is as if he were saying: A Prince who governs others must be entirely devoted at all times to carefully washing and wiping away the filth of wicked appetites and vices which he might have contracted, so that he may return to his original cleanliness and purity. And this is that "renewal of oneself" which **Zengzi** <note>original: "çem-çu"; a primary disciple of Confucius</note> wished to place first in this passage, as the root and foundation of the "renewal of the people."

*Furthermore, the ancient custom of those times is surely worthy of observation: in domestic vessels and similar furniture (such as this King's washbasin), the most beautiful examples of virtues were usually engraved or painted, even on the inner surface of the vessel itself. This was done so that even when they were washing their bodies or taking food, they would always have these lessons before their eyes. This custom, derived from the ancients, still flourishes in* China <note>original: "Sinis"</note> *today; however, with this difference: while they once painted or engraved these letters on the inside, they now mostly do so on the outside, being content today with mere outward show and a certain external appearance of virtue.*

### §. 2.

The aforementioned King **Wu** <note>original: "vù-vâm"; the founder of the Zhou Dynasty</note> says in that same book of his, the **Announcement to Kang** <gloss>1, 2, 3</gloss> <note>original: "cam-caó"; a chapter of the Classic of History</note>: <gloss>4</gloss> stir up or challenge the <gloss>6</gloss> people <gloss>5</gloss> to renew themselves. It is as if he were saying: even if the people have perhaps lived badly until now, if they wish to act rightly in the future, let the Prince be their standard; by his own example, let him studiously challenge his subjects to a new standard of a better life. For this is the true method of renewing the people.

*Since the memory of King Wen is so celebrated among the Chinese, it is helpful to touch upon a few things about him here in passing. The father of this King Wen was Wang Ji; his mother was Tai Ren, whom they record was of such modesty that she could not bear to see or hear anything dishonorable; and of such humility that no arrogance could be noted even in her words. King Wen, the devoted son of a devoted mother, fell mortally ill in the twentieth year of the reign of the tyrant Zhou (also known as Zhou Xin). When the earth had already been shaken for five days by miraculous tremors, he ascribed such a great calamity and the wrath of heaven to his own sins alone; and yet he was a man of such great virtues, and of such illustrious fame among foreign nations, that forty-four Kingdoms voluntarily submitted themselves to him. However, nothing shone so brightly in this Prince as his singular devotion of spirit toward all, of which it may suffice to bring forward one example out of many. The Chinese Annals, and the book titled "Annals of the Various Kingdoms" (Lieguo Zhizhuan), relate that when he happened to find the unburied bones of an unknown man in a field, he immediately ordered them to be buried. When there was someone among the bystanders who said that the deceased's master was unknown, and therefore no account should be taken of him: "But indeed," said the King, "he who holds the Empire is the Master of the Empire; he who holds the Kingdom is the Master of the Kingdom; I, therefore, am also the Master of this man; why should I deny him this final duty of devotion?" Saying this, he stripped off his royal robe and ordered the bones to be wrapped in it and buried according to custom. The nobles, astonished by such an example of virtue, said: "If our Prince's devotion toward dry bones is so great, how great will it be toward living men!" And*

*This <insert>Vù Cum</insert> was a <term>Petty King<note>original: "Regulus"; a ruler of a smaller state within the feudal system.</note></term> of the Kingdom of Guéi <note>The State of Wei.</note>, which today is the Province of Hônân. The judge intended to determine whether the litigant was sincere and true, or malicious and deceitful. Therefore, the first thing he ordered to be observed was the arrangement of words and the manner of speaking in the person bringing the lawsuit; this was called <term>çû-tím<note>Likely "Ci ting" (辞听) from the Zhou Li; the "listening to speech."</note></term>, that is, the observation of words. The second was the composure of the mouth and the whole countenance; this was called <term>se-tím<note>Likely "Se ting" (色听); the "listening to facial expression."</note></term>, that is, the observation of the face. The third was the manner of breathing while the plaintiff proposed the suit; this was called <term>kí-tím<note>Likely "Qi ting" (气听); the "listening to the breath."</note></term>, that is, the observation of breathing. The fourth was the readiness of the plaintiff's ears; specifically, whether the plaintiff, when interrogated by the judge in a complex or confusing manner, gave irrelevant or ambiguous answers; this was called <term>ûlh-tím<note>Likely "Er ting" (耳听); the "listening to the ears."</note></term>, that is, the observation of the ears. Finally, the fifth was the uncertain casting and blinking of the eyes, to see if anything deceitful or less than sincere appeared in them; this was called <term>mó-tím<note>Likely "Mu ting" (目听); the "listening to the eyes."</note></term>, that is, the observation of the eyes. By so many signs did that ancient <term>Areopagus<note>original: "Sinarum Areopagus"; a reference to the high court of Athens, used here by the translator to describe the ancient Chinese judicial council.</note></term> of the Chinese skillfully explore the hidden feelings of the mind; but today these things are either unknown or neglected.

Hence it happens that, neglecting that interior care and having loosened the reins of their appetites, they rush headlong into every crime; being ignorant, clearly, that their own conscience is like a thousand witnesses; and likewise all things betray themselves by their own tracks; nor is there anything so hidden that it does not eventually betray and reveal itself. Certainly, just as one who carries spices, although he carefully hides them, is betrayed by the very fragrance; and as for the one who suffers from a foul-smelling ulcer <note>original: "carcinomate"</note>, his own stench betrays him even against his will; so neither can virtue remain hidden for long, nor vice, even if you wish to hide it as much as possible; nor will any arts of feigning or simulating profit you.

### BOOK ONE

[If there is] an abundance at home, it usually causes the roofs and walls to overflow with it; and what wealth of gold and silver it has inside, it displays in the external furnishings and equipment of the whole house. In the same way, virtue, in whose soul it dwells, immediately overflows into the whole person—even into the external habit of the entire body—and it makes what is truly within appear on the outside. From this it follows that a man endowed with virtue, because he has nothing within for which his conscience reproaches him, feels his heart expand. He is soothed within by a certain deep peace, tranquility, and delight, so that these same qualities overflow into the body, expanding and filling it, as it were. This is the meaning of those words: <gloss>7</gloss> *with a heart* <gloss>8</gloss> *broad* <gloss>9</gloss> *and wide, even* <gloss>10</gloss> *the body* <gloss>11</gloss> *is expanded and prospers.* However, because that virtue which thus adorns and affects the body proceeds from and depends on the sincerity and truth of our will, <gloss>12/13</gloss> *therefore the* <gloss>14</gloss> *zealous student* <gloss>15</gloss> *of virtue* <gloss>16</gloss> *perfects* <gloss>17</gloss> *his* <gloss>18</gloss> *intention or will.*

To more fully declare what has been said, one of the disciples of Confucius brings forward here an axiom which he had heard from his Master time and again. <gloss>1</gloss> Zengzi, <gloss>2</gloss> therefore, was <gloss>3</gloss> accustomed to saying <gloss>4</gloss> constantly: "That <gloss>6</gloss> which <gloss>4</gloss> ten, or many, <gloss>5</gloss> eyes <gloss>7</gloss> see, and <gloss>8</gloss> what <gloss>9</gloss> ten <gloss>10</gloss> hands <gloss>11</gloss> point to—<gloss>12</gloss> how much <gloss>13</gloss> that is to be feared from him!" <note>This is a core teaching from the Great Learning regarding the impossibility of hiding one's character.</note> Or (as others explain it): live as cautiously as if you were watched by ten eyes and pointed at by ten hands. It is as if he were saying: most men are sluggish and indifferent regarding the interior of the soul; for because they think that those things which the mind deals with in the interior are so hidden, they vainly persuade themselves that these things cannot become known externally by any sign. From this it happens that, neglecting that internal care and loosening the reins of their appetites, they rush headlong into every crime, being ignorant, of course, that their own conscience is like a thousand witnesses; and likewise that all things betray themselves by their own tracks; nor is there anything so hidden that it does not eventually betray itself and be revealed. Certainly, just as one who carries spices, though he hides them studiously, is nevertheless betrayed by their very fragrance; and as a foul tumor <note>original: "purulento carcinomate"; literally a purulent carcinoma or ulcer.</note> betrays the one who suffers from it even against his will by its heavy odor; so neither can virtue lie hidden for long, nor vice, even if you wish to hide it most of all; nor will any arts of feigning or pretending profit you.
