So also men <gloss>18</gloss> in <gloss>19</gloss> those <gloss>20</gloss> whom <gloss>21</gloss> they hold in low esteem or <gloss>22</gloss> hate, <gloss>23</gloss> likewise <gloss>24</gloss> deflect from the right path. ->§. 2.<-

This present paragraph now shows by example how truly close and inseparable is the bond between the King’s example and the people’s imitation; and since opposites shine more clearly when placed side by side, it contrasts two of the best Kings with two of the worst. It says, therefore, that Yao <note>original: "Yaô"; a legendary sage-king and model of virtue.</note> ^1 & ^2 Shun <note>original: "Xún"; the successor to Yao, also revered as a perfect ruler.</note> ^3 ruled ^4|5 the empire ^6 with piety and mercy ^7 & ^8 and the people followed ^9 ^10 them. On the contrary, those two worst Kings, Jie <note>original: "Kie"; the tyrannical last ruler of the Xia dynasty.</note> ^11 & ^12 Zhou <note>original: "Chéu"; the cruel last ruler of the Shang dynasty.</note> ^13 ruled ^14|15 the Empire ^16 with cruelty and tyranny, ^17 & ^18 and the people likewise followed ^19 ^20 them, imitating their wickedness and crimes. But if ever ^21 those things ^22 which such Kings ^23 had commanded ^24 through public Edicts ^25 were contrary ^26 to those things ^27 which they themselves loved ^28 to do, ^29 then ^30 the people ^31 did not ^32 obey, because they saw, of course, that the kings commanded one thing abroad while doing another in their own homes. For this ^33 reason, ^34 a virtuous ^35 King first possesses ^36 virtue ^37 in ^38 himself, and ^39 then ^40 thereafter rightly ^41 demands ^42 it from ^43 others; he is first irreproachable and without fault ^44 in ^45 himself, ^46 and then ^47 thereafter rightly ^48 reproves ^49 that fault in ^50 others. This is truly "to measure others by oneself" <note>A reference to the Confucian concept of *shu* or reciprocity.</note>, and to pour out upon others the virtue with which one is first filled. For when virtue has once flowed out to others through your own example and reputation, then indeed the people, stirred by these things, will wish to imitate and follow you; and only then will you be able to effectively teach them and instruct them with the best laws; otherwise, you will waste your effort. For it is completely ^62 impossible ^63 that one who is destitute of virtue and hidden away, ^54 subject to ^53 vices ^52 in his ^55 own ^56 person, ^57 and has nothing good of his own to propagate ^57 outwardly, ^58 could ^60 nevertheless ^59 teach and rightly instruct ^61 others; for to whom can he be good, who is wicked to himself?

*I would be doing an injustice to the reader if, at this place where these four Emperors are first mentioned, I did not relate at least a few of the many things about them that are found scattered throughout all the Chinese books. Let us give the first place to the one who occurs first here: Yao, the most celebrated of the Chinese Emperors and also a Legislator. He was born to the Emperor Di Ku <note>original: "Tí-co"</note> and his Queen named Qingdu <note>original: "Kím tú"</note> in the fourteenth month after his conception. He took up the reins of government in the year 2357 before Christ, and he held them successfully for a total of 100 years; and for the last fifty, he ruled so peacefully that his subjects did not even know whether he was ruling or not. Hence, he left such a great reputation for his virtues among everyone—not only his subjects but also posterity—that the things the Chinese Annals report about him seem to be spoken not without exaggeration or hyperbole <note>original: "auxesi aut hyperbole"</note>. In piety they made him almost equal to heaven, in prudence and wisdom to the spirits, and in the majesty of his appearance and devotion, almost equal to the sun. It is certain that he was a Prince most highly endowed with all natural gifts: wealthy without pride; noble without insolence; honest and sincere without pretense. His palace was a common and humble roof; his clothing simple and not embroidered; his food frugal without seasonings...*

...ment; <note>The word likely concludes "vestimento" (clothing) or "ornamento" (adornment) from the previous page.</note> he used clay vessels, having rejected curiosities and foreign luxuries; straw was his bed. A simple carriage, not at all elaborate or painted, was pulled by white horses. The music called *Dazhang* <note>original: "Tá cham"; the traditional music of Emperor Yao's era.</note> was serious, pious, and modest; for he hated shameful songs. He was entirely devoted to serving Heaven and helping the needy. Hence came those sayings of his: "The hunger of my people is my own; the sin of my people is likewise mine." By this, he so bound the wills of his subjects to himself that they obeyed him no longer from fear of punishment or hope of reward, but with entirely willing spirits as if to a Father and Mother. Hence, upon his death, mourning was observed for three years by all the people as if for a Father and Mother, as is related in the *Book of Documents* <note>original: "Xu kim" (Shujing), Book 1, folio 16.</note>; and everyone was held by as great a longing for him as for a dewy cloud in a time of drought. He is said to be the first to have instituted the doctrine of the *Great Learning* <note>original: "Tá-hio"</note> and the *Doctrine of the Mean* <note>original: "Chum-yûm"</note> by his own example, becoming the prototype and model for all subsequent Emperors. He held court in the city of Pingyangfu <note>original: "Pìm yâm-fù"</note>, the most famous in the entire Province of Shanxi <note>original: "Xan-si"</note>. In the seventy-second year of his reign, he chose Shun <note>original: "Xún"</note> as his primary colleague in the Empire for twenty-eight years, and then as his successor, moved by the fame of Shun's obedience toward his parents; to bind him with a closer bond, Yao gave him two of his daughters in marriage. When Yao heard that his son Danzhu <note>original: "Tan chu"</note> was taking it badly because he saw himself excluded from succession to the Empire, he replied: "I prefer it to go ill for one man so that it may be well for all the people, than for it to go ill for the people and well for one son." Finally, full of days, he died in his hundred and eighteenth year; he was buried in Shandong <note>original: "Xan-tum"</note> Province.

Shun <note>original: "Xún"</note>, also known as Yu <note>original: "Yù"; here likely a title or stylistic name, though Yu is also the name of his successor.</note>, similar to his predecessor in all things, ruled the Chinese Empire with the same happiness; and because he easily gave an ear to everyone, he commanded the minds of all with wonderful ease. He delighted so much in the company of wise men that he ordered them to be sought out from everywhere, sometimes at great expense. He cultivated music no less than his predecessor. Nor did he judge it unbefitting of Royal Majesty to play instruments of five, eight, and twenty-five strings, called *Qin* <note>original: "Kîn"</note>; indeed, he himself repeatedly sang a verse, still sung today, about the kindness of the southern wind in enriching his people and making the lands fertile. From this you may see how deep a peace existed under his rule, with what great happiness the Chinese Empire then abounded, and with what great progress it advanced daily. Certainly, by the testimony of the Annals, it is clear that very many barbarian kingdoms and peoples, moved by the fame of so fortunate a Prince, voluntarily subjected themselves to him. An eagle flying throughout the Empire and new stars seen during his reign signified this happiness; the people boasted that such happy omens descended from *Shangdi* <note>original: "Xám-tí"</note>, that is, the Supreme Emperor of Heaven, who favored this King with so many blessings. Of the one hundred and ten years that he lived, he reigned most happily for sixty-one; and having rejected his son Shangjun <note>original: "Xam-kiun"</note>, he placed virtue before blood when he chose the great Yu <note>original: "Yù"</note> as his successor.

Furthermore, how much longing and praise the Lawgivers Yao and Shun...

...then those two others, Jie and Zhou, earned the execration and reproach of all posterity, being twin monsters of cruelty and lust.

**Jie** <note>original: "Kie"; the last ruler of the Xia dynasty, traditionally portrayed as a tyrant.</note>, who was also called Li-gui <note>original: "Lì-quèï"</note> by another name, was the son of Di Fa <note>original: "Tí-fa"</note>. He began to reign in the year 1818 BC, the seventeenth and last Emperor of the first imperial family called the **Xia** <note>original: "Hiá"</note>. This dynasty had already begun to threaten ruin since the time of Kong Jia <note>original: "Cùm-kia"</note>, the fourteenth Emperor of that same family. He possessed such physical strength that he could break iron with his hands. Upon the death of his father, in the nineteenth year of his own reign, he began to harass the people with tyranny and cruelty. Fourteen years later, which was the thirty-third year of his reign, he took a concubine named Meixi <note>original: "Muí-hì"</note>, whose whims he obeyed in a truly infamous servitude. Warned by his advisors, he not only failed to repent but, despising those who gave good counsel, he put them to death with the utmost ingratitude and cruelty. He was accustomed to saying that he held power just as Heaven holds the sun, and therefore he would only cease to rule when the sun itself ceased to be. He built a tower of jasper at the people’s expense. He filled entire lakes with wine, into which three thousand men were ordered to gorge themselves at a given signal. 

While he raged for a long time with these and six hundred other such foul acts of cruelty, luxury, and lust, Heaven warned him to repent through more than one prodigy: for in the fiftieth year of his reign, stars were seen openly falling from the sky, the earth was shaken horribly by unusual movements, rivers dried up, and a large part of Mount Taishan <note>original: "Tái-xan"</note> collapsed in an earthquake. Since he did not yet grow wise despite so many portents and threats, in that same year he was driven from the Kingdom by **Cheng Tang** <note>original: "Chîm-tam"; the virtuous founder of the Shang dynasty.</note> (who, among the petty kings, more zealously insisted upon the pious laws of the Ancients and ancestral institutions). He fled to a place called Nanchao <note>original: "Nân-chaò"</note>, where he died in exile three years later in the 52nd year of his reign. With him, the Xia family expired, having lasted 458 years.

**Zhou** <note>original: "Chéu"; King Zhou, the last ruler of the Shang dynasty.</note>, also named Shou Xin <note>original: "Xeù-sin"</note>, was the third-born son of his father Di Yi <note>original: "Tí-ye"</note> by his mother who had been made Queen. (For his two elder brothers were born of the same mother, but while she was still a concubine, and they were excluded from the succession by the law of the Kingdom.) He began to rule in the year 1154 BC, and was the twenty-eighth and last Emperor of the second family called the **Shang** <note>original: "Xam"</note> or **Yin** <note>original: "Yn"</note>. He was equipped with all the gifts of nature and talent beyond all others. He was so powerful in bodily strength that he could tear apart wild beasts with his hands; yet, through luxury, lust, and drunkenness, he utterly extinguished such noble talents. He did not sacrifice to <term>Shangdi</term> <note>original: "Xam-tí"; the "Supreme Emperor" or High God of the ancient Chinese.</note> nor to others, nor to the Spirits; for he would blasphemously boast everywhere that he held the <term>Tianxia</term> <note>original: "Tien-hiá"; literally "all under heaven," meaning the whole world.</note> under his feet. 

In the eighth year of his reign, having obtained the concubine Daji <note>original: "Tan-kì"</note>, he administered all things according to her lust. He built towers and sumptuous palaces at the people's expense for the purpose of breeding all kinds of foreign and wild beasts. He opened a lake of wine into which men and women, casting aside their modesty along with their clothes, would immerse themselves. He instituted a cruel type of punishment called **Paoluo** <note>original: "Paô-lo"; the "burning pillar" punishment.</note>, with that same concubine as the inventress and author. It was a bronze column, eight cubits wide and twenty cubits long, entirely hollow inside, and

...divided by three openings: one at the bottom, another in the middle, and finally one in its upper part. Into these three receptacles, fire was introduced so that the multiplied power of the heat might make that mass glow white-hot all the more quickly and violently. To this column, even a prisoner accused of lighter crimes would be most tightly bound with iron chains, suspended in such a position that he appeared to embrace it with his hands and feet. As the machine gradually became white-hot, the wretched man was roasted and scorched as if in a frying pan <note>original: "sartagine"</note>, crying out and wailing horriby until, with his flesh, nerves, and fat melting away on all sides, even his bones glowed like charcoal, and he finally turned entirely to ashes. All this time, his mistress Daji <note>original: "Tan-kì"; the consort of King Zhou, traditionally blamed for the fall of the Shang</note> watched, as if it were a pleasing and delightful spectacle for her eyes, showing no more mercy than the King for the wails of the miserable victims. Although the King's advisors frequently noted such great lust and tyranny in the King and his mistress, and strived to bring the madman back to sanity, they achieved so little that the King remained deaf to everything—indeed, he raged and fumed even more. Consequently, some of these advisors were put to death, others hid themselves in secret places, and some finally fled into the forests and the dens of wild beasts, even feigning madness.

At last, having been defeated in battle by King Wu <note>original: "Vù-vâm"; the founder of the Zhou dynasty</note>, the leader among the minor kings, he fled to a tower. There, having lost all hope of escape, he set himself on fire along with all the royal furnishings so that he might not fall alive into the hands of his enemies; this occurred in the 32nd year of his reign. With him, the Shang <note>original: "Xam"</note> family also came to an end, after it had lasted 644 years.

Such is <gloss>10</gloss> the bride or newlywed <gloss>11</gloss> when <gloss>12</gloss> she passes into the house of the groom, where she provides <gloss>15</gloss> what is fitting <gloss>13 | 14</gloss> for her <gloss>16 | 17</gloss> household, giving to each their due: namely, respect to the husband's parents, peace to the relatives, obedience to the husband, and benevolence and care to subordinates. From this it follows in turn that each and every member of her household conducts themselves properly toward her and toward one another; and so the whole house is well-ordered and composed by her example alone." ## PAGE 24

In this way, the King should establish his family or his domestic court by his own example, so that each and every person within it performs their respective duties in turn. For once the King has first <gloss>19</gloss> performed <gloss>18</gloss> what <gloss>18</gloss> is <gloss>18</gloss> proper <gloss>18</gloss> for his own <gloss>20 21</gloss> household <gloss>22</gloss>, then <gloss>23</gloss> afterwards <gloss>24 25</gloss> he will be able <gloss>26</gloss> to teach and holily instruct even <gloss>27</gloss> the people <gloss>28</gloss> of the entire Kingdom.

-> §. 3. <-

This passage from another Ode <note>The *Odes* or *Shijing* is a classic collection of Chinese poetry cited frequently by Confucius and his followers to provide moral authority</note> serves the same purpose, where the <gloss>1</gloss> Ode <gloss>2</gloss> says: let the younger brother perform <gloss>4</gloss> what <gloss>3</gloss> is <gloss>3</gloss> proper <gloss>3</gloss> for the elder; and let the elder brother perform <gloss>6</gloss> what <gloss>5</gloss> is <gloss>5</gloss> proper <gloss>5</gloss> for the younger. This should not be restricted only to biological brothers <note>original: "uterinos" — literally brothers from the same womb</note>, as if it did not equally apply to others. For in any complete domestic family, whoever is superior to us either in age or social standing is to be held by us in the place of elder brothers; and as such, they are to be won over with all reverence and obedience. Then they, in turn, will both love and cherish us as if we were their own younger brothers. This is what the Ode means: let the younger brother perform what is proper to the elder. Similarly, those who are inferior to us in age or condition are to be loved and cherished by us as younger brothers; and they, without a doubt, will in turn follow us with both honor and obedience as their elder brothers. This is what it means, as the Ode says, for the elder brother to perform what is proper for the younger. 

Zengzi <note>original: "çem-çu"; one of the most important disciples of Confucius, to whom the *Great Learning* is traditionally attributed</note>, applying these words of the Ode, says: if the King is first able to fulfill this himself at home and in his private court, and by his own example ensure that all his household fulfill and perform <gloss>7</gloss> what <gloss>7</gloss> is <gloss>7</gloss> proper <gloss>7</gloss> for <gloss>8</gloss> elder brothers and <gloss>9</gloss> what <gloss>9</gloss> is <gloss>9</gloss> proper <gloss>10</gloss> for younger ones, as was just said, "then <gloss>11</gloss> afterwards <gloss>12 13 14</gloss> he will also be able <gloss>15</gloss> to teach and rightly instruct the <gloss>16</gloss> people <gloss>17</gloss> of the entire Kingdom." He does this by bringing it about that, following his own example, the people also live according to the law of brotherhood among themselves: namely, with respect toward elders and seniors as their older brothers, and with love and benevolence toward the small and inferior as their younger brothers.

-> §. 4. <-

Finally, another <gloss>1</gloss> Ode <gloss>2</gloss> says: if the King <gloss>5</gloss> does not <gloss>6</gloss> fail <gloss>3</gloss> in his <gloss>4</gloss> example <gloss>3</gloss> in all things, his <gloss>11</gloss> kingdom <gloss>8</gloss> will be <gloss>7</gloss> rightly ordered <gloss>9</gloss> in every <gloss>10</gloss> part. Explaining these words of the Ode, Zengzi says: if <gloss>12</gloss> the King himself, <gloss>13</gloss> acting the part <gloss>13</gloss> of a father, <gloss>14</gloss> a son, an <gloss>15</gloss> elder brother, and <gloss>16</gloss> a younger brother <gloss>17</gloss> in his own home, provides himself as a sufficient <gloss>18</gloss> exemplar—that is, if he has perfectly <note>original: "adamussim" — a carpenter's term meaning "according to the level" or "exactly"</note> observed love as a father, obedience as a son, harmony and benevolence as an elder brother, and respect and subjection as a younger one—then, as the Ode says, his example will be perfect in every way, failing in nothing. And <gloss>19</gloss> then <gloss>20</gloss> afterwards <gloss>21</gloss> the people will <gloss>22</gloss> imitate him as their prototype. Parents themselves will also cultivate kindness and fatherly love; children, filial piety and obedience; and thus finally the whole Kingdom will be rightly ordered in every part.

# BOOK ONE.

-> p. 2. §. 1. <-

These three texts just cited and borrowed from the *Book of Songs* <note>original: "Carminum libro" — referring to the Shijing, the classic collection of ancient Chinese poetry</note>, although different in words, all nevertheless say the same thing: namely, this very point that was said above <gloss>2</gloss>, that rightly <gloss>3</gloss> governing <gloss>4</gloss> a kingdom <gloss>5</gloss> consists in rightly <gloss>6</gloss> establishing <gloss>7</gloss> one’s own <gloss>8</gloss> family.

Having explained those matters pertaining to the right ordering of the family and Kingdom, Zengzi <note>çem çu; a primary disciple of Confucius to whom the "Great Learning" is attributed</note> now finally approaches the last part of his Master's doctrine delivered above at the start of this book; and <gloss>1</gloss> what was <gloss>2</gloss> said there, <gloss>3</gloss> pacifying <gloss>4</gloss> the empire <gloss>6</gloss> consists in rightly <gloss>7</gloss> governing <gloss>8</gloss> one’s own <gloss>9</gloss> kingdom. He explains this with a similar discourse, saying: Because men have been allotted a soul of the same nature, therefore the nature of the passions is also the same in all. Thus we see, everywhere on earth, parents desire and love obedience in their children; elders and superiors desire subjection and reverence in their inferiors; the wretched and orphans hope for mercy and kindness in the more powerful, and so forth.

But indeed, the moderation and measure of all these things rests with the King alone, as one who, like a prime mover <note>original: "instar primi mobilis" — an Aristotelian concept describing the outermost sphere of the heavens that moves all other spheres; the translator uses this to explain the King's influence on society</note>, carries and drives his Ministers and Subjects with him by his own example, just as if they were lower spheres, toward that direction in which he himself inclines. For thus, if <gloss>10</gloss> the King at his own home fulfills all <gloss>13</gloss> parts <gloss>11</gloss> of an obedient <gloss>12</gloss> son toward <gloss>14</gloss> his own parents, then <gloss>15</gloss> the people, stirred by his example, <gloss>16</gloss> will be moved to <gloss>16</gloss> obedience toward their own parents. If <gloss>17</gloss> the King fulfills the <gloss>18</gloss> laws of <gloss>18</gloss> due <gloss>18</gloss> obedience toward <gloss>19</gloss> his own <gloss>21</gloss> elder <gloss>19</gloss> brothers <gloss>20</gloss> by birth, and any others he might have in his house as elders <gloss>21</gloss>, then the <gloss>22</gloss> people of the whole Kingdom will be <gloss>23</gloss> moved by his example to <gloss>23</gloss> subjection and reverence toward <gloss>23</gloss> their own elders. If, finally, <gloss>24</gloss> the King <gloss>25</gloss> shows <gloss>25</gloss> compassion and <gloss>25</gloss> kindness as is fitting toward those <gloss>26</gloss> fatherless and <gloss>26</gloss> orphans he has in his own house, then <gloss>27</gloss> the <gloss>28</gloss> people <gloss>29</gloss> will not act <gloss>30</gloss> to the contrary; but all and each will likewise cherish with the same kindness whichever orphans and weak persons they have in their own homes. 

So great, evidently, is the connection of the Great and Superiors with their inferiors, that in whatever things the former lead, the latter immediately follow. Whence it may be seen that, just as the nature of the passions is the same for an entire Kingdom as it is for any private family, so it is the same for the whole Empire as for the people of a private Kingdom. This <gloss>31</gloss> is <gloss>32</gloss> the reason why <gloss>33</gloss> a virtuous <gloss>34</gloss> Prince of this kind <gloss>35</gloss> possesses within <gloss>35</gloss> himself the <gloss>38</gloss> nature of a <gloss>36</gloss> measure <gloss>37</gloss> and standard; by which, measuring others by his own person, he stirs them by his example to do (or not do) the same things which he himself either loves or turns away from.

*The opportunity of this passage invites me to touch briefly here upon certain matters regarding the observance and piety of the Chinese Emperors toward the elderly, the fatherless, and others oppressed by poverty or other calamity; so that from this the European Reader may hereafter understand how much honor and observance the Chinese have always rendered to their parents, or rather how much piety, love, and care—*

->§. 3.<-

The following passage from another Ode <note>original: "Oda" — referring to a poem from the Shijing or "Classic of Poetry"</note> serves the same purpose, where the <gloss>1</gloss> Ode <gloss>2</gloss> says: let the younger brother <gloss>4</gloss> perform <gloss>3</gloss> what <gloss>3</gloss> is <gloss>3</gloss> right for the older; and let the older brother <gloss>6</gloss> perform <gloss>5</gloss> what <gloss>5</gloss> is <gloss>5</gloss> right for the younger. This is not to be restricted only to biological brothers <note>original: "uterinos fratres" — brothers from the same womb</note> as if it did not equally have a place among others. For in any single, whole domestic family, whoever is greater than us either in age or in social standing must be held by us in the place of older brothers; and as such, they are to be won over with all reverence and obedience; for then they themselves, in turn, will both love and cherish us as if we were their own younger brothers. And this is what the Ode means when it says, *let the younger brother perform what is right for the older.* In the same way, those who are inferior to us either in age or condition are to be loved and cherished by us as younger brothers by birth; and they, without doubt, will in turn treat us with both honor and obedience as their older brothers; which is, as the Ode says, *for the elder brother to perform what is right for the younger.* <term>çem-çu</term> <note>Zengzi, the philosopher traditionally credited with editing the Great Learning</note> applying these words of the Ode, says: if the King is first able to fulfill this himself at home and in his private court, and by his example bring it about that all his household fulfill and <gloss>7</gloss> perform <gloss>7</gloss> what <gloss>7</gloss> is <gloss>7</gloss> right <gloss>8</gloss> for older brothers, and <gloss>9</gloss> what <gloss>9</gloss> is <gloss>10</gloss> right for younger ones, as was just said; <gloss>11</gloss> only <gloss>12</gloss> then <gloss>13</gloss> <gloss>14</gloss> will he also be able <gloss>15</gloss> to teach and rightly instruct the <gloss>17</gloss> people <gloss>16</gloss> of the whole Kingdom; namely, by bringing it about that, according to his own example, they also live among themselves by this fraternal law; specifically, with observance toward elders and seniors as their older brothers; and with love and benevolence toward orphans and inferiors, as if they were their younger brothers.

->§. 4.<-

Finally, another <gloss>1</gloss> Ode <gloss>2</gloss> says: if the King <gloss>6</gloss> does not <gloss>6</gloss> fail in <gloss>4</gloss> all things <gloss>3</gloss> by his <gloss>5</gloss> example, his <gloss>10</gloss> kingdom <gloss>8</gloss> will be <gloss>7</gloss> rightly <gloss>8</gloss> established <gloss>9</gloss> in <gloss>9</gloss> every <gloss>9</gloss> part. Explaining these words of the Ode, <term>çem çu</term> says: if the King himself, <gloss>11</gloss> acting <gloss>12</gloss> the part <gloss>13</gloss> of father, <gloss>14</gloss> son, and <gloss>15</gloss> older and <gloss>16</gloss> younger <gloss>17</gloss> brother at home, shows himself to be a <gloss>18</gloss> sufficient exemplar—that is, if he has observed to a hair's breadth <note>original: "ad amussim" — a carpenter's term for perfect precision</note> love as a father, obedience as a son, concord and benevolence as an older brother, and respect and subjection as a younger one—it will be, as the Ode says, that his example is perfect in every way, failing in nothing; and <gloss>19</gloss> only <gloss>20</gloss> then <gloss>21</gloss> will the people <gloss>22</gloss> imitate him as their prototype. Parents themselves will likewise cultivate kindness and paternal love; children will cultivate piety and obedience; and thus finally the whole Kingdom will be rightly established in every part.

### CHINESE KNOWLEDGE
### (SCIENTIÆ SINICÆ)

...ness, the same as parents have toward their children; and as Kings have long since bestowed upon their subjects. And certainly, Christian Europe should acknowledge and esteem such great piety in that ancient Gentility <note>The author uses "Gentilitate" to refer to the pre-Christian or "pagan" era of ancient China.</note>; even if their descendants have now so far fallen away from it that they seem to have acquired a completely different natural character than those ancients possessed. 

The books of duties <note>Referring to the *Liji* or *Book of Rites*</note> report extensively and throughout that this pious custom has flourished since the time of the Legislators **Yao** and **Shun**, namely the specific care of nourishing the elderly, and indeed in a place destined for that purpose: the more honorable in the superior or Eastern Academy, and the commoners in the inferior or Western Academy. And this custom subsequently persisted constantly among the later families <note>The Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties</note> of **Xia**, **Shang**, and **Zhou**; as is made manifest from various places in the same book of duties which we omit for the sake of brevity. 

Certainly, the Annals record concerning the Emperor **Shun** (and other Kings following his example) that while he traveled through the Provinces of the Empire, he was accustomed to inquire everywhere whether there were any centenarians; and if he found any, he visited them in person. Indeed, by the testimony of the same Annals, it is established that those ancient Kings of the Chinese, after performing Sacrifices, were accustomed to change their robes and betake themselves to nourishing the elderly; and this (as is reported in the same place) because they thought that by this work of corporal mercy they might attain from heaven what they had petitioned. Furthermore, from the same book of duties, it is clear to us that this piety and beneficence of the Chinese Emperors extended not only to the elderly, but to all the wretched: orphans, widows, the mute, the lame, the maimed, and so forth.

FOR a fuller declaration of the things mentioned above, **Zengzi** <note>original: "çem-çu" — a philosopher and disciple of Confucius</note> now shows, by an enumeration of parts, in what that principle of the "measuring square" <term>mensuræ normæque ratio <gloss>xieju zhi dao</gloss></term> consists; or by what method and in what matters it is fitting to measure others by ourselves, saying: Of the men with whom you live, some are above you, some below you, some before, some behind, some finally are on the right, and others on the left; and all indeed are affected similarly, just as you are. The same things which you either wish or do not wish to be done to you by them, they also wish or do not wish to be done to them by you. 

Therefore, what you $^1$ dislike $^2$ in $^3$ your superiors, $^4$ do $^5$ not $^6$ do to your inferiors; and $^7$ what $^8$ you dislike $^9$ in $^{10}$ your inferiors, $^{11}$ do $^{12}$ not $^{13}$ do to your superiors. Likewise, what $^{14}$ you hated $^{15}$ in your $^{16}$ predecessors, in that $^{17}$ do $^{18}$ not go before your $^{19}$ successors; and $^{20}$ what $^{21}$ you hated $^{22}$ in your $^{23}$ successors, in that $^{24}$ do $^{25}$ not follow your $^{26}$ predecessors. Finally, what $^{27}$ you condemn $^{28}$ in those who are $^{29}$ on the $^{30}$ right, $^{31}$ do $^{32}$ not do to those who $^{33}$ are $^{34}$ on the $^{35}$ left; and conversely, $^{36}$ what $^{37}$ you disapprove of in $^{38}$ those who are on the $^{39}$ left, $^{40}$ do $^{41}$ not do $^{42}$ to those who are on the $^{43}$ right. 

In a word: **What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.** And $^{44}$ this is and $^{45}$ is called the true $^{46}$ principle $^{47}$ of the measuring $^{48}$ square; by the use of which any upright Prince finally achieves this: that having become, as it were, one heart and one soul with his people, wishing and not wishing the same things as the people, he may now more truly be called the father of the people than their Lord. This, **Zengzi** confirms from the *Book of Odes* <note>The *Shijing* or *Classic of Poetry*</note> with an authority clearly suited to this passage, saying:

**BOOK ONE.**

### §. 2.

<margin>1.</margin> The **Poem**<sup>1</sup> <note>original: *Carmen*; referring to the *Book of Odes* or *Shijing*</note> says: a Prince of this kind is truly praiseworthy<sup>2</sup> and lovable<sup>3</sup>; he is plainly<sup>5</sup> the father<sup>6</sup> and mother<sup>8</sup> of the people. Following this same poem, **Zengzi**<sup>9</sup> <note>original: *çem-çu*, a primary disciple of Confucius</note> says: to rejoice<sup>12</sup> in what the people<sup>10</sup> rejoice in, and to hate<sup>16</sup> what the people<sup>14</sup> hate; this is said to be<sup>19</sup> the father and mother of the people. It is as if he were to say: for a King to measure and moderate all his actions according to the feelings and will of his people, fostering and protecting them just like his own children, is the thing by which the people are primarily bound to him, and in which all subjects, both collectively and individually, are accustomed to rejoice wonderfully. If, therefore, the King himself also rejoices in this same way, so that what the people have in their prayers, he has in his works; that is when the heart of the King is so poured into the souls of his subjects that he rejoices in the same things they desire, and hates what they loathe; plainly in the manner of a father and mother embracing their son with the most intimate affection. From this, the people will in turn hold such a King in the place of a father and mother; which is the principal effect of measuring others by oneself <note>original: *metientis alios ex seipso*; a reference to the Confucian "Golden Rule" or principle of *Shu* (reciprocity)</note>.

### p. 2. §. 1.

**Zengzi** confirms the above by the opposite case, using another place from the same *Book of Odes*; where<sup>1</sup> the **Ode**<sup>2</sup> says:<sup>3</sup> "O, how<sup>4</sup> steeply<sup>5</sup> that southern<sup>8</sup> mountain<sup>9</sup> towers!<sup>6</sup> O, what a great and jagged<sup>10</sup> mass of rocks!"<sup>9</sup> Just so do you tower, to be feared<sup>12</sup> for your power and dignity,<sup>11</sup> great Master<sup>13</sup> of the Royal **Yin**;<sup>14</sup> <note>Referring to a high-ranking but oppressive official of the Yin dynasty</note> and indeed all<sup>17</sup> the people<sup>16</sup> fear and look up to<sup>18</sup> you; but they do not love you, since you consult your private interests and not the common good. Explaining this passage of the Ode, **Zengzi** says: since<sup>19</sup> the one holding<sup>20</sup> the kingdom, or the King, is established upon that steep pinnacle of Royal dignity and is never hidden from the eyes of his subjects;<sup>21</sup> he ought<sup>24</sup> not<sup>22-23</sup> to fail to watch with anxious care,<sup>25</sup> and to direct all his concerns to this end: that whatever affairs or business he undertakes, all should agree with the prayers and expectations of the people. For if he does not know how to measure others by himself, but acts in all things according to his own lust and desire, neglecting those things which are beneficial to and desired by the people; and if he does not labor to repel and turn away those things which are hated and ruinous to the people: it will undoubtedly happen that the people, their hearts alienated from him and distracted by seditions and tumults, will at last depart from him; and he, left alone, will no longer be able to protect the Kingdom from ruin or preserve it. Therefore, if the King (says **Zengzi**) swerves from this rule,<sup>26</sup> it will<sup>29-30</sup> altogether<sup>28</sup> be the setting<sup>31</sup> <note>original: *occasus*; a metaphor for the "sunset" or end of a dynasty</note> and ruin of the empire.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Confucian classic "The Great Learning," specifically the chapter attributed to Zengzi. # CHINESE KNOWLEDGE

...the people, or the love of the people, he held and ruled the Empire in peaceful possession. Because of the conformity of his virtue with Heaven, he was able—or rather, was worthy—to be admitted into the society and fellowship of the Supreme Emperor of Heaven <note>original: *supremo cœli Imperatore*; likely referring to *Shangdi*, the High Deity</note>. However, after their degenerate posterity turned away from the ancient virtue of their ancestors and lost the love of the people, they also lost the favor of heaven, or rather, the imperial authority bestowed by heaven. Therefore, it is now necessary for the descendants of our **Zhou** <note>original: *Cheu*</note> family (which succeeded the **Yin** or **Shang** <note>original: *Yn, seu Xam*</note> family in the Empire) to cast their eyes upon the **Yin** family and take care that they do not follow their bad example and lose the Empire in a similar way. "For the most high mandate of heaven, or the favor of heaven, by which Empires are granted, is not easily preserved." The Ode therefore means to say (as **Zengzi** <note>original: *çem-çu*</note> explains) that once the "love of the people" is obtained, the "kingdom" is soon obtained as well; just as, conversely, if the "love of the people" is lost, the "kingdom" is likewise soon lost.

->*folio* 12. *page* 1. §. 1.<-

Since, as has been said, the longevity and preservation of the Empire depends on the love of the people, and the love of the people depends on virtue—which alone makes a Prince lovable—therefore the **perfect King** watches over all things and applies himself to **virtue**. By possessing virtue, he will by that very fact possess the hearts and wills of the people. Having the wills of the people on his side, he will by that very fact possess the **lands**, which the people, tilling and inhabiting them, will be more than willing to have under his dominion. Furthermore, by possessing the lands, he will by that very fact possess the **wealth** and resources produced from them. Finally, by possessing wealth, he will by that very fact have everything necessary for the **use** and preservation of the Kingdom.

->§. 2.<-

This is an inference most worthy of gold and cedar <note>original: *auro cedroque dignissima*; a classical idiom meaning a work is of high value and deserves immortality</note>, by which the Author concludes that **virtue** is the more principal thing, or of greater importance for the peaceful government of the Empire. It is like the **root** from which all the safety and vigor of Kingdoms proceeds. **Wealth**, however, is less principal, or so to speak, an accessory of lesser importance; it is therefore like the **branches** of a tree, which cannot help but flourish beautifully once the root is deeply fixed and vigorous. For however much wealth may be necessary for the preservation of the Empire, it is of such a nature that wherever virtue, the mistress, fixes her home, wealth follows there of its own accord as a handmaid.

->§. 3.<-

Since virtue, according to what has just been said, is the more principal thing and of greater importance—being the root and foundation of happy governance—while wealth is less principal and of less importance—being the branches that then sprout of their own accord from that fertile root of virtue—it follows that a good Prince must have virtue first in his heart...

ought to be held as domestic <note>The author uses a metaphor of a household: virtue is a family member to be kept inside, while wealth is a "foreigner" to be kept outside the heart.</note>; but these [riches] should be less cared for, and placed outside as if they were foreign things. If therefore the King holds in <gloss>¹</gloss> the outermost place <gloss>¹</gloss> and cares less for that which is more <gloss>²</gloss> principal—that is, virtue—and holds in <gloss>³</gloss> the innermost parts, or in his heart above all else, that which is <gloss>⁴</gloss> less <gloss>⁴</gloss> principal—that is, wealth, by amassing it through right or wrong <note>original: *per fas nefasque*</note>; the people, taught by his example, will immediately do the same; they will all consume each other with disputes, lawsuits, thefts, and robberies. Therefore (says **Zengzi** <note>original: *çem-çu*</note>) such a King will provoke the people to <gloss>⁵</gloss> brawls <gloss>⁶</gloss> seditions and <gloss>⁷</gloss> disturbances <gloss>⁸</gloss>, and will <gloss>⁷</gloss> open the way <gloss>⁸</gloss> to thefts and <gloss>⁹</gloss> robberies.

<margin>§. 4.</margin>
Therefore, when <gloss>¹</gloss> wealth is scraped together by right or wrong, by <gloss>³</gloss> that very act <gloss>⁴</gloss> the people <gloss>⁵</gloss> are scattered; and conversely, where <gloss>⁶</gloss> wealth is prudently <gloss>⁷</gloss> distributed for the common necessities of the people and the Kingdom, by <gloss>⁸</gloss> that very act <gloss>⁹</gloss> the people <gloss>¹⁰</gloss> are gathered together. For indeed, the unjust accumulation of wealth is the scattering of the people, and the generous giving and distribution of wealth is the uniting and gathering of the people.

<margin>§. 5.</margin>
Furthermore, such a greedy accumulation of wealth and riches is not only the loss of the people, but is even the most certain destruction and loss of the wealth itself. <gloss>¹¹</gloss> For this reason (says **Zengzi**), just as a <gloss>¹</gloss> rash <gloss>²</gloss> word <gloss>³</gloss> having gone out <note>original: *egressum*</note> from the mouth, <gloss>⁶</gloss> also <gloss>⁷</gloss> enters [the ear of another] rashly in turn <gloss>⁸</gloss>; so <gloss>⁹</gloss> wealth <gloss>¹¹</gloss> having entered through <gloss>¹⁰</gloss> wickedness, <gloss>¹²</gloss> also <gloss>¹⁴</gloss> departs through <gloss>¹³</gloss> wickedness again. It is as if he were to say: Just as one who speaks insulting words against others must necessarily hear similar things spoken by others against himself; so wealth once badly gained cannot be preserved for long without slipping away badly again. Thus, the unjust accumulation of wealth is not so much an amassing as it is a loss. If, therefore, such unjust riches are so difficult to preserve, why should the King hold them so deep in his heart, while holding virtue in the outermost place?

<margin>part 2. §. 1.</margin>
Because the ruin of the Empire itself, by the scattering of the people, usually follows that backward love of riches, **Zengzi** confirms this by authority in these words: The <gloss>¹</gloss> **Book of Kang Gao** <gloss>²</gloss> <gloss>³</gloss> says <note>The *Kang Gao* is a chapter in the *Classic of History* or *Shujing*, containing the "Announcement to the Prince of Kang."</note>: The <gloss>⁴</gloss> mandate, or Empire, of Heaven <gloss>⁵</gloss> is <gloss>⁶</gloss> not lasting. He <gloss>⁷</gloss> means to say (says the same **Zengzi**) that a King who <gloss>⁸</gloss> is honest and a lover of virtue, by that very fact <gloss>⁹</gloss> obtains and preserves the Empire; but he who <gloss>¹⁰</gloss> || <gloss>¹¹</gloss> is wicked and values gold more than virtue, <gloss>¹²</gloss> immediately <gloss>¹³</gloss> loses it. Therefore, let the King cultivate virtue above all else, and let him hold this alone in high esteem over riches, if indeed he desires the favor of heaven to be stable in preserving the Empire for himself; for this alone, as was said above, is the most solid basis and foundation <note>original: *Firmamentum*</note> of Kingdoms and Empires.

It concludes by citing the Classic of History to show that the Mandate of Heaven is only maintained through moral integrity, not material riches.</summary>

### §. 2.

Using an example taken from the Chronicles, **Zengzi** <note>original: *çam çû*</note> shows here how truly nothing ought to be more precious to a King than virtue, while he recounts that among good Princes, virtue was formerly held in higher esteem than gold and gems. For when the Envoy of the Kingdom of **Chu** <note>original: *çû*; now the Province of Huguang</note>, named **Wangsun Yu** <note>original: *Vân-fun-yù*</note>, was once asked by **Zhao Jianzi** <note>original: *Chaò kien-çù*</note>, a Great Noble of the Kingdom of **Jin** <note>original: *çín*</note>, about the riches and precious gems of that Kingdom, the Chronicles of the same Kingdom of Chu say that he replied thus: *The Kingdom of Chu <gloss>⁷, ⁸</gloss> considers <gloss>¹¹</gloss> nothing <gloss>⁹</gloss> to be precious <gloss>¹², ¹⁷</gloss>; it considers <gloss>¹⁶</gloss> virtue <gloss>¹⁵</gloss> alone <gloss>¹³</gloss> and uniquely <gloss>¹⁴</gloss> to be precious.* As if he were to say: Although our Kingdom of Chu does not lack gold, pearls, and precious stones, we do not hold these in such high esteem that we do not consider virtue, and the men endowed with virtue who are not lacking in our Kingdom, to be far more precious and valuable than gold and gems. And indeed, at that time there lived in that Kingdom two men famous for their virtue, one called **Guan Shefu** <note>original: *Quón-xé-fù*</note> and the other **Zuo Siyi** <note>original: *çò-sù-y*</note>: for both these men, like two most firm columns, supported their King and the Kingdom itself through their wisdom, counsel, integrity, justice, and piety.

*Quite parallel to this is what the Chinese Chronicles record as having happened under **King Xian** <note>original: *Hiên-vâm*</note>, the thirty-second Emperor of the **Zhou** <note>original: *Cheu*</note> family (under whom the Philosopher **Mencius** <note>original: *Mem-çú*</note> lived). The petty King of the Kingdom of **Qi** <note>original: *çî*</note> had entered into a treaty with the petty King of the Kingdom of **Wei** <note>original: *Guéi*</note>: when the latter asked the former whether he had precious stones in his Kingdom, and he replied that he had none, the King of Wei was astonished; scarcely believing the one who answered, he said: "I, who possess a Kingdom far smaller than yours, nevertheless possess a precious stone (namely, a carbuncle) which illuminates the space of twelve chariots with its brightness; how then can I believe that in your Kingdom, which is far more extensive than mine, such precious stones are not found?" To which the King of the Kingdom of Qi replied: "I have four ministers, or Dynasts, who administer the Provinces entrusted to them with great prudence and virtue; these are my very carbuncles and precious stones, which illuminate with the rays and light of their virtue not only the space of twelve chariots, but an expanse of a thousand Chinese stadia <note>referring to 'li', a Chinese unit of distance</note> far and wide."*

*I attach to this another far more ancient and equally illustrious testimony of virtue from the same Chronicles, given by that most illustrious heroine **Queen Jiang**, the wife of the Emperor **Xuan Wang** <note>original: *Siven-vâm*</note>, the eleventh of the Zhou family, who began to reign 827 years before Christ, and more than 200 years before Confucius. For when this Emperor, in the 33rd year of his reign, was gorging himself entirely on banquets and lusts, Queen Jiang, detesting the incontinence and luxury of her spouse, first took off the earrings and precious gems she was wearing and went to the King; she intrepidly rebuked him, saying: **Vâm lo fe, ûlh vâm te**, that is, "You, O King, rejoice in luxury, and you forget virtue <note>original: *tu ô Rex, gaudes luxuriâ, & oblivisceris virtutis*</note>, which I value far more than precious stones," etc. By then discoursing further on that matter, she so changed the mind of the Emperor that he entirely...*

...with abundance and plenty; but the people in peace, union, and everlasting tranquility—but why do I say preserve? Nay, even to be a benefit to the whole Kingdom itself and a source of new growth every day. On the contrary, if there were any one of my nobles who, being entirely intent on his own individual advantages, arrogated everything to his own individual gifts and talents; and thus envied other men possessing good talents, and therefore even hated those same men; and if he, armed with a thousand tricks and arts, excluded and hindered men excelling in wisdom and virtue, doing everything so that they might not emerge: such a man, so infested with the stain of self-love <note>original: philautiæ; from the Greek 'philautia,' meaning excessive egoism or conceit</note>, and a man of such a narrow heart, truly is not able to admit or tolerate alongside himself men signally commended by virtue and nature, and much less to propose that they be raised to higher office. And so, established in the dignity of a High Official, he causes the King, finally pressed by extreme difficulties, to lose his royal spirit, while all the worst men obtain their wishes; and thus all the affairs and business of the Kingdom go to ruin. Such a man, therefore, is in no way able to protect my sons and grandsons, nor ensure that royal honor and dignity long persevere among them; nor can he preserve the people in lasting peace, for they, provoked by his tyranny and vexations, would surely rise up. Nothing of protection, nothing of defense is ever to be expected from such a man; indeed, I would dare to say that he will eventually bring the ultimate danger and ruin to my entire Kingdom and the royal lineage.

->Book 13, Page 1, Section 1<-

In this paragraph **Zengzi** <note>original: çem çu; the philosopher and disciple of Confucius traditionally credited with the "Great Learning"</note> teaches that only a pious and truly people-loving Prince—who indeed knows how to measure the feelings and wishes of his people by his own—is of such virtue and mind that, when he detects a ruinous official of this kind, or a Counselor, he immediately proscribes him and banishes him to the furthest distance from the Kingdom, out to the Barbarians of the four regions <note>original: quatuor plagarum Barbaros; referring to the non-Chinese tribes at the edges of the known world</note> and foreign nations, not permitting him to live together with the rest in the Middle Kingdom <note>original: in medio (hoc est Sinarum) regno; "the kingdom in the middle," the traditional name for China</note>; this is so that he might not be a source of harm or an obstacle to men excellently equipped by nature and virtue within the Kingdom. For in order to free yourself from a pain or anger that sticks deep in your marrow, it is necessary to uproot the very source of the evil. And this is plainly what **Confucius** had said: namely, that only the pious and perfect Prince is he who knows how to love men, and knows also how to hate men <note>original: norit amare homines, & norit item odiſſe homines; the ideal ruler is not indifferent, but possesses the moral clarity to love the good and hate the wicked</note>.

->Page 2, Section 1<-

Because **Zengzi** said above that honest men are a great benefit to the Commonwealth <note>original: Reipublicæ</note>, and the wicked a no less significant detriment, he now warns in this present paragraph that any good Prince should not show himself slow in employing the former for governance, or in removing the latter. For he says thus: "to see or know a man who is honest and wise, and not be willing to elevate and use him; or, indeed to elevate him...

<meta>This page continues the discourse on the moral obligations of a ruler, specifically focusing on the consequences of keeping a wicked advisor in power. # BOOK ONE.

...indeed, but yet not to have wished to do it <note>that is, to banish the wicked official</note> sooner, is to do an injury. But on the contrary, to have a wicked and destructive man to the state <note>original: Reipublicae; referring here to the common good or the commonwealth of the kingdom</note> established in high office, and yet not be willing to remove him from there; or, to remove him indeed, but quite sluggishly and half-heartedly; and to not be willing to remove him far away—this is a crime.

### §. 2.
**T**o know how to love people, and to know how to hate them, is to perfectly fulfill that aforementioned norm and rule of an upright King, by which he is accustomed to measure the affections of the people according to his own single person. To know upright men and yet not elevate them, or at least to elevate them later than is right; and conversely, to know wicked men who are destructive to the public good and not to drive them far away <note>original: averruncare; a term for averting or weeding out evil</note>, is to fail that same rule. And Zengzi <note>original: çem-çu; a primary disciple of Confucius and traditional author of the Great Learning</note> had dealt with both of these points in the immediately preceding paragraph; now, in this present one, he deals with the wicked Prince who not only fails to follow the said rule, but opposes it from the opposite side.

He says, therefore, that **to love what other men everywhere hate**, and **to hate what other men love**—this is said to be repugnant to the common nature of humanity. It is as if he were saying: a wicked counselor and a disturber of the public peace in the Kingdom (of whom mention was made just above) is a man hated by all; and thus he should be removed far from office and dignity. To cherish such a man nonetheless, and not only to believe his malice and deceptions but furthermore to use his service for the greatest affairs of the Kingdom—this, of course, is what Zengzi means when he says: *to love what men hate*.

On the other hand, the upright and honest man, faithful to the King, is the one whom all good people love with a unanimous affection, and who is thus worthy to be elevated as quickly as possible to the primary honors and offices in the Kingdom. Furthermore, to despise such a man, and not only to refuse him admittance but to cast him even further away—this, finally, is what the same Zengzi means by: *to hate what men everywhere love*. 

But indeed, to hate evil and to love good is the common nature of all, which every mortal has received in equal portion. Therefore, to love the one whom all others hate, and to hate the one whom all others love and esteem, is this not to fight against and oppose the common nature of all mortals? And he who thus opposes this nature, why should he not also simultaneously incur the hatred and envy of all? And thus, being hated and detested by everyone, what else should he expect from a vengeful Heaven except that, having lost the love of the people, he also loses his Empire <note>original: Imperium; the right to rule or the sovereignty</note>, as Zengzi implies with those words: **calamities will certainly be imminent for a person of that kind**.

### §. 3.

# THE CHINESE SCIENCE

$^6$That great and so often praised **rule of virtue**, $^7$by which the ruler measures the people by his own person; $^8$certainly, $^9$sincerity and $^{10}$faithfulness <note>The Latin uses *synceritas* and *fides*, referring to the Confucian concepts of *cheng* (sincerity/integrity) and *xin* (trustworthiness/fidelity)</note> (acting, that is, candidly without guile and sincerely without pretense) were the means $^{11}$by which he attained it $^{12}$; just as, on the contrary, $^{13}$arrogance and $^{14}$insolence are the vices $^{15}$by which the same rule $^{16}$is lost. 

For when you have progressed so far in sincerity that, having become the master of your own affections, you are no longer a source of deception to anyone—not even to yourself—and likewise, when you have moderated all your actions by faithfulness (that is, by a rule consistent with all things), then indeed you will find yourself possessing that integrity of mind, rectitude, and equanimity of the affections. Then you will love nothing except what good men approve, and you will hate nothing except what all good men likewise detest. Then, at last, you will be able to measure others by yourself without error, and (as was said above) happily propagate your own singular virtue through fame and example to the people and kingdoms subject to you. This is that great **norm and rule of virtue** handed down even to this point and so greatly commended to Leading Men, by which you will know how to rightly hate and love others, having become truly **the father and the mother of the people**. 

But if, on the contrary, becoming insolent through your dignity and power, you indulge your own unbridled desire—attending not to what the reason of the common good suggests, but to what your own lust <note>original: *libido*; here meaning whim or selfish impulse</note> persuades—then surely, with your heart closed to the utility of others and following will instead of reason, you will no longer strive to benefit others, but only yourself; not for the profit of the people and the state, but only for your own convenience. By loving what good men detest, and detesting what good men love and approve, and thus having become rebellious against the common nature of mankind, what can you finally expect, having lost that great rule, except calamities and ruin?

->§. 14. p. 1. §. 1.<-

**B**ecause the "accursed hunger for gold" <note>original: *auri sacra fames*; a famous quote from Virgil’s Aeneid (3.57) regarding greed</note> and the insatiable desire for amassing wealth is most often what diverts Kings and Leading Men from the royal path of virtue and drives them astray, *Zengzi* <note>original: *çem çu*; a primary disciple of Confucius to whom the Great Learning is attributed</note> in this paragraph clearly indicates the royal way, by which they may be able to achieve their desires and increase the royal wealth by perpetual growth, not only without vice, but even with great commendation of virtue. Thus, he says: $^1$for the increasing of $^2$royal wealth and resources, $^3$there is given $^4$a certain great and excellent $^5$rule: primarily, that if those who $^6$produce and increase $^7$it (or contribute their effort to increasing it) are $^8$many—leaving no one idle, but with everyone occupied in agriculture or honest trade—then wealth grows. Conversely, the Prefects and Ministers who $^9$consume, or receive their annual revenues from $^{10}$those royal riches, should be $^{11}$few, namely by cutting back the unnecessary multitude of offices and servants which is nourished by the royal treasury. Furthermore, those who $^{12}$labor and cultivate the fields should work $^{13}$strenuously; that is, they should not be distracted by other things during the proper time for agriculture, but should be skillfully occupied in the single work of farming. Zengzi argues that national wealth is best increased by maximizing producers (farmers/traders) and minimizing consumers (bureaucrats).</summary>

# BOOK ONE.

^14 Those who use them, or those who distribute those royal riches, should be ^15 deliberate and moderate, looking ahead so far into the future with provident parsimony <note>Latin: *parsimonia*, meaning thrift or frugality</note> and saving, so that in any given three-year period, for example, at least one year's revenue remains as a surplus, which they may add to the Royal treasury as a permanent increase. ^16 By this means, it will come to pass that the ^17 royal riches and resources ^18 will always ^19 be sufficient.

---

-> §. 2. <-

In the previous paragraph, <gloss>Zengzi</gloss> <note>original: "çem çu"; the name of a prominent disciple of Confucius to whom this part of the text is attributed</note> handed down the rule for acquiring and increasing wealth. Here he now teaches the right use of it, saying: ^1 a virtuous and people-loving Prince ^3 adds luster to ^4 his person ^2 through riches; on the contrary, ^5 a wicked one ^10 adorns ^9 riches ^6 with his ^7 ^8 own person.

As if he were to say: A merciful and people-loving Prince, who understands that great rule of increasing resources, strives for this one thing above all: that there is enough wealth for his people, being not at all anxious for his own individual profit. From this it follows that he himself, with the people looking up to him and applauding, is celebrated by the mouths and prayers of all, having become dear and venerable to everyone. This is what is meant here by *despising riches and exalting and adorning one's own person.* 

Conversely, a harsh and wicked man who does not know that great rule of increasing wealth, acts only to fill the Royal treasury with riches scraped together by right or wrong <note>Latin: *per fas nefasque*, meaning "through any means, lawful or unlawful"</note>, caring nothing for the needs and hardships of his impoverished people. Because of this, the hearts of his subjects are alienated from him, and he eventually brings destruction upon both the Kingdom and himself. This is what is meant by *despising the person and exalting riches.* 

Therefore, to "adorn the person with riches" is, properly speaking, to not crave riches for oneself, and yet, by binding the hearts of the people to oneself through this modesty, to never truly lack riches. Conversely, to "adorn riches with one's person" is to wish to honor the person in name, but in reality to destroy it; and once the person is lost, what use can there be in wealth?

---

-> §. 3. <-

<term>Zengzi</term> <note>A philosopher and student of Confucius</note> now confirms the things said above from the perspective of utility: "It has not yet ^1 been seen," he says, "that one ^5 placed ^3 in a ^4 superior ^2 position—that is, a King—^6 ^7 loved ^8 piety <note>Latin: *pietas*, here referring to the ruler's parental-like benevolence or *ren*</note> and mercy toward his subjects, ^6 and the ^7 subjects ^8 did not ^9 love ^10 loyalty <note>Latin: *fidelitas*, referring to the Chinese concept of *zhong*</note>, or did not respond in turn to their King with the loyalty they owe by justice." 

Nor has it been seen thus far ^11 that a ^12 people ^14 rejoiced in ^15 loyalty toward the King, and ^16 his (the King's) ^17 business and efforts ^18 did not ^19 achieve the desired outcome. For when the people adhere to their King with such loyalty, they surely consider the King's resources and treasures as their own, and they preserve them in peace and defend them in war as if they were their own property. Hence, "it has never ^20 been seen that such a ^21 faithful ^22 people ^24 did not treat the ^23 riches of the royal treasury ^25 as if they were their own." It is of such great importance to the King to have bound the people to himself through benevolence and beneficence.

### CHINESE SCIENCES

<margin>§. 4.</margin>
<gloss>Zengzi</gloss> <note>original: "çem-çu"; a primary disciple of Confucius</note> continues to emphasize further the aforementioned piety and benevolence of the King toward the people, as a virtue that can never be sufficiently recommended to Princely Men. To this end, he introduces those most beautiful and immortal <note>original: "cedroque dignissima," literally "worthy of cedar oil," a Latin idiom for works worthy of being preserved for eternity</note> warnings of that great man called <gloss>Meng Xian Zi</gloss> <note>original: "mém hién çù"</note>, who once held the chief prefecture of the Kingdom of <gloss>Lu</gloss>. Thus, therefore, Meng Xian Zi says: those who ^6. 7. maintain ^8. 9. **four-horse chariots** <note>these were the nobles called <term>Dafu</term>, who were permitted to travel in a "quadriga," or a carriage drawn by four horses</note>, since they live on a royal income, ^10 should not ^11 deal in ^12 **chickens** and ^13 **piglets**—that is to say, they should not breed a great quantity of these for the profit of their private household, thereby snatching away the livelihood of the common people, for whom this is their own proper business. ^14 Likewise, the ^16 family ^14 of those who ^15 **cut ice** <note>This refers to the <term>Qing</term>, a higher rank of Lords; in ancient China, harvesting and storing ice for ancestral rites was a privilege reserved for the high nobility</note>, because they enjoy a larger income than the ordinary nobles, should not themselves ^17 breed ^18 **oxen** and ^19 **sheep**—namely, by raising numerous herds and flocks for the base profit of their own house, which causes no small harm to the wretched commoners who depend on the small profits of that humble trade to survive. ^20 Finally, the ^22 family of ^21 **a hundred chariots** <note>These were the <term>Satrapae</term> or Governors of the petty kings, also called <term>Qing</term>; they governed a territory of ten Chinese miles and could field a hundred war chariots</note> ^23 should not ^24 maintain and cherish in their homes ^25 **oppressive** ^27 **ministers** ^26 **of taxes**, who, under the pretext of collecting revenue, monstrously "skin" <note>original: "deglubant," meaning to flay or strip bare</note> the subject people and strip them of their resources. For ^28 if ^29 that Governor should perhaps ^30 have ^31 such a ^34 minister ^32 unjustly multiplying ^33 taxes ^30 in his house, ^35 it would be better for him ^36 to have a minister ^37 openly plundering ^38 his own domestic treasury <note>original: "gazophylacium"</note> and riches; for this one harms only one person, while the other harms many. How, then, can it be that he suffers in his own home such a common thief of the Kingdom, a leech <note>original: "sanguisugam"</note> of the people, who so cruelly drains the sweat and blood of the subjects? And this was the warning of that most praiseworthy man; explaining which, Zengzi says: with ^37 these few aforementioned words, ^38 that great man wanted to say that ^39 Kings and Princely Men ^40 should ^41 not ^43 place ^42 **profit** ^41 in their own private gain, ^40 but ^47 place ^48 **profit** ^45 in their own and the people's mutual ^46 **justice and love**. As if he were to say: Princely Men ought not to burden the people with excessive taxes, nor consider treasuries filled with gold and silver as their chief profit; but they should hold only that as true profit in which the people also have a large share. When they have won over the people through love and benevolence, and made them their own, only then should they consider themselves truly to have attained power over affairs.

->P. 2. §. I.<-

What <gloss>Zengzi</gloss> <note>original: "çem-çu"</note> said in the previous paragraph—that Princes ought to measure their ^1 <term>profit</term> <note>original: "lucrum"; translating the Chinese concept of *Li* (gain)</note> primarily by the ^2 utility and ^3 advantage of their people—he now amplifies by describing the ^4 losses that await those who, ^5 neglecting the people, ^6 pursue their own ^7 private ^8 wealth. He says, therefore: if someone ^1 governs a ^2 royal ^3 house ^4 and ^5 devotes ^6 himself ^6 entirely to the ^7 hoarding of riches, this ^8 undoubtedly ^9 arises ^10 from a vile and ^10 base ^11 man <note>original: "vili & abjecto homine"; referring to a corrupt or "small" person in a moral sense</note> who, having ensnared the King with malicious counsel, induces him toward this path. Such a man suggests that a heavy burden of ^12 taxes and ^13 exactions is the most suitable ^14 industry for ^15 enriching the Kingdom; ^12 he ^13 persuades the King to ^14 hold this as ^14 good and ^14 just.

If such a destructive advisor—truly a ^15 vile and ^16 base ^16 man—is ^17 employed to ^18 govern the ^19 royal ^20 family, he will surely fill everything with ^21 plunder and ^22 theft, snatching away the goods and resources of the subjects at his own whim. Thus, with the hearts of the people alienated from both the advisor and the King, and the ^23 just anger of heaven provoked against them, ^21 calamities from heaven and ^22 ruin and slaughter from men will undoubtedly ^23 arrive ^23 together or ^23 in a heap. And ^25 although ^26 there might ^27 be ^27 some ^27 upright ^27 man who tries to help and turn away such a great force of evils, ^28 nevertheless, ^29 how ^31 will he ^31 have the power, ^30 acting alone, to prevent it? And this ^32 is what ^33 was said above: that an ^34 upright ^35 King does ^36 not ^38 establish ^39 profit ^37 in his own private ^37 gain, but ^40 establishes ^43 profit ^41 in mutual equity and love ^42 between himself and the people.

<margin>e)</margin>
*This is indeed a most fitting Conclusion to the entire doctrine of this book! It is entirely worthy for <gloss>Zengzi</gloss> to crown the end of this first book with it as his own concluding flourish <note>original: "epiphonemate"</note>; just as <gloss>Mencius</gloss> <note>original: "Memçius"</note> would distinguish the beginning of his fourth book with it as a primary inscription of things to be said. For certainly, anyone who examines all the paragraphs of this book with an open mind will clearly perceive that our Chinese Philosopher—I mean Confucius—aimed primarily at this: to show Kings and Princely men (to whom, above all others, he directed this great science of his) that virtue is necessary above all else for the peaceful and happy governance of Kingdoms and Empires. This was shown not merely from his own opinion, but from the unanimous sense of all the most Ancient men. For just as all Chinese antiquity believed—not in vain—that power is granted and taken away by Heaven, and as their descendants even today confess, long experience over so many centuries has proven that the safety and preservation of these same Kingdoms depends, after the gods, upon the love and faith of the people. Thus, by common sentiment long ago, those first Founders of this Chinese Monarchy judged—and even today the best of the Chinese confess—that it is virtue which wins together both the favor of Heaven and the high gods, and the love of the people, for Princes who deserve well of them. Thus, to pass over many others in silence, in the 3rd book of the <gloss>Shu Jing</gloss> <note>original: "xu kim"; the Classic of History</note> on folio 17, that most praised man <gloss>Yi Yin</gloss> <note>original: "y-yn"</note>, the Royal Master, as a new and young...*

*(who reigned before Christ)* in order to kindle a love of virtue more vehemently, he gave warning in these very words drawn from the text. "O King," he said, "Heaven is not moved by mere emotion; yet it knows how to duly venerate and worship, and to such a person it is always dear and gracious. Likewise, the people are not always moved; yet they are always moved by one who possesses piety. Finally, the spirits do not always listen; but they listen to him who excels in true virtue. With this one thing <note>virtue</note> held, (†) do not doubt that you will be eternally beloved by heaven, always dear to the people, and finally, never anything but pleasing to all the spirits above," etc. Since the author throughout this whole book—as is clear to the reader—has demonstrated this great prerogative of virtue over gold and riches by using various reasons and authorities, he could not, in my judgment, use a more suitable Epilogue than these very words: that is, to say that an upright King should not define ^1 <term>profit</term> <note>original: "lucrum"; translating the Chinese concept of *Li* (gain or benefit)</note> by that sordid ^2 gain of ^3 private ^4 wealth, but should define profit in the ^5 mutual ^6 equity between himself and his people. It is as if he were saying: the entire doctrine handed down by me in this book turns upon this one hinge, and teaches this one thing above all: that Kings and Princes should place the meaning of true profit not so much in treasuries filled with gold as in the mutual equity, love, clemency, and faith between themselves and the people—in a word, in virtue. For once that is possessed, all other things which can be desired or deserved—namely gold and wealth, the love of the people, a long line of descendants, and finally peace, (†) and the enduring rest and stability of the empire—follow of their own accord.

And this is that <term>Great Science</term> <note>original: "Magna Scientia"; the Latin title used by the Jesuits for the *Daxue* or *Great Learning*</note> which long ago issued from this Chinese ^1 <term>Areopagus</term> <note>The Areopagus was the high court of Athens; the author uses it here to describe the ancient Chinese assembly of sages</note>, most worthy of such a great name, whether you look at the nobility of its doctrine or its antiquity. It demonstrates its nobility from the virtue (what is nobler?) which it teaches; and its antiquity from the very beginnings of the Chinese Monarchy (what is more ancient?) from whence it was born. And although European Philosophy might compete with this Chinese one in the nobility of its subject matter—and if you were to contend in elegance of style, subtlety, eloquence, variety, and (†) grace, European philosophy might not undeservedly excel—yet I would dare to say that in antiquity, it does not even come close, but follows at a very long distance indeed. Truly, before the superstitious deities of Asia were born, virtue had already grown to adulthood among the Chinese, and the very courts of the Kings were turning into <term>Lyceums</term> <note>The Lyceum was Aristotle's school; here meaning centers of moral education</note> of virtue. At a time when Europe is believed to have still been entirely uncultivated, without king or law, the Chinese Monarchy was already governed by highly refined Kings and laws. Such was the knowledge, value, and practice of virtue among the Chinese; such was the system, force, and tenor of a more refined life, that the peace and happiness of a certain golden age seemed to flow even into the wild beasts themselves, as is clear from the <term>Shujing</term> <note>original: "Xukim"; the Classic of History</note> book 3, leaf 10. Certainly Hu Shuanghu <note>original: "hû-xuam-hû"; a 14th-century Neo-Confucian scholar</note>, the classic interpreter of the Chinese Annals, as can be seen in the chronological appendix called the *Gangjian Bu* <note>original: "Cám-Kién-pù"; a major historical work</note>, book 1, leaf 20, affirms in plain words that the entire doctrine of this book, the *Daxue* <note>original: "Tá-Hiô"</note>, consists of nothing other than the documents and examples of the Kings <gloss>Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wenwang, Wuwang, and Zhougong</gloss> <note>original: "Yaô, xún, yù, tám, vên-vâm, vù-vâm, & chêu-cúm"</note>, and of Confucius himself. # CHINESE SCIENCE
## SECOND BOOK

THIS book is indeed the work of *Confucius*, but it was published by his grandson, called *Zisi* <note>original: "çù-sū"</note>. It treats primarily the eternal mean, or that **golden mean** <note>original: "aureâ mediocritate"</note> which is, as Cicero says, the path to be held constantly and in all things between the "too much" and the "too little." Therefore, *Zhongyong* <note>original: "Chūm-yūm"</note> is the title of the Book; for *Zhong* <note>original: "Chūm"</note> signifies the **middle** or **mean**; while *yong* <note>original: "yūm"</note> (which is commonly used for the "ordinary" or "everyday") in this context, according to the Commentators, means the same as **constant** or **eternal**.

-> folio 1, page 2, section 1 <-

THAT which is bestowed upon man by heaven is called **rational nature**: that which is conformed to this nature and follows from it is called the **rule**, or that which is consistent with reason. To restore this rule through practice, by moderating oneself and one’s affairs according to it, is called **instruction**, or the discipline of the virtues.

-> section 2 <-

SINCE the said Rule is intrinsic to rational nature, it can never—and indeed must not—be absent or separated from man for even a single moment; for if it could at any time be absent or separated, it would no longer be the rule or reason implanted in nature by heaven. And this is the reason why the **perfect man** <note>The "perfect man" (Latin: *perfectus vir*) refers to the *Junzi*, often translated as the "gentleman" or "exemplary person" in Confucian thought.</note> is always so anxiously attentive to himself and keeps watch even over those things not perceived by the eyes, such as the slightest movements of the soul. Likewise, he feels such fear and awe even in those things not perceived by the ears; so that, when something must be done, he does not turn aside for even a moment from the norm of right reason impressed upon him.

<summary>This page introduces the "Doctrine of the Mean" (Zhongyong), attributed to Confucius's grandson Zisi, defining virtue as a constant adherence to a heaven-sent rational nature and the "golden mean." It emphasizes the importance of constant self-vigilance over one's internal thoughts and unseen actions.</summary>
<keywords>Zhongyong, Doctrine of the Mean, Zisi, rational nature, golden mean, self-vigilance, Junzi, Confucian ethics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the translation of the *Zhongyong* (Doctrine of the Mean).
