# BOOK TWO

->§. 1.<-

For the movements of the soul are essentially that which does not appear, because they are hidden and known to themselves alone; they are also that which is not manifest, because they are exceedingly subtle and the smallest of things. Therefore, the perfect man <note>The "perfect man" or "superior man" (*junzi*) is the Confucian ideal of a person who has achieved moral excellence.</note> watches over the secret of his heart with such anxious care, and is so cautious in those internal matters which he alone perceives. From this it follows that the secret and abstruse recesses of the heart, which are hidden from others, are nonetheless open to him alone; likewise, those most subtle movements of the soul—whether toward good or toward evil—which can hardly be perceived and are most minute, are nonetheless entirely manifest to him alone.

->§. 2.<-

Moreover, since the root of the passions is deep within the nature of man—or rather, that nature itself is this root—and since this root breaks out continually into its acts or passions, the perfect man attends to himself with the greatest vigilance so that he may moderate these passions. He uses the bridle of nature itself, insofar as nature is the principle of reason and discretion. Therefore, the passions of the soul—such as joy from prosperity, anger from adversity, sadness from loss, or cheerfulness and the joyful enjoyment of a thing obtained—before they sprout and come forth into action, are said to be **in the middle** or **the mean** <note>original: "in medio"</note>, because they are still an indifferent thing between excess and deficiency. But once they have sprouted and have all reached the dictate of right reason, they are called **concord** <note>original: "consentaneum"</note>, or a certain harmony of the passions among themselves and with reason itself. And indeed, when they are in the mean, they are called the great principle of the whole world and the foundation of all good actions; when they are in harmony with reason, they are called the rule of the universal world, or the **Royal Way** <note>original: "Regia via"</note> of the human race.

*The doctrine of holding the mean <note>original: "tenendo medio"</note>, as the fountain of all Chinese wisdom <note>original: "Sapientiæ Sinicæ"</note> flowing back through all the ages, was recommended (among other things) by Emperor Yao <note>original: "Yaò," a legendary sage-king of China’s golden age</note> to his successor Shun <note>original: "Xún"</note> more than sixteen hundred years before Confucius; and he in turn recommended it to the Great Yu <note>original: "Yù"</note> when he appointed him heir to the Empire. It contains sixteen characters, which the Interpreters explain and extol with many more words. We shall explain it here using the words of Zhang Juzheng <note>original: "Cham-colai," a prominent Ming Dynasty scholar whose commentaries were often used by the Jesuits</note>, but reduced to a compendium. Thus, the *Book of Documents* <note>original: "Xu-kim" (Shujing)</note>, book 2, folio 10, says: "The heart of man is unique: when it is led by private affection, it is called **Ren xin** <note>original: "Gîn sîn," the human heart/mind</note>, that is, the heart of man; when it acts from the dictate of the right law, it is called **Dao xin** <note>original: "Taó-sîn," the mind of the Way/Reason</note>, that is, the heart of reason. The heart or will of man, since it is a variable thing and easily moved and bent by any object, is a thing always exposed to dangers; but the same heart or will, when conformed to the good and the norm of virtue, is something excellent and hidden. Wherefore it is necessary that, by serious examination, you repeatedly purify that heart from depraved and private affections, which silently insinuate themselves; and thus separate the right heart from the depraved. Which done, reject entirely that which belongs to the human and private heart, and [hold] the right law of that heart as the sole mistress of your person..."*

Therefore, the root and foundation upon which the right administration of the world rests is the rectitude and standard of a single heart, etc. Thus says the Colaus <note>original: "Colaus"; a Latinization of the Chinese *gelao* (Grand Secretary), referring to a high-ranking official or commentator.</note>.

->p. 2.<-

WHERE, therefore, the middle and the fitting harmony have been clearly perceived, then finally the state of both Heaven and Earth follows—quiet, permanent, and peaceful—along with the uniform propagation and vigor of all things. For (*as the Interpreters add*) if man acts always according to right reason—since he forms as it were one body with the universe—it will follow that Heaven and Earth also act according to the standard implanted within them: the Planets flow without error, the four seasons of the year run their course without failure, the Young obtain their desired years of life, the Old reach an end agreeable to nature, and finally, all things obtain their proper state and place.

*Who here does not see that the Philosopher aimed only at this: that he might lead the nature of man—which the Chinese teach is upright from its origin but thereafter fallen and depraved everywhere—back to its primitive state of innocence? And so, might he not recall the rest of created things—now rebellious against man and armed for his ruin—back to their former obedience? He indicates this in chapter 1, section 1 of the book **Tà Hiô** <note>The **Great Learning**, another of the primary Confucian texts focused on self-cultivation and governance.</note>, and likewise here and elsewhere more than once. Moreover, although the Philosopher did not know that we fell from our original happiness because of the sin of our first parent <note>A reference to the Christian concept of Original Sin and Adam.</note>, he seems to have learned—through long experience and contemplation—both (α) [firstly] of the so many things that are adverse and hostile to man, and (β) [secondly] of human nature itself being so prone to worse things, that this universe, which a corrupted man had in a way corrupted, cannot be restored to its natural integrity and order unless man himself first recovers that integrity and order through victory over himself.*

->f. 3. p. 2. §. 1.<-

HERE, and in the rest of this book, **Zisi** <note>original: "çù-su"; Zisi was the grandson of Confucius and the traditional author of the *Zhongyong*.</note> quotes the words of the Master, saying: *Confucius says: the perfect man holds the mean always and everywhere; but the wicked man violates the mean either by excess or by deficiency.*

->§. 2.<-

**The Perfect Man** (explains **Zisi**) possesses the **mean**, or is always in the middle, and because he is *perfect*, he therefore always—that is, at any time, whether in adversity or prosperity—conforms himself and his actions to the mean in which he exists. He does this with that caution, vigilance, and fear regarding the smallest movements of the soul (of which we spoke above). The **wicked man** also has his own **mean** which he might hold, but because he is *wicked*, he is held by no fear or shame in violating it; for he acts everywhere according to his own lust.

### BOOK TWO.

->f. 4. p. 1. §. 1.<-

Confucius says: Oh, how sublime is that Mean! <note>original: "medium"; referring to the *Zhongyong* or the Doctrine of the Mean, the Confucian principle of perfect balance.</note> Among the common people, few are able to hold to it. Nor is this a new occurrence; this is an old disease, an ancient complaint—it has been this way for a long time.

->§. 2.<-

Confucius says: As for the reason why most mortals do not walk along this royal road of the Mean, I myself know it well. For the "prudent" <note>original: "prudentes"; here meaning those who are worldly-wise or intellectually clever.</note> of this age overstep it; and because they believe they understand things more numerous and more lofty than this Mean, they neglect it as if it were something small and insufficient. The "unlearned," <note>original: "rudes"; the simple or uneducated.</note> on the other hand, do not reach the Mean because they either do not know it or, terrified by its difficulty, they despair of ever arriving there. I also know the reason why many do not have a clear perspective of this path of the Mean, despite it being so conspicuous: for the "wise"—or those who profess the study of wisdom—exceed and pass by the Mean in their actions, or rather they sin by excess, following certain dangerous and unusual principles and paths. The "sluggish" and "dull" souls, however, do not reach it in their deeds because they despair of even knowing the Mean, let alone attaining the Mean itself.

->p. 2. §. 1.<-

That people err so widely in every direction arises from a lack of self-examination. For since that rule <note>The "rule" of the Mean.</note> is internal to man, the actions that proceed from nature would surely proceed from that stated rule for the most part, if only it were properly understood. For example, Confucius says: there is no man who does not drink and eat every day; and yet, in a matter so common, few are able to distinguish right flavors, or to pass a right judgment on the nature and efficacy of food and drink—which are often corrupted by so many seasonings. If they explored this more accurately, they would not so often exceed the limits of temperance.

->§. 2.<-

Confucius says in conclusion: therefore, the reason this path of the Mean is not frequented or observed is likewise because men (alas!) do not labor to investigate it or to know it; and thus they either exceed the Mean or fall away from it.

->§. 3.<-

Confucius, exhorting everyone to a serious examination of the Mean, brings forward the example of the Emperor Shun <note>original: "Xún"; the legendary Emperor Shun, a model of virtue in Confucian thought.</note> and says: how great was the prudence of that Emperor Shun! For he did not rely on his own judgment alone or his private prudence, but administered the State <note>original: "Rempub."; short for *Respublica*, the Commonwealth or State.</note> relying on the counsel and wisdom of his people. Thus, Shun rejoiced to consult others even on common matters; and he used to—or rather, delighted to—examine all the responses of his people, however obvious and vulgar they might be. If they happened to suggest something that was not entirely in accordance with reason, he did not use it, yet he would prudently conceal the bad that was in it through dissimulation, thus fostering...

Indeed, he made use of counsel that aligned with reason in such a way that he even praised the good within those suggestions, so that his advisors might declare their thoughts more eagerly and confidently. But if the answers given strayed slightly from the center, he diligently took hold of the two extremes of those responses; having weighed them maturely in the balance of reason, he used only the middle path <note>The "Mean" or middle way between extremes.</note> between them for the governance of the people. The *Chinese Annals* record that this Emperor was accustomed to *hang a tablet in the front courtyard of his Palace, upon which his subjects were allowed to confidently advise their King and note down anything he might have happened to do wrong.*

<margin>Page 2. Section 1.</margin>
Confucius, rebuking the deceptive prudence of his own times—which had degenerated from the path of the Ancient Kings—said: "Every man says now, 'I am prudent; I know what should be done and what should not be done.' But because he keeps only his own profit and convenience before his eyes, and not the losses and dangers thereof, he incautiously enters into a thousand nets and snares at the slightest impulse, and finally falls into the middle of a pit, from which he knows no way to escape or extricate himself. Likewise, every man says, 'I am sufficiently prudent,' and in word he selects the *Mean* for himself and acts according to it; but behold, overcome by sloth, he is not even able to keep to it constantly for the space of a single month." Of what use, then, is the science and knowledge of the Mean to them?

<margin>Section 2.</margin>
Confucius said: "My disciple *Yan Hui* <note>original: "Hoéî"; the favorite and most virtuous disciple of Confucius.</note> was indeed a truly prudent man. For he knew how to distinguish things properly and then choose the Mean; and whenever he attained one virtue, he would immediately grasp it tightly with both arms, as if in veneration, and cherish it within his breast, never letting go of it once it was grasped."

<margin>Folio 6, page 1. Section 1.</margin>
Confucius said: "*There will be those who can rule the Kingdoms of the world in peace; there will be those who are able to refuse high honors and wealth; there will be those who can bravely tread upon bare swords; but the* Mean, *although at first glance it appears easy, nevertheless cannot be obtained by anyone except with a certain great struggle and labor.*"

ON THIS occasion, perhaps, the disciple *Zilu* <note>original: "çù-lú"; a disciple known for his bravery and impetuous nature.</note>—since he was of a warlike disposition and desired military glory—asked about fortitude.

# BOOK TWO

->§ 2.<-

**C**onfucius <note>The Latin text uses "Sciscitatur ex eo," referring to his disciple Zilu (Tzu-lu), though the disciple is not named in this specific excerpt.</note> inquired of him and said: "Is it the strength of those who live in the Southern regions that is being asked about? Is it the strength of those who inhabit the Northern region? Or is it perhaps your own strength—the strength of you who cultivate wisdom?"

->§ 3.<-

**T**o behave with great generosity and gentleness, and to instruct people with a certain indulgence—not always punishing their laziness or slowness, nor exacting vengeance or penalties from the stubborn, but bearing with them patiently—that is the strength of the Southern regions. Through this, they strive to gradually subject the minds of men to reason; and this, the perfect man <note>term: "vir perfectus" (Latin for "perfect man") refers to the *Junzi* or "Superior Man," the Confucian ideal of a moral person.</note> is able to achieve.

->§ 4.<-

**T**o lie down fearlessly and securely upon spears and armor, to live in the midst of deaths and yet not be terrified nor affected by the weariness of such a life—this is indeed the strength of the Northern regions. The strong and robust are able to achieve this; however, because there is often much recklessness present here, and the rule of the "Mean" <note>The "Mean" or *Zhong*, referring to the path of perfect balance and moderation.</note> is very frequently violated, this is not the strength that I expect from you, my disciples.

->p. 2. § 1.<-

**T**herefore, the Perfect Man, always intent on the victory over himself alone, fashions and accommodates himself to the characters and temperaments of others; yet (as he is master of himself) he does not allow himself to waste away, as it were, nor to be corrupted by the habits and examples of the idle and the soft, nor does he obey everyone without discrimination—and oh, how great is this strength! Again, in the midst of others who wander from the right path, he alone stands upright and inclines toward neither side—how great is this strength! Likewise, if virtue and laws flourish in the Kingdom and he himself holds office, he does not change his character amidst these honors, nor that rule of life which he observed as a private citizen, and thus he does not swell with empty pride—oh, how great is this strength! On the other hand, if virtue and laws lie neglected in the Kingdom, and there is great political turmoil, he himself—though he may be weighed down by poverty and afflicted by many various hardships, even reduced to the point of death—does not change amidst these things. Always holding fast to the purpose he once undertook—how great and how excellent is this strength! Truly, it is situated in the constant victory over oneself. From you, therefore, my disciples, I both desire and expect this kind of strength, rather than that strength of the Southern and Northern peoples.

->§ 2.<-

**C**onfucius said: "There are those who recklessly leap over the boundaries of the Mean while they pursue I know not what virtues—strange and hidden ones—and they rejoice in performing certain wonders so that there may be those in future ages who will praise their names. But I certainly would not do such a thing."

# CHINESE KNOWLEDGE
<header>CHINESE KNOWLEDGE</header>

...matters; that which is generally fitting to know and to do, I strive to know and to do.

### leaf 7. page 1. § 1.

The Perfect Man <note>term: "Perfectus Vir" (Latin) refers to the *Junzi*, often translated as the "Superior Man" or "Gentleman" in Confucianism.</note> enters upon the ordinary path and therefore progresses in it with constancy; but there are those who either rashly strive after unusual and abstruse things, even those greater than their own strengths, or, although they have entered the path of virtue in a fitting manner, nevertheless break off their course in the middle of the way and shamefully fail. But I certainly would not wish, nor would I be able, to stop in this way; what I have begun, I shall strive to complete.

### § 2.

Therefore, the Perfect Man in all things always conforms himself to the Mean <note>original: "medio," referring to the *Zhong*, the central path of balance and moderation.</note>, doing nothing in excess and nothing in deficiency. However, to flee from the world and its honors out of a love for virtue, so as to never be seen by men, nor even recognized, and yet to be affected by no sense of sadness or regret—this is so difficult that only he who is a Sage <note>term: "sanctus" (Latin) is used here to translate *Shengren*, the "Holy One" or "Sage" who possesses innate wisdom.</note> can achieve it.

### page 2. § 1.

In this and the following paragraph, Zisi <note>original: "çù-su," the grandson of Confucius and traditional author of this text.</note> says that the rule of the "Perfect Men" <note>original: "perfectorum," referring to those who have achieved moral excellence.</note> in seeking the Mean is broad and universal in its application; and yet its internal power and logic in small matters is subtle, hidden, and recondite, and thus known by few.

### § 2.

Men and women, though they may be unrefined, can to some extent reach a practical knowledge of the Mean within their natural sphere; but to reach its most subtle peak through understanding—even if one is a Sage and well-informed—he will surely find something that he does not yet know. Men and women, though they may be the common crowd <note>original: "inutile vulgus," literally "the useless common people," a phrase used by the translator to distinguish the masses from the scholarly elite.</note>, nevertheless it is possible that in certain things they are occasionally able to act partially according to the rule of the Mean; yet truly, to reach its supreme peak—even if someone is a Sage—there will still be something he cannot attain and things he cannot maintain. Indeed, even Heaven and Earth, despite their great magnitude, perfection, and benevolence toward men, nevertheless, because of the changes of the elements and the seasons, they cannot fulfill the wishes of every individual; so much so that man finds in them things to criticize, and still has reason to complain indignantly against Heaven and Earth. Therefore, if the Perfect Man speaks of its magnitude, he must necessarily admit that the whole world cannot contain or sustain the weight of such great virtue; if he speaks of its hidden smallness and subtlety, he will likewise admit that the entire world cannot divide it or break through it by penetrating it. The meaning is this: nothing is so large that Reason <note>original: "ratio," here likely translating the Chinese concept of *Li* (Principle or Reason).</note> is not within it; likewise, nothing is so small that it lacks a certain Reason.

It highlights the contrast between the "ordinary path" of the Superior Man and the rash or inconsistent efforts of others.</summary>

# BOOK TWO. 47
<header>BOOK TWO. 47</header>

->leaf 8. page 1. § 1.<-

He confirms the aforementioned by citing an Ode <note>original: "Odam," referring to the *Shijing* or Classic of Poetry</note>, which says: *The hawk <note>original: "Avis rven," referring to the bird 'Yuan'</note> reaches the heavens in its flight; the fish plunges into the deep sea*, that is (as Zisi <note>original: "çù-su," the grandson of Confucius and traditional author of this text</note> explains) just as the flight of birds is carried to the heights of the heavens and the movement of fish is carried to the depths of the abyss; so this very virtue and reason <note>term: "ratio," often used to translate the Chinese concept of *Dao* or the Way</note>, reaching equally to the highest and the lowest, exerts and manifests itself in the greatest and the smallest things, above and below.

->§ 2.<-

Therefore, as I have said, the rule of the Perfect Man <note>term: "Perfecti Viri," referring to the *Junzi* or Superior Man</note> in maintaining this Mean <note>original: "medio," the central path of balance</note> takes its beginning from even the simplest men and women; and so this very same virtue or rule of the perfect in maintaining the Mean, since it is universal and innate to all, has its first principles also among the common folk. But indeed, insofar as it extends itself to its peak; or, if we discuss (as others explain) its highest point; it shines far and wide and is manifest and open in heaven and on earth alike.

After Zisi explained what was said above—that the rule of reason and that which is consistent with it can never be absent from man—he thoroughly explains this same point in the following paragraphs through the words of Confucius.

->page 2. § 1.<-

Confucius, in order to prove that all people indiscriminately can reach that rule which is implanted in man in their own way, explains that axiom: *What you do not wish to be done to yourself, do not do to another.* He says: The rule of reason (which is concerned, for example, with the relationship between King and subject, between Father and Son, Husband and Wife, Elders and Youths, and finally between Friends) is not far from man himself. But indeed, that rule which men manufacture for themselves, and which they wish to be far from man himself (such as certain exotic and arduous principles which do not at all harmonize with the five orders of men just mentioned), cannot be considered a rule and reason.

->§ 2.<-

He confirms this by an analogy taken from an Ode, which says: *Carving an axe-handle, carving an axe-handle;* the pattern or rule for this is not far off; for the handle itself, with which the craftsman carves the raw wood to form another, is in his hand. Confucius, explaining the analogy, says: The craftsman takes the handle in his hand to cut and form another similar handle with the axe; he looks at it from the side and examines whether it exactly corresponds to the shape and rule of the handle in his hand; yet I still consider this pattern to be further away than that rule which is bestowed upon man by heaven, because this is internal, while that is external. In carving a handle, one handle is distinct from the other: therefore, when the Perfect Man instructs a person, he does not do so through something external and remote from the person, but through the person himself...

<summary>This page explains that the "Way" (Dao) is manifest in all things, from the heights of heaven to the common life of ordinary people. It introduces the "Golden Rule" and the famous analogy of the axe-handle to show that moral patterns are found within human nature itself, not in external, abstract theories.</summary>

# CHINESE KNOWLEDGE,

...it instructs and governs man, and it is not like a person carving an axe-handle who carves something different from what he holds in his hands: For the same light of reason <note>original: "lumen rationis," referring to the innate moral nature</note> is within man; this alone it excites and commands to be as a rule; which, once done, if he attains it so that he is corrected and amended by these things, then at last he finds rest and stops, naturally setting aside the more laborious training.

### leaf 9. page 1. § 1.

**AGAIN** he says: Whoever measures others by himself with all faithfulness and sincerity, this person surely does not depart far from the rule and natural law; or rather, he is directed by that rule which he has within himself; since its first dictate is almost this: those things which one does not wish for oneself, one should likewise not do to others. <note>This is the "Negative Golden Rule," a cornerstone of Confucian ethics</note>

### § 2.

**The rules** of the Perfect Man <note>term: "Perfecti Viri," translating the Chinese *Junzi*, the ideal moral person or "Gentleman"</note> are four; but I, says *Confucius*, cannot yet observe even one of those four. 1. Just as I require from my son, so to serve my father, I myself am not yet able. <note>This refers to filial piety, the primary virtue in this system</note> 2. Just as I require from my subject, to serve the Prince with faithfulness, I am not yet able. 3. Just as I require from my younger brother, to serve the elder with such respect, I am not yet able. 4. Just as I require from my companion and friend, to give him the first place and to anticipate him with due duties, I indeed am not yet able. But the perfect man practices these ordinary and daily virtues without any pretense; he is also circumspect in his daily speech; and if there is anything in which he falls short and thus has not fulfilled his duty, then he does not dare not to compel himself so that he may finally fulfill it: if he has an excessive abundance of words, he likewise does not dare to pour them all out: and so, as a severe judge of himself, he acts so that his words correspond to his deeds, and his deeds correspond to his words. How then could such a perfect man not be solid and stable? I, meanwhile, try to imitate him, and keeping to his footsteps, follow him from afar, yet I follow.

### leaf 10. page 1. § 1.

**HERE** *Zisi* <note>original: "Çù-su," the grandson of Confucius and traditional author of the *Doctrine of the Mean*</note> teaches that the Perfect Man lives perhaps content with his own lot. The Perfect Man, he says, acts according to the reason of his status, which he holds here and now; nor does he desire anything alien to this status of his.

### § 2.

**IF** he is rich and honored, he acts as one rich and honored; yet in such a way that he does not give himself over to illicit pleasures and luxury, nor offend anyone with his arrogance and pride. If he is poor and lowly, he acts as one poor and lowly; yet in such a way that he commits nothing unworthy of a serious and upright man. If he is a foreigner outside his own country, he acts as a foreigner, or rather conducts himself as the status of one living among strangers demands, always consistent with himself. If he should be involved in hardships and labors, he acts according to the reason of his status...

<meta>catchword: status</meta>

BOOK TWO. 49
<sig>N</sig>

...of a distressed state, yet always holding fast to his great purpose. Finally, for the perfect man, there is no state of life he might enter where he is not his own master and content with his lot; and thus, his life unfolds according to his own virtuous intentions.

->§. 4.<-

If this same man is established in a high position and dignity, he does not treat those of a lower rank harshly by striking fear into them; if, however, he is placed in a lower position and rank, he does not flatter his superiors to chase after their favors. He is entirely focused on this: that he might perfect himself, and he seeks nothing from others; thus, he is never resentful toward anyone. Looking upward, he does not complain against Heaven <note>original: "cœlo," referring to the divine order or fate</note> because it does not grant him prosperity or because it afflicts him with hardships. Looking downward, he does not accuse or blame other men, for he does not attribute the cause of his misfortunes or failures to them. Indeed, always content with his own lot, he seeks nothing that is outside of the state he currently holds.

->§. 4.<-

Therefore, the **Perfect Man** <note>term: "Perfectus Vir," the *Junzi* or moral gentleman</note> dwells in a certain level and quiet region, and with a calm mind awaits the unique ordinance of Heaven <note>original: "cœli... ordinationem," the mandate or will of the divine</note> concerning himself. The wicked man, on the contrary, walks headlong down dangerous paths, and through right or wrong seeks a lot and happiness that is entirely unearned and not due to him; if he should obtain it, he must be judged to have obtained it purely by chance.

->p. 2. §. 1.<-

<term>Zisi</term> <note>original: "çù-su," the grandson of Confucius and traditional author of the *Doctrine of the Mean*</note> concludes his own thought with the words of <term>Confucius</term>. <term>Confucius</term> says:
> The <term>Archer</term> <note>original: "Sagittarius"</note> bears a certain resemblance to the perfect man: if he misses the painted target, he turns back to himself and seeks the cause of the error from no person other than his own. In the same way, the perfect man, if he should miss the target of the **Mean** <note>The "Mean" refers to the state of moral equilibrium and perfect appropriateness in all actions</note>, attributes the cause of the error to himself and not another, and so he demands an account for it from himself.

->§. 2.<-

Here <term>Zisi</term> teaches the method by which one ought to arrive, step by step, at the **perfection of the Mean**. He says that the rule or method of proceeding for perfect men is like someone making a long journey, who must begin it from the place closest to him. It is also like someone climbing to a height, who must begin his ascent from the lowest step.

->§. 3.<-

A familiar and domestic comparison follows here, by which <term>Zisi</term> proves or illustrates these sayings, first by the authority of the <term>Book of Songs</term> <note>original: "libri Carminum," the *Shijing*, one of the Five Classics of Chinese literature</note>, and then by the authority of <term>Confucius</term>. The <term>Ode</term> <note>A poem or song from the *Shijing*</note> says:
> When your wife is loving and in harmony, the family is like those who strike cymbals, enjoying that sweetest pleasure of domestic peace and mutual concord. Again, when the older and younger brothers are in harmony, the joy of their concord truly lasts a long time, flowing perpetually down to their sons and grandsons; and thus...

->§. 4.<-

Confucius likewise says: O how happily and tranquilly the father and mother of the family will live in this domestic harmony of their subordinates! For the mutual concord of subordinates—for example, daughters-in-law and sons-in-law, older and younger brothers—overflows into the joy of the parents or the elders. <margin>p. 1. §. 1.</margin>
Confucius, in order to show that one must strive with constant effort toward the aforementioned virtue of the Mean <note>term: "virtutem medii," referring to the *Zhongyong* or the Doctrine of the Mean, the path of perfect equilibrium</note>, which is so ample and sublime, takes an example from the spirits. Just as their intellectual power is more excellent, so too is their effectiveness in acting is great. Thus he says: In spirits there resides an operative power and effectiveness; and O, how outstanding it is! How manifold! How sublime!

*Although various meanings are attributed to these two words, **quei xin** <note>original: "quei xin," now typically Romanized as *gui shen*, referring to ghosts, spirits, or ancestral souls</note>, whether they are taken separately or together (as can be seen in their dictionaries), in this place our interpreter **Colaus** <note>original: "Colaus," a Latinization of *Colao* or Grand Secretary, referring to a high-ranking Chinese official and scholar, likely Xu Guangqi</note>, along with many others, rejects the airy fictions of certain interpreters. These later commentators, imbued with many errors, conflict both with one another and with themselves. Colao understands by **quei xin** those spirits for whose veneration or for the imploring of whose help sacrifices have been established. This view is supported by the common usage of both words throughout the whole Empire. It is also supported by many ancient texts and especially this one which we are now explaining, where the Philosopher <note>referring to Confucius</note> distinctly defines them and their operations, attributing to them things that can only be attributed to spirits endowed with intelligence. Finally, it is supported by the common use of so many temples everywhere, and so many rites and sacrifices, which have been dedicated to these said **quei-xin** from every age. For who would not reject the interpreters of later times <note>a reference to Neo-Confucian scholars like Zhu Xi, whom the Jesuits often criticized for being too materialistic</note> when they want **quei-xin** to be understood only as the natural operations of the two qualities **Yn** and **Yâm** <note>original: "Yn & Yâm," or Yin and Yang</note>—that is, of the cold and the hot, or the perfect and the imperfect—or merely their remission and intensity and nothing more? For who could hear without blushing that these mere material and inanimate qualities ought to be worshipped with such great honors, sacrifices, and fasts; that the prayers and vows of suppliants are heard by them; and that they approve of what is done by virtue, while condemning what is joined with vice and negligence? What of the fact that they commonly call these spirits incorporeal, asserting that they leave no trace for human senses, and deny that they have any concern for place or measure, as bodies do? However, although there are some who want these two words to be understood as the single supreme deity <note>original: "unicum numen supremum"</note> because in the books of rites and elsewhere he is sometimes called the spirit of heaven, sometimes the spirit of heaven and earth, sometimes the supreme spirit, or the spirit or the supreme Emperor of spirits, or sometimes the spirit of the supreme Emperor; nevertheless, for the most part, the discussion here seems to concern those spirits or intel—*

...intelligences whom God appointed as presiding ministers and administrators to protect and preserve created things. Elsewhere, the Interpreter calls them *Xámtí chi xîn* <note>original: "Xámtí chi xîn," referring to *Shangdi zhi shen*, the spirits or servants of the Supreme Emperor</note>, meaning the clients and subjects of the Supreme Emperor who have care of the Planets and the rest of the Stars, the Elements, as well as the regions and things of the earthly world. For it is explicitly recorded in the *Shujing* <note>original: "Xu-kimp," the *Classic of History* or *Book of Documents*</note> concerning Emperor Shun <note>original: "Xún," the legendary sage-king</note>, who was both Emperor and Legislator, that whenever he inspected the Empire, he sacrificed to the supreme Emperor of heaven. Then, with a lower rite, he made offerings to the six principal spirits: namely, the four seasons of the year (cold and heat), the sun, the moon, and the presiding spirits of the five Planets. After these, he made offerings to the spirits of the mountains and rivers, as if they were further removed from himself, and finally, he sacrificed to the multitude of spirits spread everywhere. Furthermore, in the third book of the *Rites* <note>original: "libro 3. Officiorum," referring to the *Li Ji* or *Book of Rites*</note>, it is stated: The Emperors (who ordered animals to be raised for sacrifice at the proper time throughout the hundred—that is, all—cities of the Empire) commanded the people that there should be no one who did not exert all their strength to honor the supreme Emperor of the great heaven, as well as the spirits of the more famous mountains, the major rivers, and the four regions of the earth, so that they might plead for happiness for the people. But let us follow the text and its exposition.

->§. 2.<-

Confucius teaches that there exists within the spirits mentioned above a certain power that is truly extraordinary and of a superior order. For while all corporeal things fall under the perception of the senses, spirits alone escape them. It is true, he says, that we perceive them in a way insofar as they repeatedly reveal themselves in their effects; and yet, in truth, we do not see them. Likewise, we perceive them through hearing in a way when we contemplate the "harmonious discord" and the harmony, as it were, of so many effects proceeding from them; yet we do not actually hear them. Finally, they are so intimately associated and "incorporate" themselves, so to speak, into all things—or, as others explain it, they exercise their operations around all things—to such an extent that things cannot dismiss them from themselves; or rather, they cannot exist without the spirits' direction.

->§. 3.<-

And this is the reason why spirits cause the people of the world—in whom gratitude is naturally implanted—to repeatedly refrain from vices, and ensure that the mind is pure and clean, and the body adorned with a more splendid garment. Thus, they offer sacrifices with the reverence that is fitting. At that time, while they contemplate that multitude of spirits filling all things like a vast sea, they venerate them as if they were standing above them, and they revere them as if they were standing at their left and right.

->p. 2. §. 1.<-

Confucius proves that this reverence is owed to them by the authority of the book called the *Shijing* <note>original: "Xi-kim," the *Classic of Poetry* or *Book of Odes*</note>. An Ode says: Whether the spirits arrive and approach those sacrificing, and whether they receive their vows, cannot be easily guessed...

### §. 2.

This secret subtlety of the spirits, and their no less significant manifestation through their effects, is so clear that—even though the spirits are in themselves so hidden—they truly cannot be concealed; such is how the matter stands.

*Although the existence of spirits is clear from the text itself and the mind of the Philosopher <note>Confucius</note>; it is helpful at this point to declare to the reader in his own words what Cham-colaus <note>original: "Cham-colaus," referring to the commentator Zhu Xi</note> himself thinks about the spirits (certainly according to the mind of the Philosopher himself). For he says that spirits exist, and this is certainly in accordance with reason; for they work with perpetual motion in this middle space between heaven and earth, and they exercise, according to their office, that power of blessing the upright and afflicting the wicked: therefore their agility and intelligence appear and manifest themselves clearly, and can never be hidden. In truth, it is so. Another Interpreter, of equal authority with Colaus, wonderfully supports this; he is also called Cham, with the surname Tûm-ço <note>original: "tûm-ço," likely referring to the scholar Cheng Yi</note>: he, in approximately the twentieth edition of his Commentaries on the sentence of Confucius just explained, writes thus: That word **Chîm** <note>original: "Chîm," referring to the Chinese term *Cheng* (誠), meaning sincerity or reality</note> signifies the truth of the spirits. And the meaning is: these spirits truly exist. Those words, **pú cò yèn** <note>original: "pú cò yèn," for *bu ke yan* (不可掩)</note>, mean it is manifest, or it cannot be hidden or denied. Thus he says.*

<margin>folio 12. page 1. §. 1.</margin>
Here and hereafter, **Zisi** <note>original: "çù-su," the grandson of Confucius and traditional author of the *Doctrine of the Mean*</note>, in order to explain the breadth of the reason innate in all people regarding its use, brings forward the words of his Grandfather <note>Confucius</note> concerning the virtues of the Ancient Kings; and first, indeed, concerning the illustrious obedience of the Emperor **Shun** <note>original: "Xún"</note> toward his parents. Confucius said: "Oh, how great was the filial piety <note>original: "obedientiâ," here in the sense of *xiao* or filial devotion</note> of Emperor Shun! In virtue he was a saint; from which it also followed that the parents of such a son were celebrated everywhere. In dignity he was the Son of Heaven, that is, the Emperor: this dignity, indeed, passed to his parents as well by a certain reckoning; and, if we speak of wealth, he obtained whatever the four seas (for thus the Chinese describe the world known to them) embrace within themselves. Furthermore, this pious man poured out these riches upon the truly royal worship of his parents, as well as upon their delights. In the ancestral halls, according to the royal custom and with great preparation, he performed the funeral rites for his deceased ancestors, a custom which his sons and grandsons also preserved. In this way, that so illustrious and Royal dignity remained in his family for a long time; and the memory of such a Great Ancestor was in turn perpetually preserved by posterity, especially in the ancestral duties and rites."

*Lest the word **Xím** <note>original: "Xím," for *Sheng* (聖), meaning Sage or Saint</note> or Saint offend the reader; for here it signifies nothing else...*

THEREFORE, his great virtue, not by chance but undoubtedly by a fixed plan, obtained that dignity from heaven—the imperial crown, the reward for his virtue. Likewise, he undoubtedly obtained those vast revenues and immense riches bounded by the Great Ocean; he undoubtedly obtained that name so celebrated throughout the whole world and such great fame; finally, he undoubtedly obtained that sweet reward of a long life, which is the specific reward for filial obedience that he praised just a moment ago.

*And indeed, the Emperor Shun* <note>original: "Xún"</note> *lived one hundred years. He was first called from the fields and from a rustic life to share in the Empire for twenty-eight years by Emperor Yao* <note>original: "Yao"</note> *himself. In the course of time, when Wen Wang, now the highest among the petty kings, grew old and weak, his son Wu Wang was similarly present for him. Imitating his father’s piety toward his grandfather, he stayed by the sick man day and night, serving him and providing whatever comfort or relief he could devise, to the point that he would not even refresh himself with food unless his father had eaten, nor would he give his weary body to rest and sleep before his father had fallen asleep. Amidst these things, the elder man’s health improved, and the pious son had perhaps given a little more time to sleep. Therefore, the father asked him whether any dream had come to him that night. To him Wu Wang replied: "Truly, O Father! Indeed, the most majestic image of Shangdi* <note>original: "Xâm-tí", the "Lord on High" or Supreme Deity in ancient Chinese belief</note> *appeared to me in a dream; the Emperor of Heaven gave me hope of obtaining nine Lim* <note>original: "Lim", referring to decades of years</note>, *that is, nine decades of years." Then the Father said: "You, as a ninety-year-old man, will one day count nine decades of years; for me, one hundred years of life are prepared. But come, let three years be taken from mine to increase yours, my son." It was a thing worthy of wonder (if the Books of Rites can be believed), for it happened exactly as it had been said: for Wen Wang ceased to live at ninety-seven years of age, and Wu Wang in the ninety-third year of his life; yet the brother of the latter, called the Duke of Zhou* <note>original: "Cheu-cum"</note>, *surpassed them both...*

During this time, the elder man recovered, and the pious son had perhaps given a little more time to sleep than usual. But come, let three years be taken from mine to increase yours, my son." It was a matter worthy of admiration (if the Books of Rites <note>original: "libris Officiorum"</note> can be believed), for it happened exactly as it had been said: King Wen ceased to live at ninety-seven years of age, and King Wu in the ninety-third year of his life; but their brother, the Duke of Zhou <note>original: "Cheu-cum"</note>, surpassed them both.*

...lived to be a hundred, a Prince most highly commended for his singular wisdom and filial respect.

->§ 3.<-

**I**ndeed, in the production of things, Heaven undoubtedly adapts and attunes itself to their dispositions, granting growth in accordance with them and fertilizing things with its influence. Thus, those plants it finds rightly planted in suitable places and times, it kindly nurtures and enlivens with its moisture and heat; those it finds cast down and withering, it utterly scatters and destroys, drying them up with that same heat. In this way, Heaven also adapts itself to the nature and character of individuals; it raises up and adorns the good, as was evident in this Prince Shun <note>original: "Xún"</note>; but it casts down the wicked and lets them perish.

->§ 4.<-

**T**he ODE <note>Referring to the *Shijing* or Book of Odes</note> says: O perfect man, to be praised with the commendations of all and extolled with shouts of joy! O how magnificently his illustrious virtue shines! He gives to the people what belongs to the people, and to the magistrates what belongs to the magistrates. He spreads his virtues among all, and thus deserves well of everyone. For this reason, he undoubtedly receives the most ample revenues (which signifies the Empire) from heaven; he preserves and nurtures the Empire; and so, he is heaped with one benefit after another flowing from heaven, and with all good things; and he is magnified unto a long posterity.

->§ 5.<-

**T**HEREFORE (the Philosopher <note>Confucius</note> concludes), great virtue undoubtedly obtains the Empire from heaven.

->p. 2. § 1.<-

**C**onfucius, launching here into the praises of Kings Wen <note>original: "Vén-vâm"</note> and Wu <note>original: "Vù-vâm"</note>, says: He who was always free from sorrow (a rare happiness among Kings) was Wen alone. This was because the petty King Wang-ji <note>original: "Vâm-ki"</note> was his Father, by whom he was so excellently instructed; and because Emperor Wu was his son, so similar to his father and grandfather. What the father had piously and fortunately begun, the son completed with even greater success over many years. For he founded the third Imperial family called the Zhou <note>original: "Cheu"</note>, which stood longer than all other families—namely, for 874 years, distinguished by thirty-five Emperors.

->§ 2.<-

**E**mperor Wu, by his heroic virtues, propagated the august lineage of his great-grandfather Tai-wang <note>original: "Tai-vâm"</note>, his grandfather Wang-ji, and his father Wen. Only once did he put on military armor, in order to exact well-deserved punishment from the most impious tyrant Zhou <note>original: "Cheu" — specifically the last ruler of the Shang, distinct from the Zhou dynasty name</note> (this man was the last of the second family, the Shang <note>original: "Xam"</note>). Once this tyrant was subdued, Wu obtained the Empire by the encouragement, or rather the impulse, of eight hundred lords <term>dinastarum|feudal lords or regional rulers</term> and all the people. Having been raised to this height, his person in no way lost the illustrious and celebrated fame of virtues and merits received from his ancestors and the whole world...

->55<-

...mate. <meta>The previous page likely ended with a word like "ultimate," referring to King Wu’s character.</meta> In dignity he was an Emperor; but if we speak of wealth, he possessed whatever the four seas contained within them. Nor was his piety any less, for in the ancestral halls of his forefathers, he performed sacrifices to them with imperial magnificence and ritual. This custom was preserved by his sons and grandsons, with all subsequent posterity propagating a glorious memory of their ancestors and royal lineage forever.

The *Chinese Annals* <note>Referring to the ancient historical chronicles like the *Shiji* or the *Bamboo Annals*</note> relate much concerning this illustrious lineage. Indeed, they trace it back to the Emperor *Huangdi* <note>original: "Hoâm-ti"; the legendary "Yellow Emperor" regarded as the ancestor of all Han Chinese</note> (*who began to reign in the year 2697 BC*) through a continuous series of forty generations, whose names and surnames they record accurately. Furthermore, 1,574 years passed between *Huangdi* and *King Wu*. From this point, not only the same family line but also the Imperial dignity itself was passed down to sons and grandsons for 874 years. From this, it is concluded that the nobility of that House—perhaps second to none in Europe or Asia—endured for 2,447 years, first with the title and rank of Princes and then of Emperors. (Consult the genealogical table of the Chinese Monarchy).

<margin>folio 13, page 1</margin>

Here and hereafter, Confucius shows how *King Wu* <note>original: "Vù-vâm"</note> and his brother, the *Duke of Zhou* <note>original: "Cheu-cum"; a celebrated figure in Chinese history known for his virtue and for acting as regent</note>, both maintained and passed on to their descendants the required worship and reverence toward their deceased ancestors. They did this by observing the proper times, order, and preparation for mourning, funeral rites, and burials, as well as other duties and rituals. This was the pinnacle of filial obedience, through which they were promised every happiness from heaven. 

Confucius says that *King Wu*, already an old man—specifically over eighty years old—took up the empire. Thus, since he reigned for only seven years, he could not establish laws and rituals so firmly that there was no danger of them being neglected or forgotten again. Therefore, when he left his son, named *King Cheng* <note>original: "Chîm-vâm"</note>, a boy of thirteen, as the heir to the Empire, the *Duke of Zhou* (who was his tutor as well as his uncle) put the finishing touches on this great work. He fulfilled the virtues and statutes of his father *King Wen* <note>original: "Vén-vâm"</note> and his older brother *King Wu*, honoring his great-grandfather *King Tai* <note>original: "Tái-vâm"</note> and his grandfather *Wang Ji* <note>original: "Vâm-kí"</note> with the posthumous title of Princes. 

Or (as others explain), the *Duke of Zhou* fulfilled the virtues of *King Wen* and *King Wu* by constantly calling to mind, for both himself and his ward, the royal families and the virtues of the Great-grandfather *King Tai* and Grandfather *Wang Ji*. He recounted the series of this most illustrious family over a thousand years or more, from the ancestral sacrifice <note>original: "çu can"</note> all the way to *Hou Ji* <note>original: "Héu-cie"; the legendary "Lord of Millet" and ancestor of the Zhou</note>, who was the Prince and head of the family. *Hou Ji* was the son of the fourth Emperor of the Monarchy, called *Ku* <note>original: "Tí-co"</note>, born of the first Queen, *Jiang Yuan* <note>original: "Kiam yuén"</note>. This *Ku* was the grandson of the second Emperor, whose name was *Shaohao* <note>original: "Xaò-haó"</note>; furthermore, *Shaohao* was the son of the famous "Yellow Emperor" *Huangdi* by his mother *Leizu* <note>original: "Luij-çù"</note>. Thus, he performed sacrifices to his deceased ancestors more solemnly and majestically according to the rites of Emperors, imparting to them his own dignity; which ritual thereafter passed into...

# CHINESE KNOWLEDGE
### (SCIENTIÆ SINICÆ)

...practice among all the Kings and Emperors of China <note>original: "Sinarum"</note>; namely, that each would bestow his own rank and dignity upon his deceased ancestors, even if they had not held such status during their lives. These rites for ancestors were thus extended to the *Princes* <note>original: "Regulos"</note> and the *Magnates* <note>The high-ranking nobility or "Greats"</note> of the Empire, known as the *Ta-su* <note>original: "Ta-su," referring to the *Dafu* or Great Officers</note>, down to the scholars <note>original: "literatos"</note>, and finally even to private citizens. For everyone, according to their own station and the rank they held, proceeded in this kind of duty. Thus, if a father had been one of the Magnates or Magistrates of the Kingdom, and the son was merely a *scholar*, the son buried his father with the rites due to a *Magnate*; however, he performed the ancestral sacrifices <note>original: "parentabat"</note> for him according to his own status as a scholar or *Doctoral rank*. Conversely, if the father had been a scholar but the son was among the *Magnates*, then the son buried the father as a scholar (using the rite of the scholars), but performed the ancestral sacrifices as a *Magnate*, bestowing his own dignity upon his father, even though deceased, for the sake of honor. They offer this reason for both types of ritual: the dignity of the father follows the dead even to the grave; but the ancestral rites performed for him, or the gifts offered, pertain to the income and resources—or the status—of the living son. If the son was poor, he honored his parents in the manner of a poor man; if a King, he honored them in the manner of a King. Regarding mourning: a one-year *mourning* period (which they signify not by black, but by wearing *white* funeral clothing) for the death of brothers or a paternal uncle extended only from the lowest commoners up to the *Magnates*. However, upon the death of a Father or Mother, a *three-year mourning* period extended even to the *Emperor* himself. In this three-year mourning for Father and Mother, no distinction was made between the noble and the low-born; the rule was one and the same for all. This is because what parents have earned from their children, and what children in turn owe their parents, are equal in all cases and must be valued at the same price.

*This three-year mourning was observed because a child is typically nursed for that many years and cherished in the lap of the parents. A husband mourned a deceased wife for only a three-month period; however, a wife mourned a deceased husband for three years; and this custom is still observed today by the Chinese throughout the entire Empire.*

---

->Part 2. Section I.<-

Confucius applauds the obedience just described, saying: *How widely the obedience of Emperor Wu-wang and his brother the Duke of Zhou <note>original: "Cheu-cum"</note> has spread!*

*It is helpful here to explain briefly the reasoning of this nation regarding this virtue—a people whose political philosophy is exceedingly studious of public peace and quiet. Thus they reasoned: "If a King loves and honors his own parents, he cannot fail to see to it that his subjects also honor and love their parents, following the King’s own example. For whoever loves virtue desires that it exist in everyone, especially when it is in his own interest for virtue to exist in others. Indeed, it is in the King's interest; for a King hopes in vain that his subjects will be obedient to him..."*

...were chosen <note>The Latin text begins with the suffix "gebantur," likely completing "eligebantur" (they were chosen) from the previous page.</note> from among the many, those who surpassed the rest in wisdom and virtue, so that they might rightly perform that specific duty. Then, indeed, when all members of a family—the rituals having been completed—invited one another to wine and feasts, those of a lower rank or age (for example, those younger by birth) served wine to their elders out of the reverence due to them. By this practice, the solemnity of these duties reached even to the lower and more humble members of the family. When these communal feasts were finished, all who belonged to other families departed, and only the blood relatives of the same family or name feasted together. These relatives sat not according to the order of their official rank, but by the "whiteness of their hair"—that is, by their age. ->§. 2.<-

**F**inally, the two mentioned Princes—namely **King Wu** <note>original: "Vu vam," the founder of the Zhou Dynasty</note> and the **Duke of Zhou** <note>original: "Cheu cum," the king's brother and a model of Confucian virtue</note>—constantly following in the footsteps of their predecessors, maintained the dignity of their ancestors which they had held in life, or certainly that which had been added to them in death. And so, when they displayed the ancestral tablets called *Pai Quei* <note>original: "Paî Quei"; these are the wooden tablets representing the spirits of the ancestors</note>, or the genealogies of their forefathers, in the halls of their ancestors, they arranged them according to the rank due to each. Likewise, they performed the rites of those ancestors; they played their music, to which they performed dances according to the order of rank. They venerated those things which the ancestors themselves had once held in value and honor, and they loved those things which the ancestors had loved—namely, their descendants, their subjects, the people, and so on. Finally, they served the dead just as they had served the living. Again, they served those who had died long ago in the same way as if they were serving them while they were still alive and surviving. And this, indeed, was the **pinnacle of obedience**.

*It can be proven from many very clear Chinese texts that the legitimate meaning of the aforementioned axiom is that the Chinese practice natural piety and political deference toward the deceased with the same intention and formal motive as they practiced toward them while they were still surviving. From this, and from what is said below, the prudent reader will easily conclude that these rites concerning the deceased were **purely civil** <note>The author is arguing that these rituals are social and political acts of respect, not religious worship or idolatry.</note>, instituted only for the honor and service of parents, which was not to be interrupted even after death. For if they had recognized anything divine in those rites, why would Confucius say that the Ancients were accustomed to serve the dead just as they served the living? Unless, perhaps, someone were to argue that sons bestowed divine honors on their parents even while they were still living—which is unheard of among the Chinese. Certainly, anyone who examines more closely the political governance of this nation as expressed in its ancient monuments will find reason to admire that sweet invention of continuing gratitude and respect from sons and grandsons, as long as they live, toward their deceased ancestors. Indeed, by this example, sons are moved and reminded to provide the obedience to living parents which they see so piously and constantly provided by those parents toward their own dead progenitors. These duties are provided to the living far more laboriously, especially in that...* <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword indicates the next page begins with "more laboriously."</note>

## BOOK TWO

...on the day which is the birthday of the parents, (a) the beginning of the year: you would plainly say some Divinity is being adored, so singular is the mark of observance and reverence with which the children, prostrated on the ground, worshipfully venerate their father and mother then standing by their seats. On this side and that are hung the images <note>Likely ancestral portraits or tablets used to represent the lineage.</note> of their ancestors to show off their lineage, along with the titles and the insignia of dignity or office if they happened to have held any while living. This display is prepared in the guest hall on the first day of the year, with a table of sweetmeats also set out, when the officials and others gather there for the sake of greeting them. They first exhibit honor and reverence to the ancestors of the one they are visiting, who have departed this life; soon after, the master of the house shows reciprocal reverence with an expression of thanks. But these matters have been discussed extensively elsewhere; let us now return to the text.

->Page 2. Section 1.<-

**Confucius**, wishing to intimate that **King Wu** <note>original: "Vu-vam"</note> and the **Duke of Zhou** <note>original: "Cheu-cum"</note>—the two brothers—had attained a most beautiful system of governing, says that he who has performed the debt of filial duty first to Heaven, and then to his own progenitors, will administer the Empire with all happiness. <term>Jiao</term> <note>original: "Kiao"</note> was that which was offered to Heaven, and thus it was offered on a round hill; while <term>She</term> <note>original: "Xé"</note> was that which was offered to the Earth, and thus in a marshy and square place (because they believed the earth to be square). Quite different from these were the parental rites offered to ancestors, denoted here by two words: <term>Di</term> <note>original: "Tí"</note> and <term>Chang</term> <note>original: "Cham" </note>. **Di** was the rite which the Emperor offered to his ancestors with a more solemn ritual once within five years; **Chang** were the parental rites which were performed for the same ancestors through the four seasons of the year. Thus, therefore, **Confucius** says: The rituals and duties of the sacrifices of Heaven and Earth were that by which they worshipped only the Supreme Emperor of Heaven and Earth, who is very aptly and literally signified by the two characters <term>Shangdi</term> <note>original: "Xám tí"; literally "Lord on High" or "Supreme Emperor."</note>. The rituals and duties of the royal ancestral halls were those by which the later Kings paid the required honors and service to their deceased ancestors. Therefore, he who clearly understands and fulfills the <term>Jiao-She</term> rites due to the Supreme Emperor of Heaven and Earth, and who likewise well knows the reasons for the <term>Di-Chang</term> rites and rightly performs the duties due to ancestors—will it not indeed be as easy for him to govern a kingdom rightly as it is to look at the palm of his own hand?

> This passage is famous for proving, according to the opinion of **Confucius**, that there is one primary principle; for when he had said there were two sacrifices, of heaven (a) and earth, he did not say "to serve heaven (a) and earth," nor "to serve the distinct divinities of heaven and earth," but "to serve the High or Supreme Emperor who is God." This is so even though **Zhu Xi** <note>original: "Chuhi"</note>, the atheist-political commentator, wrongly says that the divinity of the earth is missing and omitted from the text for the sake of brevity; a fiction which **Father Matteo Ricci** <note>original: "Matthæus Riccius"</note> and other Christian Doctors learnedly refute. Indeed, we shall bring forward this most illustrious passage and others of this kind elsewhere when...

->page 2, § 1.<-

Confucius, wishing to imply that **King Wu** <note>original: "Vu-vam"</note> and the **Duke of Zhou** <note>original: "Cheu-cum"</note> (who were brothers) had attained the most beautiful method of governing, says that he who first performs the duty of piety owed to Heaven, and then to his own progenitors, will administer the Empire with all happiness. *Kiao* <term>Kiao: the Jiao sacrifice, performed at the winter solstice</term> was that which was offered to Heaven, and thus it was offered on a round hill; but *Xé* <term>Xé: the She sacrifice, offered to the spirit of the Earth</term> was that which was offered to the earth, and thus in a marshy and square place (because they believed the earth to be square). Quite different from these were the parental rites offered to ancestors, denoted here by two words, *Tí* and *Cham*. *Tí* <term>Tí: the Di sacrifice, a grand ancestral ritual performed every five years</term> was that which the Emperor offered to his ancestors with a more solemn rite once every five years; *Cham* <term>Cham: the Chang sacrifice</term> were those parental rites performed for the same ancestors through the four seasons of the year. Thus, therefore, Confucius says: the rites and duties of the sacrifices of heaven and earth were that by which they worshipped only the supreme Emperor of heaven and earth, who is very aptly and literally signified by the two letters *Xám tí* <term>Xám tí: Shangdi, the "Lord on High" or "Supreme Emperor"</term>. The rites and duties of the royal ancestral halls were those by which later Kings paid the honors and service due to their deceased ancestors. He, therefore, who clearly understands and fulfills the *Kiao* and *Xé* sacrificial rites due to the supreme Emperor of heaven and earth, and who likewise properly knows the reasons for the *Tí* and *Cham* rites and rightly performs the duties due to ancestors—will it not truly be as easy for him to govern the kingdom rightly as it is to look at the palm of his own hand?

*This passage is famous for proving, according to the opinion of Confucius, that there is one first principle; for when he said there were two sacrifices, of heaven and of earth, he did not say they were for serving heaven and earth [as elements], nor for serving distinct deities of heaven and earth, but for serving the celestial or supreme Emperor who is God. This is despite the fact that the atheistic-political commentator Zhu Xi* <note>original: "Chuhi"</note> *falsely says that the deity of the earth is missing and is omitted from the text for the sake of brevity; a fabrication which Father Matteo Ricci and other Christian Doctors learnedly refute. Truly, we shall bring forward this most famous passage and others of this kind elsewhere when...*

# CHINESE KNOWLEDGE

...for those who surpassed others in wisdom and virtue were chosen from among the many to fulfill that office of theirs properly. Then, when all members of every family, having completed the rituals, invited one another to wine and banquets, those of lower rank or age—for example, the younger brothers—would serve wine to the elders out of the reverence due to them. Thus, the solemnity of these duties reached even the lower and less noble members of the group. Once these common banquets were finished, all who belonged to other families would depart, and only the blood relatives of the same family or name would feast together. These relatives sat not according to their rank of dignity, but by their gray hair—that is, by age. Thus, only the order and count of their teeth <note>original: "ratio dentium"; a Latin idiom referring to age or seniority, much like "counting rings on a tree."</note> (*or age*) was considered, with the elders occupying the primary place.

<margin>§. 2.</margin>
Finally, the two aforementioned Princes—namely **King Wu** <note>original: "Vu vam"</note> and the **Duke of Zhou** <note>original: "Cheu cum"</note>—constantly following in the footsteps of their predecessors, maintained the dignity of their ancestors which they had held in life, or which had certainly come to them in death. Thus, when they displayed the tablets called *Paiwei* <note>original: "Paî Queî"; these are ancestral tablets upon which the names of the deceased are inscribed.</note>, or the ancestral lineages, in the halls of their forefathers, they arranged them according to the order of dignity due to each. Likewise, they performed the rituals of those ancestors and played their music, to which they performed dances according to the order of dignity. They venerated those things which the ancestors themselves had once held in price and honor; they also loved what the ancestors had loved—namely, their posterity, subjects, the people, and so on. Finally, they served those who had recently died just as they had served them while living. Furthermore, they served those long dead in the same manner as if they were serving them while they were still safe and surviving. And this, indeed, was the pinnacle of obedience <note>In this context, "obedience" refers to Filial Piety, the central Confucian virtue of respecting one's parents and ancestors.</note>.

*It can be proven from many very clear Chinese texts that the legitimate meaning of the aforementioned axiom is that the Chinese practice natural piety and political deference toward the deceased with the same intention and formal motive as they practiced toward those same people while they were still living. From this, and from what will be said below, the prudent reader will easily conclude that these rites concerning the deceased were merely civil, instituted solely for the honor and deference of parents, which was not to be interrupted even after death. For if they had recognized anything divine in those rites, why would Confucius say that the ancients were accustomed to serving the deceased just as they served the living? Unless, perhaps, someone might say that sons bestowed divine honors upon parents who were still living—which is unheard of among the Chinese. Certainly, anyone who more attentively examines the political governance of this nation as expressed in its ancient monuments will find much to admire in that invention, so sweet for continuing gratitude and respect from sons and grandsons toward their deceased ancestors throughout their lives. For by this example, sons are moved and reminded to provide the obedience to their living parents which they see being so piously and constantly provided by those same parents toward their own dead progenitors. Moreover, these duties are performed for the living in a far more laborious way than that...*

...on the day which is the birthday of the parents, or the Beginning of the Year <note>original: "anni Principium"</note>: one would plainly say that some Divinity is being adored, so singular is the expression of observance and reverence with which the children, prostrated on the ground, worshipfully venerate their father and mother who stand near their seats. ->folio 15, page 2, section 1.<-

Human virtue—that is, the united mind and virtue of both the King and his subjects—makes governance efficient; it makes the proper way of ruling prompt and easy, just as the productive power of well-cultivated soil accelerates the growth of plants. Such a system of governance is therefore like river reeds <note>likely referring to bamboo</note>, which, when planted near flowing water, grow up more quickly and successfully than other plants.

->§. 2.<-

Indeed, the best method of administration (as was that of Kings **Wen** and **Wu**) depends on the men to whom this duty is entrusted by the King. However, selecting these men depends on the good composition and the standard of the royal person, who must be an exemplar for the rest. Furthermore, the composition of the royal person depends on that universal rule of reason through which he is able to discern good from evil, so that he may reject the latter and choose the former, and render to each what is his own with faith and equity. This aforementioned rule is perfected through that solid virtue of the soul and the universal love and piety toward all called ***Ren*** <term>Gìn: the central Confucian virtue often translated as "humaneness," "benevolence," or "perfect virtue."</term>.

->§. 3.<-

Thus, to love is the mark of a human being. Nevertheless, to love one’s parents above all others is man’s principal and primary duty, from which he then takes the step to love the rest. From this same love arises that distributive justice, which is itself the quality of being "fitting." Thus, to be just is a matter of equity; and although justice consists in the desire to render to each what is his own, it nonetheless requires that one honor the wise and the upright above others, by promoting them...

...promoting people to dignities and public offices is the chief duty of this form of justice. ->§. 2.<-

Since, therefore, right governance depends on wise men, and the selection of wise men depends on the virtue of the King’s own person, a perfect King cannot, above all else, fail to properly cultivate his own person. He does this first through the universal norm of reason and love toward all, upon which all other things depend. If he seriously intends to cultivate his own person through this aforementioned universal love—and since parents hold the first place among men—he cannot fail to serve his parents and love them above all others. Since this very love, or virtue, flows from the parents toward the rest of humanity (for it is a universal love), if the King seriously intends to serve his parents, he will eventually come to know other men. Among these, he will recognize those who excel others in virtue and wisdom, so that he may choose them as administrators for himself and his Kingdom. If he applies himself diligently to knowing men, it will be impossible for him not to have a clear perspective of **Heaven** <note>original: "Cælum"; referring to the divine order or the source of moral law</note>. Or rather, he will see the "Reason of Heaven" implanted in all things; this reason dictates that the person must be cultivated with virtues, parents must be cherished, the upright and wise must be honored, and finally, Heaven must be venerated. It is from Heaven that right reason—the principle and root of all virtues—is implanted in man.

->§. 3.<-

He says: There are five universal and common Rules, or paths, for the entire world; but the means by which they are practiced are three. The five Rules are: 1. Justice between the King and the subject; 2. Love between parents and children; 3. [Justice/Order] between husband and wife...

## BOOK TWO

...as a standard, you have known that by which you may rule the kingdoms of the world. For the same principle and law exists in all things as in a single person; from this it follows that the perfection of the ruler's own royal person is the foundation and the standard for the perfection of all others.

->folio 17. page 1.<-

<term>Confucius</term> <note>original: "Confucius"; the Latinized name of the Chinese philosopher Kong Fuzi</note>, according to what has been said, in instructing a King, speaks thus: Whoever governs the kingdoms of the world should hold these nine rules—precepts that are common enough, yet necessary to observe: Namely, 1. He must cultivate himself through virtues; 2. He must cherish wise and upright men; 3. He must respect and love his parents; 4. He must honor and hold in high value the superior ministers and those exercising the chief <term>magistracy</term> <note>original: "Magistratum"; high-ranking government officials</note>; 5. He must attune himself to the will of the other ministers or minor officials, whom he should regard as his own limbs; 6. He must love the people and the common masses like his own children, rejoicing with those who rejoice and grieving with those who grieve; 7. He must summon many artisans of every kind for the common benefit of the Kingdom; 8. He must receive and protect strangers and guests arriving from afar with kindness and courtesy; 9. Finally, he must lovingly and earnestly support and take to heart the <term>vassal princes</term> <note>original: "Regulos & Dynaſtas"; the local rulers or lords of smaller territories within the empire</note> and lords of the Empire, so that their love and loyalty toward the King may be secured.

->page 2. section 1.<-

If, therefore, the King observes these nine aforementioned rules, many benefits will indeed follow for the entire Kingdom. For if he cultivates himself through virtues, those universal laws and rules will soon flourish by the King's example. If he cherishes the wise, and thus makes great use of their experience and counsel, he will no longer hesitate or be perplexed in undertaking and completing business. If he respects and loves his parents, then among the rest of his kin—for example, uncles, and brothers both older and younger—there will be no complaints or rivalries, but rather a harmonious love working together for the good of the entire family. If he venerates and holds the chief ministers in high value, his vision will not be clouded, nor will he be anxious and trembling in the administration of his Kingdom, even if some crisis should perhaps arise; for men of proven virtue and unconquerable strength will be present to help their Prince, ready not only with counsel but also with their hands. If he considers the local officials as the members of his own body, adapting himself to them, then both these and those who are prefects of a higher order will render their services more earnestly and abundantly, and all will respond to the King with total loyalty and sincerity. If he loves the people like sons, then the people will in turn be encouraged and moved to love such a beneficent parent back. If, drawn by the fame of such a great King, many artisans of every kind arrive, then there will be an abundance of wealth for use and of things necessary for common needs. If he kindly receives strangers arriving from distant regions, soon from the surrounding four...
