<meta>catchword: to be received</meta>

the peoples of the world will come to him of their own accord and will rejoice to be subject to such a humane and kind Prince. If he diligently loves and supports the <term>vassal princes</term> <note>original: "Regulos"; local rulers or lords of smaller territories within the empire</note>, he will in turn have them devoted and bound to him; thus, increased himself by such great wealth and power, he will now be formidable to the whole world.

->§. 2.<-

Confucius, having listed the fruits that arise from the nine aforementioned Rules, here teaches the method by which they may be put into practice, saying: If a King abstains from vices, he becomes pure and stainless within, and externally he is clothed in a grave dignity worthy of himself; if he does not touch what is illicit or contrary to reason—these are certainly the ways by which the royal person is refined. 

If he pushes detractors far from him and stays far from carnal pleasures; if he thinks little of wealth and property but values virtue highly—these are the ways by which the wise followers of virtue are encouraged and spurred to imitation. If he values, honors, and fosters the dignity of his parents, and uses his royal revenue to increase their private income, loving and hating the same things they love or hate <note>In Confucian thought, "filial piety" involves aligning one's own will and emotions with those of one's parents to ensure family harmony</note>—these are the ways by which the rest of the people are likewise encouraged to love their parents and relatives. 

If he employs a great number of inferior <term>Prefects</term> <note>original: "Præfectorum"; administrative officials or magistrates</note> who, subordinated to the higher officials, manage all the smaller business as their duty—this is the means by which the Prefects of the higher order are encouraged, so that they may more successfully carry out their own duties by utilizing the industry and work of their subordinates. 

If the King trusts and believes in his ministers and orders that ample salaries be given according to each person's merits—these are the ways by which the royal ministers are encouraged to serve their Prince more intensely. If he occupies the people only at suitable times (namely, not during the seasons when fields must be tilled or the harvest gathered) and moderates taxes—these are the ways by which the common people are encouraged toward love and prompt obedience. 

If he examines daily, and explores for himself every month, whether the wages and food given to workers from the royal storehouses correspond to their labor—this is how artisans are encouraged to work more intensely. If the King attends to departing guests with the honors due to them and receives those arriving kindly and courteously—praising the distinguished talents of others when they possess them, employing them for public duties, and pitying the weakness of others who might be poorer—this is the way that strangers and travelers from afar are treated kindly. 

If he strives again and again to perpetuate or preserve the families of the vassal princes which are now near extinction, by appointing another member of the same family to the place and dignity of the deceased; if, furthermore, he strives to raise up and restore their collapsing Kingdoms to their former state, moderating and suppressing the seditions or riots that have arisen, and repelling and halting imminent dangers; likewise, if while the assemblies of the vassal princes are to be celebrated, and to be received

# BOOK TWO

receiving their embassies, he should do so only at the appointed times (without changing the common practice in this, so as not to be a burden to the <term>vassal princes</term> <note>original: "Regulis"; local lords or subordinate rulers</note>). Likewise, if he treats those departing sumptuously and splendidly, and receives the gifts of those arriving not greedily but with royal moderation (which was the decree of the Ancient Kings)—these are the ways, in short, by which the vassal princes who are clients of the Empire are lovingly fostered.

*It was the custom that every year the vassal princes would send gifts to the Emperor through an envoy called a <term>Ta Fu</term> <note>original: "Tá Fu" (大夫); a high-ranking administrative official</note>; likewise, every third year, they would send larger and richer gifts through an envoy of a higher rank called a <term>Kim</term> <note>original: "Kim"; likely a transliteration of "Qing" (卿), a high minister</note>; finally, every five years, the vassal princes themselves were required to present themselves to the Emperor in the assemblies of the Empire.*

->f. 18. p. 2. §. 1.<-

Confucius concludes: Therefore, whoever rules the kingdoms of the world possesses indeed these nine rules and the manner in which they should be kept. However, the means by which they must exercise them is but one: namely, a serious solidity of mind or truth without any pretense <note>This refers to the Confucian concept of "Cheng" (誠), often translated as Sincerity or Integrity</note>; which, if it were lacking in even one of the nine rules, the virtue would no longer be right, but merely disguised and superficial.

->§. 2.<-

But so that one may attain these rules and all virtues with that aforementioned solidity and truth of mind, the Philosopher <note>Commonly used in this period to refer specifically to Confucius</note> adds this: If all matters and actions relating to the aforementioned rules are thought out in advance, and, having been previously considered, are firmly established in the mind, they will for this very reason be ready and will stand firm. But if you do not meditatively prepare them, they will collapse and come to nothing. Thus, if you determine the words to be spoken beforehand—repeating them to yourself again and again, and clearly defining what and how things should be said—you will not stumble, nor will you hesitate or cause offense in your speech. If you first weigh the things to be done accurately within yourself, and firmly decide what and by what method they should be done, you will not thereafter be distressed or afflicted by their failure. If you yourself firmly pre-determine the work you are about to undertake within your mind, you will not later regret it, nor will the work begun lose its vigor, nor will you yourself be marked for levity or inconstancy (if by chance you should fail halfway through). Finally, if the rule of right reason is first fixed and firm—or if, before you undertake a task to be completed, you have long meditated upon it and strengthened your mind with that resolute strength of right and sincere judgment—then indeed such virtue and efficacy will arise that it cannot be exhausted, and its use will remain unfailing for you.

# CHINESE KNOWLEDGE

->§. 3.<-

The Philosopher <note>Referring to Confucius</note> explains the doctrine just mentioned through the example of those in lower positions in relation to their superiors, speaking thus: He who is placed in a lower rank, if he has not first won over the mind of his superior and of those placed in the highest authority, it is impossible for the people to be governed by him rightly and peacefully. Furthermore, for the winning over of the minds of Superiors and the highest Magistrates, there is also a specific method and rule upon which it rests: namely, that he must keep the faith he has given to his friends and equals. For if one does not keep faith with friends from the heart, he will not be able to obtain favor, benevolence, and trust among Superiors and the highest Magistrates; for these will not trust one who is deceptive, even if the person who proved false is a friend or intimate acquaintance. 

However, so that one may keep faith with friends, there is also its own rule and method: for if one does not seriously support and obey his parents, and thereby in some way fails in his duty, for this very reason he will neither keep nor hold faith with his companions and friends. Moreover, for the obeying of parents, there is also a certain method and rule: if anyone, looking back into himself, does not find that he obeys them truly and from a sincere mind, but only through pretense and outward appearance, he is clearly to be judged as not supporting or obeying his parents. 

Finally, so that one may sincerely and solidly perfect oneself and obtain that integrity of a right mind, there is likewise a certain rule and method, which consists in the discernment of good from evil; for unless one has a tested and clear understanding of the nature of good and evil, he will never sincerely perfect himself, and will not be able to be "solid" <note>In this context, "solid" refers to being substantial, authentic, or having integrity</note> within himself.

Above (from page 14, part 2, § 2), the Philosopher treats right governance in imitation of the Ancient Kings *Wen-wang* and *Wu-wang* <note>original: "Ven-vam" and "Vu-vam"; the founders of the Zhou Dynasty, regarded as ideal rulers</note>. Then he brings forward those five rules of nature implanted by Heaven in this universe of things <note>The Five Relationships: Ruler-Subject, Father-Son, Husband-Wife, Elder-Younger Brother, and Friend-Friend</note>, and the three virtues which are, as it were, Cardinal: prudence, love, and fortitude, by which those rules are perfected. 

Then, descending to particulars, he hands down the nine rules proper for rightly governing the Empire, all of which he says depend on the right instruction of oneself. Finally, he concludes that he who wishes to rule himself, and then the people, must begin from the intrinsic solidity of the mind, or a certain sublime perfection and truth that utterly excludes all pretense. Indeed, this truth and solidity is sometimes taken for nature itself, implanted by Heaven into man and all things in varying proportions and efficacy. This truth and solidity is explained here by the character *cheng* <note>original: "chim" (誠); often translated as Sincerity, Integrity, or Reality</note>. The interpreters explain this with four characters, namely *Zhen Shi Wu Wang* <note>original: "Chin Xe Vu Vam" (真實無妄); meaning "True, solid, and without falsehood"</note>. We, however, shall henceforth call it "true or solid perfection."

<summary>This page outlines the Confucian chain of moral dependency, where effective governance is shown to rely on winning over superiors, which in turn requires honesty with friends, filial piety, and ultimately the internal "solidity" of distinguishing good from evil.</summary>

## BOOK TWO

->folio 19. page 1. section 1.<-

So that the mind of the Philosopher <note>Referring to Confucius</note> may be understood here and from now on, I say that he treats the Holy Sage and the wise man (as it pertains to the light of reason, or to that native perfection and truth) in such a way that, although he asserts that the rational light is infused into these as well as into other men in equal measure, it is nonetheless infused into the Holy Sage in such a way that—because he never deflected even the slightest bit from that first integrity through crooked or depraved affections of the soul—he enjoys, as it were, an ever-serene sky. In this sky, he naturally and without resistance spreads the rational light of his native sun far and wide for his uses and actions. On the other hand, the same light and perfection is infused into the wise man in such a way that, because certain obstacles, vices, and stains later arrived which intercepted the light of the native sun like clouds, there is need for no small effort, study, and labor so that, by removing the clouds, he may be restored to his primeval serenity and splendor. This latter process is called *the way and method of man* <note>original: *gĭn táo* (Ren Dao)</note>, which is the rule of the wise who are striving toward the primeval origin of perfection. The former is called *the method of heaven* <note>original: *tién táo* (Tian Dao)</note>, which is the first rule instilled equally in all by heaven; it is the never-violated virtue of the Holy Sages.

The Philosopher treats both of these methods or rules almost until the end of this book, as will be clear to the reader. Dealing with both here, **Confucius** says: to be endowed with true and solid perfection is a certain heavenly principle <note>original: *ratio*</note> instilled in all; but truly, after the loss of this, to strive to recover this true and solid perfection anew, or to return through effort to that integrity which one lost, is a certain human way and method. Regarding one endowed with true and solid perfection: because such a person surely proceeds from heaven, he acts on his own part without forcing himself and without any conflict of passions, and yet he attains the mark and the end without difficulty. He does not use complex reasoning, and yet he achieves the matter; finally, with great tranquility and without any agitation, he follows reason and attains virtue; and this belongs to the **Holy Sages**. However, regarding him who strives through effort toward true and solid perfection: because he depends on the man himself, who tries to achieve it with labor, it is necessary that he first meditate seriously within himself and examine every detail. Once this is done, he then selects the good for himself, and having selected it, he then holds it firmly with his hand and preserves it; and that is the way and method of wise men, who belong to an order far inferior to the one just mentioned.

->page 2. section 1.<-

Furthermore, so that one may be able to select the good for oneself and then hold it tenaciously, it is necessary to observe five Rules. 1. That he thoroughly learns the reasons, causes, and harmonies of all things, not in passing or piecemeal, but fully and broadly; for he who strives to achieve solid perfection...

The Philosopher <note>Referring to Confucius</note> declares the doctrine just mentioned by the example of those in lower positions with respect to those in higher ones, saying: He who is placed in a lower rank, if he does not first have the mind of his superior and those placed in the highest dignity reconciled to him, it is impossible for the people to be governed by him rightly and peacefully. Furthermore, for the reconciliation of the minds of Superiors and the highest Magistrates, there is also given its own reason and rule upon which it rests: namely, that he keep the faith he has given to his friends and equals. For if one does not keep faith with friends from the soul, he will not be able to obtain grace, benevolence, and trust among the Superiors and the highest Magistrates; for these will not give their trust to a deceiver, even if the one who deceived is a friend or familiar. However, for one to keep faith with friends, there is also a certain rule and reason: For if one does not seriously comply with and obey—and thus in some way fails in his duty toward—his parents, by this very fact he will neither keep nor hold faith with his associates and friends. Moreover, for complying with parents, there is also a certain reason and rule: namely, if anyone, first turning his eyes upon himself, does not find that he obeys them truly and from a sincere soul, but only feignedly and in appearance, he is clearly to be judged as not complying with or obeying his parents. Furthermore, for one to sincerely and solidly perfect himself, and to obtain that integrity of a right mind, there is likewise a certain rule and reason, which consists in the discrimination of good from evil; for unless one has a thoroughly tested and clear understanding of the nature of good and evil, he will never sincerely perfect himself, and will not be able to be solid within himself.

Above (from folio 14, page 2, section 2), the Philosopher treats right governance in imitation of the Ancient Kings **Wen Wang** and **Wu Wang** <note>original: *Ven-vam* and *Vu-vam*; the founders of the Zhou Dynasty, held up as models of virtue</note>. Then he brings forward those five Rules of nature implanted by Heaven in this universe of things, and the three virtues, which are like Cardinals—prudence, love, and fortitude <note>original: *prudentia, amor, fortitudo*; often translated as Wisdom, Benevolence, and Courage</note>—by which those rules are perfected. Then, descending to particulars, he hands down the nine Rules proper for rightly governing the Empire, all of which he says depend on the right instruction of oneself. Indeed, this truth and solidity is sometimes taken for nature itself, implanted by Heaven in man and in all things, in various proportions and efficacy. Therefore, this truth and solidity is explained here by the character *Chim* <note>original: *Chim*; the Chinese character *Cheng* (誠), usually translated as Sincerity or Integrity</note>. The Interpreters explain this with four characters, namely *Chin Xe Vu Vam* <note>original: *Chin Xe Vu Vam*; likely *Zhen Shi Wu Wang* (真實無妄), meaning "True, solid, and without falsehood"</note>, that is, *True, solid, without fiction*. # BOOK TWO

->f. 19. p. 1. §. 1.<-

So that the mind of the Philosopher <note>Confucius</note> may be understood here and hereafter, I say that he treats the Holy One <note>original: *Sancto*; likely referring to the *Shengren* or the Perfected Person</note> and the Sage <note>original: *sapiente*; referring to the *Xianren* or the virtuous person who learns</note> in this way (regarding the light of reason, or that native perfection and truth): Although he asserts that a rational light has been infused into both of these, as well as into all other men, in equal portion, it is infused into the Holy One in such a way that—because he has never turned aside even the slightest bit from that original integrity through crooked or perverse affections of the soul—he always enjoys, as it were, a most serene sky. In this sky, he naturally and without resistance spreads the rational light of his native sun far and wide for his use and actions.

On the contrary, the same light and perfection is infused into the Sage in such a way that, because certain obstacles, vices, and stains later came upon him—which, like clouds, intercepted the light of the native sun—he needs no small effort, study, and labor to remove those clouds and be restored to his primeval serenity and splendor. This is called *gin táo* <note>original: *gin táo*; the Way of Man</note>, that is, the way and method of man, or the rule of the wise who are striving toward the primeval origin of perfection. The former, however, is called *tién táo* <note>original: *tién táo*; the Way of Heaven</note>, that is, the method of heaven, or the first rule instilled by heaven equally in all, and it is the never-violated virtue of the Holy Ones.

Both of these methods or rules are discussed almost until the end of this book, as will be clear to the reader. Dealing with both here, **Confucius** says: to be endowed with true and solid perfection is a certain celestial method <note>original: *ratio*; meaning a principle or way</note> instilled in everyone; but truly, after its loss, to strive to recover this true and solid perfection again—or to return through effort to that integrity which one lost—is a certain human way and method. 

Regarding the one endowed with true and solid perfection: because such a person surely proceeds from heaven, he acts for his part without forcing himself and without any conflict of passions, and yet he attains his aim and end without difficulty. He does not reason things out, and yet he achieves his goal; finally, with great tranquility and without any agitation, he follows reason and attains virtue; and this belongs to the *Holy Ones*. 

However, regarding the one who strives through effort toward true and solid perfection: because he depends on himself, laboring to attain it, it is necessary that he first meditate seriously within himself and examine individual things. Once this is done, he then selects the good for himself, and having selected it, he then holds it firmly with his hand and preserves it; and that is the way and method of wise men, who are of an order far lower than the one just mentioned.

->p. 2. §. 1.<-

Moreover, so that one may be able to select the good for himself and then retain it tenaciously, it is necessary that he observe five Rules.

...he must learn many things seriously. 2. Because among the things he has learned, there may perhaps be points he does not yet know well enough to prevent doubts from arising, it is necessary that he discusses what needs to be asked early on, examining each point and consulting wise men and those experienced in such matters. 3. Finally, once these things are thus perfected, it is necessary that he acts not in a faked manner, but solidly and constantly; that is, he should execute with all his strength the matters he has previously decided upon in his own mind.

->§. 2.<-

**C**onfucius continues: there are those who do not wish to learn because they do not profit by learning, nor can they immediately attain what they desire; but if they do learn, they should not stop their study until they know. There are those who do not wish to ask questions because, being slow of wit, they do not immediately grasp the answers; but if they do ask, they should not stop asking until they understand. There are those who do not wish to meditate through reasoning because they do not easily grasp what they meditate upon; but if they do reason, they should not stop or despair of their undertaking until they attain it. There are those who do not wish to argue and judge because they do not perceive the matter with total clarity and distinction; but if they do judge, they should not stop or lose heart until they perceive everything clearly. There are those who do not wish to act because they are not solid and constant in their actions; but if they do act, they should not stop the work they have begun until it is completed with all their effort. For if others can successfully attain something on the first and only attempt, you yourself—if not in one attempt or one effort—will surely achieve something on the hundredth. If others can do something on the tenth attempt, hope that you will succeed on the thousandth.

->folio 20. page 1.<-

**I**f anyone, therefore, can truly prevail upon themselves to try to keep, or act according to, these five stated rules without intermission, even if he is unrefined <note>original: *rudis*; referring to a lack of education or natural polish</note> and feels himself little aided by art or nature, he will eventually emerge clearly understanding; and even if he is currently soft and weak, he will eventually emerge strong in the exercise of virtues. *Thus far Confucius.*

# SECOND BOOK
R

...nature, or the innate virtue infused from heaven: again, to illuminate oneself and become intelligent through prior effort and study, and then to become firm in true virtue or perfection, is called **instruction** (or, as others explain: to possess a clear and perfect understanding of all things from that true and solid perfection is what is called **nature**, or a certain native virtue and perfection bestowed upon mortals by Heaven; this is *Tien Táo* <note>original: "Tian Dao", the Way of Heaven</note>, or the virtue of the **Holy Ones**, which, having never suffered any stain or vice, is positioned as if on the peak of Olympus <note>The author uses "Olympus" as a classical metaphor for the highest, most serene heaven</note> and descends to all things with the greatest ease: but truly, to ascend to that original and true perfection—that native virtue as it was first bestowed by heaven—from a clear and perfect understanding of things that was acquired through long study and labor, is called **instruction**, or the discipline of virtues that are not infused, but acquired; and this is *Gín Táo* <note>original: "Ren Dao", the Way of Man</note>, or the virtue of the **wise**, who struggle with great labor to reach the high peak of Olympus where they were first placed by Heaven. Therefore, whoever is endowed with native perfection, or is a **Holy One**, is by that very fact clearly understanding of all things, or wise; and whoever has acquired a clear understanding of things through labor and effort will soon be able, with easy work, to be solidly perfect and on an equal level with the **Holy One** himself.)

*Here he subsequently explains the doctrine of Zisi* <note>original: "çù-su", the grandson and disciple of Confucius</note> *concerning solid truth, and the supreme holiness joined with it. Although the pagan interpreters (with some exceptions) attribute this to man, the Philosopher <note>Confucius</note> makes it so sublime that in truth it seems it can be attributed to nothing but supreme truth and holiness. For when he asserts that it is supremely true, and that only this can, by understanding, exhaust the supreme nature of all things, foreknow the future, be the beginning and end of things, most ample, most subtle, perpetual, and without end; that it is something without motion, yet moving and producing, covering, sustaining, and perfecting all things; that it is something unique, supremely holy, supremely intelligent, invisible, etc., as will be clear in the text below; what else did he wish to imply than some supreme Divinity, and a most perfect mind? If we grant the knowledge of this to Confucius and his disciples, what new thing, I ask, do we say? For the Apostle himself* <note>A reference to St. Paul, who argued in Romans that even pagans could know God through reason</note> *first granted that very knowledge to many pagans, as did the holy Fathers, and finally so many great Doctors and Theologians—and even the Prince of Pagan Eloquence* <note>The Roman orator Cicero</note> *himself granted it to the barbarian nations. Indeed, while these thinkers attempt to demonstrate the existence of God through moral reasons, they draw great strength for their demonstration from that very consensus of all nations and wise men, who certainly could not agree so constantly on a falsehood.*

# CHINESE KNOWLEDGE

->f. 21. p. 1.<-

Therefore, Zisi <note>original: "çù-su"; Kong Ji, the grandson of Confucius and traditional author of the *Doctrine of the Mean*</note> says that although the nature bestowed by Heaven upon man is indeed rational when viewed at its root—being something solid, true, and without deception—nevertheless, because man has already turned away from that innocence and truth of native purity through the disordered movements of his passions, he no longer knows it clearly. Nor can he achieve it in practice as much as the condition and status of nature requires. 

Therefore, only he who is supremely perfect and holy in this entire universe can, through his understanding, fully realize <note>original: "exhaurire," literally "to exhaust" or "to drain," meaning to reach the furthest depths or full potential</note> his own nature. Moreover, he who can fully realize his own nature can, by this very fact, also fully realize the nature of other men—both by understanding them and rightly instructing them—and thus cause them to return to their original purity from which they fell away. 

If he can thus fully realize the nature of men, he will also by this very fact be able to fully realize the natures of all other things, fulfilling what they require—whether by governing or preserving them—and ensuring that every single thing obtains a state agreeable to its own nature. If he can fully realize the natures of all things, he will then be able to concur, as if by assisting, with Heaven and Earth in the production and preservation of all things. If he can thus assist Heaven and Earth in the production and preservation of things, then—since Heaven is above, cherishing and covering all in its embrace, and Earth is below, sustaining all things—the Supreme Sage, positioned in the middle between Heaven and Earth, can finally complete the Ternary Principle <note>original: "ternarium principium," referring to the *San Cai* or the Three Powers: Heaven, Earth, and Humanity</note>. These matters indeed pertain to the reason and rule bestowed from Heaven.

->p. 2.<-

Regarding those who are of the second rank—those perfect men who are next to the Sages—they act first in this way: they bend back or rectify what is crooked. With labor and constancy, they strive to restore that small portion of native goodness not yet lost and to kindle the spark of primeval light not yet fully extinguished. 

If they do this and restore that portion of native goodness, they will then be able to revive, in a sense, and regain that first vigor of solid perfection. It is not unlike a parched tree that is nearly dead; if by chance we perceive through the sign of a tiny bud or a single green twig that faint remains of life survive, we immediately apply labor and industry—now by watering it, now by adding richer soil. Furthermore, by pruning away what is beyond hope of cure and finally by bravely removing the cause of the disease and vice, we at last ensure that the original vigor and life is restored to the entire tree. 

When, therefore, they have achieved solid perfection, it will soon manifest itself. Once it has manifested, it will soon shine more and more, like the rising Sun. When it has shone forth, it will soon, like the Sun at midday, spread the rays of its light far and wide. When it has thus irradiated, by that very fact it will move the souls of others.

## BOOK TWO

For a man endowed with solid perfection must necessarily strike the minds of men with the rays and the fame of his virtues. Wherever he creates movement and a stirring of souls, he will, without them even perceiving it, induce a change in morals. For by his example, a person will feel themselves inclined toward the good, even if they do not know from where this feeling comes. Once he has induced this change in morals, a happy conversion of all things follows by that very fact. Only he in this universe who is supremely perfect and holy can bring about this conversion. Furthermore, when men of this second order <note>This refers to those who achieve perfection through diligent effort and study, rather than those born with innate holiness</note> finally arrive at solid perfection, they too, through the fame of their virtues, will be able to effect such a sublime conversion of minds, and in this way cooperate with Heaven and Earth toward that harmonic concord of the entire world.

->f. 22. p. 1.<-

Since men everywhere have their minds clouded, as if by a mist of wicked passions, they are unable to clearly know every principle; sometimes they cannot even discern what is right before their eyes, let alone those things which are most remote, such as the future. But indeed, says Zisi <note>original: "çù su"; the grandson of Confucius and author of the text being commented upon</note>, the virtue of the supremely perfect and holy man is such that he can know the future in advance. When a Royal Family is about to be established, there are undoubtedly favorable omens given everywhere; likewise, when the downfall of a Royal Family is imminent, there are undoubtedly unfavorable omens given, which are manifested in the herb called *xi* <note>original: "xi"; the milfoil or yarrow plant used in I Ching divination</note> and in the tortoise called *quei* <note>original: "quei"; the tortoise shell used for pyromancy or bone-reading</note> <gloss>above this shell some would burn the aforementioned herb, and from the marks or colors which then happened to appear, they would conjecture the future</gloss>. Also, by a prior movement or a certain trembling and fear of things to come, the four limbs or the entire human body are struck. But the supremely perfect man, if by chance calamity or happiness is close at hand, does not wait for such signs; in the case of the upright, he undoubtedly foreknows and senses that happiness, and in the case of the wicked, he undoubtedly foreknows that calamity. Therefore, since the supremely perfect man is so subtle and discerning, he is like a spirit penetrating everything from all sides; why then would he need such auguries and omens?

Regarding what pertains to lots <note>original: "sortes"; the practice of casting lots or using divination tools</note> and other observations of superstitious antiquity, that stain also seems to have contaminated China, which in those times was common to almost the entire human race. It is indeed certain that the Ancient Chinese also had their own lots and their own auguries, and from these, they were accustomed to predict the successful outcome of affairs. The Chinese were not ignorant of the fact that there is a great affinity and a most close connection between Heaven and Earth, as if both were like parts making up a single whole. In this constitution, since Heaven is by far the more noble part and that which rules over the other, it follows that all vigor and power flows from Heaven to Earth, and to us mortals who dwell on Earth, in a perennial flow as if from its head into the subject members.

# THE CHINESE SCIENCES

...might flow out. But since that heavenly flow and efficacy were such that it very frequently escaped the senses, and hardly revealed itself except through its effects—even though they were not without their own (judicial) Astrologers whom they consulted time and again as interpreters of heavenly secrets, albeit with very little reward for their effort—they were nevertheless entirely persuaded that there also existed on earth certain things which had a specific and special connection, and as if a sympathy, with heaven; by whose indication they could be made more certain about future events and the secret influences of the heavens. Just as we see happening in the human body, where the feet, though the most remote of all parts, not infrequently are the first to feel an affection of the head. 

Therefore, they thought this kind of sympathetic power was present especially in the tortoise; both because it was a certain living image (as they said) of heaven and earth, since the tortoise represents this very earth (which they established to be square) with the lower part of its body, which is likewise square; and the convexity of the heavens with its back; and also depicts the celestial houses of the planets and their circles with various streaks and markings with which its back is variegated; and also because they thought that among brute animals none could be found longer-lived than the tortoise, which, in their opinion, surpassed a thousand years and more.

The reasoning for the herb called Xi <note>original: "Herba Xi"; referring to the milfoil or yarrow stalks (Achillea alpina) used in I Ching divination</note> was clearly similar: this grew (as they themselves write) to the size of nine cubits, and being a conqueror over other herbs, was equal to the trees themselves: it was also believed to persist vigorously for a thousand years; hence its wonderful price, because it was believed to be powerful with a secret and heavenly force.

Furthermore, they say the use of both things was of this kind: they would place the Xi herb next to, or even on top of, the *Quëi* <note>original: "Quëi"; the Chinese word for tortoise (gui)</note> or the back of the tortoise; soon they would apply fire; when the said herb had caught fire, they would diligently observe what kind and how great a brightness, and what colors would shine forth from it: Again, what motion and effort there was of the tortoise itself: likewise what colors would manifest themselves on the variegated back of the shell: and if indeed they were such as the present season of the year, for example, springtime, seemed to require; they would surely prophesy well and fortunately, but if otherwise, they soon foretold that something sinister was imminent. Not much differently than if a Chinese Physician <term>Chinese Physician (Medicus Sinensis)</term> <note>the text draws an analogy to traditional Chinese pulse diagnosis, where a physician reads internal states through external rhythms</note>, by the indication of the pulses, perceives winter-like affections to be in the human body during the summer time, he affirms without doubt that some poison lies hidden and a disease is imminent: Similarly also as when someone is seized by an unexpected motion or symptom of the body, they are accustomed to be anxious and afraid: which the Philosopher also indicated in this very text.

But so that we may know for what purpose primarily, or in what matters the Ancients applied these observations, that which is commemorated in the *Shujing* <note>original: "Xu-kim"; the Classic of History or Book of Documents</note>, Book 1, page 29, will bring us much light. Emperor Shun <note>original: "Xún Imperator"; a legendary model of virtue and one of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors</note> had determined to hand over the Empire by hand to his client, named Yu <note>original: "Yu"; known as Yu the Great, the tamer of the floods</note> (he was the Founder and Prince of the Xia Family <note>original: "Familia Hiá"</note>, the first of the Imperial Families), on account of the great merits of the man, when he diverted the greatest floods of water, which had been stagnant for many years, into the sea no less industriously than fortunately.

## BOOK TWO

*But Yu earnestly refused the dignity offered to him, arguing that there were many others whose merits were far greater than his own, and that the Empire could be conferred upon one of them. If it seemed difficult to designate one of these, he suggested that the divination lots could be consulted—and indeed, in a matter of such great importance, they absolutely ought to be. To this, Emperor Xún <note>Emperor Shun (r. c. 2255–2205 BCE), the legendary successor to Yao</note> replied:*

"Whenever," he said, "a doubtful and difficult matter is presented to us, we certainly consult the lots. Nevertheless, before they are consulted, I place the matter under deliberation before my own eyes and maturely weigh what benefits or disadvantages it might bring, and which of these carries more weight. I also solicitously seek the opinions of the wise. Having heard them, I then determine within myself what must be done. Only after this do I order the great tortoise to be brought and the lots to be cast. But in this case, I have already determined and decreed that you shall succeed me in the governance of the Empire; nor is there anyone among those I have consulted who does not wonderfully approve of my decision. Since this decision has already been made public, do you not see for yourself the great zeal and applause arising from all the people? Therefore, without a doubt, the Spirits themselves favor our decision; for what other wish could they have than the wish of the entire multitude? Who, then, could doubt that the lots will produce any opinion other than the one we ourselves hold? It would, therefore, be entirely superfluous to consult them again, since it is already established that the wishes of the whole people and the Spirits themselves are in agreement with us." Thus spoke the Emperor.

*These things, explained according to the interpretation of Cham colai <note>Refers to Zhang Juzheng (1525–1582), a Ming dynasty statesman and commentator on the Classics</note>, can certainly shed no little light on our subject, as I was just saying. It becomes clear that they did not use the lots in such a way that they held the power of a primary or principal rule for undertaking or performing tasks. Indeed, the lots never seem to have been of such importance that if something appeared to be for the good of the State, and consistent with what is right and just, they would ever set it aside because of adverse lots or augurs. And indeed, does not the Philosopher <note>Confucius</note> teach in this very place that holiness <note>original: "sanctitati"; referring to the Sage-like quality of the perfect ruler</note> has no need of such divinations, because whoever is endowed with it can perceive hidden things and prudently conjecture about the future even without any divinations? Furthermore, it is entirely credible that those Augurs and Soothsayers, if they already knew the opinion and will of the Prince and the Nobles, were generally accustomed to comply with it, and to draw their "reluctant" tortoises toward that same conclusion—a common vice, to be sure, of certain Astrologers who, while casting the horoscopes of their Princes, are accustomed to prophesy (or rather, to lie) to the credulous about almost nothing but favorable outcomes: many years of life, and new increases in wealth and kingdoms.*

Our Confucius, although he himself gave little or no faith at all to these observations—indeed, he even despised and condemned them (as will be established below)—could not, however, avoid making some mention of them, both here and in the book Ye-kim <note>The I Ching, or Book of Changes</note>. ### CHINESE KNOWLEDGE

<note>original: "subtiliter observat"; the text begins mid-sentence from the previous page</note> ...closely observes) that during the reign of the **Zhou Dynasty** <note>original: "Familia Cheu"; c. 1046–256 BCE</note>, toward the decline of which the **Philosopher** <note>Confucius</note> lived, those observations were in use. Furthermore, since this practice was accepted throughout the whole Empire and recommended by its considerable antiquity, had he—being a private citizen and certainly devoid of royal dignity—undertaken to publicly condemn or abolish it, he would surely have labored in vain. He would have gained nothing from such an effort except the resentment of having fruitlessly disturbed the Empire.

But let these remarks suffice. They are said not because we wish to defend those divinations or to entirely clear the **Ancient Chinese**; rather, they are meant to make it clear to the reader that there is perhaps nothing here that can be greatly condemned, except for ignorance—which we also certainly condemn. ->Page 2. Section 1.<-

True and solid perfection <note>The Latin "perfectio" here translates the Chinese concept of *Cheng* (誠), often rendered as Sincerity, Integrity, or Reality</note> is the perfection of oneself. That is, it is perfected through itself, or is perfect by its own nature, and not through anything distinct from itself. It is its own rule; other things are measured and directed by it, such that it is not directed by anything else.

->Section 2.<-

This true and solid reason, or perfection, is the end and the beginning of all things. If this true and solid reason, or perfection, were lacking in things, they would not exist. In the same way, in moral matters, an action that lacks truth is not to be judged as virtue, but as a shadow and a mere surface of virtue. For example, if a son does not obey from a true and sincere mind, he is not to be judged obedient; nor is a subject faithful if he does not serve the King with faith and truth. For this reason, the wise and upright man values this true and solid perfection above all else.

->Section 3.<-

The **TRULY** perfect man does not only act so as to perfect himself and then stop there; rather, he also perfects other things. To perfect oneself is the work of love <note>original: "amoris"; referring to *Ren* or Benevolence</note> tending first toward its own perfection. To perfect others is the work of prudence or providence. These are indeed innate virtues. But to unite and bind these two virtues together by applying them to external things (or other people) and internal things (or oneself): this is indeed the most correct rule. Furthermore, to exercise these same virtues according to their proper times and circumstances is the work of fittingness <note>original: "convenientiæ"; referring to *Yi* or Righteousness/Appropriateness</note>. In this way, the most perfect harmony arises in this universe of things, and all things attain the end consistent with their nature.

->Folio 23. Page 2. Section 1.<-

Therefore, he who is supremely perfect and holy never stops or ceases; but he works continually and without interruption.

# BOOK TWO.

->§. 2.<-

If it never ceases, then its internal power <note>original: *virtus*</note> always persists; and if it always persists, then it cannot remain hidden for long, but must necessarily reveal itself and appear outwardly through its effects and actions.

->§. 3.<-

If it reveals itself outwardly through its effects, then it will spread far and wide through the growth of its virtues. If it spreads far and wide, then it will expand more and more—amply and deeply, with none opposing it—by that greatness of power and the fame of its operations. If it expands so amply and deeply, then it will rise higher than all else, adorned with such great virtues, becoming clear and conspicuous to all, and shining like the sun to the whole world; thus it must necessarily harmonize with **Heaven** and **earth** toward the fruitful concord <note>original: *concentum*</note> or harmonious preservation of all things.

->§. 2.<-

Indeed, because it is so vast through the growth of so many and such great virtues, and so deep in that vastness of the power of its operations, it sustains all things like the **earth** <note>original: *telluris instar*</note> with the arm of its power, while granting to each what is fitting. And because it is so sublime and so clear and conspicuous, it illuminates and protects all things by the splendor of its operations, just like **heaven**. Finally, because its power <note>original: *virtus*</note> is so widely diffused everywhere and so enduring, it brings all things to completion. From this it follows that all things perfectly enjoy a state consistent with their nature.

->p. 2. §. 1.<-

Because of its vastness and depth, it is likened to the earth; but because of its loftiness and clarity, it is likened to heaven; with these, it completes the **triple principle** <term>ternarium principium: the "Great Triad" of Heaven, Earth, and Man, which together govern the order of the universe</term>. As for its breadth and duration, it is without limit and without measure.

->§. 2.<-

For this reason, being of such a nature and greatness, it does not first display and show itself off before becoming manifest; it does not first move others by exhortation before effecting a conversion; it does not first employ a great exertion of force to do something before completing it. Or, as others explain: since its power is so great, even if it does not show itself or offer itself to be stared at, it is nonetheless manifested through its effects. In this, it agrees with the hidden power of the earth: it is not moved, and yet it moves and effects changes. Or rather, it does not seem to move anything with any outward sound or clatter, and yet, with a certain sweet tranquility, and

# CHINESE KNOWLEDGE

It brings about the transformation of things and minds without violence; thus, it harmonizes with **Heaven**, which acts through silent movements and influences. In short, it does nothing, and yet it does everything; or rather, it seems to perform no great action, yet it is always at work, bringing all things to fulfillment.

->§. 3.<-

Previously, Zisi <term>çu-su</term> <note>Zisi, the grandson of Confucius and traditional author of the *Doctrine of the Mean*</note> taught that the virtue of the supremely true and holy man works in harmony with **Heaven** and **earth** toward all things alike. Here, however, he moves on to show that the effectiveness of **Heaven** and **earth** in producing effects depends on only one thing—and that the first Principle—just as all the perfection of a holy man depends on a single perfection of the mind and the solid truth of the heart. Thus he says: The reason <note>original: *ratio*</note> of **Heaven** and **earth**, or their productive and preservative power, however great, can nevertheless be understood and exhausted in a single word: Sincerity <note>original: *Veritate*, often translating the Chinese concept of 'Cheng'</note> or solidity. And this, indeed, in producing things, is not a dual thing, but something unique and simple; and yet the method and reason of it in procreating things is beyond our understanding <note>original: *inscrutabilis*</note>.

*To provide a clearer understanding of this passage, it is pleasing to attach here the very words with which the most learned Interpreter, Zhang Dunfu <term>Cham, Tum, ço</term> <note>A Neo-Confucian commentator</note>, explains this same passage; his opinion is not exactly the same as that of the Grand Secretary <term>Colao</term> <note>A title for high officials, often used by Jesuits to refer to prominent scholars like Xu Guangqi or Zhu Xi</note>, yet it does not stray from the truth. For he says: Indeed, if we do not have a clear view of the principle of **Heaven** and **earth**, how can we understand supreme truth? For the operations of **Heaven** and **earth** are inexhaustible, or in a way, infinite. However, if we examine and look into the reason of Him who is the Lord and Author of their (Heaven and Earth's) own origin, it can be most precisely and briefly understood in a single word—namely, the word <term>Chí Chîm</term> <note>Zhi Cheng, or Perfect Sincerity</note>, that is, the highest truth or supreme sincerity, as the Interpreter Zhang <term>Cham Colaus</term> most eloquently explains the phrase "in a single word."*

*Furthermore, **Heaven** and **earth** (Zhang Dunfu <term>Cham tum ço</term> continues), although they produce things, are themselves truly contained as one thing within this principle. That is, they themselves are also contained within the number and category of produced things; for this is what the text says: <term>Kî Quêi Ve Yè</term> <note>A romanization of the Chinese phrase 'Ji Wei Wu Ye', meaning 'they too are things'</note>, which is to say, they too are things. Nevertheless, this single principle of the first cause is supremely pure and simple, and by no means two, or a composite reason; and finally, it stops here. Moreover, what we have called <term>Pú úlh</term> <note>Bu Er, literally 'not two'</note>, that is, "by no means two," means nothing else than that the productive principle of all things is only one, and is spirit: because, naturally and by its own power, it procreates the universe; nor do we know where that procreating spirit itself originated. But who can guess this by searching through their own thoughts? These are the words of that classic interpreter of Confucius, called Zhang Dunfu <term>Cham tùm ço</term>, regarding the twenty-fifth chapter of the book <term>Chum-yûm</term> <note>The Zhongyong, or Doctrine of the Mean</note> on page 37, part 1, in its first editions.*

# BOOK TWO.

-> §. 4. <-

This nature <note>original: *ratio*</note> and power of Heaven and Earth, by which they are able to produce so many and such marvelous effects, is likewise broad and deep, sublime and clear, diffused far and wide, and eternal.

-> §. 5. <-

He <note>Zisi, the grandson of Confucius</note> <insert>Zisi</insert> now enumerates here part by part this magnitude and effective power of heaven and earth, which he establishes in both solidity and truth. Now, if you look at this heaven (he says), it will seem to be nothing else—if compared with its total magnitude—than this tiny portion or quantity of light and brightness; but if in your mind you ascend to its height and its splendor spreading everywhere, it will seem to be something infinite: for indeed the Sun, the Moon, the Stars, and so many celestial signs are contained within it as if suspended; likewise, all things are encompassed and covered by it. 

Now, if you look at this earth which you tread with your feet, when compared with the mass of its whole body, it will seem to be the quantity of only a single handful of soil; but if you traverse its magnitude and depth in your mind, it supports the greatest mountains, and among the five most celebrated mountains of the Chinese (which they call *Wu Yue* <note>original: *U Yo*</note>), it supports the principal mountain *Hua Shan* <note>original: *Hóa-yo*</note>; and yet it is not weighed down by the weight of such a great mass; it also embraces the rivers and seas in its bosom, and yet it is not flooded by them, as they are restrained by the land; finally, it is the firmest support of all earthly <note>original: *sublunarium*, referring to things beneath the moon</note> things. 

Now, if you look at this mountain, what—I ask—will it seem to be (if compared with the things it contains, which are hidden from the eyes) except, in a way, a tiny portion of a single piece of stone, or as much as can be held in a fist? But if you contemplate it more diligently and come to its width and magnitude, you will immediately see a thousand plants and trees being born and sprouting there, a thousand birds and wild beasts dwelling there, and also metals and precious stones lying hidden in its depths <note>original: *visceribus*</note> coming forth into the light. 

Now, if you turn your eyes to this mass of waters, what indeed—if compared with the whole Ocean as it lies open everywhere—will it seem to you except a tiny portion of a single spoonful, or some small amount? But if you descend with the eyes of the mind to their inexhaustible abyss, you will surely find that great whales, crocodiles, horned serpents, dragons, countless scaly fish, and huge tortoises <term>testudines</term> <note>often referring to the sacred or long-lived turtles of Chinese mythology</note> are produced in them; finally, that innumerable riches and wealth arise and emerge from them. 

The meaning of this passage is the same as that found above on page 7, part 2, § 1. For these four—heaven, earth, mountains, and sea—if viewed in some small part, are not large; but if one reaches their summit, they seem something immense. In the same way, the virtue of the divine man <note>the sage</note>, even though it appears so slight and subtle, grows to such greatness that it can be compared with these, and we cannot measure it.

Zisi <note>original: *çu-su*; the grandson of Confucius and author of the *Doctrine of the Mean*</note> concludes by citing the *Book of Odes* <note>original: *Odarum librum*; the *Shijing*</note>, where it is said: "The virtue of Heaven alone—oh, how profoundly it is hidden, how perpetual and excellent it is!" It is as if he were saying (Zisi adds) that King Wen was "Wen"—that is, such a great hero—specifically because his virtue was pure and sincere, and consequently never failed or was interrupted, and was therefore rightly to be compared to Heaven.

->folio 25, page 1, section 1<-

# BOOK TWO

->§. 2.<-

THEREFORE, it is commonly said that unless there is the greatest virtue and holiness <note>original: *sanctitas*; here referring to the character of a Sage</note>, the supreme law and reason <note>the *Dao* or the Way of Heaven</note> will by no means unite; that is to say, the observance of the supreme law will in no way be perfect in every detail.

->§. 3.<-

HENCE, the student of virtue first looks up to and most highly honors, and strives to preserve, his rational virtue—that is, the natural light <note>original: *lumen naturale*; a Scholastic term for innate moral reason</note> which he received from heaven. Thus, by accurately examining all things according to the rule of right reason and by training himself, he leads forth his native virtue and extends it to its full breadth and greatness, so that it is never thereafter contracted by the vice of private love <note>self-interest or partiality</note> or desire. He likewise exhausts and perceives even the most subtle and minute details, discerning each thing so clearly that he does not wander even a finger’s breadth from the truth. Furthermore, he perfects and leads the native virtue of his mind to a certain summit of sublimity and clarity; and indeed, by doing all things according to the rule of the eternal mean <note>the *Zhongyong* or Center</note>, he reflects on the old and strives to know the new. <note>This refers to the famous Confucian maxim: "He who by reanimating the Old can know the New is fit to be a teacher."</note> Finally, he establishes and constantly strengthens what was previously gained, so that he might increase and perfect what is right and just. 

(Or, as others explain: the student of virtue honors the foundation of virtues, which is the rational nature itself and the light of right reason; and proceeding from there and training himself, he strives to act according to its dictates. Using severe examination and zeal, he is always learning, never relaxing this ardor and study for progress; and so at last he rises and reaches a certain greatness of heart, such that he exhausts even the smallest and most subtle matters. He likewise reaches a certain sublime clarity and perspicacity of mind, and with this as his guide, he acts in all things according to the rule of right reason, walking securely along that royal road of the appropriate mean. Being accustomed to and greatly rejoicing in studies of this kind, he reflects on the old things he has learned, and repeatedly strives to know more and more anew; he preserves what has been gained and constantly accumulates new things, so that by repeated actions he may strengthen within himself what is right and just. Moreover, he increases for himself the perfect knowledge and practice of law, of civil rites <note>original: *rituum civilium*; the *Li* or Ritual Propriety</note>, and the virtues contained within them, *and thus that supreme law and reason from heaven cannot help but conform to the virtue of such a man and unite as one.*)

SINCE, therefore, this kind of wise man is entirely devoted to this—namely, to bringing the virtue he cultivates in himself back into harmony with the reason of heaven—it follows that in any place, time, or state, he does nothing that is not consistent with reason. And this is also the reason why the perfect man, or the wise man, when standing in a superior place and dignity, does not become proud or insolent; and when standing in an inferior place and rank, he is not stubborn or rebellious, nor does he violate the laws and rights commonly accepted, or any new ones which...

->§. 2.<-

HERE *Zisi*, digressing slightly, speaks against those who, while they are merely private citizens, either violate the established rites and laws or rashly attempt to create new ones. On this subject, he quotes *Confucius*, who says: "If a man is unrefined and of little virtue, yet insists on following only his own judgment and relying upon it as if he possessed great experience and deep understanding; or if a man of low birth attempts to claim for himself powers and privileges that are not within his legal right; or if a man born in the present age, under its specific laws, turns back toward the past and stubbornly insists on following the outdated laws of the Ancients—if anyone does these things, I tell you truly that many calamities will befall him."

->§. 3.<-

THUS, unless one is the "Son of Heaven" <note>original: *cæli filius*; the Emperor</note>, who possesses both virtue and authority, no one else (says *Zisi*) should establish rituals <note>original: *ritus*; the formal systems of social and religious conduct</note> or the duties of etiquette. No one should introduce new court customs or change, at their own whim, the furnishings of the Royal house or the protocols of the court. Nor should anyone dare, by his own judgment alone, to change anything in the realm of literature or reform the records of ancient books. This ensures that the peace of the Empire—which is built and maintained through the uniform practice of rituals, literature, and customs—is not disrupted by such innovations; for if harmony is lost, the Empire itself is put at risk.

# BOOK THE SECOND
X

...scholarly disciplines; likewise, there is one and the same system for sacrifices and clothing, according to each person's rank. Furthermore, there is an entirely uniform design for Cities, Palaces, and Houses, so that he who has seen one City may be considered to have seen all the Cities of this Empire. Indeed, the care of the Ancient Kings <note>original: *Priscorum Regum*; referring to the legendary sage-rulers of China's early dynasties</note> and their zeal for uniformity reached such a point that it pleased them for weddings to be celebrated throughout the entire Empire at roughly the same time of year; for funerals to be conducted and the proper rites for the deceased to be performed during roughly the same days. To that end, the use of a Calendar <note>original: *Kalendarii*</note> has been constant since time immemorial, and a certain distribution of tasks to be performed throughout the days of the year was established and promulgated annually across the whole Empire. 

However, the superstition of a later age has corrupted this observation of times for performing such matters in no small way, and has harmfully twisted it toward ends far different from those intended by those ancient founders of the laws. Clearly, after idolatry introduced such a variety of sects, opinions, and thus also of rituals and other things, that praiseworthy mutual conformity of the Chinese <note>original: *Sinarum*</note> amongst themselves decreased significantly. While that conformity flourished in the past, I believe this China presented the appearance not of an Empire, nor a Province, nor a City, but of a single Family under its Head of the Household <note>original: *Patre-familias*</note>. For their letters, seals, titles, even their caps <note>original: *pilei*</note>, clothes, houses, palaces, and insignia—as well as the rites used while performing sacrifices, the dishes served during banquets, and the troupes of dancers and singers—all derived their name, order, and majesty according to the greater or lesser rank and dignity of each individual. Furthermore, such great respect for this proportionate uniformity once flourished that if anyone exceeded the prescribed limits of rituals and customs, he was frequently condemned not only for arrogance but also for ambition; and if by chance he rashly usurped those things proper to the King alone, he was summoned on suspicion and charge of rebellion. Hence, that Ancient Law in Book 3 of the *Book of Offices* <note>original: *Officiorum*; likely referring to the *Liji* (Record of Rites) or *Zhouli* (Rites of Zhou)</note>, folio 29, states:

> Whoever shall have made shameful songs, or foreign garments, or practiced unusual arts, or fashioned unusual instruments, so as to thereby disturb and deceive the people, let him be put to death.

### folio 26. page 1. §. 1.

The carriages of this modern Empire under which we live, the Zhou <note>original: *Cheu*; the dynasty founded c. 1046 BCE, often cited by Confucians as the model of perfect governance</note>, (says *Zisi* <note>original: *çù su*</note>) follow the same ruts that they followed of old, since they consist of similar wheels. Moreover, the books preserve the same method and the strokes of the characters <note>original: *ductus literarum*</note> that were in use in ancient times. There is also the same system of customs and duties as there was of old. For the same custom exists between elders and juniors, between the highest and the lowest, and among friends. By what right, therefore, would any unrefined or private person dare not to follow these modern rituals and laws of greater importance in this Empire, since they flourish here and now and depart so little from that ancient integrity?

...new music; for virtue is the foundation upon which holy laws are established. Even if someone possesses the royal virtues of those ancient rulers, if they lack their royal dignity <note>original: *regia dignitate*; referring to the formal rank or office of an Emperor</note>, they would not dare to arrogantly establish rituals and music. For this task belongs solely to one who is both a Sage <note>original: *Sanctus*; in this context, the Latin translates the Chinese concept of the *Sheng* or "Holy Sage"</note> and an Emperor.

Here, observe that the Ancients intended for a certain harmony and concord between rituals and music to be signified by the two characters *Lì* and *Yo*. This refers not only to formal ceremonies, but also to the duties <note>original: *officiorum*; the social obligations and etiquette known as *Li*</note> that people are accustomed to practicing toward one another everywhere. Indeed, both of these meanings are contained within the character *Lì*. For the Ancients clearly understood that if all rituals and duties did not proceed from a sincere heart and true virtue—as if from their natural root—they would be useless, vanishing, and deceptive things, unable to flourish or persist for long. Therefore, with all their zeal and industry, they strove to ensure that these rituals and duties, imbued with the essence of virtue, would flourish more and more each day throughout the Empire. But since they also noticed that our corrupted nature somehow shrinks from virtue and is spontaneously carried toward vice and illicit pleasures, they employed music so that men might embrace virtue more eagerly. This was especially intended for the youth of the Royal house and those of a tender age not yet corrupted by vice; they began to instill the most beautiful lessons of virtue into the minds of the innocent youth, flavored by the sweetness of music.

As for the rituals, which the aforementioned music accompanied—or rather, animated—they primarily regarded that worship which was offered to Heaven, by which I mean the <term>Supreme Spirit of Heaven and Earth</term>, as the procreator and beginning of all living things. Hence, in the book *Ye Kim* <note>original: *Ye Kim*; refers to the *I Ching* or *Book of Changes*</note>, it is expressly stated that the ancient Kings established music so that they might offer it with solemn ritual to the <term>Supreme Emperor of Heaven</term> <note>original: *supremo caeli Imperatori*; a translation of the Chinese term *Shangdi*</note>. The rituals also concerned the worship with which they honored their deceased ancestors as their progenitors. Finally, they concerned the honor given to Kings and the Teachers of the entire people, as those to whom the care of correctly instructing the people has been entrusted by Heaven, and upon whom the happy administration of Kingdoms is accustomed to directly depend.

The duties, however, were chiefly those most proper to human society, regarding the <term>five orders</term> of relationship: between the King and his subjects; between parents and children; between elder and younger brothers; between husband and wife; and finally, between companions or friends. To these may also be added the distinction and order usually observed between commoners and nobles due to their unequal condition. And these rituals and duties are truly like bonds and ligaments which most aptly bind and unite the various members of the same body, both among themselves and to the head itself. From this, there immediately arises a mutual honor and benevolence among all, and thus a certain perennial peace and happiness for the entire Empire, and an altogether admirable stability, dignity, and beauty for the political body.

Confucius, therefore, used to say that these rituals and duties were the light of the Empire, an...

### BOOK TWO. ###

...virtue; and where those things were lacking, all was blind and confused.

Indeed, because they wished for the things observed and practiced in this category to be done not falsely, but from the heart—as we were saying—and from true virtue, so that internal qualities would correspond to external ones through a certain political and moral harmony; and since this very doctrine was published to the common people mostly through musical measures, hence it was called **Li Yo** <note>original: *Li Yue*; the combination of Ritual and Music</note>, which means music is to be joined to its own rituals. This implies that the sincere heart, from which the rituals and duties proceeded, was in concord with the very rituals and duties that manifested themselves outwardly.

Therefore, the entire care and study of the ancients who established music was not directed toward the private pleasure of Princes (as the ancient author **Tai Su Cum** <note>original: *Tai Shi Gong*, the title of the historian Sima Qian</note> records at length), but especially toward the proper instruction of the youth and the entire people. It was a gentle and domestic teacher, not only of other virtues, but primarily of the harmony of the subjects among themselves and with their Prince. Furthermore, so that it might obtain more authority and trust, it could be established and spread by none other than the Emperors themselves. Yet even among these, it was not permitted for just any Prince to undertake so great a task, but only for those who had joined extraordinary virtue with Imperial dignity. How much this music was valued shortly thereafter can be understood from the fact that it was later sent to the Lords of proven virtue as a kind of great gift. Moreover, the man to whom the task of composing music was entrusted—to bring it into the light for public use, and to chant it at stated times before the Prince and the Nobles of the Empire—was by no means a man of humble or even mediocre condition. This care belonged to the **Mandarins** <note>officials of the imperial Chinese bureaucracy</note> of the higher order, and indeed to men of upright life and uncommon wisdom; they commonly called him the **Ta Su Yo** <note>original: *Da Siyue*; the Grand Minister of Music</note>.

That the use of music has been perpetual in **China**, as well as being most ancient, can be understood from the fact that **Fo Hi** <note>Fu Xi, the legendary first of the Three Sovereigns of ancient China</note>, the first founder of the **Chinese** people, was also the first master of music. He was clearly another Orpheus for his nation; for he drew rude and rustic men out of their forests and mountains with his voice and strings. Allured by the sweetness of his song, he led them gradually toward humanity and the civil society of life, and he constrained their promiscuous and wandering lust with the bond of marriage. Thus, his music was called **Fû Lâï** <note>possibly referring to the *Guqin* music attributed to Fu Xi, meant to "bring" people to civilization</note>, because it had been an invitation to men, so that they might approach him of their own accord who so excellently aided them. But even the **Chinese** language itself, consisting of about 320 monosyllabic words, can it be seen as anything other than a kind of perpetual music, composed of a harmonic variety of so many accents in each individual word? Furthermore, for other leaders of the people, each had their own study and love of music. For there exist specific names for music, each of which was received from its author among the most celebrated Emperors; and every one of them, suited to the genius of the **Chinese**, is smooth and placid, a persuasive conciliator of mutual peace and concord. This is true if you except the penultimate one, which, having as its author **Vu-Vâm** <note>King Wu of Zhou</note>, the warlike founder of the third Dynasty, is entirely full of its author and breathes of Mars and arms <note>original: *Martemque et arma spirat*; a reference to the Roman god of war, signifying a military or aggressive tone</note>. But for this very reason, to a peaceful man of letters...

->§. 3.<-

Confucius used to say: I indeed always love and recall with pleasure the rituals of the ancient Imperial **Xia** <note>original: *Hiá*</note> Dynasty; nevertheless, because the descendants of the small Kingdom of **Qi** <note>original: *Kí*; the state where Xia descendants were granted land</note> (which belonged to the Empire of the **Xia** Dynasty) have degenerated from their ancestors, they are not a sufficient witness of these things; that is, they do not suffice for me to propose them to others as legitimate witnesses of the integrity of said rituals and laws so that they might gain trust: and thus, how can I alone follow them? I likewise examined and learned the rituals and laws of the Imperial **Yin** or **Shang** <note>original: *Yn* or *Xam*</note> Dynasty, and although there are even now descendants in the modest Kingdom of **Song** <note>original: *Sum*</note> (which belonged to the Empire of the **Yin** Dynasty), among whom certain monuments exist containing those laws; yet because many things are now antiquated and obsolete, and since the pious statutes of the modern Empire are not lacking and rival those of the ancients, why should I follow those rather than these? I have, finally, accurately studied the recognition of the rituals and laws of the present Imperial **Zhou** <note>original: *Cheu*</note> Dynasty; since these are accommodated to reason and the times, and everyone everywhere now uses them—even if they perhaps differ in some respects from the ancient rituals of the **Xia** and **Yin** dynasties—I indeed shall follow these rituals of the currently ruling **Zhou** Dynasty.

->Part 2. §. 1.<-

If those who obtain and administer the Empire (says **Zi Si** <note>original: *çu su*; Confucius's grandson and author of the *Doctrine of the Mean*</note>) hold those three things to be of great importance, the men and subjects of that Empire will sin little or rarely delinquent, and thus an easy and peaceful government of the Empire will follow. These three, mentioned above on folio 25, page 2, section 3, concern **civil rituals**, **court governance**, and **the examination of books and literary matters**: for that uniformity of customs and rituals throughout the whole Kingdom, and the equal standard of action in all things, contributes greatly to mutual harmony among themselves and with the head <note>the ruler</note> itself, which is the stable foundation of the Empire.

->§. 2.<-

The Kings of former times, although they properly established laws, these have nonetheless vanished, as it were, either through the length of time, the corruption of books, or a lack of wise men; or certainly, if they have not yet perished, because the modern Kings who propose them to the people to be kept lack the proper virtue of Kings themselves, it happens that they also lack sufficient testimony among the people; moreover, since this sufficient testimony is lacking to them, trust is not given; furthermore, the people do not follow those to whom trust is not given. On the other hand, holy men established in a lower or private station—though they may properly understand and cultivate the duties of courtesy <note>original: *urbanitatis officia*</note> and be endowed with virtue worthy of the Empire—if they propose those same pious institutions of the ancients to be kept by the people, yet because they lack royal dignity, it happens that they themselves do not prevail with the due authority among the people...

### §. 2. ###

...he conformed himself to water and earth; for just as these, although they are a single mass, are nonetheless manifold and diverse in their temperament and the variety of things they produce—hardening the Northern regions with harsh frost and snow, yet nourishing the Southern ones with mild heat; opening the seas to the East, yet enriching the West with woody mountains and fertilizing its valleys—so also our Master <note>Refers to Confucius.</note>, when he traveled through the Kingdoms formerly called Lu, Song, Qi, and Chu <note>Latin: *Lù, Súm, çî, çù*; these were the central states of the Zhou Dynasty where Confucius traveled.</note>, skillfully perceived the customs and rites of each Kingdom and studiously observed them all. ### §. 2. ###

Here Zisi <note>Latin: *çu-su*; the grandson of Confucius and traditional author of the *Zhongyong* or "Doctrine of the Mean."</note> continues the praises of Confucius, not without hyperbole: "He was," he says, "like heaven and earth; and like the earth indeed, insofar as there is nothing it does not contain and sustain; and like heaven, insofar as there is nothing it does not cover and encompass in its embrace. He was likewise like the four seasons proceeding in succession and equal order; he was like the Sun and Moon, which successively illuminate all things in alternating turns. For in this way, the Sage <note>Latin: *vir Sanctus*; the "Holy Man" or "Sage" in the Confucian sense (*Shengren*).</note> also encompasses and nourishes everything in the wide bosom of his piety, and binds both citizens and foreigners within the arms of his ample charity; there is nothing he does not sustain by his fortitude and prudence; and finally, by the splendor of his wisdom, he reaches all people and all things at every place and time."

### §. 3. ###

All things that are nurtured and covered by heaven and sustained by the earth are produced together, and yet they do not harm or hinder one another. The successive movements of the Stars <note>Latin: *Astrorum*; refers to the celestial bodies in general.</note>, by which the seasons of the years are established and divided—namely the Sun and the Moon, the Princes of the Stars and Masters of the seasons—proceed and revolve continuously in their orbits in succession, as we see, and create the distinction between day and night, yet they are not contrary to one another. The cause, therefore, why in such a great succession and variety of things there is nevertheless no confusion or conflict, is this: that into every single thing, a certain thin and limited virtue <term>virtue: here meaning a natural power or essence, translating the Chinese concept of 'De'</term> has been derived from heaven, as it were, according to the requirements of each thing; this force and virtue, like a stream continuously flowing, waters the universe through a perennial channel. Moreover, that such diverse things are produced together in this universe, and act so uniformly without hindering one another—this, finally, must be attributed to a certain great and unlimited virtue. This virtue, like the source and root of all things, communicates itself incessantly to everyone far and wide according to the capacity and need of each thing; and thus it effects and strengthens the production of things, so that nothing is ever lacking. It is clear, therefore, that heaven and earth are of such great magnitude for this reason.

And thus, once this origin of transformations is finished and completed in that supreme virtue, or first cause, then that minor or subordinate virtue of secondary causes will never be exhausted. And this is clearly the reason why heaven and earth become so great; it is entirely, I say, because of this government and empire which the supreme virtue exercises, etc. Thus *Cham tùm ço* just cited, *folio* 46, *page* 2, in his first editions.

And for this reason, I said above that he is made equal to heaven—or rather, that he possesses the closest possible fellowship with heaven itself.
