# THE CHINESE SCIENCES

->folio 29. page 1. section 1.<-

Only he who is supremely perfect and a Sage <note>original: *Sanctus*; referring to the *Shengren*, the highest ideal of human perfection in Confucian thought</note> in this universe is of such a kind that he can initiate and weave together the great order and logic of the world. He is the one who can establish the great foundation of this universe, and who, finally, can possess a thorough understanding of the procreations and preservations of all things derived from heaven and earth. Since a supreme Sage of this kind is so great and of such a nature, in what way is it possible for there to be any thing in the entire universe upon which he must lean, or to which he must be attached, or upon which he must first depend and be assisted by, before he can act?

->section 2.<-

The love and piety of such a Sage are supremely benevolent and beneficial, extending themselves to the great order of this world. Likewise, the abyss of his perfections is calm and profound, possessing the power to erect that great foundation of this universe. His heaven <note>referring to his heavenly nature or mind</note> lies open and extends as widely as possible, from which so many transformations of things in the world emanate in a certain perpetual and uniform series.

->page 2. section 1.<-

Zisi <note>original: *Çu-su*; the grandson of Confucius, Kong Ji, to whom the *Doctrine of the Mean* is attributed</note>, after bringing what praise he could for the supreme Sage, concludes—to signify that he himself is unequal to declaring such great perfection—that only a Sage can speak of a Sage with due dignity, since he alone understands what it is to be a Sage and how great that state is. "Truly," he says, "unless someone is indeed of a great and searching intellect—is a Sage, I say, and endowed by heaven with such wisdom and prudence that he penetrates deeply into every virtue of heaven—how could anyone else know this aforementioned Sage, or express him in words?" Therefore, only the supreme Sage can fully grasp the virtue of the supreme Sage, both by understanding it himself and then by announcing it to others. In short: no one knows the Sage properly except the Sage.

->section 2.<-

Thus far, Zisi has treated the perfection of the supreme Sage; now he returns to explaining the virtue of the perfected and truly solid man <term>solid man: translates *viri... verè ſolidi*, referring to the *Junzi*, a person of authentic moral substance</term>, which was discussed at the beginning of this book. This virtue must certainly exclude all simulation, hypocrisy, and desire for outward glory, so that he may gradually make his way toward the virtue of the Sage. To this end, Zisi cites a poem <note>original: *carmen*; a reference to the *Shijing* or Book of Odes</note> about a very beautiful matron who added grace to her most precious garments as if by covering them with another layer put on over them. The Ode says this: if someone puts on rich and variegated clothing but wears a common cloak over it, by this very act they declare that they undoubtedly hate the ostentation and external splendor of such finery. "Therefore," says Zisi, "the perfected man hides and covers his own virtue, but it increases daily like a growing light, and even against his will, it reveals and manifests itself. # BOOK TWO

...and of a good man, his painted <note>original: *fucata*; meaning artificial or disguised virtue</note> virtue might show some appearance of virtue indeed, but in truth it is nothing but an appearance. Indeed, it is the particular industry of such empty men to show off themselves and their deeds, offering them to the eyes of all to be gazed upon; but because that is not virtue, but a shadow of virtue, it clearly happens that day by day it is thinned more and more, and at last vanishes like smoke. The virtue of a perfected man <note>the *Junzi*, or superior person</note>, if you consider its first taste, will seem somewhat insipid and dull; and yet, when through mature consideration—and much more through the practice and imitation of it—you have tasted it again and again, you will find it to be such that, although you feed upon it constantly, it does not produce nausea or loathing. Again, it seems to be something relaxed, meager, and almost contemptible, and yet, if you contemplate what is within with the eyes of the mind, how much beauty and grace, how much charm you will find there! You would call it humble, rough, and shapeless at first sight; and yet, in the center of the heart, it is polished, well-composed, and marvelously ordered according to right reason. To say much in few words: it is an Attalic garment <note>a luxurious fabric woven with gold and gems, named after the wealthy Kings of Pergamum</note>, shining with gems and gold; nevertheless, it lies hidden safely beneath a cheap cloak. The more hidden it is, the more precious it becomes. 

And understand these things indeed concerning his internal and private perfection; since its light is so great, and the force of its heat so great, that it cannot be restrained from bursting forth of its own accord and devoting itself to procuring the common good of the Republic <note>original: *Reip.*, short for *Respublica*; referring here to the state or the public welfare</note>. Therefore (Zisi <note>original: *çu-su*; the grandson of Confucius</note> adds) if such a perfected man knows the proximate principle of those things which are far off—that is, if he knows how to direct others according to his own standard; likewise, if he knows the origin of behaviors and movements—that is, if he knows how to move the hearts of others from the movement of his own heart; and finally, if he knows the manifestation of subtle and secret things—that is, if he knows that those things which lie hidden within will undoubtedly at some point show themselves outwardly; then surely, with such distinguished knowledge of things, he will be able to make progress step by step and at last reach the eminent virtue of the Sage <note>original: *Sancti*; the *Shengren*, the highest moral ideal in Confucianism</note>. 

Or, as others explain: if he knows the heart to be the principle of any actions whatsoever, that good actions proceed from a good heart and evil from an evil heart; if he also knows the origin of morals and rites <note>original: *rituum*; the *Li* or ritual propriety</note> to be founded in that symmetry of the Holy Kings <note>original: *Sanctorum Regum*; the legendary Sage-Kings of Chinese antiquity</note> which is rightly measured with the law of heaven, by which all things are directed; and finally, if he knows the manifestation of subtle and hidden things—if he can, namely, know those things which lie hidden within from those which appear outwardly; then he also, in this way, will be able to reach the virtue of the Sages little by little.

...[the perfected man] naturally finds rest; and since there is nothing of which he is ashamed, it follows that he is not displeased with himself in his own heart, by which he is no longer rebuked. Certainly, is not the interior virtue of the perfected man—that state which men generally cannot reach except with the greatest difficulty—this very thing alone which others do not see? Indeed, since this examination of the inner heart is of such a nature that the perfected man can only exhaust its depths with the greatest difficulty, is it not this very thing that other men never observe? For other men value only those things perceived by the senses, being little concerned with the internal ornament of the mind and the purity of the heart.

->Part 2. Section I.<-

ANOTHER Ode <note>From the *Shijing* or Classic of Poetry, frequently quoted in the *Doctrine of the Mean*.</note> says: *Look and look around at how you conduct yourself when you live alone in your house: furthermore, do nothing for which you could blush, even though you are in the most secret corner of your home.* Therefore (adds Zisi <note>original: *çu-su*; the grandson of Confucius and traditional author of this text</note>), the perfected man does not first begin a business and only then start to pay attention to himself; he does not first utter a word and only then think about the truth of his words: but he is always and in all things vigilant. For even before any movement of the soul arises, the perfected man already observes himself attentively and solicitously, keeping watch over himself; before he utters a word, he already fully persuades himself and believes without any doubt that what he intends to say is true. He understands this to be the reward of his labor, the fruit of his vigilance and self-examination: that even in those things and pursuits which are perceived neither by the eyes nor the ears, he conducts himself circumspectly and with a reverent fear.

->Section 2.<-

Again, the Ode says: *The Priest <note>original: *Mystes*; here referring to a ritual official or minister of sacred rites</note> entering the Temple, so that by sacrificing before all the people he may move and invite the spirits, approaches with an unusual silence and a singular composure of mind and body; and although he does not command silence from the people, nevertheless at the time of sacrifice, no voice of those conversing is heard, nor does any murmur or contention arise from the surrounding crowd.* Certainly, the virtue and probity of the one performing the sacred rites is perceived by each individual; likewise, that gravity and modesty which shines forth in his face and the bearing of his whole body is an index of his interior reverence and composure. This influence is so great that, although he himself exhorts no one and threatens no one with punishment, he nevertheless keeps everyone in their duty and brings them to perfection, so that they assist in the sacred rites with a most profound silence and veneration. In the same way (says Zisi), the perfect King, although he does not lavish gifts, nevertheless the people—moved by no hope of reward, but by the single example of their King—are stirred to imitate him and are wonderfully invited to every virtue, and to obedience in all things pertaining to their duty. Again, although he does not become angry, nor deter men from evil by threatening penalties and punishments, he nevertheless brings it about that [the people...]

...the people should stand in awe of the Royal person much more than if he were threatening the necks of his subjects while armed with the rods and axes <note>original: *fascibus & securibus*; these were the Roman symbols of a magistrate's power to punish and execute, used here to represent coercive state force.</note> of office.

Zisi <margin>§. 3.</margin> <note>original: *çu-su*; the grandson of Confucius and traditional author of the *Doctrine of the Mean*.</note> rises even higher in his instruction for Kings, finally fixing his pillars here and setting a goal for the virtue he desires in Kings, such that royal virtue and happiness cannot seem to progress any further. Seeking authority from the Ancients, he cites an Ode <note>From the *Shijing* or *Classic of Poetry*.</note> which says: if the virtue of the perfect King is so subtle and remote from the grasp and senses of the common people—so deep, hidden, and solitary—that not even a trace of it seems visible to mortal eyes, and if it remains hidden in the innermost recess of the heart, revealing itself only through heroic actions and public utility without any ostentation; then surely a hundred—that is, all—the Dynasts <note>original: *Dynastæ*; the various local rulers and lords of the Chinese world.</note> and petty kings of the Chinese world, looking up at that majesty of royal virtue as something celestial and greater than human, will each strive to zealously emulate it according to their own capacity and strength. And this is also the reason (says Zisi) why the perfect King, being conscious of this truth, cultivates it so solidly—that is, he protects and preserves his internal virtue so vigilantly, reverently, and solicitously at every time and in every place. The fruit of this vigilant reverence and wise care will be that eventually the entire world, although it cannot fully grasp such a great and secret virtue, will nevertheless enjoy perpetual peace while under the administration of such a King.

->f. 31. p. 1.<-

Zisi concludes and confirms his words with the authority of the Book of Odes, where (according to the Interpreters) Shangdi <note>original: *Xam Ti*; the Supreme Emperor of Heaven, often translated by the Jesuits as the supreme deity or God.</note> himself, the supreme Emperor of heaven, is introduced speaking.

Thus the Ode says: "I (says the supreme Emperor of heaven) embrace and love the most clear and pure virtue of King Wen <note>original: *Vén-vâm*; the founder of the Zhou Dynasty, held up as the model of a perfect, virtuous ruler.</note>." And I love it precisely because it did not ring out loudly so as to be perceived and seen from the outside. (Or as others explain: because that virtue did not seek its greatness from the sound of words or some external appearance and splendor, but from its own solidity and internal cultivation). Truly, Confucius says, these external things—such as the sound of words and external appearance or figure, I mean wealth and arms, the force of eloquence, and the splendor of Imperial majesty—intended to move and convert the people, are in truth secondary things and like the branches of a tree; but that solid truth of the heart which reveals itself in words and deeds, and a soul equipped with the protections of other virtues, are the root itself and the foundation. Therefore, this internal quality is what ought to be considered first and most important here. Another Ode says: "Virtue of this kind is something subtle and light, like a hair." However (adds Zisi), a hair, although it is...

->### CHINESE KNOWLEDGE<-

...although it is indeed something thin and subtle, there is nevertheless a sensible quality that holds an order with it, and to which it is compared and corresponds. Therefore, to further illustrate the matter, another poem is cited which says: "The workings of High Heaven <note>original: *supremi cæli res*; referring to the *Shijing* or *Classic of Poetry*.</note> far elude human senses; it has neither a sound to be heard, nor a scent by which it might be perceived." From this (says Zisi <note>original: *çu sù*; the grandson of Confucius</note>), it seems to be concluded that such a thing is a supreme reality, invisible to human eyes and indivisible, thus transcending all sensible things. This final statement clarifies the matter most fully.

*In this last paragraph, there are two things that might appear somewhat obscure and difficult to explain. First, what those words <term>Mingde</term> <note>original: *Mîm te*; often translated as "Bright Virtue" or "Illustrious Virtue".</note> signify here. Second, what is signified by <term>Shangtian zhi zai</term> <note>original: *Xám Tien Chi çai*; meaning "The actions of High Heaven".</note>; for various expositions are offered for both the former and the latter. We, however, shall follow two in particular.*

*And as for the first, we follow here those who wish for the two words <term>Mingde</term> to signify either a certain excellent virtue, and a moral one at that; or the rational portion and power which is in man. For this exposition certainly agrees fortunately with what is said in the book <term>Daxue</term> <note>original: *Tá Hio*; "The Great Learning".</note> §. 1, where <term>Mingde</term> is called that rational portion implanted in man by heaven; just as in this very book <term>Zhongyong</term> <note>original: *Chum yûm*; "The Doctrine of the Mean".</note> folio 1 and elsewhere it is called <term>Tianming</term> <note>original: *Tien mîm*; "The Mandate of Heaven" or "Heavenly Decree".</note>, and in folio 25, §. 3, <term>Dexing</term> <note>original: *Te sîm*; "Virtuous Nature".</note>.*

*Regarding the second: by the two words <term>Shangtian</term> <note>High Heaven</note>, some teach that the Providence of the Supreme Deity <note>original: *supremi Numinis Providentiam*</note> is signified; others say the highest heaven, or what we call the Empyrean <note>In medieval cosmology, the highest part of heaven, the abode of God and the blessed.</note>, namely the seat and home of blessed minds.*

*Furthermore, whatever these expositions may finally be, one thing is certain: that from this last sentence of the Book <term>Zhongyong</term>, three truths seem able to be drawn and proved to the Chinese, even though they are Heathens; namely, the existence of one Supreme Deity, that the souls of mortals are immortal, and finally, that rewards correspond to each person's merits after this life. For since the Supreme Emperor of Heaven <note>original: *supremus cæli Imperator*</note> himself is introduced uttering words, and since elsewhere the soul of the pious King Wen <note>original: *Ven-vam*; the founder of the Zhou Dynasty.</note> is said to assist at the left and right hand of the Supreme Deity, it is clear that they believed both in God and that the soul by no means perishes with the body. Again, when it is said that the same Deity embraces and loves the virtue of the said King, it undoubtedly signifies that rewards correspond to his virtue. What the ancient Chinese thought concerning the immortality of souls remains to be briefly examined here; for we have already explained to some extent the existence and Providence of the Supreme Deity in various places of this work, and we reserve it for a separate and more copious treatise.*

I do not deny that the ancient Chinese, through the common and hereditary fault of the human race, labored primarily for this present life: so that they might live here well and happily, and keep their Empire peaceful, flourishing, and unconquered...

...power: as for what fate or life might await them in time to come, they entrusted it to heavenly Providence <note>original: *cælesti Providentiæ*</note> and the Divine Power. (In their number, however, are by no means included those whose distinguished virtue, deeds, and their own writings show them to have been despisers of mortal life and human affairs, and instead devoted to the study of immortal life.) Yet, even those common men did not lack this appetite for a long-lasting and eternal life, which we mortals feel has been implanted in us by the Author of nature—and certainly not implanted idly or in vain. How vehement this appetite was in some of them can be seen in those "precious potions" or "Ambrosias of immortal life" <note>This likely refers to the "Elixirs of Life" sought by various Chinese Emperors through Daoist alchemy.</note> which even Emperors took, deluded by the hope of drinking in immortality, following the fables of impostors several centuries after Christ.

Therefore, regarding a matter that is so natural to man, it is impossible that there should not exist some traces in their ancient books and monuments. Since these traces do exist—as they truly do—and shine forth here and there like wavering and thin little sparks, why, I ask, should we not prefer to gradually revive and kindle them with a more kindly interpretation <note>original: *interpretatione benigniore*</note>, as if with a gentle breath? By doing so, we might lead those desires for a long life (or rather, for a prolonged mortality) toward the hope of true immortality and life, rather than smothering and extinguishing them with the silence of a more severe and sinister interpretation. For what fruit, after all, will arise from such silence and severity? Surely none other than that we would seem to admit tacitly that the entire ancient age of this nation is contrary to our doctrine; and thus the ruinous error of Atheists and Impious men would be most powerfully strengthened. When they see us hesitate, they will soon go further and attack us on that very ground where, if we had the courage, they could have been successfully fought by us. And so they will finally say that they prefer to persevere in that opinion in which we ourselves admit their ancestors remained for four thousand years; they would rather follow so many men most famous for wisdom, virtue, and power, than give credit to a few foreigners teaching the opposite.

Far be it, therefore, from the Preachers of the Gospel <note>original: *Evangelii Præconibus*</note> to hold this opinion: that they should think no help or light is to be sought from the authority of the Ancient Chinese <note>original: *Prifcorum Sinarum*</note> for declaring Christian truth. Indeed, such an opinion (if it is permissible to say) seems to proceed either from a certain empty fear and superstition, or certainly from a notable sluggishness or ignorance. For even if there were those among the ancients (for I am not dealing with the moderns here) who openly opposed us, believing that no reward is paid for right deeds nor punishment for crimes, and that all things end with the life of man—well, there were some among the European philosophers in that same camp. Yet the wise Cato, in the works of Cicero, calls such men "minute" <note>original: *minutos*; meaning petty or narrow-minded thinkers.</note>; and in the same author, Lelius says:

> I do not agree with those, he says, who have recently begun to argue that souls perish along with their bodies, and that all things...

...[that the soul is] destroyed by death; the authority of the ancients or of our Ancestors <note>original: *Majorum*</note>, etc., weighs more with me.) If, I say, there were those among the Ancients who openly opposed us, even if there were others who seemed to favor us, it would perhaps be safer then not to touch upon such suspect authorities. But now, since we encounter no adversary; since nowhere does even a shadow of that impiety <note>The "impiety" here refers to the denial of the soul's immortality or the existence of Divine Providence.</note> appear; but on the contrary, many things can be brought forward which—even if they do not provide absolute proof—nevertheless make it very probable that the Ancients thought well and wisely concerning the Providence of the Deity <note>original: *Providentiâ Numinis*</note> and the immortality of Souls; who, finally, of sound mind would prefer to have adversaries for himself rather than friends, and allies, and patrons? And this includes not only the Ancients, but also the Chinese of this age, who are (as we taught above) so studious and observant of their Ancestors. Who would prefer to follow the few atheists and idolaters of a later age, and suck poison from those ancient flowers, rather than sweet and health-giving honey?

That no small amount [of this honey] is contained in them has been taught not only by other writers, but especially by the Priests of the **Society of Jesus**: **Ricci**, **Pantoja**, **Vagnoni**, **Aleni**, **Monteiro**, **Buglio**, **Martini**, and others most famous in European and Chinese letters. Thus **Lactantius** says in *On False Religion against the Heathens* <note>original: *de falsa Religione contra gentes*</note>, chapter 5: "Let us truly omit the testimonies of the Prophets, lest the proof seem less suitable coming from those who are not believed at all; let us come to the *Authors*, and cite those very witnesses to prove the truth whom they are accustomed to use against us: *I mean the Poets and Philosophers*." 

Although in this, our men again imitate those Fathers: for whenever they dispute concerning the immortality of Souls and similar arguments, they seek the far greater strength from our own Christian Philosophy, and they sprinkle such a great abundance of heavenly ambrosia upon that Chinese honey, as I called it, that although the Chinese eagerly seek it as if it were their own, in reality it belongs entirely to the Europeans, or rather, to Christ.

Finally, that we may more zealously dig out this truth from the ancient monuments of the nation, this reason also moves us: that if indeed it is proved that this was clear to their Ancestors, their descendants will immediately concede that the other truth (which we supported above with so many arguments) was also clear—concerning a certain Supreme Deity <note>original: *supremo quodam Numine*</note> who created and governs all things. For there has been no nation so rustic and barbaric that it did not acknowledge an immortal God, and yet acknowledged the immortality of its own soul.

# BOOK TWO #

...its own power. Therefore, as we make use of this method, we ask first of all: do any of the ancient and classical authors anywhere claim that the souls of mortals perish, and that matters are governed by chance or luck rather than by any plan of providence? Truly, they must admit that there is no one who is so insane or impious as to say this openly.

From here, we move to positive authorities and arguments. First, we place before their eyes what **Confucius** himself thought about immortality. The *Classics* <note>original: *libri Classici*; referring to the foundational canon of Chinese literature</note> provide us with many examples—some of which he wrote himself, and others he collected and organized. I call them "Classics" because they alone carry weight among the Chinese, as they do with us. As for the things found in the books called *Kia Yu* <note>original: *Kia Yu*; the *Kongzi Jiayu* or "Family Sayings of Confucius"</note>, or the domestic discourses of **Confucius**, since they were reportedly published nearly seven hundred years after the Philosopher lived, they carry only as much weight as one chooses to give them. This is especially true since it is believable that they contain many things inserted by wicked men or fabricated by the foolishly over-eager followers of the Philosopher himself. It is certain that these books are by no means numbered among the *Classics* or those prescribed for learned men <note>The "literati" or scholar-official class</note>. Nevertheless, lest I seem to have hidden or avoided anything here, I will bring forward one passage which alone might seem less favorable to our opinion. In it, a disciple of **Confucius**, commonly called **Zi Gong** <note>original: *çì cùm*; one of Confucius's most prominent students</note>, is introduced asking his Master whether the dead retain knowledge of things. The Philosopher—who was accustomed to tailoring his answers to the temperament, capacity, time, and place of each person—replied in such a way that he did not remove the doubt of the seeker:

> "If," he said, "I say that the dead retain knowledge of things, I fear that those sons whose devotion <note>original: *pietas*; referring to the Confucian concept of Filial Piety</note> toward their parents is greatest would wish to join them, and so would kill themselves. If, on the contrary, I assert that there is no knowledge, I fear that filial devotion might wither, and there might be those who would even cast away their parents without burial. Therefore, my son, stop seeking so curiously into the condition of those who have finished their lives. There are other more necessary things I wish you to know; those things, indeed, you will learn later."

Thus spoke the Philosopher. Note that in this passage, the existence of Souls is not being doubted; rather, the disciple asks whether the Souls of the deceased (which he assumes to exist) retain knowledge of past events.

Setting aside these matters of less certain authority, let us bring forward only those whose authority is undisputed among them, and which seem more suited to proving immortality to the Chinese. Many such things are supplied to us by the Five Books <note>The *Wujing* or Five Classics, the most authoritative texts in the Confucian tradition</note> and those which we explain here, which are not only Classics, but of the highest rank.

To proceed more orderly, let us begin with the definition of death as they pass it down in their books. In this way, it will be easier to judge the remaining things that follow and to understand what the age of the Ancients thought. For as to what most Chinese of our own age, from im...

<meta>This page continues the argument for the immortality of the soul in ancient Chinese thought, moving from Confucius's personal views to broader linguistic and historical evidence found in the Classics and royal decrees.</meta>

-> ### CHINESE KNOWLEDGE ### <-

As for what the unlearned masses, at least, believe regarding death, there can be no doubt or controversy, since it is well established that most give credit to Pythagorean fables concerning the transmigration of souls <note>original: *metempsychosi*; the author is likely comparing Buddhist beliefs in reincarnation to the Greek ideas of Pythagoras to make them more familiar to European readers</note>. However, even though they deny that souls perish, they rely on the most vain and false principles; it would be plainly absurd to grant them any authority or to try to support the truth using their lies.

In ancient times, therefore, to teach that human nature consists of two parts—one mortal and the other immortal—they used two specific terms: one signifying a descent or fall, and the other an ascent. In this way, they describe the death of the Emperor **Yao** in the *Shujing* <note>original: *Xu kim*; The Classic of History, one of the oldest foundational texts of Chinese literature</note>, perhaps the most ancient of all books. These words carry the same meaning even when the terms vary, as when they describe the "ascents" and "descents" of the Kings **Shun** and **Wen**, and other Princes. By this, I mean they signify their passing, or the separation of the soul from the body. Certainly the interpreters—even the non-Christian ones, among whom our own **Grand Secretary** <note>original: *Colaus*; referring to Xu Guangqi, a high-ranking official and prominent convert known as "Colao" (Grand Secretary) Paul</note> supports us here—agree with a wonderful consensus of opinion. They explain those terms by saying that *that which rises on high is the spirit, while that which is carried downward and falls is the body*. Without a doubt, they would not have used these specific words, nor so many of them, if they had intended to signify merely the dissolution of the physical body and the end of life.

From this source comes that never-sufficiently praised saying and speech of King **Tang** <note>original: *Tà Regis*; Tang of Shang, the legendary founder of the Shang Dynasty</note>, which he used to console his followers when faced with a sudden and present danger to his life:

> *This life of ours, my Lords, is like a deposit; death, therefore, will be the return of that deposit.* <note>original: *sĕm kì yĕ, sù quĕi yĕ*. In this context, *ki* (ji) refers to a lodging or a temporary stay, and *quei* (gui) means to return home.</note>

Indeed, since these two words—the one signifying a temporary lodging and the other a return—are used together, this wise man seems to have wanted to embrace, with his own characteristic brevity, that famous sentiment of **Cicero** <note>original: *Tullianum*; referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero</note>. Cicero said that nature has given us a place to stay as guests, not a permanent home; therefore, we ought to be prepared to depart from this life as if from an inn, rather than from a house. If antiquity can lend any weight or authority to a matter, as it surely can, then a Chinese King uttered a sentiment so Christian in spirit before the time of **Abraham** himself, let alone before Cicero or the founding of Rome. 

This beautiful way of speaking passed into common usage and, along with the memory of such a great Prince, flourishes even today. Nothing is more familiar to the Chinese than to say, when someone has departed from the living, that he has "now departed from the age" <note>original: *kiú xí*</note>, or "bidden farewell to the age" <note>original: *çú xí*</note>, or "given thanks to the age" <note>original: *sié xí*</note>, and so on. This is expressed exactly in the manner of someone who has given thanks to the host with whom he lodged, said his farewells, and returned to his own fatherland. That the Chinese generally speak this way from the true conviction of their hearts—or certainly did so in the past—is proven by the custom of the ancients, mentioned more than once in the *Books of Rites* <note>original: *Officiorum libris*; likely the *Liji* or Book of Rites</note>. Whenever one of them died, they were accustomed to climb to the higher parts of the house and there, with eyes cast up to heaven and with great mourning for the deceased—

-> ### BOOK TWO ### <-

...to cry out the name <note>The text begins mid-sentence; the original Latin word was likely *interictum* or *interitum*, referring to the announcement of death</note>, mournfully repeating the call six times. Furthermore, that word, as the interpreters here affirm, signifies a return to the body, or to come back to life. **Mencius** <note>A famous follower of Confucius, known for his teachings on human goodness</note> perhaps alluded to this rite when, using the same word, he said: "If the Holy Kings were to come back to life, they would teach nothing other than what I myself teach." Certainly, in the passing of Kings as well, this rite I mentioned was employed; and although it now seems outdated, it nonetheless clearly declares what that age felt regarding immortality. This is all the more remarkable when compared to the present age of later generations, just as the ancient era excelled this one in the innocence of life and morals, as well as in a certain candor and simplicity. I believe that from the ancients also flowed that custom which is in use here in various provinces, whereby sons at the death of their parents—clothed in mourning attire and with tears and wailing—run through the neighboring places, just as if they were seeking the fleeing soul and calling it back to its former seat and lifeless body.

But if the ancients believed (setting aside our own age for a moment) that the souls of men perish, how superfluous and foolish were all these things! For can that which has perished move itself, let alone ascend? Can a deposit that is known to have perished be restored? As for a guest, if he has already expired in his inn, would not someone be either very ignorant or a trifler to say he has departed, or that he has sought his fatherland and home? And would anyone of sound mind do those things we have recounted if he judged that after death nothing exists that lives or understands?

Yet it does not escape me what might be answered here by the atheists of this time <note>The author is likely referring to the Neo-Confucian scholars of the Song Dynasty, whose more naturalistic or materialistic interpretations of the Classics the Jesuits often criticized</note>—who, although they differ greatly from the ancients, still wish to appear to agree with them most of all. They claim, of course, that many things are said for the sake of ornament and figuratively; that the mentioned rite is fleeting and useless; and that the ancients had no other purpose here than to testify to their grief and longing for the one who had perished. They say it should not seem surprising that they looked up to heaven and in a way called back the beloved <term>Manes</term> <note>original: *Manes*; a Roman term for the spirits of the dead, used here to represent the Chinese *shen* or ancestral spirits</note> from there. They argue this because they think—indeed, they even explicitly teach both here and elsewhere—that that spirit which is said to ascend here is something airy <note>original: *aërium quid*</note>, or rather nothing but mere air. They argue that he says nothing absurd or alien who says that air is carried on high. Moreover, they claim that even **Confucius** himself does not seem alien to this opinion; when asked to define the meanings of the two words <term>quei xin</term> <note>original: *quei xin* (鬼神, guǐshén); traditionally spirits, ghosts, or gods</note>, he replied that it was something airy, as is reported in the *Books of Rites* <note>original: *Officiorum libris*; likely the *Liji* or Book of Rites</note>. He was, they say, imbued with the same errors held by our own ancient poets when they sang that our soul was a "particle of air" <note>original: *particulam auræ*</note>; errors also held by **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman scholar who proposed a physicalist view of the soul</note> when he said the soul was air conceived in the mouth, warmed in the lungs, heated in the heart, and diffused through the body. And so, this way of speaking is very familiar to the Chinese—

-> ### CHINESE KNOWLEDGE ### <-

...the current state of affairs when speaking of a dying person; they commonly say that the *çivè kí* <note>original: "çivè kí" refers to *qì jué* (气绝), meaning the breath or life-force is cut off</note>, or the "cut off spirit," or the *tuón kí* <note>original: "tuón kí" refers to *duàn qì* (断气), meaning to stop breathing or expire</note>, the interrupted **spirit**—or more accurately, the **respiration**—of the man has occurred.

Perhaps those who seek to refute our position argue in this way, though it is by no means difficult to disprove them. For in interpreting the ancient rites mentioned above as "empty" or "meaningless," they do so without the authority or example of any true scholar; indeed, none of the Interpreters I have been able to consult thus far teach that these rituals were devoid of meaning. Furthermore, when they claim that the human soul is defined—or more accurately described—merely as the air we breathe, they prove nothing against the Ancients or **Confucius**. I ask you: what word or metaphor could a man, who was unaware of our more refined European logic and metaphysics, use to explain a thing he taught was exceedingly subtle and beyond the reach of the senses themselves? Could he use any other than one borrowed from the most subtle of all earthly things? Indeed, we ourselves—we Europeans, I say—when we wish to signify the rational soul with the most appropriate word possible, what word do we finally use? Is it not **Spirit**? And from where is the etymology of this word derived? From *spirando* <note>Latin: "breathing"</note>. Yet, even brute animals breathe, and the winds blow; both the beasts and the winds have their own "spirit." Likewise, among our own Physicians (and indeed among the Chinese as well), there is frequent mention of the "vital spirits." You may say this is true, but when we speak of man, the use of the word is metaphorical; and thus, the use of "air" here is also metaphorical. Shall I go deeper? It is well known that the word *animus* <note>Latin: "soul" or "mind"</note> takes its origin from the Greek word *anemos* <note>original: "ἄνεμος," meaning wind or breeze</note>. If this word signifies a "blast" or "wind" to the Greeks, would you then correctly conclude that the rational soul, in the opinion of the Latins, is something windy or full of air? Not at all, you would say; for the Latins declare what they mean when they call the soul "rational." Very well then! Do the Chinese not also declare what they themselves mean? What is more frequently on the lips, not only of the Scholars but even the common people, than these phrases: *a wise, noble, prudent, and intelligent spirit or soul, etc.*? Surely no one in possession of their reason would say such things except of a soul endowed with reason.

Now, when **Confucius** himself calls that spirit (which you claim is mere air) **animate, intelligent, and spiritual** even after it has been separated from the body, does he say nothing? When he teaches that it is something most subtle and exceedingly **pure**, and when he calls it **wise**, does he not declare what he feels? He relates that the spirit, after it has departed the body, manifests itself, diffuses its own scent, and is affected by a certain sadness and compassion for itself because it has been deprived of the long association and companionship of the body. When he says these and other things, is he saying nothing? Has he not yet declared his meaning? Furthermore, how noble and how fitting to our purpose is that pronouncement of **Mencius** <note>A primary developer of Confucianism (372–289 BCE), often called the "Second Sage"</note>! He says that there is something "most subtle" by which man differs from the brute animals. He calls it "most subtle" because he undoubtedly understood it to be entirely free from matter.

# BOOK TWO

But let us proceed. Let us suppose that they speculated somewhat crudely, and conceived of spiritual substance in a material way (just as so many Philosophers in Europe once did regarding the nature of Angels): shall we therefore immediately say they wandered completely from the truth <note>original: "aberrâvisse toto cœlo," an idiom meaning to be diametrically opposed or utterly mistaken</note>, and denied to humans that <term>substantial form</term> <note>the philosophical "blueprint" or essence that makes a thing what it is</note> of the soul which is attributed to living beings? If we grant license to both Painters and Poets when they depict those heavenly minds for us—even if they attribute to them things quite alien to their nature—shall we then immediately condemn the Chinese if, perhaps, beyond alien concepts (which we ourselves form constantly, even against our will), they occasionally use alien words and phrases?

However, because we who live among the Pagans <note>Latin: "Ethnicos"</note> must take the greatest care lest we seem to those who are unrefined—or even perverse and already lost—to be held by the same errors as they are, the members of the **Society of Jesus**, whenever the rational soul had to be discussed, very prudently abstained from the word ***Ki*** <note>original: "Ki" (Qi), often translated as "breath," "air," or "vital energy"</note>. This was partly because the Chinese use it for almost nothing else than the common air we breathe, and primarily because their ancient monuments, and even the books of **Confucius** himself, supply many quite appropriate terms by which the nobler part of man, or the immortal mind, is signified. Indeed, they clearly affirm that man himself is the most noble of all living things. They then distinguish the mind as ***Tá ti*** <note>original: "Tá ti" (dà tǐ), the "greater body" or "greater part"</note>, or the *greater and nobler substance*, from the ***Siaò-ti*** <note>original: "Siaò-ti" (xiǎo tǐ), the "lesser body" or "lesser part"</note>, which signifies the *lesser substance*. They also call it the *clear mandate of heaven* and the *clear or intelligent virtue*; additionally, they call it the natural virtue and the intellectual power—which is itself subtle, infused from heaven, and illuminated by the light of reason. What more? They sometimes attribute the same words to the rational soul that they use to signify their spirits, or ***Xin*** <note>original: "Xin" (shen), meaning spirit, god, or divine power</note>, which the book ***Ye-kim*** <note>original: "Ye-kim" (Yi Jing), the *Book of Changes*</note> elsewhere calls wandering souls. Nevertheless, since they ascribe to spirits a certain extraordinary power (as we recounted above) and many things that exceed human strength, the Jesuits chose to use the word ***Xin*** in such a way that it was almost never attributed to anything other than Angelic natures. To signify the human mind, however, they mostly employed the two terms ***Lîm sim*** or ***Lim hoen*** <note>original: "Lîm sim" (líng xīn) and "Lim hoen" (líng hún)</note>. This was done aptly; for while the word ***Hoen*** signifies the Soul, when ***Lim*** <note>original: "Lim" (líng), implying spiritual or supernatural efficacy</note> is added, it is immediately narrowed to the rational soul. Indeed, by ***Lim*** they signify the intellectual and thus spiritual power. Metaphorically, however, a certain principal beauty or efficacy even in an inanimate thing is declared by the same word ***Lim*** (or even ***Xin***), as I mentioned above. But if you add or prefix the word ***Kio*** <note>original: "Kio" (jué), meaning sensation or perception</note>, which means "sensitive," to the word ***Hoen***, you make its meaning broader; and broadest of all, if you join it with the word ***Sem*** <note>original: "Sem" (shēng), meaning life or growth</note>, meaning "vegetative." The logic for the word ***sim*** <note>original: "sim" (xìng), meaning nature or essence</note>, which signifies nature, is the same as for the word ***Hoen***.

Since they teach, therefore (to return to our earlier reasoning...

# CHINESE KNOWLEDGE

(...let us return) to the idea that the rational nature of man, or the Soul, is infused into us from heaven; or, to use the words of **Tullius** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman and philosopher</note> here, that "the heavenly soul was pressed down from its highest home and, as it were, submerged into the earth," a place contrary to divine nature and eternity. Again, since they <note>the Chinese</note> teach that the Soul came from heaven in this way—adorned with its gifts and fortified by the protection of prudence, piety, and other virtues, coming as if surrounded by such a great retinue—and since, as ***Mencius*** <note>An influential follower of Confucius, c. 372–289 BCE</note> clearly proves and teaches, and as boys everywhere learn along with the very elements of their letters, it was created with a certain innate propensity toward what is right and virtuous. Indeed, whoever are **Sages** <note>original: "Sancti," referring to the Chinese *Sheng*, the ideal moral exemplars</note> (this is an ancient opinion of the Chinese people), they are all born Sages by a certain special benefit of heaven. When, I say, the Ancients not only felt this way but even taught it, there is certainly no reason to wonder if they thought that Souls, having proceeded from heaven, return to heaven; since that most ancient **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure to whom ancient mystical and philosophical works were attributed</note> used to say: "the souls of the pious pass from death into the nature of the Gods"—from which those Philosophers whom **Cicero** writes never doubted that "we have souls plucked from the universal divine mind" might not perhaps have disagreed. Certainly many centuries later, **Africanus** <note>Scipio Africanus the Younger, as depicted in Cicero's "Dream of Scipio"</note> following these men, after he had related (in the same **Cicero**) that the Soul was given to us from the eternal fires of the heavens which we call stars and constellations—which he also says are animated by divine minds—soon added that those who cultivate justice and piety go to heaven and into the assembly of those who have already lived, and who, released from the body, inhabit a place conspicuous for its most brilliant radiance.

Therefore, in this sense, that famous passage of the book ***Ye Kim*** <note>The *I Ching* or *Book of Changes*, a foundational Chinese divination text</note> can be explained: for after it was shown how all things are drawn toward the place and end suitable to their nature, spontaneously and with a certain impulse, this is also added: that portion of man which is nobler always looks toward heaven and is carried into it as its center; but that which is more ignoble <note>The text here contrasts the *Hun* (spiritual/heavenly soul) and the *Po* (earthly/physical soul)</note> looks with downward eyes at the earth, its companion. You would say that the **Poet** <note>Likely referring to Ovid and his description of man’s upright posture in the *Metamorphoses*</note>, when he sang something very similar many centuries later, had learned it from the Chinese; and that the **Roman Orator** <note>Cicero</note> had thoroughly read their books when he said: "The Soul, stirred and exercised by the best cares and studies, flies more swiftly to the Seat of the blessed and to its own home; and it will do so even more quickly if, even then while it is enclosed in the body, it stands out beyond it, and contemplating those things which are outside, abstracts itself as much as possible from the body."

### BOOK THE SECOND.

->D 4<-
<meta>catchword: Nor</meta>

Confucius himself is the author, in the book of the first class called *Chun-çieu* <note>original: "Chun-çieu"; the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, one of the core Five Classics of Chinese literature</note>, of the account that the Soul of a certain *Chim pe* <note>Likely the Earl of Zheng (Zheng Bo)</note>, who during his life had served as a prefect, was seen after his death. Here, therefore, we already have a testimony that is most weighty among the Chinese: that the Soul does not perish along with the body itself. For who would say that a man of such proven faith and such singular prudence either fabricated what he understood to be false, or rashly believed what was legendary? Europeans, indeed, will feel about him according to their own hearts; but no Chinese person could be persuaded otherwise. However, I would not wish to place the primary weight of this argument on the testimony of a single man. The most abundant testimonies from the *Xu-Kim* <note>original: "Xu-Kim"; the *Shujing* or *Classic of History*, a compilation of ancient rhetorical addresses and historical records</note>, the most classical of books, call to me.

*Puon-kem* <note>Pan Geng, a traditional ruler of the Shang dynasty (c. 13th century BCE)</note> of the *Xam* <note>The Shang Dynasty</note> family—a family prolific among those who held power—was himself the seventeenth Emperor, who began to rule in the year 1401 before Christ. When he was forced by great floods to transfer his Court elsewhere and return it to the first location which the founder of his family, called *Chim-tam* <note>Tang the Completer, the first king of the Shang</note>, had once chosen for himself in the Province of Honan <note>Henan</note> (the name of the place was then *Po*), and when he saw that the people recoiled from changing their seats again (for during the rule of this family, they had already migrated elsewhere four times), and that they even openly clamored against and resisted his commands; he gave a public written account of his counsel. He placed before the eyes of all both the utility and the necessity of the matter at hand. Among other things he brings forward, there is one point in which he exerts a particular force: a force which would have been non-existent if the common sense and faith of the Nobles and the people had not supported the immortality of souls.

> "If I," he says, "by staying here longer, destroy both myself and you, in what way shall I finally escape the most just rages and threats of my Ancestor *Tam* <note>King Tang</note>, whose soul now dwells in heaven, and who will undoubtedly hold me alone guilty for all the calamities that befall us, reproaching me for my lack of mercy because, when I could have saved you, I allowed you to perish so cruelly?" Nor does he add much later that his Grandfather and Father were the ones who prompted the said *Tam* to take vengeance on those Nobles who greedily plotted against the resources of the wealthier citizens, etc. Writing on this passage, the Interpreter called *Vam-xi* <note>Possibly a reference to the commentator Wang Shi or similar</note> says: *Ever since the Imperial families of Chim-tam and Cheu <note>The Shang and Zhou dynasties</note>, ascending to earlier times or indeed from every age, the Chinese have never failed to serve the deceased just as they served the living.*

I ask now of the Atheists <note>The author is addressing contemporary European debates where some argued the ancient Chinese were materialists or "atheists"</note> and those who contend that the Ancient Chinese were atheists: if indeed our Soul is something airy, which, once released from the body, is soon dissipated and vanishes into the empty breezes; where, and in what manner, did the Soul of King *Tam* persist for so long, and so whole and inviolate, for three hundred years and more? For that many years intervened between his death and the reign of his great-great-grandson.

Nor is the other testimony from the same family any less illustrious—

King Zhou <note>original: "Cheu Tyrannus"; the last ruler of the Shang dynasty, traditionally depicted as a cruel and decadent tyrant</note> was ruling, a man who was equally cruel toward his own people and impious toward Heaven <note>original: "cœlum"; here referring to the divine order or Tian</note>. All honest men groaned because they saw the State being increasingly undermined, and the Empire itself now clearly threatened with ruin. One man did not endure this any longer; he was equal in dignity to many of the nobles, but surpassed them all in loyalty, prudence, and zeal for the public good (his name was Zu Yi <note>original: "çu-y"; a high-ranking official during the reign of King Zhou of Shang</note>). He approached the King fearlessly, though not unaware of the great danger to his own life; for he knew that the King relied on a certain foolish confidence in the favor of his ancestors <note>original: "Proavorum"</note> and even (if you please) of Heaven itself. Therefore, he said: "O Emperor, Heaven clearly now seems to have taken the Empire away from this family of ours; for so the men who are foremost in virtue and wisdom judge; and the divinations <note>original: "sortes"</note> themselves, which we consulted by applying the turtle shell <note>original: "admotâ testudine"; referring to plastromancy, where cracks in heated shells were read as divine omens</note>, are all grim and ill-omened, and foretell this not obscurely. Yet you should not think that the founders and princes of this family—your ancestors—are without feeling, nor that they are untouched by the misfortunes of their children and grandchildren, and by the fall of your most noble house, and indeed their own. But indeed, because you show yourself so unlike them in life and character, indulging in jokes and lust, you have effectively cut yourself off from Heaven, and have brought it about that the Souls <note>original: "Animi"</note> of your ancestors who dwell in those blessed seats—although they wish it most greatly—cannot help you unless you enter upon a different way of life, and in this way change the sentence of Heaven already passed against you." Thus he spoke.

He certainly would not have started a discourse of this kind, especially in such a place and time, if he himself had either doubted the immortality of Souls, or if he had thought the Tyrant, however impious, doubted it. Much less can it be said that he was willing to face the ultimate danger to his life merely to persuade another of something he did not feel himself, through a superficial appearance and political pretense. Certainly that foolish Tyrant, impatient of the truth, ordered his far-most faithful client—who was then advising him of the most useful things—to be snatched away immediately for capital punishment; and the reward for such rare loyalty was death.

Furthermore (which I would like the Reader to observe carefully here), the Ancients clearly seem to have believed that the minds of pious men from Heaven thus help their own, or even inflict punishments on sinners, so that they achieve this not so much through themselves, as by requesting from Heaven itself, or from the Lord of the Heavens and Supreme Judge <note>original: "Domino cœlorum ac supremo Judice"</note>, at one time rewards and at another time punishments for their descendants. Thus they were accustomed to act as patrons whenever some particular favor was hoped for from the Celestial Court <note>original: "cœlesti Aula"</note>. This fact also wonderfully confirms what we asserted above: that the Supreme Deity <note>original: "supremum Numen"</note> was known and worshiped by the Ancients, whom they believed the minds of their Ancestors—already received into heaven—assisted as their Lord, King, and Judge. He was the Founder of the third Imperial Family, called the **Zhou** <note>original: "Cheu"; the Zhou Dynasty, traditionally dated 1046–256 BC</note>, and he began to reign in the year 1122 before Christ. His brother, who was also the first minister of the Empire, commonly named **Zhou Gong** <note>original: "Cheu-cum"; the Duke of Zhou, a hero of Confucian virtue</note>, was here deeply distressed and feared that the newly won Empire might collapse if his brother were snatched from the living while the reign had scarcely begun, let alone been stabilized. Having humbly offered a petition, he willingly devoted his own life to the **Spirits** <note>original: "Manibus"; the deified souls of ancestors</note> of his Father, Grandfather, and Great-grandfather, who assist the Supreme Emperor of the Heavens, so that some relief and a slightly longer life might be granted to his ailing brother. His prayer was granted, and through such rare brotherly grace, it cost him nothing. The King then lived for five years and established the foundations of the August House; and finally, as he was dying, he commended his young son—the heir to such a great empire, then thirteen years old—to his brother. The Duke acted with the greatest loyalty as the tutor of his nephew, and by instructing him in the finest disciplines, he shaped him toward truly Royal virtues. The supreme power and the Empire were almost entirely in the hands of this one uncle until the small boy should grow up. But from this, as is customary, envy gradually arose. This was not hidden from the Prince <note>the Duke of Zhou</note>, who, fearing that the envy might be more sharply inflamed and that the **State** <note>original: "Respublica"; the public affairs of the Empire</note> might suffer some harm on his account, voluntarily yielded to the season of envy and abdicated his vicarious rule and tutelage. He had two men on his council who were outstanding in virtue and wisdom; commending the ward to them and in a way giving an account of his deed, he said, "I must depart; for if I do not turn this storm away from myself, or rather from the State itself, what shall I say one day after death to my **Ancestors** <note>original: "Majoribus"</note>? They will surely demand an account from me—not to mention deserved punishment—because, by looking to private advantage rather than public peace, I brought the entire Empire into danger." Having said this, he set out for the Kingdom of **Shandong** <note>original: "Xan tum"</note> as a spontaneous exile, and lived there as a private citizen.

But indeed, anyone who loves to remain hidden cannot remain hidden for long. For after two years had passed, as if Heaven itself were taking up the cause of such great virtue to be defended against envious rivals, a horrendous storm began to rage: thunder bellowed in the sky, and by the force of raging winds, ancient trees were torn up by the roots; and now no small destruction and devastation was brought upon the fields and cities. Seized by this crisis of affairs, the young Emperor ordered the Archive called the **Golden Casket** <note>original: "Kin tem"; referring to the "Jin Teng" or "Metal-Bound Coffer," a famous chapter of the Classic of History</note> to be opened, so he might consult the books according to custom. While he was leafing through them himself, he happened upon the petition mentioned above. He read it, was struck with amazement, and dissolving into tears and groans, he cried out that he was ungrateful, that the fatherland was ungrateful, and that they certainly deserved such great punishments from an angry Heaven. Without delay, he ordered his Uncle to be recalled with the most kind words. He went out to meet him as he returned; his former honors were restored; and lest these things be thought to have happened by chance, together with the return of **Zhou Gong** himself, serenity was soon restored to the sky and tranquility to the lands.

Many things of this same kind could be woven in here from the **Annals** <note>original: "Annalibus"; the historical records of China</note> and other sources...

...drawn from books. But indeed, I fear lest prolixity, which is always unpleasant, should also be burdensome and offensive in this our argument and discussion. Let us therefore have as a conclusion a truly beautiful warning, which **Shao Gong** <note>original: "Chao-cum"; the Duke of Shao, a high official and relative of the Zhou kings</note> once inserted into his exhortation to the Emperor **King Cheng** <note>original: "Chim-uam"; the second king of the Zhou dynasty</note>: namely, if he wished himself to be safe, if he wished for a perennial and flourishing Empire, it was necessary to insist on the footsteps of his ancestors and constantly imitate their heroic virtues. "For what do you think, O great Prince," he says, "that those wise administrators of the State and Kings of the recently extinguished Family, having forgotten human affairs, dwell in heaven and did not act so that the branch and Royal house might be preserved? This was, believe me, in their prayers; it was in their care and heart. But indeed, the impiety of the last King hastened destruction and ruin. The clamor of the whole people groaning under bitter tyranny reached heaven itself, and prevented the Ancestors from bringing help to their descendants; who, when they understood that the implacable angers of heaven were now unleashed, certainly complied with its most just will." But let us rather hear the text itself and the interpretation of the **Grand Secretary** <note>original: "Colai"; a Latinization of the Chinese term 'Gelao,' referring to a high-ranking official or commentator</note>.

*Those wise and upright ancestral Kings are in heaven, and they have not perished entirely. Therefore, how can they not earnestly implore help from heaven to assist and protect the sons and grandsons of their Family, etc.? But because (continues **Grand Secretary Zhang** <note>original: "Cham colaus"; likely referring to the Ming dynasty commentator Zhang Juzheng</note>) the impious **King Zhou** <note>original: "Cheu"; the last, tyrannical ruler of the Shang dynasty</note>, who had received from heaven the most illustrious Empire (or, the most illustrious mandate), was not able to cultivate virtue; because he rejected and cast away from his protection the elders of the people, causing upright and wise men either to flee or hide themselves; because likewise he gave the greatest trust to impure and corrupt men, he further caused those infected with this disease to obtain public offices and dignities; and since they, being depraved by similar crimes, strengthened the alliance between themselves and the King, and thus helped each other; such a dire poison tended toward the certain destruction of the people. It happened, therefore, that the people, oppressed and afflicted by such a cruel tyranny, and having nowhere left to flee or anyone before whom to plead their cause, found this as their only remedy: that the fathers of families, embracing their little sons and dragging their wives, cried out tearfully to heaven in a miserable voice, pleading that they might finally be allowed to escape the final danger of their remaining life, since they were held constrained by so many calamities on all sides, and there was no place anywhere to receive them. Truly a mournful and utterly pitiable lot for the people! But indeed, heaven silently decides the affairs of mortals within itself. When, therefore, it contemplated these peoples of the four parts of the Empire, and understanding them to be oppressed without their own fault by so many losses and calamities; could it be that it was not moved by the most tender affection of commiseration and thought to help and succor them as quickly as possible? Therefore, although the Souls of the Ancestral Kings of this **Yin** <note>original: "Yn"; another name for the Shang dynasty</note> Family reside in heaven, nevertheless even now they cannot restrain or revoke the will or decree of heaven itself, etc. Thus far Zhang the Grand Secretary.*

## BOOK TWO

Who, moreover, would believe that in a matter of such weight and importance, so great a man would have used such reasoning, if indeed the Providence of the Deity and the immortality of souls had been doubtful to him, or if he had certainly thought them doubtful to his Prince? By no means, however, were they accustomed to attribute this authority and favor in the "celestial court"—so to speak—and the zeal for patronizing their descendants to just any of their ancestors. Rather, they gave it only to those who had joined a certain exceptional probity of life and character (which they themselves called sanctity) with Royal dignity; and to those who had proven themselves sons of heaven by their virtues and the glory of their right deeds, rather than by a prestigious name alone.

Let these things suffice, therefore, so that we may understand what that philosophy of ancient sincerity <note>The author refers to the original, "pure" Confucianism before later interpretations.</note> felt concerning immortality. Furthermore, whatever we have brought forward here has been drawn from the book <term>Shujing</term> <note>original: "Xu-kim"; The Classic of History, a foundational collection of documents and speeches from ancient Chinese history</note>. It is a classic of the first authority, and one which has occupied the minds of the Chinese for forty centuries now; from here they seek their learning, from here the arguments for their scholarly works, and from here, finally, their degrees, honors, and high offices.

*Here, however, our Grand Secretary Zhan <note>original: "Colaus noster Cham"; 'Colaus' is a Latinization of 'Gelao' or 'Grand Secretary,' a high-ranking official. 'Cham' likely refers to a specific commentator, possibly Zhan Ruoshui.</note> demands, as if by his own right, that since we began this scholarly labor with him, and entered upon the journey with him as our primary guide, we should complete the whole course with the same companion; now, having reached the end, let us sit down with him as if tired from so long a journey, reviewing the whole matter together in a single glance.*

The book (he says) <term>Zhongyong</term> <note>original: "Chum yûm"; The Doctrine of the Mean, one of the Four Books of Confucianism</note>, regarding the eternal mean, when it begins with nature—which heaven has implanted in man—teaches us that the principle of acting rightly is from heaven. When, however, it treats at the end the incorporeal virtue of the supreme heaven, it indicates how the perfect man must strive to reach that purity and innocence which he received from heaven. To attain this, it is first necessary that he attend to himself, behaving solicitously and circumspectly even in those matters which do not fall under the senses of others: for thus the blessed man will hold the middle way. When, through this exercise of watching over himself, he has attained his primeval purity and innocence, then at last he will be able to gradually obtain that supreme and hidden excellence of the most subtle and unique virtue.

*These are the words of the Grand Secretary. Although the Chinese schools attribute a great deal of praise and authority to this man, I nevertheless think that Confucius—who is obscure in his more than Laconic brevity—would have received much more light, and much more applause and authority even among the Chinese themselves, from a European interpreter or a Chinese Christian than he has received from this non-Christian man <note>original: "homine Ethnico"; literally 'a pagan man,' referring to the Neo-Confucian commentators who did not share the author's Christian perspective.</note> who was ignorant of higher truths. Since he was the teacher of a Prince (or a future Emperor), he set one goal for himself: the political instruction of his Prince for governing rightly and happily. Thus, he not infrequently does violence to the text itself, and those things which transcend the clouds and stars, he shuts within the limits of an earthly Empire and the narrow enclosures of the Royal Palace. And this is, finally...*

Confucius treats each of these [states] individually <note>original: "singulis"; referring to the rulers of the various feudal domains</note>, each of whom was required to have exactly one thousand four-horse chariots <note>original: "quadrigas"; a measure of a state's military and economic power</note> ready at hand whenever the Emperor ordered them into battle. First, let the ruler handle all matters of his domain⁹ with care⁶ and consideration⁷; let him think that nothing, however small it may seem, can be neglected by him. He should remember that from a single oversight of a Prince, calamities not infrequently arise which afflict even the most extensive domain for many centuries. Second, let him cultivate faith and truth, and persuade himself that this is the most precious gem of his crown. Let his speech, therefore, be true and without ambiguity, and thus always a clear indicator of the thoughts hidden in his soul. Especially in determining either rewards or punishments, let him pursue what is equitable and just; thus it will happen that his subjects will, in turn, do whatever is commanded, and indeed do so eagerly and with faith. Third, let him moderate gifts and expenses¹², removing what is useless and superfluous; for in this way there will always be an abundance of wealth in the royal treasury and the entire kingdom. Likewise¹³, let him love¹⁴ the people¹⁵ subject to him with a truly paternal affection, helping all those whom either orphanhood and loneliness, or poverty and hunger, or other misfortunes or hardships afflict. For in this way, the subjects will in turn behave toward their Prince like sons, and they will respect him so much that they also love him. Finally, if ever the labor and work of the subjects is required for building or restoring public works, let him command¹⁶ these of his subjects¹⁷ at an appropriate¹⁸ time¹⁹; namely, when there is leisure throughout the countryside, and not when sowing, agriculture, or the harvest occupies them. In this way, a bounty of grain and food will generally be available, and public works will be completed eagerly without public detriment.

# CHINESE KNOWLEDGE
<note>original: "SCIENTIÆ SINICÆ" — This refers to the title of the work, *Confucius Sinarum Philosophus* (Confucius, the Philosopher of the Chinese), which presented Chinese philosophy to the West.</note>

### Part 2. Section 1.
<note>This begins Book 2 of the Analects (Lunyu), which focuses on government and virtue.</note>

Confucius said: If subjects are directed by a King or Governor and kept to their duty solely through **laws**; and if those who do not observe them are nevertheless kept to their duty through **terrors and punishments**: the **people** will then indeed restrain themselves from more serious crimes, driven by a servile fear; but they will do so surely in the manner of some wicked servant, namely **without shame** and without a true hatred of their crimes. Therefore, they will not persist in their duty for long; for they persist by force and with fear as their master, which is certainly a poor teacher of duty.

### Section 2.

**ON THE OTHER HAND**, if you rule and direct them through almost **virtue** alone, being yourself an example of virtue to all, everyone will undoubtedly model themselves after this. And since the condition of all people is not the same, nor can their virtue be equal; if you indeed restrain your people with prudence and humanity, and if you govern your subjects by ensuring each fulfills their own **duties**, and thus unite and bind everyone together, it will clearly happen that they are held not only by a certain noble **shame** and a filial fear of sinning; but they will also, of their own accord and with alacrity, strive for and attain all the praise of virtue.

### Folio 9. Page 1. Section 1.
<note>This begins the famous passage in Analects 2.4 where Confucius outlines the stages of his life.</note>

Confucius, candidly explaining to his followers the progress he made in the study of philosophy as his age advanced, said: When I was **fifteen** years of age, I immediately applied my mind to thoroughly learning the institutes of the great men, or philosophy.

### Section 2.

Having reached **thirty years**, I had already stood firm: I mean that I had put down such roots that I remained **steadfast** in the study of virtues and wisdom I had undertaken, and no external thing was able to distract my mind from it.

### Section 3.

At **forty**, I no longer hesitated: the clouds of doubt had vanished; for I had clearly perceived the natural harmonies of things, and I understood what perfection or imperfection was inherent in each.

### Section 4.

At **fifty**, I immediately knew the **providence** and **mandate of Heaven**, and that to each individual thing its own [nature] has been implanted by Heaven...

# BOOK THREE
<note>original: "LIBER TERTIUS" — While this section contains verses from what we now know as Book 2 of the *Analects*, the Jesuit translators categorized this as the third major division of their work.</note>

...[at age fifty, I understood] nature, its force, and its inner logic; I myself explored the perfection and subtlety of this nature; I also tracked its origin and understood what its cause finally was. 

When I was **SIXTY**, my ears were already receptive and favorable—that is, I had a ready and sharp power of understanding. My mind was cultivated through diligent study and practice over so many years, and steeped in the best precepts and disciplines, so that I could easily and clearly perceive whatever others might argue or what I myself might read.

->§. 6.<-

**FINALLY**, at **SEVENTY**, by the benefit of long meditation and victory over myself, I followed what my heart desired; yet I did not exceed the rule, nor did I leap over the bounds of honesty and right reason, to which my appetite now obeyed without struggle or trouble.

->*Folio 10. Page 1. Section 1.*<-

**Meng Yi Zi** <note>original: "Mém' ý çù" — A high-ranking official from one of the three powerful families in the state of Lu.</note>, one of the High Officials of the kingdom of Lu, consulted Confucius about the <term>filial piety</term> <note>original: "obedientia" — The Latin translates the Chinese concept of *Xiao* (filial piety), the core Confucian virtue of devotion to parents.</note> which sons owe their parents: specifically, in what does it consist? Confucius responded: "It consists in this: that one does not oppose." Having heard this, the Official left, perhaps thinking the Philosopher had said everything there was to be said.

->§. 2.<-

**THEREFORE**, Confucius explained the matter to his disciple **Fan Chi** <note>original: "fán' chì" — A younger disciple of Confucius who often served as his carriage driver.</note>, who was also his charioteer, saying: "**Meng Sun** <note>original: "mém' súm'" — Another name for Meng Yi Zi.</note> asked me about filial piety, in what it consisted? I indeed responded: *'That one does not oppose.'*" Hearing this, he immediately departed.

->§. 3.<-

**Fan Chi** said: "I pray you, Master, what is the meaning of your response?" Confucius, explaining it, said: "While parents are **alive**, a son should comply with their wishes and serve them with the required duties; when they are **dead**, he should similarly pay his respects and bury them with the required rite and ceremony; finally, every year he should make offerings or perform ancestral rites according to the logic of the funeral rites and duties. I say, let him do these things, and he shall be judged to have fulfilled all the measures of filial obedience. I do not, therefore, define it as sons never opposing the commands of their parents (since it can happen that these commands conflict with equity and reason, which must by no means be obeyed; and since even after parents have passed from life, there is still a place for obedience and piety...)"

->Book 2. Section 1.<-

**C**onfucius says <note>original: "ait"</note>: If subjects are directed by a King or Governor and kept to their duty through laws <note>original: "leges"</note> alone; and if those who do not observe these laws are nevertheless kept to their duty through terrors and punishments <note>original: "supplicia"</note>: the people will then indeed abstain from the more serious crimes, driven by a servile fear. But they will surely do so in the manner of a certain wicked slave—that is, without shame <note>original: "pudore"</note> or a true hatred of crimes. Consequently, they will not persist in their duty for long; for they persist only by force and with fear as their master, which is certainly a poor teacher of duty.

->Section 2.<-

**O**N the contrary, if you rule and direct them through virtue <note>original: "virtutem"</note> alone, being yourself an example of virtue to everyone, all people will undoubtedly model themselves after this. And since the condition of all people is not the same, nor can their virtue be equal; if you indeed hold your people together by prudence and humanity, and if you moderate your subjects through the specific duties <note>original: "officia"</note> belonging to each, thus uniting and binding them all, it will clearly come to pass that they are held not only by a certain noble shame and a filial fear of sinning, but they will also spontaneously and eagerly strive for and attain the full praise of virtue.

->Folio 9. Page 1. Section 1.<-

**C**onfucius, candidly explaining to his followers the progress he made in the study of philosophy <note>The translators use "philosophy" to describe the study of the Way or the teachings of the ancients.</note> during his earlier years, says: When I was fifteen years of age, I immediately applied my mind to thoroughly learning the institutions of the great men of old, or philosophy.

->Section 2.<-

**H**AVING reached thirty years of age, I had already taken my stand: I mean to say, I had struck such deep roots that I stood firm in the study of virtues and wisdom I had undertaken, nor could any external thing call my mind away from it.

->Section 3.<-

**A**T forty, I no longer hesitated: the clouds of doubt had vanished. For I had perceived the natural harmonies of things, and I understood the level of perfection or imperfection inherent in each.

->§. 5.<-

**B**y the age of sixty <note>original: "sexagenario"</note>, my ears were already receptive and favorable—that is, I possessed a ready and sharp power of understanding. Through the constant studies and exercises of so many years, my mind was cultivated and imbued with the best precepts and disciplines, so that I could easily and clearly perceive whatever others debated or whatever I read myself.

->§. 6.<-
