->*Folio 10. Page 1. Section 1.*<-

**M**eng Yi Zi <note>original: "Mém' y' çù"</note>, one of the high officials of the kingdom of Lu <note>original: "lù"</note>, consulted Confucius regarding the obedience <term>filial piety: the core Confucian virtue of respect and duty owed to one's parents and ancestors</term> which sons owe to their parents—specifically, in what does it consist? Confucius responded: "It consists in this: that one does not oppose." Having heard this, the high official departed, perhaps thinking the Philosopher <note>Confucius is frequently referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in these translations.</note> had said all there was to be said.

->§. 2.<-

**T**herefore, Confucius explained the matter to Fan Chi <note>original: "fán' chì"</note>, his disciple and also his charioteer, saying: "Meng <note>original: "mém' sum"</note> (this is the same man as Meng Yi Zi) asked me about obedience, and in what it consists. I truly responded: 'That one does not oppose.' Upon hearing this, he immediately left."

->§. 3.<-

**F**an Chi said: "I pray you, Master, what is the meaning of that response?" Confucius, explaining it, spoke thus: "While the parents are living, the son should comply with their will and serve them with the required duties; once they are dead, he should similarly perform the funeral rites and bury them with the proper ceremony and preparation. Finally, he should make annual offerings to the parents according to the logic of the rituals <term>Li: the traditional rites, manners, and social rules that govern proper behavior</term> and funeral duties. If he does these things, I say, he should be judged to have fulfilled all the requirements of filial obedience. I do not, therefore, establish obedience as sons never opposing the commands of their parents (since it can happen that these commands conflict with equity and reason, which must by no means be obeyed); rather, even when parents have finished their lives, there is still a place for obedience and piety..."

->Page 2. Section 1.<-

**M**eng Wu Bo <note>original: "Mém uù pĕ"</note>, the son of the aforementioned *Meng Sun*, asks Confucius in what obedience <term>filial piety: the foundational Confucian virtue of devotion to parents</term> consists. *Confucius*, who was accustomed to giving answers tailored to the habits and vices of those questioning him—much like matching a medicine to a specific disease—responds in this manner: "Father and mother are only distressed by the illness <note>The text suggests that a virtuous son gives his parents no reason to worry except for unavoidable things like sickness.</note> of their children." Therefore, whoever seeks the praise of filial obedience should take care, first and foremost, not to ruin their strength and health through lust, intemperance, or similar vices, lest they bring heavy worries, if not bitter grief, to their good parents. This young man, born into a wealthy and luxurious house, was devoted to untimely banquets and other vices, thereby putting his health and life at risk.

->Section 2.<-

**T**he disciple *Zi You* <note>original: "çù yeû"</note> likewise asks Confucius what constitutes the essence of true obedience. *Confucius* responds: "In our current age, those are commonly called 'obedient' who are able to provide food for their parents; but truly, if nothing more than that is required, one could seek the name and praise of obedience from brute animals as well. Indeed, if we speak of dogs and horses, these all can have someone to feed them. Thus, if reverence <note>original: "reverentia"</note> is lacking—if, I say, that care for supporting one's parents does not proceed from love and filial honor—what distinction will there be to differentiate the support of a father from that of a domestic dog or horse?"

->Folio 11. Page 1. Section 1.<-

**T**he disciple *Zi Xia* <note>original: "çù hiá"</note> similarly raises a question about filial obedience. *Confucius* responds: "A cheerful countenance <note>original: "Oris alacritas"</note>, or that constant filial eagerness that shines forth from the face and whole expression of a loving and reverent son, is indeed a difficult thing to achieve; but it is surely the near-certain mark of true and genuine virtue. For even unwilling or disobedient sons can perform domestic services; for instance, when there is work to be done at home, the younger brothers and the sons of the family certainly take up the more laborious tasks in place of their elders. Again, when wine and feasts are available, the younger ones then undoubtedly serve their parents and elder brothers with great duty."

->§. 2.<-

**C**onfucius says: I sometimes debate with my disciple *Hoëi* <note>original: "hoëi"; referring to Yan Hui, the Master's most beloved and intellectually gifted student</note> for an entire day; yet he listens to me in such a way that he never objects to anything, appearing like one who neither disagrees nor doubts, so much so that he seems to be a dullard <term>stolidus: a person who appears slow-witted or lacking in feeling</term> who understands nothing of what is being said. However, when he has left my presence, I then examine the man more closely, observing what he does in private; and I find that first, in silence and at leisure, he meditates on the things I have discussed; then, he acts and speaks in such a way that I clearly understand he is equipped with such talent that he not only very successfully perceives and penetrates everything I teach, but also openly practices and manifests those same things in his actual deeds and actions. Truly, my disciple *Hoëi* is by no means a dullard or unrefined.

->Page 2. §. 1.<-

**C**onfucius says: It is often very difficult to distinguish the upright from the wicked. However, so that you may discern them, first observe what the person you wish to understand does and what they are striving for; for the wicked almost always commit things that are unjust and shameful, whereas the upright do things joined with honesty and justice. But since these are not an entirely certain proof of uprightness,

->§. 2.<-

**I**nspect more deeply and consider more attentively the goal of every work; specifically, with what mind or purpose they do those things which are honest and just. For if they act hypocritically and with a false or perverse purpose, even if the things they do are the best, they can by no means be considered upright when they act in this way.

->§. 3.<-

**B**ut anyone who does not wish to err cannot stop even here: he must proceed further and inquire where the one who seems upright finds his rest <note>The text uses "conquiescat" to mean the state in which a person finds their true satisfaction or inner peace.</note>, or in what things and pursuits he takes delight. For if he does what he does with faith and justice, and even with a good end and purpose, yet does so with little will—as if by force and compulsion—so that his mind does not seek its rest and delight from the virtue or honesty of the work itself, but from elsewhere, certainly that uprightness can neither be called perfected, nor can it be lasting, whatever its nature may be.

->Folio 12. page 1. §. 1.<-

**C**onfucius said: If someone diligently recalls and practices old knowledge—whether things he once committed to memory and learned—and in this way masters them over and over by himself, or derives new insights from them (for the fountains of Truth and Philosophy are indeed fertile and inexhaustible), he will be able to reach a distinguished level of learning and emerge as a teacher of others.

->§. 2.<-

**C**onfucius said: The perfect man is not a vessel <term>vas: in this context, it refers to a tool or specialized instrument (the Chinese 'qi') that has only one function</term>; that is, he is not like a vessel or a tool suited only for one or two specific uses. Instead, because he is equipped with an abundance and breadth of various talents, he is fit to accomplish tasks however great and numerous they may be.

In a different sense, Confucius once entered the ancestral hall of the Kings and saw a certain vessel already tilted and leaning toward a fall. Sighing, he said: "An empty vessel, and likewise a vessel overflowing with liquid, is easily overturned; but a half-full vessel stands safely and upright." His disciple *Zilu* <note>original: "çù' lú"; one of Confucius's most loyal and courageous followers</note> was present as he said this and asked for the meaning of the statement to be explained to him. Then Confucius said: "If a King is either empty of virtue, or full and, as it were, overflowing with a certain arrogance and pride, he will be prone to fall into any evil, and the kingdom, along with its Prince, will be inclined toward ruin. On the contrary, if a King has adorned the excellent gifts of his nature with the best disciplines and sciences, yet does not completely please himself—remembering that although he knows many things, more things are still unknown to him; and although his merits and virtues are many, he always values the praise of others more than his own; and finally, however much he prevails in wealth and power, he nevertheless carries himself as if his status were modest—whoever reigns with this prudence, moderation, and greatness of soul will reign securely. He will walk the safest middle path <note>original: "medio tutissimus"; a reference to the classical Latin poet Ovid, suggesting that the middle way is the safest</note>, and the extraordinary gifts of nature and fortune, which are often a snare for many, will be to him a source of glory and benefit."

->§. 3.<-

**T**he disciple *Zigong* <note>original: "çù' cúm"; a disciple noted for his eloquence and diplomatic skill</note> asks Confucius about the perfect man—what kind of man he truly is. Confucius responds: He is such that he first completes with actual deeds those words with which he desires to instruct others.

# BOOK THREE.
D ij

...others, and then follows his own deeds and examples by instructing others. In a word, he first acts, then teaches. ### § 4.

Confucius says: The upright and perfect man <note>original: "probus atque perfectus vir"; a translation of the Chinese term *Junzi*, often rendered as the "superior man" or "gentleman"</note>, through a certain breadth of charity and benevolence by which he desires to deserve well of all, and to cultivate and protect the common reconciliation and association of the human race, is universal and not partisan. On the contrary, the wicked and vile man of a low and abject mind is partisan; he is led by private passions, lends his friendship for interest, and basely sells his own merits and favors for private gain or as if for a price; and thus he is not universal.

*Confucius once declared this teaching, along with the breadth of his own benevolence, in a memorable saying. For it was heard that a soldier from the kingdom of Qi <note>original: "çi"</note>, who had perhaps lost his shield and sought it in vain for a long time, finally used these words to console himself for his loss: "A man or subject of the kingdom of Qi lost a shield, but without doubt a man of that same kingdom of Qi, or one of my fellow soldiers, has obtained the lost item." To this, Confucius said: "He would have spoken much better and more laudably if he had said: 'A man lost a shield, and a man has obtained the lost item.'" In this way, he translated the soldier's charity from the narrow confines of the camp or fatherland to the breadth of the whole human race.*

### Part 2. §. 1.

Confucius says: One who gives himself entirely to practice <note>original: "exercitationi"; refers to study and the application of lessons</note> and not to meditation <note>original: "meditationi"; refers to deep reflection or thinking</note> will surely lose his labor; one who gives himself entirely to meditation and not to practice will surely be subject to error and confusion. For whoever studies and indeed learns and exercises himself, but does not constantly meditate and reflect and, as it were, ruminate upon what he has learned, will learn nothing exactly or solidly, but will struggle with a certain perpetual ignorance and a kind of darkness. Conversely, whoever is occupied by either sloth or a certain overconfidence in himself, and neither consults books nor teachers, but gives himself only to sterile and idle contemplation of things rather than to practice—he will surely attain nothing but the shadows of things and empty, often false images; nor will he rest in any solid and safe doctrine, but there will be the danger that he falls into one error after another repeatedly.

### §. 2.

Confucius also says: Whoever devotes effort to strange <note>original: "peregrinis"; foreign or heterodox</note> dogmas that differ from the teaching of the Holy Sages <note>original: "doctrina Sanctorum"; the "Saints" here refers to the ancient Sage-Kings of Chinese tradition</note>, and rashly institutes them...

# CHINESE KNOWLEDGE
### (SCIENTIÆ SINICÆ)

The Grand Secretary <note>original: "Colaus"; a Latinization of the Chinese "Gelao," a title for a high-ranking official or imperial advisor</note> enumerates four sects in this passage, and what I might call "Chinese heresies"; since both he and other interpreters condemn them with very grave words, it will be worthwhile to sample a small portion of their critiques here. Thus he says: Any law and discipline that differs from that which the Sages <note>original: "Sancti," literally "Saints," but used here to refer to the idealized ancient rulers and philosophers of China</note> handed down to us is called a heresy. Such are those whose leaders were Yang <note>original: "yâm"; referring to the philosopher Yang Zhu</note> and Mo <note>original: "mè"; referring to the philosopher Mozi</note>, and those which in our age are commonly called the Taoists <note>original: "taó kiá"</note> and the followers of Fo <note>original: "fe"; the Chinese name for Buddha</note>. (Fo is the name of an idol imported from India into China, which the Japanese also worship, but by another name, namely Shaka <note>original: "xaca"; referring to Shakyamuni Buddha</note>.) The heresiarchs Yang and Mo lived about six hundred years before Christ, during the reign of the Zhou <note>original: "cheu"</note> family, which was then already declining toward its end. The error of the former [Yang] was this: *That care for one's own affairs was enough and more than enough for each person, and that one should not be involved in the affairs of others at all; and so nothing of zeal, or work, or resources should be contributed to the State, nor to the Prince and Magistrates, nor even to one's own parents. Thus the wicked man dissociated the human race; by reducing the world to a solitude, he completely destroyed the beautiful bodies of cities and kingdoms, for he commanded each of the members (the citizens, I mean) to be vacant for themselves alone and to look after only their own interests.* Opposed to this diametrically was the doctrine of the latter, who was called Mo: *namely, that each person should neglect himself and labor only for others; but in such a way that an equal care and benevolence should be spent on everyone, with no distinction made for friends or even parents. Thus both were fools; while they sought to avoid vices—one loving himself immoderately, the other neglecting himself—they ran into opposite extremes, as usually happens.* The author of the third sect, which is called Taoism, was Lao-tzu <note>original: "lì laò kiún," referring to Li Lao Jun</note>, a contemporary of Confucius. He taught *to count as small things those riches, honors, and qualities which seem exceptional and excellent to most, and to despise them with a stable and firm mind; to be free for oneself and for the contemplation of nature. Furthermore, this sect was perhaps originally pure and not wandering far from the truth, but later followers corrupted it with so many superstitions and magic tricks, and contaminated it with such a foul stain of base pleasures, that it can now be called a heresy, and indeed a pestilential and pernicious one.*

The interpreter Cheng-zi <note>original: "Chîm çù"; likely referring to the Neo-Confucian philosopher Cheng Yi or his brother Cheng Hao</note>, writing on this passage, says: Of the four sects, the last one, which worships the idol Fo [Buddhism], indeed brings forward more things that are in agreement with truth and reason than the three prior ones; but for this very reason it is more pernicious, as it is able to more successfully hide its poison under that appearance of truth and spread it more widely. Therefore, whoever is a student of virtue and wisdom ought to turn away from and flee its dogmas no differently than they would obscene talk or alluring and shameful sights; otherwise, that plague will rapidly insinuate itself into the vitals of the unwary. *So he said.*

But the Interpreter of the Annals, Qiu Junshan <note>original: "kieū kiūm xān"; likely referring to the Ming dynasty scholar Qiu Jun</note>, with even graver words and sentences, and not without a certain bitterness, not only condemns the sect itself, but especially the folly and rashness of Emperor Ming-di <note>original: "mîm tí"; an emperor of the Han Dynasty traditionally credited with introducing Buddhism to China</note>, who...

# BOOK THREE. 17

...since he allowed the monster or idol Fo <note>original: "Fe"; the Chinese name for Buddha</note> to be brought into the Chinese Empire. Indeed, by this deed he provided an entrance for all misfortunes and calamities, so that from the very beginning of the world until the present day, nothing more unfortunate or sad has happened to the Chinese. Thus, he deserved very poorly of his ancestors and descendants; nor is there any tyrant, however ruinous or detestable they may have been, who cannot be considered more innocent and better than Emperor Ming-ti <note>original: "Mîm tí"; Han dynasty emperor Ming, r. 58–75 AD</note> on this count alone. "What, then," he says, "is more foreign to the piety and reverence owed to one's Ancestors than to seek a law from the lands of barbarians—a law which neither our Ancestors followed, nor indeed wished to follow; which, being an enemy to peace and human society, disturbs and removes all order which nature established and wished to be fostered and preserved by mutual duties between parents and children, Kings and subjects, husbands and wives, etc.? Truly, a crime of this sort reaches up into heaven." *Thus far the Interpreter of the Annals.*

Therefore, just as the Grand Secretary <note>original: "Colaus"; a high-ranking imperial official</note> along with the rest of the Interpreters vehemently condemns these sects and novelties, so he teaches that one way, and one law which the Sages <note>original: "Sancti"</note> constantly held, and which is most common to all lands and nations, must be maintained. This is undoubtedly that which is called *Ju Jiao* <note>original: "Jû kiáo"</note>, that is, the law and doctrine of the Literati, which Confucius received from the ancient Kings and Philosophers and which he himself both very strictly practiced and refined, illustrating it with so many documents and precepts. If the scholars of our age would observe this law as they profess it, the entrance would not be as difficult for them as it is now to the law of Christian truth and grace—the law by which alone that law of nature ought to be perfected.

->§. 3.<-

Confucius says¹: Do you desire to be a knower of things both in reality and in reputation, O my disciple Yu² <note>original: "Yeu"; referring to Zilu, a prominent disciple of Confucius</note>? Come now, therefore, I will teach you how to know³, or I will teach you who can truly be said to be a knower of things. Do you know⁴ something? Profess⁵ that you know it⁶. Do you not⁷ know⁸ it? Freely admit that you do not know; or conduct yourself¹¹ as one who does not know¹⁴: for this is truly to know¹⁵, and to be a knower of things. For this is not required: that one should have all the causes and natures of things clearly perceived, since not even the Sages <note>original: "Sancti"</note> could exhaust them through knowing; but that he should understand and learn thoroughly those things which belong to his duty, not taking unknown things for known, nor rashly assenting to them, and, what is worse, selling his errors to others, deceiving both himself and others. Instead, he should apply both time and diligence to considering things; he should repeatedly consult those more experienced than himself, and in this, he should imitate the prudence and modesty of the ancient Kings Yao <note>original: "Yaô"</note> and Shun <note>original: "Xún"</note>. That little scholar of a disciple was led by an immoderate desire for praise and excellence, and so he not infrequently erred in this regard; wherefore Confucius chastises him with these words as if with a gentler hand.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the governance of the Empire, illustrating the weight of an Emperor's word through a historical anecdote before transitioning to a dialogue from the Analects (Book 2, Chapter 23) regarding the predictability of future dynasties based on historical patterns of the Xia, Shang, and Zhou.</meta>

with this, Empires, however vast, are governed prosperously and peacefully.

Certainly, how much this was at heart for the Ancients, both for the Emperors and the Administrators of the Empire, can be sufficiently understood from what once happened to the second Emperor of the *Cheû* <note>the Zhou dynasty, c. 1046–256 BCE</note> family, called *Chîm-vâm* <note>King Cheng of Zhou</note>. For while he, as a youth of seventeen years, was enjoying himself in a garden with his younger brother, he plucked a leaf from a tree and applied it to his brother's forehead (imitating the rite by which a <term>Regulus: a minor king or vassal prince</term> was usually created by applying a tablet to the forehead). In jest, he said: "I create you the *Regulus* of the Kingdom of *Tâm*." *Sù yè*, one of the High Officials, said: "It is ratified, O Emperor, this creation." And when the Emperor said that he had done it for the sake of a joke, the Sage persevered, saying it was ratified; for jokes do not apply to a Prince; his word must stand. Why say more? *Xo yû* (this was the Prince's name) obtained the kingdom, in which a long series of twenty-nine subsequent *Reguli* followed as his successors.

### Part 2. Section 1.

The disciple<gloss>1</gloss> *çù châm*<gloss>2</gloss> <note>Zi Zhang, a student of Confucius</note> asks<gloss>3</gloss> of his Master, whether ten<gloss>4</gloss> Imperial families<gloss>5</gloss> <note>dynasties</note>, which in the gliding centuries might eventually follow the one which then held power, can be known in advance<gloss>7</gloss>; namely, whether it can be known even now what the laws and institutions of each will be, and what their rise and fall.

A Chinese age <note>original: "sæculum"</note> consists of only thirty years; and this is the common meaning of the word *Xí*. Here, however, it signifies all that time in which any one family rules, whether it be thirty years, or three hundred, or more.

### Section 2.

Confucius<gloss>8</gloss> responds<gloss>9</gloss>: The Imperial House of *Yn*, or *Xām* <note>the Shang dynasty</note>, (which closely succeeded the family of *Hiá* <note>the Xia dynasty</note>) conformed<gloss>10</gloss> itself to<gloss>11</gloss> the Imperial family of *Hiá*, as far as pertains to the laws and duties<gloss>12</gloss> of greater importance—the very hinges of the Empire—and changed nothing in these. However, in those matters which were of lesser importance, it can easily be known<gloss>17</gloss> what<gloss>13</gloss> it either removed<gloss>14</gloss> or added<gloss>15</gloss> anew; what it changed, I say, in the very manner and, as it were, the temperament of the laws and duties. Similarly regarding the family of *Cheû*<gloss>18</gloss> <note>the Zhou dynasty</note>, which in this age of ours holds power; it is conformed<gloss>19</gloss> to<gloss>20</gloss> the family of *Yn*<gloss>21</gloss> that immediately preceded it in the very substance of morals and laws<gloss>17</gloss>. What<gloss>18</gloss> it either removed<gloss>19</gloss> and made obsolete, or established<gloss>20</gloss> anew, can likewise be known<gloss>22</gloss>. This is certain: the first of the families <note>the Xia</note> had especially at heart faith and sincerity, and in this they placed their chief devotion and glory. The second <note>the Shang</note>, conspicuous for a certain masculine simplicity, labored primarily for the integrity of the substance of things and morals. But our own, which is the third <note>the Zhou</note>, is delighted most of all, as we see, by the ornament and elegance of all things, and by external cultivation and ceremonies <note>original: "cerimoniis"</note>. Therefore, however many<gloss>23</gloss> may perhaps<gloss>24</gloss> in the future succeed<gloss>25</gloss> the house of *Cheû*<gloss>26</gloss>, even if<gloss>27</gloss> a hundred<gloss>28</gloss> Imperial houses<gloss>29</gloss> in number, by estimating the future from the past, it can<gloss>30</gloss> already without difficulty be [known].

# BOOK THREE.

can now be known in advance from these things, or rather from the proposed condition, insofar as it can be conjectured what fate awaits each, what the future stability and glory of each will be, and likewise what growth they may achieve. Since we have examined both the members of the political body and the connections between those members—as well as the very vigor and spirit with which they are imbued—who could deny that we are able to pronounce, long in advance and with a fairly probable conjecture, the future of Empires: what the stability and power of each will be, and what their virtue and glory will appear to be in times to come.

### *F. 15. p. 1. §. 1.* <note>This refers to the original book and page numbering in the source text, specifically referencing Book 2, Chapter 24 of the Analects.</note>

Confucius<gloss>1</gloss> says<gloss>2</gloss>: If there is no<gloss>3</gloss> proper<gloss>4</gloss> spirit<gloss>5</gloss> to whom you yourself, by reason of your condition and office, can and ought to sacrifice, and<gloss>6</gloss> yet you sacrifice<gloss>7</gloss> to it, you are truly flattering<gloss>8</gloss>; or rather, through that flattering display of a worship that you should not be performing, you are importunately begging for some bit of good fortune.

*The Chinese Monarchy has always been, and remains today, most diligent in maintaining the system of due subordination, by which the lowest things are governed and moderated through the middle, and the middle through the highest. The ancient Kings and Philosophers seem to have sought the model for this from the celestial bodies and all other moving bodies, which are joined together in their fixed places and seats by a fit connection. They observed that the revolutions and movements of these bodies proceed in an orderly fashion from one supreme Mover, descending step-by-step to the lowest. Thus, in the worship of Spirits—whom they understood to be ranked one above another—they decided that a certain order of rites and sacrifices, accurately prescribed by the Ancients, should be observed. Therefore, the Emperor alone sacrifices to the Spirit and Lord of heaven and earth with a solemn rite; the <term>Reguli: minor kings or vassal princes</term> and Nobles sacrifice to the presiding spirits of the mountains and rivers; the lower Prefects sacrifice to the lesser spirits; and so on. The Philosopher therefore condemns the rashness of certain men who, in this matter, were serving their own ambition or greed more than the Spirits themselves, having neglected the order and ritual we have described.*

### §. 2.

The <term>Colao: a high-ranking official or Grand Secretary</term>, connecting this with the passage above, says: We are taught to handle those things which fall within our jurisdiction and human powers; but we should prudently abstain from searching too curiously into the secrets of the Spirits and those things which exceed our sphere. Therefore, if someone sees and understands what his duty is, and what is equitable and right here and now, and yet does not undertake<gloss>3</gloss> or complete<gloss>4</gloss> it—presumably because he is hindered by fear or desire—that is certainly not<gloss>5</gloss> the mark of a brave<gloss>6</gloss> mind. Indeed, it is a sign of shameful and abject weakness, which everyone would condemn. However, one cannot rightly condemn another simply because he is unable to have a clear perspective on the hidden and sublime natures of Spirits, which seem to escape the sharpness of our human minds.

## KNOWLEDGE,
### OF THE THIRD BOOK,
### PART TWO

Confucius, speaking of the magistrate of the Kingdom of *Lu* known as *Ki-xi* <note>Ji Shi, the head of the powerful Ji family who held real power in the state of Lu</note>, who was usurping Imperial rites, said with wonder and indignation:
> *Eight rows of dancers perform in his ancestral hall. If this can be tolerated, what then cannot be tolerated?* <note>original Latin: "Octonis choris saltatur in ejus aulâ parentali : Hoc autem si tolerabile est, ecquid tandem non tolerabile erit?" This refers to the famous opening of Analects, Book 3.</note>

According to the ancient custom of the nation, only the Emperors were permitted to present eight funeral dance troupes <term>yi, ceremonial dance groups used in ancestral rites</term> in the ancestral halls of their forefathers; each of these troupes consisted of eight dancers who moved in time to the music <note>Totaling 64 dancers, a number symbolizing the highest authority</note>. Meanwhile, petty kings <term>zhuhou, or feudal lords</term>, when they solemnly honored their ancestors, were permitted only six troupes; magistrates <term>dafu, high officials</term> were allowed four; and scholars or other officials of lower rank <term>shi, the literati class</term> were allowed two. 

To one man alone, *Cheu-cum* <note>Zhou Gong, the Duke of Zhou, a culture hero and model of virtue</note>, although he was only a minor king, the Emperor *Chim-vam* <note>Cheng Wang</note>—his nephew—once granted the funeral honors of the first rank <note>the eight troupes reserved for the Emperor</note> because of his exceptional service to the then-ruling family and the entire Empire. Since the house of the magistrate *Ki-xi* [Ji Shi] usurped these honors through remarkable arrogance, the Philosopher <note>Confucius</note> condemns them. He teaches that the neglect and violation of ancient custom and right order must in no way be endured, as such license is a kind of seed for the greatest disturbances, and like sparks from which the most serious fires of rebellion later arise.

# CHINESE
## KNOWLEDGE,
### THE THIRD BOOK,
### PART TWO.

CONFUCIUS, speaking of a magistrate of the Kingdom of *Lu* <note>The home state of Confucius</note> called *Ki-xi* <note>original: "Ki-xi"; known today as Ji Shi, the head of a powerful noble family</note>, who was usurping Imperial ceremonies, said with both wonder and indignation: *Eight rows of dancers perform in his ancestral hall: if this can be tolerated, what then cannot be tolerated?*

According to the ancient institution of the nation, it was permissible only for Emperors to produce eight funeral choruses <term>rows of dancers</term> in the ancestral hall of their forefathers; each of these consisted of as many dancers as there were rows <note>An 8x8 formation totaling 64 dancers</note>. Meanwhile, minor Kings <term>feudal lords</term>, when they solemnly performed rites for their ancestors, were allowed only six rows; Magistrates were allowed four; and the literati and other Mandarins <term>government officials</term> of lower rank were permitted only two. To *Cheu-cum* <note>The Duke of Zhou, a foundational figure in Chinese statecraft</note> alone—though only a minor King—the Emperor *Chim-vam* <note>King Cheng of Zhou</note>, his nephew, had formerly granted funeral honors of the first rank because of his extraordinary service to the reigning family and the entire Empire. When the magisterial house of *Ki-xi* usurped these honors out of remarkable arrogance, the Philosopher condemned them. He teaches that the neglect and violation of ancient custom and proper order should never be endured; for such lawlessness is a seed of the greatest unrest, and like sparks from which the most serious fires of rebellion later ignite.

<summary>Confucius condemns the Ji Shi family for using the Emperor's "eight rows of dancers" in their private rituals, arguing that violating social hierarchy and ritual protocol leads to political chaos.</summary>

->Section 2.<-

The three families of the Kingdom of *Lu*, namely the *Meng-sun*, the *Shu-sun*, and the *Ji-sun* (also known as the *Ji-xi*), whenever they offered solemn sacrifices to their ancestors, would conclude the funeral rites and clear the tables and food to the singing of the poem called the *Yong*. <note>original: "Yum"; this refers to Ode 209 in the *Classic of Poetry* (Shi Jing). The title *Yong* means "Harmony."</note> (The *Yong* is that part of the Book of Songs which contains the praises of the *Zhou* family.) Confucius, likewise condemning this license and arrogance and noting it to be worthy of ridicule, spoke thus: "When the Emperor himself offers sacrifices to his ancestors in the funeral hall, with the petty Kings <term>feudal lords</term> assisting and serving him, it is only then that the dishes are removed with that solemn song and ritual. The words of the song were these: *The ministers of the rites are only the petty Kings; the Emperor assists in such a way that in him, a completely hidden majesty, reverence, and virtue shine forth.* I ask now: when those Magistrates offer sacrifice, do the petty Kings perhaps assist them? Is the Imperial Majesty present? If none of these things are present, by what right, by what authority, and with what face are such foreign rites usurped in the ancestral hall of the three families?" Truly, for those who now invade royal rites, it is to be feared that they will soon invade the kingdoms themselves; for once the distinction between the subject <term>client</term> and the Prince is removed, the Prince himself is soon removed.

->p. 2.<-

Confucius said: "For a man who is not upright—for one, I say, who is not furnished with true and solid virtue—of what use, finally, are rites, ceremonies, and outward duties? Again: for a man who is not upright, of what use, finally, is harmony and musical accord?" For since all duties and rites ought to flow from a mind imbued with virtues, as if from its own root, if such a mind is not present, then all rites and duties will surely be a certain empty shadow of humanity and a mere lie. Again, since it is necessary for a mind devoid of virtue to be shaken by various impulses and constantly disturbed, all harmony of instruments and voices will certainly be useless in such great discord of interior movements. This paragraph once again rebukes and condemns the families who usurp Imperial rites.

->Folio 2, page 1, section 1.<-

Lin Fang <note>original: "Lin Fam"; a man from Lu known for his inquiry into the "root" of ritual</note>, a man of integrity and rectitude originating from the Kingdom of *Lu*, observed that the men of his time celebrated banquets and conducted funerals with excessive labor, magnificence, and expense. Doubting whether this was the custom of the ancient Kings or the manner of those times, he inquired of Confucius what the foundation of duties might be—or rather, in what the force and reason of civil rites and duties truly consists.

->Section 2.<-

Confucius, filled with admiration and praising the man who labored most greatly over that which is most important in every matter, spoke thus:
"O, what an excellent, what a great question!"

### BOOK THREE

<margin>§ 3.</margin>
I say, therefore, that just as in other things, so too in our duties <term>officiorum: the ritual obligations and social roles according to one's station</term>, each has its own substance, and then that which is added to that substance—a certain ornament and decorum. If both are present, then the duties will be judged as perfect in every part; but if it is necessary for one of the two to be missing, I would certainly prefer the thing itself without ornament (which happened mostly in ancient times) rather than the ornament without the thing itself. For example: In those duties most commonly practiced by the public, such as banquets and funerals, I myself—in the face of such great splendor of feasts and that prodigality with which they are now prepared—would prefer something moderate, not shrinking from the ancient simplicity and thrift of our ancestors; but above all, I would prefer mutual faith, reverence, and charity among the guests. Again, in celebrating funerals and burial rites, instead of that so expensive apparatus and funeral luxury born of mere custom, I would truly much prefer true mourning, true tears, and an immortal longing for the one whose funeral is being conducted. That luxury of rites and ceremonies, which in these <insert>*alas*</insert> times of the families <note>The "three families" of Lu who were then usurping power.</note> had grown altogether immoderately, offended the Philosopher; and he burned with a desire to recall the customs of the ancient age, which labored more for the soul itself than for the outward signs of the soul.

<margin>p. 2. § 1.</margin>
Confucius, groaning, said: "The Eastern and Northern Barbarians have a King who is a King not only in name, but in the thing itself and in authority, inasmuch as his subjects yield to him, obey him, and revere him. It is not like this miserable China of ours, which now has no King—the distinction between client <term>subject</term> and Prince having been removed, a distinction which even among the Barbarians is kept inviolate; and this is because of the insolence of certain families, which is an enemy to ancient law and order."

<margin>§ 2.</margin>
Mount *Tai-xan* <note>Mount Tai, the most sacred of the five peaks of China.</note> is a very high and most noble mountain in the Province of *Xan tum* <note>Shandong</note>, formerly in the kingdom of *Lu*. Furthermore, the previously mentioned *Ki-xi* <note>The head of the Ji-sun family, a powerful usurper.</note> was offering sacrifice to Mount *Tai-xan*—to the spirit, I mean, presiding over the mountain (as the interpreters clearly say). This was despite the fact that it was lawful for no one other than the Ruler <term>Regulo: the legitimate Duke of the kingdom</term> of the kingdom of *Lu* himself to perform this sacrifice. Confucius, offended by this matter and addressing his disciple *Gen-yeu* (for this man belonged to the family of the Magistrate <note>specifically the Ji family</note> and was a domestic Mandarin of the same), spoke thus: "Can you not then find a remedy for such a great evil?" The disciple responded: "I cannot." Then Confucius said again, after first letting out a sigh (which is expressed by the two words *U-hu* <note>original: "U-hu"; the Chinese *Wūhū* (呜呼), an exclamation of grief or lamentation</note>): "Will it then ever be said that the spirit who presides over Mount *Tai-xan* cannot be compared with that so ordinary man *Lin-fam*, who recently consulted me? He was seeking quite anxiously the reason and foundation of the Duties and rites, lest perhaps he might sin through ignorance; and shall we think that the spirit is by nature so...

(From this paragraph and the explanation of Colaus <note>original: *Colai*; likely referring to the commentator Zhu Xi or the "Great Collection" of commentaries often cited by the Jesuits</note> it is most evident what the Chinese even of old felt concerning the spirits presiding over things; namely, that they are endowed with intellect and mind, and are held by a zeal for what is fair and right.)

<margin>folio 3, page 1, § 1.</margin>
Confucius says: Among serious and upright men, there is nothing over which they contend. Indeed (you will say) is there not a contest and competition of archery? Certainly, there is. But of what kind is it? Those who are to compete with arrows, before they enter the hall destined for that exercise, reverently greet their companions three times, thrice they defer the first place to them, and then finally they enter the hall. Here indeed, he who has emerged as victor and has hit the target more successfully than the others, descends together with the defeated, whom, having courteously greeted, he again bids to ascend into the hall; and there they pour wine with their own hands and, standing, drink the "penalty wine" <note>original: *vinum pœnale*; a ritual cup drunk by the loser as a mark of respect and acknowledgement of the winner's skill</note> (so called because the defeated were "fined" with such a drinking of the same). Truly, even in the very heat of the contest, one may observe harmony, modesty, and courtesy; and it is clear that those who compete are upright and serious men. While, on the contrary, vile and wicked men, if ever they contend among themselves, are accustomed to flare up into anger and to clash together almost in the manner of wild beasts.

<margin>folio 2, page 2, § 2.</margin>

Likewise, to beautiful eyes, the fit proportion of white and black color." Truly, where the subject itself and, as it were, the ground is properly disposed, from there the ornament added to it and the form so pleasing to the eyes emerges. This last verse *Su y quei hiven hi* <note>original: *素以為絢兮 (Sù yǐ wéi xuàn xī)*; usually translated as "The plain ground is taken to make the colors" or "The painting comes after the plain background"</note> the disciple did not yet perceive: wherefore, consulting his Master, he said: "What does that verse signify?"

<margin>p. 2. § 1.</margin>

<margin>p. 2. § 2.</margin>

---

->folio 4, page 1, § 1.<-

Confucius said: Regarding the customs, institutions, rites, and writings of the ancient Xia family (this was the first of all the Imperial and Monarchical families of China), I could certainly speak and pass down the sum of them to posterity. But indeed, the kingdom of *Kî* <note>modern: Qi</note>, which is now held by the descendants of the Xia family, is not sufficient to testify to or confirm the things I would say. Similarly, regarding the customs, rites, and writings of the *Yn* or *Xam* <note>modern: Yin or Shang</note> family, the second of the Imperial families, I could speak and report many things which would serve as an incentive for our age to imitate the ancient customs and the distinguished praises of their ancestors. But the kingdom of *Sum* <note>modern: Song</note>, which has now lost much of its former splendor and size and is held by the descendants of that family, does not suffice to testify that the things I report are true. To be sure, the books and the wise men, who are very few at this time in either kingdom or among the descendants of either family, do not suffice. They are not, I say, the ones from whom our age may seek a sufficiently clear testimony; this is the reason. Otherwise, if they were sufficient, then I in turn could testify; and much light and weight would be added to my testimony by their evidence and authority. But now, since I lack such necessary supports, why should I labor in vain and speak forth things which posterity will not believe?

---

->§ 2.<-

Confucius said: Whenever that solemn rite called *Ti* <note>the great "Di" sacrifice</note> is performed—which is proper to the Emperors, and by which they are accustomed every five years in the ancestral hall of their forefathers to honor the founder of the family and the Emperors born from him thereafter—even if many things are done with sufficient gravity and correctly at the beginning, yet once the wine has been offered nine times according to custom and likewise nine times poured as a libation, whatever is done thereafter, because it is done sluggishly and with little reverence, I truly have no desire or joy to watch, even though I am compelled by the duty of my office to be present. But what here displeases me most of all is that I see those honors owed to the Emperors alone (and once granted only to the Duke of Zhou <note>original: *Cheu-cum*</note>, though he was only a minor king <note>term: *Regulo*; a vassal prince or minor ruler</note>, by the Emperor *Chim-vam* <note>modern: King Cheng</note>, his nephew, and that because of the man's truly extraordinary merits toward the whole Empire) now being deferred to other minor kings who are descendants of that same Duke of Zhou, against all right and custom of the Empire.

<meta>This page continues the translation of Book Three of the Analects. # CHINESE KNOWLEDGE

<margin>page 2.</margin>

Someone once asked Confucius for the meaning of the most solemn ancestral rite, called the *Ti* sacrifice <note>original: *Ti*; in modern pinyin, the *Di* sacrifice, a major ritual performed by the Emperor to honor the founding ancestors of the dynasty</note>. He saw this rite being performed in the Kingdom of *Lu*, but he was ignorant of its origin and purpose. Confucius replied to him, saying: "I do not know. However, I say that whoever truly understands the secret and sublime reasons for these rites and duties would find all matters concerning the governance of the Empire as clear and as ready to hand as if he saw them placed here, in the palm of his hand." As he said this, he pointed with his finger to his own palm, as has been handed down by his disciples. Truly, he who knows how to offer the due honors to his departed ancestors will easily govern men. Meanwhile, the Philosopher <note>A common title for Confucius in Jesuit translations</note> chose not to explain this mystery to the questioner for two reasons: first, because it contains the very pinnacle of filial piety and obedience, which no one seems to have reached in practice and exercise except for those ancient Kings of great virtue, and which no one seems to have reached in knowledge and understanding except the truly wise. Why, then, should he have explained it to a common man? The second reason was that those things pertaining to the rite could not be declared without immediately making evident, and more than silently condemning, the notable arrogance of the local Ruler <note>original: *Regulus*; referring to the Duke of Lu</note>, who was using this Imperial rite here against the laws and customs of the Empire. Indeed, this truth was bound to produce hatred and danger.

<margin>folio 5. page 1. line 1. §.</margin>

Confucius (as is handed down by his disciples) whenever he more solemnly reflected upon the memory of his ancestors and the benefits received from them, performed the prescribed rites with such a sense and expression of a pious and grateful soul as if the ancestors themselves were truly present and standing by. (From this manner of speaking, it can be gathered that the Chinese <note>original: *Sinas*</note> were not in the error of believing that the ghosts of their deceased ancestors actually assisted in the duties of those performing the sacrifices.) Likewise, whenever he was holding office and, according to his duty, offered the prescribed honors to the spirits presiding over certain places, he offered them with such veneration and gravity as if the spirits themselves were present and visible.

<margin>§ 2.</margin>

Confucius himself, therefore, used to say quite often: "If ever I am seriously hindered and do not assist in these duties in person and perform them rightly—even if I should immediately delegate my role to another—I am by no means satisfied. Instead, I am distressed in my soul, just as if no one had yet performed those sacred rites." This is an illustrious proof of both the piety and the very sincere veneration with which the Philosopher honored either his ancestors or the guardian spirits.

# BOOK THREE. 7

->Section 3.<-

Van sun kià <note>original: *Van sun kià*; Wangsun Jia, a powerful high official in the State of Wei</note> inquired of Confucius, saying: "What is the meaning of that proverb of ours: 'Rather than seeking the favor of the spirit called Ngao <note>original: *Ngao*; the spirit of the southwest corner of the house, representing high status and the inner sanctum</note>, who is considered to preside over the domestic hall and be of a superior rank; it would be better to seek the favor of the spirit called çao <note>original: *çao*; the Kitchen God (Zao Jun), who oversees the hearth and daily life</note>, who presides over the hearth, even though he is of a lower order?'" This official possessed the greatest influence and authority with the King of Guéi <note>original: *Guéi*; the state of Wei</note>, at whose kingdom the Philosopher happened to be staying at that time. Thinking that Confucius had come there for the purpose of obtaining a high office, he jokingly urged him through this inquiry to seek his own favor and help; for he implied that this would be, in a sense, more necessary to him than the favor of the King himself.

*The ancients believed that every home and family was committed to the protection and trust of two primary spirits. Among these, the one called Ngáo was considered more noble; however, the common people worshipped the other who presided over the hearth more diligently, persuaded (as they said) not only by its utility, but also by necessity—since life cannot be led without the hearth, and if life fails, the spirits themselves cannot be worshipped.*

->page 2. Section 1.<-

But Confucius, being well aware of where the arrogant man’s playful inquiry was heading, and judging it contrary to right reason and most unworthy of a wise and upright man to hunt for favor by flattering others, spoke thus: "It must not be done at all in the way you silently suggest to me. I do not follow the custom of the common people. For whoever has sinned against <term>Heaven</term> <note>original: *cœlum*; in this context, the supreme moral and governing principle of the universe</note> has no other higher Divinity from whom he may pray for the forgiveness of his sin."

*Here, indeed, however much certain modern interpreters may twist themselves, it must be stated that the Philosopher is speaking of the very same Heaven of which the Prodigal Son once spoke when he lamented that he had sinned against heaven <note>A reference to the Biblical parable in Luke 15:18, illustrating the Jesuit effort to find common ground between Confucianism and Christianity</note>. Nor are we lacking in interpreters who hold this view against impious citizens. First, Cum ngan <note>Kong Anguo, a famous Han dynasty scholar</note> says: 'He has no reason to pray for pardon from the spirits of the universe' (because he has offended the Lord of all spirits). Even more fully and clearly, our Colaüs <note>likely a Latinization of a specific commentator, possibly referring to the school of Zhu Xi or a specific Jesuit source</note>, in explaining the sentiment of Confucius, says: 'There is one Heaven, which must be worshipped above all else, and to which nothing is equal. From this, prosperity comes to the upright and adversity to the wicked, so certainly and so exactly that there is no room for even the slightest error. Whoever conducts his affairs so as to obey reason, a blessed lot surely awaits him; but whoever resists reason, by that very act sins against Heaven. Who can escape the calamities sent by an avenging Heaven? Or how could one turn them aside by imploring the aid of the spirits Ngáo and çáo?' From these words it is clear that a man must obey reason and serve Heaven, and must not flatter even the spirits themselves (much less men).*

<summary>Confucius rejects the advice of a powerful official to use political flattery, arguing that moral rectitude and alignment with the supreme "Heaven" are the only true sources of security. The commentary emphasizes a monotheistic interpretation of the Chinese concept of Heaven.</summary>

# CHINESE KNOWLEDGE

->§ 2.<-

Confucius said: The Zhou <note>original: *Cheu*</note> dynasty, which now holds power, looked back at its beginning upon the two dynasties of the Xia <note>original: *Hia*</note> and the Shang <note>original: *Xam*</note> which held the Empire before it. Since the Zhou possessed men distinguished in both literature and arms—most notably the Princes Wen <note>original: *Ven-vam*; King Wen, the cultured founder</note>, Wu <note>original: *Vu-vam*; King Wu, the martial conqueror</note>, and the Duke of Zhou <note>original: *Cheu-cum*</note>—it so successfully refined the laws and customs of the preceding dynasties, partly by adding certain things and partly by removing others, that it eventually emerged as the most refined state in every kind of learning, duty, and way of life. Therefore, I gladly follow the customs and institutions of the Zhou dynasty, especially since it was my lot to be born and live my life during its reign.

->§ 3.<-

During the time Confucius held office in the Kingdom of Lu <note>original: *Lu*</note>, he frequently entered that great and famous hall dedicated to the memory of the most wise Duke of Zhou <note>original: *Cheu-cum*</note>, to duly pay the customary honors to the deceased Prince alongside the other high officials of the kingdom. Furthermore, whenever he entered, he would inquire very carefully and studiously about almost every single thing: namely, what the use of the ceremonial vessels was, for what purpose, by what ritual, and in what manner each action ought to be performed. Someone, noticing this, said: "Who could be convinced, or would say, that the son of the man from Zou <note>original: *Ceu*; refers to the district of Zou</note> (thus he called Confucius, because his father Shu-liang He <note>original: *Xo leam be*</note> had once been the Prefect of the town called Zou) is skilled in the rituals? For whenever he enters this great hall, he inquires about everything, in exactly the same way as the most ignorant person would." But Confucius, having heard this, said: "On the contrary, this very practice of inquiry is itself a type of ritual, and a clear enough proof of how one is not ignorant of them." Indeed, it was exactly so: for such great care and such singular zeal in inquiring after even the smallest details clearly showed that the Philosopher understood the great importance of what was being done there, and in what high regard he held those rites and ceremonies. At the same time, it revealed the man's modesty; though he had attained an exceptional skill in rituals, he was by no means arrogant about it, nor did he trust in his own knowledge so much that he did not constantly consult others, rejoicing to profit and learn from them.

->Folio 6, page 1. § 1.<-

Confucius said: "Those who shoot arrows do not aim to pierce the hide" <note>original: *non perforant corium*; these words appear in the *Book of Rites* <note>original: *libro officiorum*</note> in the section on archery exercises</note>. He said: The praise and victory of a skilled archer did not consist in ancient times in piercing through the target (the target was made of hide), but simply in hitting it. And not without reason: because the physical strength of those competing is not equal, and the contest was not a test of brute force, but of skill and dexterity. This was the law and principle of the Ancients; from which, alas! our age has now begun to deviate, having poorly resumed the use of arms which King Wu <note>original: *Vu-vam*</note>, the founder of the Zhou dynasty...

### BOOK THREE
c

The founder had well and wisely ordered these things to be stored away. Now, once again, military strength and the arts of war are held in high esteem; but virtue is neglected, though it alone reaches the goal of true praise; and while strength cannot be acquired through learning, virtue can.

->§. 2.<-

At the end of every year, the Emperors used to distribute the Calendar for the following year—which had been prepared long in advance—to the Feudal Lords <note>original: *Regulos*; referring to the regional rulers or "petty kings" of the Chinese states</note>. The Lords would then preserve it in the ancestral halls of their forefathers. On the first day <note>original: *Calendis*; the Roman "Calends" or the first of the month</note> of each month, they would go to these halls, and having brought forth and consulted the Calendar, they would sacrifice a sheep according to the prescribed rites. By this ritual, they were said to remind the spirits of what had been done, or to give an account of themselves to them—that is, they conducted themselves as if they were testifying to their devotion and gratitude in the very presence of their ancestors' spirits. For what was this "reminding" being discussed here, if not a kind of pure public festival? This custom in the Kingdom of Lu <note>original: *Lu*</note> had already been neglected for many years; nevertheless, a sheep was still provided from the public treasury to each official who was entrusted with this duty. A disciple <note>The disciple Zigong, as indicated by the name "Su" below</note> therefore desired that the practice of offering a live sheep on the first of each month—the rite by which the spirits were reminded—be abolished in the future. He desired, I say, to be spared the expense, which he judged to be clearly unnecessary.

->p. 2. §. 1.<-

BUT Confucius, who considered the matter more deeply and wished to provide at least for future generations, by no means approved of this plan for thrift. "My disciple," he said, "Su <note>original: *Su*; the personal name of the disciple Zigong</note>, you indeed love those sheep; but I love that custom and ritual. That most praised custom is already being neglected and has been partially abolished; but if hereafter the sheep cease to be provided, even the hope of some day restoring the custom will be utterly destroyed. Surely those expenses should not be considered useless which do not allow us to be unmindful of our duty, and which will one day, I hope, rouse the heart of some King to restore the ancient custom of piety and reverence."

->§. 2.<-

Confucius said: I so obey and serve my King that I fully exhaust whatever may be required for that outward veneration and observance. Yet certain imprudent and reckless men—who either have no insight into my mind, or measure my mind by their own—judge me to be a flatterer for this very reason, as one who would meanly seek the favor of my Prince through such arts.

->f. 7. p. 1. §. 1.<-

THEN the King <note>Duke Ding</note> of the Kingdom of Lu raised a question of this sort: "When a King commands his subjects, and the subjects in turn serve their King, by what principle shall they conduct themselves?" Confucius replied: "A King should command his subjects..."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of social and ritual harmony. Having previously addressed the sacrificial rites in the Kingdom of Lu, the text now transitions to the specific virtues required of both rulers and subjects, and the domestic foundations of a stable state through the examples of virtuous royal women.</meta>

# CHINESE KNOWLEDGE

with a certain prudent moderation; he should despise none of his subjects: he should adapt himself to each according to their merits, duty, rank, and dignity; dealing more gently with some, more severely with others; more confidently with some, more cautiously with others. Subjects truly should serve the King with great loyalty and a zeal for sincere truth, not only concealing nothing from him which it is right for him to know; but also, whatever is commanded, however arduous and difficult it may be, they should nonetheless undertake it bravely and complete it with constancy: nor should they hesitate, when the situation demands, to cheerfully undergo the risk of life itself.

Confucius says: The wedding song called *Quan-çin* <note>original: *Quan-çin*; referring to the "Guan Ju" or "Crying Ospreys," the first poem in the *Classic of Poetry*</note> is indeed joyful and festive, yet not obscene: it is mournful insofar as it expresses the lover's longing and various emotions of the soul, yet it is not of such a kind that it affects anyone too violently or disturbs them. For a long time, King *Ven-vam* <note>King Wen of Zhou, a legendary model of wisdom</note> had sought for his wife a maiden named *Tai su* <note>Tai Si</note>, adorned with exceptional natural gifts and virtues: and he burned indeed with love and longing for the maiden: nonetheless, he burned in such a way that he did or said nothing unworthy of a Philosopher King. When the day of the wedding finally arrived, although the whole court resounded with the festive harmony of the musicians, nothing was heard that would offend modest ears; on the contrary, the exceptional lessons contained in those songs restrained any more wanton movements of the soul. Thus, a singular moderation is commended here, both of the Prince and of the entire Royal court.

*Among other illustrious women, three in particular, called the* San-mù <note>original: *San-mù*; meaning "Three Mothers"</note>, *that is, the mothers of the three greatest Princes, are celebrated in the praises of the writers:* Tai kiam <note>Tai Jiang</note> *mother of King* Vam-ki <note>Wang Ji</note>; Tai-gin <note>Tai Ren</note> *mother of King* Vèn-vâm, *who was the founder of the* Cheu <note>Zhou</note> *family;* Tai fu <note>Tai Si</note> *from whom was born then* Vù-vam <note>King Wu</note> *the first Emperor of that same family, and thus grandmother of* Chîm-vam <note>King Cheng</note> *the second and most famous Emperor. Nor do they hesitate to credit the prudent and virtuous instruction of these matrons for the noble upbringing of such great sons and their most prosperous successes. Furthermore, whoever desires to know more about these and other most praised women should consult the books* Quei muen pie-to, <note>likely the *Gui-men-bi-du*, "Necessary Reading for the Women's Quarters"</note> *and* Lie niu chuen <note>The *Lienü Zhuan* or "Biographies of Exemplary Women"</note>. *One will find here, among other examples of virtue, a chastity rivaling that of Lucretia* <note>A reference to the Roman heroine Lucretia, intended to provide a familiar Western comparison for Chinese female virtue</note>; *many, I say, dying most promptly for the sake of defending their modesty.*

Ngai, when he was King of the Kingdom of *Lu*, inquired about the area or a certain open circle outside the city called *Xe* <note>original: *Xe*; the "She" or the Altar of the Soil</note>, from the disciple *çai-ngò* <note>Zai Wo</note>. <margin>The previous page likely ended with the mention of the Xia dynasty.</margin>...was planted with pines; the men of the second family, the *Yin* <note>The Shang dynasty (c. 1600–1046 BCE)</note>, used cypresses; and finally the men of the third family, called the *Cheu* <note>The Zhou dynasty (c. 1046–256 BCE)</note>, which now holds the empire, adorned it with chestnuts. I say they did this so that the people would be struck with fear or shaken by a certain horror. It was the custom to execute criminals in that same place; and since the aforementioned trees presented a certain deathly and horrific appearance, some have rashly interpreted the mind of the ancients, imagining a mystery where there was none. In truth, when each of the families established their court in different places, they designated the site for sacrifice and punishments based on those trees which the nature of the place and the character of the soil itself demanded.

-> p. 2. §. I. <-

Therefore, when Confucius heard what his disciple had answered—which was certainly not very prudent nor to the point—he said: "When a matter is already completed, one must not speak of it." Indeed, even if a matter is not yet finished, but has been brought to such a point that it can no longer be hindered, one should not offer a warning, as it would be useless and in vain. Finally, when a matter is already in the past, punishments should not be exacted with the intent of undoing what has already been done; however, this does not mean one should not take precautions for the future. Furthermore, these very words have the force of a rebuke: for he could hardly have punished the disciple's rashness more severely than by not punishing him in such a manner. The Philosopher certainly wished for subjects to be kept in their duty through <term>justice and mercy</term> <note>original: *iustitia, clementiâque*</note>, rather than through threats and terrors; therefore, he took it very poorly that the King's mind had been stirred toward immoderate severity by such a false interpretation, a severity from which the age of the ancients had always been most distant.

However, because the man lacked true <term>virtue and wisdom</term> <note>original: *vera virtus sapientiaque*</note>, the Philosopher thinks and speaks of him meanly; for he judged that the true greatness of anyone, and the true praise of a capable and deep soul, must be sought and estimated from virtue alone. Only when one of these Masters or Leaders has rightly instructed himself and his own family, can the greatest benefits then finally flow down to the Prince and the subject people.

But indeed (replied the other), if the man is so splendid and so munificent, and one who so excellently provided for the right order of judgments, must it not then be said that **Quòn-chúm** <note>Guan Zhong (c. 720–645 BCE), a famous chancellor of the State of Qi</note> is well-versed in duties <term>original: *officia*; referring to the *Li*, the traditional rites and social responsibilities</term>—that is (I say), what each person's duty is and what each matter requires? **Confucius** responds: The King, with a wall standing tall, veils the main gate of his Palace, certainly according to his right and custom (for it was permitted only to the Royal house to erect a wall or a certain vestibule outside the main gate of the palace, through which a central passage was open to the King alone, with all others entering only through the side doors). Yet the family of **Quòn-chúm** similarly covers the gate of their house with a wall, just as if it were royal. Likewise, if the King at any time hosts a banquet for two Kings—if, I say, the guest is another petty King <term>Latin: *Regulus*; a minor ruler or prince</term> whom he invites to dinner—he has, according to his wealth and Royal majesty, various sideboards <term>Latin: *abacos*; referring to ritual stands or tables for drinking cups</term> where golden bowls and other vessels may be placed. The family of **Quòn-chúm**, through remarkable arrogance, similarly has sideboards furnished for cups. Truly, if **Quòn-chúm** and his family, while doing things so foreign to the duty and modesty of a subject, are still thought to know duties—or are judged to know them—then who finally will be judged *not* to know duties, no matter how much they neglect them, despise ancestral customs, and invade what belongs to another’s right?

<margin>Page 2.</margin>
The Philosopher took great delight in **Music**, not so much for the sweetness that soothed the ears, as for the benefits that the highest and lowest alike perceived from it whenever it was performed in the manner of the Ancients; so much so that sometimes a certain renewal of the entire Kingdom and a singular improvement of morals would follow. Such was the power of the teaching which the Ancient Kings and Masters had bound into their melodies. Thus, when **Confucius** returned from the Kingdom of **Guéi** <note>The state of Wei</note> to his native kingdom of **Lù**, seeing that Music was everywhere neglected and that many things pertaining to the administration of the Republic and the discipline of morals were nearly consigned to oblivion, he earnestly desired to restore everything. Addressing the Great Master of Music of the Kingdom of **Lù**, he spoke thus:
> "Of the Music which was of such great value to our Ancestors, you at least, who handle it by virtue of your office, can be skilled in it. And indeed, in the beginning, with voices and instruments sounding together in harmony..."

The border official of the town called **Y** asked the disciples of **Confucius** for the opportunity to meet and greet their master, saying: "Whenever men of proven integrity and wisdom have come here, I have never failed to see them." The disciples introduced the man to greet the Philosopher. Having greeted him, as he was leaving, he turned to those same disciples and said: "O you two or three sons <note>original: *filii*; a term of endearment for students or disciples</note>, why do you grieve and feel such anguish in your hearts because your Master now lives far from his native kingdom and is stripped of his dignity? Furthermore, it has long been that our empire lives without law: and I indeed determine that it will soon happen that Heaven, out of **Confucius**, shall create a kind of living instrument, a **Mo to**, or the sounding tongue of a bronze bell for the instruction of the whole people."

> *In former times, a high-ranking official <term>Mandarin: a senior civil servant in the Chinese imperial system</term> was chosen from among the more serious men to disseminate the laws of the empire and the sound doctrine of holy men throughout all the Provinces. He used a small bell which, although it was made of bronze, was equipped with a wooden tongue; hence it was called a **Mo to**. This is in contrast to the military bell used to announce military statutes and the laws of war, which was made entirely of bronze; and so it was commonly called a **Kin-to**. Here, therefore, it is signified that the Philosopher's doctrine would be spread throughout the entire Empire: as indeed later came to pass.*

->page 2. section 1.<-

**Confucius**, as they record, used to say of the **Shaò** music <note>original: *Xaò*; the ritual music attributed to the legendary sage-king Shun</note>, whose author had been the Emperor **Shun** <note>original: *Xún*</note>, that it had completely exhausted elegance and beauty. Likewise, that it had exhausted clemency and sweetness. However, he said of the music called **Wǔ** <note>original: *Vù*; the music of the Zhou dynasty's founder</note> (this had belonged to the Emperor **Wǔ-wáng** <note>original: *Vù-vàm*</note>) that it was indeed most excellent and full of majesty: but not likewise most sweet, for it resounded of war and arms.

->section 2.<-

**Confucius** said: If high officials are not kind, and again if those who perform the mutual duties of politeness and ceremonies do not honor one another from the heart? ->Folio 1. Page 1. Section 1.<-

**Confucius** said: It is quite rare for a village or hamlet to be so small—where, for instance, no more than twenty-five families might live—that the inhabitants are not such that mutual faith and love flourish. Let all praise and honor be sought from this one thing alone. Yet, should there be anyone who chooses a dwelling place for himself, but does not wish to reside in this "seat of charity and innocence" <note>original: *charitatis & innocentiæ*; these Latin terms are used by the translators to approximate the Confucian concept of *Ren*, often translated as "humaneness" or "benevolence"</note> which we have described: how can I judge such a man to be wise?

->Section 2.<-

**Confucius** said: The wicked can by no means remain for a long time amidst hardships and poverty; likewise, they cannot remain for a long time amidst the joys of favorable fortune. The man of integrity <note>original: *probus*; referring to the *Junzi* or "Superior Man"</note> meanwhile, whatever chance or accident may befall him, finds his rest in virtue alone. Furthermore, the wise man does not seek his own advantage or profit from virtue.

->Page 2. Section 1.<-

**Confucius** said: Only he who is truly virtuous can safely love men, and safely hate men. <note>The Latin *tuto* (safely) suggests that only a person of high moral character can trust their own emotional impulses of affection or dislike to be objective and just.</note>

->Section 2.<-

**Confucius** said: If anyone seriously and firmly applies his mind to virtue, he will commit nothing that is shameful or contrary to reason.

->Section 3.<-

**Confucius** said: Wealth and honors are those things which mortals desire. But if it is not consistent with reason itself to obtain them, the true Philosopher <term>Sage: in this context, the Latin *Philosophus* refers to the Confucian ideal of the perfected moral man</term> will by no means persist in them. He will, of his own accord, renounce them. Conversely, poverty and a lowly or humble status are things that mortals hate and flee; yet the true Philosopher, even if these things have befallen him through no fault of his own, will by no means act so as to avert the lowliness of poverty through right or wrong <note>original: *per fas & nefas*; literally "through the divine and the forbidden"</note>.

->Folio 1. Page 1. Section 1.<-

Therefore, if someone wishes to be heard as a Philosopher, and yet casts aside the study of true wisdom and virtue—being such a person, how could he deserve or win for himself the name and reputation of a Philosopher?

->Section 2.<-

The true Philosopher, not even for the tiny space of time in which the body is usually refreshed <note>a reference to the time it takes to eat a single meal</note>, would commit anything contrary to virtue and right reason. And though the most sudden accident might occur, he persists entirely in this purpose of virtue. Indeed, whatever calamities may press upon him when his affairs are overturned and ruined, he perseveres entirely upon this foundation of virtue.

->§. 3.<-

**Confucius** said: I have not yet seen anyone who truly delights in virtue and feels a genuine horror toward vice or wickedness. The reason for both is this: for the one who delights in virtue, I would wish him to be held by such an inflamed zeal and love for it that he places nothing else before it. On the other hand, for the one who abhors wickedness, I wish him to apply himself to integrity in such a way that he does not allow his character to be affected or stained by even the slightest bit of what is shameful.

->Page 2. Section 1.<-

Yet, is it truly credible that there exists anyone who, with the noble resolve of a determined mind, wishes—and indeed is able—to spend all his strength on the study of virtue for the space of even a single day, and yet does not reach it? I certainly have not yet seen anyone whose strength was insufficient for this task.

->Section 2.<-

**PERHAPS** there will be someone who is truly so weak; but I certainly have not yet seen such a person.

### p. 2.

After **Confucius** had left shortly thereafter, the disciples questioned Master Zeng, saying: "What, I ask you, do those words of the Master signify?" To them Master Zeng spoke thus: "The fundamental doctrine of Confucius, and the unique principle of living rightly, is this: whatever you do, do it truly from the soul with all your might, and from your own heart take the measure of others. In other words: be such toward others as you would wish others to be toward you; this is sufficient, and nothing else is needed." <note>This is a famous early formulation of the 'Golden Rule' or the principle of reciprocity (Shu).</note>

### f. 14. p. 1.

> **Confucius** said: The upright man and true Philosopher is exceptionally keen-sighted in those things which are consistent with reason; but the wicked, and those men who are most eagle-eyed regarding their own gains and advantages, discern most sharply only what is for their own benefit and what is against it.

### p. 2. §. 1.

> **Confucius** said: If an upright man sees anyone endowed with virtues, he immediately thinks of conforming himself to that person. If he sees a man lacking in virtue, seeking even then to gain fruit from the situation, he immediately examines himself internally to see if perhaps, by his own fault, he is similar to that man.

And even if they overwhelm him with labors and troubles, or indeed even with blows—

### §. 3.

->Folio 1. page 1. paragraph 1.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'C' with floral background patterns.</image-desc>**CONFUCIUS** said regarding his disciple called *Gongye Chang* <note>original: "Cum ye cham". For even though he was among those bound with black ropes <note>original: "atro fune vinctos", a Latin idiom for being bound in prison</note>—that is, committed to prison—this nevertheless happened through the fault of another who slandered an innocent man, and not through any fault of his own." **Confucius** therefore gave him his own daughter in marriage.

->§. 2.<-

**CONFUCIUS** said regarding his disciple *Nan Rong* <note>original: "Nan-yûn"</note>: "This man is of rare prudence, and of solid and adult virtue; therefore, if virtues and laws flourish in the kingdom, he is not neglected, but is employed in the duties of the state. If, however, the kingdom should be without virtue and laws, then by his own prudence he keeps himself safe from destruction and dangers." For this reason, **Confucius** gave his brother’s daughter to him in marriage.

->P. 2.<-

**CONFUCIUS** likewise said regarding his disciple *Zijian* <note>original: "çu-çién"</note>: "Of what great wisdom and virtue this man is! But indeed, if in this our kingdom of *Lu*, from which he himself originates, there were not so many men distinguished by wisdom and virtue—by whose examples, experience, and instruction he has steadily made progress—from where or how would he have acquired for himself such great virtue and such great wisdom?"

->folio 2. page 1. §. 1.<-

*Zigong* <note>original: "Cu-cum" or "çù cúm"</note>, who was also one of **Confucius’s** disciples, having heard the praise of his fellow disciple *Zijian* uttered by the Master himself, and being curious to know what his Master thought of him, inquired of the same, saying: "And what of me, *Si*? <note>original: "Ego sú"; Si was Zigong's personal name.</note> What kind of man am I?" **Confucius** replied: "You are a vessel." Having heard this, he asked again, saying: "Of what- <note>original: "cujus-", the catchword for the next page, beginning the question "Of what kind of vessel?"</note>
