"...what sort of vessel am I?" To which **Confucius** replied: "You," he said, "are that precious and elegant vessel called *Hù-lièn* <note>Hulian: a specialized ornate ritual vessel used for holding grain during sacrifices in the ancestral temples of the Zhou dynasty.</note>, which was especially valuable among the vessels used for the offerings that Kings were accustomed to make in the hall of their ancestors." Therefore, **Confucius** compared this disciple of his to this vessel, in order to show that he was adorned with such talents that he deserved the first place among the other Governors of the Kingdom.

->§. 2.<-

One of **Confucius's** disciples called *Yum* <note>Ran Yong, also known as Zhonggong.</note> was a man more silent than the others; someone noting this silence of his said to **Confucius**: "Your disciple *Yum* is indeed an honest man; however, he is unlearned in speech and lacks eloquence."

->§. 3.<-

**Confucius** replied: "What use, after all, is that cleverness of tongue <term>oris facundia</term> <note>Literally "eloquence of the mouth." Confucius often preferred inner virtue over superficial glibness.</note> and talkativeness? For to overwhelm and crush others with the readiness of a chattering mouth usually stirs up indignation and hatred among men. As for my disciple *Yum*, whom you assert to be an honest man; I do not know, nor do I debate his honesty; I only ask, what use is that cleverness of tongue which you value so highly?"

->p. 2. §. 1.<-

**Confucius** had ordered one of his disciples called *çie tiao cai* <note>Qidiao Kai.</note> to hold a Magistracy. He replied: "I do not yet possess or have not yet attained sufficient skill in this matter that I would dare to undertake it." **Confucius**, having heard the response of his disciple—full of prudence and modesty—was greatly delighted.

->§. 2.<-

SINCE in the times of **Confucius**, virtue lay neglected in the Kingdom of *Lù*; and the King did not employ honest and wise men for public duties: **Confucius**, who accepted honors chiefly with the intention that he hoped his teaching would thus be more easily accepted by the people; seeing himself and honest men neglected everywhere, full of sorrow, finally broke out into these words and said: "My teaching today is neglected and not spread: Why, then, do I still inhabit *China*? I shall board a raft to sail through the seas, and I shall quickly flee this age so corrupt in its morals. Without doubt, at least this one disciple of mine, *Yeu* <note>Zilu, a disciple famous for his martial spirit and impetuousness.</note> (a man equally ready and bold for attempting any difficult tasks) will follow me as I depart." *çu-lu* <note>Zilu.</note> hearing these things, was delighted. But **Confucius**, turning to this disciple of a glowing spirit, said: "Hey, my *Yeu*; in your love and zeal for bravery you indeed surpass me; but you lack that thing by which you might grasp what is more prudent; you lack, I say, maturity of judgment."

The Prefect of the Kingdom, *Lù mem* <gloss>called the Ruler</gloss> <note>Likely Meng Wubo, a high official in the state of Lu.</note>, wishing to promote some men to public offices, questioned **Confucius**, saying: "Is your disciple *çu lu* <note>Zilu, a disciple famous for his courage and military ambition.</note> a man of true and solid virtue?" **Confucius**, knowing that virtue is such an arduous thing, and therefore not easily or rashly to be attributed to anyone, replied very prudently: "True and solid virtue <term>virtus</term> <note>The Latin "virtus" here translates the Chinese concept of "Ren" (benevolence or perfect humanity).</note> is a thing hidden in the innermost recesses of each person's soul; and so, whether one possesses it or not is difficult to discern fully. Therefore, as to whether *çu-lú* is of true and solid virtue, as you ask me, I indeed do not know."

§. 2.
Not satisfied with **Confucius's** previous response, the Prefect asked him again about the virtue of the disciple *çu lu*; for he could not persuade himself that **Confucius** did not know the virtues of his own disciples. Then **Confucius** replied: "Since my disciple *Yeu* <note>Another name for Zilu.</note> is endowed with exceptional fortitude and martial valor, he could be entrusted with governing the military affairs of a kingdom of even a thousand war chariots. §. 3.
The SAME Prefect, having questioned **Confucius** about another disciple named *Kieu* <note>Ran Qiu, a disciple noted for his administrative skills.</note>, said: "What sort of man is your disciple *Kieu*?" **Confucius** replied: "To my disciple *Kieu*, a town of even a thousand families, or a noble house of a hundred war chariots, could be entrusted so that he might act as their governor. Yet, I am not certain of that inner virtue of his."

Again, the Prefect, questioning **Confucius**, said: "What sort of man is your disciple *Che* <note>Gongxi Chi, also known as Zihua.</note>? **Confucius**, wishing to stimulate one who was so idle, said: "In the earlier times of my life, when I dealt with men and heard their words, I immediately believed they would act in the same way; nor did I doubt that they would do what they said. But now, since the face of things and morals has changed, I recognize that I was deceived. Therefore, from now on, when dealing with men I will indeed hear their words, but at the same time I will observe their works and actions to see if they correspond to their words. Otherwise, I will not believe them. Having now been taught by experience with this disciple of mine, *çû* <note>Referring again to Zai Yu, whose name is sometimes rendered as Zigong in different contexts or phonetic transcriptions in this era.</note>, I have corrected myself in this regard."

But indeed, these things so constantly preached by our **Confucius**—nature and its dictate divinely implanted in man—cannot be fully grasped or thoroughly perceived, even by the most keen-sighted minds.

->page 2. § 1.<-

**Zilu** <note>original: *Cu-lú*; a disciple known for his impulsive and courageous nature.</note>, a disciple of a very ardent temperament, upon hearing of some good and praiseworthy deed, would immediately burn to carry it out. But whenever he was unable to complete what he had heard as quickly as possible, he would be troubled in spirit; he feared only that in the meantime some new lesson regarding virtue might present itself for him to hear before he had fulfilled what he had first understood in practice.

->§ 2.<-

Long ago, it was the custom among the **Chinese** <note>original: *Sinis*</note> that whoever had lived in a magistracy or high rank—whether laudably or wrongly—would be marked after death with a specific title of either honor or reproach. Therefore, **Zigong** <note>original: *çu-cum*</note>, a disciple of Confucius, knew that a Prefect of the Kingdom of **Wei** <note>original: *Guei*</note> named **Kong Yu** <note>original: *Cum-yù*</note> had committed many unpraiseworthy acts while he lived (among other things, he had prompted a man named **Tai Shujie** <note>original: *Tai xo çie*</note> to divorce his wife so that he might then give him his own daughter in marriage). And yet, after his death, he was honored with that distinguished title **Kong Wenzhu** <note>original: *Cum-wen-çu*; the title Wen means "The Accomplished" or "The Refined."</note>. Greatly marveling at this, **Zigong** asked the Master, saying: "That Prefect **Kong Wenzhu**, for what reason was he called after his death by the honorable name of *Wen*, which signifies ornament?" 

Confucius replied: "Although that Prefect was himself sharp and perceptive by nature, he nevertheless delighted in studying books repeatedly and learning more; nor was he ashamed or did he disdain to consult even his inferior ministers, and indeed even commoners, even regarding matters that those being consulted perhaps did not fully understand. Because he was adorned with such singular modesty while he was among the living, he was therefore rightly and deservedly titled 'Accomplished' after his death." For the book from which such posthumous titles are usually drawn says: *Kìn hiŏ háo vén yuĕ vén* <note>original: "勤學好問曰文"; translated as: 'Those who, while they lived, studied diligently and consulted others willingly, are to be titled "Accomplished" after death.'</note>.

->folio 6, page 1, § 1.<-

For in conducting his own affairs, he is extremely moderate and of a modest and humble spirit, never praising himself or his own deeds; yet he publicly praises others who are conspicuous for their integrity and willingly places them above himself. Furthermore, in serving and obeying his Prince and his superiors, he conducts himself with great reverence and performs commands promptly and eagerly. Moreover, in preserving and protecting the people, he is exceedingly beneficent, anxiously procuring what is advantageous and profitable for his subjects, and warding off what is harmful." ### BOOK THREE

Finally, he himself <note>The text refers to Yan Pingzhong, a famous statesman of the Spring and Autumn period.</note> displays great equity and justice in governing the people and administering the law, favoring no one too much and treating no one more harshly than is right; he is fair toward all. **Confucius** said: **Zang Wenzhong** <note>original: *Cam vên chúm*; a high official in the state of Lu.</note> hid in his house a great tortoise called **Cai** <note>original: *çai*; large tortoises were used for divination and were usually reserved for the Emperor or high ritual use.</note>; or rather, he lives in a house which, in its appearance, resembles the native place of that tortoise called **Cai**. # CHINESE KNOWLEDGE

But indeed, this nature which our Confucius so constantly preached, and its dictates implanted in man from heaven <note>The translator refers to the Confucian concept of *Xing*, which the Jesuits often interpreted through a theological lens as a gift from God.</note>, cannot be fully grasped or deeply understood even by those of the most keen intelligence.

->p. 2. §. 1.<-

**Zilu** <note>original: *Culú*; one of Confucius’s most famous and impetuous disciples.</note>, a disciple of a very fervent nature, whenever he heard of something good and praiseworthy, he burned to put it into practice immediately. But whenever he was unable to quickly complete what he had heard in action, he was troubled in spirit; he feared only that in the meantime some new teaching regarding virtue might present itself to be heard before he had finished putting into practice what he had previously understood.

->§. 2.<-

It had long been a custom among the Chinese that one who lived in a magistracy or high rank, whether they had lived praiseworthily or poorly, would be assigned a specific name of honor or reproach after death <note>This refers to the system of posthumous titles (*shìhào*), which served as a moral judgment on a person's life.</note>. **Zigong** <note>original: *çu-cum*; a disciple known for his eloquence and business acumen.</note>, a disciple of Confucius, knowing that the Prefect of the Kingdom of **Wei** <note>original: *Guêi*</note> called **Kong Yu** <note>original: *Cum-yù*</note> had committed many unpraiseworthy acts while alive (among other things, he had encouraged a man named **Taishu Ji** <note>original: *Tai xo çie*</note> to divorce his wife so he could give him his own daughter in marriage), and yet after death he had been granted and called by the honorable title **Kong Wenzi** <note>original: *Cum-wen-çù*; the suffix *Wenzi* means 'The Refined' or 'The Cultured'.</note>; being quite surprised, he asked the Master: "For what reason was that Prefect **Kong Wenzi** called and honored after death with the character **Wen**, which signifies refinement or culture?"

Confucius replied: "Although that Prefect was himself sharp and naturally discerning, he took constant joy in studying books and learning; nor was he ashamed or did he disdain to consult even lower ministers, or indeed commoners, even about things that those being consulted perhaps did not fully understand. Because he was adorned with such singular modesty while he lived, he was therefore rightly and deservedly named 'Refined' after his death." For the book from which such posthumous titles are typically drawn says: *Kin xue hao wen yue wen* <note>original: *Kín hiǒ háo vén yvĕ vén*</note>. That is: Those who, while living, studied diligently and willingly consulted others, are to be named 'Refined' after death.

->f. 6. p. 1. §. 1.<-

Confucius, repeatedly praising the Prefect of the Kingdom of **Zheng** <note>original: *Chím*</note> called **Zichan** <note>original: *çú chàn*; a famous and highly respected statesman.</note>, said: "The Prefect **Zichan** possesses four virtues proper to a perfected man. For in conducting his own affairs, he is exceedingly moderate, and is of a modest and humble spirit, never praising himself or his deeds; yet he openly praises others who are conspicuous for their integrity, and willingly prefers them to himself. Second, in serving and obeying his Prince and his superiors, he carries himself with great respect, and does what is commanded promptly and eagerly. Furthermore, in preserving and protecting the people, he is extremely beneficent, anxiously procuring what is for the benefit and profit of his subjects, and warding off what is harmful." Of

### BOOK THREE

Finally, he himself, in governing the people and administering justice, displays great equity and justice, favoring no one too much and treating no one more harshly than is right, being fair toward all. Thus the Kingdom of **Zheng** <note>original: *Chim*; a state in the Spring and Autumn period famous for its central and precarious geographic position.</note>, although it lies between two most powerful kingdoms, **Qin** <note>original: *çín*</note> and **Chu** <note>original: *çû*</note>, situated in the middle, nevertheless, with such an administrator of its affairs <note>The text refers to the famous statesman Zichan, known for his legal reforms and diplomacy.</note>, it excellently protects its liberty and wards off all force and snares of the neighboring kingdoms. Such indeed is the protection found in the wisdom and virtue of even one man.

->§. 2.<-

Confucius said: **Yan Pingzhong** <note>original: *Tén pîm chûm*; a celebrated diplomat and minister of the State of Qi.</note> (this was the name of the Prefect of the Kingdom of **Qi** <note>original: *çi*</note>) fulfills all expectations in cultivating friendship with men: For he is an old friend, and yet he is respectful, just as if the friendship were even now new.

->§. 3.<-

Confucius said: **Zang Wenzhong** <note>original: *Cam vên chûm*; a high official in the State of Lu.</note> kept a great tortoise called **Cai** <note>original: *çai*; referring to a species of tortoise used for divination, named after the state from which it came.</note> in his house—or rather, he lives in a house that by its appearance resembles the native place of that tortoise, called *Cai*. For he has the lintels of the doors carved with the shapes of mountains, and the small columns painted with the figures of marsh herbs. What kind of prudence, I ask, can be attributed to him who, having forgotten the people committed to him, seeks or hopes for happiness from a place of this sort? <note>Confucius critiques Zang Wenzhong for his superstition and for usurping the architectural styles—mountains and duckweed—reserved for the Son of Heaven (the Emperor) or for ancestral temples.</note>

->p. 2.<-

The disciple **Zizhang** <note>original: *çû-cham*; a younger disciple known for his ambition and inquisitiveness.</note> asked Confucius, saying: The Governor of the Kingdom of **Chu** <note>original: *çu*</note>, named **Ziwen** <note>original: *çu vên*</note>, was promoted three times to office and held the supreme magistracy called **Lingyin** <note>original: *Lîm yn*; the highest administrative post in the state of Chu, equivalent to Prime Minister.</note> without any appearance of joy showing on his face. Likewise, he was dismissed from office without any appearance of indignation showing on his face. Moreover, he would infallibly inform the new governor who succeeded him about the past administration of his office as *Lingyin*, candidly indicating to him without any envy whatever he had learned through experience could be useful or harmful for the successful administration of the city. What should be said of this man? Confucius replied: He was indeed a faithful and upright man. The disciple pressed further and said: Can he not be called a man of solid virtue? <note>The disciple asks if Ziwen possesses *Ren*, the highest Confucian virtue of perfect humanity or benevolence.</note> The Philosopher replied: I do not yet know. For how could I know whether he attained solid and true virtue of the soul?

Where, when he found similar wicked men...

When he encountered Prefects who were disloyal to their King, he immediately said: "These Prefects are similar and entirely of the same grain as our Prefect **Cui Zi** <note>original: *qui çu*; a powerful minister in the state of Qi who assassinated his ruler.</note>. Therefore, let me have nothing to do with them." Proceeding from there, he arrived at another Kingdom: where, similarly encountering wicked Prefects, he likewise said: "These too are entirely similar to our Prefect **Cui Zi**." Wherefore he departed from there as well to go elsewhere. What do you think of this man? **Confucius** replied: "He certainly deserves to be called what he truly was: a pure and upright man." **Zizhang** <note>original: *çu cham*; a prominent disciple known for his ambition and formal manner.</note> asked again: "But should he be called a man of solid virtue?" <note>The Latin *virtus* here represents the Chinese concept of *Ren* (benevolence or perfect virtue).</note> **Confucius** replied: "I do not know. For since true and solid virtue lies hidden in the inner heart and cannot be certainly perceived in external actions, how can I immediately grasp or know whether he has acquired true and solid virtue?"

->Book 2, Section 1<-

Formerly, a Prefect of the Kingdom of **Lu** named **Ji Wenzi** <note>original: *Ké vên çù*; a high official known for excessive caution.</note> was a man who was morose and a procrastinator in dispatching affairs. Indeed, he would weigh each thing three times within himself, and only then would he carry it out. **Confucius**, hearing this, said: "To weigh everything maturely a second time, or twice, is truly sufficient. There is no need thereafter to delay longer or deliberate further; lest while we aim to be wiser than is right, we sin greatly against wisdom itself."

->Section 2<-

**Confucius** said: **Ning Wu Zi** <note>original: *Ním vù çù*; a minister of the state of Wei.</note>, Prefect of the Kingdom of **Wei** <note>original: *Guéi*</note>, was considered wise by everyone when integrity flourished in the Kingdom or the Royal House. If, however, the Kingdom was without law and integrity, such that it began to be disturbed and endangered, he would timely withdraw himself and remain so hidden, removed from the eyes of the common people, that he never ceased to support the tottering State with his wisdom and counsel. However, because he performed these things as a private citizen and in secret, he was then called unrefined, timid, and unskilled in managing affairs. But I judge thus regarding his wisdom: one might easily reach and imitate that wisdom by which he excelled in the kingdom during times of peace. But as for that most wise 'simplicity' <note>Confucius uses a word that implies feigned ignorance or "folly" as a protective mask during political upheaval.</note> of his, while all things were in turmoil, looking after both his own safety and that of the public, it can be reached only with the greatest difficulty and by very few.

->Folio 8, Page 1<-

When **Confucius** was in the Kingdom of **Chen** <note>original: *Chin*</note> and saw that his teaching was not being accepted, he said: "I shall return, therefore; I shall return to my native Kingdom of **Lu**. At least my young fellow-citizens and disciples, as they are of a loftier spirit aspiring to all the highest things and despising lower, common things, so they weave their speeches and nightly labors into elegance and ornament; yet meanwhile they do not know what or by what means they should correct themselves, being ignorant of that rule by which we are accustomed to prudently prune away whatever is excessive or flourishing beyond the bounds of what is right."

**Confucius** said: **Boyi** and **Shuqi** <note>original: *Pĕ y* & *Xŏ tś*; legendary brothers famous for their integrity and for choosing exile over compromising their principles</note>, the sons of the King of the Kingdom of **Guzhu** <note>original: *Cu chŏ*; an ancient state in northern China</note> (of whom we shall treat in part 4), did not dwell upon, or call back to memory, the past crimes of others. Although they held the wicked in hatred because of their crimes, if those people sincerely repented, the brothers embraced them as if they had never committed any sin. Therefore, complaints and grumblings against these Princes were extremely rare; so dear were they to everyone, and burdensome or hateful to none.

->Section 2.<-

**Wei Sheng-gao** <note>original: *Vi ſem cao*; a man of the state of Lu</note> was a man who, in the opinion of the common people, was considered quite sincere and candid. But **Confucius**, who had observed the man, wanted to show how liable the judgments of the ignorant multitude are to error. Recounting one of the man's actions, he said: "Who, I ask, can say that **Wei Sheng-gao** is an upright and sincere man? For recently, when someone asked him for some vinegar, even though he did not actually have any, he did not honestly admit this. Instead, feigning the opposite, he secretly went to ask his neighbor for a loan of it and gave it to the person who asked." Furthermore, let those who so highly praise the man's candor see now whether the reality matches his reputation. <note>Confucius criticizes this as a form of "staged" virtue—trying to appear helpful at the cost of simple honesty.</note>

->folio 9. page 1. Section 1.<-

**Confucius** used to say: Affected words of polished speech with which you might soothe and tickle the ears of men; an affected appearance of a fawning face with which you might entice the eyes of others; and finally, excessive ceremonies with which you might capture the favor and minds of others—these are the arts and industries of shallow and deceitful men, who speak according to the will of their audience rather than according to the truth. In a word, they are the arts of flatterers. That distinguished man **Zuo Qiuming** <note>original: *ço kieu mim*; traditionally identified as the author of the *Zuo Zhuan* or *Zuo Commentary* on the Spring and Autumn Annals</note> used to blush at these things and condemn them; and I, too, no less blush and condemn them. Furthermore, the mutual association of men requires, above all, loyalty and candid truth. Therefore, to hide a hatred conceived in the soul and then to pursue that very same man whom you truly hate with the false duties of a feigned friendship—that most wise man **Zuo Qiuming** likewise blushed at and hated this, and I also detest it and blush at it.

The **Chinese** in ancient times used only animals of a single color for sacrifices; however, the specific color changed from time to time according to the variety of the eras and the families <note>meaning the ruling dynasties</note> who held the Empire. In the time of the **Zhou** Empire, red was held in high esteem. **Confucius**, therefore, speaking of his disciple <gloss>Ran Yong</gloss> **Chum cum**, and wishing to praise him through an appropriate metaphor, spoke of the calf or son of a spotted or multicolored cow, which was entirely red <note>original: *rufo toto*</note> and equipped with elegantly rounded horns: "Even though most men might not wish to use it for sacrifice because it was born of a spotted mother, will the mountains and rivers—that is, the presiding spirits of the mountains and rivers—reject it for that reason if it is offered? I think not." Thus, therefore, this disciple of mine, even though his father is a man of low and abject condition, similarly marked by various stains of vice and thus like a spotted ox; he himself is distinguished by virtue...

<margin>*The virtue of **Ren** (**Gîn**) is that interior and solid perfection of the soul by which we constantly follow the natural light granted by heaven, so that we do not stray from our chosen course for even a small moment of time.*</margin>
**Confucius** said: "Only my disciple **Yan Hui** <gloss>Hoéi</gloss> possessed a mind that, through self-mastery for a space of three months, never lost this virtue of **Ren** <gloss>Gîn</gloss>. They eventually stop, and soon they are driven backward; what they gained with great labor, they suddenly lose."

...from the foreign Kingdom of **Qi** <gloss>çi</gloss>. He was indeed an illustrious Philosopher, who valued the hardships of exile more than the dignity and wealth offered by a wicked man.

<margin>Folio 14, page 1.</margin>
It was an ancient custom of the Chinese <gloss>Sinarum</gloss> that those who were confined to bed by illness would place their small bed by the northern window of their house, positioned directly opposite the southern side of the same house. Because a king sat in a very similar position whenever he held court—namely, turned toward the North so that he faced the South directly—it followed that whenever a King visited a sick person, the patient's bed was immediately moved to the southern part of the chamber. This was done so the guest of such high honor could be received in the proper place of dignity. 

Therefore, when **Bo Niu** <gloss>Pe nieu</gloss>, a disciple of **Confucius**, happened to be ill and Confucius came to visit him, the disciple wished to receive his Master with the greatest possible honor. He ordered his bed to be moved just as if he were awaiting the King. But Confucius, sensing what was happening and certain that he should not accept an honor due only to a King, very kindly inquired after his disciple's health; however, he refrained from entering the room. Instead, from the outside, through the very window where the sick man had placed his bed, he took hold of his hand. Noting the certain signs of approaching death, he groaned and said: 

> He must die. This is the will of Heaven <note>original: *cæli voluntas*; referring to *Tian*, the guiding providence or natural order</note>. Alas, the grief! Is it possible that such a great man should have such a disease! Is it possible that such a great man should have such a disease!

<margin>Page 2, Section 1.</margin>
Intending to celebrate the joyful poverty and frugality of his disciple **Yan Hui** <gloss>Yen hoéi</gloss>, Confucius said: 

> Oh, how wise and upright was **Hui**, my most dear disciple! Content and cheerful with a single small basket <note>original: *quasillo seu fiscella*</note> of cooked rice for food and a single bowl of water for drink, he lived in a mean and deserted corner of an alley. Other men certainly would not be able to endure such great harshness in their food and lifestyle—a life so full of weariness and gloom, as they would think. But indeed, that great Philosopher **Hui**, always true to himself, in no way changed his joy. Oh, rare man! Oh, truly wise man, my disciple **Hui**.

->§ 2.<-

**Ran Qiu** <gloss>Gen Kiêu</gloss>, a disciple of a more faint-hearted character, speaking with his Master Confucius, said: "It is not that I do not love and esteem your teachings, Confucius, or that I make little progress in them for that reason. Rather, my strength is not sufficient." Confucius replied: "He whose strength is truly insufficient gives up in the middle of the path. But now you, my good man, through your own laziness, have set a limit for yourself before the journey has even begun."

<vocab>Confucius, Bo Niu, Yan Hui, Ran Qiu, Chinese, custom, philosophy, wisdom, poverty</vocab>

### BOOK THREE

->Folio 15, page 1, section 1.<-

**Confucius**, addressing his disciple **Zixia** <gloss>çù-hiá</gloss>, said: "You, my disciple, must be one of those perfect, truly great, and Royal scholars <gloss>literati</gloss>. You must by no means be one of those petty scholars <gloss>literatulis</gloss>, or those who are base and dishonest." 

<note>Confucius distinguishes between the *Junzi Ru* (the noble or "Royal" scholar who studies for self-improvement and public good) and the *Xiaoren Ru* (the petty scholar who seeks only status or narrow expertise).</note>

->Section 2.<-

**Ziyou** <gloss>CU yeu</gloss>, a disciple of Confucius, was formerly the Governor of the town of **Wucheng** <gloss>Vu-chim</gloss> in the Kingdom of **Lu** <gloss>Lù</gloss>. Confucius, turning his attention there, asked: "Have you found any remarkable man in that town who has become your close associate?" The disciple replied: "There is one man here from the family of **Tantai** named **Mieming** <gloss>Mië mên</gloss>, a man who is exceedingly serious and upright. He walks along the Royal path of virtue <note>original: *Regiam virtutis viam*; a reference to the 'Great Way' or Dao of public righteousness</note> and never turns aside into the crooked paths of private interests. Therefore, unless there is some public business to attend to, he does not even visit my house, though I am his friend."

->Page 2.<-

Confucius, praising the military commander **Meng Zhifan** <gloss>Mem chi fan</gloss> for a certain singular modesty, spoke with great admiration: "**Meng Zhifan** never boasts. Recently, during the burning war between the kingdoms of **Lu** and **Qi** <gloss>çi</gloss>, when our army was scattered after a chance conflict and turned to flight amidst a slaughter, he remained with a steady spirit in the very rear of the column <note>original: *extremo agmine*; the 'rear guard' is the most dangerous position during a retreat, as it faces the pursuing enemy</note>. There he held back the momentum of the victor, diligently performing the duties of both a leader and a soldier. But when most of his men had reached safety and he himself was just about to enter the gates of his own city, he then spurred his horse, entering last of all, and said: 'It was certainly not because I was brave that I held the rear of our fleeing army after our defeat; it was simply that this horse of mine, broken by exhaustion, would not move forward.'"

->Folio 16, page 1, section 1.<-

Confucius, seeing that in the Kingdom of **Wei** <gloss>Guei</gloss> only those who excelled in the grace of a silver tongue or a handsome face were promoted, sighed and said: "Unless a man possesses either the talkativeness of the Governor **Zhuo Tuo** <gloss>Chô tò</gloss> or certainly the elegance and charm of the handsome **Song Zhao** <gloss>Sum chao</gloss>, it is difficult to escape the current age without being crushed by the snares of the envious and the hatred and injuries of enemies."

<note>Confucius laments a political climate where superficial traits like eloquence and physical beauty are valued over substance and virtue.</note>

->Section 2.<-

Confucius said: "Who can leave a house without going through the doors of that house? Why then do we not walk through the Way itself? Why, I ask, do we not—by a similar logic—ensure that whatever business we undertake or whatever matters we approach, we enter through the proper 'doorway' or natural path of the thing itself? In this way, we might bring our work to the end we have set for ourselves."

<note>This is a metaphor for the *Dao* (the Way). Just as a door is the only proper exit from a room, the "Way" of virtue is the only proper path for human conduct, yet people often try to find "shortcuts" or irregular routes.</note>

<summary>This page discusses the distinction between noble and petty scholars, the integrity of Tantai Mieming, the famous modesty of the commander Meng Zhifan, and the necessity of following the "Way" (Dao) despite the corruption of the times.</summary>
<keywords>Zixia, Ziyou, Tantai Mieming, Meng Zhifan, modesty, Kingdom of Wei, the Way, Dao, eloquence vs virtue</keywords>

CHINESE KNOWLEDGE

->§. 3.<-

**Confucius** said: If the simple quality of one's nature exceeds outward ornament and refinement—that is, if nature is left entirely to itself and receives no support or decoration from art or culture—then that person will undoubtedly be something rough, rustic, and wild. On the other hand, if art, or more truly that outward ornament and cultivation, exceeds one's natural simplicity, then something affected will arise, something merely political <note>original: *merè politicum*; here meaning "superficially polite" or "socially calculated"</note> and merely fussy. But indeed, if that outward cultivation and ornament is joined to the inner simplicity and sincerity of nature in such a way that they correspond to one another without the excess or defect of either—with a pleasing diversity but a just proportion—then at last the true <term>Kiun çu</term> <note>original: *Kiun çu* (Junzi); the "Superior Man" or "Noble Person"</note> will emerge. There will emerge (I say) something illustrious and perfect in all its parts: the most beautiful appearance of a man who is both serious and refined. It is just as the body is made most beautiful by a proper shape of the limbs joined with a certain sweetness of color.

->page 2. §. 1.<-

**Confucius** said: Man is born upright. If he is depraved, his continued life and escape from death is a matter of mere chance and is undeserved.

->§. 2.<-

**Confucius**, discussing three classes of men who profess virtue, said: Those who understand and have a clear perspective on what virtue is and how greatly it is to be sought are not to be compared with those who love it—that is, those who pursue virtue with zeal and affection. Furthermore, even these lovers of virtue are not to be compared with those who already find joy in possessing what they love. <note>This is the famous hierarchy of learning: knowing it, loving it, and finding delight in it.</note>

->§. 3.<-

About to hand down the correct method of teaching others, **Confucius** said: Starting from men of mediocre talent and ascending upward, one can certainly propose more sublime teachings, for they will grasp them and learn successfully. But starting from men of mediocre talent and descending downward, one cannot propose more sublime things: for both the students themselves and those who wish to teach them will waste their "oil and labor." <note>original: *oleum & operam perdent*; a Latin idiom for wasting time and effort.</note>

->folio 17. page 1.<-

The disciple **Fan Chi** <gloss>Fân chî</gloss> questioned his Master about Prudence <note>original: *Prudentia*; often translated as Wisdom (*Zhi*)</note>, or the prudent man. **Confucius** replied: "Whoever exerts himself earnestly in human virtues, or those which most become a man; and who likewise honors the spirits <note>original: *spiritus*; referring to ancestral or local deities</note> while dealing with them only from a distance—this man can finally be called truly prudent." The disciple **Fan Chi** then questioned him about the virtue <term>Gîn</term> <note>original: *Gîn* (Ren); often translated as Benevolence, Humanity, or Perfect Virtue</note>, or about inner, solid, and consummate virtue. **Confucius** replied: "If a man of true and solid virtue works first, and only afterwards obtains the fruit, then he can be called a man of true and solid virtue."

<summary>This page defines the "Junzi" (Noble Person) as a perfect balance between natural sincerity and cultural refinement, while also categorizing the levels of devotion to virtue and defining wisdom as a focus on human duty over spiritual interference.</summary>

<keywords>Junzi, Ren, Fan Chi, nature vs culture, education, wisdom, spirits, virtue, humanism</keywords>

# BOOK THREE

->page 2. Section 1.<-

**Confucius** said: People who are perceptive of what is fair and true, and who are industrious, delight in water; but men of solid virtue delight in the mountains. For the former—that is, the perceptive and industrious—are in perpetual motion like flowing streams while they investigate things and the search for the causes of things; they deduce one thing from another, and are always active and striving. The latter, however—men of solid virtue—remain firm and immobile in perpetual rest, just like the mountains. The perceptive and fair indeed live joyfully; however, those who possess virtue live long lives because they live so placidly and so tranquilly.

**Confucius** said: Regarding the Kingdom of **Qi** <note>original: *çi*</note>, if by some stroke of fortune it should one day be restored, and even if that change for the better or restoration occurs, it would still hardly reach the current state of our Kingdom of **Lu**. But the Kingdom of **Lu**, as soon as it allows for a similar change or renewal, will immediately attain the virtue and governing principles of its Ancient Kings. For since that civil courtesy and respect still flourish there, nothing is greatly lacking except to restore and renew the method of ruling subjects with clemency and justice, which has nearly collapsed.

->folio 18. page 1. Section 1.<-

To teach that every mortal ought either to live up to their name <note>meaning their title or role in society</note> or else set it aside, **Confucius** used a metaphor taken from the square tablet commonly called a *gu* <note>original: *cu*</note>, which the Chinese used to use as paper for writing. He said: If that square tablet, the *gu*, is not four-cornered, how can it be called square? If a King does not perform what belongs to a King, or a man what belongs to a man, how can they be called a King or a man?

->Section 2.<-

**Zai Wo** <note>original: *CAIngo*</note>, a disciple, professed to follow virtue (and especially piety), though he did not yet fully grasp the nature and properties of this virtue. Questioning the Master, he asked: Should a truly pious man, a lover of others, be such that even if someone of uncertain reliability reports there is a man in a danger in a well, he would immediately follow the messenger and lower himself into the well at the risk of his own life? To this question, **Confucius** replied: Why would he act in this way? A perfected man is indeed bound to help those in danger, but he is neither bound nor lawfully able to do so at such immediate risk that he helps neither the other nor himself. Therefore, it is acceptable to be deceived, but it is not acceptable to perish.

# CHINESE KNOWLEDGE

<gloss>Page 2. Section I.</gloss>
**Confucius** said: A true Philosopher is engaged in a very wide study of all books and sciences; examining everything, he limits and directs his findings to the rule of right reason. And in this way, it will be possible for him to never deviate from truth and virtue.

<gloss>Section 2.</gloss>
**Confucius** once held a magistracy in the Kingdom of **Wei** <term>Guéi: one of the central states during the Spring and Autumn period</term>, during the reign of King Ling <note>original: *Lim*</note>. Furthermore, the King's wife, named **Nanzi** <term>Nân-çu: an empress historically notorious for her influence and alleged scandals</term>, was seized with a desire for the Philosopher. The Philosopher, well aware that the woman was of ill repute, had repeatedly excused himself from a meeting. But when she persisted (since it was the custom then that all who held magistracy were also presented to the Queen), **Confucius**, fearing to cause offense, finally approached Queen **Nanzi**. His disciple **Zilu** <term>çu-lu: known for his impulsive and bold character</term> did not quite approve of his Master's action. But **Confucius**, relying on the excellent testimony of his own conscience, without hesitation bound himself by a religious oath, saying: "If I have admitted anything wicked or shameful into my heart, if I have committed any sin, may Heaven curse me! May Heaven curse me!"

The same King **Ling**, *as the Chinese chronicles record, while inspecting the city one day with Queen **Nanzi** riding together in the same chariot, happened to encounter Confucius and invited him to board one of the chariots following the Royal one. But the Philosopher, greatly offended by such immodesty of the man and woman—even though they were spouses—sitting together in the same chariot, indignantly refused the honor of the offered chariot and departed.* <note>The "immodesty" refers to the public display of the King and Queen together, which Confucius viewed as a breach of ritual propriety.</note>

---

<gloss>folio 19. page 1. Section 1.</gloss>
**Confucius** said: The golden mean <note>original: *Aurea mediocritas*</note>, or holding the middle path in all things—even in daily and ordinary actions—this at last is the mark of true and perfect virtue. But how arduous and sublime it is! That it belongs to only a few mortals is by now an old saying; it is an old evil and an old complaint.

<gloss>Section 2.</gloss>
The disciple **Zigong** <term>çu: refers here to Zi-gong, one of Confucius's most eloquent students</term>, when speaking about that virtue of **Ren** <term>Gin: the core Confucian virtue of humaneness or benevolence</term> insofar as it is called piety <note>original: *pietas*; likely referring to universal love or filial devotion</note>, consulted **Confucius**, saying: "If there were someone who bestowed benefits most generously upon others and was also able to assist everyone, what would you think? Could such a person be considered and called truly pious?" **Confucius** replied: "How could such a thing be accomplished solely by the kind of piety you propose? Here, holiness <note>original: *sanctitas*</note> is also necessary. Even **Yao** and **Shun** <term>Yâo & Xún: legendary Sage-Kings of China's golden age</term> themselves struggled with this; they felt their own strength was unequal to attaining this virtue."

<gloss>page 2. Section 1.</gloss>
THAT holiness, then, or charity and piety which I require, my disciple, is a constant affection of the soul consistent with reason, by which one, having cast aside all care for one's own utility or convenience, embraces all the people of the world just as if they were one and the same with oneself.

# BOOK THREE

<note>original: *LIBER TERTIUS*</note>

...and indeed he possesses and displays a shared feeling with others in times of both prosperity and adversity. For example, such a pious man, desiring to be uplifted and to flourish himself, immediately by his counsel, resources, and effort, also uplifts any others who are either held down to the ground by natural poverty and weakness, or who have been afflicted and thrown down from a height by a more serious misfortune. Likewise, he who wishes to successfully penetrate into matters cannot bear to see others who either wander blindly or succumb, overcome by labors and difficulties; but he himself leaves nothing untried and strives by every means to help both the former and the latter. In this way, he enables others to also penetrate and break through the difficulties standing in their way, and to finally struggle successfully out of the darkness of errors and ignorance. Furthermore, once this charity or piety <note>The Latin *charitas* and *pietas* are used here to translate the Chinese concept of *Ren* (仁), which the translators interpreted through the lens of Christian love and social duty</note> has settled in the minds of mortals, then indeed the whole world will be like a single family; indeed, all men will be like a single man, and whatever exists anywhere will seem to be of one and the same substance, because of that wonderful connection and order between the highest, middle, and lowest things.

->§. 2.<-

Therefore, let us love others as we love ourselves: Let us measure others by ourselves: Let us estimate the labors and advantages of others based on our own. Finally, to embrace everything in a few words, to know how to take or establish a comparison with others from near at hand (that is, from ourselves), wishing or not wishing for them everything that we ourselves wish or do not wish to happen to us—this, finally, can be called the art and rule of practicing the virtue of <term>Gin: the Jesuit transcription of *Ren* (仁), the foundational Confucian virtue of humaneness or benevolence</term>, or the aforementioned charity and piety.

# OF THE THIRD BOOK
## PART FOUR

->Folio 1, page 1, paragraph 1.<-

Confucius says: I am a messenger, or a narrator, and not the author of the doctrine which I make known. I believe in and love antiquity, from which I studiously borrow and select those things which serve my purpose; imitating in myself that famous old man *Lao Peng*: <note>original: *Pùm*. This refers to Lao Peng, a legendary figure in Chinese culture renowned for his longevity and his role as a preserver of traditions.</note> for he was the first to hand down the monuments of the ancients to posterity with a similar effort.

<margin>The Chinese say that this Lao Peng lived for seven hundred years with a body that was always vigorous; and that he lived during the times of the Shang <note>original: *Xam*</note> family; while they were ruling, he also held a magisterial office.</margin>

->page 2, section 1.<-

Confucius says: To devote oneself to silence, and to recall to memory those things which we have either seen or heard; to apply oneself to studies seriously and constantly, and not to be affected by weariness; to teach others, and not to be broken or exhausted by the labor of teaching: in what way have these three things ever truly been present in me? <note>Confucius often spoke with great humility, questioning if he lived up to his own high standards of constant learning and tireless teaching.</note>

->section 2.<-

Confucius says: Not to have cultivated virtue more studiously; not to have discussed the best sciences and disciplines more frequently; to have heard what is right and consistent with reason, yet not to have been able to apply myself to them; finally, not to have been able to correct my vices according to my desire: these four things, I say, are my grief and a just cause for sorrow.

->section 3.<-

The disciples celebrated their Master *Confucius* everywhere with this praise: "Our master Confucius," they said, "whenever he lived at home alone and free from business, how pleasant and affable he was, with what an open and serene mind! How courteous and calm!"

<summary>This page presents Confucius as a humble "transmitter" of ancient wisdom rather than an innovator, while recording his personal anxieties about his progress in virtue and his disciples' admiration for his serene private character.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the reflections of Confucius on his own life and his methods for teaching and attaining virtue. It transitions from his general humility to specific steps for self-improvement and his requirements for students.</meta>

# BOOK THREE. 2
<note>original: *LIBER TERTIUS*</note>

### Folio 2, page 1, section 1.

Confucius, now an old man, used to say: "My physical weakness is truly great now. It has been a long time since I have seen that great master **Zhou Gong** <note>original: *cheu cum*. Referring to the Duke of Zhou, a hero of early Chinese history whom Confucius considered a model of virtue.</note> in my dreams, as I used to do when I was in the vigor of my youth."

### Section 2.

In this paragraph and the four that follow, the Philosopher declares the manner in which the study of virtue is completed and perfected—that is, what a student of virtue must do to become perfect in it. **Confucius** therefore says: "First, the mind must be fixed upon the agreeable dictates of reason, or upon that which reason demands of us."

### Section 3.

Second, virtue must be seized or grasped with a serious and great spirit.

### Section 4.

Third, one must firmly apply oneself to the absolute perfection of interior virtue.

### Page 2, section 1.

Fourth, so that practice may flourish, one should seek that ease and skill in the **liberal arts** <term>liberal arts: The "Six Arts" of ancient Chinese education: ritual, music, archery, charioteering, calligraphy, and mathematics.</term> and duties which follow from such exercise.

### Section 2.

It was a long-accepted custom among the Chinese that anyone who entrusted himself to another to be instructed in the liberal disciplines should offer a <term>minerval: a tuition fee or gift for a teacher, named after Minerva, the Roman goddess of wisdom.</term> to the Master upon their first arrival. Furthermore, the humblest kind of tuition gift was a bundle of dried meat consisting of at least ten pieces. **Confucius** says: "Whoever has come to me to be admitted into my teaching—starting from those who offered a bundle of dried meat, the lowest kind of gift, and ascending to others who offered more sumptous things—there is not one of them I have ever failed to instruct and teach."

### Section 3.

Confucius says: "In the school of wisdom, if a man does not exert effort, I certainly will not instruct him. Likewise, if he does not open his mind to me through words (perhaps because he is unwilling or unable), I will neither understand him nor be able to perceive his errors or doubts. Finally, if I present one corner of a square to him and he cannot infer the other three corners for himself, I will certainly not repeat the same thing to him in vain." <note>original: *crambem*. This refers to the Latin proverb *crambe repetita* (reheated cabbage), meaning a tedious repetition of the same material.</note>

### Folio 3, page 1, section 1.

In this and the following paragraph, the disciples praise their Master. They say: "**Confucius**, having performed funeral rites and sitting afterward at a solemn banquet beside those who had led the funeral, would hardly think of the food placed before him and never satisfied his hunger; he was so gripped by grief and longing for the one who had died."

<summary>This page outlines Confucius’s four steps for attaining perfection—reason, grasping virtue, internalizing it, and practicing the arts—while describing his inclusive but rigorous teaching philosophy and his deep respect for mourning rituals.</summary>
<keywords>Duke of Zhou, steps to virtue, liberal arts, tuition, dried meat, pedagogical method, mourning rituals, grief</keywords>

# BOOK THREE
## PART FOUR

->Folio 1, page 1, paragraph 1.<-

Confucius says: I am a herald <note>original: *Præco*</note>, or a transmitter, and not the author of the doctrine which I make public. I believe in and love antiquity, from which I studiously borrow and excerpt those things which pertain to my purpose; imitating in myself that famous old man **Lao Peng** <note>original: *Pùm*. Likely referring to Lao Peng, a figure in Chinese tradition often compared to Methuselah, known for transmitting ancient knowledge.</note>: for he, in earlier times, handed down the monuments of the ancients to posterity with a similar effort.
The **Chinese** <note>original: *Sinenses*</note> say that this **Lao Peng** lived for seven hundred years with a body that was always vigorous; and that he reached the times of the **Shang** <note>original: *Xam*</note> family; during whose reign he also held a magistracy.

->page 2, section 1.<-

Confucius says: To devote oneself to silence, and to recall to memory those things which we have either seen or heard; to apply oneself seriously and constantly to studies, and not to be affected by weariness; to teach others, and not to be broken or exhausted by the labor of teaching: in what manner have these three things been in me at any time? <note>This is a rhetorical expression of humility, suggesting he has not yet mastered these qualities to his own satisfaction.</note>

->section 2.<-

Confucius says: Not to have cultivated virtue more studiously; not to have discussed the best sciences and disciplines more frequently; to have heard things that are right and consistent with reason, yet not to have had the strength to transfer myself to them; finally, not to have had the strength to amend my vices according to my wish: these four things, I say, are my grief and a just cause for sorrow.

->section 3.<-

The disciples celebrated their Master **Confucius** everywhere with this praise: "Our master Confucius," they said, "whenever he lived at home alone and free from business, how pleasant and affable he was, with what an open and serene mind! How courteous and calm!"

->Folio 2, page 1, section 1.<-

Confucius, now an old man, used to say: "Truly, my weakness is now great. It has been a long time since I no longer see—as I used to when my youth was vigorous—that great master **Duke of Zhou** <note>original: *cheu cum*. The Duke of Zhou was a cultural hero whom Confucius considered the architect of the ideal social order.</note> in a dream."

->section 2.<-

In this paragraph and the four following ones, the Philosopher declares the manner in which the study of virtue is finally consummated and perfected; or rather, what the student of virtue must do to emerge perfect in it. **Confucius** therefore says: "First, the mind must be fixed upon the consistent dictates of reason, or upon that which reason demands of us."

->section 3.<-

"Second, virtue must be seized or grasped with a serious and great spirit."

->section 4.<-

"Third, one must apply oneself firmly to the absolute perfection of interior virtue."

->page 2, section 1.<-

"Fourth, one must ensure that practice flourishes, along with the ease and skill in the liberal arts and duties that follow from such exercise."

->section 2.<-

It was an ancient custom received among the **Chinese** <note>original: *Sinas*</note> that whoever gave himself to another to be instructed in liberal disciplines should offer a <term>minerval<gloss>a fee for instruction, named by the translator after Minerva, the Roman goddess of wisdom and weaving</gloss></term> to the Master upon their very first arrival. Furthermore, the humblest kind of tuition gift was a bundle of dried meat <note>original: *fasciculus siccatæ carnis*; in Chinese tradition, this is the *shixiu*.</note> consisting of at least ten pieces. **Confucius** says: "Whoever has come to me to be admitted into my discipline, beginning from those who offered a bundle of dried meat—the lowest kind of tuition—and ascending from these to others who offered more lavish gifts; I have never failed to instruct and teach any of them."

->section 3.<-

Confucius says: "In the school of wisdom, if someone does not apply effort, I indeed will not educate him. Likewise, for one who does not open his mind to me with words—because he either will not or cannot—I will neither understand him, nor will I be able to perceive his errors or doubts. Finally, when I present one corner of a square, and yet he does not infer the remaining three corners for himself; for such a person I will certainly not repeat the same <term>monotony<gloss>original: *crambem*, referring to the Latin proverb *crambe bis cocta* or 'twice-cooked cabbage,' used to describe tedious repetition</gloss></term> anymore in vain."

->Folio 3, page 1, section 1.<-

In this and the following paragraph, the disciples praise their Master. They say: "**Confucius**, having performed funeral duties and then sitting at the side of those who led the funeral during the solemn feast; thinking hardly at all of the food set before him, he never filled his hunger: so great was the mourning and longing he felt for the one who had died."

<summary>This page outlines Confucius’s path to moral perfection through reason and the arts, his policy of teaching students regardless of their wealth, and his requirement for students to be self-driven. It also highlights his profound emotional commitment to ritual mourning.</summary>
<keywords>Duke of Zhou, path to virtue, education, tuition gifts, dried meat, pedagogical method, mourning rituals, Chinese customs</keywords>

# CHINESE KNOWLEDGE
<note>original: *SCIENTIÆ SINICÆ*. This refers to the "Chinese Sciences" or "Chinese Knowledge," the title of the work translated by Jesuit missionaries.</note>

->Section 2<-

This same **Confucius**, on a day of mourning, would weep profusely for the deceased, and on such days he would not sing at all. <note>Ritual propriety was central to Confucius; he believed that one's internal state of grief should be reflected in their outward behavior, such as abstaining from music.</note>

->Section 3<-

**Confucius**, speaking to his disciple **Yan Hui** <note>original: *Yen yven*</note>, said: "When we are called upon and employed for public duties, let us take up the affairs of the State <note>original: *Rempublicam*</note> immediately and without hesitation. Conversely, when that dignity is lost, let us immediately hide away in our private homes without complaint or distress of mind. I believe only you and I are of such a character."

->Page 2, Section 1<-

The disciple **Zilu** <note>original: *çu lu*</note>, hearing the Master praise his fellow student, and being conscious of his own military courage, said: "If the Master (speaking in the third person out of reverence, according to the common custom of the nation) were to lead the **Three Armies** <note>The "Three Armies" was the standard full military force of a large state in ancient China.</note>, whom would he choose as a colleague?"

->Section 2<-

**Confucius**, in order to dampen the vain and warlike spirit of his disciple, replied: "I would certainly not wish to lead troops with a man who would attack a wild tiger with his bare hands, or commit himself to a wide and rapid river without a raft or boat—one who might face a thousand deaths and yet feel no fear. For such rashness has rarely been useful; it brings loss very often, and honor never. It is indeed necessary not to be perturbed in difficult circumstances; but when a doubtful and unforeseen danger presents itself, then most of all must one use the counsel of a present mind, and conduct oneself with consideration and vigilance. I would much prefer someone who strives to anticipate, and indeed takes pleasure in perceiving, what might happen in the future, determining beforehand what might occur on either side of a situation."

->Folio 4, page 1, section 1<-

**Confucius**, criticizing the insane efforts of men in amassing wealth, said: "If riches could indeed be obtained by human strength and industry, I would even act as a **groom** <term>groom<gloss>original: *Agasonem*, a stable-hand or horse-keeper; considered a very humble occupation</gloss></term> to obtain them, if it were necessary. But if abundance and wealth cannot be prepared by human strength and industry, but depend on Heaven alone, I shall instead follow what I love, and what I am bound to and able to follow: the light and the guidance of reason bestowed upon me by Heaven."

->Section 2<-

Three things are said to have been the focus of **Confucius’s** greatest vigilance, care, and effort: **ritual purification** <note>original: *abstinentia*. Specifically, the fasting and spiritual preparation required before performing religious sacrifices.</note> before performing sacred rites, the conflict with an enemy, and illness.

# BOOK THREE

### §. 3.

**Shao** <note>original: *Xao*. This refers to the ritual music of the legendary Emperor Shun.</note> is the name or genre of music formerly established by the Emperor **Shun** <note>original: *Xún*</note>, in which are contained the virtues and praises of that great Lawgiver called **Yao**; by whom **Shun** himself had been first admitted into a partnership of the Empire and thereafter into the succession. Therefore, while the **Zhou** <note>original: *Cheu*</note> family was gradually collapsing, **Confucius**, being by chance in the Kingdom of **Qi** <note>original: *çi*</note> and hearing that **Shao** music there, was suddenly affected by such a great sense of pleasure that, although he was nourished by it for a full three months, he did not perceive the flavor of the meat he was eating. Indeed, he himself used to say: "I never would have thought that the one who composed this music had reached such sweetness."

### P. 2. §. 1.

Formerly, when the King <note>The title used is *Lim cum*, referring to Duke Ling of Wei.</note> of the Kingdom of **Wei** <note>original: *Gŭéi*</note> had a son named **Kuai Kui** <note>original: *Quái quei*</note>: this man, because he had attempted to kill his adulterous stepmother, was expelled from the Kingdom by his father. He therefore fled to the neighboring Kingdom of **Jin** <note>original: *çin*</note>, but left behind his son, whose name was **Zhe** <note>original: *Che*, also known as Duke Chu of Wei</note>. In the meantime, Duke **Ling** <note>original: *Lim cum*</note> died. The people placed the son of the fugitive Prince upon his grandfather's throne. Those who had given refuge to the father heard of this. They condemned the act. They brought the fugitive father back. The son resisted and, having secretly sent a band of armed men, prohibited him from coming. Amidst these events, there were various rumors and opinions among the people. Some denied that it was lawful for a son to hold the Kingdom while his father was alive and against his will. But others, on the contrary, argued that the father had long ago forfeited his right to the fatherhood and the Kingdom by laying a trap for the life of the Mother <note>Refers to his father's wife, the stepmother Nanzi.</note>, even if she was not his own biological mother. Certainly, it seemed the scepter should be deferred to no one other than he who was both innocent and a son. Furthermore, at the same time, **Confucius** was living in this very Kingdom of **Wei**. Therefore, his disciple **Yan Hui** <note>original: *Gen yen*</note> asked his fellow student **Zigong** <note>original: *çu cum*</note> whether **Confucius** also favored this same **Zhe**, Prince of the Kingdom of **Wei**? **Zigong** immediately replied: "Very well; I shall find out."

### §. 2.

In the Kingdom of **Guzhu** <note>original: *çu cho*</note>, the King had three sons: the eldest was called **Bo Yi** <note>original: *Pey*</note>, the youngest **Shu Qi** <note>original: *Xo çi*</note>, and the name of the second is not recorded. The Father, who loved the youngest more tenderly, declared him the heir of the Kingdom when he was close to death. But after the Father died, the subjects wanted the eldest to reign, for they believed the crown was owed to him by right of birth and order. But he, placing the will of his Father above both his own right and the wishes of his people, voluntarily ceded the Kingdom to his brother. But the younger brother, no less mindful of fraternal love than the other was of filial observance, constantly urged his brother to undertake the government of the Kingdom, because he was the first-born. When this contest of such rare grace had lasted a very long time, and neither could persuade the other of what each felt was owed to the other by a certain right; so that an end might finally be put to such an unusual contention, both finally fled secretly from their own people, retreating from the court into the wilderness—both victors, and both vanquished. And so, the second of the brothers took up the [throne] left behind by...

...he took up the kingdom with the common consent of the people and the nobles. Furthermore, this contest between the brothers, as to which should yield the crown to the other, was diametrically opposed to that contest which (as we mentioned a little above) then existed between the father and the son <note>This refers to the conflict between the exiled Prince Kuai Kui and his son, Duke Zhe, who had taken the throne.</note>. Therefore, the disciple **Zigong** <note>original: *çu cum*</note>, cleverly seeking the Philosopher’s opinion through a roundabout way, entered to consult the Master. He asked, "What sort of men were the two brothers **Boyi** and **Shuqi**?" <note>original: *Pe y* & *Xo-çi*</note>. The Philosopher, noticing where that inquiry was heading, replied: "**Boyi** and **Shuqi** were entirely among the men of proven virtue and wisdom of old." The disciple **Zigong** pressed further and said: "But is it believable that they remained steadfast, and did not later repent of their deed and their flight?" Then **Confucius** said: "In this deed, both sought true virtue, and they found true virtue. Why then would repentance have come upon them where neither error nor sin preceded it?" By this response, **Confucius** sufficiently declared what he thought of the wicked **Zhe** <note>original: *Che*</note>, the usurper of his father’s sovereignty; for while he thus praised for their virtue and wisdom those who had yielded the Kingdom to one another, he certainly condemned him whose impious rashness and ambition had violated the piety owed to a father, however much a fountain of faults <note>original: *fonti* (likely a typo for *fontem*, referring to the father as a source of trouble)</note> he might be. **Zigong** therefore went out and said to his fellow disciple **Ran You** <note>original: *Gen yeu*</note>: "**Confucius** by no means favors the faction of Prince **Zhe**."

->folio 5. page 1.<-

**Confucius** used to say: I eat mostly very common and easily obtained food; I drink water, and while I refresh my strength with a brief sleep, I bend my elbow and place it under my head, and it serves as my pillow. In the meantime, I affirm this: that a Philosopher’s pleasure still stands firm in the midst of this. Virtue entirely has its own delights in the midst of hardships. However, whoever is devoid of virtue, even if the same man be rich and wealthy, and thus—as usually happens—honored; to me he will certainly be like a passing cloud.

->page 2. section 1.<-

**Confucius**, at seventy years of age, used to say: If Heaven were to grant me a few more years of life, so that I might thoroughly learn the doctrine of the book **Yi Jing** <note>original: *Te kim*; the "Book of Changes," an ancient manual of divination and philosophy</note>, that is, of changes; I would be able, certainly, to be free from at least any more serious fault or crime.

->section 2.<-

**Confucius** (as the disciples record) had three things which he used more frequently in his discourses. The **Odes**, that is, the Maxims of the ancient Sages and Kings, bound in meter. The **Chronicles**, or the deeds performed—whether rightly or wrongly—by the same Kings and their ancestors. Finally, the duties and rites studiously observed and practiced by those same Kings. These three, I say, were almost everything of which **Confucius** would discourse here and there.

# BOOK THREE <note>original: *LIBER TERTIUS*</note>

->Folio 6, page 1, section 1.<-

<margin>When</margin>The Governor of the city of **She** <note>original: *Xe*</note>—an arrogant man who rashly claimed a title far superior to his actual office—asked the disciple **Zilu** <note>original: *çu lù*</note> what kind of man his Master was. **Zilu** did not answer him.

->Section 2.<-

When **Confucius** learned of the governor’s inquiry and his disciple’s silence, he said to him: "Why did you not respond in this way? 'He is the kind of man who labors at nothing more than his tireless progress in the study of virtue and the fine arts. If there is anything he has not yet fully mastered, he exerts all his strength and effort toward it, even to the point of forgetting to eat until he achieves it. Once he has succeeded, he is filled with such joy that he no longer remembers the previous sadness or hardship; nor does he notice that, in the midst of all this, old age has already nearly arrived.' This," I say to you, "is how you could have answered the inquiring governor."

->Page 2, section 1.<-

**Confucius** said: "I was not born with wisdom (or, I am not one who appeared in this world wise from the start). Rather, from my earliest years, I have always been a lover and a student of antiquity, applying all my effort and diligence to it. It is through these means that I have acquired whatever wisdom is attributed to me."

->Section 2.<-

**Confucius** (as his disciples record) spoke only very rarely, and then briefly, about four things: namely, about exotic, unusual, or foreign things, such as monsters and portents; about political factions, dissensions, and public disturbances; and finally, about spirits. He avoided the latter because their power, efficacy, and nature are so subtle and sublime—and so far removed from human senses—that there is a danger in speaking of them in a manner they deserve.

->Page 2.<-

**Confucius** said: "If even only three of us walk together, there will undoubtedly be a teacher for me among them. There will be, I say, two from whom I may profit. For example: let one be upright and the other wicked. I will soon select the good points or virtues of the former and follow them by imitation; as for the latter, I will silently observe his evils or vices and examine myself. If I find myself guilty of the same, I will soon correct it."

->Folio 7, page 1, section 1.<-

**Confucius** had traveled from the Kingdom of **Wei** <note>original: *Guéi*</note> into the Kingdom of **Song** <note>original: *Sum*</note>, where he exercised his disciples every day in the shade of a very large tree. Furthermore, the local prefect, named **Huan Tui** <note>original: *Von túi*</note>, because he hated **Confucius** and his doctrine, ordered that tree to be cut down. This event struck fear into the hearts of the disciples, who were afraid that the Master himself might be removed from the living...

...would ponder. But **Confucius**, recognizing the fear of his followers, spoke thus: "Since Heaven has produced virtue and the gifts of nature within me, and since my life depends entirely upon Heaven, why then should that prefect **Huan Tui** <note>original: *Vân tûi*; a military official in the State of Song who attempted to assassinate Confucius</note> harass me so? Does a mortal attempt to fight with Heaven?"

->§. 2.<-

Wishing to free his disciples from a certain suspicion, **Confucius** said: "Is it really so, my two or three disciples, that you think of me as hiding something from you regarding the pursuit of virtue and wisdom? Truly, I affirm to you that I employ no reticence or concealment with you. In truth, I have never done anything that I have not shared and made known openly to you, my disciples. This is certainly the kind of person I am."

->Page 2, Section 1.<-

Although **Confucius**, as was just said, concealed nothing of sound doctrine from his followers, he nonetheless instructed them primarily in four areas: In literature—that is, the books **Shijing** <note>original: *Xi kim*; The Classic of Poetry</note> and **Shujing** <note>original: *Xu kim*; The Classic of History</note>—as well as in every liberal discipline and science. Secondly, in the use and practice of all they had learned. In the third and fourth place, he constantly urged his followers to persist in a thoroughly serious and sincere will in whatever they did, joined with faith and constancy, and with a certain strength of an unconquerable mind.

->§. 2.<-

**Confucius** said: "I have not yet been able to see a holy man; however, that I might one day be able to see a man who excels others in virtue and wisdom—this indeed could still happen."

->§. 3.<-

**Confucius** also said: "I have not yet been able to see a man who is thoroughly upright and of perfect integrity. However, if I might be permitted to see someone who possesses strength and constancy in the pursuit of virtue and wisdom that they have undertaken; this indeed could still happen."

->§. 4.<-

**Confucius** said: "To not possess, and yet to pretend to possess; to be empty and devoid of doctrine and virtue, and yet to pretend to have an abundance and fullness of them; to be meager and thin, and yet to display some kind of greatness and excellence: a pretender of this sort, though he may perhaps deceive men for a very short time, will nonetheless struggle greatly to maintain the consistency of his acting, so that his fraud and pretense will eventually be revealed."

->Folio 8, Page 1, Section 1.<-

**Confucius**, as his disciples used to recall, when he happened to spend time in private fishing or fowling <note>the hunting of birds</note>, would fish only with a single hook and a rod, and not with nets. Similarly, when he went fowling, [he used] a cord [attached to] an arrow...

...[he used a cord] to strike, with which he would seek one or two birds flying past; but he did not strike those at rest. <note>This passage refers to Confucius's practice of fishing with a line rather than a net and shooting only birds in flight, demonstrating a sportsmanlike compassion even in hunting.</note>

### §. 2.

**Confucius** said: "How is it that there are men so ignorant of things, yet so active and ready? I, at least, do not have this fault: hearing many things, selecting the best from them and following it; likewise seeing many things and remembering them all, so that I might profit from everything. This is the second rank of knowledge <note>original: *sciendi secunda classis*; the first class being those born with innate knowledge</note>, which is the one I apply myself to."

### §. 3.

The village of **Hu-xiang** <note>original: *Hu hiam*</note> was a difficult place for discussions on virtue to be taken seriously, due to the wickedness or dullness of its inhabitants. One day, a boy from there appeared and presented himself openly to **Confucius**, who kindly admitted him as he requested. Seeing this, the disciples were somewhat offended.

### P. 2. §. 1.

**Confucius**, becoming aware of this, said: "I admitted him just now so that he might enter my teaching; I did not admit him so that I might immediately cast him out. Why then this vehemence and your offense? Whenever any man has renewed himself so that he may be admitted into my school and discipline, I shall certainly accept this renewal and his purpose of a new life. However, I am not a sponsor or a guarantor for his future life, nor for whether he will persevere."

### §. 2.

**Confucius** said: "Is virtue perhaps far away from us? Surely, if I desire virtue, this very virtue has come to me. It is not to be sought outside, for it is born with us."

### §. 3.

A high official <term>Mandarin <gloss>a senior administrative official</gloss></term> of the **Kingdom of Chen** named **Su-pai** <note>original: *Su pai*; likely the Sima or Minister of Justice of the state of Chen</note> asked **Confucius** whether **Duke Zhao** <note>original: *Chao*</note>, the Prince of the **Kingdom of Lu**, was well-versed in the sacred rites and laws. **Confucius** replied that he was indeed well-versed in the rites.

### f. 9. p. 1. §. 1.

After **Confucius** had left, the official greeted a disciple of **Confucius** named **Wu-ma-qi** <note>original: *Vû ma ki*</note>, who happened to cross his path. Approaching him, he said: "I have always heard that the perfect man does not engage in flattery. Does the Philosopher, then, also flatter at times? Is it not well known that the Princes of both the kingdoms of **Wu** and **Lu** share the same surname, **Ji** <note>original: *Ki*</note>? And yet, the King of your **Kingdom of Lu** took a wife from the royal family of **Wu**, who has the same surname as his own—a thing forbidden by the Laws of the Kingdom. Indeed, to better hide the matter, he did not call his bride by her true and proper surname, **Wu Meng-ji**; but by the fictitious name **Wu Meng-zi**. Truly, if that King is considered an expert in rites while he thus mocks them, then I ask you: what mortal would not be considered an expert in rites and laws, even if he violates and despises them?"

Seeking to free his disciples from a certain suspicion, **Confucius** said: "Is it truly so, my two or three disciples, that you think of me as hiding anything from you that pertains to the study of virtue and wisdom? ->p. 2. §. 1.<-

Although **Confucius**, as was just said, concealed nothing of sound doctrine from his followers, he nevertheless instructed them primarily in four things: First, in letters—that is, the books of the *Shijing* <note>original: *Xi kim*; The Classic of Poetry</note> and the *Shujing* <note>original: *Xu kim*; The Classic of History</note>—as well as in all the liberal disciplines and sciences. Second, in the use and practical exercise of everything they had learned. Third and fourth, he diligently impressed upon them that they should persist in an entirely serious and sincere will in whatever they did, joined with constant faith and a certain strength of an unconquered mind.

->§. 2.<-

**Confucius** said: "A holy man <note>original: *hominem sanctum*; referring to the 'Shengren' or Sage, the highest ideal in Confucianism</note> I have not yet been able to see; but that I might one day be able to see a man who excels others in virtue and wisdom—this indeed may still be possible."

->§. 3.<-

**Confucius** also said: "A man who is thoroughly upright and of integrity, I have not yet been able to see. But that I may be allowed to see someone who possesses the strength and constancy in his chosen study of virtue and wisdom—this truly may still be possible."

->§. 4.<-

**Confucius** said: "A man who does not have, yet pretends to have; who is empty and void of doctrine and virtue, yet pretends to have an abundance and fullness of them; who is meager and small, yet shows off some sort of greatness and excellence—a pretender <note>original: *Simulator*</note> of this kind, though he may perhaps deceive men for a very short time, will nevertheless struggle greatly to maintain the consistency of his pretense, so that his fraud and simulation do not eventually come to light."

->f. 8. p. 1. §. 1.<-

As his disciples used to recall, when **Confucius** was perhaps privately occupied with fishing or bird-catching, he fished only with a hook and rod, and not with nets. Similarly, when he went bird-catching, [he used] a cord [attached to] an arrow... <note>This passage emphasizes the Master's compassion; he would not use a net to take all the fish at once, nor shoot birds while they were nesting.</note>

# BOOK THREE
