...[The Master used a fishing line] but did not use a net; he would shoot at birds flying by, but he would not strike those at rest. <note>This describes Confucius's restraint and compassion even when hunting or fishing, refusing to take unfair advantage of animals.</note>

->§. 2.<-

**Confucius** said: "How is it that there are men so ignorant of things, and yet so active and ready to act? As for me, I at least do not have this fault: having heard many things, I select the best from them and follow them; likewise, I observe many things and remember them all, so that I might profit from everything. This is the second class of knowledge, to which I indeed apply myself." <note>Confucius distinguishes between innate wisdom (the first class) and the knowledge acquired through diligent study and observation (the second class), placing himself in the latter category.</note>

->§. 3.<-

The place of *Hu hiam* <note>Huxiang</note> was a difficult place for holding discourses on virtue, due to the wickedness or the slow-wittedness of its inhabitants. One day, a boy from that place appeared and openly presented himself to **Confucius**; the Master kindly admitted him when he requested an audience. Seeing this, the disciples were somewhat offended.

->p. 2. §. 1.<-

**Confucius**, learning of their reaction, said: "I admitted him just now so that he might enter into my discipline; I did not, however, admit him so that I might immediately repel him. Why, then, is there this vehemence and offense among you? Whenever any man has renewed himself so that he may be admitted into my school and discipline, I shall surely accept this renewal and his purpose for a new life. However, I am not a sponsor or a guarantor for his future life, as to whether he will persevere."

->§. 2.<-

**Confucius** said: "Is virtue perhaps far distant from us? Certainly, if I desire virtue, this very virtue has come to me. It is not to be sought outside ourselves, for it is born within us."

->§. 3.<-

The Minister of Justice <note>original: *Su pai*; the official title *Sibai*</note> of the Kingdom of *Chin* <note>Chen</note> asked **Confucius** whether *Chao* <note>Duke Zhao</note>, the Prince of the Kingdom of *Lù*, understood the rites and laws. **Confucius** replied that he did indeed understand the rites.

->f. 9. p. 1. §. 1.<-

After **Confucius** had left, the Minister greeted a disciple of **Confucius** named *Vù ma kì* <note>Wuma Qi</note>, whom he happened to meet, and approaching him, said: "I have always heard that a perfect man does not practice flattery. Does the *Philosopher* then sometimes flatter? Is it not well known that the Princes of both the kingdoms of *U* <note>Wu</note> and *Lù* are of the same surname, *Kì* <note>Ji</note>? And yet the King of your Kingdom of *Lù* took a wife from the royal family of *U*, who is of the same surname as his own, which is forbidden by the Laws of the Kingdom. <note>Ancient Chinese law strictly forbade marriage between people with the same surname, as they were considered to be of the same bloodline.</note> Indeed, so that the matter might be better hidden, he did not call his bride by her true and proper surname, *U mem kì* <note>Wu Meng Ji</note>, but by the false surname *U mem çu* <note>Wu Meng Zi</note>. Truly, if that King is considered skilled in the rites while he thus mocks them, who among mortals, I ask you, is not skilled in rites and laws, even if he violates and despises them?"

->p. 2 §. 1.<-

**Confucius** (as his disciples recall), while singing together with others, if he noticed that someone sang beautifully, would always ask for the song <note>original: *symphoniam*; referring here to a musical harmony or melody.</note> to be repeated, for he was nourished by it. ->§. 3.<-

**Confucius** said: "As for what pertains to holiness and that solid perfection of a sincere mind, with which the common people suppose me to be endowed; how indeed would I dare to claim such things for myself? Or perhaps they mean this one thing: that in the exercise and effort by which I strive toward perfection, I do not grow weary; and in teaching and instructing others, I am not exhausted? If so, they might be said to mean something: for this alone, and nothing more, I confess I am able to do." The disciple **Gong Xi Hua** <note>original: *Cum si hoâ*.</note>, hearing the Master say these things, sighed and said: "You do not allow yourself to be called holy and perfect, O most wise Master; yet you confess that your mind is eager and constant in the study of cultivating virtue, and utterly tireless in the instruction of others. ### BOOK THREE.

...with well-deserved humility; then indeed to demand those things which are auspicious and prosperous from them <note>The spirits or ancestors.</note>. As for me, I have not yet dared, by word or deed as far as I know, to offend the spirits; but I have done this: throughout my whole life, I have worked at this—to obey reason in all things. ->p. 2. §. 1.<-

**Confucius** said: "A man of integrity is always even-tempered, tranquil, and calm. A wicked man, however, is never without a troubled and bitter mind."

->§. 3.<-

**Confucius** (as his disciples testify) was gentle, courteous, and approachable; yet at the same time, he was venerable and composed. He was serious and strict when the situation demanded it; yet he was by no means morose, harsh, or fierce. He was dutiful, attentive to others, and respectful; yet in such a way that it was very temperate, pleasant, and without causing trouble or annoyance.

> **Tai pe** and **Yu chum** <note>Zhongyong</note> were the elder sons of **Tai vam**. When they knew that their younger brother **Ki lie** <note>Jili, the father of the future King Wen</note> was loved more dearly by their father, and that the Kingdom was intended for him, they became voluntary exiles for the sake of both and sought out the lands of the southern Barbarians. To hide their noble birth, they cut their hair and disfigured their bodies with tattoos and the marks of slaves. By this man [Tai pe] was founded the Kingdom of **Nanjing** <note>original: *Nankim*.</note> in the city of **Suzhou** <note>original: *Sucheü*.</note> around 1160 years before Christ, where his tomb still exists today.

...will hesitate and tremble at every single thing. If a man is brave and vigorous, yet lacks the restraint and moderation of wisdom <note>original: *prudentiæ*</note>, so that he rushes headlong into any task, he will surely become a disturber of both his household and the state. ->§. 2.<-

If indeed a person who holds a government office <note>The text uses the Latin *Magistratu fungitur*, referring to anyone in a position of public authority.</note> conducts himself with integrity and constancy toward his parents, then without a doubt his subjects, inspired by this example, will also flourish in virtue. Likewise, if he does not neglect or cast aside those who are older in age or superior in merit, his subjects will do the same; they will honor and care for their fellow citizens, whether they are burdened by years or distinguished by their service.

<margin>Folio 12, page 1, section 1</margin>
**Zengzi** <note>original: *Cem-çu*; a primary disciple of Confucius known for his focus on filial piety.</note>, the second among the disciples of Confucius and by far the most devoted to filial piety, was gravely ill and close to death. Having called together the disciples of his school, he said: "Come, uncover my feet, uncover my hands. These limbs, which I received from my parents, I have kept healthy and whole as far as I was able, so that I might more readily and for a longer time employ them in their service." This, he said, the **Book of Odes** <note>original: *Odarum liber*; the *Shijing*, an ancient collection of Chinese poetry.</note> taught him when it says: *Be fearful and trembling, anxious and cautious, like one approaching the deep and rapid bed of a river, or like one treading upon thin ice* <note>This is a metaphor for the constant vigilance a virtuous person must maintain to avoid moral failings.</note>, lest you commit anything that might grieve or offend your parents. "But indeed," he continued, "the end of my life, as I feel, is now at hand; and therefore I understand that from this moment forward I can be released from such cares." Having said this, he called out to them again, saying, "My fellow disciples," exhorting them with this final address to follow his example.

> Because of this beautiful—not to say foolish or superstitious—ideal of filial piety and obedience, many, under the rule of the **Tartars** <note>The Manchu Qing Dynasty, who had recently conquered China at the time of this Latin translation. They mandated the 'queue' hairstyle, which required shaving the forehead.</note>, preferred to be drowned or strangled by a noose rather than lose their hair. Indeed, it has always seemed more desirable and honorable here to end one's life by the noose than to be "diminished by the head" <note>This refers to both beheading and the forced shaving of the head.</note>. For it seems intolerable to the Chinese to return to their fathers and ancestors, as they say, without a head, and to afflict the spirits of their ancestors with such a spectacle and disgrace. They believe they would stand guilty of so heinous a crime if they were forced to offer to their parents' sight a body—which they received whole—now mutilated and truncated like the **Headless Ones** <note>original: *Acephalorum*; a reference to mythical or monstrous headless beings.</note>.

->§. 2.<-

When **Zengzi** was thus ill, the Governor of the **State of Lu** <note>The home state of Confucius and Zengzi.</note> named **Meng Jingzi** <note>original: *Mem-kim-çu*</note> came to visit him and inquired about his health.

### BOOK THREE

->p. 2. §. 1.<-

**Zengzi** <note>original: *CEM-çu*</note>, addressing a Prefect, said: "When birds are about to die, their song is mournful and full of sighs. But when men are close to death, their speech is then especially good and sincere."

->§. 2.<-

The Philosopher <note>Referring to the "Superior Man" or *Junzi*</note> said: "There are three things that a man of wisdom values most in the practice of true philosophy. First is the movement, form, and bearing of the body; by this means, he removes anything coarse or undisciplined. Second is a true and sincere expression of the face: for in this way, one comes closest to faithfulness and truth. Third is the grace of speech flowing from a wise mouth: for this will keep away anything that is unseemly or contrary to reason. As for the wicker and wooden vessels <note>These are the *dou* and *bian*, ritual containers for food</note> intended for the use of sacrifices and offerings, there are surely others whose duty it is to care for and look after them." <note>Zengzi suggests that the true gentleman focuses on his internal character and deportment rather than the technical minutiae of ritual ceremony, which can be left to minor officials.</note>

->f. 13. p. 1. §. 1.<-

**Zengzi**, recalling the virtue of his fellow disciple **Yan Hui** <note>original: *Yen hoei*, the favorite disciple of Confucius who predeceased him</note> who died long ago, said: "He was one who was powerful in wisdom and counsel, yet still sought advice even from the unskilled; he was one who flourished in genius and was rich in experience, yet would inquire for the sake of learning from those who were duller or less gifted; he possessed extraordinary talents, yet acted as if he had none. He was full, yet acted as if empty, because of a humble mind <note>original: *animi demissionem*</note> that thought most modestly of himself and highly of others. He was one who, when offended or provoked by another, did not become angry. Among thousands, there was only one such as my former companion **Yan Hui**, who was always laboring and training himself in this kind of pursuit of virtue."

->§. 2.<-

The same **Zengzi** said: "He to whom a 'six-palm' youth <note>original: *sex palmorum*; a metaphor for a young orphan prince or ward, roughly fifteen years old</note> can be entrusted; he to whom a dynasty <note>original: *dynastia*</note> of a hundred Chinese leagues <note>original: *stadiorum Sinicorum*</note> can be entrusted; and who, when a sudden calamity strikes and everything is at risk, cannot be shaken or discouraged so as to allow anything contrary to his dignity and constancy—should such a man not be judged an altogether exceptional man? Indeed, he should be judged an altogether exceptional man."

->p. 2. §. 1.<-

The same **Zengzi** said: "Men of letters <note>original: *litterati*, referring to the *Shi* or scholar-class</note> must not lack a broad and great spirit, as well as strength and constancy. For the burden, or duty, that rests upon their shoulders is exceedingly heavy, and the journey they must complete is long."

# CHINESE KNOWLEDGE

->§. 2.<-

True and sincere virtue is their own chosen burden; is it not truly heavy? Furthermore, it is only when death arrives that this labor and the necessity of sustaining such a great burden finally cease. Is it not, therefore, a long and lasting task, a span of time that equals the length of one's whole life? <note>Zengzi is describing the lifelong commitment required of a Confucian scholar to maintain moral integrity.</note>

->§. 3.<-

Confucius said: We who are lying down and crawling upon the ground are, in a certain way, raised up and set upright by the *Book of Odes*. <note>original: *Odarum librum*, referring to the *Shijing* or Classic of Poetry. Confucius believed poetry provided the initial emotional and moral awakening.</note>

->f. 14 p. 1. §. 1.<-

Furthermore, we stand firm and truly persist—preserving decorum and constancy throughout all of life—by means of the *Books of Rites*. <note>original: *Officiorum libros*, referring to the *Liji* or Book of Rites, which provides the structure for social conduct.</note>

->§. 2.<-

Finally, we are brought to perfection through music—that is, the music which, through its harmonic teaching, soothes and refines our very wills.

->p. 2. §. 1.<-

Confucius said: The people can indeed, and truly should, be commanded to follow the execution of the laws; but they cannot be commanded in the same way to pursue the study of deep knowledge. <note>This passage (Analects 8.9) is historically interpreted to mean that while the masses can be guided to act correctly, the intellectual "why" behind the virtue is a matter of personal cultivation that cannot be forced.</note>

->§. 2.<-

Confucius said: If a man is bold in spirit and delights in his own physical strength and power, yet also holds a deep hatred for the poverty that happens to weigh upon him, he will easily become a disturber of the public peace. Similarly, a wicked man—even if he is truly worthy of being disliked—will become a source of unrest if he is hated too vehemently or agitated by others. *Confucius* preferred to heal such people through the power of clemency rather than exasperating them with severity.

->§. 3.<-

Confucius said: Even if a man possesses the talents of the great **Duke of Zhou** <note>original: *Cheu-cum*, a legendary figure of virtue and statecraft from the early Zhou Dynasty</note> and all the excellence of his many faculties: if he should happen to lift himself up with arrogance and pride, and consequently become envious of the praise and glory of others, then whatever else remains in such a man—even if it is truly great—is not worthy for us even to turn our eyes toward.

->f. 15. p. 1. §. 1.<-

Confucius said: It is by no means easy to find a man who devotes himself to virtue and wisdom for a long time without having his mind fixed on a salary. <note>original: *censu*, referring to the official stipend or wealth gained from office.</note> If such men are found, the King should summon them and never let them go; but (adds the **Grand Secretary**) <note>original: *Colaus*, from the Chinese *Ge Lao*, a term for a high official or commentator</note> he should reject mere seekers of profit so completely that he never summons them at all.

->§. 2.<-

Confucius said: The philosopher who believes with firm faith in the truth he has been taught, and who spares no labor or study, will remain consistent within himself throughout the entirety of his life until death; he will always be in perfect harmony with virtue and the dictates of right reason.

<meta>catchword: § 3.</meta>

### BOOK THREE

<note>original: *LIBER TERTIUS*. While the header indicates Book Three, the content corresponds to the eighth book of the *Analects* (Taibo).</note>

->§. 3.<-

Therefore, a Philosopher does not enter a Kingdom that is in danger in such a way; nor does he ever live in a Kingdom that is in a state of turmoil. If virtue and respect for the laws exist within the Empire, then he makes himself known publicly. But if virtue is lacking in the Empire, then he remains hidden—living as a private citizen, certainly, but safe. <note>This reflects the Confucian principle of "timely" service: one should serve when the government is just and withdraw when it is corrupt to avoid compromising one's integrity.</note>

->p. 2. §. 1.<-

Conversely, when a Kingdom possesses virtue and the laws flourish, then to waste away in the leisure of a private life, wishing to live in poverty and remain neglected, is a cause for shame. However, when a Kingdom lacks virtue and the laws lie neglected, then for one who wishes to be called a Philosopher to serve the times and desire to increase his wealth and honors is an unworthy thing, and most especially scandalous and shameful.

->§. 2.<-

Confucius said: If you are not appointed to this or that office, you should not deliberate upon or involve yourself in its administration. <note>Analects 8.14. This emphasizes focusing on one's own duties rather than interfering in the responsibilities of others.</note>

->§. 3.<-

Confucius said: In my home Kingdom of *Lu*, when the Grand Master *Zhi* <note>original: *Chi*</note> began the musical performance, and the final stanza of the *Guan Ju* <note>original: *Quan-çi͡u*, the first poem of the *Classic of Poetry*</note> resonated with the fullest harmony of voices and instruments—oh, how sweetly and pleasantly it filled and soothed the ears.

->f. 16. p. 1. §. 1.<-

Confucius said: A person who is a clever lover of both glory and himself, and is therefore not upright; likewise, one who is naturally dull yet remains reckless and headstrong; and finally, one who is unrefined and inept at handling business, yet is also not truthful or sincere—of such people, I say, I truly do not know what kind of men they are, or how anyone might be able to help them. <note>Confucius is expressing frustration with people who lack even the basic redeeming qualities that usually accompany their flaws (e.g., a simple person should at least be honest).</note>

->§. 2.<-

Confucius said: Learn in such a way as if you have not yet reached your goal. Indeed, even if you have learned something, fear that you might lose it.

->§. 3.<-

Confucius said: Oh, the greatness! Oh, the sublimity of the virtue and wisdom of *Shun* and *Yu*! <note>Shun and Yu were legendary sage-kings of China's golden age.</note> Both were most wise, and they lived quite contentedly in their lot, even though it was originally humble and did not match their illustrious lineage. Their own virtue raised them both to the Imperial throne. Thus, they both held this vast Empire of the Chinese <note>original: *Sinarum Imperium*</note>; yet they, in turn, were not "held" by it. This means (as the *Colaus* <note>term: *Colaus* (from the Chinese *Gelaou*) refers to a high-ranking official or Grand Secretary, likely used here to refer to a specific commentator like Zhu Xi</note> explains) it was as if the Empire were of no personal interest to them. They clearly considered all things of little value compared to the single nobility and excellence of their own minds. For they knew that such a mind was created by Heaven for the possession of virtue and wisdom—a possession that is not uncertain, nor dependent on chance or luck.

Confucius, sighing, said: As the old proverb says, "great talents are difficult to find and rare"; is this not true? The fourth was <term>Bi Gong</term> <note>original: "Pie cum"; the Duke of Bi.</note>. The fifth was <term>Rong Gong</term> <note>original: "Yum cum"; the Duke of Rong.</note>. The sixth was <term>Tai Dian</term> <note>original: "Tai tien".</note>. The seventh was <term>Hong Yao</term> <note>original: "Hum yao".</note>. The eighth was <term>San Yisheng</term> <note>original: "San y fem".</note>. The ninth was <term>Nangong Kuo</term> <note>original: "Nan cum quo".</note>. Within the palace, however, the Queen wife <term>Tajiang</term> <note>original: "Te kiam"; the wife of King Wu, who was regarded with such high status that she was counted among the ten ministers.</note> governed the Royal family and the affairs of the Palace with admirable virtue and prudence.

---

->f. 17. p. 1. §. 1.<-

Confucius, sighing, said: What is said in the old proverb—that great talents are difficult and rare—is this not true? Scarcely only that most beautiful society and succession which was formerly called <term>Tang and Yu</term> <note>original: "Tam & Yu"; referring to the legendary reigns of Emperors Yao and Shun.</note>, otherwise known as <term>Yao and Shun</term>, can be rightly judged to have flourished with such illustrious administrators alongside this Empire of our <term>Zhou</term> <note>original: "Cheu"</note> family. And this Empire of ours, with doubled happiness, counted ten in all. And among these ten is given one woman, namely the Queen <term>Tajiang</term>, the wife of Emperor <term>King Wu</term> <note>original: "Vu-vam"</note>; and thus only nine men are to be counted, and no more. Therefore, that old saying is most true: great talents are difficult and rare.

->§. 2.<-

The Philosopher passes to the praise of Prince <term>King Wen</term> <note>original: "Ven-vam"</note>, whose son was <term>King Wu</term>. He says: although he already possessed two out of three parts of the Empire (insofar as he held the devotion and will of all the people), yet even so, he could not be drawn away from his duty as a most excellent subject. Instead, holding loyalty to the Empire as more important, he obeyed and served the <term>Yin</term> <note>original: "Yn"; also known as the Shang dynasty.</note> family (though it was by then tyrannical) with invincible patience. For this reason, the virtue of the <term>Zhou</term> family can truly be called the supreme virtue, to which nothing can be added.

->p. 2.<-

Confucius said: As far as it pertains to Emperor <term>Yu</term> <note>original: "Yu"; Yu the Great, legendary founder of the Xia dynasty, famed for flood control.</note>, I do not have, nor can I find, anything to criticize. He was frugal and wonderfully temperate in his food and drink; yet the same man was most liberal, magnificent, and pure toward the spirits. His clothing was everywhere quite common and ordinary; yet the same man possessed a certain supreme adornment and splendor in his priestly robes and crown whenever he performed sacred rites. His Palace was humble and least expensive; yet the same man put forth and exhausted all the resources of his mind and treasury in the channels for diverting waters into the sea and in reservoirs for times of drought. In <term>Yu</term>, therefore, I do not have, nor can I find, anything to criticize.

*Because of this strong humility we have described, his virtue and wisdom recalled him to the ancestral dignity of his first lineage. Indeed, on account of the greatness of his merits, he was so dear and held in such high value by Emperor <term>Shun</term> <note>original: "Xun"</note> that, after he had taken him as a colleague in the Empire for his final 17 years, he did not hesitate (following the example of his predecessor <term>Yao</term>) to pass the throne to him, firmly rejecting his own legitimate son, whose name was <term>Shang</term> <note>original: "Xam"; Danzhu, the son of Yao, or Shangjun, the son of Shun, both often cited as unworthy heirs in Confucian texts.</note>.*

# CHINESE KNOWLEDGE
### BOOK THREE

...[Shun], being already ninety years old, designated him heir to the Empire. But **Yu**, escaping in a noble flight, hid himself in retreats <note>Yu famously attempted to decline the throne out of humility, a recurring theme in stories of "Sage Kings."</note>. But finally discovered by the lords, he was raised to the throne, however unwillingly. There shone in him a certain admirable ease and affability toward everyone. He ordered a **bronze bell** <note>original: "æs campanum"</note> to be erected in the very courtyard of his Palace: at the first stroke of which he would rush out eagerly to hear his subjects. Thus it happened sometimes that during the time of a single meal he would rise ten times from the table; likewise from the bath, where he was washing his body, he would run out once, twice, and a third time—and indeed with his hair still loose and uncombed—so that at the first signal of the bronze bell he might hear either the petitions or the complaints of his people.

Among the many other laws he established, there was one by which **wine** was strictly forbidden to everyone, and the inventor of wine was sent into exile. He used to say: "Wine will one day ruin the affairs of the Empire and our family"; and indeed it happened so, as will be mentioned elsewhere <note>This likely refers to the later fall of the Xia and Shang dynasties, which traditional history blames on the decadence and drunkenness of their final rulers.</note>. He ruled alone for ten years with such success, abundance, and tranquility that his times could deservedly be called "golden"; and if it is indeed right to believe the Chinese in this matter, it is said that **gold** actually rained for three days during his reign.

While traveling once, he happened to encounter a man bound in chains; immediately leaping down from his chariot, when he learned the man was guilty of a capital crime and was already being hurried to his execution, he wept. When his followers wondered at this, he said: "The men of a former age shaped their lives and morals according to the examples of King **Yao** <note>original: "Yao"; the first of the three legendary Sage Kings.</note>; but now, while I, a man of modest virtue, administer the Chinese state, not a few of my people, as I see, lead their lives according to their own whims and less than honorable pursuits." 

**Yu** lived for one hundred years, so free from all private affection that as he was dying, he proposed as successor to the Empire a man of proven virtue named **Ye** <note>original: "Ye"; likely referring to Bo Yi.</note>, neglecting his own son **Ki** <note>original: "Ki"; Qi, the second ruler of the Xia dynasty.</note>. However, both the lords and the people wanted the son to be the heir of his father's Empire, as he was the heir of his father's virtues; and from then on, the election of Emperors passed into the hereditary succession of sons and grandsons. 

And these things, which we note here and elsewhere, are recorded by the Royal writers of those times and authentic annals, and are often confirmed by the philosophers **Confucius** and **Mencius**. The aforementioned **Yu** died in the 20th year of the ninth cycle, called *Guiwei* <note>original: "Quéi vi"; one of the 60 terms in the Chinese sexagenary cycle.</note>, which corresponds to the year **2208 before Christ**.

# BOOK THREE
## PART FIVE

->Folio 1. page 1. paragraph 1.<-

The disciples used to recount that **Confucius**, their master, spoke very rarely—and then only with difficulty—concerning personal gain and profit, or about fate—that is, the heavenly decrees; and also about ***Ren*** <note>original: "Gin." This refers to the core Confucian virtue of "Humaneness" or "Benevolence."</note>, which is to say, that heaven-bestowed innocence and purity joined with the protection and ornament of all the virtues.

The inhabitants of a village called **Daxiang** <note>original: "A hiam." This refers to a specific district or village mentioned in Book 9 of the Analects.</note> happened to be speaking of **Confucius**, saying: "Oh, how great a man is Confucius! His skill and learning in every branch of knowledge is most extensive; and yet, there is no single thing for which his praise and fame are specifically proclaimed, since he is supreme in everything."

**Confucius**, hearing this by chance and addressing his disciples, said: "I think those simple country folk wish for me to apply myself more earnestly to some specific trade. What, then, should I take up above all else? Among our **six liberal arts** <note>The "Six Arts" of ancient Chinese education: Rites, Music, Archery, Charioteering, Calligraphy, and Mathematics.</note>, there are two more suited to the nature of common people: namely, charioteering and archery. Shall I therefore take up the art of charioteering, or shall I take up the art of archery? It is well; I shall take up and cultivate the art of **charioteering**, which is both easier and—precisely because it is humble—dear to me." <note>This is a classic example of Confucian humility and irony; he mocks the idea that a great sage should be known for a single technical skill.</note>

->page 2. paragraph 1.<-

**Confucius** used to say: "In former times, a ceremonial cap woven from fine hemp was the proper custom for formal ritual. But now, in our current age, silk is used, and it is less expensive and requires less labor. I, although this departs from the custom of the **Ancients**, follow the majority because no moral error is committed; in this matter, I adapt to the times."

<vocab>
**Confucius**: The Latinized name of the philosopher Kong Fuzi.
**Ren (Gin)**: Humaneness, the central virtue of Confucianism.
**Daxiang (A hiam)**: A village where the people praised Confucius's broad knowledge.
**Liberal Arts**: The six foundational skills of a gentleman.
**Charioteering (aurigandi)**: One of the six arts, considered lowlier than archery.
**Archery (jaculandi)**: One of the six arts, often associated with ritual and nobility.
**Fate (fatum)**: The "Mandate of Heaven" or the predestined path of a life.
**Heavenly Decrees**: Divine will or the natural order of the universe.
</vocab>

# THE CHINESE SCIENCES

->§. 2.<-

Greeting the Prince from a distance and from the lower courtyard was the custom and rite of the Ancients. Now, however, the custom of greeting the Prince up above in the hall itself is truly excessive and almost arrogant. Therefore, even though I may oppose the crowd in this matter, I follow the ancient rite of greeting from the lower courtyard.

->§. 3.<-

Confucius (if it is right to believe his disciples) was entirely free of four things. Regarding future matters, he had no personal prejudice or preconceived intention. Likewise, he had no stubbornness of mind or fixed determination; nor did he have obstinacy once a matter was undertaken, holding tooth and nail to a particular way of doing things. Finally, he did not have himself or his own conveniences before his eyes. <note>These are known as the "Four Avoidances" of Confucius: prejudice, dogmatism, obstinacy, and selfishness.</note>

->f. 2. p. 1. §. 1.<-

Confucius, perhaps being in danger, conducted himself with care and vigilance in the place called **Kuang** <note>original: "Quam loco."</note>. The cause of the danger was a physical resemblance to another former prefect of that same place named **Yang Hu** <note>original: "Hiam hù."</note>, whom the inhabitants of the place—remembering the injuries he had once inflicted on them—sought to kill. Consequently, the Philosopher's inn was besieged by armed men for five days.

->§. 2.<-

To strengthen his disciples, who were struck by such unexpected danger, **Confucius** said: "It has been nearly six hundred years since **King Wen** <note>original: "Ven-vam." The founder of the Zhou Dynasty, held by Confucius as a model of wisdom and culture.</note>, that wise King, died. But has that illustrious law, and as it were the light of the law, which shone forth through his work, perished for that reason? Does it not exist here among us even now?"

->§. 3.<-

"If **HEAVEN**, therefore, intended to extinguish this light of the law, I, who was born after that King and was likewise destined to die, would not have been able to contribute my efforts toward promulgating this law to some extent. But if Heaven did not wish the proclamation of this law to be extinguished, it will certainly also wish to look after our lives. What, then, can the inhabitants of this place **Kuang** <note>original: "Quam."</note> finally do to me?"

->§. 4.<-

One of the Prefects, a **Taizai** <note>original: "Tai çai." A title for a high official, often translated as Grand Commandant.</note>, inquired of Confucius’s disciple **Zigong** <note>original: "çu cum."</note>, saying: "Is your Master Confucius a holy man? For if he were not such, how could he be skilled in so many things?"

->p. 2. §. 1.<-

**Zigong** <note>original: "CU-cum."</note> replied: "As for our Master, Heaven has indeed perfected him with lavish generosity so that he might be a holy man. But in addition, he also possesses great skill in many sciences."

->§. 3.<-

**To** confirm this saying of **Confucius**, it is related by his disciples that **Lao** <note>A disciple of Confucius, not to be confused with Laozi.</note>, their fellow student, frequently recounted what **Confucius** himself used to say: "**I**, in the early times of my life, was not called to manage the affairs of the State <note>original: "Reipublicæ."</note>; therefore, I learned and mastered the liberal arts."

->§. 4.<-

**Confucius**, taking it poorly that he was commonly held to be the most expert in all things, used to say: "Am I to be thought to have such great knowledge? On the contrary, I do not have it. I confess indeed that when some common and humble man appears, who asks me something, even if he is quite unrefined and dull-witted, I soon undertake to handle the two ends <note>original: "duo quasi capita." Likely referring to the pros and cons, or the beginning and end of a matter.</note> of the very matter about which he consults me, and I exhaust these through discussion."

->§. 1.<-

**Confucius**, deploring the calamity of his times and despairing of their improvement, used to say: "The Phoenix <note>original: "Aquila (aut solis avis)." Literally 'the eagle or bird of the sun,' used here to describe the mythical Feng Huang.</note> no longer arrives. No map <note>original: "mappa." Referring to the *He Tu* or Yellow River Map.</note> (or monster depicted with various signs) comes forth from the river. These two things were the omens of returning happiness. It is all over for me and my doctrine, alas!"

->§. 2.<-

**The Grand Secretary** <note>original: "Colaus." A Latinization of the Chinese *Gelao*, a title for a high-ranking official or academician.</note> rightly notes that the order of the characters is disturbed here, which ought to be as this version indicates. **Confucius**, seeing men dressed in mourning clothes for the death of their parents; and others likewise distinguished by the cap and dress of a Mandarin <note>original: "Mandarinico."</note>, even though they were of a younger age, or even those deprived of their sight; nevertheless, upon seeing them, he would undoubtedly rise out of respect. And when passing by them, he would undoubtedly quicken his step. (*Following the dutiful custom of the Chinese <note>original: "Sinarum."</note> as if yielding the place to another in haste out of respect*)—that is to say, he had scarcely any regard for his own age or authority, but certainly the greatest regard for the piety and dignity of others.

->§. 2.<-

**Yen-yuen** <note>Yan Hui, the favorite disciple of Confucius.</note>, sighing deeply, used to say: "The doctrine of our Master is something altogether sublime and most profound. To me, as I look up at it and already take a step toward it, it appears always higher and higher. Again, as I penetrate into it, I find its firmness..."

->§. 2.<-

**Confucius**, hearing these things, said: "Does that Grand Steward <note>original: "Tai çai." A high-ranking official or administrator.</note> truly know me well? ### CHINESE SCIENCE

...it is always found to be more and more firm and impenetrable. At times I contemplate it (as if placed before my very eyes), and I am carried as if into its embrace, when suddenly, behold, it stands behind my back, having slipped, as it were, from my very hands. <note>This is a famous passage from the Analects where the disciple Yan Hui describes the elusive and sublime nature of the Master's "Way" or path of wisdom.</note>

**AND** yet, in imparting this very doctrine to men, our Master knew how to allure and lead people where he wished, step by step and gently, in his own particular order: he expanded my mind with the supports of his Philosophy, and drawing all things back to a single point, he drew me together toward the single moderation and rule of heaven-sent reason.

<margin>§. 4. p. 1.</margin>
**BUT** when I wished to stop and enjoy what I had already gained, I was utterly unable: so when I had, in a sense, exhausted the powers of my mind, it was just as if something were given that stood upright before my eyes. Moreover, although I ardently desired to attain and embrace it, I still had no way or means by which I might fulfill my wishes; and thus I remained astonished at the height and depth of this doctrine and virtue.

<margin>p. 2. §. 1.</margin>
**Confucius** was ill, and not without danger: having learned this, the disciple Zi Lu <note>original: "çu lu." One of Confucius’s most loyal but impulsive students.</note>, wishing to please the Master, secretly sent and ordered several disciples to attend the sick man, acting as a kind of honorary retinue, and even to arrange a funeral, if it should be necessary, with splendor and pomp. <note>Zi Lu was attempting to accord Confucius the funeral honors of a high official, even though Confucius was no longer in office.</note>

**BUT** when the disease abated somewhat, Confucius, having discovered the matter, by no means approved of this desire to please him; "Ah!" he said, "for how long now has this disciple You <note>original: "Yeû." Another name for Zi Lu.</note> been acting neither rightly nor sincerely! In the past, custom and reason permitted me that crowd of attendants and domestic splendor: but now, since I have retired from my magistracy <note>original: "defunctus sum magistratu." Confucius had previously served as a high official in the state of Lu.</note>, and therefore have no public Ministers, as is fitting; if, nevertheless, behaving ambitiously, I should seem to have these Ministers, whom then would I deceive? Surely, though I might deceive the eyes of mortals, would I also deceive Heaven itself?"

<margin>§. 3.</margin>
**AND** indeed, regarding that death to be faced amidst the service and hands of those ministers, would it not have been much more pleasing and sweet to die in the hands of two or three disciples? Certainly, even if I could not then have been carried out with that magnificent funeral proper to high officials; would I therefore, dying among you, have died on the public road and lain there unburied?

The **Commentator** <note>original: "Interpres." Referring to the traditional Chinese scholars whose explanations were integrated into this Latin edition.</note> concludes the three preceding paragraphs with these words: *The words of the Sage end here.* <note>original: "Xím gîn yû çiĕ." A transliteration of the Chinese "Shèng rén yǔ cǐ," meaning "The Sage spoke this."</note>

### BOOK THREE

*yû çié pím guêi pé chi cum, lh sú tien chì chîm, xeù lì chi chím, yé hâo pú keù jù çù çù sò y guêi ván xí fá yè*, <note>This is a phonetic transcription of a Chinese passage using an early Jesuit romanization system.</note> that is to say: *A holy man, when faced with the crisis of a severe illness, remains sincere in his will to obey Heaven and maintains the rectitude of following what reason dictates; he does not act rashly, even by a hair's breadth of his head, as is evident here.*

**Zi Gong** <note>original: "CU cum." One of Confucius’s most eloquent and commercially successful disciples.</note> was encouraging his Master to use his talents for the public good. He said: "If a man had a beautiful gem of rare value in these troubled and turbulent times, should he keep it hidden away in a chest? Or, on the contrary, should he seek someone to buy it at a fair price?" **Confucius**, being well aware of what this metaphor signified, replied: "Let it be sold! By all means, let it be sold! But I am waiting for someone who truly knows its value to make an offer. It is not our way to go out searching for a buyer." <note>Confucius suggests that while he is willing to serve in government, he will not compromise his dignity by campaigning for a position; the ruler must seek him out.</note>

->p. 2. §. 1.<-

**CONFUCIUS**, weary of the times in which he lived, desired to leave his homeland and go to live among the nine tribes of the Barbarians. <note>original: "novem gentes Barbarorum." This refers to the non-Chinese peoples of the East. Confucius's statement is a rhetorical expression of his frustration with the lack of virtue in the "civilized" Chinese states.</note>

->§. 2.<-

**IT** happened that someone, wishing to dissuade him, said: "Those people are lowly and uncouth. How could this be done? How could you live there?" **Confucius** replied: "Wherever a sincere follower of virtue and wisdom dwells, how could anything there be considered lowly or uncouth?"

->§. 3.<-

**CONFUCIUS** said: "When I returned from the Kingdom of **Wei** <note>original: "Guêi."</note> to my native Kingdom of **Lu**, it was then that, through my efforts, music was restored to its ancient order and purity. The poems of the *Ya* and the *Song* <note>original: "Yà" & "çum." These are specific sections of the *Shijing* or *Classic of Poetry*, consisting of courtly odes and sacrificial hymns.</note> each finally regained their proper place—namely, their harmony and their original majesty."

->§. 4.<-

**CONFUCIUS** said: "While abroad and in public life, one should serve the Prince and the other officials as is fitting. While at home, one should serve parents and brothers with the required respect. In times of mourning and funeral rites, one must not fail to exert all his strength. Finally, at banquets, one must not do anything through the excessive use of wine that might be grave or dangerous. Although these four things seem easy at first glance, they are in truth difficult; and so, how well do I fulfill them?"

->§. 5.<-

**CONFUCIUS**, perhaps standing by a riverbank and contemplating its eternal flow, suggested that one must never stop on the path of virtue, saying: "How they go and flow in this way, these waters, never ceasing their course by day or by night!"

# BOOK THREE <note>original: "LIBER TERTIUS"</note>

Who would not rejoice? However, to make progress here, and to "ruminate" <note>original: "ruminari," a metaphor comparing deep meditation to a cow chewing the cud to extract all nutrients</note> on those things repeatedly—this is indeed the first and most necessary requirement. For if someone only rejoices, and meanwhile does not weigh and ruminate on that which he enjoys, he is not nourished by the food by which he seems so much delighted. Likewise, if someone reverently receives sincere and upright advice, and meanwhile does not conform his habits to them and corrects nothing, I certainly do not know how to deal with such a man: the deed is done, and we lose both our oil and our labor <note>original: "oleum & operam perdimus," a Latin idiom meaning to waste time and effort, like a lamp burning oil for no result</note>.

**Confucius** said: "Let nothing be as close to the heart as sincerity of heart and faithfulness. Do not enter into friendship with one who is less good than you yourself are. Have you sinned? Then do not hesitate or fear to correct what has been committed."

->§. 1.<-

**Confucius** said: "From an army of three legions <note>that is, 37,500 soldiers</note> fighting with the greatest resistance, its leader can sometimes be snatched away and carried off into slavery. Yet from the lowliest and most humble little man, the free judgment of the mind cannot be snatched away by any force."

**Confucius**, praising his disciple <term>Teû</term> <note>Also known as <term>Zi Lu</term> (çù lù), a disciple known for his bravery and bluntness.</note>, said: "He who, dressed in a worn and torn cloak made of common hemp, stood together with other companions dressed in fox skins and the skins of the <term>hǒ</term> <note>The *hǒ* is a species of small animal whose skin is of rare value; likely the raccoon dog or a similar fur-bearing creature</note>, and yet was in no way ashamed—he was truly the disciple <term>Teû</term>."

He confirms the same praise from an ode which goes thus: "Whoever is neither envious nor greedy; for what use, finally, will he not be exceptionally well-suited?"

->§. 2.<-

**Zi Lu**, happy with his Master's public praise, thereafter recited this little verse throughout his whole life. Noticing this, and wishing to restrain a disciple who was pleasing himself more than was right, **Confucius** said: "That praise and virtue by which you are free from envy and greed—how is it enough to make you immediately and exceptionally suited for all things, so that nothing more is now desired?"

->§. 3.<-

**Confucius** said: "Only in the winter time is it finally known whether the pines and cypresses will then lose their leaves." <note>The pine and cypress are symbols of constancy because they remain green while other trees wither.</note> "A brilliant example of those men," says <term>Colaus</term> <note>likely referring to the Chinese scholar-official and convert Xu Guangqi, known as Paul Xu or "Colaus" (from the title *Kolao* or Grand Secretary) to the Jesuits</note>, "whom a peaceful State proves to be very similar to one another, but whom a troubled and afflicted State then proves to be very different, clearly distinguishing the strong from the weak, and the foolish from the wise."

...who would not rejoice? However, to profit in this and to ruminate upon those teachings repeatedly is indeed the first and most necessary thing. ### §. 1.

> Whoever is not envious, nor greedy;

**Çu-lú**, happy with the public praise from his Master, proceeded to recite this little verse throughout his whole life. ### §. 3.

**Confucius** said: "Only in the winter season is it known whether the leaves of the pines and cypresses will then fall." <note>A famous metaphor: just as only the cold reveals which trees are truly evergreen, only times of crisis reveal who is truly virtuous.</note> This is an illustrious example (says the <term>Colaus</term> <note>original: "Colaus," a Latinization of the Chinese "Ge Lao" or Grand Secretary, referring here to a high-ranking commentator on the text.</note>) of those who, in a peaceful Republic <note>Translated here from "Republica," referring to the state or the social order.</note>, appear very similar to one another; but when the state is disturbed and afflicted, they are proven to be most unlike. <meta>This page continues the "Scientia Sinica," transitioning from the discussion of the indomitable human will to the nuances of character discernment and the psychological nature of pursuing virtue. It includes a rare instance of a literary analysis by Confucius regarding an ancient poem.</meta>

<page-num>60</page-num>
<header>CHINESE KNOWLEDGE</header>

**Confucius** said: The wise man does not hesitate while being of two minds; the truly upright and innocent man does not grieve; the brave and great-souled man does not fear or tremble.

**Confucius** said: There are some with whom you may equally begin the study of virtue and wisdom; yet you cannot then run the path itself with those same people, or practice the specific works of the wise. There are others with whom you can run the path already begun, yet you cannot then persist for long in that way and course with them, because they lack constancy. Again, there are others with whom you can constantly persist in the path and course begun, yet you cannot then, with those same people, weigh all matters and actions of the entire life according to the most exact equilibrium of virtue and wisdom. <note>Confucius here describes four levels of companionship in learning: starting together, practicing together, persevering together, and finally, achieving a shared moral judgment or "equilibrium."</note>

Here is cited a verse taken from an ancient Poem, in which someone living outside his homeland and being far away, and perhaps having caught sight of a tree similar to one he had seen in his native soil, remembered a friend whom he had left in his homeland, and sang in this manner: "The leaves and flowers of the plum tree <note>original: "arboris pruniferæ," likely referring to the wild plum or cherry blossom often found in Chinese poetry.</note> are continually tossed now this way, now that, by the blowing west wind <note>original: "zephyro," the gentle west wind.</note>. Ah! how could I not think of you, how could I not long to see you? But alas! those prayers are empty! For the house of each of us is far removed from the other."

**Confucius**, seeking the essence of the teaching from this, said: He says indeed that his homeland and friend are being thought of by him; but in truth he does not think of them: for what distance, after all, is given here? <note>Confucius argues that physical distance is an excuse; if the desire were genuine, the heart would bridge the gap.</note> It is as if he were to say: if indeed the thought were serious, he would have prepared himself for the journey long ago. We also, with far less justice, complain that virtue and wisdom are distant from us, about which we think in such a way that we *only* think: otherwise, if the thought were serious, virtue—which is innate to us—would already of its own accord rush into our embrace.

*Plainly unusual, <gloss>α)</gloss> which might seem to have exceeded the limit, was the diligence with which the disciples observed not only every smallest word and <gloss>α)</gloss> deed of Confucius, but even all his postures and movements, and committed them to writing for the memory of posterity; and we too thrust this upon the European, fastidious though he may be, just as it stands.* <note>This is a translator's note from the 17th-century Jesuit editors, acknowledging that European readers might find the upcoming detailed descriptions of Confucius's daily habits and posture somewhat tedious or overly "minute."</note>

**Confucius**, when dealing with those who were of the same clan or family as himself, had a certain way of acting very sincerely and candidly. He seemed not to prevail by any eloquence or learning above the rest.

<meta>This page marks the beginning of Book Three (traditionally Book 10 of the Analects), shifting the focus from Confucius's philosophical teachings to a detailed description of his personal conduct, ritual propriety, and courtly etiquette. It provides a vivid portrait of how the sage embodied his principles through his physical bearing and interactions with various social ranks.</meta>

<header>BOOK THREE</header>

->§. 1.<-

The same man <note>referring to Confucius</note>, whenever he moved within the royal courts of the Great Nations, or in the royal Palace, spoke clearly and distinctly, yet always in such a way that nothing was said without mature consideration, careful thought, and focused attention.

<margin>folio 10, page 1, section 1</margin>
In the hall of the royal Palace, during the time he was waiting for his King along with officials of various ranks, he conducted himself with a certain solid gravity when speaking with those of lower or equal dignity to himself. However, when speaking with superior officials, he tempered that gravity with an affable and easy courtesy.

->§. 2.<-

When the King was present, he assisted with a singular and almost anxious reverence for the Royal majesty; yet he did so in such a way that he remained simultaneously calm and always present of mind.

->§. 3.<-

When the King summoned him and ordered him to receive visiting lords <note>original: "dynastas," referring to high-ranking nobles or local rulers</note>, then indeed the color of his face would change somewhat; likewise, his feet and his gait seemed to be hindered <note>This indicates a state of ritual tension and profound respect, where his movements became deliberate and cautious in the presence of authority.</note>.

->§. 4.<-

Whenever any guest lord approached to greet the King, if **Confucius** was then assisting in his official capacity, he would respectfully signal to those who were assisting with him, whether to his left or to his right. (He did this *respectfully, that is, with nearly the same gesture by which grave men greet one another: namely, with arms somewhat arched and hands folded together, extended slightly forward from the chest.*) In that movement of the arms, his robe, both in front and in back, never failed to appear elegantly arranged.

->P. 2. §. 1.<-

Therefore, once the power to introduce the guest into the sight of the Prince had been granted, **Confucius**, introducing the guest with an accelerated pace, would spread the loose sleeves of his flowing robe on both sides like wings, moving them with even balance.

*The acceleration of the pace is a sign of reverence, so that the Prince should not have to wait for the visiting guest for even the smallest space of time.*

->§. 2.<-

When the guest had finally withdrawn from the sight of the Prince, **Confucius** would report this to the Prince without delay, saying: "The guest no longer looks back," which is to say, he has departed.

*For it is the custom that a departing guest turns back again and again toward the one he visited—if he is being escorted out—or certainly toward the hall where the visitation took place, to perform the final duty of salutation.*

->§. 3.<-

It is now explained in what manner *Confucius* would conduct himself whenever he presented himself before the King: When he entered the gate of the royal apartments, out of reverence not only was his mind humble, but his body was also lowered and thoroughly bowed, just as if the gate were not large enough to contain him as he entered.

->§. 4.<-

IF he had to stand anywhere, he certainly never stood in the middle of the gateway—through which the King himself was accustomed to go out and enter. Passing through the same, he did not tread with his foot upon the threshold of the gate itself <note>Stepping on the threshold was considered a sign of disrespect or a breach of ritual boundaries.</note>.

->§. 5.<-

Having progressed now into the interior of the Palace, and perhaps passing before the Royal throne, even though the King was not yet present, even then the color of his face seemed to change. Likewise, the feet and the gait of the one passing by seemed hindered. Furthermore, his very speech seemed even more constrained.

<margin>folio 10, page 1, section 1</margin>
->f. n. p. i. §. 1.<-

IF at any time he had to approach closer to the King sitting upon his throne, lifting his robe with both hands, he would ascend the stairs into the hall with his body greatly lowered and inclined, not daring even to raise his eyes: meanwhile, he so carefully suppressed his breath that he seemed, in a way, not to breathe.

->§. 2.<-

Upon departing from the King's sight, as he was now descending one or two steps, he immediately regained his former facial color and appearance, looking now as if he were cheered. Then, from the last step, he proceeded somewhat more quickly with a mind now freed not only from cares, but also with the sleeves of his robe more spread out here and there <note>This describes the "bird-like" or "wing-like" grace of a scholar’s sleeves when moving rhythmically.</note>, walking elegantly; and returning to the proper place of his office, he stood there among the other officials with care and a certain reverence.

->§. 3.<-

Whenever **Confucius** was sent as an envoy by his Prince <note>referring to the Duke of Lu</note>, who was of the first rank, and presented himself to another, he held in his hand the insignias <note>original: "insignia"; these were jade tablets (gui) that served as symbols of delegated authority.</note> of his Prince, with his body reverently bowed, just as if he were not equal to sustaining the weight of such great dignity. Whenever he raised them, he shaped his arms as if reverently greeting another; if he lowered them a little, he used a gesture as if offering something to someone else. Meanwhile, however, because of the care by which he was held and the fear <note>in the sense of ritual awe or profound apprehension</note>, his color changed, just as the color of combatants, their faces and eyes, usually change at the beginning of a contest. His gait, likewise, was like one both accelerated and yet entangled, exactly as if he were dragging some weight attached to his feet.

### p. 2. §. 1.

**W**henever he offered gifts in the name of his King to another petty king or local ruler; he maintained a facial expression tempered with both affability and gravity.

### §. 2.

**H**owever, when he subsequently offered private gifts in his own name; then a certain touch of extra cheerfulness was added to that same affability.

### §. 3.

**IN THIS** and the following paragraphs, it is explained what kind of clothes Confucius usually wore, in what manner, and at what time. Our Philosopher <note>Confucius</note> never applied to common use or everyday dress decorations of a flame-like and darkish color, nor red or purple colors, sewn as collars or borders on the upper and lower edges of his garments: for he used the latter color only for funerals, and the former for sacrifices.

### §. 4.

**LIKEWISE**, he never made garments for common and domestic use out of that common red color, or violet verging toward red, so much did the Philosopher delight in the natural simplicity of things: also because those same colors were valued and used by matrons and young women.

### §. 5.

<margin>Co pu</margin>
**DURING** the summer months, he would always wear over another inner garment that simple and thin dress which was then commonly in use (whether it was finely or coarsely woven) made of <term>Co pu</term> <note>original: "Co pu"; likely a transliteration of *gebu* (葛布), a fabric made from kudzu fiber</note> (which seems to be a species of hemp); and thus he made that summer dress the outermost layer: undoubtedly out of a desire for modesty, propriety, and decency, so that nothing of the body's nakedness might otherwise show through.

### f. 12. p. 1. §. 1.

**FOR HIM**, in the winter time, beneath a black gown made of lambskins, there was likewise a black gown: Under a white garment made of the skins of young deer, likewise a white gown: Under a saffron garment made of fox skins, likewise a saffron gown.

### §. 2.

**THAT** fur gown which he commonly used at home was indeed long: yet the right sleeve of it was somewhat shortened, so that he might be more agile in handling things.

### §. 3.

**HE HAD** his own nightdress for rest, quite long so as to cover the whole body, and it additionally had another half <note>The Latin *alteram medietatem* implies an extra length of fabric for wrapping or double coverage.</note> covering the same body. Furthermore, his primary use of this garment was during times of fasting.

Indeed, as <term>Colaus</term> <note>original: "Colaus"; a Latinization of a Chinese commentator's name, likely referring to the traditional commentaries used by the Jesuits</note> concludes, the Saints venerate the spirits as if they were present before them; for this reason, they devote themselves to abstinence and self-control so diligently and carefully.

...if it happened to be tainted, he would not eat it. If the smell was likewise tainted, he would not eat it. If it lacked the proper preparation or seasoning, he did not eat. Anything unripe, such as grains or fruit, he did not eat.

->f. 13. p. 1. §. 1.<-

If something was not cut fitly or correctly, he did not eat. (*Since the Chinese consider it a mark of rusticity to touch food with the fingers—indeed, any food at all—they instead carry even the rice itself to the mouth with <term>twin sticks</term> <note>original: "geminis paxillis"; a description of chopsticks, which were unfamiliar to many European readers at the time of this text's composition</note>, which are oblong and handled with great skill and dexterity. For this reason, almost no meat is brought to the table that has not been cut into pieces beforehand.*) If any food did not have its proper <term>sauce</term> <note>original: "embamma"; a Greek-derived term for a dipping sauce or condiment</note> or dip, he did not eat.

The Chinese do not place bare salt on the table as we do; but in its place, they provide various kinds of dips, as well as vegetables and legumes seasoned with salt, which are very well-suited for eating rice more heartily.

->§. 2.<-

Even if there was an abundance of meat, he did not make it his primary food, or rather, he did not eat it in such a way that its quantity exceeded that of the rice or grain-broth. Only regarding the use of wine did he have no fixed measure that he prescribed for himself; however, he never used it immoderately, so that he never reached a state of mental confusion.

->§. 3.<-

Wine bought in public markets or at crossroads, and likewise dried meat bought there, he would not use, fearing that they might not be clean.

->p. 2. §. 1.<-

He did not abstain from eating ginger, but added it to almost every dish, because it especially arouses the spirits of man and wards off things contrary to health.

->§. 2.<-

Finally, on the whole, he was not a man who ate much.

->§. 3.<-

During the time when ancestral offerings and feasts were held in the Royal Palace, **Confucius** did not keep even for one night those meats which the King himself, following custom, sent as gifts to his Magistrates and clients after the Rite was finished. However, in the private rite of his own home, when he himself offered meals and meats in memory of his own ancestors, he did not keep the food beyond three days. Anything that had already exceeded three days was not eaten by anyone, as it had already begun to spoil.

->§. 4.<-

While eating, he did not converse; while resting, he did not speak, unless perhaps he was asked a question.

->§. 1.<-

Even though he might eat very common and easily obtained food—for example, a broth prepared from vegetables—he would nevertheless always offer a libation from it, both to his ancestors and to those whose labor and industry had provided these things to the human race. Thus, it was clearly a kind of perpetual practice of fasting and <term>denying his own nature</term> <note>original: "geniique fraudandi"; a Latin idiom for self-denial or abstaining from pleasure</note>.

->f. 14. p. 1. §. 1.<-

The ground itself, covered with mats, served as a seat for the <term>Ancients</term> <note>The text uses "Priscis" to refer to the early Chinese people of the Sage-Kings' era</note>. Therefore, if a mat was not properly placed, he would not sit upon it; such was his care for what was right, even in the smallest and lowliest of matters.

->§. 2.<-

When his relatives, kinsmen, and fellow townsmen feasted together: as soon as those using a staff—that is, those who had just passed their sixtieth year—departed at the end of the banquet, he himself would follow immediately after. He was never one to fail in venerating <term>gray hair</term> <note>A poetic reference to the elderly</note>.

->§. 3.<-

When these same townsmen performed the <term>supplication</term> <note>original: "supplicationem"; referring to the *Nuo* ritual, a traditional ceremony to drive away evil spirits and pestilence</note> during the winter months to ward off disease-bearing spirits (as they called them), he would put on his more solemn ceremonial robes and stand at the entrance of his house, on the eastern steps, where he was accustomed to meet a guest who came to visit him.

>*The commentators teach that the use of this ceremony began almost at the same time as the <term>Zhou dynasty</term> <note>original: "Cheu"</note>, and <term>Zhu Xi</term> <note>original: "Chu çù"</note> indeed suggests it was not unlike a festive game. But <term>Zhang Nanxuan</term> <note>original: "Cham tûm ço"</note> observes that here Confucius showed some of his respect toward the Emperor, who himself allowed this rite or "game" to be performed in his court during the autumn.*

->§. 4.<-

When sending someone from his household to politely inquire after the health of a friend living in a different region, he would bow his body reverently and salute the absent friend again and again, just as if he saw him present before him. Even if the one he sent was a servant, he would nevertheless lead him out with honor, honoring the person for whom the message was intended through the messenger.

->§. 5.<-

<term>Ji Kangzi</term> <note>original: "Ki cam çu"; a powerful minister of the State of Lu</note>, the Governor of the Kingdom of <term>Lu</term>, had sent a gift of medicine to Confucius. Confucius, accepting it with thanks and with signs of honor, said candidly: "I do not have sufficient knowledge of what power and efficacy it possesses; and therefore, I do not yet dare to taste it."

->P. 2. §. 1.<-

The stable of Confucius, while he was serving as Governor, had by chance burned down. Upon his return from the court, when a messenger met him with the news of the domestic calamity, he said: "Alas! Did the fire hurt any person?" Meanwhile, he asked nothing at all about the horses.

->§. 2.<-

**Whenever** the Prince of the Kingdom of **Lu** honored him with a gift of food, he would most certainly arrange his mat, or seat, just as if the Prince himself were present. First, he would <term>offer a libation</term> <note>original: "delibabat"; a ritual pouring or tasting of a portion of the food to honor spirits or ancestors</note> from the gift himself, and then he would share it with the others. When the same Prince sent him an honorary gift of raw meat, *Confucius* would without fail cook it first, then offer it to his ancestors <note>original: "majoribus vitâ functis"; literally, "the elders who have finished with life"</note>. Finally, if his Prince sent him a living animal as a gift, he would undoubtedly nourish and maintain it with great care, by no means daring to consume a living testament to the Royal beneficence.

->§. 3.<-

**If** ever he was sitting at the side and feasting together with his Prince, and the Prince was about to offer the customary libations from each of the dishes to his own ancestors, *Confucius*—out of modesty and unwilling to exercise his right as a guest, which would have allowed him to offer libations similarly—did only this: Very skillfully anticipating the Prince, he would taste each of the foods first. You would have said he was not so much the Prince's guest as his <term>official taster</term> <note>original: "praegustatorem"; one who tastes food for a monarch to ensure it is safe or properly prepared</note>.

->§. 4.<-

**If** *Confucius* were ill and the King came to visit the sick man, he would turn his head toward the east <note>The east was considered the direction of life and growth, and the proper orientation for receiving a superior</note>. Likewise, he would place his more solemn ceremonial robes upon himself as he lay in bed (the ones he was accustomed to wearing whenever he went to greet the King). Over these very clothes, he would lay his large and most honorable girdle.

->f. 15. p 1. §. 1.<-

**When** summoned by the King, *Confucius* would not wait for his own household carriage, but would immediately set out on his way on foot.

->§. 2.<-

**Whenever** he entered the Great Ancestral Hall dedicated to the memory of the Prince <term>Duke of Zhou</term> <note>original: "Cheu cum" (Zhou Gong); the virtuous founder of the state of Lu whom Confucius greatly admired</note>, he would ask questions about nearly every single thing therein.

->§. 3.<-

**If** one of his friends happened to die and had no one to whom he could turn for the management of the funeral, *Confucius* would then say: "Let the care of managing this funeral be upon me."

->§. 4.<-

**When** gifts and presents were sent to him by friends, even if they were chariots and horses or other things of greater value, he showed no special honor to any of them, with the sole exception of meat that had been offered to ancestors according to the <term>ancient rite</term>.

->§. 5.<-

**Whenever** he lay down for the sake of sleeping, being even then mindful of modesty and decency, he did not lie like a corpse—that is, flat on his back and unseemly sprawled out. When living with his family at home, and within private...

->Part 2. Section 1.<-

**When** he caught sight of someone dressed in mourning garments <note>original: "veste lugubri"; traditional Chinese mourning involved wearing coarse white hemp</note>, even if it was someone otherwise very close to him, he most certainly changed his facial expression, moved by a deep internal sense of a compassionate soul. Likewise, if he saw someone wearing a <term>solemn cap</term> <note>original: "solemni pileo"; a formal head covering indicating official rank or ritual status</note>, such as those belonging to the Magistrates, or if he saw someone deprived of sight <note>original: "orbatum luminibus"; a blind person</note>, even if he were dealing with them in private, he undoubtedly treated them with reverence and honor.

->Section 2.<-

**To** anyone wearing mourning clothes, even when he himself was riding in a carriage, he would rise as a sign of honor, leaning forward toward the front of his carriage. He rose in the same way for the person carrying the <term>Public Register</term> <note>original: "Codicem publicum"; the census or official records of the population</note> containing the names of the entire people; in doing so, he showed his veneration for the people as a whole.

->Section 3.<-

**If** ever a rich and splendid banquet was held in honor of *Confucius*, upon seeing the table set with so many courses and the rest of the preparation, he undoubtedly changed his expression and immediately rose to give thanks to the host for the honor bestowed upon him.

->Section 4.<-

**At** sudden claps of thunder, as well as at fierce and terrible winds, he never failed to change his expression, struck by a certain sacred awe, clearly declaring his reverence toward the <term>supreme majesty of heaven</term> <note>original: "supremam cæli majestatem"; referring to the concept of *Tian* (Heaven) as a moral and natural authority</note>.

*But this was by no means new for a Philosopher, since (a) the **Ancient Kings of the Chinese** (a) were also accustomed to spring from their beds even during the night hours when the sky was flashing with lightning or thundering; and, dressed in their more solemn cap and robe, they would duly strive to appease the celestial anger, as is clear from their own books.*

->Section 5.<-

**When** *Confucius* entered a carriage, he always stood upright while taking hold of the reins.

->Section 6.<-

**While** inside the carriage, he did not turn his eyes behind him; he said nothing hastily or rashly; and he pointed at nothing with his finger.

->Book 16. Page 1. Section 1.<-

**A bird**, at the first sight and appearance of a <term>fowler</term> <note>original: "aucupis"; a hunter of birds</note> from whom it sees a trap being set, immediately flies on high; and flying far away, it removes itself, and then, looking around for a suitable and safe place, it settles there, secure and at rest.

->Section 2.<-

**Confucius**, as his disciples recall, once caught sight of a wild pheasant <note>original: "gallinam sylvestrem"; likely referring to the mountain pheasant mentioned in Analects 10.27</note> while in the countryside. Sighing, he said: "The wild pheasant I see there on the mountain peak—how well it knows its own time! How well it knows its own time!" He meant, of course, the time for flying, the time for resting, and so on, following nature as its sole mistress in all things. As the Philosopher was saying these things, his disciple *Zilu* <note>Latin: "çu lu"</note> stood nearby and gazed at the bird from a distance, not without a desire to capture it. But the bird, chirping three times, quickly took flight and soared away; by its very act and flight, it confirmed in a way what had been said above.

Our <term>Colao</term> <note>original: "Colaus"; a Latinization of the Chinese *Ge-lao* or "Grand Secretary," a title the Jesuits used to refer to high-ranking scholar-commentators</note> draws a wholesome teaching from this: *while he wished us to learn even from the brute animals themselves, he suggests that the time and opportunity for doing things rightly must not be neglected by man, for whom not only nature, but also reason itself, is a Leader and Mistress.*

## PART SIX

->Folio 1. page 1. paragraph 1.<-

**Confucius** said: Our predecessors, or our ancestors, in their mutual respect and harmony—that is, in the performance of their duties—were rustic men <note>original: "subrustici"; meaning plain or unrefined</note>, at least if we listen to the opinion of our own fastidious age. But the later men—meaning ourselves, who under the rule of the **Zhou** <note>Latin: "Cheu"</note> family flourish with such a great abundance of luxury, rites, and ceremonies—are supposedly distinguished and most illustrious men in our mutual respect and harmony.

§. 2. Nevertheless, as far as the use and practice of that respect as well as that harmony is concerned, I shall certainly follow my predecessors.

§. 3. Confucius, remembering his disciples—some of whom had met their end, while others were serving as Magistrates elsewhere—said with a sigh: "Those who once followed me in the Kingdoms of **Chen** and **Cai** <note>Latin: "Chin" and "çai"</note> no longer come to this <term>gymnasium</term> <note>original: "gymnasium"; used here in the classical sense of a school or place of study</note> of mine."

...for skill and eloquence, *Zai Wo* and *Zi Gong* <note>Latin: "çai ngo" and "çu cum"</note>. For the art and industry of governing the State, *Ran You* and *Ji Lu* <note>Latin: "Gen yeu" and "Ki lu"</note>. For skill and elegance in literature, *Zi You* and *Zi Xia* <note>Latin: "çu yeu" and "çu bia"</note>.

§. 2. **Confucius** said: Of them all, *Hui* <note>Referring to Yen Hui, the philosopher's favorite student</note> was the only one who did not "help" me—meaning he never raised doubts or objections. Indeed, among all my speeches and opinions, there was not even one in which he did not find great joy; he evidently considered it unnecessary to question anything.

§. 3. **Confucius**, exclaiming in praise of his disciple, said: What a man of rare filial piety and obedience is *Min Ziqian* <note>Latin: "Min çu kien"</note>! Indeed, the reports of strangers do not differ from the words of his father, mother, or his elder and younger brothers, all of whom celebrate his devotion. There is but one voice from everyone—a wonderful consensus.

*This disciple gave a sweet example <note>original: "specimen"</note> of charity and prudence even while still a boy. He had lost his mother, and his father had taken another wife. By this second wife, two sons were born to him, whom she cherished as a mother; but, against the harshness of winter, she provided them with garments lined with warm cotton, while she neglected her stepson. One winter day, his father ordered the boy to drive his carriage. Because he was so poorly dressed, the boy nearly froze stiff with cold. When the father discovered the cause, he was filled with indignation and decided to cast his wife out of the house. Observing this, the pious son pleaded with him <note>original: "supplex"</note> with tears: "Spare her, O father! Spare the mother, so that you may spare the sons. For if she stays, I alone must suffer some discomfort; but if she is sent away, then three sons in total will suffer greatly." This voice of love broke the father’s anger, and transformed the stepmother into a true mother.*

Folio 2. page 1. §. 1. The disciple *Nan Rong* <note>Latin: "Nân yum"</note> would daily repeat, a second and third time, the ode called *The White Scepter* <note>Latin: "Pe quei"; an excerpt from the Book of Odes</note>, which contains various lessons, but especially those teaching us to speak with prudence and consideration. For this reason, **Confucius** gave him the daughter of his own elder brother in marriage.

§. 2. *Ji Kangzi* <note>Latin: "Ki cam çu"</note>, a Governor of the Kingdom of *Lu*, asked **Confucius** which of his disciples was the most studious. **Confucius** replied: "There was one, *Yen Hui*, who was the most studious of all. But unfortunately, after a very brief enjoyment of this life, he died prematurely. Now, alas, it is over; I see no hope of finding another disciple like him."

Page 2. §. 1. §. 2. **Zilu** <note>Latin: *çu-lu*</note>, the chief minister of the very powerful **Ji** family <note>Latin: *Ki*</note>, had used his authority and favor to arrange for his fellow student **Zigao** <note>Latin: *çu-cao*</note> to serve as the Governor of a certain small district called **Bi** <note>Latin: *Pi*</note>.

**Folio 8, page 1. §. 1.** It happened that four disciples, namely **Zilu**, **Zeng Xi** <note>Latin: *çem sie*</note>, **Ran You** <note>Latin: *gen yeu*</note>, and **Gongxi Hua** <note>Latin: *cum si hoâ*</note>, were sitting by the Master's side.

§. 3. "When you live as private citizens, you often say (I think): 'I am not recognized, and so there is no one who makes use of my service.' What, I say, would you do?"

§. 2. "But you, my disciple *Kieu* <note>Latin: *Gen yeu*; the disciple Ran You</note>, what do you have in your mind?" Furthermore, it is nothing other than this: at the end of spring, dressed in spring clothes—that is, simple and light, and now suited to an elderly body—together with five or six companions who have already left their youth behind <note>original: *pileatis*; literally 'the capped ones,' referring to those who had undergone the manhood ceremony</note> and share my studies; likewise with six or seven young men, to walk in the southern suburbs. Then, indeed, I would catch the breeze in the shaded grove of *Wuyu* <note>Latin: *Vu yu*; a place where they used to sacrifice to heaven whenever they prayed for relief from drought</note>. And finally, we would sing in turns sweetly, and thus, happy and cheerful, at last return home."

...to seek. Confucius, delighted by this simplicity of the noble old man <note>Zeng Xi, the father of the philosopher Zengzi</note>, applauding him and yet sighing at the same time, said: "Well said!
