*Various reasons for this approval are offered by Colaus <note>likely referring to a Mandarinate official or a specific commentator like Ge-lao</note> and other Interpreters: 1. That the Philosopher might show that he in no way approved of the lust for power. 2. To teach that all boasting and vanity are foreign to a wise man. 3. "But indeed," (the elder said here again) "concerning the third disciple, *Gongxi Hua* <note>original: *che*</note>, surely he had no Kingdom in his wishes?" Confucius replied: "He too is not free from the desire for power. For the ancestral halls of the princely ancestors and the funeral rites, likewise those extraordinary or general assemblies—if these are not the proper business of the petty Kings <note>original: *Regulorum*; feudal lords</note>, then to whom do those matters belong? However, because he said he wished to act as an assistant of a lower rank in such a place and time, I suspect his speech; for a man like *Gongxi Hua*, of such great quality and born for all the greatest things, if he acts as a..."

*Yan Hui* <note>original: *Yen yven*; Confucius's favorite and most virtuous disciple</note> consulted the Master regarding that innocence and perfection of the heart <note>This refers to the core Confucian virtue of *Ren*, often translated as benevolence or humaneness</note> which is bestowed by heaven upon all mortals; he sought the method of recovering it. *Confucius* replied: "To conquer oneself, and thus return to that original temperament of rational nature, is what it means to have attained innocence and perfection of the heart. Nevertheless, whether one applies effort to recovering that perfection depends entirely upon the man himself. How could it possibly depend on or arise from other men?"

Govern the people and assign them public works as if you were offering a great sacrifice that must be performed with all due rites. In a word, treat your subjects with reverence. Finally, do not do to others what you do not wish to be done to yourself. In this way, whether you serve as a public administrator in the kingdom, there will be no one who hates you or complains about you; or whether you are at home, there will be no one among your household who struggles with hatred or envy toward you." Having heard this, *Zhonggong* replied: "Though I am hardly quick-witted, let it nevertheless be permitted for me to carry out these your teachings."

...speech is delivered with moderation and slowness, he shall soon be called perfect of heart." *Confucius* responds: "To act rightly is arduous and difficult; who then can speak rightly without that slow-speaking moderation of the tongue?" <margin>folio 13, page 1, section 1</margin> The same *Sima Niu* <note>original: *Su ma nieu*; a disciple of Confucius known for being talkative and for his family's involvement in a rebellion</note> asked about the upright man. *Confucius* responds: "The upright man is neither saddened nor afraid, just as you are, who exhaust yourself with excessive fear and sorrow because of your rebellious and fugitive brothers."

<margin>section 2</margin> "Now then," he asked, "is he who is neither sad nor afraid to be called an upright man for that very reason?" *Confucius* responds: "If, when examining the inner reaches of the soul with a severe scrutiny, one finds nothing of error or fault to repent or be ashamed of—so much so that he has done nothing that cannot be made public among men, and has turned no thought in his mind that he would not wish Heaven to be aware of (<note>original: *Vu yo nien pu co yu tien chi*</note>)—such a man, I say, why on earth should he be sad? <margin>page 2, section 1</margin> The same *Sima Niu*, while nonetheless grieving and distressed on account of his brothers, whom he foresaw were soon to perish, said: "Miserable me! Most men have older and younger brothers, and I alone (as I sadly suspect) will soon have none."

<margin>section 4</margin> "Wherefore, the true Philosopher <term>Philosopher: refers to the *Junzi*, or the 'superior person' who pursues wisdom</term>, acquiescing to the judgment of Heaven alone, does one thing: namely, he attends to his own perfection, and loses or neglects nothing that might be of use for this end. Toward other men, however, of whatever age or rank they may be, he practices respect and benevolence. Yet he does so in such a way that all things are tempered by their proper rites and duties. Furthermore, for one who conducts himself thus toward himself and others, all men who exist within the four seas—that is, in the whole world—are his older or younger brothers, as if poured out from the same womb of the same mother. Why then should the Philosopher be distressed in mind because he has no brothers?"

To not listen to accusations, nor to believe them immediately: this can be judged and called **perspicacity** <note>original: *perspicacitas*; meaning sharp discernment or insight</note>, and nothing more is required. I say again: by showing yourself very slow and cautious in lending your ears or your trust to those deceitful slanders that gently instill their poison—as well as to those accusations about some clearly received loss, artfully composed to move one to pity—one can truly be said to see through things, however hidden or remote, with a certain extraordinary and almost inscrutable discernment. Nor is anything else needed here.

*When the Commentator* <note>original: *Colaüs*; likely referring to a specific Chinese commentator or the collective interpretation used by the Jesuit translators</note> *had explained this passage with a copious paraphrase, he finally concluded that this teaching ought to be especially dear to the heart of a Prince. For since he must reach all the affairs of his dominion, however vast, through his own eyes and ears alone; if he should happen to have ears that are too easy and open, or eyes that are insufficiently discerning, there is a danger that the lies and calumnies of the malevolent, envying one another, might—like hidden waters—a) fill up and b) dull the senses of the supreme head through treachery, and shortly an unexpected torrent and flood of calamities would overwhelm and ruin the body of the entire Kingdom.*

§. 2. **Zigong** <note>original: *çu-cum*; a prominent disciple known for his eloquence and political skill</note> consults the Master on the right method of governing. Confucius responds: Let there be an abundance of food for your subjects. Let there be an abundance of soldiers and things necessary for the uses of war; finally, let there flourish among the people a trust <note>original: *fides*; the mutual confidence between the ruler and the ruled</note> that answers to the faith and benevolence of the Prince himself.

p. 2 §. 1. To these things **Zigong** said: I have indeed understood the matter well; but a new doubt arises in me. What if it were absolutely impossible to do otherwise than to give up one of these three? Which would you give up in the first place? Confucius responds: I would give up the soldiers. For their own trust toward the Prince will arm the unarmed crowd, and mutual love and concord will make them invincible.

§. 2. **Zigong** asks again: What if it were absolutely impossible to do otherwise than to take away something here as well; of these two, namely food and trust, which would you allow to be taken away first? Confucius responds: I would allow food to be taken away or given up. For from every age, we are all entirely mortal. Confucius preferred, therefore, that the subjects die with their trust intact rather than depart from their human condition destitute of it. Certainly, where a people is destitute of mutual trust, they are so far from being raised up or coalescing into a **Commonwealth** <note>original: *Rempublicam*</note>, that on the contrary, it is necessary for it to perish.

§. 2. To this **Zigong** said: "Oh, how lamentable is that speech of yours and your judgment concerning the wise man! Such a speech, once [it is uttered...]"

<margin>page 18. part 1. § 1.</margin> The same **Ji Kangzi** <note>original: *Ki cam çu*; a powerful head of the Ji family in the state of Lu</note> again seeking the way of governing correctly from **Confucius**, spoke thus: "If I were to put to death the wicked and the lawless everywhere, so that I might more conveniently invite and promote the upright and the observers of the laws, what would you think of that?" **Confucius** replied: "If you indeed govern as is proper, why use punishments so frequently? <margin>§ 5.</margin> **Confucius** said to this: "What you describe is indeed being well-spoken of and being called illustrious, but it is not *being* clear and illustrious. For being talked about and actually being something are two different things."

<margin>Folio 19, page 1, section 1</margin> **Fan Chi** <note>original: *Fan chi*; a disciple known for his practical questions about farming and morality</note>, a disciple, while following **Confucius** as they walked in the lower part of the grove called <gloss>Wuyu</gloss> <note>original: *vu yu*; refers to the 'Rain Altars,' a place for ritual and relaxation</note>, spoke thus: "Might I dare to ask of you, Master, and learn three things especially necessary for any man who wishes to live well and happily? The third, finally, is how to skillfully discern and thoroughly examine the clouds and disturbances of the mind, so that I may dispel them at their very origin."

<margin>Section 2</margin> **Confucius** exclaimed, saying: "O, a question worthy of praise!"

<margin>Section 3</margin> And responding immediately, he said: "To busy oneself primarily with the study itself of accumulating virtues, and not to value highly or count for anything that which has already been accumulated of virtue and merit, nor that which is hoped for in the future as reward or utility—is this not the way to accumulate virtues? As if to say," says the Interpreter <note>The "Interpreter" refers to the traditional Chinese commentaries, such as those by Zhu Xi, which the Jesuit translators used to explain the text</note>, "whoever in the pursuit of virtue constantly considers in his mind that the path of virtue is long and arduous, and—driven by that thought—proceeds so vigorously as if he had completed none of the way; indeed, the prudent man never thinks of the progress already made or the distance left behind him. Rather, he neglects those things and holds them in the lowest regard, lest such a thought should somehow steal away his progress by enticing him to leisure and rest while he is still running. Whoever, I say, possesses such prudence and skill, is it not possible that he should profit daily, and through increments that escape his own notice, pile up great treasures of virtue and wisdom?

Again," says **Confucius**, "to declare war on oneself, to attack one's own vices and errors day and night; and by no means to rashly and idly inquire into the manners of others, nor to rebuke and attack the vices and errors of others while being unmindful of one's own: is this not truly to heal oneself from within and correct one's own vices and errors?

Finally, a very brief anger, even of a single morning, if not soon restrained, often destroys one's own person, reaching even to one's parents, kinsmen, and the whole family. Is this not indeed the affection of a blind and disturbed mind?"

<margin>Section 3</margin> To a doubting disciple, **Confucius** said: "Whoever elevates and promotes the upright and honest to the administration of the State, while setting aside all who are corrupt and wicked, will be able to ensure that the wicked themselves also turn toward what is right and honest."

<margin>Section 4</margin> **Fan Chi** did not yet fully grasp his Master's reasoning, which was so brief <note>original: *laconica*</note>. He left, and not long after, while visiting his fellow disciple **Zixia** <note>original: *çu hia*</note>, he said: "I want you to know that I was recently in the presence of our Master and consulted him about wisdom. The Master replied: 'Elevate the honest, set aside all the wicked; in this way, you can ensure that the wicked become honest.' What, I ask you, does this mean?"

<margin>Folio 20, page 1, section 1</margin> **Zixia**, understanding the matter immediately, exclaimed: "O, what a rich and fertile thought from our Master! I shall explain this to you using the example of two Emperors."

<margin>Section 2</margin> "Long ago, when **Shun** <note>original: *Xun*</note> held the Empire, he used mature deliberation and finally selected for himself one man from among all others, elevating him to the office of his supreme assistant: the wise **Gao Yao** <note>original: *cao yao*</note>. Once this fact was made known throughout the Empire, every wicked person or those devoid of virtue was removed so far away that you would have thought wickedness itself had vanished. Similarly, Emperor **Tang** <note>original: *Tam*</note>, after he obtained the Empire, chose from among all men and promoted to the highest dignity the wise **Yi Yin** <note>original: *y yn*</note>; and behold, every wicked man either returned to a productive life <note>original: *ad frugem rediit*</note> or withdrew so far that it was as if he had ceased to live."

*Gao Yao is believed to have descended from the lineage of **Zhuanxu** <note>original: *Chuen hio*</note>, the third Emperor of the Chinese Monarchy. His descendants were later granted the dynasty of **Liao** <note>original: *Leâo*</note>, which they governed for nearly ten centuries until they were extinguished by the Prince of **Chu** <note>original: *çu*</note>. Illustrious records of such a great man concerning the method of correct governing still exist in the second book of the **Shujing** <note>original: *Xu kim*; The Book of Documents</note>, which is titled the **Counsels of Gao Yao** <note>original: *Cao yao meu*</note>. These are written in the form of a dialogue between himself and the Emperor; a work worthy of European printing presses if only for its antiquity (being more than two thousand years before Christ). Among other things regarding the correct administration of the people, he teaches how he who commands on earth ought to shape and accommodate himself to the desires and wishes of his subjects, and to be such a ruler as the merits or demerits of the subjects require. He should take the example and standard of highest Heaven <note>original: *supremi Caeli*</note> for himself. For although the Emperor of this [Heaven]—or rather the Ruler of this [Heaven]—hears and understands everything (as **Grand Secretary Zhang** <note>original: *Cham Colaus*; referring to the Ming Dynasty scholar Zhang Juzheng</note> literally explains), since every mind, reason, and counsel has been placed in us by Him; and although He repays each individual what is fair according to their merits; nevertheless, He exerts these very effects of His Providence in such a way that His governance begins, in a sense, from the common wishes and merits of mortals. He tempers Himself so that the voice and mind of the people is the voice and mind of Heaven itself, or of the Lord of Heaven. Thus it happens that whatever the whole people hears, sees, and perceives through a natural instinct toward the good—and likewise whatever it loves and...*

...hates: heaven likewise hears, sees, perceives, loves, and hates this very thing. *Or as it is said in another place: heaven sees through the eyes of the people, and hears through the ears of the people, and so is moved beforehand by the people themselves; in a way, heaven is determined by them so that it may decree rewards or punishments according to the merits of each.* And hence also, more than once in this book, the **Shujing** <note>original: *Xu kim*; The Book of Documents, one of the Five Classics of Chinese literature</note>, it is said: **Shangdi bu chang** <note>original: *Xam ti pu cham*</note>, which means the Supreme Emperor of Heaven <term>Shangdi</term> <note>The highest deity or "Lord on High" in early Chinese theology</note> does not have a fixed determination, but if he sees the wicked, he punishes them, and if he sees the upright, he blesses them. From this it follows, as stated elsewhere, that whether heaven sends down calamities or blessings depends upon one's virtue. And indeed, one may still escape the calamities brought by heaven, but those which a person crafts for himself through his own crimes cannot be so easily avoided, unless, of course, he amends his ways. If the people do not obey virtue nor submit themselves to the correction of their crimes, heaven certainly warns and moves them through ill omens so that they may be called back to their own rectitude and virtue.

Another of the wise men, **Yi Yin**, traced his lineage from the illustrious Counselor <term>Colao</term> <note>A high-ranking minister or Grand Secretary, from the Chinese *Gelaoyue*</note> **Jie Mo**, who approximately eight hundred years before this grandson of his had been an advisor to the first Emperor of the Monarchy, named **Huangdi**. Therefore, when **Yi Yin** found himself in most turbulent times, he wisely remained in hiding and devoted himself to agriculture. When the King **Tang** invited him five times in vain, he finally compelled him—not without a kind of friendly force—to assist him and serve as his counselor. Not long after, he sent him to the impious **Jie**, the last Emperor of the first dynasty <note>The Xia Dynasty</note>, not without hope of recalling the man to a sound mind. However, when he had profited nothing there, having despaired of the matter, he returned to King **Tang**. **Tang** was subsequently raised to the Empire and conferred the highest rank after his own upon the sage, making great use of his work and counsel for the foundation of his family, called the **Shang**. 

He was also the author of opening gold mines, namely for the relief of the people, who had been severely afflicted by sterility and famine for a full seven years—during which time, perhaps, both Egypt and (as the sacred pages testify) the entire world then labored. <note>The Jesuit translator here draws a parallel between the ancient Chinese famine and the biblical famine of Joseph in Egypt.</note> Upon the death of Emperor **Tang**, when by chance the youth **Tai Jia**, who had succeeded his grandfather, began to shrink from public cares and business and give himself over to sloth and youthful pleasures, the Counselor **Yi Yin**, intending to crush so much evil in the seed, kept the young man in the garden of his father's tomb as if under domestic guard. For three whole years (which was the time designated for paternal mourning), he instructed and refined him with quite severe discipline, using the vicarious power he held. As a result, when the youth emerged, he was already a different person, surpassing his age in wisdom and maturity; as a rival to his grandfather's praise, he thereafter governed the empire quite wisely for thirty years.

The Counselor **Yi Yin** died over a hundred years old, in the 8th year of Emperor **Wo Ding**, who was the third of that family. This Emperor performed the royal funeral rites for him; and deservedly so, as one who had once administered the Empire for three years with such great faithfulness, and with vicarious power. He was buried about half a league from the tomb of the founder in **Henan** Province. He was succeeded by his son **Yi Zhi** <note>original: *Y pu*</note>, who was the Counselor to **Zhong Ding** <note>original: *hutim*</note> and the four Princes who followed in succession.

The instructions and warnings of this man, worthy of being preserved in cedar <note>original: *cedro digna*; a Latin idiom meaning "worthy of immortality" or highly valuable</note>, are extant in that same book, the **Shujing** <note>original: *Xu kim*; the Classic of History, one of the foundational texts of Chinese tradition</note>. First among these is titled **The Instructions of Yi** <note>original: *Y hiun*</note>, which are the documents of **Yi Yin** <note>original: *Y yn*</note> himself, in which he fortifies the young prince—not yet corrupted—with certain antidotes and armor, as it were. The second consists of a more severe discourse, in which he chastises the same prince with paternal authority when he had already begun to change for the worse. The third is written for the prince when he was already coming to his senses; at which time, the three-year period of mourning being finished, on the first day of the twelfth month, the same **Minister** <term>Colao</term> <note>original: *Colaus*; from the Chinese *Gelaoyue*, referring to a high-ranking Grand Secretary or advisor</note> brought him the purple robes and the diadem. He led him back, joyful, from his funeral watch to the hall and his ancestral throne. Finally, in the fourth chapter, he exhorts him to protect what has been gained and to courageously pursue the path of virtue he has begun. Lastly, there is another chapter titled **The Single Virtue** <note>original: *Ye te*; likely referring to the *Xian yi zhi de* or "Common Virtue" chapter</note>, which is a sharp exhortation regarding one virtue in particular as the unique foundation of government. Meanwhile, in all these writings, frequent mention is made of **Heavenly Providence**, which it is right to obey, and of the **Supreme Emperor of the Heavens** <note>original: *supremi cælorum Imperatoris*; referring to **Shangdi**</note>, who often appears under the name of "Heaven" itself, according to the very common custom of the **Chinese** <note>original: *Sinis*</note>. Indeed, because these monuments of the past are so ancient, I believe Europeans would rejoice to see them printed by their own presses; they would learn from them, above all, that the law of nature, along with the knowledge of the true **Deity** <note>original: *Numinis*</note>, was not lacking even in the farthest reaches of the earth. They would also see, not without admiration, what arts and what precepts for ruling an Empire—founded on a single religion and virtue—flourished even then in **China** <note>original: *Sina*</note>, namely, in the year 1750 before Christ.

It is helpful here to sample one or two warnings from among many, given by the faithful minister **Yi Yin** to the Prince as he was returning to a state of virtue, just as our native interpreter <note>referring to a Chinese commentator or collaborator</note> explains it along with others.

> The royal person, he says, has the august heaven above him, by whom he is watched; below he has the people, by whom he is likewise watched; and before and behind, to the right and to the left, the spirits stand by. This is truly a matter to be greatly feared. Although Heaven regards the King as a son, it has not yet determined whether it will always favor him or whether it will eventually oppose him and take away his Empire; thus, Heaven is not guided here by a fixed affection or leaning. But if the Prince knows how to conduct himself reverently and obey heaven—if he watches himself, and in every movement, action, speech, and thought, always carries himself as if heaven is looking upon the King and is present to assist him—and if he does not dare to admit even a single wicked thought, then certainly a reverent mind and thought of this kind penetrates heaven itself. Soon, heaven lovingly helps, protects, and expands the Empire delegated by it. Likewise, although the people always have their minds and eyes fixed on their King and all their hopes placed in him, one must not always trust the disposition of the people, since they can be turned now to the good and now to the bad side; thus, their owed subjection is not something stable and immutable. But if the Prince fosters and protects the people with piety, if he loves them like sons and does not allow even one lowly man or poor woman to go without rejoicing in the royal beneficence, then surely a heart of such great piety will be poured out upon the people, who will so venerate and love him in return, and will rejoice to submit themselves voluntarily to such a pious and...

Since these things are so, if indeed a King, established in a dignity granted by Heaven, admits even a single improper thought, Heaven will immediately loathe and turn away from that King; if even a single matter loses its proper order, the people will by this very fact be alienated. Finally, in another chapter, fortifying the Prince against presumption, he says with a sigh: *That you rule over the nine Provinces of the Empire* <note>The "Nine Provinces" (*Jiuzhou*) traditionally represented the entirety of the Chinese world</note> *is truly nothing other than a mandate from supreme Heaven. # BOOK THREE
## PART SEVEN

->Folio 1, page 1, paragraph 1.<-

**Zilu**, a disciple, asked his Master about the method of governing. *Confucius* replied: "Ensure that you lead and shine before your subjects by the best examples of virtue; then, see to the affairs of the people yourself, and willingly take your part in the public labor."

§. 2. The disciple asked the Master to suggest more. *Confucius*, wishing to cure the disciple's restlessness <note>original: *morbo*, literally 'disease' or 'affliction,' here referring to a spiritual or mental habit</note>, replied: "I have nothing to add; let those two things be observed, but constantly, and let there be no laziness, boredom, or weariness."

§. 3. Another of the disciples named **Zhonggong**, who was then serving under **Ji Shi**, the Great Prefect, as a Governor of a smaller territory, likewise inquired about the method of governing. *Confucius* replied: "First, ensure you have junior officials through whose effort and service you may accomplish things. Be a wise leader by looking the other way and forgiving minor faults. Elevate to public honors and bring into the administration of the Commonwealth <note>original: *Reipublicæ*; used here to refer to the state or public affairs</note> men of proven virtue and wisdom: for in this way you will provide excellently for yourself and your people."

p. 2. §. 1. "But," said the same **Zhonggong**, "how shall I recognize the qualities of such wise men so that I may then elevate them?" *Confucius* replied: "First, make sure you elevate those whom you have recognized yourself—even if it is only a single person, if you have known only one. As for those you have not recognized personally, will not others also know them, and thus they will be brought forward rather than passed over and neglected?"

§. 2. Upon the death of **Duke Ling**, the ruler of the Kingdom of **Lu** <note>The text mentions Lu, though Duke Ling is historically the ruler of the Kingdom of Wei; the translator may be conflating the states or the events</note>, he was succeeded by Prince **Zhe**, his grandson. Meanwhile, the Prince's father had been neglected and sent into exile against what was right and just; furthermore, when the father prepared to return, he was prevented by force of arms. During these events, *Confucius* happened to return from the Kingdom of **Chu** <note>original: *çu*</note> to the Kingdom of **Wei**, where at that time his disciple **Zilu** held office. Addressing his Master, Zilu said: "The Prince of the Kingdom of **Wei** has long desired your presence and eagerly awaits receiving you as his Master so that you may take up a position in the magistracy. If this should happen, I wish to know: what is the very first thing you, as Master, would do?"

<margin>§. 3.</margin> Confucius replied: By no means should the law and order be violated, by which nature subjects and binds a son to his father. Now your Prince **Che** <note>This refers to Duke Chu of the state of Wei, who was involved in a succession dispute with his father.</note>, since he has neglected his father and his father's right, and calls the one who is his grandfather "father," so that by a more plausible name he might possess a dominion not yet due to him: I, before all things, would strive to heal such a foul disturbance of right order and wounded piety; and thus I would entirely reform his name <note>This is the doctrine of *Zhengming*, or the "Rectification of Names," holding that social harmony stems from things being called by their proper titles and individuals acting according to those titles.</note>.

<margin>Folio 2, page 1, §. 1.</margin> **Zilu**, not considering the Master’s words maturely enough—as if they were less relevant to the matter at hand—said somewhat recklessly: "Is it as you say? You, Master, so it seems to me, are far from the truth here. To what end, I ask, is this so superfluous 'reformation of names,' when there are other matters of far greater importance which, in this state of affairs and times, seem rather to be handled?"

<margin>§. 2.</margin> Confucius, somewhat offended by such a hasty response, said: "Alas! How unrefined and rustic you are, my **Zilu**! A wise man, in matters he does not yet properly perceive, certainly acts like one hesitating and doubting; he does not rashly blurt out whatever comes into his mind.

<margin>§. 3.</margin> Hear now, therefore, what I wished to signify in few words: If the name of the Prince himself is not 'right,' nor of such a kind as rightfully belongs to him; and so, if a lie shines out, as it were, on the very forehead of the man; then certainly his speeches and commands will by no means be received with favorable ears and minds. But if the speech of the Prince is not received with favorable ears and minds, then without a doubt public affairs and business will by no means be completed.

<margin>§. 4.</margin> When, however, things are stuck and not completed, then that bond of human society—namely, the order of duties and the mutual harmony of all—will not flourish. With that order and harmony not flourishing, then punishments and penalties will not reach the goal established by the laws. With punishments wandering from the goal of the laws in this way, then the unhappy people, uncertain of what to pursue or avoid, simply have no place where they may safely set their feet and hands. Furthermore, the head and root of so many and such great evils is the neglected filial piety <note>original: *pietas*</note> of a son, masked by that false right and name.

<margin>§. 5.</margin> Therefore, a Prince, as far as concerns his name and title <note>original: *compellationem*</note>, must beyond doubt be of such a kind that it can be uttered without shame or offense to his subjects, so that he is called a son, if he is a son; a grandson, if he is a grandson. Now, when the name is uttered in this way, the affairs and business of the whole Kingdom will beyond doubt proceed successfully and without resistance from the subjects. Wherefore, let a Prince have or admit nothing in his words that is empty or rash; and let this indeed suffice, so that you yourself may understand how much importance there is in that change of name which I required at the beginning."

<margin>p. 2. §. 1.</margin> The disciple **Fan Chi**, weary, I think, of the corrupt morals...

...of his life, asked to be taught agriculture. Confucius replied: "I am not as skilled in the rustic arts as a veteran farmer; consult those who are experts." Again, he asked to be taught gardening. Confucius replied: "I am not like an old gardener; go and consult those whose duty that is."

As he was leaving, Confucius criticized him, yet in such a way that he might at the same time encourage him to pursue the study of virtue and wisdom more strenuously: "O," he said, "what a small-minded and common man you are, Fan Chi!" <note>The term used here is *xiaoren*, literally "small man," referring to someone of narrow vision who focuses on petty or material gains rather than moral cultivation.</note>

<margin>§. 3.</margin> Those who hold a superior place in the Republic—if indeed they delight in both outward and inward order <note>original: *compositione*, likely referring to *Li* or Ritual propriety</note>—then none of their subjects will dare not to honor and revere them. Again, if these same superiors delight in equity and justice, then none of their subjects will dare not to comply with them in all things. Finally, if superiors delight in good faith, maintained in both words and deeds, then none of their subjects will dare not to exercise, in turn, a sincere and ready will. If these things are so, then the people of the four regions—that is, the whole world—will carry their little infants wrapped in cloths upon their shoulders and will come hastening of their own accord in great crowds. Thus, there will be no lack of cultivators for the fields, nor food for the cultivators. Why then should you apply your mind to agriculture, when you can cultivate your own soul and the souls of others, and in this way provide most greatly even for agriculture itself?

*Lest anyone should perchance think that the Chinese Philosopher despises agriculture—which no Chinese philosopher has failed to hold in high esteem—our translator Couplet <note>original: Colaus. This refers to Philippe Couplet, the primary editor of this 1687 Latin edition.</note> tries here to explain Confucius's response in such a way that he does not hesitate to reconcile it with that famous exhortation by which the Duke of Zhou <note>original: Cheu</note>, while he was the Prince, studiously commended agriculture to the Emperor King Cheng <note>original: Chim vam</note>, for whom he was uncle and tutor. This is recorded in the Book of Documents <note>original: Xu kim</note>, Book 8, under the title "Against Idleness" <note>original: Vu ye</note>. Above all, it teaches how much Kings ought to value, and how solicitously they should protect and cherish agriculture as the very foundation of the Empire—the very element of the people, by which they are preserved no differently than a fish in its water. To this end, he brings forward the examples of the ancient Kings Shun, Yu, Wen, and King Wu <note>original: Vu-vam</note>, his father and brother, who had once joined the study of philosophy with the study of agriculture. What? Did not even Kings judge it not beneath Imperial dignity to move their royal hands to the plow-handle, plowing a portion of the field themselves every year? From this, the cakes and wine for the sacrifices to be offered to the Emperor of Heaven were afterward sought, as Mencius <note>original: Memcius</note> testifies, citing the books of rituals. Although there was also another reason for such a rare example: namely, that by this practice the Princes might learn to pity the hard labors of their colonists. So that he might refresh the memory of these things from time to time, one of the Emperors even ordered a plow to be hung up in the Palace. In addition to these, he also brings forward this reason for the exercise of the fields by Kings...*

§. 3.</margin>§. 3. Confucius responded: *By no means should the law and order be violated, by which nature has subjected and bound a son to his father. Now, your Prince Che <note>This refers to Duke Chu of the State of Wei, who was embroiled in a succession crisis with his father.</note>, insofar as he has neglected his father and his father's rights, calls the one who is actually his grandfather "father," so that by using a more respectable name he might possess a dominion that is not yet his by right. I, above all else, would strive to heal such a foul disturbance of right order and wounded piety; and thus, I would completely reform the names used by him.*

folio 2. page 1. §. 1. <gloss>Zilu</gloss> <note>original: "çu-lu"</note>, not sufficiently weighing the Master's words and thinking they were less relevant to the current situation, said somewhat thoughtlessly: "Is it truly as you say? You, Master, as it seems to me at least, are far from the truth here. To what purpose, I ask, is this so-called 'reformation of names'—a thing so superfluous—when there are other matters of far greater weight that ought to be dealt with in this state of affairs and times?"

§. 2. Confucius, somewhat offended by such a hasty response, said: *Alas! How unrefined and rustic you are, my You! <note>"You" is Zilu’s personal name; Confucius uses it here in a stern, paternal rebuke.</note> A wise man, in matters he does not yet properly perceive, certainly acts like one who hesitates and doubts; he does not rashly blurt out whatever comes into his mind.*

§. 3. *Hear now, therefore, what I wished to signify in few words: If the name of the Prince himself is not correct, nor of such a kind that belongs to him by right; and if, as it were, a lie shines right upon the forehead of the man; then certainly his speeches and mandates will by no means be received with favorable ears or minds. But if the speech of the Prince is not received with favorable ears and minds, then without a doubt public affairs and business will in no way be accomplished.*

§. 4. *Furthermore, when affairs are stuck and not accomplished, then that bond of human society—namely the order of duties and the mutual harmony of all—will not flourish. When that order and harmony do not flourish, then penalties and punishments will not reach the goal established by the laws. When punishments wander from the goal of the laws in this manner, then the unhappy people, uncertain of what to pursue or what to flee, quite literally have no place where they may safely set their feet or hands. Moreover, the head and root of so many and such great evils is the neglected piety of a son, masked by that false right and false name.*

§. 5. *Therefore, a Princely man, in what pertains to his name and title, must beyond doubt be of such a kind that he can be addressed without shame or offense to his subjects; so that he is called a son, if he is a son; a grandson, if he is a grandson. Now, when the name is uttered in this way, the affairs and business of the entire Kingdom will be able to proceed successfully and without resistance from the subjects. Wherefore, a Princely man should have or admit nothing in his words that is hollow or rash; and let this suffice, so that you yourself may understand how much weight lies in that change of names which I required at the beginning.*

### BOOK THREE

In his time, Fan Chi <note>A disciple of Confucius known for his interest in practical affairs.</note> asked to be taught agriculture. *Confucius* replied: "I am not as skilled in the rustic arts as a veteran farmer; you should consult the experts." He then asked to be taught gardening. *Confucius* replied: "I am not like an old gardener; go and consult those whose duty that is."

§. 2. *Fan Chi*, frustrated in his hope, went out; as he was leaving, *Confucius* criticized him, while simultaneously encouraging him to diligently pursue the study of virtue and wisdom, saying: "Oh, what a common and humble-minded man you are, my *Fan Chi*!"

§. 3. Those who hold a superior place in the Republic <note>The translator uses "Republic" (Respublica) to refer to the State or the Commonwealth.</note>, if they truly delight in both outward and inward composure <note>This refers to the practice of 'Li' or ritual propriety.</note>, then none of their subjects will dare not to honor and revere them. Again, if these same superiors delight in equity and justice, then none of their subjects will dare not to comply with them in all matters. Finally, if superiors delight in good faith, maintained in both words and deeds, then none of their subjects will dare not to show, in turn, a sincere and ready will. If things are managed in this way, then the people of the four regions—that is, the entire world—will carry their little infants wrapped in cloths upon their shoulders and will hasten to arrive in crowds of their own accord. Thus, neither will the fields lack cultivators, nor will the cultivators lack food. Why, therefore, would you apply your mind to agriculture, when you can cultivate your own mind and the minds of others, and in doing so, provide the very best service even to agriculture itself?

*Lest anyone should perchance think that the Chinese Philosopher despises agriculture—which no Chinese Philosopher has failed to hold in high esteem—our translator Couplet* <note>original: "Colaus Interpres" refers to Philippe Couplet, the primary editor of this 1687 Latin translation.</note> *attempts here to explain Confucius's response in such a way that he does not hesitate to reconcile it with that famous exhortation by which the Duke of Zhou* <note>original: "Cheu"</note>, *when he was prince, studiously commended agriculture to Emperor Cheng of Zhou* <note>original: "Chim vam"</note>, *for whom he was uncle and tutor. This is recorded in the Classic of History* <note>original: "Xu kim"</note>, *Book 8, under the title "Against Idleness"* <note>original: "Vu ye"</note>. *Above all, he teaches how much Kings ought to value, and how solicitously they should protect and foster agriculture as the foundation of the Empire, and as a kind of element for the people, by which they are preserved just as a fish is by its water. To this end, he brings forward the examples of the ancient Kings Shun, Yu, Wen, and King Wu* <note>original: "Xun, yu, ven & Vu-vam"</note>, *the father and brother of the Duke; who had once joined the study of agriculture with the study of Philosophy. Indeed, Kings did not judge it beneath their Imperial dignity to put their royal hands to the plow-handle, annually plowing a portion of the field themselves. From this field, the cakes and wine were later obtained for the sacrifices to be offered to the Emperor of Heaven, as Mencius* <note>original: "Memcius"</note> *testifies when citing the books of rites. Although there was also another reason for such a rare example: namely, so that by the experience itself, Princes might learn to pity the hard labors of their farmers. To refresh the memory of these labors, one Emperor even ordered a plow to be hung in the Palace. Besides these, he offers another reason for Kings to practice agri—*

<summary>Confucius rebukes his disciple Fan Chi for wanting to learn manual labor rather than statecraft, arguing that a virtuous ruler naturally attracts and provides for the people. The commentary clarifies that Confucius and other Chinese sages actually held agriculture in high religious and political esteem.</summary>

Folio 3, page 1. *Confucius* says: Suppose someone has thoroughly learned the three hundred chapters of the **Odes** <note>The *Shi Jing* or Classic of Poetry, essential for any scholar-official</note> through laborious toil and study. Yet, if the duty of governing the State <note>original: *Reipublicæ*</note> is conferred upon him, and he does not have a clear grasp of the affairs of his office—so that if he goes as an envoy to the four quarters of the Empire, he cannot by his own skill and on the spur of the moment give appropriate answers to the inquiries of the petty Princes <note>original: *Regulorum*</note> to whom he is sent—then of what use, after all, will these many things be to him, though they were acquired with great study? It is a useless burning of the midnight oil <note>original: *lucubratio*</note> which you cannot put forth in real matters and deeds.

Page 2, § 1. *Confucius* says: If the person of the ruler is himself upright and composed toward every virtue, then even if he uses no warnings or exhortations, the subjects will nevertheless of their own accord turn themselves toward every virtue and praise, drawn along by the example of the governor. On the contrary, if the person himself is not upright, even though he uses constant prodding and exhortations, the subjects will still not follow. For words may attract, but deeds more powerfully turn them away.

§ 2. The **Duke of Zhou** and **Kang Shu** <note>original: *Cam xo*</note>, sons of King Wen <note>original: *Ven-vam*</note>, each received their own dynasties: to the latter fell the Kingdom of **Wei** <note>original: *Guei*</note>, and to the former, **Lu**. § 3. *Confucius* used to say regarding the Prefect of the Kingdom of Wei called **Jing** <note>original: *Cum çu kin*; referring to Prince Jing of Wei</note>, who by chance lived content with his lot: he lived at home as a well-pleased and private citizen. As soon as he had even a little, he immediately said to himself in silence: "I have accumulated enough." Then, when he had a little more, he nonetheless said: "I have plenty at hand." But when an abundance of things was finally his, he immediately said: "I have enough even for splendor."

§ 4. The disciple asked again: "Once an abundance of things is present, what would you add furthermore?" He responded: "**Right instruction.**"

§. 5. *Confucius used to say*: If there were any of the local lords or petty kings <note>original: *dynastis ac Regulis*</note> who would employ me, making use of my work and my counsel, within the cycle of a single year I would have accomplished something significant, and the value of my efforts would already become visible, at least in the removal of the more serious vices. After three years, I might even dare to hope that the state of affairs would be fully perfected.

page 2. §. 1. *Confucius*, citing a proverb from ancient times, says: A Prince who is well-schooled in honesty <note>original: *probitate*</note>, and who governs his Kingdom through his own efforts and through sons and grandsons like him, would certainly be able, within a span of a hundred years, to transform and return to goodness even the most wicked and savage of men; indeed, he could even abolish the punishments of death themselves. This is because love, rather than terror, keeps subjects within their duty. Oh, how true are these words of our ancestors!

§. 2. *Confucius says*: But if a Prince were granted who rules with rare virtue and wisdom, then it would clearly come to pass that, once thirty years have flown by, the native virtue implanted in everyone would then happily bloom.

folio 5. page 1. §. 1. *Confucius says*: If a man properly orders his own person, what trouble or difficulty will he have in undertaking a magistracy <note>term: *Magistratu* — here referring to a public office or government position</note>? §. 2. **Ran Qiu** <note>original: *Gen-çu*; a disciple of Confucius known for his administrative talent</note>, a counselor to the Prefect **Ji Kangzi** <note>original: *Ki-xi*; the head of the powerful Ji family who often usurped the authority of the Duke of Lu</note>—a man of a turbulent nature—happened to be coming from the court of that same Prefect. *Confucius said*: "Why so late?" For if public matters had been discussed, even though I am not currently employed to manage the State at this place and time, according to the accepted custom whereby retired officials are consulted from time to time, I would undoubtedly have been consulted as well and heard something of the matter." Here, the Prefect is silently rebuked—as is his disciple and counselor—because they were secretly plotting something against the King.

...the Kingdom, or, can that which explains what usually brings destruction to Kingdoms also be given? *Confucius* responds: By the same token, such a thing—which is the summit of all evils—cannot be so easily determined by a single word. There is a common proverb that says: *I do not rejoice in, nor do I wish to act as King; but if I do, then I certainly and vehemently desire that my words and Royal edicts be obeyed, and that no one at all opposes me.*

§. 4. *Confucius* reasons: If these words of the ruler are good, and suited to equity and the public good, and because of this no one at all opposes them; will this not truly be magnificent and a rare happiness? On the contrary, if the ruler's words are not good, nor joined with the equity and utility of the subjects, and yet again no one at all opposes or argues against the Prince ruling badly; will you not then have determined by almost a single word that which overthrows a Kingdom; or, that which contains the destruction of a kingdom? For just as not opposing evil is the ruin of Kingdoms; so not opposing good things is their peace and foundation.

<margin>folio 6. page 1. §. 1.</margin> In the Kingdom of *Chu* <note>original: *Çu*</note>, the Governor of the town of *She* <note>original: *Xe*</note> inquired about the method of governing correctly.

§. 3. The disciple *Zixia* <note>original: *Çu hia*</note>, when he was Governor of the district of *Jufu* <note>original: *Kiu fu*</note> located in the Kingdom of *Lu*; consulted the Master on the method of governing correctly. *Confucius* said: two cautions are necessary for you: first, do not wish to be over-hasty or headlong, by sharply and improperly urging that what has been commanded be finished immediately. The other, that you should not focus on tiny gains of little importance, or small advantages. For wishing to accelerate everything, and to hurry always and everywhere; then certainly you will not have a clear view of things, the knowledge of which is usually reached only slowly. Now, if you attend to certain meager gains and comforts; then it will happen that even the greatest matters and business will not be completed.

For a father, if something more serious has perhaps been committed by the son, even for the very reason that he is his son, hides the matter; likewise, a son, if something has perhaps been committed by the Father; even much more so, because he is the Father, hides the matter and conceals it from others, especially the judge; and as it seems to me, a certain simplicity and uprightness exists even in this very devotion of the father and son to hiding [the fault] <note>This passage highlights the Confucian priority of family loyalty (filial piety) over legalistic or abstract "truth," suggesting that social harmony begins with the integrity of the family bond.</note>.

§. 3. **Fan Chi** <note>original: *Fan-chi*</note> questioned the Master on the method of acquiring true virtue. **Confucius** responded: The study of virtue is necessary in every place and at every time. If you live as a private citizen, ensure you constantly maintain decorum and gravity. If you must set your hand to any public work or business, conduct yourself with diligence, maturity, and composure. In dealing with others, let loyalty and truth be at your heart. Even if you should travel among barbarian and uncultured nations, it is not permitted to cast aside these pursuits of virtue for even a single moment.

<margin>Folio 7, page 1, §. 1.</margin> **Zi Gong** <note>original: *çu cum*</note> questioned him, saying: In what way can someone succeed and be deservedly called an extraordinary and primary man? <note>This refers to the *Shi*, often translated as "scholar" or "knight."</note> **Confucius** responded: He who is modest in the affairs and actions proper to his own person, such that he fears and recoils from even the first appearance of baseness and iniquity; likewise, he who is sent as an envoy by his Prince to the four corners of the Empire and does not disgrace the Prince’s mission through negligence or imprudence, but handles affairs with the local rulers skillfully—he can be called an extraordinary and primary man.

§. 2. The disciple said: May I be permitted to ask again, within this rank of men who rise above the common crowd, who are those of the second degree? **Confucius** responded: The second are those who are rightly and deservedly judged and proclaimed as "obedient" <note>meaning filial</note> by their relatives and kin. Likewise, those who are judged and proclaimed by their fellow townsmen as "respectful to their elders."

§. 3. The disciple said: May I be permitted to ask yet again: among these very people, who are those of the third degree? **Confucius** responded: Those who, in their speech, bring a mind determined toward the truth, even if they lack the sharp wit to distinguish perfectly between the true and the false. Likewise, those who, in all their affairs and actions, bring a mind determined to complete the work they have undertaken. These kinds of men possess a certain hard and persistent constancy—though of how little capacity and talent they are! Nevertheless, can they not also be judged second to those others, especially since they are generally a harm to no one, and while they look to their own affairs, they may still possess something that deserves praise?

§. 4. **Zi Gong** interrogated him again: Regarding those who are currently employed in governing the Republic <note>the state</note>, what is your judgment of them, Master? **Confucius** responded: Alas! They are men of such meager capacity and talent, clearly like the <term>Teu and Siao</term> <note>original: *Teu & Siao*; small bamboo measures or vessels of little volume</note> vessels; how could they deserve to be counted of any number or value?

**Folio 8, page 1, §. 1.** **Confucius** said: Among the people of the south, there is a common proverb which says: "A man who lacks constancy cannot practice the art of either divination or medicine." I praise and approve of this.

**§. 2.** He confirms this proverb by the authority of the **Prince of Zhou** <note>original: *Cheu-cum*; refers to the Duke of Zhou, a foundational figure of Chinese civilization whom Confucius greatly admired</note> in his commentaries on the *Book of Changes* <note>original: *librum mutationum*; the *I Ching* or *Yi Jing*</note>, at figure 32, titled *Heng* <note>original: *Hem*; the 32nd hexagram of the I Ching, representing endurance and constancy</note>, that is, constancy, where he says: "Whoever does not perpetuate and constantly cultivate his virtue will eventually bring shame and disgrace upon himself." **§. 3.** Sighing here, **Confucius** said: "Alas! Blind mortals do not seek out or weigh this truth. It is over!"

**§. 4.** **Confucius** said: A man of integrity and wisdom, as far as divine law and reason permit, agrees with everyone, yet in such a way that he does not become one and the same with the indiscriminate crowd: on the contrary, the wicked and foolish man, with no discernment, makes himself one and the same with everyone, and yet he agrees with no one insofar as divine law and reason prescribe.

**§. 5.** **Zi Gong** <note>original: *Tçu cum*; one of Confucius's most prominent and eloquent disciples</note> asked, saying: "If all the common people like someone, what will you think?" **Confucius** replied: "That is not yet enough to determine anything certain about his virtue and wisdom." "But if all the common people hate someone, what will you think of him?" **Confucius** said: "This too is not yet enough. It is far better and safer if the most upright of the common people like him, and the most wicked of them hate him. Of such a man, I would dare to safely affirm that he is a man of integrity and wisdom."

## BOOK THREE

...if you flatter and please him, even if you do so shamefully and illicitly, he is nevertheless delighted. But when acting toward him as toward a master or a leader of the people, he urgently and unmercifully demands from his subjects things that are perfect in every respect <note>original: *omnibus numeris absolutas*; a Latin idiom meaning complete or perfect in every detail</note>.

**§. 2.** ***Confucius says***: The wise man enjoys a deep peace, yet he is not puffed up with any haughtiness or pride. The foolish man, however, is pleased with himself and applauds his own actions, yet he is a stranger to true peace because he is a stranger to true goodness and true virtue.

**Folio 9, page 1, §. 1.** ***Confucius says***: By the strength of a constant mind, by brave patience, by pure simplicity, and finally by a certain slowness in speaking—by these four steps, as it were, one approaches nearly to that integrity and innocence of soul implanted by heaven into our nature.

**§. 2.** ***Zilu*** <note>original: *çu lu*; one of Confucius’s most loyal and daring disciples, known for his bravery</note> asked, saying: "In what way can someone be called a Master among his own people?" ***Confucius replied***: "Let there be a certain ardor of love and zeal in pursuing virtue. Let a certain exactness and effectiveness be applied in reminding others of their duty. To these, let a serenity of countenance and an affability of speech be added; such a man can be called a Master. Furthermore, toward friends and associates, let there be an ardent zeal for mutual virtue, as well as a sharp and accurate requirement of mutual duty. But toward brothers, both older and younger, let a gentler and more pleasant manner be applied."

**§. 3.** ***Confucius says***: If a man of probity and integrity should teach the people what pertains to their duty, whether toward their parents or toward the Prince, and if he should teach this for seven years, then the citizens and subjects will even be able to emerge as skilled in military affairs.

**Page 2, §. 1.** ***Confucius says***: To employ a people not yet properly instructed in virtues for military service is truly and rightly said to be "throwing one's own away" <note>original: *abjicere suos*; to abandon or discard one's people to certain death</note> and exposing the fatherland to grave danger.

**§. 2.** The disciple ***Yuan Xian*** <note>original: *Yven hien*; a disciple known for his purity and preference for a simple life over wealth</note> asked what things ought to be considered shameful. ***Confucius replied***: "In a Kingdom, while the laws are in force, to hold public office but contribute nothing by effort or counsel to the public good—and meanwhile to enjoy a royal stipend—is a matter worthy of shame. Again, in a Kingdom, while the laws lie dormant, to dissolve into the same idleness and sloth when one should most especially be consulting for the endangered fatherland, and nonetheless to enjoy a royal stipend; this is a thing to be vehemently ashamed of."

**§. 3.** The same disciple proposed a question of this sort: "If someone," he said, "were free from the four most common vices, and thus if—out of an excessive appetite for glory and excellence, or through self-complacency and boasting, or through anger, or finally through the desire for possessions—he did nothing at all; could he, in my opinion, be considered endowed with that primary virtue and innocence which was implanted in man?"

**§. 4.** ***Confucius*** replied: "To do nothing in conjunction with those things which..."

# CHINESE KNOWLEDGE
(SCIENTIÆ SINICÆ)

...you have listed, such as disturbances of the mind, it can indeed be considered very rare and difficult. But regarding that primeval command of reason or innocence, and whether he is endowed with it or not, I truly do not know.

**Folio 10, page 1, §. 1.** ***Confucius says***: A man of gravity and wisdom who labors chiefly for this, and meditates on this constantly—how to live comfortably and pleasantly at home—is unworthy of being considered a wise man.

**§. 2.** ***Confucius says***: If in any kingdom the law and authority of a good Prince flourish, speak out confidently and bravely; act confidently and bravely. If in a kingdom the laws and authority of the Prince lie neglected, then one must still act confidently and bravely; however, let your speech have more than the usual ease and submission, lest you aggravate the disease of an already sick body rather than healing it.

**Page 2, §. 1.** ***Confucius says***: He who possesses virtue undoubtedly also has words and teachings at the ready with which to recommend it to others. However, those who have words at the ready do not always, by any necessary consequence, possess virtue. Again, whoever excels in integrity and innocence of life is undoubtedly endowed with a certain strength of mind and fortitude. Yet a brave man is not necessarily endowed with that integrity of which I spoke.

**§. 2.** The disciple ***Nan cum quo*** (also known as ***Nan yum*** <note>original: *Nan-rong*</note>) asked Confucius, saying: "In ancient times, the ruler of the Kingdom of *Yeu kium* <note>original: *Youqiong*</note> called *Heu y* <note>original: *Hou Yi*, the famous mythological archer</note>, who was also a <term>Colaus</term> <note>a Latinized version of the Chinese *ge-lao*, meaning a high-ranking minister or Grand Secretary</note> under *Chum cam* <note>original: *Zhong Kang*</note>, the fourth Emperor of the *Hia* <note>original: *Xia*</note> dynasty (about 1700 years before Confucius), was a man of immense strength and simultaneously most skilled in archery. Another contemporary of the same, named *Ngao* <note>original: *Ao*</note>, the son of *Han cho* <note>original: *Han Zhuo*</note>, could move ships here and there on dry land with no effort, so prodigious was his physical power. Yet both of these men did not meet a natural death; both were murdered. On the other hand, two others, *Yu* <note>Yu the Great, founder of the Xia dynasty</note> and *çie* <note>original: *Qi* or *Xie*, the ancestor of the Zhou lineage</note>, though not distinguished by physical strength or wealth—since they tilled the fields with their own hands and lived humble and poor lives—nevertheless obtained the Empire of China. *Yu* indeed succeeded the Emperor *Xun* and was the founder of the first *Hia* dynasty; *çie* truly, insofar as the great *Vu vam* <note>original: *Wu Wang*, the Martial King</note>, founder of the third *Cheu* <note>original: *Zhou*</note> dynasty, was born from his line (though about 1300 years later). But why was this so?" Confucius did not answer at that time. But as soon as the disciple *Nan cum quo* had left, Confucius exclaimed: "O, how excellent this man is! O, how much this man, *Nan cum quo*, values and truly appreciates the price of virtue!"

**Folio 11, page 1, §. 1.** <term>Gin</term> <note>original: *Ren* (仁); often translated as benevolence, humaneness, or perfect virtue</note> is the native virtue of the heart, and is almost nothing other than a constant alignment of the mind with the laws of heaven. But because the heart itself is so inconstant and restless, it often happens that, even without us noticing, this virtue is obscured as if by certain mists, if not lost entirely. Therefore, Confucius rightly says: A man of both probity and wisdom may yet sometimes...

### BOOK THREE
<note>In this edition, "Book Three" likely refers to a specific division within the larger work or the third book of the *Analects* as organized by the translators.</note>

...is granted as being entirely devoid of that purest and most tender virtue. In a word: a slight error, a light sin, may befall a wise man. But there has never yet existed, nor indeed can there exist, a man who is at once wicked and at the same time endowed with that virtue *Gin* <note>original: *Ren*, the Confucian core virtue of "humanity" or "benevolence"</note>: for such a person would be in harmony with heaven and not in harmony with it at the same time.

§. 2. *Confucius* says: Can anyone who loves another not also subject them to hard discipline? Again, can anyone who is a faithful and true Minister to his Prince not also remind him of his duty?

§. 3. The Kingdom of *Chim* <note>original: *Zheng*</note> was certainly modest in size, situated in a central location between the two powerful Kingdoms of *Qin* and *Chu*. However, the virtue and prudence of its Prince, known as *Hien cum* <note>original: *Duke Xian of Zheng*</note>, combined happily with the faithfulness, harmony, and skill of his Ministers. This not only made the kingdom invincible against the ambition and power of its neighbors, but also allowed it to flourish, blessed with peace and wealth. Confucius, intending to give here an example of that harmonious skill and the faithfulness of those serving the Prince—estimating the strength and elegance of the whole body from a single finger <note>a metaphor for judging the whole by a small part</note>—says thus: whenever something had to be announced in the Prince's name to the neighboring petty Kings, first the Prefect *Pi xin* <note>original: *Pi Chen*</note>, having well understood the Prince’s mind, would begin to set it out in a first draft with a rougher pen; soon after, *xi xo* <note>original: *Shi Shu*</note> would examine the writing and confirm it by applying reasons and examples from the Ancients. A third man, *Hin gin* (this is the name of his office) called *çu yu* <note>original: *Ziyu*</note>, would prune those things which seemed superfluous and add what he judged was missing, arranging and adorning everything in a more refined style and order. Finally, a fourth, born in the territory of *Tum-li* and named *çu chan* <note>original: *Zichan*, a famous statesman</note>, would add his own grace and charm to the work, removing anything antiquated that might have crept in. Furthermore, because the work was completed by four illustrious men in such harmony, could it possibly fail to achieve the desired outcome?

**Page 2, §. 1.** Confucius explains in this paragraph and the two following ones what he thinks of certain men and Ministers of various princes. Thus, when someone asked what he thought of *çu chan* <note>Zichan</note>, Confucius replied: "He is a benevolent man, and is regarded as such by all, even though he is also a strict critic, censor, and judge."

§. 2. Asked what he thought of *çu si* <note>original: *Zixi*</note>, he replied in a dismissive manner: "That man? That man?" For he favored the dynast of the Kingdom of *Chu*, who was legitimate in his line but who claimed the title of King against the law of the land <note>referring to the Chu rulers' usurpation of the title 'King' which was reserved for the Zhou Emperor</note>.

§. 3. Asked about *Quon chum* <note>original: *Guan Zhong*</note>, the Prefect of the Kingdom of *Qi*, who had formerly been the advisor to *Huon cum* <note>original: *Duke Huan of Qi*</note>, then the leader of the petty Kings; he replied: "This was the man for *Huon cum*." Certainly, when he had deprived one of the prefects (named *Pe xi* <note>original: *Bo Pi*</note>) of the district of *Pien* and its three hundred families because he was guilty of a certain crime, and when he had transferred this district to himself, *Pe xi* was then reduced to poverty, even to eating the cheapest rice; yet, until the very end of his life, he did not utter <note>The text cuts off here at "protu-", likely for "protulit," meaning he did not utter a complaint.</note>

...never a word of an unfair or indignant mind. For he reflected constantly both on what failings he might have committed, and how great were the merits of the other who had succeeded him in that command.

**f. 12. p. 1. §. 1.** *Confucius says*: To live in poverty and yet not to hate it is extremely difficult. To be wealthy and yet be without pride or arrogance is easy.

**§. 2.** *Confucius says*: Regarding the former Great Officer of the Kingdom of *Lu* <note>The home state of Confucius</note> named *Mem cum cho* <note>Meng Gongchuo</note>: he is certainly well-suited to serve as the chief steward for the *Chao* and *Guei* <note>Zhao and Wei</note> families in the Kingdom of *Qin* <note>original: *çin*, referring here to the powerful state of Jin</note>, even though they are quite distinguished and wealthy; he surely has enough ability and industry for that. But he cannot even serve as the Governor of the smallest dynasties such as *Tem* or *Sie* <note>Teng or Xue, two minor states</note>.

**p. 2. §. 1.** *çu lu* <note>Zilu, a prominent and bold disciple of Confucius</note> asks what things especially make a man perfect in every respect? *Confucius* answers: If one possesses the knowledge and prudence of the Great Officer of the Kingdom of *Lu* called *cam vu chum* <note>Zang Wuzhong</note>; likewise the moderation of mind, free from desire and greed, of the aforementioned *Mem cum cho*; furthermore, the strength of both mind and body of the Officer of the district of *Pien* called *chuam çu* <note>Zhuangzi of Bian, a man famous for his bravery, not to be confused with the Daoist philosopher</note>; and finally the industry and skill in the liberal arts of your fellow student *Gen kieu* <note>Ran Qiu</note>—if, I say, someone adorns these gifts and merits, and tempers them in a certain way with duties and civil rites, and with music—that charming teacher of mutual harmony and the best morals—then indeed such a person can be considered a man perfect in every respect <note>original: *vir numeris omnibus absolutus*, a Latin idiom for "a man complete in all his parts"</note>.

**§. 2.** But how can one person embrace all these things? We can conceive of such perfection in our minds, but we can hardly find one who is endowed with it. Nevertheless, why is it so necessary for the perfect men of our own age to be such? Certainly, if someone seeing a chance for profit immediately meditates on justice; likewise, seeing a crisis for the State or the Prince, eagerly exposes and offers his life; and in old pacts and promises, does not forget nor deny his lifelong words, and never fails the faith once given—one who is like this may also, in his own way, be considered a perfect man.

**f. 13. p. 1. §. 1.** *Confucius*, inquiring about the Great Officer of the Kingdom of *Guei* <note>Wei</note> named *cum xo ven çu* <note>Gongshu Wenzi</note> from a certain native named *cum mim kia* <note>Gongming Jia</note>, speaks thus: "Is it believable, as is commonly said, that your master does not speak, does not laugh, and does not accept anything?"

**p. 2. §. 1.** *Cum min kia* replied: "Those who tell these things exceed the limits of truth. My master speaks only when the time for speaking is right, and when the place and reason demand it; and so people do not grow weary of his words. If there is cause for joy, where a just reason for laughter and cheerfulness is given, then he laughs; thus people do not grow weary of his laughter. Finally, if justice and equity allow it, then he accepts what is offered; in this way, people are not offended by his acceptance of gifts." Such moderation, because it is not common...

### BOOK THREE
<note>original: *LIBER TERTIUS*. In this 1687 edition, the translators have divided the work into "Books" that may differ slightly from modern numbering of the Analects.</note>

...is in our time; therefore my Lord is commonly said neither to speak, nor to laugh, nor to accept anything. Hearing this, **Confucius**, full of wonder and like one who somewhat doubts, said: It shall be as you say. A marvelous thing indeed and of rare praise: but how, nevertheless, is it really thus?

**§. 2.** **Zang Wuzhong** <note>original: *çam vu chum*</note>, a prefect of the Kingdom of **Lu**, had gravely offended the Prince, and fearing punishment, had fled to the neighboring dynasty called **Chu**. But not long after returning from there to his Fatherland, and to the territory formerly under his jurisdiction, he asked the inhabitants to entreat the Prince for his former possession for at least one of his descendants. But **Confucius**, by no means approving of these roundabout ways, spoke thus: **Zang Wuzhong** procures and seeks for his descendants from the Prince of the Kingdom of **Lu** regarding his former territory: but I fear lest those prayers be armed <note>Confucius suggests that since Zang Wuzhong held the city of Fang, his "request" was actually a veiled military threat</note>, and although he himself says, "I want nothing from the King through deceit or force," I nevertheless do not believe him. I would believe him if he had gone straight to the Prince and not to his former subjects.

**f. 14. p. 1. §. 1.** **Confucius** says: The Ruler of the Kingdom of **Jin** <note>original: *çin*</note>, **Duke Wen** <note>original: *Ven cam*</note>, was deceitful and craftily industrious in the expeditions he undertook, and was not upright and sincere. On the contrary, the Ruler of the Kingdom of **Qi** <note>original: *çi*</note>, **Duke Huan** <note>original: *Huon cum*</note>, was sincere, and performed with good faith whatever he had promised, and was not at all deceitful; for this reason, he is clearly to be preferred far above the other.

**§. 2.** After the death of **Duke Xiang** <note>original: *Siam cum*</note> of the Kingdom of **Qi**, a grave sedition arose among the inhabitants, some demanding the elder son for the Kingdom, others the younger, and this not without force and arms. Meanwhile, the elder, **Duke Huan**, fled together with his follower and counselor **Bao Shuya** <note>original: *Pao xo ya*</note> into the Kingdom of **Ju** <note>original: *Kiu*</note>, to gather soldiers there. The younger, however (whose name was **Prince Jiu** <note>original: *cum çu kieu*</note>), betook himself to the Kingdom of **Lu** with two other followers, **Shao Hu** <note>original: *Chao ho*</note> and **Guan Zhong** <note>original: *Quon chum*</note>. When the younger was finally defeated, the elder entered the Kingdom of **Lu** and compelled the terrified inhabitants to the slaughter of the fugitive Prince; however, he ordered both companions of the flight to be cast into prison. One of these, **Shao Hu**, could not bear to survive his Lord; but by a voluntary death, he forestalled the shame of chains. **Guan Zhong**, yielding to fortune, accepted the chains: but having then been released from these by order of the victor, he was even created his supreme Counselor and administrator, with the support of **Bao Shuya**. The success of the matter surpassed the hopes and prayers of everyone: for when the neighboring Barbarians had invaded the Kingdom of **Qi**, the new administrator soon brought it about by his counsel and prudence not only that the Kingdom of **Qi**, having conquered and routed the Barbarians, should recover its former peace and liberty; but also that many of the Rulers should again obey the Imperial House of **Zhou** <note>original: *cheu*</note>, which at that time lay inglorious, and should pay their tributary homage. Therefore the disciples **Zilu** <note>original: *çu-lu*</note> and **Zigong** <note>original: *çu cum*</note>, seeking the opinion of their master, **Zilu** indeed spoke thus: **Duke Huan** killed **Prince Jiu**, his brother. **Shao Hu** likewise died with his Lord, a faithful companion of flight and death. **Guan Zhong** was certainly different from this man, not...

...he died; but like a rebel and a deserter, he followed the victor. Therefore, shall it be said that he was not pious <note>original: *pius*. **p. 2. § 1.** **Confucius** said: **Duke Huan** <note>original: *Huon cum*, referring to Duke Huan of Qi</note>, as you know, gathered and joined various dynasts and minor kings in study and arms, by whose labor he expelled the Barbarians in such a way that he provided for the honor and safety of the Imperial house. **§. 3.** **Confucius** replied:

If **Guan Zhong** had not existed, I and you would now be serving barbarians; and according to the custom of barbarians, I would have this hair loose and flowing, and not gathered according to our custom, and I would fasten my garment with a buckle on the left side, and not on the right, as is the barbarian ritual <note>Confucius argues that Guan Zhong saved Chinese civilization itself, which is more important than the "small fidelity" of dying for a single prince</note>.

**p. 2. §. 1.** There was a servant and domestic minister named **Zhuan** <note>original: *Siven*</note> under a certain famous prefect in the Kingdom of **Wei** <note>original: *Guei*</note> named **Gongshu Wenzi** <note>original: *cum xo ven çu*</note>. ...to promote one of such humble status to a rank equal to his own.

**§. 3.** **Confucius**, while living in his native Kingdom of **Lu** <note>original: *Lu*</note>, remarked that Prince **Ling** <note>original: *Lim*</note> of the Kingdom of **Wei** <note>original: *Guei*</note> lived without the character or restraint of a good Prince. **Ji Kangzi** <note>original: *Cam çu*</note>, the Prefect of the Kingdom of **Lu**, asked: "If this is so, why has the Kingdom of **Wei** not perished?"

**§. 4.** **Confucius** replied: "**Zhongshu Yu** <note>original: *Chum xo yu*, also known as Kong Wenzi</note> holds the office of receiving envoys and guests. **Zhu Tuo** <note>original: *Cho to*</note> is in charge of the ancestral halls of the ancestors. **Wangsun Jia** <note>original: *Van sun kia*</note> is the Prefect of the military camps. These three men administer the matters entrusted to them with great prudence and skill. When things are so, and if a Kingdom relies on men of such stature, how could it perish—no matter how much the Prince himself lives unmindful of his duty?

f. 16. p. 1. **§. 1.** **Confucius** said: Whenever a man's speech is imbued with a certain shame <note>original: *verecundiâ*, implying a sense of modesty or moral restraint</note> or modesty and moderation, it is well; but when words are brought forth with rashness and boasting, it is certainly very difficult to fulfill them with deeds and actions. Therefore, when you find someone speaking grandly, observe what he actually does; remember that a poverty of deeds is not rarely joined with a bounty of words.

**§. 2.** **Chen Chengzi** <note>original: *chin chim çu*</note>, a Prefect of the Kingdom of **Qi** <note>original: *çi*</note>, was plotting a secret rebellion. His Ruler already suspected and hated him for this, and had ordered a faithful man named **Han Zhi** <note>original: *Han chi*</note> to watch him diligently. But the traitor, sensing the investigation, first killed his own spy, and then even killed the Ruler himself, **Duke Jian** <note>original: *Kie cum*</note>.

**§. 3.** **Confucius**, who shortly before had held a high government office <note>Confucius had served as the Minister of Justice in Lu</note>, was moved by the atrocity of such a wicked murder. Following custom, he first washed his body <note>original: *lavit corpus*. This refers to ritual purification performed before a solemn religious or state act</note> and then immediately proceeded to the court to inform **Duke Ai** <note>original: *Ngai cum*</note>. When he came into the Duke's presence, he said: "**Chen Heng** (which is another name for the murderer) has killed his King. I ask you to send the army to seize and punish the traitor. Since his Kingdom is neighbor to yours, you should be the first to seek vengeance for a crime that Heaven itself will by no means tolerate."

**§. 4.** The Duke, as he was now old and nearly useless for managing affairs—and moreover possessed little authority, since the three families ruled with almost royal power—replied to **Confucius**: "Go, and report this matter to my three clients <note>original: *clientibus*. These were the heads of the three powerful clans that actually controlled Lu</note>: **Mengsun**, **Shusun**, and **Jisun** <note>original: *Mem sun, Xo sun, & Ki sun*</note>."

**§. 5.** **Confucius**, before he departed, said: "O King, although I do not hold office now, because I once did, and because I am next in rank after your prefects, I did not dare not to inform you of a matter of such great importance." The King said again: "Go, and report the matter to those three clients."

**§. 2.** When <gloss>cum</gloss> a disciple, hearing these things, said: "In this way indeed, O Master, out of your singular modesty, you both feel and speak regarding yourself."

**§. 3.** When <gloss>cum</gloss> [this disciple] was entirely occupied in comparing the characters and morals of men with one another, Confucius, rebuking him, said: "And you, O my disciple **Zigong** <note>original: *Su*.
