For my part, I do not have enough leisure even for my own affairs and concerns; how much less then to inquire inquisitively into the characters and lives of others."

**§. 4.** Confucius said: "Do not be distressed in mind or torture yourself because men do not know you. Rather, be distressed and tortured by that powerlessness and weakness of your own, by which it happens that you are not yet able to have fully understood, and much less to fulfill, those things which are of your duty."

**p. 2. §. 1.** Confucius said: "If anyone does not anticipate, with anxious suspicion and care, a deception and fraud still far removed, nor is among the number of those who are continually afraid of everything even when it is most safe; if anyone also has not long before determined in his mind that credit will not be given to him when he is about to say or do something; if anyone, I say, is a man of this kind, so that he is never entangled in those cares and suspicions which are so hostile to human society and mutual dealings; yet if that same person should prevail with a certain exceptional shrewdness and perspicacity regarding either men or things, and thus immediately scents and foresees whatever fraud or deceit may happen to lie hidden—he is surely a man of insight and prudence." <note>The Master is arguing for a middle way between being overly suspicious and being easily fooled.</note>

**§. 2.** One from the number of the wise, but who kept his leisure for himself alone <note>A reference to a "hermit" or "recluse" philosopher who avoids public service</note>, named **Wei Shengmu** <note>original: *Vi sem mu*</note>, addressing Confucius, spoke thus: "**Qiu** <note>original: *Kieu* (read as *meu*). Now you are in the Kingdom of **Qi** <note>original: *çì*</note>, now in the Kingdom of **Lu** <note>original: *Lù*</note>. You offer your teaching for sale everywhere, but nowhere do you find those who will buy; is this not to be exactly like a street-peddler, talkative and garrulous, seeking the empty applause of the ignorant multitude, and perhaps even begging for some position of dignity?"

**§. 3.** Confucius, in order to blunt the man's pride a little, responds in this manner: "I would not dare to sell trifles and words, nor to act the talkative man. Moreover, I even hate and condemn the man who is stubborn and fixed to a single thing and opinion, and who, at the first impulses or threats of public calamity, immediately seeks a hiding place, and cannot even endure to think about restoring the laws and correcting the depraved morals of men." <note>Confucius defends his travels as a moral duty to fix society rather than a search for fame.</note>

**§. 4.** Confucius used to say: "In a rare and excellent horse, it is not so much its strength that is praised as its **virtue** <note>original: *virtus*</note>, that is, its docility, gentleness, and tractability."

**§. 2.** Confucius responded: He who acts in such a way <note>meaning: one who repays an injury with a benefit</note>; with what then will he compensate good deeds? For the reward and the reasoning ought to be different for one who deserves well and for one who deserves ill.

**§. 3.** This, therefore, is my opinion: compensate injuries and hatred with that which is right and just; compensate good deeds with good deeds. 

The **Interpreter** <note>This refers to the traditional Neo-Confucian commentaries used by the Jesuits</note> explains these words in this way: Someone seems to have brought an injury upon me; I will not dwell on it, nor will I consider it only as it was done to me; rather, I will weigh every aspect of it on the fair scales of reason, so that I may determine what here is worthy of hatred, what of love, what of avoidance, and what of pursuit. Having weighed everything, if I find that the person who hurt me is, in other respects and simply speaking, worthy of love, I certainly will not, because of a private offense, cast any envious shadows upon his praise and virtue. But if there are many things that make him hateful and worthily to be cast out, I will then obey reason, which teaches us to pursue and eliminate wickedness and other vices with hatred. And this is what it means to repay hatred with that which is right and just.

*You have here, **Christian Reader**, the opinion of a Heathen Philosopher <note>Confucius</note> on so difficult a matter. But notice also the Interpreter’s exclamation, likewise a Heathen, yet worthy of a Philosopher; although it does not reach the height of **Evangelical holiness** <note>The teachings of the Christian Gospels</note>, how much milder is this speech, and how much more humane than that crude Pharisaic axiom: **you shall hate your enemy**. Nevertheless, Confucius seems to have been not far from the **Evangelical Light** (if it is permitted to speak thus), since it is recorded in the *Book of Rites* <note>original: lib. Offic. 9. fol. 38.</note>: **"To compensate hatred with benefits; this is indeed the virtue and piety of a most expansive heart."** <note>original: "Y te pao yven, çe quon xin chi gin ye" — this is a transliteration of the Chinese *Yi de bao yuan, ze kuan xin zhi ren ye*</note>*

**§. 4.** Confucius, in order to provoke his disciple **Zi Gong** <note>original: çu cum</note> to inquire about something, sighed and said: "There is no one of all men who knows me."

**§. 5.** Hearing this, **Zi Gong** said: "Master, how is it that there is no one who knows you?" Confucius responded: "First of all, I do not resent Heaven, nor do I blame mortals. Having begun from the lower things, I learn about the world not without labor and constancy, and thus, making my way step by step, I emerge and penetrate into the more sublime. Meanwhile, that which has a clear view of me is Heaven itself."

***I*** *(explains **Colaus** <note>A reference to the commentator Huo-lao or a similar authority</note>), although I am humble and weak, and have not experienced that bounty of Heaven which is commonly valued so highly, I nevertheless do not resent Heaven or murmur against it. Nor do I bring a charge against men because they do not make use of my work. I do this one thing: I cultivate myself, and having begun my journey from the foot of the mountain, I strive step by step toward its summit. I tread the **Royal Way**; I flee from things that are new and unusual. It is no wonder, then, that I remain hidden and unknown. Meanwhile, I do not blush to lift my eyes and look trustfully toward Heaven, as long as I do not cease from that study I mentioned—of preserving my own mind. For it is believable that supreme Heaven, in the midst of that secret and hidden darkness, watches over me and has a clear view of me.*

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book 14 of the Analects (here labeled Book Three). On the preceding page, Confucius reflected on how no one truly knows him, except for Heaven. BOOK THREE. 107

...so it is; what then, I pray, does it matter if I am seen, recognized, and celebrated by men?

Thus ends the paraphrase of the *Grand Secretary* <note>original: "Colai"; a transliteration of the Chinese term *Ge-lao*, referring to a Grand Secretary or high official acting as a commentator</note>, who concludes with his own summary statement: "This is exactly how things stand," he says. "After the Saints have, through their labor and constancy, reached the point where they clearly perceive the supreme disposition of Heaven toward themselves, they finally join and associate that splendor of virtues, which they secretly contain within themselves, with Heaven itself. But as much as this matter is clearly seen by Heaven, it is just as obscure to the majority of mortals."

**p. 2.** A man of the Kingdom of *Lu*, named *Gongbo Liao* <note>original: "Cum pe leao"</note>, was slandering the disciple *Zilu* <note>original: "çu lu"</note> to *Ji Sun* <note>original: "Ki sun"</note>, whose official and follower he then was. *Zifu Jibo* <note>original: "çu fo Ki pe"</note>, a Prefect of the same Kingdom, offended by the insolence and boldness of the slanderer, reported the matter to *Confucius*, saying: "My master *Ji Sun* clearly suspects something sinister and wishes your disciple ill because of *Gongbo Liao*, by whom he has been incited to suspicion and accusation. If you permit it, I am able, by my own authority and power, to punish him, and to remove that wicked slanderer from our midst and cast him out into the public square."

**f. 20. p. 1. §. 1.** *Confucius*, in order to turn the Prefect away from his purpose of inflicting death, said: "That the righteous administration of any Kingdom proceeds successfully is a matter of the heavenly decree <note>term: "decreti caelestis" refers to the *Tianming* or Mandate of Heaven</note>. That the righteous administration of any Kingdom is neglected and perishes is likewise a matter of the heavenly decree. What, then, does *Gongbo Liao* have to do with this decree of heaven? Could he perhaps prevail in destroying one whom heaven protects? Or could he protect and defend one against whom heaven is hostile?"

**Our Interpreter** <note>The Jesuit commentator</note>, after explaining this response of the **Philosopher** <note>Confucius</note> in almost such a way as if all human affairs were held by an inevitable law of the fates, finally declares the mind of the **Philosopher** and his own opinion. He plainly denies that it belongs to a wise man—when he is able to be free and to follow reason and nature as his guides in all things—to voluntarily bind himself with the fatal chains of such a harsh necessity. Meanwhile, he explains that *Confucius* was prudently adapting himself to the time and the character of the men: he spoke this way partly to comfort and appease his offended disciple; partly to dissuade the other from an agitated revenge as if it were superfluous; and finally, to rebuke the slanderer himself by this reasoning.

**§. 2.** *Confucius* said: The wise sometimes flee the age <note>or "the world"</note>, so that they utterly reject all honors and public cares.

**§. 3.** Next to these are those who sometimes flee the region where they live because they see it is disturbed; and they migrate to another which is rightly governed.

**§. 4.** Next again to these are those who flee the sight of their Prince, when they see that he is of disordered character.

**§. 5.** Finally, next to these are those who flee the speech or conversation of such a Prince.

**§. 6.** *Confucius*, sighing, said: Those who have thus fled from public cares...

<summary>Confucius argues that the success or failure of governance depends on the Mandate of Heaven rather than the schemes of slanderers, and he outlines the different degrees to which a wise man might withdraw from a corrupt society.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the translation of Book 14 of the Analects. The previous page discussed various disciples and the concept of withdrawing from a corrupt world. This page focuses on several "hidden sages"—recluses who chose to live in obscurity—and their critiques of Confucius’s active efforts to reform a failing society.</meta>

# CHINESE KNOWLEDGE

...whether due to public dangers or a desire for private leisure and quiet, there were seven men in total (their names are not extant).

### §. 7. 
Once, while **Zilu** <note>original: "çu lu"</note> was following the Master as he migrated from one kingdom to another, he happened to spend the night in a place called **Shimen** <note>original: "Xe muen"; literally "The Stone Gate"</note>. The gatekeeper, who was himself one of the hidden sages, asked him, "Whom do you follow?" **Zilu** replied: "I follow **Confucius**." Then the other said: "Is he not that man who, understanding that a thing is not suitable, nevertheless does that very thing which is not fitting? Does he not wish, in vain, to bring aid to a struggling Empire?"

<margin>p. 21 §. 1.</margin>
**Confucius**, in order to soothe the sorrow of a mind so afflicted by public calamity, happened to be striking a stone musical instrument <note>original: "instrumentum musicum lapideum"; referring to the *qing*, or lithophone, ancient Chinese stone chimes</note>—one that remained true to its own strings—at the time he was staying in the **Kingdom of Wei** <note>original: "Guei"</note>. One of those hidden sages, who was carrying straw baskets, passed before **Confucius's** door. From the very nature of the music, which was entirely mournful, he skillfully recognized the feelings of the Philosopher lamenting the public disaster. Full of wonder, yet appearing somewhat annoyed, he said: "Can this be? Indeed, as I see it, he possesses a sense of public calamity just as we do, which he reveals clearly enough by striking the instrument in this way."

### §. 2. 
Then, after he had stopped for a little while, hearing him playing again, he said: "O, what a common and stubborn man! <note>original: "O vilem hominem & pertinacem!"</note> There is absolutely no one who knows him, or certainly no one who wishes to know him and make use of his service. Let him therefore desist from such troublesome and useless study! Already, he has tried and hurried about more than is enough. You ought to remember the Proverb of our Kingdom: *If the river is deep, which you wish to cross on foot, then cross it clothed according to our ancient custom; if it is shallow and of modest depth, then tuck up your garments.*" It was as if he were saying: Why, having already explored the state of our times, does **Confucius** not adapt himself to it, and prudently abstain from such useless care and commotion?

<margin>f. 21. p. 1. §. 1.</margin>
**Confucius**, having heard the speech of the somber and stern philosopher, sighed and said: "O, a man too stubborn in his purpose! There is indeed no difficulty in doing what he does—to withdraw oneself from labor and danger. But my heart certainly cannot bear to act in such a way."

*Our Interpreter, adding his own opinion to this saying of the Philosopher, says: "The mind of the Saints <note>In this Jesuit translation, "Saints" refers to the ancient Chinese Sages (*Shengren*)</note> is like heaven and earth. (Though heaven and earth may be beset by clouds and feel the blasts of winds and storms, they never desist from their duty of procreating and nourishing things through their influence. Similarly, the wise man, however harsh and calamitous the times may be, always acts so as to deserve well of the human race. Below, he always pities his mortal companions; above, he constantly reveres the inviolable nod and will of heaven.)"*

<summary>This page recounts two encounters between Confucius's circle and reclusive "hidden sages" who critique the Master for his persistent, though seemingly futile, attempts to reform a collapsing society. Confucius responds by acknowledging the ease of withdrawal but asserting his moral obligation to continue his work, comparing the Sage's duty to the unceasing functions of Heaven and Earth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Confucian classics, specifically addressing a passage from the Analects concerning ritual mourning and the historical reign of Emperor Wu Ding. It follows previous discussions of disciples and the Master's interactions with various figures.</meta>

### BOOK THREE

§. 2. The disciple **Zizhang** <note>original: "çu cham"</note>, asking a question, said: In the **Classic of History** <note>original: "xu kim"; the *Shujing*, one of the five foundational texts of the Confucian canon</note>, the annals of the Ancient Kings, it is narrated that Emperor **Gaozong** <note>original: "Cao çum"; also known as **Wu Ding**</note>, living in seclusion in **Liang’an** <note>original: "Leam ngan"; the name of the royal burial garden or grove where his father **Xiao Yi** was entombed</note> for three years, gave himself over to such pious mourning that he did not speak. What does this signify? For it is indeed difficult to understand.

§. 3. **Confucius** said: "Why, I ask you, do you wish this to be so for only one man, **Gaozong**? Nearly all the Ancient Kings were of this sort. Consult the books of duties, where it is taught that upon the death of a Prince of a Kingdom or Empire, his successor and son would devote himself entirely to mourning for three years. Meanwhile, all the Prefects and Magistrates performed their respective duties; for they received their orders from the supreme administrator, who acted in place of the mourning Prince; and this continued for the three-year period."

**Gaozong**, or **Wu Ding**, was the twentieth Emperor of the second Imperial family, called the **Shang** <note>original: "Xam"</note>, who began to reign in the year 1324 before Christ. Regarding this most religious Prince, it is recorded in the **Classic of History** <note>folio 28</note> that while he was living in seclusion in the burial garden of his father **Xiao Yi**, anxious and meditating deeply on how to renew the Empire, there was presented to him by **Shangdi** <note>original: "Xam ti"; the supreme Emperor of Heaven, often translated as God by the Jesuit authors</note>, through a dream, the appearance of an unknown man. **Gaozong** described this man to his Senate in words, and he was depicted in colors and sought everywhere. At last, he was found among the masons in a place called **Fuyan** <note>now called the town of **Pinglu** in the province of **Shanxi**</note>. From his work in the mud, the Emperor raised him to the supreme dignity of a counselor.

This man was commonly named **Fu Yue**. There exist in the **Classic of History** three chapters containing his excellent advice, from which Emperor **Wu Ding** (also known as **Gaozong**) profited so much that for 59 years he governed the Empire happily and peacefully with piety and religion.

Here it is truly delightful to see how the most famous interpreter, named **Zhu Xi** <note>original: "Chu hi"</note>—the leader of the later school of atheist-politicians <note>the Jesuit authors often characterized Neo-Confucianism as "atheopolitica" because it emphasized abstract principle over a personal deity</note>—struggles with himself; yet the poor man is unable to escape the difficulty. On one hand, he is forbidden from denying the truth of these events by the authority of the ancient text (which is sacred among the Chinese); on the other hand, whichever way he turns, he cannot free himself from the presence and majesty of a certain supreme Deity. Thus, in his major commentaries, he says:

"When Emperor **Gaozong** dreamed of **Fu Yue**, there was distinctly and clearly a real **Fu Yue** who existed there. **Gaozong** truly did not know the one whose likeness was offered in the dream; for he had never seen such a man himself. Since **Gaozong** dreamed of **Fu Yue** as someone who actually existed there, it must be that there truly was a certain **Emperor of Heaven** who said to **Gaozong**, 'I assign to you a faithful helper.' Now, however, people say that by the word **Ti** <note>Di; Lord or Emperor</note>, nothing other than a 'Lord and Governor' is understood; and they say he is without body or form. But I think the matter may not have been quite like that."

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Emperor Gaozong (Wu Ding) of the Shang dynasty, specifically debating the nature of his divine dream and shifting into the teachings of Confucius on self-cultivation and leadership.</meta>

# CHINESE KNOWLEDGE
### (SCIENTIÆ SINICÆ)

(Certainly, this Writer did not understand how one who is without a body could, by assuming a visible form, be revealed to a man.) As for what pertains <note>original: "quod attinet"</note> (the **Interpreter** <note>The "Interpreter" refers to **Zhu Xi** (Chu Hsi), the influential Neo-Confucian philosopher whose commentaries became the standard for imperial examinations.</note> continues) to him who in our current age is called **Yo-hoam-ta-ti** <note>original: "Yo-hoam-ta-ti"; the **Jade Emperor** (Yuhuang Dadi), a high deity in the Taoist pantheon</note>, that is, **Yo-hoam** the Great Emperor (of heaven), I truly think it cannot be said that it was he (for it certainly cannot be said: How could that man **Yo-hoam** have appeared, who was born several centuries after **Gaozong** <note>original: "Cao çum"</note> and then, only after several more centuries had passed, was granted the title of Supreme Deity through the insane superstition of the Emperor called **Huizong** <note>original: "Hoeci çum"</note> of the nineteenth family, known as the **Song** <note>original: "Sum"</note>?) Again (the **Interpreter** continues), how far from empty or accidental that dream was, the success itself proved: for when King **Gaozong** dreamed that a faithful assistant was assigned to him by the Emperor of Heaven, the Emperor of Heaven was undoubtedly present to him in his sleep to point that man out; and in no way can it be said that the matter was otherwise. Nor can it be said here that this was merely that "celestial reason" which we call **Li** <note>original: "Li"; a central concept in Neo-Confucianism referring to the underlying "Principle" or "Pattern" of the universe.</note>. (And thus far indeed the **Interpreter Zhu Xi**, not knowing which way to turn; yet by that very ignorance and perplexity of his, he favors—even if unwillingly—the **Truth and Providence of the Deity**. This **Li** is a certain figment of the "atheist-politicians" <note>A derogatory term used by Jesuit translators for Neo-Confucian scholars who interpreted the universe in naturalistic rather than theistic terms.</note> invented by modern interpreters forty centuries later. By **Li**, they understand a certain power or natural influence lacking mind and will, yet the principle of all things, to which they attempt to refer everything, twisting the monuments and meaning of all antiquity to their own opinion.)

§. 4. **Confucius** says: He who is placed in charge of others, if indeed he delights in the proper contemplation of duties, always making a fair distinction between the humble and the honored, between the highest and the lowest: then he will easily rule the people.

P. 2. §. 1. **Zilu** <note>original: "çu lu"; one of Confucius’s most famous and impetuous disciples</note> inquires about the wise man, and one who stands far above the common crowd; **Confucius** replied: "Let him cultivate himself, so that in this way he may emerge upright through constant self-vigilance and attention." **Zilu** asks: "When he has done this, will it suffice?" He replied: "Let him therefore cultivate himself, and cultivate himself in such a way that he fulfills the wishes of others, just as he desires his own to be fulfilled." The disciple insists: "When the matter stands thus, will nothing more be required?" He replies: "Let him cultivate himself, and let him spread the wealth of virtue and industry he has acquired so broadly that he procures peace and fulfills the wishes of the entire people. But indeed, this is a difficult thing; and in this study of self-cultivation, so as to fulfill the wishes of the entire people, **Yao** and **Shun** <note>original: "yao & xun"; legendary sage-kings of China's golden age</note>—men who were such great Princes—nevertheless they too labored vehemently and were held by a kind of perpetual sickness of soul and anxiety, lest by chance there should be even one person among all whose love and benevolence they did not obtain. To such an extent did they love their own people no differently than themselves."

# BOOK THREE

*Confucius has long been known to you.* <note>original: "Confucium jam olim tibi notum." The author is addressing the reader directly, assuming a prior introduction to the philosopher's life.</note> **Confucius**, condemning such rustic manners in a man and other vices of a whole life, said: "Indeed, when you were a youth, you were not of a humble mind nor observant of your elders. Having become older, you possessed no virtue or praise that might be proclaimed. Now that you are an old man, if indeed you do not die soon, this will truly be a harm to many by your wicked example and habits." Having said this, he lightly struck the man's legs with a staff, so as to warn the rustic man of the gravity and decorum that was his due. <note>This anecdote refers to Confucius’s meeting with his old acquaintance Yuan Rang, who was sitting in a disrespectful posture.</note>

§. 2. From the district called **Que** <note>original: "Kive"</note>, several native boys who had recently been handed over to **Confucius** for instruction were carrying the Master's commands to guests, and in turn, their responses back to the Master. Someone, perhaps having inquired, asked: "Are those boys making progress?"

§. 3. **Confucius** replied: "They ought to stand not in the middle of a gathering, but at the side; and while following an elder, they should follow behind. But now I see them rashly seating themselves in a place of honor. I see them walking side by side with their Master without any interval; thus they do not observe the behaviors proper to their age. Therefore, I judge that they are not studious of their own progress. However, I shall take up this duty: I desire to cultivate and perfect them through good manners and disciplines once that rudeness is removed as soon as possible. Nevertheless, I shall do so by starting from the easiest and lowest things, and lead them by the hand step by step toward greater things as they age."

**Folio 2. Page 1. §. 1.** **Confucius** said: "My disciple **Zilu** <note>original: "Yeu", alias "çu lu". Zilu was known for his courage and directness.</note>, those who have a deep understanding of virtue are few."

*Under the rule of this family, the new moon that was nearest to the sun's entry into the 15th degree of Aquarius established the beginning of each year; because this system of time was so well-suited to agriculture and other uses of human life, it was greatly approved by Confucius. **§. 2.** "While performing sacred rites, wear the ceremonial cap of the **Cheu** family, which currently rules." <note>The Zhou (Cheu) dynasty (c. 1046–256 BCE) was the era in which Confucius lived; he admired their refined rituals and headgear.</note>

# BOOK THREE #

**§. 4.** **Confucius** says: To sin and not to amend your ways—this is truly what is called sinning.

**p. 2. §. 1.** **Confucius** says: I have often spent whole days without eating and whole nights without sleeping, so that I might devote myself to meditation; and yet I reaped almost no benefit. There is nothing better than to devote effort to the written records <note>original: *monumentis literarum*, referring to the classical texts or ancient literature</note>, so that you might translate what you have learned into practical use and exercise.

**§. 2.** **Confucius** says: The philosopher <term>Philosophus: Used here by the 17th-century translators to represent the *Junzi* or "superior man," the Confucian ideal of a moral person</term> works for virtue; he does not work for food. Indeed, hunger and unexpected barrenness often follow the work of agriculture itself; but in the study of virtue, the rewards and "harvest" never fail. Therefore, the philosopher is anxious about his virtue; he is not anxious about his poverty.

**§. 3.** **Confucius** says: If you have attained something through wisdom <note>original: *prudentia*</note>, unless you are strong enough to preserve it through inner virtue, then even if you have gained it, you will undoubtedly lose it.

**§. 4.** If you have attained something through wisdom and are strong enough to preserve it through inner virtue, but you do not also apply a gravity of manners and authority to govern rightly, then your subjects will not respect you.

**f. 8. p. 1. §. 1.** If you have attained something through wisdom, and are strong enough to preserve it through inner virtue, and also apply an external gravity of manners and authority to govern rightly; unless you move your subjects in a suitable and proper manner, the work is not yet perfect.

**§. 2.** **Confucius** says: An excellent man cannot be immediately known or judged as fit to handle great things based on small matters, even if he has performed them brilliantly. On the contrary, great things should not be demanded of a common man—nor one equipped with only modest natural gifts—let alone undertaken by him. Rather, what he is capable of in modest and common things is what ought to be recognized.

**p. 2. §. 1.** **Confucius** says: Virtue is more necessary to the people than water and fire. I have seen those who stepped into water and fire and perished; I have not yet seen one who walked the path of virtue and perished.

**§. 2.** **Confucius** says: When undertaking the cultivation of the soul through virtues, one should not yield even to a Master, nor allow the first place in the study of virtue to be deferred to another. <note>Confucius suggests that in the pursuit of moral excellence, one must take personal initiative rather than passively following a teacher.</note>

**§. 3.** **Confucius** says: The perfect man is upright and constant, but not stubborn.

**§. 4.** **Confucius** says: A servant who serves the King as is proper holds most dear, above all things, those duties which belong to his office; and he puts his own wealth and wages after these.

**f. 9. p. 1. §. 1.** **Confucius** says: Let there be instruction without distinction. <note>This is the famous Confucian principle that education should be available to all, regardless of social class.</note>

**§. 2.** **Confucius** says: Those who differ in their path will by no means agree with one another when consulting on any matter.

**§. 3.** **Confucius** says: Let words be understood (that is, the naked truth of the words without the deception and the luxurious elegance of our current age), and let this be sufficient.

**§. 4.** The Master of Music, named **Mien**, had come for the sake of visiting **Confucius**. As he approached a certain step, **Confucius**, warning his guest (who was indeed blind), said immediately: "Here is a step." When the guest had proceeded into the hall intended for receiving visitors and approached a mat, **Confucius** said again: "Here is a mat." Soon after, when the Master of Music and the other guests were seated together, **Confucius** informed him, saying: "Titus <note>original: *Titus*—the Latin translators used common Roman names like Titus and Sempronius as placeholders, much like "John Doe" or "Person A" and "Person B" today</note> is here, or is sitting on this side; Sempronius is on that side." This was so that he might more fittingly fulfill the duty of greeting and honor owed to each person.

**§. 5.** When Master **Mien** had left, one of the disciples named **Zi Zhang** <note>original: *çu cham*</note> asked **Confucius**, saying: "Is there also a rule from the principles of your philosophy for speaking and acting in this way with a Master of Music?"

**§. 6.** **Confucius** replied: "This is indeed the rule for assisting blind Masters, established of old."

**p. 2. §. 1.** In the Kingdom of **Lu**, there were three very powerful and noble families who, being all but rebels against their King, had divided the four regions of the Kingdom among themselves. **Meng Sun** <note>original: *Mem sun*</note> had seized one; **Shu Sun** <note>original: *Xo sun*</note> another; and the Governor **Ji** <note>original: *Ki*</note>, more powerful than either, had claimed the third and fourth for himself. Not content with these (such is the insatiable lust for power <note>original: *insatiabilis dominandi libido*</note>), he was planning to invade another dynasty situated in the very center of the Kingdom, which was subject to him by feudal right. Thus, **Ji Xi** (or **Ji Sun**) was in a state of preparation to attack the territory of **Chuan Yu** <note>original: *chuen yu*</note> with war.

**§. 2.** **Ran You** <note>original: *Gen yeu*</note> and **Ji Lu**, standing before **Confucius**, said: "Our Lord **Ji Xi** is very soon to have a conflict with the ruler of **Chuan Yu**." Both were disciples of **Confucius** and happened to hold magisterial office at the time; they did not approve of this kind of invasion.

**§. 3.** **Confucius** said: "**Ran Qiu** <note>original: *Kieu*, the personal name of Ran You</note>, is this crime not also yours?"

**f. 10. p. 1. §. 1.** Further arguing against the injustice of the war, he proved it on three main grounds. "This territory of **Chuan Yu**," he said, "was long ago made the mistress of Mount **Meng** <note>original: *mum*</note> by the ancient Emperors of the **Zhou** <note>original: *Cheu*</note> family, being situated in that same territory where the local rulers care for the sacrifices which are duly performed for the presiding spirit of the mountain. Secondly, it is situated in the middle of the Kingdom's borders. Finally, it is subject and a <term>vassal: *clientelaris*, a state that owes allegiance to a higher lord</term> to the royal house and family; by what arrangement, then, and by what right does that wicked man claim it for himself and invade it?"

**§. 2.** The disciple **Ran You**, now better informed by this speech of his Master, said: "Our Lord **Ji Xi** strongly desires that territory; we two, as his ministers and subjects, certainly do not desire or approve of it."

<meta>catchword: equitable</meta>

...also to challenge and condemn by both words and deeds; and if they should not succeed by advising and challenging, they should renounce their duty. Thus he says: "My disciple **Ran You** <note>original: *Kieu* — Confucius's disciple, also known as Ran Qiu</note>, there exists a saying of that ancient and famous Historian **Zhou Ren** <note>original: *Cheu gin*</note> which is very much to our purpose: 'If anyone,' he says, 'has the strength and faculties to manage the State <note>original: *Respublica* — here referring to the governance of the territory</note>, let him indeed accept the public office; but if he is not able to perform the requirements of his duty, let him stop, and abdicate his rank, if by chance he holds one.' For such a man, being closest to a precipice, is endangered, and yet is not held by the hand, or is not warned, because he is obviously impatient of being warned. He falls forward, and yet, while falling, he is not supported by the hand; for indeed there is no one who dares to move a hand to help, and it is clear he intends to go headlong to his ruin. For what use, then, is that assistant or guide to a man who is blind, or rather, to one who is insane?"

<margin>p. 2. §. 1.</margin>
"And so, regarding what you were just saying—that war is being prepared against your will and disapproval, so that all the blame might be diverted onto the Governor—this itself is your second crime; and indeed it is the more shameful, as it is joined with a shameful error. For I ask you: if a certain tiger or wild buffalo has escaped outside its enclosures and its bars; or likewise, if a tortoise-shell <note>The shells of rare tortoises were highly prized for divination rituals</note> of rare craftsmanship, or other furniture of precious stone has perished or been damaged, even though it was placed in the middle of a chest: whose crime, then, will this escape and this loss be? Will it not be his to whose faith and care both the enclosures and the treasures had been committed?"

<margin>§. 2.</margin>
The disciple **Ran You** <note>original: *Gen yeu*</note>, understanding himself to be accused by this argument, and undertaking to defend both his own cause and his Lord's under the plausible name of necessity and justice, spoke thus: "Now this territory of **Zhuanyu** <note>original: *chuen yu* — a small, independent state within the region</note> is strong and fortified, and it is possible that it may become more fortified day by day. At present it is not hostile to its neighbors, but who can guarantee it will never be so at any time? Furthermore, it is neighboring and bordering on **Bi** <note>original: *Pi*</note>, the ancestral territory and patrimony of my Lord **Ji Sun** <note>original: *Ki xi*</note>. Therefore, if he does not occupy it now, while he can and while time and fortune favor him, it will undoubtedly be a source of bitter grief and late material for repentance for his sons and grandsons in the future."

<margin>§. 3.</margin>
**Confucius**, having thus exposed the hidden wound <note>A metaphor for the moral corruption or intellectual dishonesty</note> of both the disciple and the Governor, said: "A true Philosopher, O **Ran You**, hates and detests that kind of man who is evasive and unwilling to candidly profess his greed, anxiously hiding other diseases of the soul, and meanwhile violently making a pretext of words, or wordy evasions, by which he eludes the truth."

<margin>§. 4.</margin>
"Hear now, therefore, what I think. I have always heard thus: those who hold a Kingdom or a dynasty <note>original: *dynastiam*</note>, or who have an ample and splendid family—provided they are honest and wise—are not accustomed to be distressed in spirit or tormented by the fewness of the subjects they rule; but they are tormented and distressed that each person does not receive his own..."

<summary>Confucius rebukes his disciple Ran You for failing to restrain the Ji family's imperialistic ambitions, using metaphors of a blind man's guide and a negligent zookeeper. He argues that a minister is responsible for the ruler's failures and should not hide greed behind political excuses.</summary>

...as justice and reason demand. I have likewise heard that they <note>referring to wise rulers</note> are not distressed because their domain suffers from a lack of resources, but are distressed and afflicted because it does not enjoy the desired peace and harmony. And rightly so; for if useless expenses are removed, if immoderate luxury is forbidden, and if to each is granted what equity demands, then although some will be wealthier than others, they will not be suffering from want or beggary. Likewise, where harmony flourishes, there is no scarcity; there is no desolation. For as long as they enjoy harmony, they will also enjoy the peace that is born from it. While peace and tranquility flourish, there will be no room for ruin, nor any danger of a more serious calamity.

**Folio 11. Page 1. § 1.** These three—justice, harmony, and tranquility—if they are maintained and flourish in the manner I have described: then even if more remote peoples do not subject themselves to so sweet a yoke, one must act to further perfect and, as it were, polish the Royal virtues. In this way, foreigners will eventually come, conquered not by deceit nor by arms, but by the fame of those virtues. When they have so arrived and passed into your jurisdiction, then you should lovingly provide for their interests and their peace.

**§ 2.** But now, oh my disciples **Zilu** <note>original: *Yeu* — also known as Zhong You</note> and **Ran Qiu** <note>original: *Kieu*</note>, you are indeed the assistants and advisors to your Lord **Ji Shi** <note>original: *Ki xi* — the head of the powerful Ji clan in the State of Lu</note>. But to what end is your labor? With what fruit? Not only do the foreigners not obey you, but because true virtue is lacking in your administration, they cannot even bring themselves to migrate to your land. The Kingdom of **Lu** has collapsed, miserably divided and torn into parts and factions; it has all but perished utterly, and thus it can no longer be preserved in its current state.

**Page 2. § 1.** And as if these things were not enough to cause public calamity and destruction, now that Governor [Ji Shi] even plots to take up new arms—and in such a way that a fierce war blazes up in the very vitals of the Kingdom. But I truly fear that the grief or ruin of the grandsons of the **Ji** family will not arise from the neighboring territory of **Zhuan Yu** <note>original: *Chuen yu* — the small state the Ji family intended to attack</note>, but will instead arise from within their own domestic walls, and be consumed at last by its own internal fire.

**§ 2.** **Confucius said:** When the Empire is at peace and administered with proper authority, the standard for duties, music, and military expeditions proceeds from the Emperor <note>the Son of Heaven</note>. When the Empire is in disorder, the standard for duties, music, and military expeditions proceeds from the Princes <note>original: *Regulis* — the feudal lords or petty kings</note>. If they proceed from the Princes, then within the space of ten generations, there will be very few among them who do not lose their Kingdom. If they proceed from the Great Officers <note>original: *Præfectis* — the high-ranking ministers like the Ji family</note>, within the space of five generations, very few will not lose them. If household retainers <note>original: *Domestici clientes*</note> usurp the mastery of the kingdom, within the space of three generations, very few will not lose what was wrongly acquired.

**Folio 12. Page 1. § 1.** If the law flourishes in the Empire, then absolute administration will not be in the hands of the Great Officers; for it will not even be in the hands of the Princes themselves.

# BOOK THREE

**§ 2.** If the law flourishes in the Empire, then the people will not interfere in public councils. For all subjects will gladly and eagerly conform to that norm of administration, which they understand to be exactly aligned with the pattern of heaven and right reason.

**§ 3.** Confucius says: Tax revenues have been absent from the Royal house for five generations. The administration has passed to the prefects for four generations. Therefore, those three descendants of King **Von cum** <note>original: *Von cum* — likely referring to King Wen of Zhou or a high ancestor of the Three Families of Lu</note> have been diminished. Confucius seems to confirm what he had said by the local example of the Kingdom of **Lu** <note>the home state of Confucius</note>, his own fatherland, in which twelve kings ruled in succession. For after the death of the sixth king, **Ven** <note>King Wen of Lu</note>, after his little son and legitimate heir was killed, the brother of the slain man, called **Siven** <note>King Xi of Lu</note>, was raised to the Kingdom. From that time, the administration of that kingdom began to collapse, and revenues passed from the Royal house to the private families of the Prefects; who, relying on their nobility because they were descended from the lineage of **Von cum**, the second king, gradually claimed the royal right for themselves.

**p. 2. § 1.** Confucius says: Three types of friends are useful; likewise, three types of friends are ruinous. An upright friend, a faithful friend, and a friend who has heard much <note>meaning one who is well-informed or widely learned</note> are useful. A friend who is only composed and serious on the outside, a fawning and soft friend, and a talkative and gossiping friend are ruinous.

**§ 2.** Confucius says: Three joys are useful; three joys are ruinous. To rejoice in the proper use of duties <note>referring to the performance of ritual and social obligations</note> and music; to rejoice in speaking of the good words and deeds of others; to rejoice in the friendship of many wise men—these are useful. To rejoice in the vanity of pride; to rejoice in idleness and a life of license; to rejoice in the jests and pleasures of feasts—these are ruinous joys.

**f. 13 p. 1. § 1.** Confucius says: There are three errors committed by those assisting a Prince. If the words of the inquiring prince have not yet reached you <note>meaning he has not finished speaking or the turn to speak is not yet yours</note>, or concern only yourself, and yet you speak, it is called rashness. If the words have reached you and yet you do not speak, it is called a moody and useless silence. If you have not yet observed his face beforehand <note>to read his mood or receptivity</note> and yet you speak, it is called blindness.

**§ 2.** Confucius says: A follower of virtue has three things to guard against. In the time of youth, when the blood and spirits are not yet settled, what must be guarded against is lust <note>original: *res venerea* — sexual matters</note>. Having reached mature age, with blood and spirits now strengthened, what he must guard against is quarreling. Having reached old age, with blood and spirits now languishing, what he must guard against is the desire for gain <note>avarice or greed</note>.

**p. 20 § 1.** Confucius says: The wise and upright man has three fears: He fears the **Mandate of Heaven** <term>Mandatum Cœli: the divine authority or moral law that grants a ruler the right to lead</term>; he fears great men; he fears the words of the **Sages** <note>original: *Sanctorum* — literally "the holy ones," used here by the translator to denote the ancient Chinese sages</note>.

**§ 2.** The wicked and foolish man does not acknowledge the Mandate of Heaven, and therefore does not fear it. He despises great men; he mocks the words of the Sages.

### § 3. Confucius says:
> Those who are born already possessing knowledge—as if they had breathed in the knowledge of things along with the very air and spirit of life—are to be considered sages of the highest order. Those who learn, however, and apply themselves to a Master, and in this way become knowledgeable, are second after those first ones. But those who are duller of mind, and yet learn through shameless labor and constancy, these are again second to those I just mentioned. Now, those who are dull and yet do not learn are considered the lowest and most useless among the common people; although they may otherwise be upright and innocent men.

**f. 14. p. 1. § 1. Confucius says:**
> The student of virtue and wisdom employs nine considerations. While observing anything with his eyes, he meditates on **perspicacity**—that is, that he must perceive what is set before his eyes clearly and correctly. While hearing anything, he meditates on an **acute power of hearing**, to properly perceive voices and the meanings of words. Regarding the appearance and habit of his face, he meditates on a certain **serene placidity**, for there is no other "color" <note>meaning facial expression or demeanor</note> that wins over souls more powerfully or sweetly. Regarding the posture and formation of his whole body, he meditates on **gravity joined with reverence**. When he must speak, he meditates on **faithfulness and truthfulness**, so that the tongue corresponds to the heart. While he acts or strives at anything, he meditates on **diligence**. In doubtful and perplexing matters, he meditates within himself on **whom he should chiefly consult**, and by what means he might seek light in that darkness. Feeling his mind stirred by anger and a desire for contention or revenge, he early on reflects upon the **inconveniences and losses** that usually arise. Seeing an opportunity offered to increase his family wealth, he immediately sets **justice and equity** before his eyes.

**§ 2. Confucius says:**
> Contemplate what is good in another as if you have not yet reached it yourself; contemplate what is evil in another as if you were touching boiling water <note>meaning to withdraw from it immediately with caution</note>. I have seen such a man; I have heard such a proverb.

**p. 2. § 1.** While still living as a private citizen, he prepares his methods and industrious plans for governing rightly. Afterward, while performing the public office of a faithful minister, he then puts into practice those methods and plans he had previously meditated upon. I have heard this proverb, but I have not yet seen such a man.

# CHINESE KNOWLEDGE

...can be said to have followed in his writing, where he says: The wife of a Prince who holds a certain broader jurisdiction—for example, a Minor King, a Governor, or a Lord—is called by her husband his "consort," "spouse," or "helper." This wife of a Prince, when naming herself in the presence of her husband, being mindful of due submission and modesty, says: "I, a simple girl" <note>original Latin: "Ego rudis puella"</note>. Yet the people and subjects of this jurisdiction, when addressing her, call her the "Queen Consort" or the "Prince’s Helper," because she is surely the governess of the domestic palace and the Royal family, just as the Prince himself is the governor of the entire territory. Again, this same Princess, when naming herself before foreign nations—that is, their ambassadors or even their Princes—says: "I, a small Princess of modest virtue." But the people and ambassadors of foreign nations, when naming her, do so just as her own subjects do, calling her the "Queen Consort" or the "Prince’s Helper."

*From all memory of the past, and even in this age, there has been an almost incredible variety and abundance of names among the Chinese. These are assigned differently according to the variety of place, time, or condition, and also at the whim of the Emperor ruling at the time; these titles are given not only to the same men, but also to families, territories, cities, public offices, and even to the very words and deeds of men. Nor is there any lack of modesty, gravity, and reverence contained within that abundance and variety. What is even more remarkable is that there is no rank or sex of people, almost no age, nor anything so crude and rustic among the forests and mountains, that has not perceived some use of this variety and abundance almost with their nurse's milk.*

*Although it might seem unnecessary to explain this with more examples, since these books we have in our hands supply not a few, it may nevertheless be helpful for the sake of delighting the reader to briefly set forth what we ourselves, who have come from Europe to China, have been forced to learn and are compelled to practice in almost daily use: that Chinese courtesy and civil elegance.*

Whenever it happens that one of our companions speaks with the Emperor of the nation himself, he names himself in almost no other way than "Distant Subject" <note>original: "Yven chin," likely *yuanren*</note> or simply "Subject" <note>original: "Chin," likely *ren*</note>, that is, a subject and newcomer from remote lands. The Prince himself, when addressing us, uses either the pronoun "thou" or our common name. We address the Emperor, as all the Chinese do, as "Ten Thousand Years" <note>original: "Van sui," referring to the phrase *Wansui*, a wish for long life</note>, by which words the most welcome vow of a long age—namely, a myriad of years—is contained. Now, if we have a conversation with the Minor Kings or the Grand Secretaries <note>original: "Colais," from the Chinese *Gelao*</note> of the Empire, who are the highest magistrates, we attribute to ourselves the name "Foreigners" <note>original: "Liu gin," likely *liuren* or *liumin*</note> with almost equal modesty. To the Minor Kings we give the title "Prince and Lord" <note>original: "Vam ye," or *Wangye*</note>, as well as "A Thousand Years" <note>original: "çien sui," or *Qiansui*</note>, by which we pray for a thousand years of life for them. To the Grand Secretaries, we give the honorable name "Venerable Lords" <note>original: "Lao ye," or *Laoye*</note>. In turn, we are usually honored by them with the name "Seniors" or "Masters" <note>original: "Sien sem," or *Xiansheng*</note>; meanwhile, the Minor Kings address us in the same manner as the Emperor himself.

<summary>This page describes the intricate system of titles and self-address in Chinese society, illustrating how modesty and hierarchy are maintained through language. It notes specific terms used by Jesuit missionaries when interacting with the Emperor and high-ranking officials.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the detailed description of Chinese social etiquette and honorifics. While the previous page focused on the titles of royalty and the inherent modesty required of noblewomen, this page shifts to the specific titles used for officials, the Jesuit missionaries themselves, and the complex system of humble and exalted vocabulary used in everyday speech and letters.</meta>

### BOOK THREE

S 2

Since, in truth, the rest of the **Officials**, by whom all parts of the Empire are administered, are classified either as literary or military; we address the military officials by no other name than **Lords** <note>original: *Lao ye*</note>. To the literary officials, however, we grant either that same title or, certainly, **Senior Masters** <note>original: *Lao sien sem*</note>, a title that is especially weighty and honorable for their office. Speaking of ourselves, however, we use no other name than **Disciples** <note>original: *Hio sem*</note>, or if a greater familiarity and intimacy should arise, we use the name **Younger Brothers** <note>original: *Siao ti*</note>. They, in turn, with an equal expression of both modesty and honor, give the name of **Masters** to us, while calling themselves **Disciples** or **Brothers**. A similar system of courtesy is observed with any man who is generally respected, even if he does not hold a public office. Yet there are some who call us by the somewhat more familiar name of **Bachelors** <note>original: *Siam cum*</note>, which is proper to those holding the first academic degree <note>the *Xiucai* degree, equivalent to a Bachelor of Arts</note> and is quite common today. Finally, the new converts, if they are educated men, call us **Senior Teachers** <note>original: *Lao su*</note>; if they are commoners, they call us **Lords**.

When, however, one approaches the tribunal of penance <note>the Sacrament of Confession</note>, they call us **Spiritual Fathers** <note>original: *Xin fu*</note>. In this setting, absolutely everyone (and many even at any time or place) call themselves **Sinners** <note>original: *çui gin*</note>. Usually, however, the educated converts call themselves **Disciples** <note>original: *Muen sem*</note>; while servants and others of the lowest class use the very humble term **Little Men** <note>original: *Siao tie*</note> in our presence. The culture is such that, apart from the Emperor and the high Princes, there is almost no one among them who would dare to use the simple pronouns **I** or **You** <note>original: *Ngo*, *ni*</note>. Furthermore, the same logic of courtesy and duty exists among themselves as it does with us, except that they are accustomed to granting more honor and the first place to foreigners.

In general, whenever they speak of matters pertaining to themselves, they not only speak with great modesty but almost always attach a term most expressive of humility. For instance, they call their own country a **Humble Kingdom** <note>original: *Pi que*</note>; their own name a **Vile Name** <note>original: *çien çu*</note>; and their son a **Small Son** <note>original: *Siao lh*</note>. Even an illness, if asked about their health, they call a **Vile and Lowly Affliction** <note>original: *çien yam*</note>. Conversely, they call a guest's fatherland an **Honorable Kingdom** <note>original: *çun que* or *quei que*</note>; his name a **Sublime Name** <note>original: *cao sim*</note>; and his offspring an **Ingenious Offspring** <note>original: *Lim lam*</note>. Finally, even the guest's illness, no matter how foul or offensive it may be, they call either a **Precious Affliction** <note>original: *quei yam*</note> or an **Honorable Affliction** <note>original: *çun yam*</note>. Whenever someone names their own father or mother before others, they call them **Father of the Household** <note>original: *Kia fu*</note> or **Mother of the Household** <note>original: *Kia mu*</note>. A guest's father is called **Your Honor** <note>original: *Lim çun*</note>, and his mother **Your Hall** <note>original: *Lim tam*—referring to the domestic quarters</note>. One's own home or family is called a **Cold or Poor House** <note>original: *Han kia*</note>, while another's is an **Honored House** <note>original: *quei kia*</note>. This is similarly observed in all other things, both in familiar conversation and in the style of letter-writing, which differs greatly from any other.

<summary>This page describes the intricate system of Chinese honorifics and self-deprecating titles used by officials, commoners, and the Jesuit missionaries. It highlights how social hierarchy and modesty are embedded in the language, where one's own belongings are "vile" while a guest's are "sublime."</summary>

**Yang Huo** <note>original: *Yam ho*; a powerful official in the state of Lu</note> (a subject and minister of the **Governor Ji** <note>original: *Ki*; one of the three powerful families who had usurped the authority of the Duke of Lu</note>) desired that he should be visited by **Confucius** first. But **Confucius**, because he understood the man to be a troublemaker and part of the family that had seized the rightful Prince’s law and authority for himself by force, did not visit him. In the meantime, **Yang Huo** sent a gift of food to **Confucius**, specifically a young pig <note>original: *porcellum*</note>, according to the custom of the people used at that time. Bound by this small gift, since **Confucius** could not, without violating the law of human courtesy, fail to approach the man to give thanks, he deliberately chose a time when the man himself would not be home, and he went there then to pay his respects; when, behold, they met each other on the road itself.

§. 2. **Yang Huo**, immediately addressing **Confucius**, said: “Come, I beg you; for I have words to share with you.” Soon he said: “If someone should hide a precious gem in his cloak and guard it anxiously, while meanwhile his native Kingdom is disturbed and afflicted, and yet he is unwilling to sell it to heal the public calamity—can someone like that be called pious?” **Confucius** replied: “He cannot be called pious.” The other insisted: “If someone enjoys and greatly desires to always do something and strive for what benefits the Republic <note>here referring to the state or commonwealth</note>, yet meanwhile repeatedly neglects and loses the offered opportunity—can someone like that be called prudent?” **Confucius** replied: “He cannot be called prudent.” Here the other, concluding, said: “The days and months flow past like a torrent; and yet of your years, you give nothing to me, not even when I demand it? Why do you not wake up, and, looking out for your studious self and your country, take up a **Magistracy** <note>original: *Magistratu*; a public office</note>?” To this, in order to free himself from the persistent prompter, **Confucius** said: “Very well; I shall take up a **Magistracy**.”

Page 2. **Confucius** said: “By nature and the light of reason, men are closely joined to one another; yet through their studies and habits, they often become very distant from each other.”

Leaf 2, page 1, section 1. **Confucius** said: “Only those who are born with wisdom and integrity itself, just as those who are born with ignorance and wickedness itself, are not easily changed through mutual association.”

§. 2. **Confucius**, arriving one day at the small town of **Wucheng** <note>original: *Vu chim*; a town in the state of Lu</note>, which his disciple <margin>**Ziyou** <note>original: *çu yeu*; a disciple known for his literary and musical talents</note></margin> was governing, happened to hear the residents playing stringed instruments and singing a symphony with great effort, precisely according to the standards and gravity established by the **Ancients**.

§. 3. **Confucius**, as if wondering that such solemn and laborious music should be instituted in such an unremarkable town, smiled gently and, using a common proverb, said: "When you are about to slaughter a chicken, why would you use an ox-cleaver?" <note>A famous Confucian metaphor suggesting that the great "tools" of state ritual and music might be overkill for a small village.</note> He said this as if to say: the narrowness of this place cannot contain such a great apparatus and majesty of music.

p. 2 §. 1. The Prefect of the place, who was also the author of this musical exercise, <margin>**Ziyou**</margin>—believing that his Master seriously disapproved of his work—replied in this manner: "In the past, I have frequently heard from you, my Master, when you said: 'If the Prefect of others is indeed a student of virtue and wisdom, he surely loves, instructs, protects, and cherishes his people. In turn, the common people, moved by the example of their studious Prefect, if they also study virtue and wisdom according to their own capacity, will be very easy to command and keep in their duty.'"

§. 2. **Confucius**, having called his disciples together, said: "O you two or three, or however many of you are here, my disciples! The speech of your fellow student **Yeu** <note>the personal name of Ziyou</note> is true and consistent with reason. What I said a moment ago was certainly for the sake of a joke and lightheartedness, and I did it to test him; for I am not ignorant that the vigor of the laws pertains to the towns as well."

[He] asked what those five virtues were. **Confucius** said: they are watchful self-observation; a broad and merciful spirit; faith and truthfulness; persistence and diligence; and love and benevolence. Indeed, if you conduct yourself with gravity and maturity always and everywhere, there will be no one who neglects or despises you; on the contrary, all will revere and respect you. If you possess a great, liberal, and merciful spirit, you will win over everyone—I say, you will win the devotion, love, and goodwill of all. If you maintain faith in your words and deeds, then all men will rely on you with confidence, committing themselves and their affairs to your trust. If you are swift, hardworking, and briskly diligent in handling business, you will achieve success and bring matters to the desired conclusion. Finally, if you are benevolent and love those under you, this will certainly be enough for you to rule your people most happily.

p. 2. §. 1. Six of the leading men were governing the Kingdom of **Jin** <note>original: *çin*; a powerful state in northern China during this period</note>, not without great civil unrest. Two of them, namely **Fan Zhong** <note>original: *Fan chum*</note> and **Jian Zi** <note>original: *Kien çu*</note>, were not only divided in their counsel and spirits, but even in their troops and weapons. During this time, **Bi Xi** <note>original: *Pie hie*</note>, who held a magistracy under [Jian Zi], summoned **Confucius**, and **Confucius** desired to go.

§. 2. The disciple **Zilu** <note>original: *çu lu*</note>, wishing to dissuade his Master from setting out, spoke thus: "In the past, **Yan** <note>original: *Yen*; Zilu’s personal name, used here as a humble self-reference</note>—that is, I—heard from you, my Master, when you said: 'A virtuous man does not enter the presence of one who is personally acting wickedly.' For he fears that by such association, he might bring harm and disgrace upon himself. Now, however, this **Bi Xi** who invites you is plotting a rebellion in the district of **Zhongmou** <note>original: *Chum meu*</note>. To what end, I pray, would you, O Master, go to such a man?"

§. 3. **Confucius** replied: "It is so; I did once have this conversation with you. Have I not also often said that a thing which is naturally very white may be dipped in black dye, yet it does not turn black within, nor ever lose its native brightness?"

f. 4. p. 1. §. 1. "How can I remain idle and useless? Am I like a great gourd of bitter flavor? How, I say, could I bear to remain hanging and motionless like that gourd, which is not eaten by anyone, feeds no one, and is of use to no one?" <note>Confucius uses this metaphor to explain that his talents are meant to be 'consumed' or used for the public good, rather than left 'hanging' like a decorative, bitter gourd.</note> Nevertheless, the Philosopher did not go to the man, because he later understood him to be the kind of man who could not be cured.

<page-num>127</page-num>

§. 4. He who delights in embracing everyone with the widest breast of benevolence <note>original: *charitas*; referring here to the Confucian concept of *Ren* or universal love</note>, and in doing good to all, but does not meanwhile delight in learning what the proper use and measure of that benevolence should be: the vice of such a man—into which the virtue itself will degenerate—will be a certain coarseness and blindness, for he will bestow benefits without judgment or limit, driven by a blind impulse of goodwill like one tossed by the wind. He who delights in prudence <note>original: *prudentiâ*; likely *Zhi* or wisdom</note>, or the clear perception of truth, but does not meanwhile delight in learning, investigating, and taking counsel: the vice of such a man will be a perpetual ambiguity and uncertainty of a wavering mind. He who delights in faith <note>original: *fide*; likely *Xin* or trustworthiness</note>, or the constancy and truth of words and agreements, but does not meanwhile delight in learning the proper time and manner: the vice of such a man will be frequent and serious offense, resulting in harm either to himself or to others. He who delights in rectitude and frankness, and hates deceit, evasions, and whatever is feigned or simulated, but does not meanwhile delight in learning what limit should be observed here as well: the vice of such a man will be the anxieties of a cramped mind and most difficult entanglements, into which his own simplicity and the fraud of others will cast him, as he is too candid and knows not how to dissemble. He who delights in acting and enduring anything generously and bravely, but does not meanwhile delight in learning the use and limit of this virtue: the vice of such a man will be insolence, and the disturbance and rebellion of the **State** <note>original: *Reipublicæ*</note>. He who delights in an adamantine <note>hard as diamond; unyielding</note> strength of mind and constancy, but does not meanwhile delight in learning where, when, how, and with what moderation it should be applied: the vice of such a man will be foolishness and madness.

p. 2. §. 1. **Confucius**, exhorting his disciples to the study of the Ancient Poems, said: "O, my children, why do you not study those books of Odes?" <note>The *Shijing*, or Classic of Poetry, one of the Five Classics of Chinese literature.</note>

§. 2. "For indeed, if we crawl upon the ground, if we lie useless and inglorious, through the lessons of the odes we can be lifted up, in a manner of speaking, and rise to true honor."

§. 3. "In the odes, as if in a mirror, we can contemplate what best suits us, and what, on the other hand, is unbecoming; and by contemplating these things, be wholesomely moved."

§. 4. "By the aid of the odes we can become social, affable, and pleasant. For just as music properly tempers sounds, so does this **Poetry** <note>original: *Poësis*</note> temper our impulses and desires."

§. 5. "We can hate without bitterness, or feel any other natural impulse, and yet follow it without falling into vice."

§. 6. "These same poems teach us how we may serve our father at home, and how, when absent and far from home, we may serve even the **Prince**."

§. 7. "Finally, by their benefit, we acquire a knowledge full of pleasure and especially rich regarding the proper names and natures of birds, four-footed animals, herbs, and trees."

<summary>Confucius explains how six major virtues (benevolence, prudence, faith, sincerity, bravery, and persistence) turn into dangerous flaws if not tempered by learning and moderation. He then presents a passionate defense of the "Book of Odes," arguing that poetry refines the character, aids in social harmony, and provides practical knowledge of the natural world.</summary>

He asked what those five virtues were. **Confucius** said: they are vigilant self-observation; breadth and clemency of spirit; faith and truthfulness; assiduity and diligence; and love and beneficence. For if you conduct yourself with gravity and maturity always and everywhere, there will be no one who neglects or despises you; on the contrary, everyone will revere and respect you. If you possess a great, liberal, and clement mind, you will soon win over the zeal, love, and goodwill of all people. If you maintain faith in your words and deeds, all men will then rely upon you with a sense of security, committing themselves and their affairs to your trust. If you are swift, industrious, and eagerly diligent in handling business, you will achieve your goals and bring matters to their desired conclusion. Finally, if you are beneficent and loving toward your people, this alone will surely suffice for you to rule over them most happily.

**part 2. §. 1.** Six of the leading men were administering the **Kingdom of Jin** <note>original: *çin*; the State of Jin during the Spring and Autumn period</note>, not without great political disturbance. Indeed, two of them, **Fan Zhong** and **Jian Zi**, were at odds not only in their counsel and spirit, but even with their forces and arms. While this was occurring, **Bi Xi** <note>original: *Pie hie*; a governor under the Zhao family in Jin</note>, who held a magistracy, summoned **Confucius**, and **Confucius** desired to go.

**§. 2.** The disciple **Zilu** <note>original: *çu lu*; one of Confucius's most loyal and brash students</note>, wishing to dissuade his Master from the journey, spoke thus: "Once I, **You** <note>original: *Teu*; Zilu’s personal name, which Confucius uses familiarly</note>, heard from you, my Master, when you said: 'An upright man does not associate with one who acts wickedly in his own person.' For he fears that by such association, he might bring both harm and disgrace upon himself. But now this **Bi Xi** who invites you is plotting a rebellion together with the district called **Zhongmou**. Why, I pray, Master, would you go to such a man?"

**§. 3. Confucius** replied: "It is so; I did once have this conversation with you. But have I not also sometimes said that a truly hard thing is rarely worn away, yet it is not broken; it is rubbed and worn, but not consumed? Have I not likewise often said of a thing that is inherently most white, that it may indeed be stained with a black color, yet inwardly it does not turn black, nor does it ever lose its native brightness?" <note>Confucius uses these metaphors of hard stone and white jade to argue that a truly virtuous man cannot be corrupted by his surroundings.</note>

**folder 4. part 1. §. 1.** "How can I cease my work, remaining useless and idle? Am I like a great <term>bitter gourd</term> <note>original: *cucurbita*; a reference to a plant that is hung up for decoration rather than eaten</note>? How, I say, can I endure to remain suspended and motionless like that gourd, and—since I am not 'eaten'—feed no one and be of use to no one?" However, the Philosopher did not ultimately go to the man, because he later understood him to be the sort of person who could not be mended.

**§. 2.** By chance, the disciple **Zilu** had seated himself at his Master's side; he was a man more studious of military glory than of literary pursuits. **Confucius** said: "My disciple, **You**: Have you ever heard the names of the six more illustrious virtues? And likewise the six vices that corrupt or obscure those same virtues?" The disciple, rising to his feet, replied: "I have not yet heard them."

**§. 3.** "Then stay here a little while," said **Confucius**, "until I explain them to you."

**§ 4.** One who delights in embracing all people with the widest arms of <term>charity</term> <note>original: *charitas*; here referring to the Confucian concept of *Ren* or human-heartedness</note>, wishing to do well by everyone, yet does not also delight in learning how that charity should be used and measured: the fault of such a man—into which the virtue itself will degenerate—will be a certain coarseness and blindness. Indeed, he will bestow favors without judgment or measure, driven by a blind impulse of benevolence as if tossed by the wind. One who delights in <term>prudence</term> <note>original: *prudentia*; the virtue of *Zhi* or wisdom</note>, or the perception of truth, but does not also delight in learning, searching, and taking counsel: the fault of such a man will be a perpetual ambiguity and an uncertainty of a wavering mind. One who delights in <term>faith</term> <note>original: *fides*; the virtue of *Xin* or trustworthiness</note>, or the constancy and truth of words and agreements, but does not also delight in learning their proper time and manner: the fault of such a man will be frequent and serious offense, causing harm either to himself or to others. One who delights in <term>uprightness</term> <note>original: *rectitudo*; the virtue of *Zhi* or sincerity</note> and sincerity, and hates deceits, evasions, and whatever is false or feigned, yet does not also delight in learning what measure must be observed here: the fault of such a man will be the distress of a narrow mind and very difficult entanglements. His own simplicity and the fraud of others will cast him, being too sincere and knowing not how to hide his feelings, into these traps. One who delights in acting or suffering anything <term>nobly and bravely</term> <note>original: *generosè ac fortiter*; the virtue of *Yong* or courage</note>, yet does not also delight in learning the use and measure of this virtue: the fault of such a man will be insolence, and the disturbance and rebellion of the Commonwealth. One who delights in a certain <term>adamantine strength</term> <note>original: *adamantino robore*; the virtue of *Gang* or firm constancy</note> of mind and constancy, yet does not also delight in learning where, when, how, and with what moderation it should be applied: the fault of such a man will be folly and madness.

**part 2. § 1.** **Confucius**, exhorting his disciples to the study of the <term>Ancient Poems</term> <note>original: *Priscorum Poëmatum*; referring to the *Shijing* or Classic of Poetry</note>, said: "O, my children, why do you not study those books of Odes?"

**§ 2.** For indeed, if we crawl upon the ground, lying useless and inglorious, we can be raised up in a certain way through the teachings of the odes, and rise toward true honor.

**§ 3.** In the odes, as if in a mirror, we can contemplate what is most becoming to us, and likewise what is unbecoming; by contemplating these things, we may be healthfully moved to change.

**§ 4.** By the protection of the odes, we can become social, affable, and pleasant. For just as music tempers sounds into harmony, so does this Poetry temper our inner movements and desires.

**§ 5.** We are able to hate without anger, or to feel any other movement of our nature, and yet follow it without falling into vice.

**§ 6.** These same poems teach us how we may serve our father at home, and how, when we are away and far from home, we may serve the Prince.

**§ 7.** Finally, by the benefit of these poems, we acquire a rich and especially fruitful knowledge regarding the proper names and natures of birds, four-legged animals, herbs, and trees.

**§ 8.** Confucius, addressing his son *Pe yu* <note>Bo Yu, the only son of Confucius</note>, said: Have you applied yourself to the first chapters of the Odes called *Cheu nan* and *Chao nan*? <note>original: *Cheu nan* & *Chao nan*; referring to the "Zhou Nan" and "Shao Nan" sections of the *Classic of Poetry*</note> Whoever does not exercise himself in these chapters (he said) is like a man standing with his face directly against a wall; that is, he is useless for all things, as he can neither move forward a single step nor perceive the reality of things.

*These odes contain the wedding song of King Wen-vam and his bride Tai gin, a maiden most celebrated for her prudence and virtue. She was the mother of Vu vam, the founder of the third dynasty, the Cheu <note>The Zhou Dynasty</note>, who began his reign in the year 1122 before Christ. Furthermore, these songs celebrate the praises of both spouses: first, because they labored wisely to cultivate virtues within their own souls; next, for rightly ordering their family; and finally, for their administration of the entire Kingdom situated in the North—the noble pattern of which they later transmitted to the southern kingdoms as well.*

f. 5. p. 1. **§ 1.** Confucius, enduring the hypocritical "trumpeters" of ancient texts with a certain sarcasm, said: "To what end are all those citations and mere words? The *Book of Rites* says, '*The Book of Rites says...*'? Do those precious vessels, the various insignia of rank, and the silk robes say anything to you? Again, the *Book of Music* says, '*The Book of Music says...*'; what book, finally? Do the bronze bells or the drums tell you what your duty is? Meanwhile, the most beautiful teachings—for the sake of which our ancestors established rites and music—you certainly do not express in your life or character."

**§ 2.** *Confucius* said: Those who are grave, constant, and severe in their outward appearance, and yet inside—in their souls, I say—are wavering and weak, are rightly compared to certain base and wicked men who, while actually being thieves in the night, play the part of a grave and honest man by day. Thus, these people are exactly like those thieves who bore through or leap over a wall in the hours of the night.

p. 2. **§ 1.** *Confucius* said: Of the same cloth as those "night-thieves" I just mentioned are those commonly held by people living in the country to be honest, simple, and dutifully companionable. In appearance they are such, but in truth they are deceptive, malicious, cunning, old rogues, and shifty—in short, the true "thieves of virtue" <note>original: *virtutum latrones*; a translation of the Chinese term *de zhi zei*, referring to "village worthies" who lack true moral substance</note>, a plague and a ruin.

**§ 2.** *Confucius* said: To hear the principles and precepts of living well and happily upon the road, and then immediately to speak of them on the road—to pour them out from the mouth the moment they are perceived by the ears, without first applying them to yourself before sharing them with others—this is a throwing away of virtue, a contempt and a rejection of it.

**§ 3.** *Confucius* said: As for those who are base and low in their condition and character...
