...how can such men serve the Prince and the State?

**§ 4.** They certainly cannot. For men of this sort, even before they obtain what they desire, are tormented in their innermost feelings until they obtain it by right or by wrong <note>original: *per fas & nefas*; literally "through divine and human law," meaning by any means necessary</note>. But once they have obtained it, they are again tormented and racked with pain lest they lose it.

**§ 5.** And indeed, when they fear losing the wealth and dignities they have thus acquired, there is nothing they will not stoop to. There is nothing, I say, so abject, so shameful, so unjust that they would not do or endure it.

**Book 6, Part 1, § 1.** **Confucius**, lamenting his own age as it grew heavy with the vices and diseases of the soul, spoke thus: The ancients indeed had three primary "diseases" <note>Referring to character flaws or moral failings</note> from which they suffered even then; yet they were neither severe nor widespread. But now it might perhaps be said that these no longer even exist <note>Meaning the original, milder versions have vanished, replaced by something far worse</note>; for the force of evil has grown so much that it seems to have passed into human nature itself.

**§ 2.** The "disease" of the ancients was a certain immoderate appetite for honor and glory, and from this was born a certain looseness, or at least a neglect of humbler things and matters of lesser importance; and nothing more. But in this time, that appetite has become such a violent dissolution of the soul that men recklessly trample upon all that is right and just. Another disease of the ancients was severity—heavy and inexorable, to be sure—yet it was not of the kind that, content with fear alone, excluded almost all love. But the severity of our age is quarrelsome; it produces almost nothing except hatred, brawls, bitterness, despair, and one disturbance after another. The simplicity and rusticity of the ancients were honest, open, and straight; the rusticity and simplicity of our age are mere pretenses, mere frauds and deceptions, and nothing else.

**Part 2, § 1.** **Confucius** said: Men of affected speech and eloquence, as well as those with a flattering face, possess little true virtue <term>virtus: Here, 'virtus' translates the Chinese concept of 'Ren' (仁), signifying benevolence, humanity, and moral excellence</term>.

**§ 2.** **Confucius**, wishing to declare by an analogy of similar things how much harm is caused by—and how worthy of universal hatred is—the appearance of a feigned face and the eloquence of a flattering and lying tongue, spoke thus: Among colors, I hate the color violet, insofar as it takes away and, in a way, steals the native purple <note>original: *purpureum*; in the context of the *Analects*, this refers to the "pure" primary color (vermilion) being replaced by a "debased" secondary color</note>, thereby diminishing its value and the love people have for it. Similarly, I hate the music of the Kingdom of **Zheng** <note>original: *Chim*; referring to the State of Zheng, whose music was traditionally criticized by Confucians as being licentious or distracting</note>: for it disturbs and, with its pleasures, weakens that music of the ancients which is called **Ya** <note>The *Yayue*, or "Elegant Music," used in court rituals to promote harmony</note>, the teacher of shame, modesty, and gravity. Finally, I hate that sharp and wickedly eloquent mouth, equipped with a thousand arts of pretending and flattering. For it ruins and utterly overthrows royal houses and the most noble families.

**§ 3.** **Confucius**, about to exhort his followers toward the practice of silence, and to insist upon deeds and facts rather than copious and ornate speeches...

...guide others; hereafter, he said, I wish to say nothing more.

**§ 4.** Zi Gong <note>original: *çu cum*; a prominent disciple known for his eloquence</note>, marveling at this statement from the Master, said: "Master, if indeed you say nothing further hereafter, then what shall we disciples learn, and consequently, what shall we report to others? What shall we impart to posterity when we ourselves receive nothing?"

**§ 5.** **Confucius** said: "How does Heaven speak? In what voice or by what reason does it teach and instruct us? Behold the four seasons of the year, how they complete their course; likewise, how all things are most happily brought forth. These things clearly declare and, with a most eloquent silence, proclaim that hidden principle of theirs, in which all things alone turn. Therefore, if Heaven speaks such hidden matters so eloquently, in what manner does it finally speak?" <note>Confucius suggests that truth is found in the natural order and action rather than just words.</note>

**Book 5, Part 1, § 1.** **Ru Bei** <note>original: *Ju poi*</note>, a man of letters whom **Confucius**—by order of King **Ai** <note>original: *Ngai*; this was the twelfth ruler of the Kingdom of Lu</note>—was instructing in funeral rites, desired one day to visit **Confucius**. **Confucius** excused himself, claiming ill health. And while the servant, who had received his master's command, was leaving through the chamber doors to announce this to the guest, the Philosopher took a musical instrument in his hands and sang with deliberate effort, so that the guest might hear him singing. In this way, the guest would understand that the Philosopher was not refusing him because he was truly unwell, but because he himself had committed some fault for which this rejection served as a deserved punishment.

**§ 2.** **Zai Wo** <note>original: *çai ngo*</note>, a disciple, consulted his Master regarding the three-year period of mourning upon the death of parents, asking what he thought of it. "For," he said, "it has long been the case that only a single year, and no more, is granted to mourning."

**§ 3.** "And in my judgment, it is plainly sufficient. For if a man of gravity and integrity, occupied with domestic mourning, does not perform any civil duties for three whole years, those duties will undoubtedly be gradually erased and perish through disuse. Likewise, if he does not practice music for three years, music will undoubtedly fall into ruin."

**Part 2, § 1.** "What of the fact that the very nature of things seems to teach us that a mourning period longer than a year is by no means required? For the beginning and end, the birth and death of most things, is defined by the span of a single year. We see certainly that when the adult and mature crop has been reaped and gathered into the granary, it has in a sense already ceased to live; the new crop which succeeds it immediately shows its budding greenness, which, leaning on the fibers of the roots and gradually uniting, now rises with a jointed stalk and is enclosed as if coming into its youth. Furthermore, just as there is a different method for plants and trees in almost every season of the year, so too the very fire, which is drawn out by boring into wood, is itself changed through each of the four seasons. <note>Referring to the ancient Chinese ritual of changing the type of wood used to produce "new fire" at the start of each season.</note> Therefore, the span of a year can entirely suffice for mourning."

<summary>This page covers Confucius’s philosophy on the "eloquence of silence" in nature and records a sharp debate over the traditional three-year mourning period, which the disciple Zai Wo argues should be shortened to one year for the sake of social and cultural continuity.</summary>

**§ 2.** **Confucius** replied in this way: "The ancient books of duties and rites prescribe for sons that during the funeral rites for parents, they should eat only very common and poorly cleaned rice for three years; they should drink water and wear garments made of hemp, which is coarse and humble. If you now, after only a single year has passed, cast off your mourning, eating once more that finer rice and wearing those precious silk garments, will your mind be at peace? Will your conscience not be tormented by your neglected filial piety <term>pietas; the central Confucian virtue of duty, love, and respect toward one's parents and ancestors</term>?" The disciple replied: "It will not torment me at all; I shall be at peace."

**§ 3.** "**Confucius** said: If indeed you will be at peace doing these things, then do what you please. To a man of integrity and wisdom who is dwelling in mourning and filth <note>original: *sordibus*; this refers to the unkempt appearance and simple living required during the mourning period</note> because of his lost parents, although he might eat rich and delicious banquets, they do not taste sweet or flavorful to him. Similarly, if he should hear a musical performance, he takes no delight in it, just as if he did not hear it. Although he might lie down softly and luxuriously, he finds no rest; such is the power of pious sorrow, such is the great and lasting longing for excellent parents. For this reason, he would never allow himself to shorten the duration of mourning established by the ancestors. But now, since you can bear to do so, then do what you please."

**Folio 8, page 1, § 1.** When the disciple **Zai Wo** <note>original: *çai ngo*</note> had left, **Confucius** turned to the others and said: "The disciple **Yu** <note>original: *Yu*; this is the personal name of Zai Wo</note> is not endowed with true and genuine virtue, since he has decided that ancient customs can be so easily neglected and the institutions of the ancestors violated—institutions which nevertheless seem consistent with the laws of nature and reason. For a child, once born, is nurtured for three years and only then released from the embrace of father and mother. What then is more just than for children to respond to those three years of love with three years of piety and mourning? This three-year mourning period is certainly most ancient, and it is a mourning custom spread and practiced throughout the whole Empire. Did the disciple **Yu** perhaps not also receive three years of care and love from his own parents, like the rest of mortals, that he so favors this novelty and defends the errors of our age?"

**Page 2, § 1.** **Confucius** said: "Those who gorge themselves with food and drink all day long, and have no serious matter to occupy their minds, oh, how hard they will work to show anything worthy of a human being! But is there not the game of chess <term>ludus scacchorum; likely a reference to *liubo* or *weiqi* (Go), which the translator has rendered as the more familiar 'chess'</term> with which they might occupy themselves? At least those who apply themselves to such games to flee idleness are certainly wiser in this one thing than those others."

**§ 3.** The disciple **Tzu-kung** <note>original: *çu cum*; a prominent disciple known for his eloquence and success in business</note>, posing another question, spoke thus: "Does an excellent man and Philosopher, provided he is bound by the desire to deserve well of all people, nevertheless also find himself bound to hate certain others?" **Confucius** replied: "He is bound to hate. He hates above all those who broadcast the vices and sins of men. He hates those who, although they are low and base, nevertheless impudently and rashly disparage and murmur against those who hold a superior place and dignity. Furthermore, he hates the strong and spirited who act without custom or measure. He also hates a certain kind of man who foolishly pleases himself—those who are so tenacious in their own opinions, so stubborn and obstinate, that they rashly attempt anything without giving place to reason."

**Folio 9, page 1, § 1.** Having said these things, **Confucius** said: "I now ask you in turn, my disciple **Su** <note>original: *Su*; another name for Tzu-kung</note>, whether besides those I have mentioned, you also have those whom you hate?" He replied: "I do, and they are of three kinds: I hate those who, although they possess little insight and understanding of affairs, are nevertheless sharp critics of others, thinking this to be a mark of prudence. I hate men who are not submissive and who, through pride, are contentious, regarding this as a mark of a brave and noble spirit. Finally, I hate men who, imprudently and mockingly, rebuke others for vices known only in secret, and who regard this as being of a candid, sincere, and upright mind."

**§ 2.** **Confucius** said: "It is almost only small-minded women <note>original: *mulierculas*; here referring to the women of the household or those of lesser education</note> and men of the lowest condition, such as those who serve us, who are extremely difficult to manage in such a way that you keep them satisfied. For if you become closer to them through a certain indulgence and ease, they will no longer carry themselves submissively, but will become insolent, and will not (as is proper) honor and revere you. If you remove yourself from them, and only rarely deal with them—and then with a certain authority and severity—they will soon complain, and you will be held in hatred as one who is austere, ungenerous, and unkind."

**Page 2, § 1.** **Confucius** said: "A man who reaches the age of forty and yet, because of his wickedness and folly, still appears to be—and is held to be—troublesome and hateful to all; the correction of such a man is desperate. He will persist in this way even until the end."

Having said this, he proceeded into the Royal chamber and with the authority of a kinsman admonished his nephew; that he should finally come to his senses at last; that he should consult for himself and his people. But the tyrant, impatient of the truth and now more brutal from the warning itself, intended to kill his innocent uncle—even as he was suggesting things most useful—not without insult and mockery. Turning himself to the surrounding nobles, he said: "This Bi Gan; if you do not know, thinks himself to be a holy man. Having spoken these words, on that very spot he ordered his uncle to be slaughtered, and the heart to be extracted while he was still breathing.*

And where, therefore, would I not be deprived of my dignity a third time or more? ### BOOK THREE

And while he was being carried in a carriage together with his disciple **Zilu** <note>original: *çu lu*</note>, who was himself the driver of the carriage, they by chance encountered two Philosophers also originating from the Kingdom of **Chu** <note>original: *çu*</note>, who were hiding away with the same purpose and weariness of those most miserable times as the man mentioned before. (**Changju** <note>original: *Cham ciu*</note> and **Jieni** <note>original: *Kie nie*</note> were their names; they were devoted to the work of agriculture, and were then together plowing some deserted fields). **Confucius**, having traveled a little way past them, ordered his disciple **Zilu** to ask them for the location of a ford across the nearby river, which they needed to cross.

§. 3. The first of them, **Changju**, questioning **Zilu**, said: "Who is that there who guides the carriage?" **Zilu** replied: "It is **Kong Qiu** <note>original: *Cum kieu*; the formal name of Confucius</note>." "Is that," he asked, "the **Kong Qiu** originating from the Kingdom of **Lu**?" He replied: "It is he." The Philosopher said: "He himself knows the ford of the river, he who goes back and forth on this road so many times. Why does he order you to ask?"

§. 4. Having received such a biting response, the disciple inquired of the other, named **Jieni**, where the ford of the river might be. **Jieni** in turn questioning him said: "Young man, who are you?" He replied: "I am **Zhong You** <note>original: *Chum yeu*; another name for **Zilu**</note>." Then the Philosopher said: "Are you perhaps a disciple of the Philosopher originating from the Kingdom of **Lu** whose name is **Kong Qiu**?" At this, **Zilu** understood the man he was speaking with was a wise man. Therefore, answering, he said: "I am indeed." But the other, intending to condemn the pursuit of the Master and the disciple alike, spoke thus: "Like a rushing torrent, all the affairs of the Empire rush headlong together; and who could bring about a change, and a sort of flowing back to the original state? Truly, compared to what you are doing—that is, following a Master who flees from men (for in the manner of a fugitive he changes his seat constantly)—how much better would it be for you to follow the Philosophers who flee from the world?" Having said these things, he went on covering the seed and did not cease from his work; nor did he himself indicate the crossing of the river.

p. 2. **Zilu** departed to inform his Master of these things. **Confucius**, sighing deeply, said: "Birds and four-footed beasts cannot be gathered together in the same place <note>Confucius means that humans cannot live in isolation with animals; we are social beings</note>. But if I do not associate myself with these men of my time, with whom then shall I associate? If the Empire were at peace, I would not be necessary to bring about change."

*Clearly this is how the matter stands (these are the words of the **Colao** <term>Colao: a title for a Grand Secretary or high-ranking official in the Chinese imperial court</term> speaking in his own name, and no longer in the name of the Philosopher): Heaven produces holy and wise men for this chief purpose: that they may be of benefit and salvation to as many as possible. Thus, in the past, those great Kings and Founders of our Empire considered the common calamity of the people to be their own; for the hunger and want from which their subjects sometimes suffered tormented no one as much as themselves. For this reason, they strove with even more burning zeal to strain every nerve of their talent and industry so that they might remedy the public calamity as quickly as possible. Unhappy would be the fatherland, and miserable the human race, if it were right to follow the doctrine—or more truly the despair and sluggishness—of those [recluse] philosophers.*

<vocab>Confucius, Zilu, Changju, Jieni, Kong Qiu, The Colao, Kingdom of Lu, Philosophy, Empire, Heaven</vocab>

A concluding commentary argues that true sages work for the public good rather than withdrawing into isolation.</summary>

Book 12, page 1, §. 1. While **Zilu** <note>original: *çu lu*</note> was traveling together with the Master, and perhaps following him at a slower pace, he fell some distance behind. The Master suddenly vanished from the disciple's sight. While Zilu stood there uncertain of which path to take, he met an old man carrying a basket suspended from a staff. **Zilu** questioned him, saying: "Good man, have you perhaps seen my Master?" The old man did not answer the question directly, but instead rebuked him with a stern speech, saying: "You indeed, good youth, wandering and wasting away in idleness, as I see, do not have a body hardened by labor, while I, a man of this age, devote my efforts to **Agriculture** <note>original: *Agriculturæ*</note>. Since you neglect this, you perhaps cannot even distinguish the **five types of grain** <note>The traditional "Five Grains" of ancient China: usually rice, broomcorn millet, foxtail millet, wheat, and beans</note>, though they are most well-known, being ignorant of the difference between beans, millet, and wheat. And you—who is this 'Master' you speak of to me? Who is that Master of yours?" Having said these things, he fixed his staff in the ground and began weeding the field, rooting out the useless weeds.

§. 2. **Zilu**, who recognized from that speech and the demeanor of the man's face and body the hidden wisdom of a concealed Philosopher, gave no sign of taking offense. Instead, pressing his hands together and curving them before his chest to show honor (as is the custom of this nation), he stood there with a remarkable display of modesty and respect.

§. 3. The old man admired and took a liking to this example of such a composed mind and natural character. Therefore, he led **Zilu** to his home and kept him there to stay the night. He killed a chicken, prepared a meal, and refreshed his guest with "unbought feasts" <note>A poetic way of describing simple, home-grown food</note>. Then, he brought out his two sons, the elder and the younger, so that they might greet the guest courteously and properly according to their respective ages.

§. 4. When the next day dawned, **Zilu** departed to inform **Confucius** of everything. **Confucius**, having heard the sequence of events, said: "Without a doubt, he is one of the number of wise men, but he is hidden and keeping to himself." He therefore ordered his disciple **Zilu** to return and visit the old man again. He went and reached the house, but the old man had already departed.

§. 5. **Zilu**, intending to explain his Master's mind and his opinion on those hidden wise men to posterity, spoke thus: "Neither divine law nor reason allows one to refuse to hold office, even in this state of affairs and in this most miserable time, provided you are fit to hold it. For indeed, if it is a crime to violate the order and mutual rights of two brothers, elder and younger, which are established by the accidental time of their birth (he seems here to allude to what he had seen a little before in the house of the old Philosopher), then by what logic shall the mutual right and duty of King and subject be violated? These good men certainly desire to look out for the integrity and innocence of their own persons, as they say; but meanwhile, they do not consider that they disturb...

### BOOK THREE

...[they disturb] and violate that great order of the human race and the tightest bond by which subjects are bound to their Prince (especially while he is in danger) and citizens to their struggling fatherland. Therefore, an upright and wise man manages the Commonwealth <note>original: *Rempublicam*; referring to the state or public affairs</note> even in the midst of turmoil, and fulfills his duty as an honest citizen; by the very fact that ancestral customs and laws no longer flourish, he understands this duty of the upright and wise citizen—which was just mentioned—namely, to come to the aid of the fatherland even at the risk of his life, rather than sitting as idle spectators of the public ruin in the manner of those old men <note>A reference to the recluses mentioned in the preceding text</note>.

Folio 13, page 1, §. 1. In this paragraph, seven hidden sages are recounted who, having either lost their dignity or even voluntarily cast it aside, led private lives; not all of them, indeed, in the same manner or with the same purpose, yet they did so wisely and with praise. They were **Boyi**, **Shuqi**, **Yu Zhong**, **Yiyi**, **Zhuzhang**, **Hui of Liuxia**, and **Shaolian** <note>original: *Pe y, Xo çi, Yu chum, y ye, chu cham, Lieu hia hoei, & Xao lien*</note>.

> Confucius said: Those who in no way abandoned the purpose of a free and unconquered mind, and in no way brought shame upon their person, were the two brothers **Boyi** and **Shuqi**. If we speak of **Hui of Liuxia** and **Shaolian**, they did indeed lower their freedom and will to some extent; they brought shame (though by the injury of others) upon their person. Yet their words were consistent with reason, and their deeds responded to the wishes of men:
->These were such men, and nothing else.<-

§. 3. Again, if we speak of **Yu Zhong** and **Yiyi**, they also lived as hidden men; they spoke quite freely. Yet their persons attained purity, and although they were cast down in appearance, they nonetheless attained an equilibrium of the heart.

Page 2, §. 1. I, however, am different from these; indeed, I have nothing that I always approve, nor anything that I always disapprove. The end for all of them was the same; the means were different, the goal was the same, but the paths varied. I do not condemn them; I praise them rather. Yet I do not wish to imitate them at all; I serve the place, the time, the people, and the Prince; insofar as I consult all these things whenever something is to be done or omitted, and I accommodate myself to all, so that I may deserve well of all, as far as it can be done.

§. 2. The Great Master of Music, whose name was **Zhi** <note>original: *Chi*</note>, moved to the Kingdom of **Qi** <note>original: *çi*</note>. *Elsewhere we have already mentioned how much this political Monarchy, especially in ancient times, attributed to music—or more truly, to that doctrine and instruction which, bound to musical rhythms and then tempered by a variety of sounds, penetrated the minds of the listeners. Why say more? For music to have collapsed and for the Kingdom to have collapsed were nearly the same thing. Here, certainly, so that it might be clear to everyone that the Kingdom of **Lu** was already near ruin, nothing other than the cessation of music and the flight of the Musicians is described; who, dismissed by families becoming insolent with power and deprived of their income, sought other jurisdictions and Kingdoms.*

§. 3. He who directed the music for the second course or the Royal meal, named **Kan** <note>original: *Can*</note>, moved to the Kingdom of **Chu** <note>original: *çu*</note>. He of the third meal, **Liao**...

§ 3. The second, or assistant, Master of Royal Music, named **Tan** <note>original: *Tam*</note>: Likewise another who played the stone chimes, named **Xiang** <note>original: *Siam*</note> (who was the very teacher of Confucius in musical matters), went into the sea, that is, to the islands of the neighboring sea.

§ 4. **The Duke of Zhou** <note>original: *Cheu cum*</note>, second to almost no one among the Chinese Princes in his reputation for wisdom, spoke to his son **Bo Qin** <note>original: *Pe Kin*</note>, who had just been created as the governor of the Kingdom of **Lu**. Providing him with the most necessary precepts before his departure, he spoke thus: A wise and princely man does not despise or cast away his relatives and kin; he does not make the chief ministers of his Kingdom feel like strangers to him, giving them cause for just offense or hatred by not employing them; he does not suddenly strip them of their dignity, either for some tiny fault or for no reason at all, without providing an explanation for his action and so heavy a punishment. A prudent man avoids offenses of this kind: for he understands that the whole body is ill-served when the head does not agree with its limbs. He certainly does not discard noble and ancient families unless there is a grave and atrocious cause; rather, as many of them as are fit to manage the Commonwealth, he admits to public service without hesitation. Those who are indeed not fit, he nevertheless allows to enjoy their income because of the merits of their ancestors. A wise King does not demand that all talents be present in one and the same man; but prudently matching the burdens to each man's strength, he treats his people much like vessels, seeking different uses from different men according to the capacity of each.

> There exist in the annals other precepts of this same Prince, with which he instructs his same son: that he should bear with a great soul the grumblings and slanders of his people; that he should seriously look into himself and inquire whether he has perhaps given them cause; and that he should strive by his equity, patience, and especially by the innocence of his life, to soften the hostile minds of those speaking ill of him and bind them to himself. Likewise, placed at that high summit of power, he should take the greatest care to avoid pride, arrogance, and vanity; he should watch himself vigilantly, not only for his own sake, but for the sake of the whole province of which he is the head. Finally, about to add more vehement stings from his own example, he said: "You know, my son, that I am the son of **King Wen** <note>original: *Ven vam*</note>, the brother of the **Emperor Wu** <note>original: *Vu vam*</note>, and the uncle and tutor of the **Emperor Cheng** <note>original: *Chim tam*</note>. And yet, though I am such and so great a man, I have not hesitated three times in one day to leap out of the bath where I was perhaps tending to my body, with my hair still loose, and three times during the same meal I rose from the table at the signal that was given, for no other [reason]..."

<margin>page 2. §. 1.</margin> The Imperial house and the family of **Chen** <note>The text refers to a legendary or historical lineage of sages</note>, at the time when it held power and was most flourishing, had eight wise men. All were brothers, and not only of the same parents, but even twins, whom their mother brought forth in four births. They are named in the order in which they are noted here with paired characters. What greatly increases the rarity of this miracle is that all of them are said to have been so endowed with the gifts of nature, such gravity of character, and such integrity of life, that they were easily judged as the leaders among the wise men of their age. If this is indeed the case, it shows that whenever Heaven sends down Kings and Princes to pacify and restore the affairs of the Empire, it also kindly sends helpers for these Princes, who may aid their efforts with industry, virtue, and wisdom. # THE THIRD BOOK
## PART TEN

->Folio 1. page 1. paragraph 1.<-

The disciple **Zichang** <note>original: *çu cham*; likely Zi Zhang, a prominent student of Confucius known for his formal manner</note> used to say: A grave and wise man, seeing a serious danger to the kingdom and the Royal family, risks his life for the public safety without any hesitation. This same man, however, when seeing an opportunity for profit, first considers within himself what justice and equity permit. When applying himself to sacred rites, he is mindful of veneration and reverence; finally, in funerals and burial rites, he is mindful of grief and compassion. Such a man is worthy of his name as a sage, and nothing else is required.

§. 2. **Zichang** used to say: Consider the man who indeed takes hold of virtue and applies himself to it, but not fully; he does so only fitfully, with meager zeal and effort, bringing (so to speak) the tiny vessel of a narrow heart. Consider also the man who lends his ears and his faith to the best teachings and disciplines, but not with that firmness or constancy which is fitting, so that he wavers and fluctuates, moved by every wind or breeze of opinion. Of such a man, how can it be judged that because he exists, anything has been added to this world? And how, again, can it be judged that because he does not exist, anything has departed from this world? <note>Zichang is arguing that a half-hearted or inconsistent commitment to virtue makes a person's life inconsequential.</note>

...above all; however, they differed in their opinions and ways of living. **Zixia** <note>original: *çu hia*</note> whatever he did, he did very seriously, diligently, and steadily; he was content with his own rank and his shared resources. On the other hand, **Zizhang** <note>original: *çu cham*</note>, impatient with rest and mediocrity, always aspired to higher things. Therefore, one day the disciples of the one named **Zixia** posed a question about friendship to **Zizhang**. **Zizhang**, questioning them, said: "What does your Master **Zixia** think of this? What does he say?" They responded: "Our Master **Zixia** says: 'With those who are worthy of friendship—because they are upright, sincere, and love to learn, and are the kind of people from whom you in turn might learn—bind yourself with the closest possible bond of friendship. But those who are not worthy of it, because they can neither be of use to you nor wish to be of use to themselves, remove them far from you.'"

**Zizhang**, hearing this, said: "I marvel at what you say; for it differs greatly from what I myself once heard: namely, that a wise man studiously cultivates the company of the wise, yet admits all others into a most wide embrace of charity <note>original: *charitas*; here used in the sense of universal benevolence or 'Ren'</note> and kindly includes them. He honors and extols those endowed with excellent gifts, and has pity on the weak, whom he raises up from where they lie, sustaining and strengthening them with advice and resources. Therefore, whatever others may be, and whatever I myself may be, I would never wish to reject anyone. Am I perhaps a great sage? If so, who among men is there whom I should not admit and embrace? If, on the contrary, I am not one of the wise, but a rude and lowly man of the common people, then surely others will easily, and not unjustly, reject and neglect me. To what end, then, is my rejection of other men? With what face should I, who am myself contemptible, hold anyone in contempt?"

§. 2. The disciple **Zixia** said: "Although a small art or method may be suited only to the most common and meager things—for example, agriculture and mechanical exercises—it nevertheless possesses something worth looking at and worthy of being observed and learned. But if you then wish to extend that same littleness and apply it to sublime matters far removed from the common folk—for example, the administration of the Empire and the Royal family—I fear that you will then immediately get stuck, as if in the mud, and make no progress. For this reason, the wise man who has been called to manage the State does not deal in such things."

->Folio 2. page 1. paragraph 1.<-

**Zixia** said: "A man who diligently searches every day and correctly understands what he lacks, and who similarly refreshes his memory every month regarding the things he has learned—forgetting nothing of what he has once perceived—can be called a **Philosopher** <note>The text uses the Latin *Philosophus* to translate the Chinese concept of a 'Ru' or 'Junzi' (a superior man/scholar)</note>; nothing more is required."

§. 2. **Zixia** said: "To embrace all the sciences with a certain tireless <note>original: *improbo*, literally 'wicked' or 'immoderate', here meaning 'unrelenting'</note> zeal for learning, and to bring to them a firm, sincere, and wholehearted will; in addition, whenever a doubt arises, to diligently and accurately consult the experts, and finally to weigh deeply within one's own mind, or to ruminate..."

### BOOK THREE

...to discern secret and solid truths: who does not see that virtue itself is already present in these very attempts to seek out virtue, especially since what is sought is innate to the mind of the seeker and impressed from heaven? <note>This continues a thought on how the search for wisdom is itself a virtuous act because the seeds of wisdom are divinely implanted in the human soul.</note>

**§ 3.** **Zixia** <note>original: *çu hia*; a prominent disciple of Confucius known for his devotion to study and literature</note> said: All craftsmen and mechanics dwell each in their own marketplace, so that by this arrangement they may complete their work usefully and conveniently. Similarly, the **Philosopher** <note>meaning the scholar or seeker of wisdom</note>, established in the school of virtue and wisdom, diligently studies and learns so that he may perfect that virtue to which he is entirely devoted; he would deservedly be ranked below even a lowly craftsman if, due to inconstancy or laziness, he did not complete his work.

**p. 2. § 1.** **Zixia** said: The foolish and the wicked undoubtedly cloak their sins with a false appearance of right and honor, so that they may persist in them more licentiously and with greater impunity.

**§ 2.** **Zixia** said: A man of integrity and wisdom, although he is always consistent with himself, nevertheless has—or rather, appears to others to have—three transformations. To those watching him from a distance, he appears very grave and severe, such that his appearance somewhat keeps them from approaching more closely. However, to those who approach more confidently and closely, he immediately appears as he truly is: easy, affable, and kind. But then, to those hearing his words, which are so upright and far removed from all pretense or appearance of falsehood, he again appears somewhat severe and rigid.

**§ 3.** **Zixia** said: Whoever manages the **State** <note>original: *Rempublicam*</note> and is a minister to the Prince should be a man of proven loyalty, and only then may he confidently impose any burden upon the people. But if he does not yet possess such a reputation and trust among the common people, then if he imposes any burden, the people will judge that they are being harassed. Similarly, once you are known for your loyalty, you may then confidently advise the Prince: he will listen to the one advising him, and will honor and love him. But if you are not yet known as faithful—because in truth you are not so—then even if you advise the best course of action, he will turn away, judging that you are not so much advising as slandering him.

**f. 3. p. 1. § 1.** **Zixia** said: In matters of greater importance, namely those by whose protection human society is best preserved, and upon which as if on hinges the most important duties turn—for example, the duties of sons toward parents, or of subjects toward their Prince—we must by no means cross the threshold, or the order and measure established by nature and laws. But in matters of lesser importance, which are in a way subservient to those greater ones, we can sometimes stand on either side of the threshold: in these, I say, a place is given for <term>equity</term> <note>original: *epikeiæ*; from the Greek *epikeia*, referring to a lenient or merciful interpretation of the law rather than a rigid adherence to the letter</note> and indulgence, especially when the ignorance of the offender deserves concealment and pardon. For the disciple must not be thought to have felt that even a blemish could be tolerated in one who glories in the name of a wise man, nor to have been ignorant of that ancient proverb: "Small things must be avoided, lest great things be lost." With this also agrees the excellent sentence of the book **Shujing** <note>original: *Xu kim*; The Classic of History, one of the Five Classics of Chinese literature</note>, *Pu kim*...

<meta>catchword: Knowledge</meta>

...to him, <note>original: "fi him, chum lui ta te"</note> to neglect minor matters is ultimately harmful to matters of great importance.

**§ 2.** **Ziyou** <note>original: *çu yeu*; a disciple of Confucius noted for his literary style and knowledge of rites</note>, mocking the disciples of his friend **Zixia**, said that they were so intent on matters of minor importance that they seemed to labor less than they should on the very hinge and foundation of things. He said: "The younger disciples of my friend Zixia, when they perform the duties appropriate to their age—namely, sprinkling the floor with water, sweeping, responding properly to others, entering, and exiting—certainly perform them well enough. But these are minor matters, like leaves and flowers; the root and the foundation are missing. Why is this?"

**§ 3.** **Zixia**, hearing this by chance, said: "Oh, how much **Ziyou** <note>original: *ren yeu*, another name for Ziyou</note> goes astray here, while he thinks that I, having neglected the root, labor only on the leaves. I deliberately begin from the lowest and easiest things, intending to then make a step toward higher and more difficult things. In the method and reasoning of a wise man in instructing his followers, is there anything so fixed and certain that it must be handed over in the first place, or anything that must be more laboriously instilled in the second place in the aforementioned instruction? It is entirely the duty of a prudent Master to diligently seek out what the shoulders of his disciples are able to bear, and what they refuse to bear; what the age of each and what the strength of their genius can grasp; and then to temper his instruction to the capacity of each individual. Just as various kinds of herbs and plants, according to their own species and proper virtues, are very aptly distinguished for various uses by one skilled in them, and are then applied with great utility. Surely I would play a fool's part and deceive myself and my followers if, without first exploring the strengths of each, I were to teach anything rashly, and impertinently thrust the most difficult things upon those not yet mature. How can the method of a wise Master in instructing his followers be mocked and mock others in this way? To embrace the beginning and the end at once, or the root and whatever grows from it, belongs to the **Holy One** <note>original: *Sancti*; here referring to the "Sage," a person of perfect innate wisdom</note> alone; to whom, indeed, wisdom would be infused from heaven along with the vital spirit. I profess that neither am I such a person in teaching, nor are my disciples such in learning."

**f. 4. p. 1. § 1.** **Zixia** said: If someone is moved to public affairs and concerns, and yet among these has plenty of leisure and strength to devote to studies, let him devote himself entirely to his studies. Let him continually increase the acquired wealth of his genius and prudence from the monuments of the ancients and the best disciplines. On the other hand, if someone is free for studies and has already acquired enough ability and strength to hold office, then let him not hesitate to undertake a Magistracy, and let him expend the private wealth of his genius and industry for the common benefit of the fatherland.

**§ 2.** **Ziyou** said: When just rites are paid to the dead, especially to parents, the pious grief of children should fully exert itself in a certain vehement compassion and an intimate feeling of the mourning and failing heart...

### BOOK THREE. 2

...those mourning their lost parents; and let the sons stand firm here, and not labor greatly for luxury and the elaborate displays of our current age—in which there is often more vanity than piety <note>original: *pietas*, here referring specifically to filial piety</note>—even if their resources are not sufficient.

**§ 3.** **Zengzi** <note>original: *çen çu*; a major disciple of Confucius known for his focus on filial piety</note> said: "My companion **Zizhang** <note>original: *çu cham*</note> certainly possesses the spirit and the ability to complete arduous and difficult tasks; nevertheless, he is not yet endowed with that internal and solid virtue from which all praise for true strength must be sought."

**§ 4.** **Zengzi** said: "How magnificently grave is the bearing of the face and body of my friend **Zizhang**; but for that very reason, it is extremely difficult to practice internal and solid virtue together with him, in such a way that either he might profit from others, or others might profit from him in turn. For what mutual help toward the interior cultivation of the soul can be hoped for, when more effort seems to be spent on a certain ostentation of virtue than on virtue itself?"

**p. 2. § 1.** **Zengzi** said: "I once heard from my Master that, commonly among men, there is no one who fully exhausts the powers of his soul in the exercise of any particular virtue. But if such a thing does occur, it truly occurs during the mourning and funeral of one's parents."

**§ 2.** **Zengzi** said: "I once heard my Master say, when he spoke of the excellent piety and obedience of **Meng Zhuangzi** <note>original: *Mem chuam çu*</note>, the Prefect of the Kingdom of **Lu**, which he clearly demonstrated at the death of his father **Meng Xianzi** <note>original: *Hien çu*</note>, also a Prefect: 'That [piety] another might also be able to perform and imitate! But this one thing—that he did not change his father's ministers and subjects, whom the father had employed in office, nor did he change his father's method of governing—this, I say, is extremely difficult to achieve.'"

**§ 3.** **Zengzi**, the disciple of **Confucius**, also had seven disciples. **Meng Shi** <note>original: *Mem xi*</note>, the Prefect of the Kingdom of **Lu**, had ordered one of them, named **Yang Fu** <note>original: *Yam fu*</note>, to act as a judge of crimes and the Prefect of the public guard. He therefore consulted his Master, **Zengzi**, on how he should conduct the office assigned to him. **Zengzi** replied: "At this time, the higher magistrates, who ought to shine before others with the best examples, have everywhere turned away from their own path and standard of living and governing rightly. Therefore, it has been a long time since the people have also gone astray, becoming scattered and distracted by evil pursuits and opinions. If, therefore, while you examine the cases and crimes of individuals, you find them to be of this sort—that is, if you are certain of the nature and causes of the crimes that are commonly committed—then, although those who are guilty cannot avoid being punished, always use compassion and mercy. By no means should you rejoice, as if pleasing yourself <note>as the **Colaus** <term>Colaus: a high official or commentator, likely referring to the standard neo-Confucian commentaries used by the translators</term> explains</note> because you have cleverly detected the hidden crimes of the miserable. Instead, remember that not all the fault lies with them, since they have been deceived by their own ignorance as well as the corrupt examples of their superiors."

...punishments may be decreed according to the gravity of each person’s offense. The moderation and clemency of **Emperor Shun** <note>original: *Xun Imperatoris*; a legendary sage-king of China</note> are famous; in giving various precepts to the governors of the people, he repeatedly concluded with these words: **"In the exercise of punishments, I wish for you to show mercy"** <note>original: *Gueî hîm fió çái*</note>. Concerning these matters, see the final book of the ***Shu Jing*** <note>original: *Xu kim*; The Classic of History, one of the Five Classics of Chinese literature</note> under the title ***Lü Xing*** <note>original: *Liu hîm*; "The Marquis of Lü on Punishments"</note>, which was composed about one thousand three hundred years later by the Prince of Lü, by order of **King Mu** <note>original: *Mo vam*</note>, the fifth ruler of the **Zhou** <note>original: *Cheu*</note> family, who began to reign in the year 1001 before Christ.

**folio 5. page 1. § 1.** **Zigong** <note>original: *çu cum*; a prominent disciple of Confucius known for his eloquence and diplomatic skill</note> said: "The wickedness of **King Zhou** <note>original: *Cheu*</note>, the last Prince of the **Shang** <note>original: *Xam*</note> family, although truly cruel and lustful, was nevertheless not so heavy and unheard of that it did not appear very similar to that of others. And yet, whenever there is talk of any more serious crime, this **King Zhou** alone is immediately brought forward as an example. As if he were guilty of all crimes, he is still lashed today by the tongues of all men. This is for no other reason than that he was simultaneously a wicked man and an Emperor. His wickedness was more powerful and a greater stumbling block because he cast himself down into the mire of vices from such a sublime height. Therefore, a Prince should truly dread to live even for a short time in such a mire and sink <note>original: *sentina*; literally the bilge water of a ship, used here as a metaphor for a gathering place of filth</note> of errors and depravities. For the sins and evils of the entire Empire—even those for which he is in no way responsible—will all be brought together and flow into him alone, just like dregs and water into a sink. The stain of a very short time will be followed by the hatred of all ages and perennial disgrace, just as happened to that **King Zhou**."

**§ 2.** **Zigong** said: "Those who do not labor to mend their sins try to cover them and spread them over with dye <note>original: *fuco*; refers to cosmetic paint or a deceptive outward appearance</note>. For this reason, the sin of a wise man (and especially of a Prince) is like an **eclipse of the sun or the moon**. For a sin that he does not hide, and which his own high station and dignity betray, is watched by all men. Likewise, when he changes for the better—specifically when, noticing his own failure and sin, he soon returns to his former brightness and splendor like the sun and moon—all men look up to him and proclaim it joyfully."

**§ 3.** A Governor of the **Wei** <note>original: *Guei*</note> Kingdom, whose name was **Gongsun Chao** <note>original: *Cum sun chao*</note>, asked **Zigong**, saying: "**Zhongni** <note>original: *Chum ni*; the courtesy name of Confucius</note>, or Confucius your Master—how did he study?"

**page 2. § 1.** **Zigong** replied: "The doctrine, laws, and institutions of **Kings Wen and Wu** <note>original: *Ven & Vu*; the virtuous founders of the Zhou Dynasty</note>, although they themselves ceased to live nearly six hundred years ago, have not yet fallen to the earth; they have not yet perished or been utterly obliterated. Indeed, they still exist and persist in men, and the wise certainly retain in their memory all their principal headings. Even the ruder sort among the common people still remember certain smaller details of minor importance. Whether you consider the great things or the small, there is nothing of them all that does not still exist in the teachings of our founders..."

The wisdom of other men is like a hill or a mountain, which, though it may seem high to those looking up from the plain, can still be climbed. But truly **Confucius**—the doctrine and wisdom of **Confucius**, I say—transcends the mountains themselves; because of its sublimity, it is in a way the **Sun** and the **Moon**, and there is no one who can transcend or surpass it. Though degenerate and wicked men may desire and strive to cut themselves off and remove themselves as far as possible from the best institution and doctrine, how can they ultimately harm this Sun and Moon of our age? It is now plainly evident that detractors of this sort do not know how to give the proper measure to things small and great, low and high."

<note>Ziqin, the interlocutor from the previous page,</note> did not yet know how to estimate the sublimity of his doctrine, addressing **Zigong** <note>original: *çu cum*; a prominent disciple known for his eloquence</note> only as an admirer of his Master; "Indeed," he said, "when you think and speak so excellently of **Confucius**, you lower yourself, led by an excessive veneration; for how is **Confucius** actually any wiser than you?"

§. 4. **Zigong**, scorning either this man's error or flattery just as he had the other's, replied: "A philosopher is not rarely judged to excel in prudence from a single word, and conversely, the same is often judged to suffer from imprudence from a single word. **Part 2. §. 1.** "Thus I think, and thus I say: As for my Master (in what pertains to his virtue and doctrine), he cannot be reached, almost in the same way that heaven cannot be ascended by a ladder; although we may look up at its vastness and beauty from afar, and wonder at it with a certain pleasure."

§. 2. **Zigong**, now about to declare that the praises he had bestowed upon **Confucius** were not empty—briefly weighing here one example out of many, namely his sweet effectiveness—said: "My Master, having once obtained a great domain to be administered on behalf of the **Prince of the Realm** <note>original: *ditionis Principe*; likely referring to the State of Lu</note>, fulfilled all the duties of a wise and benign governor in this order and manner. First, that which is commonly said and commanded to governors: 'raise up and sustain the people,' namely, through a fair division of lands and watchful industry, so that none of those things necessary for the sustenance and care of the body are lacking. With **Confucius** administering affairs, the people were immediately raised up, and grew like a well-tilled field. Once a great abundance of things was available in this manner, that which is commanded next followed: 'by your words and examples, guide and direct the unrefined people toward every right and honest way of living and discipline.' With **Confucius** directing, the people immediately followed him willingly and gladly, and stood constant in the path that had been shown. Once the **State** <note>original: *Republicâ*; used here to mean the commonweal or organized society</note> was established in this way with the best laws and disciplines, that which is commanded next followed: 'procure peace for the people,' so that each, content in his own place and condition, might find rest in his native soil as if in his center. The rare skill and prudence of **Confucius** procured this as well. Immediately, many outsiders from neighboring lands, driven by the fame and desire for such longed-for peace, came flocking in. But once public tranquility was secured, that which is commanded next followed: 'move and rouse the people,' and renew the study of virtue and mutual charity and respect among all through other industries; lift up the faint-hearted, and spur on those already running. With **Confucius** thus rousing them, harmony immediately flourished among all, along with those things that accompany it: the rites and duties of citizens who honor and love one another. Indeed, as the summit of these praises, it was added that they were held in such high regard..."

...the movements of souls occurred without any visible movement or noise from the one who moved them; in almost no other way than the silent and hidden power of the heavens, which, while it achieves so much on earth, remains most secret, and escapes not only the eyes but also the intellect of mortals. For these and other reasons, his life was altogether most glorious; and his death was truly most tearful, as evidenced by the common and long-lasting mourning that followed it, testifying that he was held in honor by his fellow citizens no differently than a father by his children; and almost in no other way than a gentle mother is accustomed to be held in delight and love. Since these things are so, how finally can he be reached?

*Behold how that hyperbolic praise <note>original: *praedicatio*; meaning a public proclamation or preaching of his virtues</note> did not depart far from the earth, which at first glance seemed to carry **Confucius** above the clouds and stars. It seemed to exceed the limits of nature; yet suddenly it confined itself within the narrow boundaries of a single, small people, whom he had undertaken to govern wisely and peacefully. Therefore, I believe there will be nothing here that offends the European reader, who is no less candid than benevolent.*

*folio 7, page 1, paragraph I. This <note>referring to the previous section</note> is explained in the following paragraphs by the disciples, who had very frequently heard from their Master which arts and industries the first Legislators of the Chinese nation, and the first founders of the three princely families—the **Xia**, **Shang**, and **Zhou** <note>original: *Hia, Xam, Cheu*</note>—had chiefly used; also what they wished to be the principles <note>original: *quasi fundamenta*; acting as foundations</note> of their politics. While succeeding one another, they managed the affairs of a very vast empire so successfully—not indeed at the same time, but by nearly the same rule—and with such constant favor of Heaven, that these three families alone, together with the two Legislators **Yao** and **Shun** <note>original: *Yao, Xun*</note>, held power for far longer than the nineteen dynasties that followed thereafter, up to this year 1670; for all those 19 together count 1929 years, while these first three count 2108 years.*

*Most of these maxims are excerpted, though in summary, from the very ancient and first-authority book called the **Shu Jing** <note>original: *Xu Kim*; the "Book of Documents," one of the Five Classics of Chinese literature</note>, which the simplicity of the style, characteristic of those times, sufficiently reveals. Furthermore, the **Shu Jing** is a brief history of certain ancient Kings, furnished with their excellent teachings. We, however, for the sake of clarity, will explain those things which are of a historical nature, sometimes more fully than is our custom, and more so than **Couplet** <note>original: *Colaus*; referring to Philippe Couplet, the Jesuit editor of this volume</note> himself, who either passed over most things here in silence or touched upon them only with a word, because he understood them to be very well known to his reader.*

***Yao**, the Legislator of the Chinese nation (of whom we have made mention above quite often), an Emperor, if not the first, certainly the most celebrated, began his reign in the year 2357 before Christ. He ruled for 100 years. He, therefore, taking no account of his own sons or domestic glory, but only of virtue and wisdom—now elderly and about to resign the empire to **Shun**, whom he had long before called from the plow-handle <note>original: *stiva*; referring to Shun’s humble origins as a farmer</note> to a certain partnership in the Empire because of his excellent praise for piety, obedience, and prudence—encouraged him with this speech, saying: "O you, my **Shun**, Heaven has decreed the succession of the Empire..."*

...to exist in your person. With faith, see that you apprehend and hold fast to the <term>Mean</term><note>The "Mean" (*Zhong*) refers to the Confucian principle of balance and moral rectitude, avoiding extremes.</note>. If the people within the <term>four seas</term><note>A traditional Chinese term referring to the world or the Chinese empire.</note> suffer from want and poverty, the rewards of heaven will cease forever.

*Be of good courage (these are the words of the Interpreter), administrator and partner of my labors and cares. The time is now at hand for me to resign all cares and honors to you alone. I once received this empire from heaven, and the ancient Kings likewise received theirs. But now, by heaven’s nod, I hand it to you: heaven must be obeyed. This will favor you if you favor your own people; if you consult, I say, the safety, convenience, and tranquility of your subjects. The burden of the empire's affairs is heavy, I do not deny it, and the cares are infinite. Yet each has its own proper measure and fittingness, which we call the **Mean**, which is impatient of all excess and deficiency. Hold this, therefore: weigh and measure all things by this scale if you wish your people to be happy and flourishing. But if you neglect my counsel and depart from the middle path of which I spoke, disasters will undoubtedly rush in, one after another; and all this region contained within the four seas, distressed by hunger and want, will pay the penalty for your sin. But even now I warn you, that you also will pay, and indeed most heavily; and you shall be stripped forever of the dignity conferred from heaven.*

**Shun** <note>original: *Xun*</note> also gave these final precepts in words of this kind to **Yu**, his successor, to whom he similarly resigned the Empire after he had successfully administered it alone for fifty years. He also had a son; yet, following the example of his predecessor, he judged that the Empire was owed to the excellent wisdom and greatest merits of **Yu** himself, who had channeled the immense floods of water into the sea. Furthermore, although **Yu**, following in the footsteps of both, had similarly neglected his son and intended the Empire for the petty king **Yi** <note>original: *Ye*</note>, who was then most celebrated for the fame of his wisdom; nevertheless, since the virtue of his own son—who was truly worthy of empire—was added to the merits of his father, both the people and the nobles desired him to rule when the father died. Because the Imperial dignity then passed to sons and grandsons, the name of "founder" is attributed to **Yu** himself; the founder, I say, of the first Imperial family called the **Xia** <note>original: *Hia*</note>, which, in the space of 458 years, counted 17 Emperors succeeding in order.

All others being passed over in silence, the following paragraph deals with **Cheng Tang** <note>original: *Chim tam*</note>, the founder and Prince of the **Shang** <note>original: *Xam*</note> family, the second among the Imperial families. But before we follow the text, it is helpful here to set forth what is reported in the *Book of Documents* <note>original: *Xu kim*</note> concerning the last Emperor of the preceding family, called **Jie** <note>original: *Kie*</note>; for in this way, the things brought forward in our text will be better understood. Especially illustrious is the passage concerning the impious Prince **Jie**, which the prime minister of the empire and brother of the Emperor **Wu Wang** <note>original: *Vu vam*</note>, the **Duke of Zhou** <note>original: *Cheu*</note>, cites in an oration held before him, where he says:

> I have heard a saying of the Ancients which goes thus: The Supreme Emperor of Heaven, while he directs men peacefully and quietly, does not do this through the reception of any physical voice, but the heart of man receives quiet...

...that quiet and calm direction, and works so fervently and without interruption: And this internal direction of the Supreme Emperor of Heaven <note>The Latin *supremi cœli Imperatoris* refers to the Chinese concept of *Shangdi* or the personified Heaven, which the Jesuit translators often equated with the Christian God.</note>, since it is granted by heaven and equally bestowed upon all, in what way could King **Jie** <note>original: *Kie*</note> have been excluded from it? But indeed, King **Jie** had buried (that is, utterly ruined) that natural goodness of the heart, and he himself did not wish to follow that silent and calm direction of the Heavenly Emperor. Nevertheless, the Supreme Emperor directed him earnestly and truly, but King **Jie** truly and constantly fled from and rejected Him. Yet the Supreme Emperor still looked upon him and had not yet utterly rejected him, but sent down calamities and wonders upon him to manifest His counsel and intention, just as if He were striking King **Jie** with a crash of thunder (*so that he might return to his senses*). But King **Jie** by no means knew how to fear or be moved, nor did he wish to reverently utilize the will and favor of the Supreme Emperor, but instead rushed into crimes and unbridled luxury. And although he occasionally uttered certain insulting and deceptive words—( *or as others say* ) feigned words like those of one repenting—nevertheless Heaven took no account of such words, and finally despised hearing them and destroyed his great Empire, sending down from on high the well-deserved punishments. And so, the Imperial **Xia** <note>original: *Hia*</note> family came to an end.

*So says **Zhou** <note>likely referring to the Duke of Zhou or a commentator on the Book of Documents</note> according to the exposition of the non-Christian interpreters, especially **Cai Shen** <note>original: *çai xin*, a famous Song dynasty commentator</note>. However, the pious Prince **Tang** <note>original: *Tam*</note>, who was over eighty years old, was urged daily by the people and the lesser lords to finally release them and his own people from the bitter and long-lasting yoke of the most impious King **Jie**. He himself, however, as one fearing* <margin>A</margin> *the Supreme Deity and His mandate, and thus not daring to disobey Him, remained perplexed and uncertain about what he should do. Therefore, **Zhong Hui** <note>original: *Chum hoei*, a minister to Tang</note> and others who were the Prince's advisors, reassured him concerning the will of Heaven:* <margin>B</margin> *namely, that the people are created by Heaven with their own passions, and if there is no one to rule them, they will bring ruin upon themselves and the Empire through sedition. Furthermore, the power of reasoning, as well as the* <margin>C</margin> *talents of judgment and intellect in other mortals, come from Heaven; and moreover, by Heaven’s grace, he was* <margin>D</margin> *granted fortitude of soul and wisdom, by which he might be able to liberate the Empire from the danger of ruin now imminently threatening. Therefore, let him obey* <margin>E</margin> *the will of Heaven. They knew indeed that those who treat the spirits impiously* <margin>F &</margin> *and the people cruelly are not long preserved by Heaven; but those who venerate* <margin>G</margin> *the laws of Heaven, will [be preserved] eternally.*

# CHINESE KNOWLEDGE

...to preserve the favorable will of Heaven <note>original: *cœli voluntatem*; this refers to the "Mandate of Heaven" (*Tianming*), the divine right to rule based on virtue</note> toward oneself. The impious **Jie** <note>original: *Kie*; the last ruler of the Xia dynasty, traditionally depicted as a tyrant</note> refused to subject himself to this will **H**, and thus he accumulated crime upon crime through a notable madness. He wished to deceive Heaven, rashly boasting to the people that Heaven’s favor toward him would never fail; he even asserted that he would only cease to rule when the Sun in the sky ceased to exist. Undoubtedly by the decree of an avenging Heaven, both **I** he himself and his family **K** <note>The Xia dynasty</note> now seem destined for destruction. He was not ignorant of the fact that Heaven conferred the Empire upon his family not out of some private **L** affection or favor, **M** but only in consideration of virtue: specifically, that it is a unique and purest virtue alone which attracts the favorable will of Heaven **N** toward a ruler. From that time, everyone congratulated the victorious and avenging Family <note>The Shang dynasty, led by Tang</note> for the peace now established and the happiness received from Heaven. In turn, the Royal house itself also congratulates its own people; for just as a small infant is watched over by its mother, so too are the people **O** looked upon and protected by the kind eyes of Heaven. They are surely meant to be blessed for a long time, unless through new crimes they themselves **P** cut short their desired years of life and summon calamities. Such disasters do not arise from any other source than the crimes of men; for Heaven inflicts them so that **Q** crimes may be made manifest. Thus, since it is difficult for anyone to escape those evils which they voluntarily bring upon themselves through **R** their own crimes, it is necessary that we devote ourselves to virtue and not slide back into sin—especially since Heaven itself warns us again and again with new wonders and calls us back to a fruitful life, so that we might **S** conduct ourselves in this manner.

**M** <margin>It is not that Heaven favored my Shang family <note>original: *Familiæ Xam*</note> for private reasons: Heaven only helps those who possess pure virtue.</margin>
**N** <margin>Those who possess a unique and pure virtue can receive the heart and will of Heaven into themselves and obtain the clear Mandate of Heaven.</margin>

**P** <margin>Heaven contemplates the subject people in their entirety: of those to whom it grants years, some are long-lasting and others are not: but it is not that Heaven has shortened the years of the people, but rather there are those among the people who have cut off their own lives through their crimes.</margin>
**Q** <margin>The reason and law of Heaven is to bless the upright and cast down the wicked: therefore, it sends calamities upon the Xia family to make their crimes public to the world.</margin>
**R** <margin>One may escape the calamities that Heaven inflicts: but those calamities which a man fashions for himself through his own crimes, he cannot evade.</margin>
**S** <margin>If the people do not follow virtue nor subject themselves to the correction of their crimes, Heaven certainly warns them through portents to rectify their minds.</margin>

# BOOK THREE

...[Tang] took up the empire, compelled by the great consensus and enthusiasm of the people and the lords <note>original: *satraparum*; likely referring to the feudal lords or provincial governors of ancient China</note>. Returning now to the court located in **Henan** province, there, in a vast and highly celebrated assembly of the whole Empire and all the people, he delivered the following speech (called the ***Tang gao*** <note>The *Tang gao* or "Announcement of Tang" is a famous chapter in the *Classic of History* or *Shujing*</note>). In this speech, giving an account of his actions before the Supreme Emperor of the Heavens, he began thus:

"O all you inhabitants of every land, hear clearly and understand this, the warning of me, a single man: From what source do you think the nature of mortals has flowed, endowed as it is with the five virtues: **filial piety, justice, prudence, sincerity, and integrity**? <note>original: *pietate, justitiâ, prudentiâ, fide, honestate*; these are the *Wuchang* or Five Constant Virtues of Confucian thought</note>. From the beginning, surely, it was that alone, the August and Supreme Emperor <note>original: *supremus (caeli) Imperator*; a translation of *Shangdi*, the "High Sovereign" or "Lord-on-High"</note>, who, when he began to create the human race, bestowed from Heaven that nature which is the most perfect **standard of the Mean** <note>original: *medii rectissima norma*; referring to the *Zhongyong* or Doctrine of the Mean</note> upon the people subject to him. If the people obey their nature, so richly endowed with gifts, it will follow that this nature—which is implanted identically in everyone—shall remain immutable. However, so that the people may lead their lives peacefully and placidly according to that heavenly standard, they depend primarily on the person of the King. He must constantly encourage his subjects through his own example, through teaching, and through righteous administration to observe that standard," etc.

Finally, rendering an account of his actions before Heaven, he continues: "I, the little one, **Li**—<note>The King calls himself a 'little child' out of submission and modesty, though he was an old man of eighty-seven; he also uses his humble, personal name, **Li**</note>—dare to offer a bull as a black-colored sacrifice <note>original: *nigri coloris hostiam taurum*; black was the ritual color associated with the Shang dynasty</note>. I dare also, openly and clearly, to give the reason for my actions before the thrice-greatest and most august King and Emperor of the Heavens—or, as the two *Colai* <note>original: *Colai*; the *Gelao* or Grand Secretaries of the imperial court</note> and the Chinese dictionaries explain: before the spirit of the most august Heaven and the all-encompassing Earth.

Grave and manifold were the sins committed against Heaven by the Emperor of the **Xia** <note>original: *Hia*; the previous dynasty</note> family. I did not dare to pardon him or to withhold just punishment. I would not dare to hide wise and deserving men—those subjects and followers so dear to the Supreme Emperor of the Heavens—nor would I fail to make their virtues and merits known. This is especially true since they are each clearly visible in the heart of the Supreme Emperor." <note>The scholar **Zhu Xi** <note>original: *Chu hi*; the famous Neo-Confucian philosopher</note> explains these words thus: Heaven knows all things, good and evil, as if it held every single sin noted and numbered in its proper order. It truly seems to be so.</note> "If you possess any good, it is already placed within the heart and mind of the Supreme Emperor. If I commit any evil, this likewise resides in the heart and mind of the Supreme Emperor."

[The speech of King Tang continues]: "If I myself, through human frailty, have committed some crime, I now humbly beseech and entreat that it not be held against my subjects, nor should all my territories bear the blame. Let the Supreme Emperor punish me alone, for I alone am at fault. But if anyone from all my territories should ever transgress, then let those offenses be attributed to my person alone." ...I undertake to accept [responsibility]: nor do I refuse any punishments, as I who am the one most guilty of all, since by my bad example and bad administration I provided the occasion for sinning to everyone.

*And thus far spoke King Tang <note>original: "Chim tam Rex"; referring to Cheng Tang, the founder of the Shang dynasty</note> according to the explanation of the Chancellor <note>original: "Colai"; likely referring to the title Ge-lao, or Grand Secretary</note>. Truly, how great was the religious zeal of this same Prince toward Heaven, or the Supreme Lord of Heaven <note>original: "supremum cæli Dominum"; a reference to Shangdi</note>, joined with a remarkable piety toward his own people, is wonderfully confirmed by this primary example which may be added here from the annals—an event which even today is celebrated in the writings and speeches of everyone. We also repeatedly assert this in speech and writing to persuade this political nation <note>The Jesuit authors are referring to the Chinese people, whom they often praised for their sophisticated civil society</note> that it was not unworthy of divine and infinite majesty to become man, and a spontaneous victim for the eternal salvation of the human race.*

For seven years (says the text) a great drought persisted. (Whether this was the Egyptian famine which the Holy Scriptures testify prevailed in the whole world in Genesis 41, we leave for chronologists to discuss.) He who was the prefect of Astronomical matters <note>The Royal Astronomer or Court Astrologer</note> indicated to the King that Heaven must be appeased no longer with the blood of calves or sheep (as was the custom), but only with human blood, if indeed a final remedy for such great evils was sought. To him the King replied:

> I, he said, wish to entreat Heaven for the safety and life of my people. But if, by taking this away from them, I shed human blood, I would surely be acting against myself. Rather, so that the safety of my people may be provided for, let me alone be the victim.

Without delay: intending to make a sacrifice of himself to Heaven, he first hid himself in a more secret place, according to custom, and fasted for three days; then, though he was now more than ninety years old, he ordered the venerable white hair of his head and likewise his beard to be shaved, and his nails to be clipped—indications, of course, of the deepest mourning. He then commanded a chariot with two white horses (this being the color of those in mourning) to be yoked. He himself, dressed in sheepskins, climbed into the chariot; and with the whole court following with equal grief, he hastened to the place called *Sanglin* <note>original: "Sam lin"; the "Mulberry Grove," a site of ritual significance</note> (that is, the grove of mulberry trees). Here, about to become a victim to Heaven for the safety of his people and Empire, he climbed a hill; he ascended, however, crawling on his hands and feet (as some write) so that he might appear more like a sacrificial victim. Then, lifting his eyes to heaven, he prayed as a suppliant that the safety and life of the whole people should not come into danger on account of his own personal defects in ruling. Then, being ready to ascribe to himself alone whatever sin might have occurred, and prepared for any punishments, he questioned Heaven concerning six matters in particular (which are contained in 24 characters):

1. Whether perhaps his method of governing lacked due moderation and equity? 
2. Whether his subjects were failing in their duty? 
3. Whether the expenses for the Palace and things relating to it were immoderate? 
4. Whether sin was being committed by the women of his harem through luxury of dress and neglect of modesty? 
5. Whether bribes reigned in judgments, or likewise fraud and avarice in trade? 
6. Whether in Festivals and Songs occasion was given for any detraction or corruption of morals?

All writers record a matter truly worthy of admiration: that the pious Prince had scarcely finished speaking...

*These events occurred in the 38th year of the 16th cycle, that is, in the year 1756 before the era of Christ; specifically in the seventh year of King Tang's <note>original: "Chim tam"</note> reign, in the 94th year of his age, and seven years before his death. This dual speech of so merciful and pious a Prince—delivered and written down before all the people more than a hundred years before Moses and the tables of the law, and so many years before Christ—does it not clearly testify how strongly the law of nature and the knowledge and veneration of the Supreme Deity <note>original: "supremi Numinis"</note> flourished at that time in this furthest Orient? Then, he ordered the guards and prisons to be opened, and those accused of crimes to be released.
