...towards all those who were most highly commended for their faith, integrity, and wisdom. Thus, every best man was then the wealthiest; provided and adorned, I say, with the most ample honors and the most ample estate.

§. 2. These are the words of the Emperor King Wu <note>original: "Vu vam"; King Wu was the founder of the Zhou Dynasty (c. 1046 BC). He is a central figure in Confucian political philosophy</note>: "Although," he says, "there are many quite closely related to the Shang <note>original: "Xam"</note> family, to whom all the chief offices and dignities seem to be owed by a certain right of royal lineage and primary nobility: nevertheless, since most of them are not to be compared with others—and those most numerous—from our own Zhou <note>original: "Cheu"</note> family, men of proven faith, integrity, and wisdom; it is certain to me that I should employ these rather than those as my counselors and administrators of my affairs. Moreover, provided with the protection of so many excellent men, if I nevertheless fail myself, and do not exact punishment from the impious Zhou <note>This refers to King Zhou of Shang, the tyrannical last ruler of the previous dynasty, whose name happened to be phonetically similar to the new dynasty, Zhou</note>, nor suppress the insolence and license of his followers as is right; then certainly I shall be held guilty not only of a single instance of laziness and sluggishness: but also, whatever my multitude of subjects may sin, they will attribute it most especially to me alone; and the stains and damages of the whole body will most justly fall upon my head alone." <note>This reflects the "Mandate of Heaven" concept, where the Emperor is personally responsible for the moral and physical welfare of the state</note>

§. 3. Therefore, since he was held by such wholesome care and fear, and was not unaware of how much vice had crept into the Commonwealth, before all things he placed the greatest zeal and vigilance in recalling weights and measures to equity and their ancient standard. He likewise examined all laws and constitutions, both those containing the duties, rites, and rights of citizens, and those containing the matters and arts of Music. He also recalled to the court and to their former dignity, and raised up, the Prefects of Cities and Provinces who had been cast down and afflicted under the impious Zhou; and thus, with affairs excellently renewed and established, the administration of the four regions—that is, the whole Empire—followed a most desired course.

§. 4. The same man restored the provincial lordships <note>original: "satrapias"</note> extinguished by the impious Zhou, and restored them to their legitimate lords. He recalled and established to be perpetuated the ancient and noble lineages of the Ancient Princes—now cut off and nearly deleted—arising from the most noble stock of the Yellow Emperor <note>original: "Hoam ti"; the legendary ancestor of the Chinese people</note>, the founder of the Chinese Monarchy; as well as those of the Legislators, namely Yao, Shun <note>original: "Xun"</note>, and Yu, and those originating from the Princes of the immediately preceding Shang <note>original: "Xam"</note> family. He enriched the descendants of all these, adorned with dynasties, also with an ample estate; having also recalled the various titles of dignity: Marquis, Duke, Count, Viscount, and Baron <note>original: "Heu, Cum, Pe, çu, Nan"; these are the five ranks of Zhou nobility: Hou, Gong, Bo, Zi, and Nan</note>; doing this primarily, and vehemently desiring, that such illustrious progeny of the greatest men should not only themselves flourish for as long as possible, but also preserve the memory of their ancestors with the greatest splendor, and rightly and piously with the customary duties and parental offerings <note>This refers to the crucial Confucian practice of ancestral veneration</note>; so that even when parents were dead, the piety and observance of the sons might always live and endure. Furthermore, he raised up and brought to the administration of the Commonwealth men lying low and hiding, [who were distinguished] by their virtue...

# BOOK THREE

...and distinguished in wisdom; but who, of their own accord, had renounced their status during the earlier storm of the disturbed Empire, cautiously fleeing to the leisure of private life as if to a harbor. When the affairs of the entire Empire had been established in this excellent manner, the people submitted themselves willingly and from the heart; they joined their own desires and efforts with those of the best Prince all the more readily because they realized how happily they now harmonized with him, as if they were most obedient limbs joined to a beloved head.

f. 8. p. 1. §. 1. Finally, there were three matters which the mentioned Emperor <note>King Wu of Zhou</note> held very close to his heart regarding the governance of his people, and which he considered to be of great weight and importance: First, the grain supply <note>original: "annona"; refers to the state's responsibility to ensure food security</note> for his subjects, so that there would always be an abundance of those things which are commonly necessary to sustain life. Second, funerals and burial rites, so that they might be performed with the proper ritual and manner. Third, the ancestral rites <note>original: "Parentalia"; the author uses the Roman term for festivals honoring deceased parents to describe Chinese ancestor worship</note>, or funeral honors and certain solemn offerings usually presented at fixed times of the year in memory of deceased parents and ancestors. By these rituals, children were reminded of the gratitude, piety, and respect they owed to their parents who were still living, as they saw such careful and anxious devotion practiced toward those ancestors already long dead.

§. 2. Having briefly explained the method of governing held by Yao and Shun <note>original: "Xun"</note>, the two Lawgivers of the nation, as well as Yu, Tang <note>original: "Tam"</note>, and Wu <note>original: "Vu"</note>—the founders of the three royal dynasties <note>original: "familiarum"; the Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties</note> who held supreme authority for so many centuries—the authors finally conclude that these rulers differed slightly from one another according to the requirements of their times. Nevertheless, in their zeal and skill for protecting their people and for preserving and expanding the Empire, and in the very substance of their deeds, they were very much alike. They summarize this similarity through four characters <note>original: "litteris"</note> which express four royal virtues. They speak thus:

If a Prince is munificent toward his people and possesses a great and liberal soul—protecting all like Heaven and sustaining all like the Earth, while doing nothing with cruelty, greed, or meanness—then he will win over everyone; that is, he will gain the admiration, the love, the efforts, and the goodwill of all. 

If he preserves faith and truth, remaining always a stranger to all pretense, lies, and fraud, then his subjects will lean upon him without any fear or hesitation, committing themselves and their affairs to the incorruptible faith of the Prince. 

If he is vigilant, industrious, and diligent in averting public harms and procuring the benefits of his people, and if he never neglects or despises anything, then he will achieve a happy outcome and the perfection of whatever affairs he undertakes; in turn, his most loving subjects will industriously, diligently, and constantly complete whatever public work might happen to be commanded. 

In exacting punishments and conferring rewards, if he is upright and fair to all, and grants nothing to private hatred or personal love, then the subjects will rejoice, and will act toward the most just Prince in all matters with eagerness and promptness...

<summary>This page describes the stabilization of the Zhou dynasty through the recruitment of wise recluses and the establishment of state priorities: food security, funeral rites, and ancestor worship. It concludes by defining the four essential virtues of a Confucian ruler: generosity, honesty, diligence, and justice.</summary>

# CHINESE WISDOM

...they will act in accordance. These indeed were the arts of the five mentioned Princes, these the sinews and the foundations by which they supported the weight of so great an Empire so successfully and for so long. Whatever has been recorded from the seventh leaf up to this point by the disciples of *Confucius* was recorded specifically for this purpose: so that posterity would know that the doctrine of their master, which they wished to spread as much as possible, did not differ at all from the decrees and institutions of the ancient Legislators, *Yao* and *Shun*, and the Kings.

§. 3. The disciple *Zi Zhang* <note>Latin: *çu cham*</note> questioned *Confucius*, saying: "By what means can someone rightly govern the State?" *Confucius* replied: "He who values five good things and removes four evils will be able to govern the State rightly and successfully." *Zi Zhang* spoke again: "What are these five good things?" *Confucius* replied: "Let the Governor of the State be beneficial, and yet spend or consume nothing. Let him be a burden to his subjects, and yet not be hated. Let him desire, and yet not seek with greed. Let him be great, let him be blessed and flourishing; and yet let him not be carried away by pride and arrogance. Let him be severe and dignified; and yet let him not be harsh and ferocious."

P. 2. §. I. *Zi Zhang*, not fully understanding the Master’s brief response, said: "What, I pray, does it mean to be 'beneficial and yet spend nothing'?" *Confucius* replied: "To constantly follow and favor those things and arts which are profitable to the subjects—namely, *Commerce* and *Agriculture*, and others of this kind—and thus to procure their profit; skillfully protecting and preserving those common benefits of heaven and earth. Through this, it eventually happens that there is a great cheapness of grain <note>original: "annonae vilitas"; referring to low prices resulting from a surplus food supply</note> and an abundance of things everywhere. Is this not truly being beneficial and yet spending nothing of either private or public wealth? Similarly, if you make a selection of those who are capable of bearing labor and burdens, and burden only those; if you have, I say, a just and accurate account of place, time, age, and the strength and resources of each person whenever some burden or public work is to be commanded; who then will hate either the commands or the commander? To crave what belongs to another is wicked and shameful; but indeed, if you desire or seek true virtue, and if you successfully obtain that true virtue so laudably sought and then fulfill all its requirements, how could you be considered viciously greedy? If a Prince, among those states so fertile with favoring fortune, remains true to himself and does not pay great attention to the number of his followers, whether many or few—as if he would scorn the latter and yield something to the former; and again, if he does not pay great attention to whether the things he must perform are of great or small importance, but treats the smallest and largest matters with almost equal care; and if there is no man, however humble and lowly in condition, whom he dares to hold in contempt; he who commands himself and restrains himself in this way, is he not, even in great peace and wealth..."

<summary>This page contains a dialogue between Confucius and his disciple Zi Zhang concerning the "Five Goods" of governance, emphasizing how a ruler can benefit the people through economic support and fair labor practices without depleting the state's resources.</summary>

...[with abundan]ce and glory, he becomes blessed and flourishing; yet will he not be carried away by pride? Finally, dignity and severity, if they lack proper measure, will easily degenerate into a hateful harshness and ferocity. But if a Prince, free from all such passions, remains content with a certain moderation—for example, if he wears his clothes and cap with gravity and decency; if he imbues his very face and eyes with a certain modesty and reverence; if in every movement, gesture, and posture of his body he preserves decorum—without a doubt, all people will gaze upon him and revere him with a truly singular respect. And is this not to be severe and dignified, and yet not harsh and ferocious?

§. 2. *Zi Zhang* <note>Latin: *çu cham*</note> asks again: "What are the four evils that anyone who governs the State <note>Latin: *Rempublicam*</note> ought to avoid and remove from himself?" Confucius responds: "Not to teach the subjects accurately whatever pertains to public law and the duty of individuals; and yet, if by chance they should fail on any given day, to punish the wretches on the spot and kill them quite mercilessly—this is truly called exercising tyranny. When some public work or service is to be demanded, not to warn the subjects beforehand or prepare them in some way so that things may be done more conveniently and orderly, but instead to overwhelm the wretches suddenly and wish to see the prescribed work finished and perfected in the blink of an eye, mercilessly urging the work and severely punishing all delays—this is truly called cruel violence. To order public works for the subjects hesitantly and coldly, but then, with a sudden acceleration, to shorten the previously established time frame, demanding the same things with fierce and inexorable severity—this is deservedly said to be like a bandit <note>Latin: *latrocinantis instar*</note>, who, as if from an ambush, oppresses the unwary and thus brings harm to his own people. Finally, to be stingy and illiberal; for example, to behave in a certain way when something must be given to others—such as when the wages of soldiers must be paid, the fair price of work to laborers, or when ranks and honors are to be conferred on others—showing stinginess and greed with a hand that is slow and unwilling, appearing now like one offering a gift and then like one demanding it back even as he gives it. Although what each person is legally owed is eventually given, because it is given in such a way that it seems more extorted than granted, it does not even deserve thanks, whereas if it had been given with a liberal mind, it would have been like a great gift. Thus, this is not the way a Prince acts, but he is deservedly called a petty official of the lowest sort for the public treasury <note>Latin: *ærarii publici*</note>."

# CHINESE KNOWLEDGE

...the light of reason implanted by heaven in mortals, by which all the affairs of one's life should be ordered, so that he may flee what is perverse and pursue what is right. A man of this kind <note>One who ignores this inner reason</note> will surely find no path to becoming honest and wise; instead, he will commit many things unworthy of a human being while he chases after what is illicit or beyond his strength, or succumbs to those evils which he tries in vain to escape.

§. 2. Whoever is ignorant of the proper measure of each thing, as well as the civil rites and duties <note>This refers to *Li*, the traditional Chinese system of ritual and social propriety</note>—which are the bonds of human society and the unique honor and strength of every person—will have no means by which to stand tall or emerge as a man of gravity and constancy, useful to himself and others. For he will constantly slip, drift in uncertainty, and eventually lose even that virtue which he might have happened to acquire.

§. 3. The tongue is the index of the heart; and it is not rare for a short speech to betray whatever lies hidden within the whole man. Therefore, whoever does not understand the speech of men—so as to aptly discern how rightly or wrongly something is said—will have no way to truly know men themselves: specifically their errors, character, intentions, and abilities.

Furthermore, whoever has properly understood these three—namely, the providence of heaven <note>The concept of *Ming*, often translated as Fate or the Mandate of Heaven</note>, the proper measure of things, and finally men themselves—and lives in such a way that his life and morals correspond to this knowledge; he may truly be said to have fulfilled all the parts of a rare sage, one who stands far above the common crowd.

*And here at last is the end of the three books of Chinese Knowledge <note>original: "Scientiæ Sinicæ"</note>, whose explanation, translated from Chinese into Latin through the singular zeal and shared labor of four companions <note>Referring to the Jesuit missionaries Philippe Couplet, Prospero Intorcetta, Christian Herdtrich, and François de Rougemont</note>, was made possible by the leisure forced upon those who have kept us now in our fourth year of exile in the Province of Canton since 1686. They compelled us, very much against our will, to cease from propagating that far more sublime doctrine <note>A reference to the Christian Gospel</note> which is the one light of the world, and without which all science and learning is mere darkness and ignorance. Furthermore, the author of these three books is considered to be Confucius, although they contain many sayings either uttered by his disciples or by philosophers and princes contemporary to him, or even pronounced by the first Kings of the nation and ancient sages. Some of these lived six hundred years before Confucius himself—and thus before the foundations of the city of Rome; others a thousand years before; and some even about one thousand seven hundred years before. That the Chinese <note>original: "Sinas"</note> are no less worthy of respect than other nations, those will easily judge who consider with an open mind the industry, faith, and diligence of this people, who have been accustomed to entrust their affairs to the monuments of their literature from every past age. They have done this through their sixty-year periods <note>The sexagenary cycle used in the Chinese calendar</note>, as will be clear from the Chronological Table which it has pleased us to annex to this work, along with a genealogical table of the three princely families who are repeatedly mentioned in the aforementioned books. In our version of the Chinese Knowledge, however, we have deliberately condensed many things; and although at times the explanation may seem more copious, let the reader know that this is by no means the translator's invention...*

# BOOK THREE. 159

In richness and abundance, the commentary of the Grand Secretary <note>original: "Cham Colai." This refers to Zhang Juzheng (1525–1582), a Ming dynasty Grand Secretary whose commentaries were the primary source for the Jesuit translations</note>, whom we chiefly follow, is truly comparable. As has been indicated elsewhere, we consistently follow in his footsteps. Therefore, if one sets aside those things which we have interspersed from other authors of the same nation for the sake of scholarship or clarity, the remainder belongs to our Interpreter. The entire paraphrase, I say, belongs to this one Grand Secretary; all the sentiments are his. No one should suspect them of belonging to a European man—even though they are expressed in a European language and style, and sometimes even through the sentiments and words of European philosophers.

I do not deny, however, that there are not a few things which might rightly be considered common, if not to say frivolous; these would undoubtedly have been omitted if we had labored solely for the amusement of Europeans. But we have already sufficiently and eloquently indicated at the very threshold of this work <note>In the preface or prolegomena</note> that these things are written primarily for those who are about to enter this vineyard of Christ <note>A common Jesuit metaphor for the mission fields in China</note> and who, we hope, will henceforth labor within it. 

Yet it is also right for us to remember that not all mortals share the same palate; many things which Europeans might find distasteful are delicacies to this nation. What is more unpleasant to a European than a hot drink? <note>A reference to tea, which was still a novelty or strange custom to many in Europe at the time of publication in 1687</note> Yet the Chinese take such delight in this that they do not abstain from it even during the summer days. Our ears generally reject Chinese music; yet, in turn, that "discordant harmony" <note>original: "discors illa vocum concordia." Referring to European polyphony, which sounded chaotic to ears accustomed to the monophonic melodies of Chinese music</note> of our voices, if it does not outright offend them, certainly offers them little delight. Thus, in much the same way regarding speech and thought, something may have its own charm and grace in China which might provoke laughter or even annoyance in Europe. However the matter stands, a fair reader cannot fail to admit that there are many things here which deserve their own value even now in Europe. Nor will he doubt that the administration of this most ancient Monarchy was excellent whenever those precepts taught here—whether for living piously and rightly or for governing the Kingdom properly—were in full force.

There now follows the fourth book of Chinese Knowledge, called *Mem çu* <note>Mencius (372–289 BC)</note>, the second Philosopher of the Chinese, who lived one century after Confucius. His work consists of seven parts or chapters; if you look at the moral aspect, it is entirely equal to the Confucian work, and even superior in a certain way if you consider only the genius, abundance, and eloquence of the author. However, in the integrity of doctrine, that ancient simplicity, and a certain secret sublimity which the Chinese so greatly admire and praise in their Confucius, Mencius must rightly be placed second. Therefore, God willing, we shall bring Mencius forth into the European light, provided we understand that Confucius has obtained his own place and approval in this most learned age and most ample theater of all sciences.

### End of Book Three of the Analects.

#### From where Chinese Chronology takes its beginning.

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'Q'. Within the letter 'Q' is a scene featuring a figure on horseback, possibly a monarch or military figure, set against a background of classical architecture including columns and a cityscape.</image-desc>

**THOSE WHO** *have written the Annals of the Chinese [Sinae] almost all begin from him who was the Founder of the Empire, called Fohi <note>Fuxi, the first of the Three Sovereigns in Chinese mythology</note>. He, moreover, began to rule in the year 2952 before Christ. However, the things which some historians mention as having happened before the times of the aforementioned King Fohi are, for the most part, rejected as apocryphal and of no reliability, even by the Chinese commentators and more serious historians themselves. Certainly, Tai su <note>original: "Tai su"; likely referring to Sima Qian, known as the Taishigong or Grand Historian</note>, a writer of the highest authority, testifies in clear words that those things which occurred before the times of Xinnum <note>Shennong, the Divine Farmer</note>, the second Founder, are unknown to him. Also, the author of the Great Annals, which consist of nearly one hundred and fifty volumes, even though he relates those things which happened before the time of Fohi, nevertheless sufficiently suggests that he does not want anyone to place faith in them when he says that he himself does not believe everything that has reached the ears of posterity concerning those most remote times through no other testimony than that of popular rumor and its various forms; but that he believes the Kim <note>original: "Kim"; referring to the Jing or the Confucian Classics</note> books to be certainly authentic, and so there is no doubt in his mind that all writers ought to begin their history from the Founder Fohi himself. And not without merit, since most of those things which*

#### ON THE CHRONOLOGY OF THE CHINESE

*...recorded to have occurred before Fohi <note>Fuxi, the legendary first emperor of China</note>, they immediately appear to be somewhat fabulous at first sight. For they record that Heaven was created between the eleventh and twelfth hour of the night; and the Earth, truly, between the first and second hour of the night. That the first Man was created between the third and fourth in the morning; and Woman after midday between the third and fourth. Likewise, they say that first man (whom they call Puon cu <note>Pangu, the primeval giant in Chinese creation myths who separated heaven and earth</note>, and say is buried in the city of Yam cheu <note>Yangzhou</note> in the province of Nan kim <note>Nanjing</note>, or, as others say, in the province of Pe kim <note>Beijing</note> in the territory of the city of Ho kien <note>Hejian</note>) was born from sterile earth, and was equipped with an admirable knowledge of things, and held dominion over all; yet his origin is unknown. Finally, they tell that there were three Emperors: the first of heaven, the second of earth, and the third of men; and that the brothers of these succeeded one another for more than 49,000 years. After whom again another 35 families ruled in a continuous series for several thousands of years. Although the Chinese <note>original: "Sinae"</note> themselves, as I have said, reject all these things as false, I cannot deny—as a European man considering each point more studiously—that I know not what sparkle of ancient truth glimmers again amidst those fables, like a tiny sliver of very thin light in the midst of thick darkness. I affirm this all the more confidently because almost all fables have their origin in that which is not fabulous. Certainly, it is entirely believable to me that they received certain things from the grandsons of Noah <note>original: "Noëmi"</note> concerning the first creation of things, and how vigorous and long-lived the men of the first age were. When these things were then passed down, as if from hand to hand, to sons and grandsons, it was certainly prone for that ancient truth to be gradually worn away, as it were, or even corrupted by the addition of lies and fables. And indeed, the fact that they assign the creation of heaven and earth, sea and woman, to determined times, already clearly enough confesses that the World has not existed from eternity, as many of the Philosophers and Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher whose views on the eternity of the universe often conflicted with Christian doctrine</note> himself once* <meta>catchword: docuerunt: (taught:)</meta>

He argues that the existence of these timelines proves the Chinese did not believe in an eternal universe, aligning them more closely with Christian thought than with Aristotelian philosophy.</summary>

# PREFACE.

...they taught: and thus it is easy to conclude by reasoning here that the *Chinese* <note>original: "Sinenses"</note> knew of some supreme Divinity, by whom all these things were created at such fixed intervals of time. Furthermore, one may understand from this that they were not ignorant of the long-lived age of the first men <note>A reference to the Biblical patriarchs who lived hundreds of years; early European scholars were eager to find parallels in other cultures</note>, because they attribute eight or ten thousand years to some of their ancestors, and over ten thousand to others. And since *Chinese* interpreters say that one hundred should be counted for a thousand, or (as others say) that lunar months should be calculated instead of solar years, they cannot indeed be said to have wandered far from the truth in all matters. Add to this that the third *Chinese* Emperor, whose name was *Huangdi* <note>original: "Hoam ti"; the "Yellow Emperor," a legendary ancestor and cultural hero</note>, and who began to rule 256 years after *Fuxi* <note>original: "Fo hi"</note>, began that book which he ordered to be written *concerning pulses and the art of healing* <note>original: "de pulsibus & de medendi arte"; referring to the *Huangdi Neijing*, the foundational text of Chinese medicine</note> (for he was also a Prince and Master of the medical art) in such a way that he posed this question before all else: *Why, since the ancient men lived so vigorously and were so long-lived, is the life of the men of his own age so short?* Finally, it is evident from the older *Chinese* books that there was a man famous for wisdom, distinguished by his holding of office during the reign of the second *Shang* <note>original: "Xam"</note> dynasty, commonly named *Lao Peng* <note>original: "Lao pum"; referring to Pengzu, a legendary figure in Chinese culture said to have lived over 800 years</note>, whom *Confucius* also mentions, and who is said to have lived exactly seven hundred years.

Regarding the universal Deluge <note>The Great Flood, which the author is attempting to identify with the flood of Noah</note>, I have as yet found nothing certain or fully explored in the books and monuments of the *Chinese*; however, that they possessed some knowledge of this, however crude and confused, perhaps someone will prove from those books entitled *Xingli Dachuan* <note>original: "Sim li Ta ciuen"; *The Great Compendium of Nature and Principle*, a massive philosophical encyclopedia compiled during the Ming Dynasty</note>; these books were indeed published about three hundred years ago during the reign of the *Ming* <note>original: "Mim"</note> dynasty, when by order of the third Emperor <note>The Yongle Emperor, who reigned 1402–1424</note> (who began to rule in the year of Christ 1402) an assembly of several scholars was gathered, by whose labor those books I mentioned were compiled; but just as they are full of their own fictions, so too are they full of lies and errors: which is by no means...

### TO CHINESE CHRONOLOGY.

*At the very beginning* of the Chinese *annals, in the times of* Fuxi <note>original: "Fo hi"; the first of the Three Sovereigns of ancient China</note> *the Founder, there was both an extreme crudeness among mortals, and the mortals themselves were exceedingly rare. From where, however, the error of certain people flowed—who thought that mention is made of the universal* Great Flood <term>Diluvium: the biblical flood of Noah</term> *in the* Chinese *annals—is now plainly clear: for in the times of* Yao, *the fifth Emperor (or, if you count from* Fuxi, *the seventh), who began to rule in the year 2357 before* Christ, *in the 61st year of his reign and the 41st of the seventh Cycle, it is recorded that vast overflows of water occurred, which for a total of nine years inundated many lands far and wide. Therefore, since the said* flood *occurred very nearly six hundred years from the time of* Noah, *if we follow the* Vulgate <note>The Latin version of the Bible used by the Catholic Church</note> *computation, it was certainly easy for a* European *man—especially then, when the full system of the annals had not yet been examined—to fall into an error of this kind. But enough on this for now.*

*Otherwise, that the* Chinese *history, as it takes its beginning from* Fuxi *himself, the Founder of the nation, is worthy of being given credit, can be proven by several arguments. First, indeed, because even today among the* Chinese, *that monument is of the highest authority, written in characters (if indeed in characters, and not rather in small lines) which is called the* I Ching <note>original: "Ye kim"; the *Classic of Changes*, an ancient divination text</note>, *and is attributed to* Fuxi *himself by all posterity without any dissent. These 64 small lines or figures (each of which consists of six lines, partly whole and partly broken) were commented upon nearly 1,800 years later by King* Wen <note>original: "Ven vam"; King Wen of Zhou</note>, *and his son* Zhou <note>original: "Cheu cum"; the Duke of Zhou</note>, *and nearly 600 years after that by* Confucius *himself. Likewise, there is the "Little Herbal" of* Shennong <note>original: "Xin num"</note>, *the second Founder of the Chinese nation. Also the first books of the Founder of the Monarchy and simultaneously the Emperor* Huangdi <note>original: "Hoam ti"; the Yellow Emperor</note> *concerning the pulse and the art of medicine; the assistants and indeed the writers of this work were* Lei Gong, Qi Bo, *and* Sun <note>original: "Lui cum, Ki pe & Souen"; legendary figures in Chinese traditional medicine</note>, *three most noble Physicians, whose books are everywhere read accompanied by the commentaries of so many Interpreters even down to these times—*

<header>ON CHINESE CHRONOLOGY</header>

### SECTION II.

->By what rule of time, and by what number of years—as if a "golden number"—the Chinese use.<-

In order to construct a *Chinese Chronology that is as reliable as possible, we must proceed according to the Cycle or period of sixty years,* which is the sole standard for this people. *We begin this history from **Huangdi** <note>original: "Hoam ti"</note> himself, or from the year 2697 BC, when he perfected that Cycle.* For although *historians assign the years of the reigns of the six preceding Emperors fairly consistently even before the time of **Yao**, most do not calculate them using Cycles. There are a few exceptions who begin this method of counting with the third Emperor, **Huangdi**, because he completed the aforementioned Cycle that had been devised by **Fuxi** <note>original: "Fo hi"</note>. Be that as it may, it is clear that the Cycle was in use at least before the time of Emperor **Yao**, because all Chinese annals uniformly begin the first year of his reign not from the first year of a Cycle, but from the forty-first year, called *Jia-shen* <note>original: "Kia xin"</note>.* We must briefly explain what the Chinese mean by this sixty-year Cycle and how they use it.

It should be understood, then, that this *Cycle* is nothing more than a *period, or—if I may call it so—a certain "golden number"* <note>In the Western calendar, the "Golden Number" is a 19-year cycle used to determine the date of Easter; the author uses the term here to emphasize the cycle's importance and recurring nature</note> *of sixty years. Each year is designated by two characters that serve as names; once these are finished, they begin again from the start or "unity" until they have completed sixty, and so they begin again and again.* This is done in much the same way as when the first *Olympiad* <note>A four-year period used by the ancient Greeks for timekeeping</note>—or the four years of which it consisted—was finished, they moved on to another four years,

He notes that while earlier records exist, the consistent use of the cycle for dating began with Huangdi and was firmly established by the reign of Emperor Yao.</summary>

*...and so to the second Olympiad, and thus the Greeks proceeded to the third and fourth, yet with this difference: that since each Olympiad* <note>The Ancient Greeks measured time in four-year periods called Olympiads, named after the Olympic Games.</note> *consisted of only four years, making the occurrences of Olympiads quite frequent, the Greeks were careful to specify not only which year of an Olympiad an event occurred in, but also which number Olympiad it was, lest the system of time otherwise become entirely uncertain and confused. The Chinese, however, although they indicate the total count of the Cycles themselves in their summary calculations, do not trouble themselves to remind the reader of this repeatedly throughout the course of their history. They are content to indicate only the current year of the Cycle and its name; from that name, it is easily inferred which year of the Cycle it is. Since this period almost equals the lifespan of a man and comprises a sufficiently large series of sixty years, it seemed superfluous to repeatedly state which Cycle it was. Nonetheless, at the end of their annals, writers usually provide the exact total of all Cycles.*

*We, however, in this Chronological Synopsis* <note>original: "Synopsi Chronologica"</note>, *to be clearer, will also indicate which number each Cycle is—as we have read in some authors—and call it, so to speak, a Chinese Olympiad* <note>original: "Olympias Sinica"</note>. *Furthermore, each year has its own character, as I said, and its own name, which consists of only two letters* <note>The author refers to the Chinese characters as "letters." These pairs form the "Sexagenary Cycle" names still used today.</note>. *These letters consist partly of those twelve by which they distinguish the twelve hours of the day and night (for they count twelve hours, not twenty-four like us); and partly of ten other letters which we will call radicals or cardinals* <note>In modern terms, these are the Ten Heavenly Stems and Twelve Earthly Branches.</note>. *Now, they use both sets in such a way that they join the first hourly character to the first cardinal, then the second hourly to the second cardinal, and so on. When the count of ten is finished, they join the eleventh hourly character back to the first cardinal, the twelfth to the second, and then the first hourly character to the third cardinal...*

...the first, etc. and thus, since the hourly markers exceed the cardinal markers by two letters or numbers, it happens that any hourly marker is always joined to a different cardinal one. This continues until the total of sixty years is exhausted, at which point each marker returns to its first position and, so to speak, its original partnership. To make this more transparent for the reader, we provide here a Chinese Paradigm—or rather, a European one that corresponds to the Chinese. This is constructed from the first ten letters of the Alphabet repeating six times, and twelve numerical or hourly marks repeating five times.

### A PARADIGM OF THE SIXTY-YEAR CYCLE
### arranged from ten letters of the alphabet and twelve hourly
### numbers.

| A I. | B II. | C III. | D IV. | E V. | F VI. | G VII. | H VIII. | I IX. | K X. | 10. |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| A XI. | B XII. | C I. | D II. | E III. | F IV. | G V. | H VI. | I VII. | K VIII. | 20. |
| A IX. | B X. | C XI. | D XII. | E I. | F II. | G III. | H IV. | I V. | K VI. | 30. |
| A VII. | B VIII. | C IX. | D X. | E XI. | F XII. | G I. | H II. | I III. | K IV. | 40. |
| A V. | B VI. | C VII. | D VIII. | E IX. | F X. | G XI. | H XII. | I I. | K II. | 50. |
| A III. | B IV. | C V. | D VI. | E VII. | F VIII. | G IX. | H X. | I XI. | K XII. | 60. |

<note>The letters A through K represent the ten "Heavenly Stems" (Tiāngān), while the Roman numerals I through XII represent the twelve "Earthly Branches" (Dìzhī), which are also associated with the Chinese Zodiac signs and the twelve double-hours of the day.</note>

*And this is that "golden number" of the Chinese which we present here, called by them the* <term>lo xe hoa kia</term> <note>original: "lo xe hoa kia," modern Pinyin: Liùshí Huājiǎ, meaning the "Sixty-year cycle of Flowers."</note>, *which is to say, the "construction of sixty rotations." This number, like an ever-flowing river, always holds its own course regardless of whatever changes in affairs may occur. It rolls on through the very rises and falls of Royal families and will continue to roll, as the poet said, "gliding on for all eternity"* <note>original Latin: "in omne volubilis ævum," a quote from the Roman poet Horace, Epistles 1.2.43, describing a river that flows forever.</note>. *By this system, not only years, but also months, days, and hours are marked in their proper proportions throughout the entire Empire.*

*Therefore, so that this Chronology may be woven aptly and clearly...*

<header>PREFACE</header>

And so, that there may henceforth be no danger of error, that **Cycle** of sixty years which I mentioned ought to serve as our rule. For by this **Cycle**, **Historiographers** lead the **Reader** as if by the hand to the proper times of each **Emperor**, both the years in which he began his **Reign**, and those during which he held and administered it. If any discrepancy is observed among **Writers** when they calculate the years each man reigned, this **Cycle** quickly settles the dispute; and if any error has perhaps crept in by a flaw of time or the negligence of **Printers**, it corrects and emends it like an accurate **Censor** <note>In the Roman sense, a supervisor of public records and official accuracy.</note>. *The matter will be made clear by examples.*

It is a custom among the **Chinese** <note>original: *Sinas*</note> that the year in which an **Emperor** dies, even if he died in the first month of the year, is nevertheless ascribed entirely to the deceased; consequently, he who succeeds to the **Empire** does not begin the years of his own **Reign** until the first month of the following year. By contrast, the **Chinese** commonly count the year in which they were born as a whole year of their age, even when they were born on the very last day of the year. Thus we say that CHRIST was born in the sixth year of the **Emperor** of the **Han** family called **Hiao ngai ti** <note>Emperor Ai of Han (r. 7–1 BC). The author notes the name means "the obedient and merciful Emperor."</note>, even though he died in the sixth month of that same year—and thus five months before the **Savior** was born. For the **Savior** was actually born under his successor, who held the surname **Hiao pim ti** <note>Emperor Ping of Han (r. 1 BC – AD 6). The author translates this as "the obedient and peaceful Emperor."</note>. Since that **peaceful Prince** entered into his **Reign** in the ninth month of that year, it follows that the birth of the **King of Kings and the truly Peaceful One** fell in the third month of the new **Emperor's** rule, which corresponded exactly to the **European December**. This was the eleventh month of the sixth year, which is officially attributed entirely to the deceased **Emperor**. And this is also the reason why **Historiographers**, even though they mention those **Empe-**

<header>ON CHINESE CHRONOLOGY</header>

...of those whom it happened to have commanded for only a few days or months of the same year in which their predecessor died; nevertheless, they exclude them from the series of **Emperors**, since the year in which they began their rule cannot be ascribed to them.

Furthermore, it not infrequently happens that some **Emperors**, contrary to the custom already mentioned, have arbitrarily wanted to claim for themselves that year in which their predecessor died. This occurs especially when an old family has been extinguished and a new, victorious one begins its rule, whether they do this for the sake of capturing good fortune for their new dominion, or for other reasons, as has clearly occurred in our own times. For to the one who began the <term>Manchu-Chinese Monarchy</term> <note>The Qing Dynasty, established by the Manchus (historically referred to by Europeans as "Tartars").</note>, the Emperor called <term>Shunzhi</term> <note>The first Qing emperor to rule over China proper, r. 1644–1661.</note>, eighteen years are attributed, even though only seventeen ought to be granted if we were to strictly observe the custom and style mentioned before. But the **Manchu** <note>original: *Tartarus*</note> undoubtedly claimed for himself that year in which the last **Emperor** of the <term>Great Ming</term> <note>original: *Ta mim*</note> family, called <term>Chongzhen</term> <note>The last Ming emperor, who reigned 1627–1644.</note>, ended his life and his empire with a noose. Thus, when it is said that this **Chongzhen** reigned for seventeen years and the **Manchu** for eighteen, while the latter in truth reigned for only seventeen (and those incomplete), it is evident that two years are erroneously counted as a single one. 

I said "incomplete" because **Shunzhi** died in the second month of his eighteenth year, which, according to ancient custom, is attributed entirely to him, just as if his son <term>Kangxi</term> <note>The Kangxi Emperor (r. 1661–1722), known for his long and stable reign.</note> had not succeeded his father until the following year. Therefore, the **Reader** should not be disturbed if he happens to find in one **Writer** a certain name for the cyclic year in which someone began to reign, and in another writer, a different name. For what is added to the years of the predecessor, for example, is subtracted from the years of the successor. Consequently, the <term>Cycle</term> <note>The 60-year sexagenary cycle used in Chinese dating.</note>, revolving in its eternal course, always corrects this error and others of this kind. If this cycle is neglected, and one blindly calculates all the years—which are ascribed as more by some and fewer by others to each of the **Emperors**—one will wander far from a just calculation of years...

[xvij]
<header>PREFACE. xvij</header>

*...it is very easy to go astray; whereas, on the contrary, if one guides oneself by that rule of the <term>Cycles</term> <note>The Sexagenary Cycle, a 60-year repeating calendar system used in China to ensure chronological consistency.</note>, one will with no difficulty soon remove or balance out whatever might be superfluous or unequal.*

*Indeed, there will be no danger of error even when a gap of several years or some other discrepancy between writers occurs. For it has happened from time to time that while the previous family was not yet completely extinct (because its Emperor, though obscure and already defeated, was still surviving), the victor claimed for himself the years of the defeated contrary to custom. Thus, to the first Emperor of the twelfth family, called the <term>Sui</term> <note>The Sui Dynasty (581–618 AD), which reunified China.</note>, twenty-four years are attributed by some historians, when nevertheless only sixteen ought to be granted. This is because the Emperor of the preceding family, called the <term>Chen</term> <note>original: *Chin*; referring here to the Chen Dynasty (557–589 AD), the last of the Southern Dynasties.</note>, was not extinguished until the seventh year of the Sui Emperor's reign. Since writers do not subtract those seven years from the family that was defeated, and yet they assign the same years again to the victorious one, it was certainly very easy to make a mistake, unless the <term>Cycle</term> immediately showed that those years were being counted twice.*

*Furthermore, historians sometimes omit not only those Emperors who ruled for just a few days or months, but even those who held the Empire for several years. Thus, before the Emperor <term>Yao</term> <note>One of the legendary Five Emperors of China's golden age.</note>, it is said that <term>Zhi</term> <note>original: *Chi*; Emperor Zhi, who according to tradition reigned before his brother Yao.</note>, the son of the Emperor called <term>Ku</term> <note>original: *Tico*; Emperor Ku, one of the legendary Five Emperors.</note>, ruled for eight or nine years; but because he later degenerated and turned away from his father's examples and institutions, he was deprived of his Empire by the <term>Local Princes</term> <note>original: *Regulis*; referring to the feudal lords or regional rulers.</note>, and King <term>Yao</term> was substituted in his place; this is something that has happened not infrequently elsewhere as well.*

*And for these reasons, a not insignificant variety sometimes exists among writers, especially those who, following abridged histories, labor more over the weight of events and opinions than over that exact calculation of time. Hence, if a <term>European</term> <note>original: *Europæus*</note> researcher here consults only one or two writers, there will certainly be a danger that he will err in calculating the years; on the other hand, if he consults many, he will be able to reconcile them all with each other with almost no effort.*

It highlights the transition between the Chen and Sui dynasties as a specific example of where counting the same years for two different rulers can cause confusion.</summary>

<header>TO CHINESE CHRONOLOGY.</header>
<meta>catchword: very easy [original: proniß, short for pronissimum]</meta>

*But it will also be worthwhile to point out another matter here, which must be carefully observed by readers of the Chinese Annals: the Emperors of the fifth family, the <term>Han</term> <note>The Han Dynasty (206 BC – 220 AD), a golden age of Chinese history. The author refers to them as the "fifth family" according to his chronological numbering.</note>, established certain characters or rather "year-nicknames" <note>original: *cognomenta annorum*; these are known as <term>Nianhao</term> or era names.</note> composed of two characters, in addition to those which each year receives in its own order from the <term>Cycle</term>, as we said above. Furthermore, they imposed new names not only in the year in which each man began his reign, but also in other subsequent years at the whim of each Prince, leaving behind the previous nickname along with its years. In this way, they began to rule under new auspices, as it were, whether they did this for the sake of capturing some new good fortune, or for renewing the Empire in themselves and their kin. Nicknames of this kind among many are the following:* **eternal principle, eternal strength, tranquility, truth, joy, concord, sanctity, glory, happiness; likewise, supreme virtue, martial virtue, overflowing war <note>original: *mars inundans*; likely a reference to a period of great military expansion or the "Great Martial" era.</note>, supreme law, supreme peace, governance, harmony, prosperity, long-lived piety; heaven’s help, heaven’s law, heaven’s treasure, heaven’s work, heaven’s glory, heaven’s favor, heaven’s joy, heaven’s strength, heaven’s stability, heaven’s prosperity,** *etc. There were some, therefore, who changed the year-nickname ten times in proportion to the many years they ruled; in addition to this, some gave a single year to individual nicknames, others four, others six or seven, and finally others wanted all the years they ruled to be marked by one and the same nickname.*

*Since, therefore, historians—when recording the acts of any Emperor regarding the computation of time—primarily take account of that nickname which had been most recently established by him, counting the years of the reign from that point no differently than if he had actually begun his reign in that year, it is certainly very easy <note>original: *pronissimum*</note> for the reader to hesitate repeatedly, and even to err, in calculating the years of that reign,*

The author warns that this practice often confuses historians who attempt to calculate the total length of a reign based on these shifting labels.</summary>

# ->PREFACE<-

(although the <term>Cycle</term> <note>The 60-year sexagenary cycle used in China to track time continuously, regardless of who is on the throne.</note> itself retains its own number and undisturbed course) unless the reader is made aware of this practice. The whole matter will become very clear through an example. We say that **CHRIST** the Lord was born in the year *Han¹ Ngai² Ti³ Yuen⁴ Xeu⁵ Lh⁶ Nien⁷*, which is to say, in the second⁶ year⁷ of the era of "Original⁴ Longevity⁵" of Emperor³ Ngai² of the Han¹ family (the two characters *Yuen Xeu*, or "Original Longevity," are the nickname for the year), or rather, in the second year after the said nickname began to be used. Furthermore, this second year is actually the sixth year of the said Emperor’s reign, if we calculate the years according to the infallible counting of the Cycle.

But this Emperor established two nicknames for his reign: the first was *Kien pim*, meaning "establishing peace," <note>original: *Kien pim*, referring to the *Jianping* era (6–3 BC).</note> which nickname took its beginning with the very start of his rule and was in use for four years. After these had passed, he imposed that other name, *Yuen xeu*, which means "original longevity," <note>original: *Yuen xeu*, referring to the *Yuanshou* era (2 BC – 1 AD).</note> in the fifth year of his reign; from that point, however, the years of his reign began to be counted anew from the start, exactly as if the other four years had not preceded them. Furthermore, this nickname lasted only two years (for he himself lived no longer); and since **CHRIST** was born in the second year of that same nickname, if you calculate according to the sixty-year Cycle, it is actually the Emperor's sixth and final year, even though it is only the second year of the nickname he established. 

And this custom, introduced as far back as the fourth Emperor of the Han family in the year 196 BC, has continued without interruption until these times. However, from the penultimate family called the *Mim* <note>The Ming Dynasty (1368–1644).</note> and this current Tartar-Chinese one, <note>The Qing Dynasty (1644–1912), ruled by the Manchus, whom the author calls "Tartars."</note> individual Emperors have each assigned only a single nickname to their own reign.

And let these things said about the epoch of Chinese chronology, or the sixty-year cycles and their use, be sufficient; now let us proceed to the Chronological Table itself.

# THE FIRST FOUNDERS OF THE CHINESE.

**FOHI** <note>Also known as Fuxi, the first of the Three Sovereigns of ancient China.</note>, the Founder of the Chinese nation, originated from the province of **Shaanxi** [*Xen si*], from where he moved his seat of government to the town of **Chenzhou** [*Chin cheu*] in **Henan** [*Ho nan*] province. He offered sacrifices to the Spirit of Heaven and Earth, for which purpose he reared animals. From the contemplation of the heavens and of earthly things, he devised the book or chart called the **I Ching** [*Ye Kim*] <note>original: *Ye Kim*, meaning the "Book of Changes."</note>, that is, the *Book of Changes*; nearly 1,800 years later, King **Wen Wang** [*Ven vam*] and his son **Zhou Gong** [*Cheu cum*] worked to provide commentary on it, as did the philosopher **Confucius** 600 years after them. Fohi gradually led the inhabitants of the Far East away from a barbarous and wild life toward civilization. He established marriage by a law that decreed unions could only be entered into between families of different surnames; this law remains in force even today. He laid the six foundations of writing (in place of which they previously used knots <note>A reference to "quipu" or knotted strings used for record-keeping before the invention of characters.</note>). He also invented musical instruments, one with 27 strings and another with 36. He desired the **Dragon** to be the emblem of the nation, which **Wu Wang** [*Vu vam*], the founder of the third dynasty <note>The Zhou Dynasty.</note>, later decreed should have five claws for the use of the Emperors alone. He is said to have reigned for one hundred and fifteen years.

**XIN NUM** <note>Also known as Shennong, the "Divine Farmer."</note>, born of his mother **An Deng** [*Ngan tem*], was a man of gentle character who won over the neighboring barbarians by his clemency. He moved the seat of the court from **Henan** to **Yanzhou** [*Yen cheu*] in the province of **Shandong** [*Xan tum*]. He invented the plow and taught the people how to cultivate and sow the fields. He acted as a physician. In a single day, he is said to have discovered twelve poisonous herbs and as many antidotes. He compiled a small herbal manual. He manufactured salt from seawater. He established commerce and designated a marketplace for fairs. He is said to have died while surveying the territories of **Huguang** [*Hu quam*]. It is recorded that he reigned for 140 years and was buried in the city of **Chen** [*Cim*].

Seven of his descendants or successors are counted over a period of 380 years; it is uncertain whether or how they administered their domains in private. They certainly mention that the descendants of **XIN NUM** were granted the dynasty of **Chao** [*Ciao*] by **Wu Wang**, the founder of the third **Zhou** [*Cheu*] family, about 1,700 years later. Some also write that **XIN NUM** was the brother of the next following Emperor, **HUANGDI** [*HOAM TI*], both being from the same father, namely the petty king of **Youxiong** [*Yeu hium*].

I. **HUANGDI** <note>original: *HOAM TI*</note>,

---

**HUANGDI** <note>The "Yellow Emperor," a legendary ancestor and cultural hero in Chinese mythology.</note>, that is, the "Yellow Emperor," was born to his mother *Fu-pao*. As the Founder of the Monarchy, he began to rule at the age of twelve, having been elected by the petty kings. He held his court at *Zhuolu* <note>original: *Cho cheu*</note> in the province of **Beijing** <note>original: *Pe kim*</note>. He dedicated a Temple of Peace to **Shangdi** <note>original: *Xam ti*</note>, that is, the Supreme Emperor or God, although it later became customary to perform sacrifices in the open air. He defeated the rebel *Chiyou* <note>original: *Chi yeu*</note>, of the lineage of *Shennong* <note>original: *Xin num*</note>, in a third battle. The majesty of the Empire began under him; the diadem and the color yellow were permitted for the Emperors alone.

Utilizing the work of *Da Rao* <note>original: *Ta nao*</note>, he perfected the sixty-year cycle <note>The sexagenary cycle, a system of sixty terms used for recording days and years.</note>. He invented tables for Astronomy and Arithmetic, as well as Music and musical instruments. Likewise, he invented weapons, the bow, nets, chariots, ships, the crafts of the smith and the potter, and measures and weights.

He cast 12 bronze bells, corresponding to the 12 months of the year.

He appointed *Ju Gong* <note>original: *Ciu cum*</note> and *Cangjie* <note>original: *çam kie*</note> (who also invented writing characters) as Chronologists.

He created six **Colaos** <note>original: *Colaos*; a term used by early European writers to describe the Grand Secretaries or supreme Ministers of the imperial court.</note>, or supreme Ministers of the realm.

He defeated five rebel Princes.

Queen **Leizu** <note>original: *Luy su*</note> taught the people how to rear silkworms, weave silk, and dye it with colors.

---

**HUANGDI** also wrote several books on the medical art of pulses, which is still used today, with the assistance of *Qibo* <note>original: *Ki pe*</note>, *Suwen* <note>original: *So ven*</note>, and *Leigong* <note>original: *Luy cum*</note>.

| | | He [Emperor Ku] had four Queens, setting a new precedent. The first, after making a vow to God, obtained a son named **Qi** <note>original: *Cie*; also known as Hou Ji, the "Lord of Millet"</note>, who deserved very well of posterity for his great work in agriculture. The second, called **Qingdu** <note>original: *Kim tu*</note>, gave birth to **Yao** <note>original: *Yao*</note> in the fourteenth month after conception. The third, after offering a sacrifice to God, conceived **Xie** <note>original: *Sie*</note>. The fourth had a son named **Zhi** <note>original: *Chi*</note>. |
| **CYCLE VI.**<br/>Year before Christ:<br/>2397. | **Ku** <note>original: *Ti co*</note> reigned 8 years. | **Ku** <note>original: *Ti co*</note> established public teachers to educate the people. He instituted vocal music to encourage mutual harmony and the study of virtues.<br/><br/>In the 32nd year of the Cycle, **Ku** died at the age of 105 and was buried in **Beijing** <note>original: *Pekim*</note>. In the 33rd year, his son **Zhi** <note>original: *Chi*</note>, born of the fourth Queen, succeeded him; but because he was lawless and degenerate, he was deprived of the Empire by the regional lords in the 40th year of the Cycle. He is excluded from the official number of Emperors. |
| | 5. **YAO**, otherwise called **Tang** <note>original: *Tam*</note> and **Tao**, reigned 100 years. | In the 41st year, **Yao**, son of **Ku**, was placed in charge of the Empire. He reigned alone for 72 years, and for an additional 28 years with his colleague **Shun** <note>original: *Xun*</note>. His court was in the city of **Taiyuan** <note>original: *Tai yuen*</note> in the province of **Shanxi** <note>original: *Xan si*</note>.<br/><br/>This Emperor was both a ruler and a lawgiver, as was his successor **Shun**; both served as a standard and exemplar for the princes of all posterity. He was pious toward the poor and respectful of the elderly; it is believed that the custom of maintaining a certain number of elderly people in every city today with royal provisions originated from him. |
| **CYCLE VII.**<br/>Year before Christ:<br/>2337. | | Although **Yao** abounded in wealth, he ruled while content with common food, simple clothing, a plain house, and a modest bed. He attributed the faults of his subjects and public calamities to himself alone.<br/><br/>With the help of the astronomers **He** and **Xi** <note>original: *Ho* and *Hi*</note>, he organized the 12 lunar months—six of 30 days and six of 29—and even intercalary months, which recur seven times within 19 years <note>This refers to the Metonic cycle used to align the solar and lunar years</note>.<br/><br/>He established six supreme tribunals <note>The Six Ministries of traditional Chinese government</note> which persist even today, as well as five orders of titled nobility.<br/><br/>He ruled so gently for 50 years that his rule was hardly felt.<br/><br/>In the 40th year of the Cycle, there was a massive nine-year flood. **Gun** <note>original: *Quen*</note> was put in charge of draining these waters. He paid for his sluggishness with his life <note>original: *capite luit*; literally "paid with his head"</note>. His son **Yu** was substituted, who successfully spent 13 years draining the waters into the sea and elsewhere, destined to receive the scepter for his merits.<br/><br/>In the 50th year, **Shun** <note>original: *Xun*</note> was elevated from the fields to the prefecture by **Yao**, who was moved by the mere reputation of his obedience. **Yao** gave him his two daughters in marriage.<br/><br/>In the 53rd year, **Shun** was elevated to a partnership in the Empire for 28 years. Whenever he surveys the Empire, he first sacrifices to **Shangdi** <note>original: *Xam ti*</note>, or God. He tames four rebels from the lineage of **Huangdi** <note>original: *Hoam ti*; the Yellow Emperor</note>. He instituted five types of punishments, recommending compassion in their execution. See the **Shu Jing** <note>original: *Xu kim*; The Classic of History</note>. |
| **CYCLE VIII.**<br/>Year before Christ:<br/>2277. | | **Shun** constructed a sphere of the seven planets out of precious stones; he divided the Empire into 12 regions.<br/><br/>In the 20th year of the Cycle, **Yao** died at the age of 118, leaving behind 9 sons; he was buried in **Qufu** <note>original: *Kio feu*</note> in the province of **Shandong** <note>original: *Xan tum*</note>. The people mourned him for three years as if for a father and mother. |

<meta>This page continues the chronological history of the Chinese emperors, moving from the decline of the first imperial dynasty (the Xia) to the establishment of the second (the Shang).</meta>

# THE CHINESE MONARCHY

**CYCLE XV.**
The year 1857 before Christ.

**CYCLE XVI.**
The year 1797 before Christ.

**CYCLE XVII.**
The year 1737 before Christ.

<column-break/>

15. **TI CAO**
reigned 11 years. <note>original: "Ti Cao," refers to the Emperor Gao of the Xia dynasty.</note>

16. **TI FA**
reigned 19 years. <note>original: "Ti Fa," refers to the Emperor Fa of the Xia.</note>

17. **KIE**
reigned 52 years. <note>original: "Kie," refers to Jie, the last ruler of the Xia dynasty, traditionally depicted as a tyrant.</note>

---

1. **CHIM TAM**
reigned 13 years. <note>original: "Chim Tam," refers to Cheng Tang, the founder of the Shang dynasty.</note>

2. **TAI KIA**
reigned 33 years. <note>original: "Tai Kia," refers to Tai Jia.</note>

---

3. **VO TIM**,
reigned 29 years. <note>original: "Vo Tim," refers to Wo Ding.</note>

4. **TAI KEM**,
reigned 25 years. <note>original: "Tai Kem," refers to Tai Geng.</note>

<column-break/>

In the 5th year of the Cycle, **CHIM TAM** is born, the future founder of the following dynasty.

In the 9th year, when **KIA** <note>Emperor Kong Jia</note> dies. In the 10th year, his son **TI CAO** succeeds him, a man devoted to luxury and lust.

In the 20th year, **TI CAO** dies. In the 21st year, his son **TI FA** succeeds him.

The tributary princes visit the Emperor according to custom.

In the 39th year, **TI FA** dies. In the 40th year, his son **KIE** succeeds him, a man both tyrannical and lewd.

A prince endowed with great natural talents, he possessed such physical strength that he could break iron with his hands.

To please his mistress *Muy hi* <note>Meixi, a famous femme fatale of Chinese history</note>, he constructed a tower of precious stone; he killed those advisors who tried to warn him, while others fled the court.

He created a lake of wine in which 3000 people might indulge in debauchery.

---

The Wise Man *Y yn* <note>Yi Yin, a legendary minister</note> is sent by the Prince of *Tam* to lead King **KIE** back to a life of virtue; he returned in the fourth year, despairing of the King's correction.

In the 21st year of the Cycle, *Tam* is sent to prison by **KIE**, but is soon released. *Tam* is incited against **KIE** by 800 lords and the people, and he is forced, even against his will, to take up arms.

In the 31st year, **KIE** is deserted by his own troops and, becoming a fugitive outside the borders of China, he dies after three years. The first Imperial dynasty is extinguished.

In the 32nd year, **CHIM TAM**, a descendant of **HOAM TI** <note>Huangdi, the Yellow Emperor</note> and 17th in line, comes to the Empire at the age of 87 and founds the *Xam* <note>Shang</note> dynasty, which held power for 644 years under 28 Emperors. The court was in the city of *Quei te* <note>Shangqiu</note> in the province of *Honan* <note>Henan</note>. He was a pious and modest prince.

He began the year from the Moon which is closest to the winter solstice, which corresponds to January. He used the color white for banners and insignia, just as the preceding *Hia* <note>Xia</note> family used black, and the following *Cheu* <note>Zhou</note> family used purple <note>or red</note>.

Under this ruler there was a seven-year famine, perhaps the same one which is written of in the Holy Scriptures as having occurred in the whole world in Genesis 41.

**CHIM TAM** offered himself as a victim to God on behalf of the people; Heaven granted his prayer with pouring rains. He opened gold mines and established music for public rejoicing.

In the 44th year, **CHIM TAM** dies at the age of 100. In the 45th year, his grandson **TAI KIA** succeeds him, the firstborn son **TAI TIM** having already died. *Y yn* the <term>Colao<note>A Western transcription of the Chinese "Gê-lǎo," referring to a Grand Secretary or high-ranking minister.</note></term> confined the degenerate Prince in the garden of his grandfather’s tomb until, after three years, having come to his senses, he was restored to the throne.

---

**TAI KIA** became a model of a pious and dutiful Prince.

In the 17th year of the Cycle, **TAI KIA** dies. In the 18th year, **VO TIM**, another grandson of the Founder, succeeds him. He followed the advice of the <term>Colao</term> *Y yn*.

In the 25th year, *Y yn* the <term>Colao</term> dies at the age of 100. The Emperor performs his funeral rites with royal splendor; his son *Y pu* then served as an advisor to five Emperors.

In the 47th year, **VO TIM** dies. In the 48th year, his brother **TAI KEM** succeeds him.

<summary>This page records the transition from the Xia dynasty to the Shang dynasty, contrasting the decadent tyranny of Emperor Jie with the virtuous rule of Cheng Tang. It notably attempts to synchronize Chinese history with the Bible by linking a seven-year famine to the story of Joseph in Egypt.</summary>
<keywords>Xia Dynasty, Shang Dynasty, Emperor Jie, Cheng Tang, Yi Yin, Chinese Chronology, Biblical synchronism, Genesis 41, Henan, cultural colors</keywords>

The Grand Secretary <note>original: "Colaus," a Latinization of the Chinese title *Gelaos*, referring to a high-ranking official</note> **Ye pu** <note>Yi Zhi, a famous minister</note> teaches that omens are inferior to virtue. The affairs of the Empire are restored. |

| **CYCLE XIX.**<br>Year before Christ:<br>1617. | | He transfers the court to the province of **Ho nan** <note>Henan</note> because of frequent flooding from the **Yellow River** <note>original: "fluvii Crocei"</note>, which occurred quite often; the court was moved now to one side of the river, now to the other. Under this Emperor, there was great peace for about 70 years. Envoys from 76 kingdoms attend the assemblies. The ancient laws regarding the support of the elderly and the proper payment of funeral rites for the dead are restored. |
| | 8. **CHUM TIM**,<br>reigned 13 years. | In the 55th year, **TAI VU** dies. In the 56th year, his son **CHUM TIM** <note>Zhong Ding</note> succeeds him. Under his leadership, marauding barbarians are subdued. Due to flooding, the court is moved from the province of **Po** <note>Bo</note> in **Xan si** <note>Shanxi</note> to **Ngao** <note>Ao</note> in the province of **Ho nan**, and later to the province of **Pe kim** <note>Beijing</note>. |

In the 9th year, his brother **VAI GIN** <note>Wai Ren</note> succeeds him. He changes the seat of the court. From this time, the beginnings of wars between sons and brothers for the right to the Empire lasted for nearly 200 years. |

He transfers the court to **Kem** <note>Geng</note>, now the city of **Xun tu** <note>Xingtai</note>; later, due to flooding, he moves to the East. He restores the collapsed affairs of the Empire: hence, a deep peace. The lesser princes frequently come to celebrate the assemblies. |
| | 12. **ZU SIN**,<br>reigned 16 years. | In the 51st year, **ZU YE** dies. In the 52nd year, his son **ZU SIN** <note>Zu Xin</note> succeeds him. |

Having found him among the masons, he creates him a **Grand Secretary** <note>original: "Colaum," a Latinization of the Chinese term *Gelao*</note>; he is called **Fu yue**, whose excellent advice you may see in the book **Xu kim** <note>The *Shujing*, or Book of Documents</note>. <br> Great peace throughout the whole Empire, and a prosperous reign. <br> While he is offering ancestral sacrifices according to custom, a pheasant flies in and perches on the handle of the Imperial vessel and soon chirps; he takes this as an omen of his own happiness. But the Minister **Zu ki** <note>Zu Ji</note> teaches him that the omen of happiness must be grasped through virtue alone. See the **Xu kim**. |

The Tartars seek safety in flight; thus, with the matter unfinished, he returns to the court. |

| | 8. **KING XIAO** <note>original: **HIAO VAM**</note>, <br/> reigned 15 years. | **In year 48 of KING YI**, the king dies at age 50. **In year 49,** his brother **KING XIAO** succeeds by force. <br/> He was so devoted to horses that he granted the prefecture of the stable to *Feizi* <note>original: *Fi xu*</note> of the *Qin* <note>original: *Cin*</note> dynasty; the descendants of this man would later unlawfully found an Imperial family from this line. <br/> An unusual hailstorm slaughters oxen and horses. |
| **CYCLE** <br/> **XXXI.** <br/> Year <br/> before Christ <br/> 897. | 9. **KING YI** <note>original: **Y VAM**; a different king from the 7th monarch</note>, <br/> reigned 16 years. | **In year 3 of the Cycle, KING XIAO** dies at age 63. **In year 4,** his son **KING YI** succeeds, a man so dull-witted that he hardly dared to admit Ambassadors or petty kings out of shame. When the petty kings arrived for the Assemblies <note>original: *Comitia*</note>, he was the first to descend by one step to receive them, at the expense of his royal majesty. |
| | 10. **KING LI** <note>original: **LI VAM**</note>, <br/> reigned 51 years. | **In year 19, KING YI** dies at age 60. **In year 20,** his son **KING LI** succeeds him. <br/> A prince cruel in both deed and name, proud, and a spendthrift with the resources of the citizens. <br/> He is mocked in public speeches and writings. He decrees the death penalty for any subjects caught speaking or even whispering to one another. A harsh silence was maintained for three years. <br/> **In year 52,** the Emperor is sought for execution by a raging mob; he flees. His family was killed by the furious people, except for a young son, whom *Shao* <note>original: *Chao*</note> had hidden with the <term>Colao</term> <note>a Grand Secretary or high minister</note>. When the matter was discovered, the common people demanded the child; the *Colao* handed over his own small son instead, who was torn to pieces by the people unaware of the trickery. The *Colao* tried in vain to restore the Emperor, who remained a wanderer and exile for 17 years. |
| **CYCLE** <br/> **XXXII.** <br/> Year <br/> before Christ <br/> 837. | 11. **KING XUAN** <note>original: **SIUEN VAM**</note>, <br/> reigned 46 years. | **In year 10 of the Cycle, KING LI** dies in exile. **In year 11,** his son **KING XUAN** succeeds him. <br/> He remained under the guardianship of Duke *Shao* and Duke *Zhou* <note>original: *Chao cum* and *Cheu cum*</note> for 15 years. He provides a model of a good Prince, summoning wise men from their places of exile everywhere. <br/> He neglects the rite by which the ancient Kings cultivated a portion of the field with their own hands, despite the *Colao* resisting this change in vain. <br/> In this age, quadruplet sages flourished, whom a single mother had brought forth in a fourfold birth. The petty kings and local lords return to their dutiful service. <br/> He forces the rebellious Southern peoples of *Huai'an* and *Huquang* <note>original: *Hoay ngan* & *Hu quan*</note> to obey Chinese laws through military force. <br/> The most prudent Queen *Jiang* <note>original: *Kiam*</note> writes a book on the instruction of the women's quarters <note>original: *Gynæcæi*</note>. |
| | 12. **KING YOU** <note>original: **YEU VAM**</note>, <br/> reigned 11 years. | **In year 56, KING XUAN** dies. **In year 57,** his son **KING YOU** succeeds, a man who fell short of his father’s virtues. <br/> He wages wars against the Western Tartars <note>referring to the nomadic Rong or Di tribes</note> unsuccessfully. Captured by love for his mistress *Bao Si* <note>original: *Pao fu*</note>, he repudiates the Queen and his son. <br/> **In year 57,** a part of Mount *Qi* <note>original: *Ki*</note> collapses in an earthquake. |
