# Note on the Second Table.

A. He is the son of **Ti co**, the fourth Emperor, and a grandson from the fourth generation of the lineage of **Hoam ti** <note>original: *Hoam ti*, likely referring to Huangdi, the Yellow Emperor</note>. From his lineage, the series of the second Imperial family is continued.
B. **Chim tam** <note>Cheng Tang, founder of the Shang dynasty</note>, Prince and Founder of the second family called *Xam* <note>Shang</note>, and later *Yn* <note>Yin</note>: which was continued by 28 Emperors over 644 years.
C. **Tai tim**, the firstborn of **Chim tam**, died while his father was still living, leaving his son as heir.
D. **Ki çu**, the son of **Tai tim**, the 26th Emperor, having been released from prison, was created King of Korea by Emperor **Vu vam** <note>King Wu of Zhou</note>; he was clearly a master of his own law and free from any obligation of vassalage.
E. **Pi can**, the son of Emperor **Tai tim**, was cruelly put to death by **Cheu** <note>King Zhou, the last Shang ruler</note>, the final Emperor, who could not bear his warnings.
F. **Vi çu**, the firstborn son of Emperor **Ti ye**, had fled into the forests during the reign of the tyrant **Cheu**. Having been recalled from there, he was created the Lesser King of the kingdom of *Sum* <note>the State of Song</note> in the province of *Ho-nan* by **Chim vam** <note>King Cheng</note>, the second Emperor of the third family. He was exempt from the burden of vassalage and permitted to rule according to the specific rites of his own family. Furthermore, this family, after a son died prematurely, was transferred to the brother **Vi chum** and continued through 32 Lesser Kings until it was finally extinguished by the Dynast of the kingdom of *Ci* <note>Qi</note>. Moreover, the head and prince of the kingdom of *Ci* was later created by **Vu vam** as *Tai cum vam*. This man's family continued through 28 Lesser Kings, until it was extinguished by the High Official <term>Colao: a Romanization of "Gelao," referring to a Grand Secretary or high minister</term> called *Tien ho*. *Tien ho* was then created the Lesser King of that same kingdom of *Ci* by **Ngan vam**, the 30th Emperor of the *Cheu* family. This was the lineage continued through 7 Lesser Kings, and finally extinguished by the Lesser King of the kingdom of *Cin* <note>Qin</note>.
G. **Cheu**, the third son of Emperor **Ti ye**: because of his tyranny, the *Xam* family was extinguished, with the third family, the *Cheu*, succeeding them.
H. **Vi chum**, otherwise known as **Chum yen**, the second son of **Ti ye**, the second-to-last Emperor: he lived in his brother’s kingdom of *Sum*, where his sons and grandsons performed public duties. They describe the lineage of *Confucius*, the Philosopher of the Chinese, as being continued from this man.
I. **Vu kem**, the son of **Cheu**, the last Emperor of the *Xam* family; when he rashly spread many rumors among the common people against **Chim vam**, the second Emperor of the now-new *Cheu* family, he was killed by **Cheu cum** <note>the Duke of Zhou</note>.
K. **Cum fu kia**, the son of **Chim cao fu**; from whom the family name of *Confucius*, *Cum* <note>Kong</note>, was bestowed, which is preserved in the family even today.

<column-break/>

L. **Xo leam he**, the son of **Pe hia**, Governor of the district called *Ceu*. When he had fathered nine daughters but no male child, and being already seventy years old, he married the young woman **Chim**, descending from the **Yen** family, which was then of the highest nobility. Although he himself was considered somewhat obscure, because it was nonetheless established that he drew his lineage from Imperial blood (however remote), he obtained the desired marriage: from these was born *Confucius*.
M. *Cum fu çu*, or *Confucius*, the son of **Xo leam he**, was born in the 12th year of Emperor **Lim vam**, in the year 551 before Christ. He was a man noble among the Chinese for his moral nobility, which is sought through virtue and letters; so too in the nobility of his blood, he is perhaps second to no one of other nations. For besides the fact that he descends in a direct line from **Hoam ti**, the first Emperor of the nation, his own sons and grandsons have preserved the splendor of their house for more than two thousand two hundred years unto this very day. Today, his descendant in the 67th (or perhaps 68th) generation resides in his ancestral city of *Kio feu* <note>Qufu</note> in the province of *Xan tum* <note>Shandong</note>, the proper and ancient seat of that family, with the title *Que cum*, that is, Duke, the only person among the Chinese who remains free from tribute <note>tax-exempt</note>. Therefore, by calculating the years from Emperor **Hoam ti** until the birth of *Confucius*, there are 2,146 years; if you add to these the 2,237 years which have passed from the birth of Confucius until the year 1683 of this century, it must be admitted that one and the same lineage has been propagated through sons and grandsons in an never-interrupted series for 4,383 years total—at least if faith is to be placed in the Chinese records.
N. **Pe yu**, the only son of *Confucius*, died in the 50th year of his life, when his father was 69 years old.
O. **çu fu** <note>Zisi, the grandson of Confucius</note>, the son of **Pe yu**, having performed great duties in the Empire, wrote the book *Chum yum* <note>Zhongyong</note>, or "On the Mean," according to the mind of his grandfather *Confucius*, of whom he can therefore be considered an interpreter. He was also the teacher of the second Philosopher of the Chinese, whose name is *Memcius* <note>Mencius</note>; whose posterity, although obscure at its origin, nevertheless perseveres to this point, and is also decorated with its own titles of honor by the Emperors in the court.

B

<meta>This page continues the genealogical and historical record of the Chinese dynasties, specifically focusing on the lineage of the Zhou (Cheu) family, transitioning from their agricultural origins to their rise as imperial rulers.</meta>

### Notes on the Third Table

<margin>A.</margin> **Hou Ji** <note>original: "Heu cie"</note>, the son of **Di Ku** <note>original: "Ti co"</note>, the fourth Emperor of the world <note>the Latin "Monarchiæ" refers to the Five Emperors of Chinese antiquity</note>, was the founder of the third family, later called the **Zhou** <note>original: "Cheu"</note>. He was entrusted with the care of agricultural matters by the Emperor **Shun** <note>original: "XUN"</note>, and because of his great merit, he was created the Dynastic Ruler of the territory of **Tai** in the province of **Shaanxi** <note>original: "Xen si"</note>. His lineage is recorded as continuing through the two royal families of the **Xia** <note>original: "Hia"</note> and the **Shang** <note>original: "Xam"</note> for forty generations. Here, however, writers record primarily the names of those who left behind some memory-worthy deed, even if they are perhaps listed more fully in other books that are lacking here.

<margin>B.</margin> **Buzhu** <note>original: "Pu co"</note>, of the lineage of Hou Ji, held a government office under the first family, the Xia. However, when he saw the laws and rights of the kingdom being destroyed and the royal family verging on ruin, he resigned his office and fled secretly to the lands of the barbarians <note>a term used by the author for non-Huaxia tribes</note>. There, he began to establish agriculture (the ancient and proper duty of his family), a deed by which he bound the hearts of all people to himself. From him, the family was again propagated through sons and grandsons down to **Gong Liu** <note>original: "Cum lieu"</note>.

<margin>C.</margin> Although **Gong Liu** held a territory surrounded by barbarians, he nevertheless instructed his people in such a way that he was also held in love and veneration by his neighbors. Consequently, as the number of his people increased daily, he moved to the ample territory of **Bin** <note>original: "Pin"</note>, now called **Binzhou** <note>original: "Pin cheu"</note>, in Shaanxi province. This occurred in the 22nd year of the Emperor **Jie** <note>original: "Kie"</note>, who was the 17th and final ruler of the first family, the Xia. Nine generations are counted from Gong Liu down to **Tai Wang** <note>original: "Tai vam"</note>.

<margin>D.</margin> **Tai Wang**, or **Gugong** <note>original: "Cu cum"</note>, restored the somewhat collapsed state of the family. After defeating the barbarians in the place called **Qishan** <note>original: "Ki xan"</note> (where the city of **Fengxiang** <note>original: "Fum ciam"</note> in Shaanxi province is now located), he established a stable seat there. He bestowed upon his family the new name of **Zhou**, which remained the name of the Imperial family thereafter. This migration from the territory of Bin to Qishan took place in the 26th year of **Xiao Yi** <note>original: "Siao ye"</note>, the nineteenth Emperor of the second family, the Shang.

<margin>E.</margin> **Taibo** <note>original: "Tai pe"</note> and **Zhongyong** <note>original: "Yu chum" or "Chum yum"</note> (both praised by **Confucius**) were the elder sons of Tai Wang. Knowing that their younger brother **Jili** <note>original: "Ki lie"</note> was more dearly loved by their father and that the kingdom was destined for him, they both went into voluntary exile for the sake of their brother’s favor, seeking out the territories of the Southern barbarians. To hide their noble origin, they cut their hair and deformed their bodies with tattoos and marks of servitude <note>this act of "yielding" is a high virtue in Confucian thought</note>. Nevertheless, Taibo was elected as the petty king of the kingdom of **Wu** <note>original: "V"</note> by those barbarians. He founded the noble city of **Suzhou** <note>original: "Su cheu"</note>, where his tomb still stands today in the province of **Nanjing** <note>referring to the Ming-era Southern Metropolitan Region</note>. They also write that the great-grandson of this Zhongyong was appointed a petty king of the same kingdom of Wu by **King Wu** <note>original: "VU VAM"</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>F.</margin> **Jili**, or **Wang Ji** <note>original: "Vam ki"</note>, succeeded his father Tai Wang in the territories. Through his remarkable piety and justice, he bound the hearts of the petty kings to himself. By order of the two Emperors **Wuding** <note>original: "Tai tim"</note> and **Di Yi** <note>original: "Ti ye"</note>, he successfully subdued the **Northern tribes** <note>original: "Pekinenses" — likely referring to the Rong or northern nomads near modern Beijing</note>. He died in the seventh year of the reign of Di Yi, leaving behind his son **King Wen** <note>original: "Ven vam"</note>, who was then 47 years old.

<margin>G.</margin> **King Wen**, son of Jili. As the imperial family of Shang fell toward ruin, forty petty kings submitted themselves to him. Out of the three parts of the Empire, he held two <note>a reference to the "Two-thirds of the world" trope in Chinese history</note> bound to himself through his benevolence and the veneration of his virtues. He is not, however, placed in the formal series of Emperors. He left twelve sons, among whom was **King Wu** <note>original: "VU VAM"</note>, the founder of the third family, the Zhou.

<margin>H.</margin> **King Wu**, son of the very powerful King Wen, was himself the Prince and Founder of the most extensive **Zhou** family, which was propagated through 35 Emperors over 873 years. This Emperor conferred various kingdoms upon his brothers; he also desired that his sons and grandsons should excel in dignity just as each of them excelled others in virtue.

<margin>I.</margin> **Bo Yikao** <note>original: "Pe ye cao"</note>, the eldest son of King Wen, was among the nobles of the Emperor **Zhou** <note>original: "CHEU" - referring to the tyrant Zhou Xin, last of the Shang</note>. While Bo Yikao's father was being held in chains, the Emperor killed the son. He ordered the flesh of the murdered man to be fried, seasoned, and offered to the father, King Wen, as a delicacy from the Royal table. The tyrant added that if the father were truly a holy man, he would undoubtedly know beforehand what kind of food it was.

<margin>K.</margin> **Guan Shu Xian** <note>original: "çao vo chin"</note>, a son of King Wen, died prematurely.

<margin>L.</margin> **Bi Gong Gao** <note>original: "Pie cum cao"</note>, a son of King Wen, was one of the nobles of the Empire. He was appointed by his brother King Wu as the petty king of the kingdom of **Bi** <note>original: "Pu"</note>, which is now the capital of Shaanxi province, called **Xi'an** <note>original: "Singan"</note>.

<margin>M.</margin> **Kang Shu** <note>original: "Cam xo"</note>, son of King Wen, was appointed by his brother King Wu as the petty king of the kingdom of **Wei** <note>original: "Guei"</note> in the province of **Henan**. After more than 800 years, his family was extinguished by the King of **Qin** <note>original: "Cin"</note>, after having been propagated through 37 petty kings.

# PREFACE

->The continuous series of Imperial Families is presented here in summary.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' featuring a cherub sitting at the base of the letter, surrounded by vine-like scrolls, with an armillary sphere or geometric instrument depicted at the top.</image-desc>Before I provide the second Chronological Table of the Chinese Monarchy after Christ, it is helpful to first present a summary of the Imperial Families of the Monarchy—both those that flourished before and those after Christ—offering them to the reader at a single glance. Chinese commentators rightly note that just as the elements and the entire sublunary <term>sublunary: the earthly realm below the moon, subject to change and decay</term> world have their own cycles of things and times, so too do kingdoms and empires, and even those families in whose hands the empires themselves rest. Thus, while one falls, others arise; while these thrive and flourish, those wither and grow old. Indeed, almost nothing is more constant than the cycle and inconstancy of things itself. The Chinese Monarchy is a most abundant witness to this truth.

Thus, the first founder of the Chinese people, **Fo hi** <note>Modern Pinyin: Fu Xi</note>, first led wandering and rustic men toward a certain social life, and soon, gently bound by marriage, began to shape them toward civilization. From **Xin num** <note>Modern Pinyin: Shen Nong, the "Divine Farmer"</note> they were then taught agriculture and provided with other protections for sustaining life. Afterward, they obtained as leaders and teachers that famous **Hoam ti** <note>Modern Pinyin: Huangdi, the Yellow Emperor</note>—from whom we began the sixty-year period <note>The sexagenary cycle, a traditional Chinese system of numbering years</note>—and his three successors (namely **Xao hao** <note>Shaohao</note>, **Chuen hio** <note>Zhuanxu</note>, and **Ti co** <note>Emperor Ku</note>). Steeped in the basics of a more refined life, they gradually grew into this Kingdom and Empire of the Far East.

# ON CHINESE CHRONOLOGY

<sig>H</sig>
<meta>catchword: they report</meta>

Following the six founders and princes of the Chinese nation were two very famous emperors who were also lawgivers: **Yao** and **Xun** <note>Modern Pinyin: Shun</note>. As for why **Confucius** in his books, and **Mencius** <note>The Latin text uses "Memcius"; he was a later follower of Confucius whose teachings helped shape the state ideology</note>—who is considered closest to him, though separated by a century—make mention of these two princes most especially and not the preceding six, there was, I believe, no other reason than that both were kings as well as lawgivers, and from them proceeded all the principal civil rites and political institutions. The reigns of these two emperors or lawgivers fill 150 years; if these are added to the 587 years of the preceding six, the total is 737 years.

Following the two founders of the nation and the six emperors, there came the Imperial Families, in whose hands the supreme dignity and the monarchical administration of the Chinese have remained until these times. In total, twenty-two families are counted: specifically, nine major ones and thirteen minor ones—at least if we include the very last family, which is currently in its prime: I mean the **Eastern Tartars** <note>This refers to the Manchus, who established the Qing Dynasty in 1644, shortly before this text was written</note>, under whose rule we are writing this.

Furthermore, those three families that preceded the others in time also surpass them in fame and praise; for in the integrity of their morals, their beautiful institutions, and their clemency, justice, and faith in governing the state, they were truly the leaders of all others. Among these, the first, called the **Hia** <note>Modern Pinyin: Xia</note>, counts 17 emperors who held power for 458 years. The second, called the **Xam** <note>Shang</note> and later the **Yn** <note>Yin</note>, had 28 emperors over 644 years. Finally, the third, commonly named the **Cheu** <note>Zhou</note>, was ruled by 35 emperors for 873 years; this family surpassed all others in both the number of princes and the span of years. The years of these three families together total 1,975.

Many things are also commemorated by *Tai su* <note>original: "Tai su"; likely referring to the *Taishi* or Grand Historian, a title often associated with the keepers of royal archives</note>, who lived more than two centuries before Confucius; and by *Lao kiun* <note>original: "Lao kiun"; known today as Laozi, the legendary founder of Taoism</note>, who was a contemporary of Confucius, though older than him. As for the rest, the **Zhou** <note>original: "Cheu"</note> family—the last of the three principal imperial families, as we have already mentioned—was the most flourishing in its earliest times and therefore provided more abundant material for writing. However, as the years slipped by, it too began to decline and gradually experienced the deceptive whims of human affairs. Certainly, by the time the Philosopher lived, the dynasty had already lost much of its ancient customs and its primitive integrity and strictness. He indeed labored for several years, acting with a clearly burning zeal through both his spoken words and his writings to recall that golden age and the innocence of the Ancients, but he labored with no success, or certainly very little. Therefore, the three principal families finally perished, after eighty Emperors from among them had held the Chinese Empire for a total of 1,975 years. And—such is the misfortune of the human condition—the ancient faith, sincerity, and innocence perished along with them. Moreover, heresies were growing strong from the time of Confucius himself, and not many centuries later, the wretched plague of idols <note>A common term used by Jesuit missionaries to describe Buddhism</note> brought in from India began to contaminate this most cultured nation in a miserable way with foul and insane superstitions. [dynasties], which followed the three just mentioned, worked tirelessly to restore the institutions of the Ancestors, their discipline, and former customs. Yet they were never able to ensure that some stain of an age once corrupted—something wrinkled and aged, as it were—did not persist; and thus, much of that ancient integrity and strictness (as all observers note) was found wanting. 

Meanwhile, it is certainly worth remembering what **Yangzi** <note>original: "Yam cie"; likely Yang Xiong (53 BC – AD 18), a philosopher and historian of the Han dynasty</note>, a most serious author among the **Chinese**, notes in his Prologue—which is typically prefixed to all historical annals: namely, that the ruin of these three so illustrious families arose chiefly from three concubines, each of whom brought destruction to her respective dynasty. 

Although this wise man observed this with good reason, many others have noted that another factor contributed to the ruin and downfall of this third family <note>The Zhou dynasty</note>. Specifically, its founder **Wu Wang** <note>original: "Vu vam"; the first king of the Zhou dynasty, traditionally praised for his virtue</note>, a Prince renowned for military glory and remarkably generous toward his followers, had granted seventy kingdoms or **dynasties** <note>The author uses the term "dynasties" here to refer to the various feudal fiefdoms or states</note>—and even more—to those who had served the **Empire** well, as well as to his own kinsmen. This munificence, as is often the case, provided fuel for greed and ambition, leading to wars that were truly long-lasting and mournful. 

Certainly, as time passed, eighteen major kingdoms were consumed by mutual wars. Finally, during the reign of **You Wang** <note>original: "Yeu vam"; the twelfth king of the Zhou dynasty whose reign is traditionally cited as a point of decline</note>, who was the twelfth of the **Zhou** family to rule the **Empire**, the entire hope of victory and the burden of war had fallen to seven Princes or petty kings. It reached the point where the final seven Emperors, besides the august title **Son of Heaven** (meaning "given from heaven"), the seal, and the nine **Imperial** vessels <note>original: "novem vasa Imperialia"; the Nine Tripod Cauldrons, ancient bronze vessels that symbolized the right to rule China</note>, retained hardly anything except the mere images and shadows of power. Indeed, for the man who was the very last of them all, nothing remained of that vast empire of lands except a tiny domain of seven towns. <header>PREFACE. 27</header>

...yielded to the one called **Qin** <note>original: "Cin"; the Qin dynasty (221–206 BC), from which the name "China" is derived</note>, which, after it had contended against six other Kingdoms for supreme dignity for a total of two hundred and ten years, finally emerged as the victor of all. It achieved its desires and gained possession of the vast **Empire of the Chinese** <note>original: "Sinarum Imperio"</note>; yet it held it for a very short time indeed. Certainly, on the third day after he occupied the throne, he was carried to his tomb; his son followed the father after a three-year period had barely passed, robbed alike of both hope and life, and with him the entire lineage and family collapsed. Thus, the happiness—or rather the mere hope of happiness—was so brief and fleeting, a goal for which the ambition of so many years had carved a path through so many slaughters and wounds.

However, the one who succeeded next, called **Shi Huangdi** <note>original: "Xi Hoam ti"; the First Emperor of a unified China, known for his legalist reforms and the Great Wall</note>, and who was finally the victor of all, protected the name of the **Qin** family (into which he had been adopted from a different lineage) for the 37 years in which he ruled. He employed a truly appropriate plan not only for preserving but even for perpetuating his Monarchy: he reduced all the **Petty Kings** <note>original: "Regulos"; the various feudal lords of the Warring States period</note>, who were leaders of factions and wars, into rank and file, and converted the Kingdoms into **Provinces**. 

Yet finally, even that name was extinguished along with him. It would indeed have been immortal among posterity—had he not foully stained the glory of his deeds (which were certainly very great) and the merits of the nearly immense wall built against the **Tartars** <note>original: "Tartaros"; referring here to the Xiongnu or northern nomadic tribes against whom the Great Wall was constructed</note> with a certain unheard-of hatred of literature and learned men, as well as by his own tyranny and cruelty. 

Indeed, when he realized that he was now hated by so many, and fearing treachery and the violence of his own people, he ordered not only weapons but all bronze and iron to be removed from private homes. But he soon learned that weapons are taken away in vain from those whom hatred and fury have armed. Certainly, their patience finally turning into rage, they attacked the tyrant with canes hardened and charred by fire. Having slaughtered and routed his armies more than once, they would have finally stripped him of both his empire and his life, had nature not anticipated his death. The leader of this deed, however, was a man of ignoble birth from the common crowd, to whom

# THE CHINESE MONARCHY

12. **JIANWEN TI**
reigned 2 years.

13. **WU TI**
reigned 24 years.

14. **AN TI**
reigned 22 years.

15. **GONG TI**
reigned 2 years.

<column-break/>

The <term>Colaus</term> <note>original: "Colaus"; a title used by early European writers for a Grand Secretary or high minister, derived from the Chinese *Gelao*</note> *Huan Wen* defeated the Prince of *Yen* in the North in battle, but the Prince, reinforced by the troops of the Prince of *Cin*, attacked *Huan Wen* in turn and slew nearly 30,000 of his men.

In the 7th year, **TI YE** <note>Emperor Fei of Jin</note> was cast down from the throne by the <term>Colaus</term> *Huan Wen* and made Lord of the fortress of *Haishi*, where he died 15 years later at the age of 43. In the 8th year, **JIANWEN TI** succeeded him; he was the younger son of *Yuan Ti*, the fifth Emperor, and was elected by the leading men of the state.

In the 9th year, **JIANWEN TI** died at the age of 53. In the 10th year, his son **WU TI** <note>Emperor Xiaowu of Jin</note> succeeded him.

*Fu Jian*, the Northern Emperor, contemplated seeking war in the South; he was advised against it on the grounds that the *Jin* <note>original: "Cin"</note> family ruled by the Mandate of Heaven and had not yet sinned so greatly as to lose its favor. Despising this counsel, it is written that he sought the South with 600,000 cavalry and 270,000 infantry, and that his marching column occupied 700 <term>stadia</term> <note>An ancient unit of distance; here used to convey an immense, miles-long line of troops</note>. Before the full force of the enemy could gather, the Southern Emperor suddenly attacked their camp with a few thousand select men out of the 80,000 armed troops he possessed. He struck with such force and bravery that the enemy was seized by a panic; he so shattered them that out of such a vast army, scarcely 30,000 escaped. Afterward, the Emperor *Fu Jian* himself was defeated by his own leaders, captured, and finally strangled in a nearby temple.

Thereupon, various other kingdoms in the North rebelled. The Southern Emperor, however, gave himself over to wine and luxury, though he might have brought everything under his own jurisdiction if he had chosen to follow up his victory.

*In the 12th year, 10th moon; the 18th year, 6th moon; the 21st year, 10th moon; and the 28th year, 5th moon: Eclipses of the Sun.*

In the 20th year of the Empire, a **Comet** appeared; another Northern war-emperor offered a drink to it, hoping to turn the sinister omen away from himself.

In the 33rd year, **WU TI** died, having been secretly smothered in his bed. The cause was a certain joke, in which he had told his second Queen (who was then 30 years old) that she seemed like a little old woman to him.

In the 34th year, his son **AN TI** succeeded him; he was dull-witted and obtuse. Seven kingdoms, both small and great, rose in rebellion.

*Tuoba Gui*, the grandson and remaining heir of the Prince of the Kingdom of *Tai* (after the sixth generation had been abolished), utterly defeated the King of the Northern *Yen*. Having plundered the court, he laid new foundations there for his own family, which would endure for 149 years under 13 Princes.

*Liu Yu*, once a traveling shoe-seller and then a soldier, and later a General of war, paved his own way to the Empire through many famous victories; he was soon to become the founder of the following dynasty.

*In the 37th year, 6th moon; the 40th year, 4th moon; the 44th year, 7th moon; the 51st year, 9th moon; and the 54th year, 1st moon: Eclipses of the Sun.*

In the 55th year, **AN TI** was killed by *Liu Yu* at the age of 37, in which year a **Comet** appeared.

In the 56th year, **GONG TI**, the brother of his predecessor by the same mother, was put in his place.

# THE CHINESE MONARCHY

<margin>
CYCLE LXIII.
Year 1024 AD.
</margin>

A prince truly pious in both deed and name, who loved peace and his people more than war; because of this, the Barbarians <note>Refers to the Liao and Western Xia dynasties bordering the Song Empire.</note> were emboldened to renew their conflicts. He entered into a peace with them that was considered unworthy of his majesty. He cast out all idols from the palace. He forbade the offering of foreign gifts to him, whether they were of rare value or considered auspicious omens. When the <term>Chancellor</term> <note>original: "Colao"; a title for a high-ranking official or Grand Secretary</note> **Zhou** <note>original: "Ziu"</note> was ill, and had been prescribed a powder made from the hairs of a beard, the Emperor ordered his own beard to be shaved and sent it to him.

When, during a banquet, a dish of twenty-eight small oysters was served, each of which had cost a thousand copper coins, the Emperor, upon learning this, said: *“Far be it from me that with the grasp of two small sticks <note>An early European description of chopsticks.</note> I should cast twenty-eight thousand coins into a gluttonous mouth.”*

In the 26th year of his reign, when it finally rained after a great period of drought, the nobles congratulated the prince. He replied: *“During all that time when we labored under a scarcity of water, I daily entreated Heaven with the proper burning of incense. At night, when I heard thunder, I rose from my bed, took up my belt and cap, and stood under the open sky. As soon as it rained, I fell to my knees, and reverently saluting Heaven, I gave thanks to the same; only then did I dare return to my bed. Now, I desire one thing above all: that you signifies to me with confidence wherein I might perhaps be sinning. For I fear that I bear a hollow name, and that I make more of outward display than is proper. O, how noble it is, and how much it matters, to bring a heart that is entirely pure both morning and evening, whenever we pray to Heaven, even in secret and in private!”*

This pious Prince tarnished his praises by the repudiation of his wife; the cause was his desire for male offspring. Many condemned this, while others approved, citing examples. However, the <term>Chancellor</term> **Tao fu**, a descendant of **Confucius**, taught that examples should be sought from the legitimate masters of virtue, **Yao** and **Shun** <note>Legendary sage-kings of China's antiquity.</note>. The <term>Chancellor</term> **Fu Bi** <note>original: "Fu pie"</note> is praised because, through his efforts and counsel, he saved the lives of more than 500,000 people who were wasting away from hunger.

**Xingzong** <note>original: "Hien çum"</note>, then the seventh King of the **Liao** <note>original: "Leao"</note> Barbarians, demanded through legates the return of ten cities in the Beijing region, which the founder of the [Song] family had recovered by force of arms. **Fu Bi** was sent as an envoy. Ultimately, the Emperor, being more desirous of peace, promised 200,000 pieces of gold and 300,000 rolls of silk annually in place of the cities. This was done—most shamefully—using the character *na* <note>original: "na"; 納</note>, which denotes a tributary payment or pension.

In the 41st year, **Yingzong** <note>original: "YM ÇUM"</note>, the son of the predecessor’s thirteenth brother, succeeded to the throne. The <term>Chancellor</term> **Han Qi** <note>original: "Han ki"</note> prudently reconciled the Prince with the Empress [Dowager], who was then holding the reins of the Empire.

At this time flourished the <term>Chancellor</term> **Sima** <note>original: "Sa ma"; referring to Sima Guang</note>, the most famous among historians, who compiled a massive work from two thousand volumes; he began his annals from **Huangdi** <note>original: "HOAM TI"</note>, the founder of the Chinese Monarchy.

...of wisdom. He favored literature immensely: he honored Mencius, the second philosopher of the Chinese <note>original: "Sinarum Philosophum"</note>, with the posthumous title of Duke.

Under this emperor and the following one, the authors of the "New Philosophy" <note>This refers to the Neo-Confucian movement, which sought to revitalize Confucianism in response to Buddhism and Taoism.</note> and interpreters of the ancient books flourished: **Cheng, Cheng, Zhang, Shao, etc.** <note>These are the influential thinkers Cheng Hao, Cheng Yi, Zhang Zai, and Shao Yong.</note> they were decorated with various titles of honor both in life and after death. When, during a time of famine, the sorrowful Prince withdrew to his private chambers, devoting himself to fasting and solitude to appease Heaven, **Wang Anshi** <note>original: "Vam ngan xe"</note>, a politician with atheistic views, said: 
> *“Why, O King, are you afflicted? There is no reason to fear Heaven; calamities happen by chance, not by design.”* 
To whom **Fu Bi** <note>original: "Fu pie"</note>, the <term>Chancellor</term> <note>original: "Colaus"; a high-ranking official or Grand Secretary</note> replied: 
> *“If the Prince does not fear and revere Heaven, what will there be eventually that he will not perpetrate?”* 
The same **Fu Bi** advised the prince not to seek out the sins of his subjects with excessive severity and scrutiny. 
> *“Greater evils,”* he said, *“arise from this. Let the ruler rather be like Heaven, which contemplates all things, both the right and the wrong; especially since these things themselves, sooner or later, reveal themselves and bring back either their reward or their punishment.”*

**Wang Anshi**, as he was a man from the highest class of the literati and possessed a versatile, shifty intellect, was the author of the "Ten Taxes" <note>Refers to the 'New Policies' (Xin Fa), a series of controversial socio-economic reforms.</note> to be established, a measure which greatly embittered the hearts of the people. Famine followed; the edicts and burdens were revoked, and behold, with a profusion of rain, Heaven rewarded the clemency of the Prince.

In the 2nd year of the Cycle, **SHENZONG** <note>original: "XIN ÇUM"</note> dies at the age of 38. In the 3rd year, **ZHEZONG** <note>original: "CHE ÇUM"</note>, his sixth son, succeeds him. His grandmother, the Empress, served as his guardian. A petition was offered by the Chancellor, recommending ten points in twenty words: 
1. Fear Heaven. 
2. Love the people. 
3. Perfect yourself. 
4. Devote yourself to study. 
5. Promote the wise. 
6. Listen to those who give counsel. 
7. Reduce taxes. 
8. Mitigate punishments. 
9. Shun extravagance. 
10. Beware of moral decay.

The Emperor repudiated his legitimate wife, defending his actions by the example of his predecessors. To this, the Chancellor said, *“It would be better, O Prince, to imitate the virtues of your ancestors than their sins.”* Flaring up in anger, the Emperor deprived his advisor of his magistrate's office.

In the 17th year, **ZHEZONG** dies at the age of 25. In the 18th year, **HUIZONG** <note>original: "HOEI ÇUM"</note>, the eleventh son of **SHENZONG**, succeeds him. He was well-instructed in the liberal arts, but being intent on luxury and jests, he committed the government to his grandmother. He immensely favored the eunuchs, whom he decorated with the dignity of petty kings <note>A rank usually reserved for the highest imperial nobility.</note>, which was usually given only to princes of the royal blood. He was also most addicted to superstition and the **Taoist** <note>original: "Tao"</note> sect.

In the 16th year of his reign, he bestowed the title of **Shangdi** <note>original: "Xam ti"</note> or "Supreme Deity" upon a certain famous hermit of that sect named **Zhang** <note>original: "Chamy"; likely referring to Zhang Daoling, the first Celestial Master of Taoism.</note>, who had flourished under the fifth **Han** dynasty.

# CHINESE MONARCHIES
<meta>catchword: year</meta>

...and he wished to be called the Supreme Pontiff of that sect <note>Emperor Huizong was deeply devoted to Taoism and took the title "Sovereign Lord of the Dao," effectively making himself the head of the religion.</note>. Sacred writers attribute the many subsequent evils and the ruin of the Empire to the atrocity of this sacrilege, by which the true Majesty of Heaven was so utterly despised and cast down.

The Emperor entered into an alliance with the *Kin* <note>The Jin Dynasty of the Jurchen people.</note> or Eastern Tartars against the *Liao* <note>The Khitan people who ruled northern China.</note> barbarians, whom he defeated in several battles. This extinguished the Liao kingdom, which had stood for 209 years under nine Princes. Its remnants fled to the West and founded a kingdom <note>This refers to the Qara Khitai or Western Liao.</note> which would be completely destroyed 100 years later by the Western Tartars <note>The Mongols.</note>. The Eastern Tartar now aimed for the Empire. He gave the name *Kin* <note>original: "Kin", meaning "Gold"</note> to his dominion and captured Beijing <note>original: "Pe kim"</note>, Shaanxi <note>original: "Xen si"</note>, and other regions. The Emperor, invited to negotiate the borders, went to the Tartar. He returned without success. The unhappy man set out again at the request of his advisors; but he was treacherously detained by the Tartar and forced, after laying aside his royal regalia, to travel beyond the kingdom and the Great Wall of China.

<margin>9. QINZONG, reigned 1 year.</margin>
In the 42nd year of the cycle, Huizong <note>original: "HOEI ÇUM"</note> died a captive in the *Shamo* <note>The Gobi Desert.</note> wilderness of Tartary at the age of 54. In the 43rd year, his eldest son Qinzong <note>original: "KIN ÇUM"</note> succeeded him, having been named by his dying father. At his father’s command, he removed six ministers guilty of treason. The Tartars invaded the court in Henan <note>original: "Ho nan"</note> province and led the Emperor and the Queens away into Tartary, leaving behind Empress Meng <note>original: "Mem"</note> because she claimed to have been repudiated. Many of the leading nobles forestalled the shame of barbarian captivity by choosing a voluntary death. The captive Emperor, however, died 30 years later at the age of 61.

<margin>10. GAOZONG, reigned 36 years.</margin>
In the 44th year, Gaozong <note>original: "CAO ÇUM"</note>, the ninth son of Huizong by his repudiated wife Meng, succeeded in the meantime. He transferred the court to the South, to Nanjing <note>original: "Nan kim"</note>, from which he was later compelled to move to the city of Hangzhou <note>original: "Ham cheu"</note> in Zhejiang <note>original: "Che kiam"</note> province. From this point on, they were called the Southern Song <note>original: "Sum"</note> family.

This Prince was a lover of peace and literature. In his first years, he won several victories over the Tartars and bandits through his most valiant general *Cum ye* <note>Likely the celebrated General Yue Fei, though the transcription "Cum ye" varies from other Latin accounts.</note>, who had emerged victorious in thirteen battles in the North. But this same Emperor, neglecting wise men, admitted wicked and perverse people into his council. He was so devoted to the sect of the Bonzes <note>Buddhist monks.</note> that he committed the administration of the Empire to an adopted son so that he might devote himself more intensely to superstitious meditations.

During this time, the King of the Tartars, wishing to win over the scholars as the foundation and flower of the Empire, personally visited the Academy <note>original: "Gymnasium"</note> and the temple of Confucius to pay him posthumous honors. When there were those who said there was no reason to honor a common man with royal rites, he replied:
> *“Although Confucius was not of a rank to deserve these honors, nonetheless his doctrine is worthy of being venerated with Royal rites.”*

He entered into peace with the Tartar, the Chinese Majesty not hesitating to sign with the name *Chen* <note>original: "Chin", meaning "subject" or "minister"</note> and *Gong* <note>original: "Cum", meaning "tributary"</note>, provided that the bodies of his parents, who had died eight years earlier—pledges dearer than the Empire itself—were restored to him. Once this was done, public joy and an amnesty were declared. Writers marvelously extol this filial piety of the son toward his parents.

In the 35th year of the Empire, the peace was broken, and the King of the Tartars headed south with 600,000 men. The city of Yangzhou <note>original: "Yam cheu"</note> was captured. Drawing his scimitar, the King threatened his own men with death unless they overcame their fear and crossed the Yangtze River <note>original: "Kiam"</note>. A mutiny arose in the army, in which the King himself was killed. Thus, with the task unfinished, they returned to the North.

In the 19th year of the Cycle, GAOZONG <note>original: "CAO ÇUM"</note> resigned the Empire to his adopted son; he died 25 years later without children, aged 84. In the 20th year, XIAOZONG <note>original: "HIAO ÇUM"</note> succeeded him, who was a grandson of the founder of this family after the sixth generation. A Prince commended for his piety, he ruled peacefully in every way, because the Tartar King SHIZONG <note>original: "Xi çum"</note> was likewise pious, wise, and of a peaceful disposition.

During his reign flourished Zhu Xi <note>original: "Chu hi"</note>, the most famous interpreter of the ancient books. He died over seventy years old, in the 16th year of the reign of Ningzong <note>The original text says "Kim çum," which may refer to the Tartar Jin Emperor or a transcription error for Ningzong.</note>. Having performed various duties under four Emperors, he was honored after death with the title *Wengong* <note>original: "Ven cum", meaning "Prince of Letters"</note>, and obtained posthumous titles alongside the other disciples of Confucius. Their names are displayed on tablets in the Temple of Confucius, a custom that still flourishes today; for when a man's virtue, wisdom, and integrity in office are established, the Emperors are accustomed to record them in the register and order of Confucius's fellow disciples, so they may share in the honors presented at stated times by the City Prefects.

In the 46th year, XIAOZONG died at age 68. In the 47th year, GUANGZONG succeeded, the third-born son of his predecessor.

In the 51st year, while before an assembly of his nobles, GUANGZONG was seized by a stroke and fell to the ground, and could not be restored to himself. He died later at age 54.

In the 52nd year, NINGZONG <note>original: "NYM ÇUM"</note>, the third-born son of the predecessor, was elevated to the throne, though he resisted greatly. A Prince of peaceful disposition in both deed and name, pious and modest; he allowed himself to be ruled, if not deceived, by his own people. He issued an edict forbidding anyone to publish annals according to their own whim.

In the 8th year of the Empire, a fire in the Palace lasted four days. Likewise, 36 years later, a fire occurred in the royal city of Hangzhou <note>original: "Ham cheu"</note>, by which 530,000 houses were consumed.

<margin>11. **XI ZONG**, otherwise known as *Jiajing*, which means "exalted tranquility." He reigned 45 years.</margin>
In the 19th year of the Cycle (1522), *Shi Zong* <note>The Jiajing Emperor</note>, the second-born of his predecessor, succeeded him at thirteen years of age.

In the beginning, he showed the qualities of a good Prince, being pious and prudent. He repeatedly examined petitions personally. He was excessively fond of *Poetry*. During times of famine, he asked to be warned if he had committed any sin, while providing for his subjects from the royal treasury and the King’s food stores. He ordered the Great Wall to be repaired. He was intensely devoted to the dreams and prayers of the <term>Bonzes|A term used by early missionaries to describe Buddhist monks</term>, and was even more studious regarding the *Ambrosia of Immortality* <note>Referring to Daoist elixirs intended to grant eternal life</note> and the *Art of Alchemy*, sending envoys through every province to seek these out. Indeed, in the 18th year of his reign, he considered abdicating the Empire for a time and handing over the care of affairs to his son and heir, had the high officials not stood in his way; they had argued in vain through repeated petitions that the two sects of *Fo* <note>Buddhism</note> and *Lao-kiun* <note>Laozi, representing Daoism</note> should be completely eliminated. He renewed the Law of the Founder regarding the title of *Confucius*, whom he wished to be called nothing other than *Sien su*, which means "the deceased Master" <note>This was a significant move to strip Confucius of kingly titles and emphasize his role as a teacher</note>. Furthermore, he forbade the casting of statues of him, allowing only a commemorative tablet. A poor man, forced by poverty, intended to sell and prostitute his two daughters; upon hearing this, both girls threw themselves into the river. The Emperor ordered a tomb to be built for them, titled "The Pair of Virgins."

In the 47th year of the Cycle, the 29th of his reign, the Tartars approached the court with an army of 60,000, but they were cut down and put to flight by the Chinese army, with more than 200 military leaders captured. The following year, the Tartar leader sent an embassy asking for forgiveness for his deed, requesting permission to come every year to sell horses. The Emperor agreed, but because experience taught that this provided an excuse for seditions and brawls between the Governors and Merchants, and that they carried out plundering under that pretext, the horse trade was later forbidden.

In the 49th year of the Cycle, the 31st of the reign (which was the year 1552 of the Christian era), on the second of December, the Apostle of the East, *St. Francis Xavier*, fell asleep in the Lord on the Chinese island of *Shangchuan* <note>original: "Sancheu"</note>, belonging to the province of *Guangdong* <note>original: "Quam tum"</note>, in the 55th year of his age.

### THE CHINESE MONARCHY
#### Page 86

In the 50th year of the cycle, maritime pirates under the leader **Hoam che** <note>original: "Hoam che"; likely referring to the notorious pirate lord Wang Zhi</note> infested the Chinese coasts with a fleet of 100 ships.
In the 52nd year, the **Japanese**, who previously used to come frequently with gifts as subjects in a tributary relationship, now arrived as pirates and open enemies. They landed on the coast of the **Zhejiang** province <note>original: "Che kiam"</note> numbering four thousand. 1,800 were slaughtered to the point of extinction; the rest slipped away in flight and were swallowed by the sea while seeking their ships. In the following year, ten thousand landed again, but they were cut down in four battles by a leader of only 900 soldiers named **Cao lim**; soon after, they were surrounded on all sides by arriving soldiers and utterly wiped out. After seven more years, new Japanese forces invaded the maritime coast of the **Fujian** province <note>original: "Fo kien"</note>. The military leader **Cie** <note>likely the famous general Qi Jiguang</note> attacked the unprepared enemy by surprise and destroyed them. In the North, the military leader **Lieu han** advanced beyond the Wall <note>The Great Wall</note> with an army to fight against the **Tartars** <note>A European term for the Mongol tribes</note>; however, as they had slipped away into the interior and their own forests, he achieved nothing of value except for 28 Tartar heads and 170 camels.

<margin>
**CYCLE 72**
The year of Christ 1564.
</margin>

In the 3rd year of the Cycle—the 45th and final year of the Emperor <note>the Jiajing Emperor</note>—a humble petition was offered to him. In it, he was severely warned to look to himself and the Empire, so that the end of his reign might match its beginnings. It stated that for twenty years and more, the statutes and laws of the ancestors had been falling into ruin; unless help arrived, the Empire was verging toward destruction. It noted that the son and heir to the Empire was rarely admitted to speak with his father; that advisors of incorruptible faith were cast off or treated harshly; and that because of the Emperor's mistrust and suspicions, they were unworthily punished for trivial reasons. The petition accused him of indulging more than was right in the pleasures of gardens and leisure with flocks of girls, neglecting in a way his legitimate wife, the Empress. It further claimed that men ignorant of war, and more greedy for gold than honor, were placed in charge of armies; the treasury was being exhausted on building palaces and gardens, on the "nonsense and prayers of the Buddhist monks" <note>original: "Bonziorum naeniis"; the author uses a dismissive term for Buddhist rituals</note>, and on the **pharmacies of feigned immortality** which they falsely claim descended from heaven itself. It argued as if anyone had ever been found immune to the law of dying since the times of **Yao** and **Xun** <note>legendary Sage-Kings of ancient China</note>. The Emperor burned with rage at these words and threw the petition to the ground; but picking it up again and re-reading it, he sighed, showing signs of regret—though it was too late. For in the 10th Moon <note>the tenth lunar month</note>, he was seized by illness; having taken the **poison of immortality** <note>original: "immortalitatis toxico"; referring to alchemical elixirs containing mercury or lead, which the Emperor believed would make him immortal but which actually caused his death</note>, he felt himself to be mortal and died at the age of 58.

However, the Prince was impatient with being warned, and frequently cast down those who offered warnings to a lower rank of dignity; he changed many things that had been rightly established by his father according to his own whim.

# HISTORY OF THE CHINESE MONARCHY

<page-num>92</page-num>

...kept the marriage bed inviolate <note>This refers to the Emperor’s personal morality and fidelity to his Empress, contrasting him with more decadent predecessors</note>. This Emperor had advised his predecessor brother to eliminate the Prince of the Eunuchs (named Guei cum <note>original: "Guei cum"; refers to the infamous Wei Zhongxian</note>), who was by far the most powerful and cruel. He warned that from this man's arrogance and insolence, the ruin of both the Court and the Empire was imminent. Guei cum, therefore, conscious of his own guilt, soon took poison during this Emperor's reign to prevent a more severe punishment. The dead man's body was cut into pieces by the raging people; a vast amount of gold and pearls was confiscated for the treasury; and many temples, which had been erected to his memory while he was alive by flatterers throughout the Empire, were destroyed by fire and leveled to the ground.

The Emperor, because a fierce war had to be waged against domestic enemies—namely, the rebels—sent the Eunuch Yuen <note>likely referring to General Yuan Chonghuan, though the text identifies him here as a eunuch</note> with a new army and broad powers to negotiate with the Tartar <note>The Manchus</note>. However, Yuen, a deceitful and treacherous man, was secretly corrupted by gold and negotiated under unfair conditions. The Emperor rescinded the peace. To force the Emperor to accept it, Yuen first removed his rival, the most loyal General Mao ven lum <note>Mao Wenlong</note>, by poisoning him at a banquet, and then encouraged the Tartar to invade Peking <note>Beijing</note> by another route. The expedition proceeded as desired right up to the court, which they besieged. General Yuen was called to help; he arrived and allowed himself to be brought in over the city walls, fearing nothing, but soon after an investigation was held, he was convicted of treason and executed. Upon hearing this, the Tartar lifted the siege and returned to Leao tum <note>Liaodong</note> laden with spoils. After this, the fortunes of war were uncertain for both sides for about eight years.

***

*In the 8th year of the Cycle (1631), the first members of the Holy Order of Preachers <note>the Dominicans</note>, and later the Order of Saint Francis <note>the Franciscans</note>, enter China.*

*In the 10th year of the Cycle, the 6th year of the Emperor (1632), the pious Paul Xu <note>original: "Siu Doctus Paulus"; refers to Xu Guangqi</note> died; he was a Grand Secretary <note>original: "Colaus"</note>, former President of the Ministry of Rites, and a pillar of the Christian cause. To defend it, he offered an Apology <note>A formal written defense</note> during the persecution, in which he offered his estates, his resources, his family, and even himself as a security, if it could be proved that the Christian Law <note>original: "Lex Christiana"</note> contained anything unholy. To promote and strengthen this cause, he successfully proposed Fathers Terentius <note>Johann Schreck</note>, Rho <note>Giacomo Rho</note>, and Adam <note>Johann Adam Schall von Bell</note>, etc., to the Emperor to restore Astronomy and the Calendar. He left Peter Li <note>Li Tianjing</note>, also a Grand Secretary, as successor to this task. Through the work of the Eunuchs, the leading ladies of the Women's Quarters <note>the Gynaeceum</note>, with the Empress’s consent, received the faith and baptism.*

***

*In the 12th year of the Cycle, the 8th year of the Emperor [1634], the Tartar King Ticum <note>Nurhaci</note> died; he was succeeded by his son, called çun te <note>Hong Taiji, whose reign title was Chongde</note> for his cultivation of virtue, who was the father of the one who would found the next dynasty. He was a prudent and courteous prince, for as a boy he had lived hidden among the Chinese and was excellently learned in Chinese letters, language, and customs. Because of this, through his kindness, he won over and attracted many Chinese generals and officials, who were weary of such corrupt governance and alienated by the severity of the [Chinese] Emperor, who was raging fiercely because of his unfortunate military failures.*

In this and the following years, there was nothing but internal wars, slaughter, and plundering by eight armies of bandits, which was the primary cause of the Empire’s ruin; for it seemed already sufficiently fortified against the invasions of the Tartars <note>The Manchus</note>. Eight leaders of the rebels fought among themselves for supreme power, until finally the whole force of arms devolved to two rebel princes, *Li* <note>Li Zicheng</note> and *Cham* <note>Zhang Xianzhong</note>. These two, lest they be consumed by one another, withdrew from each other: *Cham* indeed applied his mind and army to the Western provinces of *Sü chuen* <note>Sichuan</note> and *Hu quam* <note>Huguang</note> (of whom more will be said later); *Li*, however, turned toward the North. From the province of *Xen si* <note>Shaanxi</note>, which he had partially occupied, he laid siege to the capital of *Ho nan* <note>Henan</note> province <note>The city of Kaifeng</note>, but he was forced to break it off after a defeat. The siege was resumed and lasted six months with such steadfastness from the besieged that human flesh was put up for sale as food. Finally, the Emperor's army arrived to bring supplies, but while expecting and fearing no such thing, it brought utter destruction: for while it attempted to destroy the army of bandits by breaking the dikes of the Yellow River <note>original: "Crocei fluminis"</note>, it happened that the entire city, with 300,000 inhabitants, was swallowed by the waters. This wretched slaughter occurred on the ninth of *October* in the year 1642.

*Li*, meanwhile, having gained control of the whole province and then *Xen si*, killed all the officials wherever they were and fined former officials, but he treated the common people kindly, even remitting their taxes and burdens. As a result, many Imperial troops flocked to him, and *Li* himself, the leader of the bandits, now grown so powerful, claimed the title of Emperor for himself. Soon, after subduing the province of *Xen si*, he entered the region of Peking <note>Beijing</note> and marched securely toward the Royal City itself. Long before this, he had secretly sent thousands of spies who were to stir up trouble upon his arrival; he was not at all doubtful that the city would be surrendered, thanks to the extreme treachery of traitors and the discord between the officials and the Eunuchs. 70,000 garrison troops were in charge of defending the city, and yet on the third day after his arrival, the gates were opened voluntarily. He entered with an army of 300,000 and went straight to the palace of the Emperor himself. The Emperor, intent on establishing fasts and prayers to the Bonzes <note>term: Buddhist monks</note> and ignorant of all that was happening, finally recognized he had been betrayed. He tried to go out through the gates with 600 armed men to fall gloriously in battle, but in despair of both counsel and circumstances, and deserted by everyone, he returned to the palace and withdrew into the garden. There, on the hem of his garment, he wrote these words in his own blood:

-> My people have betrayed me, <-
-> decide concerning me as you please, <-
-> so long as you do not harm my people. <-

Then, with a drawn sword, while he tried to kill his marriageable daughter lest she fall into the hands of the bandits, she dodged the blow and fell unconscious, her arm mutilated. Finally, having wrapped a sash around his neck, the Emperor hanged himself in the 36th year of his age. With him, the name and the whole of the Empire...

In this and the following years, there was nothing but internal wars, slaughters, and plunders carried out by eight armies of bandits. This pitiable slaughter occurred on the 9th of October in the year 1642.

Because of this, many Imperial troops flocked to him, and *Li* himself, once a leader of bandits, increased in power so much that he now claimed the title of Emperor for himself. Soon, having subdued *Shaanxi* province, he entered the province of Beijing <note>Pekinensem</note> and marched securely toward the Royal City itself. Long before his arrival, he had secretly sent thousands of spies there to stir up crowds when he appeared. He had no doubt the city would be surrendered, largely due to the extreme perfidy of traitors and the discords between the Governors and the Eunuchs. Though 70,000 guards were in charge of defending the city, the gates were opened voluntarily on the third day of his arrival. He entered the city with an army of 300,000 and went straight to the palace of the Emperor. The Emperor, intent on observing fasts and Buddhist prayers <note>original: "Bonzaicis supplicationibus"</note> and ignorant of all that was happening, finally realized he was betrayed. He tried to leave through the gates with 600 armed men to die gloriously, but his plans and affairs were hopeless. Deserted by everyone, he returned to the palace and withdrew into the garden, where he wrote these words in his own blood on the hem of his garment: <note>original: "Mei me prodiderunt, de me statue quod placuerit, modò populo meo ne noceas."</note> *My own people have betrayed me; do with me what you please, so long as you do not harm my people.* Then, drawing a scimitar, he tried to kill his daughter of marriageable age so she would not fall into the hands of the bandits; she dodged the blow and fell unconscious, her arm mutilated. Finally, wrapping a sash around his neck, the Emperor hanged himself at the age of 36. With him, the name and the whole of the Empire...

# THE CHINESE MONARCHY

<meta>catchword: the West-</meta>

The imperial lineage, consisting of 80,000 members as they say, was gradually extinguished. Following this example, the supreme Grand Secretary <note>original: "Colaus," a Latinization of the Chinese term *Gelaos*</note> hanged himself there, as did the queens and the more faithful Eunuchs in other places. The royal corpse <note>Emperor Chongzhen</note>, sought for a long time, was finally found by chance on the second day and brought before the Tyrant <note>The rebel Li Zicheng</note> sitting on the throne; by him, it was treated with many barbarous insults. The Emperor's two young sons were beheaded (for the firstborn had escaped by flight), and all the Prefects were most cruelly slaughtered. The entire city was then abandoned to the fury and lust of the soldiers. Soon after, the Tyrant prepared himself to subdue the most faithful General *Wu Sangui* <note>original: "V fan quei"</note>, who commanded the Chinese army with supreme power against the Tartars <note>The Manchus</note> in *Liaodong* <note>original: "Leao tum"</note>. The city and its very strong fortress, located 70 leagues from the Royal city, were besieged. In order to compel the son to surrender, the bandit placed the father himself before the city walls, threatening him with a most bitter death unless the city was handed over. *Wu Sangui*, looking at his father from the wall, begged his forgiveness on bended knees, attesting that he owed more to the Emperor and the fatherland than to his father, and thus he would rather die a thousand times than serve a bandit shamefully. The father praised his son and steadfastly offered himself to the executioner for the sake of that same fatherland. But the son, seeking to avenge the death of both the Emperor and his father, sent an embassy with gifts to the Tartar King, inviting him to take up arms and bring aid against the Tyrant under agreed conditions. The King arrived eagerly with 60,000 men. The siege was broken, and the forces of the robbers were routed. The Tyrant *Li*, having returned to the palace but finding no safety there, plundered the royal treasures, gave the city and palace to the flames, and fled with his army into the province of *Shaanxi* <note>original: "Xen si"</note>, while the Tartar pursued the fleeing crowd with swift horses and weapons. Meanwhile, the Tartar King *Hong Taiji* <note>original: "çum te"</note> died at the entrance to China, after he had declared his younger son the heir, entrusting the care of the war and the Empire to the Prince Regent *Dorgon* <note>original: "A ma vam," from the Manchu *Ama-wang* or Father-Prince</note>, the boy's uncle. Soon the six-year-old boy, wise beyond his years, entered the city in triumph; he was received with the common congratulations and applause of the whole people as the Defender of the fatherland, placed upon the throne, and hailed as Emperor. Everyone acclaimed with one voice: *“Long live the Emperor, long live (Wan sui, Wan sui) for ten and ten thousand years”* <note>original: "vivat Imperator, vivat (Van sui, Van sui) decem & decem millibus annorum"</note>; and this voice of the people conferred the Empire upon him.

**SHUNZHI** <note>original: "XUN CHI"</note> was the name of the Emperor, and he was the founder of the new Tartar-Chinese Imperial family called the *Qing* <note>original: "Tai cim"</note>, which means *Great Purity*. He established the first year of his Empire—as if it were a good omen for himself—as the very year which was the seventeenth and most fatal for his predecessor *Chongzhen* <note>original: "çum chim"</note>. It was the 21st year of the 73rd Cycle, and the year 1644 after Christ.

*Wu Sangui* (by whom it is believed the Tyrant *Li* was killed in battle), now recognizing too late that to keep away the dogs he had incautiously admitted lions, accepted from the Tartar the dignity of a Prince and the title *Pingxi* <note>original: "Pim si"</note>, or "Pacificator of the West- <note>The text breaks here at the catchword "occa-" for "occidentalis"</note>

The bandit <note>The rebel leader Li Zicheng</note> fled, having designated the royal metropolis of **Xi'an** <note>original: "Si ngan"</note> in the province of **Shaanxi** as his seat, which he had previously devastated with fire and sword. The Tartar <note>The Manchu Qing forces</note>, having successfully subdued the Northern provinces, turned his mind and his weapons toward the Southern ones. From there, the army marched to the metropolis of **Zhejiang** province, in which the Prince of **Lu** <note>original: "Lo vam"</note> refused the title of Emperor. Seeing the city surrounded by the Tartars, and wishing to prevent the slaughter of his people, he knelt on the walls in a posture of supplication, saying:

> "Decide what you wish concerning me; behold, I offer myself as a victim for my subjects."

Having said this, he went out from the city and surrendered himself to the Tartar; this piety, if it did not save the Prince, certainly saved the city and its citizens. In the province of **Fujian**, another grandson of **Wanli**, called **Longwu** <note>original: "Lum vu"</note>, was proclaimed Emperor, but he was soon killed after the Tartar occupied the entire province peacefully. There was at that time a Great Admiral <note>original: "Architalassus"</note> originating from **Fujian** named **Zheng Zhilong** <note>original: "Chin chi lum," also known as Nicholas Iquan</note>, who had first served the Portuguese at Macau and, having been washed in the sacred font <note>baptized</note>, had received the name **Nicholas**. From small beginnings and through great commerce with the Spaniards and the Dutch, he rose from a famous pirate to become a commander of vast fleets. He had submitted himself first to the Emperor **Longwu**, and then to the Tartar, though only feigningly. Created a Prince by the Tartar and invited to a solemn banquet—deluded by the appearance of attaining greater honors at court—he was honorably escorted there <note>where he was actually taken captive</note>. Meanwhile, his son **Koxinga** <note>original: "Que sim," referring to Zheng Chenggong</note>, having become more cautious, succeeded to the command of his father's entire fleet; he could be moved from his purpose of loyalty toward the King and fatherland by neither his father's exhortations nor the Tartar's promises.

Now the Tartar army descended to subdue the provinces of **Guangdong** <note>original: "Quam tum"</note> and then **Guangxi**, capturing every city and place in its path with ease. However, in the province of **Guangxi**, the course of victories was halted somewhat. There was a Viceroy there named **Thomas Qu** <note>original: "Kiu Thomas," referring to Qu Shisi</note>, and the supreme commander of the entire military (which had fled there from various provinces), **Luke Chen** <note>original: "Chin Lucas," referring to Jiao Lian</note>; both were Christians. The battle was fought fiercely; at last, the Tartars were defeated and cut down. Soon the victorious Chinese elected **Yongli** <note>original: "Yum lie"</note> as Emperor, a descendant of the **Wanli** line. Having been brought from the metropolis of **Guizhou** province where he had been acting as Prince, he established his royal seat in the city of **Zhaoqing** in **Guangdong** province. His chief counselor was the Eunuch **Achilles Pang** <note>original: "Pan Achilleus," referring to Pang Tianshou</note>, who was most zealous for the Christian faith. Through his efforts and those of Father **Andreas Koffler**, the Emperor's own mother, his wife, and his son—the heir to the Empire—were washed in the sacred font <note>baptized</note>. Soon the six-year-old boy, wise beyond his years, entered the city in triumph. He was received with the common congratulation and applause of the entire people as the Deliverer of the fatherland, and placed upon the throne, he was hailed as Emperor. Everyone acclaimed with one voice: "Long live the Emperor, long live! (**Wan sui, Wan sui** <note>original: *Van fui*, meaning "Ten thousand years"</note>)." This voice of the people conferred the Empire upon him. The Emperor was called **SHUNZHI**, and he was the founder of the new Tartar-Chinese Imperial family called **Qing** <note>original: *Tacim*, from *Da Qing*, meaning "Great Purity"</note>. He established the first year of his Empire—as if it were a good omen—to be the same year that was the seventeenth and most fatal year of his predecessor **Chongzhen** <note>original: *Cum chim*</note>. This was the 21st year of the 73rd Cycle, which was the year of Christ 1644.

**Wu Sangui** (by whom it is believed the Tyrant **Li** was killed in battle), now recognizing too late that he had incautiously admitted lions to ward off the dogs, accepted from the Tartar the dignity and title of Prince **Pingxi** <note>original: *Pim si*, meaning "Pacificator of the West"</note>...

[Beijing having fallen] was assigned as the seat of the government, replacing the royal capital **Xi'an** <note>original: *Si ngan*</note> in the province of **Shaanxi** <note>original: *Xen si*</note>, which a bandit had previously devastated with fire and sword. The Tartar <note>The Manchus of the Qing Dynasty</note>, having successfully subdued the northern provinces, turned his mind and his weapons toward the south. By the following year, **Hongguang** <note>original: *Hum quam*, the first Southern Ming emperor</note>, the grandson of Emperor **Wanli**, had already been proclaimed Emperor in the capital of **Nanjing** <note>original: *Nan kim*</note>; but he was soon captured and led away to Beijing, where he was strangled along with the firstborn son of **Chongzhen** <note>original: *çum chim*</note> (though whether this son was the real one or a pretender is uncertain). From there, the army moved to the capital of **Zhejiang** <note>original: *Che kiam*</note> province, where the Prince of **Lu** <note>original: *Lo vam*</note> refused the title of Emperor. Seeing the city surrounded by the Tartars, and wishing to prevent the slaughter of his people, he knelt in supplication upon the walls. "Concerning me," he said, "decide what you will; behold, I offer myself as a victim for my subjects." <note>original: *de me, inquit, quod vultis statuite, pro meis subditis ecce me victimam*</note>. Having said this, he went out from the city and surrendered himself to the Tartar; this act of piety, if it did not save the Prince, certainly saved the city and its citizens. In the province of **Fujian** <note>original: *Fo kien*</note>, another grandson of Wanli, called **Longwu** <note>original: *Lum vu*</note>, was proclaimed Emperor, but he was soon killed after the Tartars peacefully occupied the entire province. There was at that time an Admiral <note>original: *Architalassus*</note> hailing from Fujian called **Zheng Zhilong** <note>original: *Chin chi lum*, also known as Iquan</note>, who had first served the Portuguese at Macau and, having been washed in the sacred font <note>baptized</note>, had received the name **Nicholas**. From small beginnings, and later through great trade with the Spanish and the Dutch, he rose from being a famous pirate to a leader of vast fleets. He first subjected himself to the Emperor **Longwu**, and later to the Tartar—though only in pretense. Created a Prince <note>original: *Regulus*</note> by the Tartar and invited to a solemn banquet, he was deceived by the prospect of attaining greater honors at court and was honorably led away there [into captivity]. Meanwhile, his son **Koxinga** <note>original: *Que sim*, also known as Zheng Chenggong</note>, having become more cautious, succeeded to the command of his father's entire fleet; he was not to be moved from his purpose of loyalty to the King and fatherland by any of his father's exhortations or the Tartar's promises.

Now the Tartar army descended to conquer the provinces of **Guangdong** <note>original: *Quam tum*</note> and then **Guangxi** <note>original: *Quam si*</note>, taking whatever cities and places were in its path with little effort. However, in the province of **Guangxi**, the course of victories was somewhat halted. The Viceroy there was **Thomas Qu** <note>original: *Kiu Thomas*, i.e., Qu Shisi</note>, and the supreme commander of the entire military (which had fled there from various provinces) was **Lucas Jiao** <note>original: *Chin Lucas*, i.e., Jiao Lian</note>; both were Christians. The fighting was fierce; finally, the Tartars were defeated and slaughtered. Soon the victorious Chinese elected **Yongli** <note>original: *Yum lie*</note> as Emperor, a descendant of the **Wanli** line. He was brought from the capital of **Guizhou** <note>original: *Quei cheu*</note> province, where he had been acting as Prince, and established his royal seat in the city of **Zhaoqing** <note>original: *Chao kin*</note> in Guangdong province. His chief counselor was the head Eunuch **Achilles Pang** <note>original: *Pan Achilleus*, i.e., Pang Tianshou</note>, who was most zealous for the Christian faith. Through his efforts, and together with Father **Andreas Koffler**, the Emperor's own mother, his wife, and his son—the heir to the Empire—were washed in the sacred font. And indeed, it was hoped that this son, in name as well as in deed, would become the "Constantine of the Chinese." <note>The heir was baptized with the name Constantine</note>. The Queen, with the Emperor's consent, certainly sent **Michael Boym** as an envoy to offer obedience to the Holy See, as the City [Rome] and the World have acknowledged.

# THE CHINESE MONARCHIES

The Emperor, of whom mention was made above <note>This refers to the Yongli Emperor, the last claimant to the Ming throne</note>. He had himself fled into the Kingdom of Mian Guo <note>original: *Mien que*, known commonly as Pegu, or modern-day Myanmar</note>, which borders the province of Yunnan, when the Manchus <note>original: *Tartarus*, a common 17th-century term for the Manchu people</note> arrived with fresh troops. After sending threatening letters to the King [of Burma], the Manchu general demanded the return of the fugitive; he was handed over without delay along with his entire family. The unfortunate Yongli <note>original: *Yum lie*</note> was brought to the capital and strangled with a bowstring. Two Queens—his mother and his wife—along with others, were taken to Beijing <note>original: *Pekinum*</note> and are kept even today with honor in a separate palace; as is well known, they remain constant in the Christian faith they once embraced <note>Many members of the Southern Ming court, including the Empress Dowager and the Empress, had been converted to Catholicism by Jesuit missionaries</note>.

This year was also fatal for the Manchu-Chinese Emperor Shunzhi <note>original: *Xun chi*</note>, whose reign began better than it ended. The cause of his untimely death was his unbridled love for a young woman for whom the wretch was dying of passion. In order to possess her, he summoned her husband to him, and as if rebuking him for poorly managing his duties, he struck him with a blow and dismissed him. This man returned home and died three days later, consumed by sorrow. Upon learning this, the Emperor called the wife to the court and, contrary to custom, created her as a Queen second only to the legitimate Empress. This new bride bore him a young son. His birth was celebrated with royal solemnity. After three months, the infant died, and the mother soon followed. How mournful the death of both proved to the King is clear from the fact that, maddened by fury and grief, he would have committed suicide with a sword had the Queen Mother and the Eunuchs not restrained his impulse. Nevertheless, he wished to appease the spirits of his concubine with the voluntary deaths of thirty men—an execrable rite among the Chinese <note>original: *Sinas*</note>, a barbaric custom which his successor later abolished. He also ordered not only the nobles of the court but the governors of the entire Empire to wear mourning and funeral attire for a month, and the common people for three days, as if for an Empress—a title with which he honored her after her death.

Indeed, the extravagance of the funeral preparations exceeded all dignity and propriety. The concubine's body, enclosed in a sarcophagus of rare value and covered in pearls, was placed on a pyre according to the Manchu <note>original: *Tartarico*</note> custom. Into this fire, a great quantity of gold, silver, silk, and royal furniture was thrown and consumed by flames. Two hundred thousand gold pieces were also distributed among the soldiers and the poor. The King himself, wailing like a woman, placed the ashes of the deceased into a silver urn with his own hands; the dying Queen had uniquely entrusted him with her love. Meanwhile, crowds of Bonzes <term>Bonzes <gloss>A Portuguese-derived term used by early missionaries to refer to Buddhist monks</gloss></term>, numbering about two thousand, had so maddened the wretched King with their chants, dirges, and foolish superstitions that he invited the palace maidens and eunuchs to take up the habit of priests. Furthermore, falling into a depraved state of mind, he shaved his head and dressed in the food and clothing of the monks. He even erected three shrines within the Palace itself to worship the Idols he had previously despised, visiting one temple after another throughout the city.
