However, having been admitted a few days before the Emperor's death, and being forbidden to kneel in his presence, the guest heard the Emperor speak and was then offered a drink of tea <note>original: *cha*</note>; having spoken no more, the Emperor sent him home. Meanwhile, the Emperor was heard by his attendants accusing himself of negligence. To give proof of a serious, though late, repentance, he took up a brush and wrote twelve points of amnesty to be proclaimed throughout the Empire. Finally, feeling that his time to depart had come, he called four great lords <note>These were the four regents: Sonin, Ebilun, Suksaha, and Oboi</note> to him and confessed that the Empire had been poorly administered through his own fault: that he had shown too little patronage to his father and grandfather, as well as to the minor princes and those who deserved well; that he had despised his mother's advice; that out of a greed for gold he had defrauded the nobles of their stipends; that being addicted to "curious things" <note>This likely refers to his interest in European gadgets, clocks, or perhaps religious curiosities brought by the Jesuits</note> he had uselessly squandered much; that he had not treated the people as his children; that he had admitted and nurtured eunuchs; and finally, that he had loved the recently deceased Queen <note>Consort Donggo, whose death in 1660 devastated the Emperor</note> immoderately, and in mourning her had been a burden both to himself and his subjects. Lastly, commending his eight-year-old son to the guardianship of the four-man council, and being ready now to see his ancestors <note>original: *patres suos*</note>, he asked for a garment; when he had put it on, he immediately said farewell, and drawing together his legs and arms, he said, "Behold, I depart." Soon after, he died of smallpox <note>original: *variolis*</note> around midnight, in the 24th year of his age.

The following morning, all the Buddhist monks <term>Bonzes: a word used by early European writers to describe Buddhist or East Asian clergy</term> were ejected from the Palace. Around midday, the body was placed in a coffin, to be set upon a funeral pyre one hundred days later (as is the custom for those who die of smallpox). The next day, the eight-year-old heir was placed on the throne and was duly saluted as Emperor by all.

The father had chosen him, leaving aside the firstborn, according to the custom used among the Manchus <note>original: *Tartaros*</note>, where the father’s will alone is observed as if it had descended from heaven.

In the beginning, under the four guardians, the state was administered moderately and peacefully. The chief of the eunuchs, as the torch and instigator of so many evils, was beheaded. Four thousand eunuchs were banished from the palace, with a thousand remaining reserved for the lowest and most menial services. An edict was promulgated by which, under penalty of death, the inhabitants of the entire sea coast across six provinces were ordered to move their soil and migrate nearly three leagues <note>approximately 9-10 miles</note> into the interior of the mainland. Their villages, forts, and coastal towns were leveled to the ground, and all maritime trade was strictly forbidden. # MONARCHY OF CHINA

...they were dragged along and perished from hardships and hunger. Not a few Christian temples, along with the shrines of idols, were abolished; indeed, even the city of Macau was about to suffer the same ruin, with the Portuguese being ordered to relocate, had not Adam <note>Johann Adam Schall von Bell (1591–1666), a German Jesuit and astronomer who became a high-ranking official at the Qing court</note> especially come to the aid of the city in its peril. From this time, the power of the maritime enemy <note>Refers to the Ming loyalist Koxinga and his forces</note> was finally so weakened that after about 20 years, the island of Formosa <note>Taiwan</note> would eventually fall into the power of the Tartars <note>The Manchu Qing Dynasty</note>.

In the 41st year of the cycle, the 3rd year of the Emperor Kangxi <note>original: *Cam hi*</note> (1664), a most grave and universal persecution was stirred up against the preachers of the Christian Law, regarding which consult the reports of Fathers Gabiani, Rougemont, and Grimaldi <note>original: *Grelon*</note>. An edict of the King was promulgated against the Religion as a teacher of rebellion and wicked doctrine. Its head, Johann Adam, and three companions were driven as defendants, weighted down with nine chains, and dragged from prison to various tribunals. All European priests were summoned to the court. Christian books, medals, and similar items were ordered to be committed to the flames as tokens of rebellion; however, the violation of churches and sacred images, and the harassment of Christians, was forbidden.

In the year 1665, on April 16th, in a general assembly of all the Orders, Adam was condemned first to the noose, and then to a type of most cruel punishment in which the body of the living person is mutilated by very small dissections <term>lingchi</term> <note>often called "death by a thousand cuts," this was a form of execution used in China for high treason</note>. The sentence was brought to be confirmed by the assembly of Princes and the Council of Four <note>The four regents: Sonin, Ebilun, Suksaha, and Oboi</note>, when suddenly the whole city trembled and was shaken by repeated movements <note>An earthquake, which the court interpreted as a celestial sign of displeasure</note>. A public amnesty was declared, and the prisoners were released from the jails, with the exception of Adam alone. After a month, when the palace had burned down on the day before the King's birthday, he was released from his chains and sent away free. The European priests who had come to the court were banished (with four exceptions) to the capital of Guangdong <note>original: *Quamtum*</note> province; these included three from the Order of St. Dominic, one from the Seraphic family <note>The Franciscans</note>, and 21 from the Society of Jesus. On August 15th, Father Adam died piously and peacefully; he was later to be declared innocent and granted a large estate for his burial, as well as his former titles and a eulogy from the Emperor.

In the 45th year of the cycle (1666), Sonin <note>original: *Sony*</note>, the eldest of the Council of Four, died. Kangxi <note>original: *Cam hi*</note> took up the governance of the Empire with solemn ritual, which he moderates today with great praise for his prudence and equity. At the beginning, he certainly gave a specimen of his own justice, or rather divine justice, in the case of another of the Council of Four named Suksaha <note>original: *Su ca ma*</note>. As this man was eminent above the others in counsel and authority, so he was a more bitter enemy of the Christian name the more he concealed it. Accused of twenty faults, he was snatched away into chains, and with his goods confiscated to the treasury, he was condemned to a most bitter death. The King signed the sentence, mitigating the punishment of the sick man and commuting it to execution by the noose. Therefore, publicly on the day before the Nones of September, seven of his sons and grandsons were beheaded, his third son was cut into small pieces, and finally, the father’s throat was crushed by a cord.

->### OF THE CHINESE MONARCHY<-

...as well as **Guangxi** <note>original: *Quam si*</note>. The King <note>original: *Regulus*; this refers to the feudatory princes who ruled semi-autonomous regions</note> of **Fujian** <note>original: *Fô kien*</note>, broken by so many disasters and distrusting his own people, again shaved his head <note>A symbolic act of submission to the Manchu (Tartar) custom</note> and surrendered to the Tartar Emperor. He was kindly received and temporarily placed in charge of a military legion. However, the King of **Guangdong** <note>original: *Quam tum*</note>, because he had been granted a lower title by the rebel leader **Wu Sangui** <note>original: *V san quei*</note> than he felt was his due, broke his alliance and brought his entire province back under the rule of the Tartars. In the same year (which was 1675), on July 12th, the Emperor visited our temple and residence. There, with the imperial brush, he wrote two characters, each a cubit in height: ***Jing tian*** <note>original: *Kim tien*</note>, which means "Revere Heaven," or "Revere the Lord of Heaven." He marked these with the imperial seal and entrusted them to our fathers. Copies of this inscription, placed at the entrances of the temples and houses of the three Religious Orders throughout the Empire, carry the weight of a silent approval of the Christian religion.

In the 56th year of the Cycle, the 18th year of the Emperor's reign (1679), **Wu Sangui** died, worn out by old age. His young grandson, called **Honghua** <note>original: *Hum hoa*</note>, was proclaimed Emperor by the rebels. In that same year, on September 2nd, around ten o'clock in the morning, such a horrific earthquake shook the royal city [Beijing] and the neighboring areas that countless palaces, temples of the gods, towers, and city walls collapsed. Over 400 people were buried under the ruins in the city, and in the nearby town of **Tongzhou** <note>original: *Tum cheu*</note>, more than thirty thousand people were crushed beneath the wreckage of their homes. Because the earthquake continued to repeat at intervals for nearly three months, though with less force, the Emperor himself, the princes, and the nobles left their palaces to live in tents. The poor commoners dragged out their lives in the open air, but the pious Emperor consoled them, drawing funds from the treasury so that the poor buried under the ruins could receive a proper coffin and the collapsed houses could be restored.

In the final month of that same year, which was already January 1680, a fire suddenly broke out in the Emperor's palace and consumed it within a few hours. The damage exceeded 2,850,000 gold pieces. Four days after the fire, the Emperor set out to the suburban forest for hunting, a pastime he loved dearly. Let it be permitted here, in passing, to offer an example of the reigning Prince's <note>The Kangxi Emperor</note> piety and justice, which he displayed while hunting. It happened that he saw from a distance a magnificent monument. This was the tomb of the last Emperor of the previous [Ming] dynasty, **Chongzhen** <note>original: *Cun chim*</note>, whom the current Emperor's father, **Shunzhi** <note>original: *Xun chi*</note>, had arranged to be buried honorably. The Emperor quickly turned aside toward the tomb, and kneeling before it with tears in his eyes, he cried out: "O Emperor Chongzhen, you know that we were not the cause of your pitiable death; your own rebellious subjects drove you to this." Then, having lit incense according to custom and prostrating his face to the ground, he performed the proper rites for the deceased. Another time, while hunting far from the crowd and unrecognized, he came upon an old man bitterly weeping for his only son, who had been taken away by force by a Tartar Prefect. In the 57th year of the Cycle (1680), the Prince <note>original: *Regulus*; refers to Shang Zhixin, the feudatory ruler of Guangdong</note> of the province of **Guangdong** <note>original: *Quam tum*</note>, although already a subject, was nevertheless suspected by the Tartar <note>The Manchu rulers of the Qing Dynasty</note> because he, being a man of a turbulent spirit, was becoming extremely powerful through maritime trade with the **Spaniards** and **Dutch** <note>original: *Hispanis & Batavis*</note>, contrary to the King’s decree. Furthermore, he was intent on the ruin of the city of **Macau** <note>original: *Macaensis*</note> and held great authority over an army of 40,000 men. Therefore, when he was ordered by the Emperor to take up arms against the rebels in the province of **Guangxi** <note>original: *Quam si*</note>, and when he had by chance retired into a certain city while his army was scattered here and there, he was led back to the province of **Guangdong** and his palace by a certain ruse. There, after some months had passed, two magnates who had flown there from the court in the space of 17 days, ordered him—on the 9th of October very early in the morning—to tighten his own throat with a noose <note>The "silken cord," a form of forced suicide granted to high-ranking officials to avoid the shame of public execution</note>, which was offered to him as a mark of honor. At that same time, 112 associates of his faction (among whom were three of his brothers) were beheaded. He was a prince otherwise worthy of a better fate, as he thought very well of God and our Law <note>The "Law" refers to the Christian religion</note> and had always favored its preachers more than can be expressed. But because the Tartar longed to add his immense wealth to the treasury, it was decided to open the sarcophagus of the Prince’s father, who was not yet buried, to investigate whether the corpse was dressed in Chinese habit and cap <note>Wearing traditional Chinese clothing instead of the mandated Manchu/Tartar dress was a sign of rebellion</note>. When they found it was dressed in the Tartar fashion, all the goods passed to the remaining brothers, among whom was the Emperor’s son-in-law and others who were related.
> *In the same year, at its end, the Reverend Fathers of the holy family of St. Augustine from the Philippines, having reached Macau, entered China.*

In the following year, the Prince of **Fujian** <note>original: *Fokien*; refers to Geng Jingzhong</note> (of whom we spoke above) was cut into pieces <note>The "slow slicing" or *lingchi* execution</note> in the court before all the people, and his flesh was thrown to the dogs, chiefly on account of the tyranny he had exercised against many Prefects suspected by him while he was rebelling. His brothers, although innocent, were beheaded. The capital of **Yunnan** <note>original: *Yun nan*</note> province was occupied by the Tartar. The Emperor **Honghua** <note>original: *Hum hoa*; the grandson of Wu Sangui</note> anticipated the Tartar execution by a voluntary hanging. The bones of **Wu Sangui** <note>original: *V san quei*</note>, who had died some time before, were dug up from the tomb and transported to the court; they were partly fixed in various places as a sign of infamy and to cause terror, and partly ground into powder and scattered to the air and winds in mockery.

This year, 1681, is also the hundredth year of the propagation of the Christian Religion in China by the Society of Jesus.

In the 59th year of the Cycle (1682), the three Princes <note>The "Three Feudatories" who led the great rebellion against the Qing</note> having now been extinguished, the 15 provinces successfully subdued, and peace established throughout the Empire, the Emperor decided to visit his native land and the tombs of his ancestors...
